Ok, sooo...
After experiencing Verdun for quite a few months by now (heck, what am I talking about, I got it since May 2015, that's two damn years ago!!!), I can see myself fit to write an, at least half-legible, poorly-translated-from-my-native-language, review about this fine work of entertainment.
200 hours? In two years? Maybe a bit too little time - some may say - to give a full, in depth, description of the game's subtelties about why it is indeed a superior form of art. But, due to the nature of my work, I just couldn't invest more in it... bear with me please!
On a positive note; well, this game has offered me something that I have not experienced in quite some years now – heck too many years to be honest - playing a FPS in which I am not bothered by extreme discrepancies between veteran players and fresh recruits; dare I call them like this; and a game that truthly encompasses what a shooter should feel like.
There is no pay to win mentality, unlike most triple A shooters today (looking at you Crap of Duty). The community is almost overwhelmingly and annoyingly friendly; to be honest with you, I haven't met anyone hostile really, well at least not too hostile to be a hinderence (expect the average troll from time to time, "for teh lulz", you know...). But with all the humor aside, the players are cool people! You get this sense of - how to put it - community. It is a relaxed atmosphere (quite ironic considering what this game simulates), players are playing mostly for fun; yet that doesn't mean it lacks the sense of competition.
It’s realistic – yes! ArmA like realistic – not quite. But truth be said if we were to make a 100% realistic WWI shooter, that would just mean creating a getting-mowed-down-by-machine-guns simulator 2017, and I guess nobody would really play that, would it now? It has balance in it, yet the balance is quite subtle. Don’t get me wrong machine guns will mow you down, but maybe not as often as you would expect.
For most players that are out there and are tired of all these damn pieces of publicly appealing crap (ahem! again COD), Verdun might sound for a good alternative and believe me, it is. Honestly enough I am really glad that I decided to spend - what I vaguely remember as being - 10 Euros on that late May day, wanting to buy this game; it really feels it was worth it.
Another strong point to this game is the setting; I mean, to this date, WWI hasn't got its proper FPS (yeah, yeah BF1, I know; but honestly do you want a somewhat legit representation of The War to End All Wars, or do you want Hollywood-style special effects?). I know that game developers see this historical period as something rather dull; truth is that this war was indeed a meat grinder. And, as the war was, expect to die in this game, and die a lot. Yet despite all this death and misery, you realise the true value of this game and the awesome work the devs have done. I mean they turned one of the saddest and most brutal chapters from the history of mankind into a quite exciting and – well, I say it now - authentic experience.
Thus, if you feel it's worth a shot, try this game out; one may be pleasantly surprised by it.

This game is made to be an accurate historical respresentation of WW1 trench warfare. It does a hell of a job doing just that. As someone who likes WW1 and WW2 history, I love it.
Fighting in the Great War through Verdun is an experience I will never forget. In the deadliest battlefields of WW1, there is no greenery. your only landmarks are sandbags, downed planes, muddy hills and even bodies. The bodies fill the trenches and shell holes. More and more bodies hit the mud as the machine guns keep firing. The wounded lay writhing and screaming in pain. The waterlogged trenches run red with blood. Artillery shells blow the legs off of men, leaving them to scream in pain as they bleed out. The shells leave craters to take cover in... if you don't mind the putrid odor of the corpses that lie in them. GAS GAS GAS! You are quick and throw on your gas mask as the yellow green cloud creeps into your trench. Your fellow soldier is not quick enough. He staggers around, choking, clutching his throat before he collapses, blood flowing from his mouth. Soon after, the opposing army drops into the trenches, bayonets and clubs and shovels and other brutal weapons at the ready. It's a massacre. Men are impaled and bludgeoned as chaotic hand to hand combat insues. Death and blood and rot are everywhere. Your fellow countrymen are dead. Your best friend just took a bullet to the neck and lays gurgling, choking, sputtering next to you, bleeding all over himself and you and the ground. Now he is dead. You're next. You could retreat, but that would be deserting. You know what happens to those poor, shell shocked ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s. There is no escaping your own gruesome, agonizing death. War is Hell. Do not play this game unless you are ready to experience all of this.
No other game I have played conveys the brutality, destruction, endless trench warfare and sheer loss of life in the Great War like this game does. And war in general at that. It accurately shows you exactly what WW1 was like, with attention to every detail. It shows you exactly what the cost of war is. It may be a game, and it may be fun, but it has a much deeper meaning to it than just that. If you learn anything from playing this game and experiencing the horrors of the most brutal war ever, it is that War is Hell.

First off, I'm always a little reserved when purchasing games that are specifically built for online play, but I have to admit, I was completely blown away by Verdun.
This is not your average, run-of-the-mill First Person Shooter: You cannot sprint at 30 mph for ridiculous distances and every engagement doesn't turn into an absurd, full-auto firefight. You can't chuck a grenade halfway across the map, like in Call Of Duty, and bullets are nearly always a single shot kill. Not to mention that your screen jerks and becomes disorienting when incoming fire comes near you, and bullet ballistics force you to lead your target and aim higher at longer distances in order to hit.
The map times are long (about 30 minutes per match), allowing your team the time to actually make an attack successful, even with heavy losses. But that also forces a considerable amount of stress on your team when defending your own trenches.
Instead of the standard FPS gameplay type, that counts wins or loses soley on bodycount, Verdun has implemented a unique system, one that (as the makers of Verdun state) "Realistically portrays the Tug-of-War style of trench warfare." The matches start in the middle of the map, with both teams in their respective trenches, separated by a streach of No-Man's-Land. One side is tasked with attacking the other team's trench, the other with defending it. The attacking team has 3 minutes to gain a foothold, and the attack will continue in "overtime" for as long as there are attackers entering the trench. This leads to a full fledged melee with shovels, clubs, knives, bayonettes, and point blank gun shots, until the trench is either captured or the attack is repelled. If captured, the capturing team must brace for a counter attack and now defend their newly captured trench. If the attack is repelled, the initally attacking team must trudge back across No Man's Land, under enemy fire, to defend their trench. With three separate trench lines behind each team, each game quickly turns into gorey, gut wrenching, dismembering bloodbath.
As far as graphics and aesthetic go, the Verdun team has done an outstanding job capturing the historic accuracy of uniforms, voices, weapons, and cratered earth. Simply watch an online stream or YouTube some Verdun gameplay, and you'll see what I mean.
There is way too much good in this game to talk about here and this "review" is getting a little long, so I'll wrap it up: This game's style is so contrastingly different to Battlefield and Call of Duty, that this game will continue to be playable for years to come. If you're on the fence about it, just buy it. Play it. If you don't like it after 10 matches, just go through the Steam return policy. Besides, this game will probably give you more fun than two large pizzas for the same price.

Was toying with the idea of picking this up, and the free weekend was my chance to see if it lived up to the high standards set by the first game. It didn't.
The game seems to be a reboot of the Homefront series, rather than a sequel. In the first game, the North Koreans overpowered South Korea, then Japan, and allied with China to invade the US. In this game, North Korea is portrayed as affluent and technologically advanced, allowing them to invade America after the US defaults on a loan. Seeing as N. Korea has something like the 3rd largest standing army in the world, the first scenario seems much more likely and realistic to me.
I see a lot of people throwing around the word "unplayable" on Steam recently, but by and large, I think people are overreacting. This game isn't glitchy and bug-ridden to the point of being unplayable, just unenjoyable. Many times, I would enter a safehouse without the game registering that I had entered a safehouse. This means I could still fire my weapon, even killing everyone inside, often without my allies' weapons even loading into their hands.
The AI is honestly some of the worst I've ever seen in a modern game. Countless times I have mowed down a KPA soldier, with his buddies standing not 10 feet away, with no reaction from them. Other times, specifically in yellow zones, I've been on the run from the KPA, and I've made a single turn, or hid behind something directly in the KPA's path, and they've simply given up the chase.
I know a lot of people who really want to like this game (and believe me, I REALLY wanted to love it) will look at my almost 4 hours playtime and think "that's not enough to judge this game by", and it kills me to say that it really is. Within 3.7 hours, I bought every gun and upgrade, with only a handful of the game's districts unlocked. This game truly has nothing else to offer me, aside from buggy character animations, a truly broken spawn system, and a drab, uninspired story. I've played games that are much, much worse. But for the reduced price of $24, you could certainly do much better.
Thanks for the free weekend, Homefront, but no thanks.

The game itself is very good. The art was very well done, the voice acting was great, and the ambience was terrific. I'd give it a 10/10 on the aesthetics.
[Spoiler Ahead]
The thing is, the story was alright, not really the "greatest video game love story of our time" I thought I was going to get. I will admit I was touched at some parts but when it comes down to it the story is about a kid who drops out of highschool to runaway with her girlfriend after her paretns express their disproval. Now this would be very powerful if this was experienced through that character's perspective, but you're experiancing this from the perspective of her sister who has come home after being gone for atleast a year and finding the house is empty. So yeah, finding out my kid sister had ranway from home to be with her highschool sweet heart before I could even see her or talk this out with her had me less than enthused. Story I'd give a 6/10.
Now here is mostly why I wouldn't recommend it. The cost and the amount of time it will take you to finish it. The games origianal price is $20, and the game only has about an hour of gameplay, maybe more if you get stuck. I have nothing against a walking-simulator, I did enjoy exploring the house, but I feel that a game that can be completed in an hour isn't worth the steep cost of twenty bucks. Maybe if it was on sale for under $5 and you like story-based games, with good atmosphere and don't mind a lack of game-play, then it might be worth a playthrough, but it really isn't worth the full-price.

This game is basically a huge bait-and-switch, a turn-off, and leaves you feeling tricked into buying into the wrong kind of game. In the latter part of my Reasons-This-Game-Is-Pretty-Bad, I will be going into detail about the story of the game. So, Spoiler Warning, whatever. Not even worth it.
The amazing atmosphere, the feeling of creeping around and seeing things you probaly shouldn't have ("Gosh, Dad..."), the ability to understand that you were in a house that's lived in, the sense of humanity and life and love that has obviously been experienced in this place, and it made you feel less of a stranger and more of a relative who hasn't visited in a while. The effort and detail that went into every item and object and path that you take is incedible (you could even say tedious...) and when you really look hard enough you can think of all the ways of what went on in the house. You're
It pulls you in for all the wrong reasons. It's full of missed potential. You explore everything in the whole game and feel dissatisfied with what's left at the end. You're in a big, spooky house trying to figure out what happened, why you're parents are missing and why your sister seems to have just up and left without a prior notice. The setting is perfect for a good ol' spookfest in gaming. It's even got the perfect setup for a good mystery: you and your family live in the middle of the woods, who had only recently aquired it about a year or so ago from a recently deceased (and crazy?) relative. It's horribly dark out, with the pattering of rain and booming voice of thunder bearing down on you from the other side of the old, creaky walls. The the lights have been previously switched off, and those that have been left on flicker eerily against the dark, threatening to hide something amongst the messy rooms. In reality, it's much less mysterious than it seems. As you progress, you discover that Mom is a forest keeper, Dad is a dimestore-fiction novelist, and your sister Sam... is a raging homosexual? Basically, you just
to come back home from a long trip to Europe while your Mom and Dad went on a camping trip for their wedding annevesery, and your sister packed her bags as quickly as she could and ran away from home to find her lover and live happily ever after with her. It's the least-classic tale of wrong place, wrong time.
Why would you go to all the trouble of setting up a creepy, unsettled environment like this -even going all the way as to make secret rooms and passageways into the house; even going out and making the previous owner of the house a
; even going so far as to
- all for a cheezy love story between two punk girls?! Everything about this game except the story itself
MYSTERY and HORROR all around it, and yet I find myself listening to the cutesy, cheery giggle of a girl who happens to just
for some kind of cliche dime-a-dosen love story?!?! But no, alas, it's just all the shenanigans of two lesbians who forgot to clean up the pentagram under the stairs after they got hyped up on soda after reading a book about ghost possessions.
Frankly, what a waste of time, money, and effort, both on my part, on the developer's part, and everyone else's. There is so much wasted potential in a game like this, and it's used up on something that could have been perhaps made better if it weren't so misleading in the first place. Ultimately, I mean no direspect to the developers of this game, but I really feel that this is the truth in the matter.

Have you ever watched a movie that looked really great in all the trailers, but then turned out to be a big let down when it finally comes out? This describes Gone Home perfectly. The store page in Steam looks great. It looks like a mystery game with a 90's flashback kind of twist.
Then you start playing. The game environment is gorgeous to say the least. The way the lights and shadows look, the sound of the raging thunderstorm outside, your footsteps on the old wooden floorboards. The ambiance is beautiful. The developers did a great job of sucking you into the game world. But that's sadly where the praise stops.
When they said it's a short game, they aren't kidding. You can finish the game in an hour or two, depending on how thorough you are in your exploration. The story is rather vague to start out, which I suppose is good for a mystery game. But halfway through all the pieces just suddenly and abruptly fall into place, and you know the answer to all your questions at once. There are still a few things left to do before the game is "done", but you already know how it all ends.
As for the story plot, the word cliche comes to mind, and the little side story (I won't tell you what it is should you still want to play) abruptly ends in a trail of loose ends. This is sad because it was actually more interesting than the main plot.
Oh well. At least there was the nostalgia.

I played this game just over 10 hours now, but I must say: what a great game.
Weapons here really hurt (mostly one shot one kill) and it is frustrating to jump in a trench and get immediately killed. Since balance is not really the point here, you get the feel that anything goes during a match: camping, running, grenading, bayoneting... everything to stay alive a couple seconds more.
Running from crater to crater trying to reach the enemy trench gives you a very small taste of what soldiers back in the day felt. One really becomes anxious when you are ordered to go over the top, running and dodging bullets, desperately trying to reach the enemy trench and, with luck, establishing a foothold. Fighting in trenches filled with green toxic gas gives it a truly other-worldly feeling, with enemies wearing masks looking even more menacing suddenly poping out of the smoke.
It is not the vibe one usually gets with other shooters and I recommend this game for precisely that reason. Aiming is not easy, getting kills neither, and staying alive is even harder. You get your blood pumping and the frustration of being shot as soon as you step on the enemy trench after dodging bullets over no man's land is more than compensated when you and your squad finally manage to conquer said trench against all odds.
Very innovative (and fun) gameplay, great atmosphere, and very good history lesson. 10/10

I don't know why all the hate but to me this game is amazing. It has everything that I wanted.
First, a lot of people complaining about bad performance. I have a gtx980ti and I run everything maxed at 90-70 FPS. It drops to 57-54 there and there sometimes but nothing really bad. So to me the game is running smoothly and well.
The engine is amazing. The graphics, the animations, the rain, the lighting and the whole atmosphere look very nice. Oh and the cutscenes. They are beautiful, movie like, but not overdone, yet interesting to watch. Actually, this is one of the few games that got me really interested into them and not willing to skip.
The world doesn't feel empty. There is always something to loot, a secret to find or a piece of land to claim. You can always pick what you want to do next - a main mission, a small mission from the mission board or maybe conquest a stronghold or a sniper nest. Also there are dynamic objectives that popup when you are close to them - i.e. somebody contacts you via a radio saying they are pinned and need help to defend their outpost. Or find that juicy loot crate. And you can always pick the approach. What is even better, there are lots of NPCs around which you can recruit to help you with a simple button click. You can have up to 5 I think and each NPC in the world carries its unique loadout. They will help you by shooting enemies, throwing frags, some even carry rocket launchers - all accessible from a get go.
Gun fights are satisfying. There are no crosshairs so you have to aim, compensate the recoil and distance. Weapons have tons of upgrades and each of them have what the game calls a conversion system - i.e. you can convert an assault rifle into a machine gun or a sticky mine gun, a crossbow to a flamethrower etc.  in a blink of an eye during the combat or before and then switch back when you want the previous weapon version right on spot. Weapons also have lots of mods and upgrades.
Yes, you can say that it is just an another average AC or Far Cry clone but this game is a blast to play provided you have a good enough system. What's most important to me - the game atmosphere and events shown in the cutscenes and during other moments really made me immersed in the game world willing to help the rebels win the war.
10/10

I definitely recommend this game.

This is a wonderful game. The premise is a bit spooky - you come home after backpacking for a year to an empty house that your family moved into while you were away, and you wander around trying to piece together what's going on. It's a setup for a survival horror, but it plays like an adventure game. The narrative is very well done, and it's a delight to just wander around exploring the place and finding out what your family has been up to over the previous year. My only complaint is it's a bit short, although in reality if it took you longer than a couple of hours of snooping to figure out where your family was, you'd have a pretty messed-up family. On the other hand, the fact you are snooping at all instead of just crashing kinda makes the protagonist seem a bit creepy, but hey, it's a computer game. Probably not worth full price, but a really great story that all narrative-driven adventure fans should jump on during a Steam sale.

So, because the developers tell me to everytime I quit the game, I'm writing my review for Verdun. I wasn't too sure what to expect when I bought this game. It was half price and had been looking into it for a little bit, and I have to say that I'm very happy with it. It feels very different to other FPS games that I have played but there is something about it which keeps me playing it. For one thing, it is one of the few WW1 games that exists, (yes I know BF1 is coming out soon) which has a huge impact on the weapon variety. There are basically, rifles, LMGs and some old-timey pistols, and when it comes to choosing which one to use, it normally depends on which one looks the coolest, because all the guns seem to do the same damage as each other. 1 shot for rifles, 2 shots for LMGs, 3 shots for pistols and 1-2 shots for revolvers. Having said that, I like the guns in the game. They're not guns that we're normally used to in FPS', and in looking into the guns in real life, I've learnt some history.
The maps are pretty good. There are plenty for what the game is. My fav is Dauauauauaumont, (or however it's spelt) mainly because of the fortification part if the map. Other maps, are not so great, and this is mainly due to No man's land. Some maps seem to have a lack of cover, and seeing as some of these players have aimbotting accuracy, I normally end up dead before i've decided which leg I should use to start running with.
Community is very very good indeed. No hackers for one thing. And no ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s. But this is probably due to the lack of communication. The only people that can hear you via mic are people in your squad, but there's only 4 players per squad. Nethertheless, Verdun is a teamwork game, and fortunatly, the community seem thrilled to work as a team. There is no friendly fire as well, which for this game is perfect. I dread to think of my fellow rifleman stabbing me in the back with his bayonet because it's "banter."
The game is pretty damn realistic as well. There was an update a while back that allowed players limbs to be shot and blown off, making it rather entertaining for everyone. And the shooting mechanics are decent. I'd rather the game didn't go for the CS:GO approach of things, where moving heavily decreases accuracy, an when youre using a bolt-action rifle 75% of the time, this can be annoying.
Because my fingers are getting pins and needles from intense typing, I'll make my last point about gameplay. It's pretty simple. The teams have to defend their trench whilst the other team attacks it and tries to capture it. If they succeed, then you are pushed back a trench and have to attack the one they're in. If you defend you're trench for long enough, you have to attack their trench. And this goes on for about 20 minutes per game depending on how good your team is.

Good game, great, modern, realistic FPS, nice design (actually, I expected something of this level for Fallout 4), interesting concept, but only partially developed. The game feels incomplete at times, but I had a great time and the bugs didn't, not once, impede a good gaming experience. The hate probably comes from the early players. At this stage, Homefront is superior to most games around (even at this stage, I should say). It's rare to see good single-player games these days, but this is one of them. There are problems, as I said, but I didn't care much about them. I'd say there are more opportunities than problems. The game beginning presents an awesome concept which keeps you asking for more, but there is little of the same quality for the rest of the game. I could play the game at around 50-55 fps, there are some frame drops, but they never took place during crucial moments, so, despite there being room for improvement, the experience is nonetheless amazing. I think the game is worth 40hrs of enjoyment, I have explored only to some extent the multiplayer, which seemed very entertaining, but lacking diversity - I suppose that it will continue in this state, after all the marketing failures of the game. I had a great time, I applaud the effort to produce a complex single-player game, and I do recommend it with the above minor qualifications.

Dark Souls II...
I was drawn into this game immediately due to its gorgeously somber atmosphere. The elements of isolation, futility, and enigma are woven masterfully into the game's core mechanic of repeated death.
There is no winning in Dark Souls 2, there is only a perpetual push forward, and you will always find yourself lagging a tad behind as your humanity is chipped away from you, and greedy invaders make forays into your realm.
Not only does this game boast a well-rounded RPG system, and an also decent, fleshed out action based playstyle, it is thematically sound and meshes well with the game itself.
It is an overall amazing experience.
Few cons...
1. Play this game with a controller.
2. Many weapons and enemies suffer from "phantom range" which causes many senseless deaths.
3. Inventory is cluttered.
4. Connectivity with friends is kind of a pain.

It is important to know what to expect in this game. The general horror/supernatural vibe that it gives off in the beginning is a facade. This is a game entirely about its story, told in a way that I found refreshing and exciting, and more than a little gut-wrenching, but that's probably me just being a softy.
You play Katie, a protagonist who, but for the intro, is silent, who returns home from travelling Europe to find her family's new house empty, her parents and sister gone. The game plays out almost like a miniature metroid-vania style, searching the house for clues and keys to open up new areas, maps that reveal secret passages, etc.
Through searching the various rooms of the house you'll find notes and letters which detail the lives of your family; your father's struggling writing career, your mother's advancing career and a potential office romance.
However, the story is primarily about your sister, Sam, and how she reacts to moving to this new house, and a burgeoning romance. While the rest of the family's story is played out entirely in text (letters and notes and such), Sam's story is told through a combination of similar notes, but also especially through audio-log-style narrations that trigger as you explore and find specific objects.
I don't want to spoil Sam's story here, but suffice it to say that it was, to me, heartfelt, relevant, and toward the end gutwrenching, all aided by a fantastic voice actress playing her part. I was very nearly in tears by the end.
The only downside, I would say, is that it is very short. It can be completed in less than two hours and it left me wanting to find out more about the family's pursuits (the mother and father stories build up slowly through numerous notes and letters and then seem to reach conclusion very swiftly, or don't at all). And at its normal price, its probably a hard investment to justify for some.
Again, its necessary to understand what this game is and isn't. There isn't a lot to it, as I mentioned, and the general vibe at the beginning is a bit misleading. However, if you're in the mood for a heartfelt, tear-jerker of a story-based game, I cannot recommend Gone Home highly enough. It is a fantastic experience.

Gone Home is a short story told via an exploration game. As a story, one gets to use multimedia to discover the main plot and several subplots of the story. There are even a few "red herrings" added to keep one guessing. As a game, Gone Home is much less novel. The mechanics are fairly standard. Players are unlikely to find anything that they've not already experienced in another game. Once the house is explored, the puzzles solved and the story completed, there is little incentive to "play" the game (story) a second time.
As a game, Gone Home, provides too little entertainment for its normal retail price. As a story, Gone Home, touches the heart, but fails to justify its pricey presentation as a game. If one can find Gone Home on sale for under $5.00, then pick it up,
Want an exploration, puzzle game that tells a story and that is replayable? Try Dear Esther.
Want an action game, with puzzles, an interesting story and is worth the retail price? Try the Bioshock Series.

SotfS was my first DS2 experience and was ok overall. Hated all the random NPC invasions and ambushes around every corner but after I found the Large Club it got super easy. Like ridiculously easy. Forlorn fights became a game of whack-a-mole as I sit there and R2'd him into the pavement, wait for him to get up then proceeded to R2 him again in the same spot. Most other enemies died really easy to it too because they're pretty much all in armor and weak to blunt. Despite enemies going down pretty easy they also hit hard which can suck if you're being ambushed/stunlocked by dual weilding ones (aka the beginning of the game).
I played this and DS1 blind just to get a true experience and after DS1 this one felt like a game made by someone who was trying to capture what media claimed the game was about (a super hard game where you die a lot) rather than implement some of the smart design choices made throughout the original. The "a super hard game where you die a lot" thing about the original was just a result of the original design and not 100% the intention.
With all that said these are my pros and cons:
Pros:
- Large Club
- Large Club
- Lots of weapon/armor choices
- The one shop keep who becomes cocky as you buy more stuff from him
- Fast travel and few more design changes made things move a bit more fluidly
- Large Club
Cons:
- Enemy and level design was a bit meh
- Maybe it's SotFS specific but the difficulty of some levels preceeding boss fights was way off wack. On more than one occassion I've been faced with really hard to get through levels and stupidly easy/uninteresting bosses to finish out the area.  Made the overall experience just feel overall forgettable.
- Estus, AGL and a few more design changes seem to just be there for added "difficulty" rather than via smart design choice. There are ways to add difficulty other than handicapping the player and forcing them to grind out levels to get back to default DS1 style gameplay.
- Forlorn coming out of nowhere despite being easy/clubable (and apparently I may just specifically have bad luck because every single one popped out to face me. Every. Freaking. Time.)
If I could give this a middle of the road review I would. It's pretty meh but not terrible. Just get yourself a Large Club and make sure you AGL is 99+ and you should be fine. Also I hear the DLC is good so idk maybe that'll make it more worth it when I play it.

Very fun overall.
Interesting backstory with a twist.
The new animatronics are quirky and fun.
Has a great difficulty for more experienced gamers.

CONS:

Can be impossible to beat at times.
Rage inducing.
Too fast paced at some times.
You need perfect reaction timing to get past the later nights (3 and on).
Overall, I recommend it, but the first one is slightly better. This one is still very good, though.

This was the weirdest first-person exploration game I have ever played.  It starts out with this tone of "something scary is about to happen", but never really happens.  The various things hinting at a horror experiance are red herrings, as it is more about the story of the side character (and narrater) Sam.
This game captures the perfect feel of exploring a new home in the dark, storming night.  Dark hallways and creaking floorboards instill a forboding fear in your chest.
The story itself is good-ish, but could stand to be a bit longer then the two hours it took me to complete it.  It did an exellent job of keeping you speculating on what is actually happening.
Overall, I say only get this game when it goes on sale.  (I got it for ~$2 at the summer sale.)  $20 is quite a bit too much for a game you will beat in a single sitting.

But SPOILER ALERT: the house is not haunted and your family is fine.
Other than that exploring your home and seeing the way your family lives can be neat I suppose. There are no real changes to how you play from the beginning to the end, you simply get answeres to puzzles as you explore, either blatently having answers spoonfed to you, or having progress blocked until you backtrack and eventually find the answer. I don't feel it to be worth twenty dollars: I took my time on the game and blew through it rather quickly.
Really, the only saving grace is the setting, as seeing old things from the nineties suddenly resurface when I hadn't thought of them in years sometimes made me smile. The story? You play no real part in it, so it might as well have been an audio book. You can probably find it on youtube with some ease, as its entirely told through cassette tapes left around the house. I felt it was worth what I paid, but I didn't pay very much: I got this from a Humble Bundle some years ago.
How much would I pay now? Well, I can get a meal at mcdonalds for five bucks, and this lasted longer than that, so I'd say five bucks, perhaps a bit more, is a fair enough price. But its basically an audio book with a small game wrapped around it, so know what you're buying.

Played it over a year ago (ignore my playtime, I bought it for the sake of having it on PC). Gone Home isn't really what you are expecting it to be, but that turns out to be a good thing. There's an eerie atmosphere to the world (well, the house) that is constantly tugging away at you as you figure out more about the house and the people who live in it.
The game plays more like an exploratory narrative rather than a traditional video game, as you traverse a large mansion in search of answers or clues as to where the residents (your family) are, or what happened to them. Almost everything in the world is able to be picked up and looked at, hucked around, or admired, all the detail and attention paid really make the characters and the environment feel real.
The game is accompanied by an EXCELLENT voice cast, with almost all props going to the voice heard the most through the story (which is that of the main character's sister), she is incredibly well written and acted, and I'm disappointed she's not in more games that I'm aware of. The atmosphere and the music are incredible, the entire game has a nostalgic feel to it, with references to old consoles and movies strewn about this home set (present) in the 90's.
Overall the story moves and flows as you uncover secrets, pictures, and notes that piece the narrative together through exploration and investigation. Finding secret rooms and hidden notes, the story evolves and I found myself caring more and more about the characters (specifically the sister) and their stories.
I will say this game is not for everyone, it doesn't play like traditional games, but acts more as a wonderful narrative experience, but those looking for a horror game will be disappointed. This is an atmospheric story driven experience filled with nostalgia, great music, amazing voice acting, an incredible sense of place, and a touching narrative that centers mainly on the confusion and stress of life from childhood through adolescence (from a female perspective).
But that's just it, this is an EXPERIENCE, and it's one I'm glad I had. This game is the main reason I gave "Life is Strange" a try, and LiS is now my favorite video game. If you're looking for a wonderful experience, sit back, turn out the lights, put on your headphones and enjoy the feels created by this wonderful game, no, this experience.

This game is not a horror game. It is not a gameplay-based game. It is more of an interactive story.
Now, a lot of people are angry that this is considered a game. But, there are graphic novels and such on the market that people seem to love and are even LESS of a game.  I don't see anyone bashing those - but whatever. Personally, I like games where you find clues that lead you to new clues and, thus, unravelling the mystery.
The game (or story) is great. Nostalgic for anyone who grew up in the 90's (references to pop culture, SNES, riot grrrl punk, etc.)
But, let's get down to it. As you play, you'll realize that it's a love story.  I ain't one for love stories, but this one is damn touching. I'll admit that I cried. I'm a sappy ♥♥♥♥ for certain things deep inside.
Basically, you go around the house picking up objects finding clues that lead you to the next - all for the sake of trying to find out what happened to your sister.  There's no combat or anything. Just walking and picking up/moving/reading objects.
If you go into this game thinking anything else, you're going to be disappointed. You have to go in knowing you're playing an interactive story.
The atmosphere is pretty great.  Being alone in a huge dark house on a stormy night leaves a really earie feeling on the player. I loved it. Especially for the fact that there is litterally nothing to be afraid of. I feel that it taps into our little selves and how we used to be (or still somewhat are) afraid of the dark and being alone, say, in the basement of our house. If that's what the devs were going for - bravo to them.

A very good game that is at times overshadowed by the success of Dark Souls 1 and marred by some questionable design choices. Excellent for its replay value, player agency and multiplayer interactions. Also a perfect PC port with excellent performance, in contrast to its predecessor.
Dark Souls 2 introduced a lot of improvements to the series that are often overlooked. The weapon upgrade system is no longer so obtuse that it punishes players that don't read guides. The implementation of weapons is excellent and eschews the fairly pointless slow attacks that were present in the first game (ie: black knight sword R2). Movement and control as a whole feels very smooth and has been improved to the point that DS1 actually feels somewhat unrefined by comparison.
Perhaps the most important improvement is the sheer volume of this game. Compared to DS1 there are more weapons, armor sets, rings (and ring slots), spells, and the areas are longer and more numerous. All of these factors contribute to greater replayability and more rewarding experiences in multiplayer. In my experience the limit of ten character slots is not nearly enough for the immense value you can get out of this game. An online community that often prioritises fashion over utility speaks volumes of the creativity of the Dark Souls 2 player base and the game itself.
The overall experience is somewhat inconsistent in terms of presentation and quality. At its best Scholar of the First Sin is visually impressive, but still retains the lacking appearance of some areas such the Shaded Woods and Earthen Peak. Many areas of this game lack the detail present in other Souls games. Rather than presenting a location that people are supposed to have lived in, many areas  consist of featureless rooms and hallways with varying placements of items and enemies. The lack of small details detract from the overall believability of the world, which is undoubtedly a significant part of the series. The music is also a mixed bag, ranging from the greatly thought provoking and compelling to the uninspired and generic.
There are some other issues with the game. The enemies often ignore the rules placed on human players, such as stamina and poise. Defining a 'fair challenge' can be difficult when you are expected to fight enemies many times your size, but these instances are a simple lack of internal consistency, which makes the game feel cheap and unrewarding. Conversely many bosses are far too easy to overcome, such as the Covetous Demon or Giant Lord. Unfortunately in Scholar of the First Sin almost any area that could be considered a challenge has at least one overpowered NPC summon available to trivialize the area. The addition of an NPC white phantom to Belfry Sol, a PVP area without a boss, is lamentably stupid.
Despite the many criticisms I could list about balance and design this is still an excellent game. When I got all of the achievements I thought I had seen everything and was done. As it happens I could enjoy over a hundred more hours playing this game. There is always a new weapon to try out, a new character you can make, an enemy attack you've probably never seen before and endless multiplayer elements to enjoy. Even though it appears that Dark Souls 3 will be great improvement for the series, I will look back on this game fondly.

As a big fan Soulsborne, I really wanted to enjoy this game as much as I enjoyed Dark Souls and Bloodborne. I had to learn the game all over again.  After the first 10 hours of the frustration from the changes in game mechanics, I started to like it.
Dark Souls 2: Scholar of the First Sin is a really beautiful game, just like the first one. Didn't really like the art style, for whatever reason it didn't really get to me as it did for the first game. PC Port for this one was way better than Dark Souls: Prepare to Die Edition for PC, which is one of the thing that immediately made me enjoy the game more. The game is, once again, typical Souls game: Hard, but fair. However, there were lots of times when the game felt cheap because of the changes that came with the Scholar of the First Sin. I haven't played the vanilla version of the game, but I've heard from other players that the vanilla version was way easier, and they decided to add more enemies, make them "smarter", and they added enemies from other locations on areas to make it more challenging. There are way more bosses in this game than there were in the first Dark Souls, but almost every one of these bosses lack the spirit that Dark Souls 1's bosses had.  Their design is alright, most of them feel lazy, they feel like From Soft didn't have any new ideas. There were couple of them that were actually really good, but overall they could've been much better.
Areas in this game are not really connected as they were in the first game (except for Majula, Iron Keep and its neighbour areas). The thing I really disliked about game's locations is the lack of creativity, once again.
Once again, this game also has lots and lots of items, and the content is pretty good.
Crown DLCs are quite enjoyable. Areas are well designed, they've certainly upped the difficulty in all three DLCs. Most of the bosses are exceptionally good, better than any in the main game.
- More Dark Souls
- Very good graphics
- PC port is much better now (no need for any mods to play it)
- Atmosphere of the game is pretty cool.
- More attributes to level up
- Better PVP
- Torch system
- Warping between the bonfires is immediately accessible)
- Good, but not so great of a story
- Soundtrack is not so memorable
- Enemies do not respawn after killing them couple of times, so the areas are no longer as farmable
- Lazy bosses (couple of exceptions like Looking Glass Knight, Executioner's Chariot, The Lost Sinner, and most of DLC bosses)
- Non-connected areas (only connected areas are Majula and the Iron Keep IIRC)
- Cheap feel for a lot of areas
- NPC's are not really interesting

: THIS REVIEW CONTAINS SPOILERS :
Let me say this right off the bat.
I believe that games can be used to tackle issues and controversial topics like violence, human psychology and homosexuality. Just because it's interactive doesn't mean it can't be emotional and thoughtful. "Gone Home" has been said to be one of those games. This game has been praised since 2013 as one of the most touching and thought-provoking games ever to be made. That's the reason i heard about "Gone Home", and that's the reason i payed 7 euros for it.
I wish i hadn't.
First of all, i didn't really mind the games extremely short length, as a game isn't automatically bad even when it's short. I've seen people beat this game in just 60 seconds, and it took around 70 minutes to complete. But that's where the problem comes up. Half of that time was just me wondering that what the hell should i do. There's no clear direction of things happening, and over 70 percent of the actions i performed were just me going walking around slamming my mouse to do something with the items on screen. Next, the gameplay itself. If you decide to buy this, then expect walking around slower than a sloth in a wheelchair and clicking on random things. That's really all there is to it.
Let's talk about the story, and that's what bothered me the most.
You see, "Gone Home" tells the story of Kaitlin and Samantha, two sisters who are three years apart from age, Samantha being the younger one. Kaitlin returns from a year-long trip from Amsterdam and enters his family home only to note how no-one is home. Including Samantha. Samantha explains in a brief note about how Kaitlin should NOT go to the attic and can't tell mom and dad, about, something. What's that, you ask? This sounds actually exciting? Well, prepare to be disappointed, because the story is so obvious after the half of the game, and even the ending doesn't really help it.
SPOILERS :
If you haven't already heard the basis of this game, Samantha is a lesbian who falls in love with a girl named Lonnie.
Lonnie is a rebellious kind, coming from a pretty twisted family. She's anarchistic, weird and crazy. They have their great moments, but they have to keep their relationship a secret due to Samanthas parents being very homophobic. Now, the story tells about how Lonnie decides to join the army, and then they have to break-up. Now, up to this point i kinda got the whole jist of the story.
1.Person X and Person Y fall in love. 2.*romance commences* 3.Something tragical happens, eventually leading up to them to go on their own ways.
Can you guess what happens next? Well, Lonnie decides NOT to go the army, and writes Samantha a letter asking her if she would love to live with her in a new town, to run away.
I don't want to sound too needy, but when a game is surrounded with as much hype and praise as this one, you'd at least expect something greater and bigger than a typical high-school love story as the plot. And in my opinion, this game doesn't even take the whole "tackling issues about being gay and acceptance"-idea that well.
As you may have understood about this rant, i was disappointed with this game. It wasn't worth the 7 euros, and i can only feel sorry for the unfortunate that spent the full price on this. This game was said to be one of the most important pieces of gaming history and one of the few emotionally touching games, but it really isn't that. I think "To The Moon" is a better example of that.

______________________________________________________________
A visceral, brutal and deeply rewarding WW1 shooter.
Deep trench, no man's land, mud crawling, mustard gas, bayonets at-the-ready.
Blown apart by mortar fire, pistol gut shot, hacked down with MG's - lie down and moan and cry and pray and beg for the mothers sweet embrace.
Fort, trench, forest or field. Mind your exposure or you will fall prey to a sniper bullet to your felt hat.
Mortar crater pocketed and crisscrossed in front. Hands and knees to the carcass of a dead horse on a berm. Come upon the crest slow and deliberate. Find any movement. Fire and retract. Rise again, fire and move. If you stay still you are dead.
Retreat. The enemy advances. He moves fast. Make your shot and retreat. Retreat or be shot for desertion.
Hold the line. They move left. Send in a recon plane. It doesnt show much. You know they are out there and moving forward but you see nothing. See but dont be seen. They've breached the hill on the right flank. Move and counter or die where you lie.
Your enemy scans the plain, he sees shadow and corpse, wire and burnt out wagon hull and wheel. He sees the slightest twitch on a ridge, could be a shadow, could be a body, could be nothing. He fires and ducks down. Someone will have seen his muzzle fire. He didnt know what it was at first but he hit his target.
You are dead. He guessed and guessed right.
You are dead forever and your mother mourns you. War is terrible.

I want to recommend this game because I have a lot of respect for anyone attempting to tell meaningful stories or alternative narratives in video games.  It's hard to do and the amount of hate that the author has received is really distressing.  It's work worth doing, and this is a decent stab at it.
But I wasn't engaged here - mostly because it feels like a snowglobe.  You find a whole house sort of frozen in time, but there's nothing fun or interesting about this house.  It's just a middle-class family home in the 80s/90s with lots of nostalgia and a bizarre amount of notes laying around.  The writing is fine, but imho it's the artwork that really needed to be a lot better.  There's nothing beautiful to find in thi world.  There's nothing that catches your eye or really makes you want to explore.  And that's really important.  People are (mostly) willing accept a game like Proteus, which has literally nothing but random creatures and trees that make sounds - and I would venture that it's because Proteus has a really fun and interesting audio-visual component.  Gone Home does not.
Worth playing perhaps, but I'm not sure it succeeds as a whole.

~Long-ish Dino D-Day Review~
Summary: Dino D-Day is a 1st/3rd Person Shooter with a relatively small player base. Do not let this fool you, though. The game itself is actually quite fun. The game is akin to the play style of TF2 and CS:GO. It offers a few different gamemodes as well as a nice array of characters to choose from (everywhere from run-n-gunners to snipers and...DINOSAURS). The best thing this game has to offer is its raw concept, dinosaurs in WW2. Let me tell you, that stays enjoyable.
Ignore the Critics: The game does have poor reviews from Metacritic and a few notably bad reviews on Steam. Don't let this deter you. These reviews were written a LONG time ago and the game has since fixed (not all but) most of the bugs that ruined gameplay.
Should You Buy?: Personally picked up the 4-pack at $3.00 coming out to 75 cents per copy (90% off). This is a more than acceptable price for the game. I would highly recommend the 4-pack when the game is on sale. Playing with friends is a blast and the DLC (Last Stand) is decent if you have some buds to play with. The DLC is definitely not necessary for you to enjoy the game.
Quick Pros:
-Playing as a dinosaur in WW2 is just as fun as it sounds.
-Really good deal when it's on sale (90% off).
Quick Cons:
-Small online community.
-Couple bugs here and there.
All in All:
8.1/10 Would Recommend (on sale...)

Needs some work still.  Somewhat enjoyable atm, it has its moments of fun and hilarity but overall I just can't recommend it.  Maybe that will change in the future if they update and fix the right stuff.
Main issues with the game so far
1. Bolt action rifles are just too strong.  they 1 shot everywhere, leg, arm, pinky finger.  all a 1 shot.  Really takes away from the skill of aiming for headshots (especially for scoped weapons).  They should be 1 shot head shot ofc, but not 1 shot body/arm/leg.  Heroes and generals does this well, Its pretty rare to see a 1 shot body shot in there and its alot better for enjoyment in gameplay.  Maybe its not the most realistic but... its a game and needs to be enjoyable.  I'll take a history class If I really need some realism, know what I mean?
2.  Mortars are silly at full 100 level.  they strike like 20-30 times and its just way to overpowered atm.  Also the cooldown is too quick for mortar strikes imo.  Few days ago I was killed 6 times in a row (honestly 6 times) by mortars within a few minutes.  Just not fun.
3.  Map design is ok, but a few of them are just too open imo.  Its more "open field warfare" than "trench warfare" as it promotes.  Really liked champagne map and hope to see more like that.
4.  Hit registry seems off.  I'll go to aim at someone and the I'll be right on them but the shot doesn't connect.  Even happens multiple times in a row sometimes, with people standing still sometimes too.  Not a big fan of the flash hit detection, Much prefer projectile mechanics, but whatever they just need to tighten things up it feels, and It could work.  Had my friends saying the same thing too, issues with hit registry.
5.  The few times I used scopes/binoculars I was quiet suprised at how zoomed in it was... for such a cqc game.  Doesn't feel right, a reduction in zoom for at least bino's would be nice (scopes I get should be long range).  The weird coloration on the zoom gives me a headache as well.  Not sure why that was really needed.  Some things just don't work well for immersion in gaming.  fun to try them out in development but for funs sake its best to make things gamey instead of realistic ( at least most of the time I feel).  Also the sensitivy when I zoom in with binos is way to fast.  super hard to control which is annoying.

At launch Homefront: The Revolution was met with bad to average reviews. The major complaint was the bugs and the poor performance resulting from terrible optimization.
So now, months after release, you might be asking yourself; is the title any good? Have the bugs been killed? Is the performance smooth?
Yes, the bugs are gone. Yes, the game is buttery smooth and yes, the title is very good indeed.
The story of Homefront: The Revolution does a much better job to sell you it's idea of a north korean invasion than the first one. It's still absurd, but so is most alternative history stuff.
You play as Ethan Brady, forgettable silent protagonist #831, who could've avoided the majority of bad situations if he only opened his damn mouth.
You're part of the Resistance, the only people in america fighting against the oppressive force of the KPA.
That's all you really need to know. The characters are rather forgettable, at times even downright ♥♥♥♥ing annoying. Looking at you, Dana. You ♥♥♥♥ing Psycho.
The gameplay and atmosphere is where Homefront's strength is really at. After a short opening sequence, you begin the game in a red zone. There are several red zones in the game and they are the place where the game shines the most for me. It's night, in you're sitting in a building devastated by bombs and rockets, overseeing the rain soaked streets, you notice the red scanners of the KPA zeppeline scanning the area, resistance fighters whispering in the shadows, planning out their ambush on a KPA patrol.
Do you remember the flashback scenes Kyle Reese had in Terminator 1? This is it, man. All Red Zones look like that.
The lighting and colors do a lot to create a really immersive and fantastic atmosphere. Unlike most games in which you play some sort of Guerrilla fighter, this time you actually feel like it. Each of your weapons have been crafted and are modifiable on the fly. You use pipe bombs, molotov cocktails and other DIY weapons. It really helps a lot in selling the idea that you're just part of a resistance that's fighting for survival against an overwhelming force.
Instead of going completely open world, the game has hubs, each hub is a bit different, but they are usually either red or yellow zone. Those hubs are further divided into areas that you can recapture for the resistance. This results in less patrols, less powerful weapons for the KPA and less drone presence. Red Zones are usually bigger and also allow you to travel faster by using bikes.
Yellow Zones are - unlike Red Zones - still intact. The streets are less open, the focus is more on small alleys and stealth, since the KPA is more aggressive here. Normal citizens live here, all of them suffering from the KPA occupation and ready to fight back. This is where the Hearts and Minds System comes into play.
When you retake areas, destroy KPA forces, destroy propaganda, or rescue prisoners, the Hearts and Minds meter will go up. You'll start seeing more and more streets being vandalized by graffiti, more people in the streets shouting anti KPA messages, more civilians joining the resistance until you manage 100% and the streets will be flooded with burning cars and civilians outright attacking KPA forces.
It's absolutely glorious.
It sounds very similar to Far Cry 4, but it's done much, much better.
A lot of elements from this game will remind you of Far Cry 3/4, the comparison is more than justified, as the game took clear inspiration from the series. That said, I think Homefront fleshed out a lot of elements that Far Cry didn't focus on, like the before mentioned Hearts & Minds System. It's a more focused experience.
I think I played for 20 hours before completing the game, because I focused on retaking as many areas as possible. In all that time the game only crashed once on my computer (happened during the Time Splitters 2 demo). There are other bugs, but none are game breaking, they are usually funny glitches, like people standing on air, or cars driving into people during a cutscene that simply disappear as they weren't supposed to be there for the cutscene. Stuff like that.
The performance is rock solid, on a mediocre to good PC you should be fine on the highest settings. The only thing bothering me is the stuttering whenever the game quick saves, but that doesn't happen all too often and you get used to it quickly.
Sound is good as well, each weapon has it's own distinct sound effects, the KPA usually only talks in korean and the drones sound amazing. The Zeppeline sticks out, as it always makes that dreadful sound when it sees you, again reminding me of Terminator. I just wish there was more variation for the recorded dialogs for the civilians and resistance.
Honestly, the developer should sit down and make this game moddable. Allow people to make a Terminator mod, because this game is just a few models away from being the wet dream of all Terminator fans.

As I prepare for Dark Souls 3, and most likely will put this game away for the foreseeable future, I thought I should write a review, because doing otherwise would be a huge disservice to a game that I’ve had enormous amounts of fun playing.
I played a bit of the first Dark Souls on Xbox 360, and I could never get very far.  Still, it was fun to watch videos of competent people playing it, and I really liked the lore, so the series grew on me.  I saw the sequel, watched videos of it, and decided to try it for myself when SotFS came out, pledging to myself that I would finally git gud.
During my first ten or twenty hours of playing, I probably said “What?  That’s ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t!” or some variation of that phrase more times than I ever had before.  I had all the standard frustrated, annoyed thoughts of “Why did I buy this?  Why did I want to torture myself by playing this?” and so on.  I saw the difficulty as unfair, unreasonable.  This is the standard initial response of the vast majority of people playing a Souls game.  If I had recorded my gameplay during those first hours, I’m certain I would cringe constantly watching all my easy mistakes.  Eventually, I managed to beat the main story, and became relatively good at PvP.  I later created a second character and optimized it better, having a more clear end-game idea in mind.  With this second character, I managed to beat many of the secret bosses not put directly in the path of the main story.  In short, I had reached my goal.  I had learned, improved, struggled, and git gud.
For all the pain that comes with learning the game, destroying all the enemies in an area once you’ve learned how to beat them is quite possibly the most satisfying thing I’ve experienced in a game.  The same goes for when you get invaded, and rather than hiding and getting killed, you can outplay the invader and win.  Your mindset changes completely once you make some progress, find a playstyle that suits you, and overall become more comfortable with how the game works.  The arrival of an invader becomes less of a vague “Oh no there go my souls” feeling of dread and instead becomes an interesting challenge.  When you learn to overcome the obstacles the game lays out in front of you, it feels amazing.  You know that you earned your victory, and nothing made it easy for you.  Whether you finally learned the attack patterns to dodge that boss you were stuck on, or discovered the weapon/spell that works for you in PvP, it’s a feeling of triumph I honestly hadn’t felt before in a video game.
As I said earlier, it wouldn’t be fair not to review this amazing game.  However, it also wouldn’t be fair to neglect to mention the relatively few aspects of it that I found genuinely frustrating, even after having become relatively competent at it.  The DLC areas are extremely cruel in their difficulty, and even after my first 100+ hours of playtime, I was unable to beat them without significant multiplayer help.  They are significantly harder than the rest of the game.  Granted, some people would see that as more of a neutral point, or maybe even a positive.  I can only really think of one thing that objectively worsened my experience with the game, and that’s the PC setup.  The keyboard controls aren’t very good, and the tutorial shows the controller controls rather than keyboard controls, leaving you to figure out how to play for yourself.  I eventually got used to it and became capable enough at PvE and PvP alike with a keyboard, but overall I’d say you should probably skip the hassle and buy this on a console, assuming that’s an option for you.  The one final negative point is that the storytelling in Dark Souls 2 does not live up to the original Dark Souls.  However, that’s just my opinion, and I know some disagree.
Dark Souls 2 is not a relaxing game.  You shouldn’t play it if you’ve had a long day and just want to unwind for an hour or so after work/class/whatever.  You’ll almost certainly stress yourself out more.  But if you want a real, meaningful challenge, and you have some time to commit to it, I cannot recommend this game enough.  I don’t mean any of this to mock people who want a more relaxing experience.  But this game is not for them.
(One aside: SotFS has some significant differences from the original Dark Souls 2, primarily in enemy placement.  I’ve never played the original, so I can’t speak to whether or not these are improvements.  However, SotFS does include the DLCs, so that’s something to consider when budgeting.)

Well, let's see:
Absolute toxic community: I only played "PVE" and sometimes I just wanted to thrash my living room: As long as you don't play with friends, noone will listen or advise any kind of tactics. Or you get downed and signal your medic to rez you and he just runs headlong into the thickest throng of enemies and gets instantly mauled. Ah, good times...
Repetitive and boring gameplay: Well, you have four classes, Rifleman, Sniper, Medic and Engineer. Three of those four classes have an actual role in this game, the sniper is just.. I don't know, useless. Why? Because all maps are narrow, small and absolutely not suited for long-range-sniping. Plus all classes have a skill, needed if playing team-based. Except the sniper. Medics can rez, Riflemen can give you ammo and Engineers restore your armor. Snipers just.. No, the don't have any of this..
The "missions" are all the same: get to the evac-point, slaughter as many bad guys as you can and extract. So, yeah, it's like CoD with bad graphics and no story at all (well, not that CoD's storys are THAT awesome...)
Pure grind: I remember when Cryteks CEO said, that after Warface no AAA-Game could survive without beeing F2P. Well, more P2W. The game is free, don't get me wrong, but the best equipment can only be bought with premium-coins, which, as usual, cost real money. You can get most of the stuff by playing missions, but the progress is so slow, you could well be in your 80'ies before you even get to the good stuff.
So, did Crytek stay true to their CEO's words? Nope, not even close..
Would I recommend this game? If you have a godlike-tolerance for curse-words, grinding the grind till it grinds and have absolutely no interest in any kind of story aside from some words at the start of your mission, then yes, by all means, play this game!

Dino D-Day might've just presented me with the must uncanny perspective I've ever took the chance of seeing WWII through. And it was, overall, good while at it. The story, while nowhere near a saga, is quite developed and credible, especially if you consider Nazi secret weapons such as dinos something less than impossible. The game doesn't really aim to be truthful though, opting for the establishment of a light and somehow refreshing humorous atmosphere through the snarky remarks of the balanced and specialized characters. Those include both Allies and Axis humans, also including several reptile killing machines - a term I've chosen here both to refer to the dinos ingeniously armed with guns and to those wielding the weapons nature gave them -, adding up to a fairly even roster, which could only be improved, in my opinion, if there were a few more German humans to choose from.
The guns in the game are quite well-modeled, even though their Half-Life basis makes them feel a bit weightless. The arsenal includes pretty much all of the most popular guns from the Great War, from American and French guns to even some British and Soviet ones. The gameplay itself is pretty straightforward, considering the game bases itself on Half Life 2's source engine. For that same reason, one can already wonder about the graphics, which - at least on my end - were average for the segment. A noteworthy aspect of it, though, was that for my computer the game ran somewhat poorly, which I believe was due to a weak optimization. Multiplayer in it seems to be fun, although my attempts to host it were clad in hardship and, when I played, there weren't many servers around. To be fair, it seemed mostly that the game had been a bit neglected both by its developers and its fanbase at the time.
Well, for starters, it is unlike me disliking WWII-based games - I really like the weaponry. Secondly, I believe this game may have potential, especially considering its background and the funny atmosphere it has. To top it off, it'd probably be unfair to let issues that maybe only happened in my computer taint the game's "recommendability", specifically because its Source base makes it ever so versatile. Still, for all I've cited, I close this review with a
.

I was happy to see Homefront 2 coming out. Happy enough to pre-order (which I don't usually do). It had an interesting setting, story was so-so and over acted (so was the original Homefront -- it was to be expected). But the more I played this game, the excitement diminished more and more and frustration took its place. It wasn't frustrating because it was difficult or challenging. No, it was frustrating because there were so many stupid things to deal with. Either bad design, random puzzle mechanics (especially those where the mechanics were not properly introduced or apparent), ugly dev shortcuts (patrols randomly popping into view?), and bugs. As another reviewer stated, you could start seeing the “cracks” appear. The story, the acting, that all would've been forgiveable. But the engine was ridiculous.
I understand the issues with development and changing hands and all that, but when you take a game and patch it only to make it worse, you really have to question what is going on. Some of those changes were not even needed, yet the developers messed with them and screw it up even more.
I recorded my playthrough and put it on YouTube, but by the end of the series, I was basically muttering “this is so stupid” the entire time.
The multiplayer is okay, but not worth the hassles you have to go through to paly it. If you can actually find a game, you have to hope that you’re a decent enough player to not fail the mission for your team. And of course, you have to hope that you get decent teammates. It’s not bad if you have to exit a game because of those issues, but it takes forever to find enough players for a game you could spend your entire ‘gaming time’ allotment sitting there waiting. the multiplayer is nothing like the original Homefront.
And on that note, the guns/shooting/etc feels nothing like the original Homefront. Those had some good feeling to it, but Homefront 2... man...
Summary: Do not buy it at full price (terrible mistake on my part). Buy it at around $5.99 USD (okay, maybe $8.99) for some fun that you can jump out of when it gets tedious. Or better yet, watch it on YouTube.

Homefront The Revolution is a heavily flawed game.
The first Homefront was a CoD copy and not even a good one. Homefront The Revolution plays like Far Cry 3 and 4 but without a great story or memorable missions.
How to free the checkpoints is the only thing HTR does better than FC 3+4. In the Ubishooters you have to climb towers over and over again. In HTR you have to complete different objectives, like killing certain targets or hack a computer but here the developers made some mistakes too: One computer was hidden in a building and I found a different way to it. I could have easily jumped up and climbed through the window but was forced to take a different route to it. Funny that I could jump out of that window to get back on the streets. On another checkpoint I could have climbed over a fence but wasn't able to do so. I had to climb up on another building and jump on the rooftop.
The modular weapon system may have been a great idea on the paper but the Crysis trilogy does it a lot better. In HTR it just takes too much time to switch the weapons and the enemies take way too much bullets even with the upgraded guns.
The programmers said that you are no CoD hero but why do I still have to kill dozens of enemies per mission? Many of the main story missions didn't feel much different than your average CoD massmurdering.
The story itself is also very weak: You play as a guy named Brady who doesn't speak and gets mixed up in the resistance where you are some sort of John Connor because you alone can do what dozens of other fighters can't and you have your Resistance buddies like the typical leader, the nice doctor and a female psycho. Oh and there is a traitor too! Surprise!
What the game does get right however is the atmosphere. When you start in a yellow zone the people are depressed and the KPA shows up just everywhere. The more you liberate the zone the more the people will rise up and you can actually see it. First there are some people protesting and later on the start to kill the KPA and the whole zone atmosphere changes.
But that is also the only cool thing about the game. The rest just feels mediocre and in the final mission you even have some heavy bugs. You have to escort two vehicles but they can get stuck. First time on some debris the second time on each other. Had to exit to the main menu to avoid the first bug and the second time when the car didn't continue and dozens of enemies spawned from nowhere I got killed but when I reloaded the checkpoint the car continued. Totally annoying!
Overall this game is boring and repetitive and brings nothing new to the shooter genre. It copies heavily from other games but doesn't even get that right.
So I really can't recommened this game.

Let me preface this by saying that I think Dark Souls II is a fantastic game, and above most titles coming out today. I do very much like the game, but do believe that it has some faults that are fairly significant.
First of all, my main issue with the game all together was the let down in world design, especially coming off of just playing the original game and Demon's Souls for the first time. Those games had their amazing interconnectivity, while Dark Souls II, while having some elements of a connected world, felt too straight forward and linear in terms of where to go (note, the DLC, especially the Burnt Ivory King, but also the others, achieve this, and almost exceed in this design completely).
Besides that, my miscellaneous issues typically are directed towards the art design and certain gameplay elements (damn you, hitboxes!). Soul memory was also kind of poorly implemented and shouldn't have been there, and the same goes for the Agility stat. Otherwise, I thought the game was quite fantastic, with its interesting level design, cool, mysterious characters, and exciting boss fights (especially those in the DLC and end-game of the base game). My favorite fight overall has to be the Burnt Ivory King; I just really love his moveset (although it is basically Gwyn 2.0), but also the area you fight him in and his whole backstory. He's just an overall awesome character and fight.
The combat needs to mentioning; it's just as fantastic as the first game. It's got a perfect blend of speed and clunkiness, to suit different players' styles, and is in general fun, challenging, and intense.
In short, I highly recommend playing this game. Even if you enjoyed the other games' feats, some of which absent in this game) I can undoubtedly say that you will enjoy this one. Don't listen to the hate! Most of them still really enjoy the game. It's got great boss fights, fantastic combat, amazing DLC, and interesting level design and characters and general story.

So, to start things off, I'll have to say that this is the first game I've ever asked for a refund over.
I'll start off with what I like about it first, and I'm not a big proponent of listed items.
I think the visual fidelity of the game is good, you can tell it was built on Cryengine, it LOOKS good, it was hard to get a good framerate when I played it, however that was right around the time it was released, and I returned it quite fast after playing it.
The gameplay foundations are also there, I can tell that this could be a solid game experience and its bothering that it simply but these features fall so flat on their face with some of the issues that just ruin everything that could be good.
One of the biggest design decisions was to make everything sort of open world and Far Cry-esque, but when you die, what the hell happens? You get stuck about a minute or two back in the game, or if you happened to get stuck by a checkpoint, good job. But if you didn't get to a checkpoint and happened to use a vehicle to get to your objective thats about a minute away with enemy patrols on your way? Well good luck, because that vehicle is no longer there anymore, and you lost a "valuable item" or something like that simply for dying. So you get punished in a good few different ways just for dying! Enemies are randomized in their locations, you get set back fairly far in gameplay, you lose a valuable item, and if you used a vehicle? Good ♥♥♥♥ing luck, its gone off into the oblivion. Its just so bloody confusing when you die, no idea where your progress was last set, so its just not worth trying to figure that out in my opinion.
This hurts though, because I love this sort of 'America has fallen' style game, Red Dawn is one of my favorite movies ever, but this game just doesn't work for me.
If someone ever comes back and tells me that these issues have been fixed, I'll give this game a try again, because believe me, I really wanted this game to be good.

Although I was gifted this game, I can definitely say this game would be worth buying. (Especially if you get it on sale).
This game could be considered "competetive". I can most compare this to Red Orchestra 2: Heroes of Stalingrad.
Although the game is not as easy as a run and gun. It definitely has its moments of derpyness, and it is really fun to create a squad of friends and to go out charging into the battlefield (Most of the time you'll end up dead).
Pros:
-Forward spawn (and this varies for different squad types). This allows there to be some mobility on the map, as squad leaders advance and take cover, your squadmates can spawn on you.
-Variety of different weapons and squads.
-Squad Abilities capture arty spam of WW1 well.
-The maps are very well balanced. Sometimes it is balanced so well, specific maps will end in a stalemate 9/10 times.
This can be seen as a pro and a con if you don't like static games.
-It is still in development and the devs seem to do a good job at fixing bugs that appear in the latest patches, the patches don't add pointless stuff to the game.
-Squad Progression: I don't think there is an "OP" squad ability, even as your squad levels up. Bonuses to your squad are well balanced, but still worth achieving. How you level up your squad, is mostly affected by how many matches you play with the people in your squad. Because of this, you pretty much need to play this game with friends if you want to unlock squad abilities. As for unlocking new weapons, you will get career points over time that you can spend on particular positions in different squads.
Cons:
-There are still glitches that appear after each patch, but these seem to be rapidly decreasing over time.
-The game is still being optimized. Even if you have a half decent graphics card, you might get frame drops every now and then until they optimize it more.
-Sometimes it is hard to find a full game depending on what time you're playing, and where in the world you live. Most of the time you can just switch to another server like EU and there will be full games.
-You will die a lot in the beginning.
Overall people who don't like slower paced games where you die a lot won't like this too much.
