As I prepare for Dark Souls 3, and most likely will put this game away for the foreseeable future, I thought I should write a review, because doing otherwise would be a huge disservice to a game that I’ve had enormous amounts of fun playing.
I played a bit of the first Dark Souls on Xbox 360, and I could never get very far.  Still, it was fun to watch videos of competent people playing it, and I really liked the lore, so the series grew on me.  I saw the sequel, watched videos of it, and decided to try it for myself when SotFS came out, pledging to myself that I would finally git gud.
During my first ten or twenty hours of playing, I probably said “What?  That’s ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t!” or some variation of that phrase more times than I ever had before.  I had all the standard frustrated, annoyed thoughts of “Why did I buy this?  Why did I want to torture myself by playing this?” and so on.  I saw the difficulty as unfair, unreasonable.  This is the standard initial response of the vast majority of people playing a Souls game.  If I had recorded my gameplay during those first hours, I’m certain I would cringe constantly watching all my easy mistakes.  Eventually, I managed to beat the main story, and became relatively good at PvP.  I later created a second character and optimized it better, having a more clear end-game idea in mind.  With this second character, I managed to beat many of the secret bosses not put directly in the path of the main story.  In short, I had reached my goal.  I had learned, improved, struggled, and git gud.
For all the pain that comes with learning the game, destroying all the enemies in an area once you’ve learned how to beat them is quite possibly the most satisfying thing I’ve experienced in a game.  The same goes for when you get invaded, and rather than hiding and getting killed, you can outplay the invader and win.  Your mindset changes completely once you make some progress, find a playstyle that suits you, and overall become more comfortable with how the game works.  The arrival of an invader becomes less of a vague “Oh no there go my souls” feeling of dread and instead becomes an interesting challenge.  When you learn to overcome the obstacles the game lays out in front of you, it feels amazing.  You know that you earned your victory, and nothing made it easy for you.  Whether you finally learned the attack patterns to dodge that boss you were stuck on, or discovered the weapon/spell that works for you in PvP, it’s a feeling of triumph I honestly hadn’t felt before in a video game.
As I said earlier, it wouldn’t be fair not to review this amazing game.  However, it also wouldn’t be fair to neglect to mention the relatively few aspects of it that I found genuinely frustrating, even after having become relatively competent at it.  The DLC areas are extremely cruel in their difficulty, and even after my first 100+ hours of playtime, I was unable to beat them without significant multiplayer help.  They are significantly harder than the rest of the game.  Granted, some people would see that as more of a neutral point, or maybe even a positive.  I can only really think of one thing that objectively worsened my experience with the game, and that’s the PC setup.  The keyboard controls aren’t very good, and the tutorial shows the controller controls rather than keyboard controls, leaving you to figure out how to play for yourself.  I eventually got used to it and became capable enough at PvE and PvP alike with a keyboard, but overall I’d say you should probably skip the hassle and buy this on a console, assuming that’s an option for you.  The one final negative point is that the storytelling in Dark Souls 2 does not live up to the original Dark Souls.  However, that’s just my opinion, and I know some disagree.
Dark Souls 2 is not a relaxing game.  You shouldn’t play it if you’ve had a long day and just want to unwind for an hour or so after work/class/whatever.  You’ll almost certainly stress yourself out more.  But if you want a real, meaningful challenge, and you have some time to commit to it, I cannot recommend this game enough.  I don’t mean any of this to mock people who want a more relaxing experience.  But this game is not for them.
(One aside: SotFS has some significant differences from the original Dark Souls 2, primarily in enemy placement.  I’ve never played the original, so I can’t speak to whether or not these are improvements.  However, SotFS does include the DLCs, so that’s something to consider when budgeting.)

Verdun is a game that throws you straight into WW1's gruesome combat. You can play as a variety of soldiers, ranging from snipers to snipers. The game differs from many other FPS games right now due to its very quick time to kill. Call of Duty, CS:GO, and Battlefield players might have a difficult time transitioning to the 1-2 shot weapons in Verdun. Although the gameplay is really good, it seems to have some latency issues. Being killed behind walls, and trade killing happens quite often. For me at least, the issues really didn't hinder my enjoyment of the game. It's fast paced in the sense that you don't know what's next in the trench, but slow enough to be too similar to other FPS games. With a squad, Verdun is far more fun, and I'd recommend it above playing alone (Playing alone is still fun!). You also get to roleplay as Pre-Nazi Hitler, which boosts the "fun level" immensely!
8/10

Last year, I was tasked with writing a paper in an intoductary level college history course. This involved selecting several academic works and writing a 10 page paper incorporating said sources. The paper I wrote addressed the battle of Verdun, specifically raising the question over where the line between Total War and Genocide should be drawn, and using the battle to examine this question. I read (and highly recommend) Paul Jankowski's Verdun: The Longest Battle of the Great War. The first hand accounts referenced by Jankowski portray a war of which can never, and frankly, should never be recreated to a high level of historical accuracy; men condemned to share trenches with cadavers of all stages of decay, towering explosions bringing down enough fresh soil to bury alive those caught beneath, and a day to day life so wrought with desiese and insanitation that it compels the modern reader to the brink of tears. Bearing this in mind, this game from a historical perspective is fantastic, and the recently added Horrors of War expansion brings a new level of intensity to the experience. I do not know of any other game in which soldiers continue shouting long after they have been "killed", and it confronts players with an uncomfortable understanding of war's awful reality. Though a video game is not likely to enlighten players to any true representation of history, anyone concerned with playing an authentic military experience should look no further. This game is pretty goddamn fun, too.

*This is not a game in the typical sense. There is no combat, no leveling, and no fail state (that I am aware of). With that out of the way, here is my review. Enjoy.
Gone Home is best described as an exploration game. There isn't any combat, scoring points of any kind, or even a "game over" state. You spend your time exploring your parents’ home trying to figure out why no one is around, picking up clues and story notes along the way. There is an overwhelming feeling of dread from the moment you take your first steps through the front door. Now, I won't spoil anything like several reviews I have read, but the game is not quite what it seems. The atmosphere in the game is building you up to expect a certain outcome but once you reach the game's climax you are given something different to absorb.
I feel that this game does earn a lot of its praise. It gave me an experience different from the normal violence and action I regularly enjoy in games. I was left thinking about the plot long after I shut it down, more than I can say about the latest One Man Army Simulator I'm currently playing. The fact that I spent time thinking about the story and how it affected me personally speaks volumes. I think some of these reviewers need to take a look at themselves for how they view Gone Home. We shouldn't be closed minded about a game because it jarred our expectations; we should embrace, or at least acknowledge it for trying to find its own voice
Now whether or not this game is for you is entirely subjective. I found it intriguing throughout my entire 90+ minute play through. But $20 is a high asking price for something that you will probably be spending less than 2 hours on if you feel that time = money. If you are truly unsure about it, wait until you can pick it up for a couple of bucks, turn off all distractions, let the game slowly unfold in front of you, and enjoy the tale.
I wish I could experience it for the first time again.
8/10

I'm a fan of walking sims. Hell, Dear Esther is one of my favorite games of all time. It was an amazing game with a beautifully told and gripping story, not to mention the environments were gorgeous and fun to explore.
THIS is no Dear Esther. The story is okay, I'll give it points for tackling homosexuality as well as it does, but everything else is pretty bad. Dear Esther knew it had little to no gameplay so it kept things nice and simple: walk from point A to point B, explore some dead ends. There are some attempts at nonlinear gameplay and puzzles in Gone Home but all it does is stretch out the game and it becomes tedious very fast.
Gone Home feels like the devs wanted to make a paranormal survival horror game but changed their minds halfway through. Occult imagrey is everywhere in the early scenes of Gone Home; there's a Oijua Board, tons of notes and books about ghosts, and lots of creepy atmosphere, such as the creepy storm warning seen on a TV. Had there been a paranormal story worked in and some critters to avoid this could have been good, but instead Gone Home only gets recognition for having a story about homosexuality.
Also, I am NOT homophobic at all so don't use that excuse for me not liking this game.

PROS:
- Authentic WW1 shooter with actual WW1 weapons and trench warfare (not as many explosions)
- Very balanced game....snipers or tanks (there are no tanks) DO NOT dominate games
- Decent amount of unlocks and levels which are easy to get
- Very pretty looking game on ULTRA graphics captures WW1 atmosphere and battlefields well
- Friendly helpful community for new players
- You can quickly get into matches and join with friends nice and easily
- Gas attacks and gas masks are a cool and unique game play mechanic
- Lots of nations to play as and variation in attacking/defending squad and soldier types
CONS:
- Spawn system can spawn you in front of enemies if they are in your trench
- Extremely hard difficulty with one shot kill on most weapons
- Tactical game play and moving between cover won't be enjoyable for COD/ACTION players
- Sometimes the games glitches as a machine gunner and makes you stand up for no reason
- Can be long periods of hiding and trying to spot enemies with not much else going on
Verdun is an excellent shooter not perfect but very good and we finally have an authentic World War 1 shooter on PC. This game is authentic enough to offer an alternative to BattlefieldOne at half the price, it's more historically accurate thant BFone. BFone tends to deal with bigger battles with more explosions and chaos where as Verdun focuses on smaller battles but its still essentially a WW1 shooter that involves going over the top. Verdun is pretty much set to the BFone gamemode operations that involves trench warfare... there are no tanks or planes it is purely man vs man combat. I would say Verdun is a more team and squad focused game than BFone. Both are good games but this will suit people who can't afford mountains of paid DLC from EA but want to experience a Great War shooter.
I have found in this game every now and then with my headphones on when crawling through craters or ducking behind barbed wire with bullets suppressing me I get a wow moment not many games do that! Immersion in this game can be amazing especially as I have an interested in history and WW1.
In the short time I've played I've had a lot of fun and would highly recommend it to players that prefer tactical shooters over quick paced sniper and tank wars. This game is a lot like Red Orchestra 2 in the way it plays and it's gun mechanics. If you make a mistake you're dead and you need patience, good judgement and good reactions before assaulting an enemies trench. Players who run around like headless chickens will die K/D doesn't have a massive bearing on the match outcome if you are holding objectives.
In terms of game play Verdun only has one game mode worth playing which is essentially trench warfare when teams take it in turns attacking and defending trenches. Sometimes lines are pushed forward, other times back but a lot of games are a fierce and grilling stalemate. Some players might get bored there is deathmatch and coop wave mode but 95% of the player base seem to be in the trench warfare mode which is called Frontlines.
What I like about this game is it's very hard, it's a hardcore experience and because it's in the WW1 era there aren't many snipers and no tanks to dominate the battlefield. Team work, finding decent cover and picking the correct time to attack or defend is key. There are 9 maps which are all different but they all capture the atmosphere of WW1 nicely, if the devs added some weather or a day and night cycle I think they'd have a perfect game. There are a couple of maps I feel if it was raining or they were played at a different time of day they would be utterly amazing.There are two night maps but it would be cool to see you the maps at different stages of light and cover.
My biggest worry was that being only 16v16 it wouldn't quite be on a big enough scale to capture how WW1 battles were but that isn't a problem the game is very good and matches are always full and your never far away from enemy fire.
When you play you'll be constantly ducking for cover in craters, checking your NCO's alive waiting for their attack order and avoiding enemy fire and grenades. When you jump into the enemies trench all hell breaks lose. The classes overall are balanced very well and there are attacking classes and defensive ones and you can change squad type during the game according to if you are on the attack or being pushed back. Verdun games are made up of 4 man squads the NCO is the leader who can give orders, lay down support gas attacks, mortar fire or request a recon plane. Everyone else fulfill the grenadier, gunner and marksman roles.  Because there are so many nations and soldiers there are a lot of loads outs to choose from you get 3 per soldier. Global levels with perks sit in the background and things like better aiming or less recoil are gained with global level. For example you can pick a better weapon and have less grenades or pick a lighter weapon and take more grenades on the Grenadier. Marksmen isn't always a sniper by the way! The retreat mechanic that forces you to run away and not camp when your trench is over run is amazing. It's so cool to watch and pick off retreating enemy and gives you a real sense of how many men must have been slaughtered during this bloody period in real life.
Machine guns and snipers rifles are available but aren't overpowered you really need to find a good location to setup and holding your breathe is key. Snipers don't dominate games 30 kills to 1 death. There's plenty of muzzle flash and suppression going on to stop people camping and you really get a feel for how new the automatic weapon and sniper technology must have been back then. The trench system means you cannot get behind the enemy to spawn camp with op weapons but you can invade their trench if lucky enough to make it over the top. I liked the idea: Deathmatching and Dino's, but it just feels like the developer took that idea and did the bare minimum of what they thought people would want. Do the dinosaurs add an extra dimension to the gameplay? No. If you took the dinosaurs out then it wouldn't make much of a difference in gameplay terms.
It's still a WW2 FPS, it's still got multiple classes, the weapons are still as accurate as shooting lemons through a drainpipe. I gave it a strong couple of play sessions making sure to try out all classes before giving it the thumbs-down, hoping that the game would rescue itself. It didn't, it just started to irritate the longer i played.
The graphics are nice, the execution is fine and there are some familiar references in one-liner's from the characters, but it's not much fun after you've got past the "Oooh wow, Nazi's and Dinosaurs".
Furthermore:
- 75% of the Allied classes are completely useless. This is due to the tiny dino's being impossible to hit thanks to players employing the age-old technique of jumping around all over the place.
- The accuracy of the weapons is period relevant. In other words, you can't hit a barn door from 5ft even if your aim is good.
- When playing as a human you're given a limited stamina reserve which is way WAY too small. Literally you cannot dash across a street without it completely draining before you've made it to the other side. Soldiers have never been more unfit than in this game.
- Part of playing any deathmatch game is being aware of noises that indicate foes nearby. Unfortunately your teammates are always noisier no matter what side you're on, plus there's the ambient sound of distant gunfire which is nothing to do with your battle. Basically you may as well play with the sound off, you'll be no worse off.
- If you've started a match and realised you've chosen one of the crappy classes, then your only way of changing is to quit the match and come in again; you can't change mid-game.
- You'll find a lot of players can shoot through walls.
- The maps are poor. Just a load of random passageways and smaller than you'd hope. Most games descend into who can surround the other team's spawnpoints first.
- Playing as any kind of dinosaur does not give you a feeling of strength, you're just as vulnerable as the humans.
- Even the Dino guns are next to useless, they spray out bullets like spittle in every direction except where you're aiming.
- If you log more time as one faction then the game simply won't let you play as the other one. I fancied a change from playing humans and selected Axis, but every time someone joined it booted me back to Allied side. It did this 6 times, despite me leaving and returning to try and be on the side i wanted to be on.
- Apart from the expected familiar Source engine sound effects, there are also a lot of Unreal ('98) sound effects. Couldn't the developer make their own? Or could they just not be bothered?
If they do another free weekend then by all means play it for nothing, you'll be sick of it by the time the weekend is over and should feel smug that you didn't pay any money to find that out.

Dark Souls 2 is a great game, but has its share of blemishes. Soul memory is arguably the worst of these... Sure, it helps with twinking, but it also drastically reduces the frequency of invasions and leads to high level pvp being an unbalanced mess. Level design takes a different direction as well, largely for the worse. As a consequence, the dense style of atmosphere of Demon's Souls and DS1 is simply not there. World geography and level transitions are just nonsensical in most places. Parries are weird, where enemies get knocked on their butts when you bat away their weapon, staring at you for about 4 seconds before thinking to get up. "What were they thinking?" is a question you may ask yourself quite a bit while playing this game.
That said, DS2 brings good stuff to the table as well. Variety is its saving grace. There are lots of weapons, miracles, sorceries, and pyromancies, allowing for much more build variety than in DS1. The addition of power-stancing only helps in this regard as well. Summoning is smooth as butter this time around (no more waiting 10 minutes to see signs, far fewer "summoning failed" errors). The abundance of armor means that Fashion Souls is very much alive and well, arguably moreso than in DS1.
This has turned into something of a rant. Altogether, DS2 is a sometimes confusing mix of questionable design choices, but is still does enough right to make it a solid game that will probably take up a lot of your time if you give it the chance.
Oh, but the SoTFS "buy the game twice" ploy was total bs. FFS Bamco.

Dino D-Day is a multiplayer team-based first-person action video game developed by 800 North and Digital Ranch and published by Valve Corporation. It was released as a digital download, via Steam, on April 8th 2011.
The game is developed as a total conversion modification on the Valve Corporation's Source engine.
The premise of the game is that during World War II, Adolf Hitler found a way to resurrect dinosaurs for use in the war effort. Players can battle online choosing to serve either the Allied nations or the Nazis.The game has been described as a new twist on "the overdone World War II FPS ... that has become a running joke in the industry and gaming press".
Upon the game's initial release, both the Allies and the Axis had six different classes of soldier. The Allied classes range from assault troops, medics and heavy support. However, the Axis have three human and three dinosaur classes. The human classes comprise assault troops, snipers and medics; while the dinosaurs comprise an attack Velociraptor, Dilophosaurus, and a Desmatosuchus with a cannon mounted on its back. Additional classes were added to both teams at later dates bringing the total to seven classes for the Allies and nine for the Axis. The Allies gained a dinosaur class of their own, a Protoceratops with a mounted machine gun. The Axis gained a Stygimoloch with a mounted gun, a Compsognathus that acts as a kamikaze bomber with a grenade and a flying Microraptor. In certain maps, an Axis player can also be chosen at random to play as a Tyrannosaurus with a jaw-mounted machine gun. While powerful, the class counts as three kills in a team death match.

I Keep Seeing Reviews that say "This is so Bad" or "Worst game I've ever Played" So, in response to this, I think its time I Shed some light on how I feel about this Game.
So, First off, Is it good? Well, it kinda depends if you dont really care about the story or stuff like that. It is Fun... But if you're looking for something like Destiny or Halo, you're in the wrong place my friend. The Story starts out great at first, but it fades off around mid-game. The gameplay itself is fun, its what you'd expect from any fps. The aiming is a little clunky, and the AI is somewhat stupid, but its enjoyable. Before patch 1.5, it was broken, not horribly, but it was broken. The only real downside now is how bad its optimizations are, but I'll cover why its like this soon.
Secondly, the Multiplayer: It's Okay, there is no PvP (Sorry all of You Cod and Halo Fans, but this isn't for you!) This is a Bluntly stated PvE Experience. This doesn't mean its bad, the missions are enjoyable. There's Just a Lack of Multiplayer maps, But Dambuster studios said that they'd Make More maps for FREE (Everyones Favorite Word!)
Thirdly, My opinion as to why this game was bad at first: This is most likely on combination of 2 reasons,
ONE: This was rushed by the publishers, the Devs were probably going to take more time with this, but the publishers probably said, "This needs to go out now, or we wont release it."
TWO: Inexperince with Making a Game like this. If you never knew what Dambuster Studios was before this, well... You're not alone. This Is Dambuster's  FIRST GAME. If you were in their shoes, and It was your first time making a game like this, It's obvious that you're going to have problems with your game, This Is also most likely why this game is badly optimized,they dont Quite Know what to do yet. Dambuster studios have made a great first impression with this game however, they obviously have some raw talent. This game was, and still is, Glitchy and Buggy, but Again, It's their FIRST TIME Doing something like this.(Give 'Em Some credit at least!)
IN CONCLUSION/ TL;DR: This game is Wonky, but it's clearly not as bad as people say it is, its a solid 7/10, its release price was kinda High, but if you can find it on sale, Go for it.
FINAL EDIT: I have waited a long tome before I started playing again, as the online was dead. Now, after a very, very long time. People are actually PLAYING ONLINE. Its as if history repeated itself, as I remember that the original homefront suffered a similar fate. This will be my last edit, as it seems no longer necessary to update my review due to almost all of the games performance and stability issues have been fixed.

Not looking at the short game duration and lack of gameplay, which are pretty common with games like these. The game gives you a nice and relaxing atmosphere, while slowly telling you it's story on a soothing way. Without spoilers; the story line isn't anything fancy, but it's something most of us can relate to. Even though the story doesn't have any twists and the ending is pretty straight forward, it's really nicely written. Expecially the voice over is down really well, and you can really feel the emotions just by listening to the speakers voice.

I played it on a pretty decent laptop which can run most games on high settings without a problem, but even on the lowest settings the framerate dropped often below 10fps. If it was any other game I would probably have just quited there and then, but because you don't really need the fps for this type of gameplay, it was just annoying.
I recommend it only to those who really like these kind of games, and want more of these. Don't expect anything new or unique, just enjoy the relaxing story with a good voice over.

Homefront: The Revolution is an excellent game. While it brings virtually nothing new to the table, it combines various elements of game series known and loved by many, including similar social stealth elements reminiscent of Assassin's Creed, and the enjoyable gunplay and customization of Crysis. It also bears tribute to Far Cry in the capturing of various outposts and 'towers'. What really makes this game shine, however, are the stunning visuals, which really bring the battered city of Philedelphia to life. The game especially shines at nightime, and if it's raining. There are some bugs, mostly related to AI Pathfinding and some animation errors (Characters getting stuck in T-poses) but overall, it's a fairly polished game with acceptable optimization. Creds to the developers, as this game was in development hell for a long time. A solid 7/10.

Verdun is a one-of-a-kind game , offering rarely seen WWI gameplay in an FPS format. It has very interesting concepts and game mechanics, and will appeal to history geeks or players expecting a fresh experience. Unlike conventional FPS shooters, Verdun is punishing and takes a while to master. However, there were several downsides to my playtime. The squad and level system in this game is never really explained, and it took a long time to figure out. Numerous bugs/glitches are also present and sometimes gamebreaking. All in all, I would recommend taking a look at Verdun, simply because it offers new content and gameplay. It tries to do something new, although not perfect in presentation.

Hmm. I quite enjoyed this "game" after all. Not because it can be seen as artsy, I really disliked The Bridge for that very reason. The exploration mechanics are neat (would love to see the same thing in a larger project) and there's been a lot of detail put into the house and subtle little jokes thrown in that I giggled at. There's not so much of a story unfolding in the game, you're just unraveling details about what has happened previously. It's cute at times and quite serious also. I think the game handles the topic very well and makes it seem realistic or at least believable.
Puzzles... are dreadfully easy. If you can call them that. It's really just looking through drawers and stuff finding codes and clues. Seeing how short the game is (I think I was quite thorough in my reading of the back of chips packages and still only clocked in 1,5 hours) this really isn't something you should get this game for. It tells a story and does so pretty well, but it offers little else. Replay value is pretty close to zero, but there is dev commentary and some other minor options to change.
But then there is the issue of pricing which a lot of other people have brought up. I picked this game up in a bundle with other games for a price I can't remember - but had I picked this up for the 20€ the steam store is asking for I would have been horribly disappointed. I would again stress that I don't find the game really bad in any aspect, but in the grand scheme of things the attention to detail doesn't excuse the poor length and lack of replay value. I don't want to spoil things for anyone else, but I enjoyed the game the most early on when you didn't know what to expect from it. Looking back... it's ok.
So to sum up, great exploration with much detail put into even small objects. Super short. Great atmosphere, but doesn't do much with it. Probably horribly disappointing if you were expecting more of a... well, game.
I really wish you could do neutral reviews on steam.

Besides the mandatory PvP(which I despise), I like this game. It looks good and has great environments.
You can summon help in the way of NPCs which range from derpy to completely competent. You can summon other players as well and most of the them are competent.

There are minuses though. The hitbox for weapons(especially Boss and Player Invader) is laughable at times. I recently got invaded, the weapon was a pike or something, glowing and hitting me with almost a virtual foot between the tip and my character. Think the vets call that lagstabbing?
Projectiles hitting air near objects. Just hanging out, mid-air, defying gravity, clipping, logic, etc...
Player invaders completely prepared for PvP invading have an almost overwhelming advantage. I get it, there are covenants that reward players for killing other players.
Invaders are prepared for invading, while the invadee is usually trying to not get killed by NPCs and environmental hazards. The invaders are completely ignored by the NPCs. It doesn't happen very often anymore but I usually just try to get to the nearest bonfire and wait for the inevitable.
Enemies will suddenly ramp up their attacks after you stroll through an area several times. I think my son was calling it false or inflated difficulty or something. They just seem buffed at times. Fight them and learn their movesets and strenths and poise and then it changes slightly. Kinda cool if a little frustrating. Thinking you are gonna walk your way to your 30K souls when BAM the mob that normally takes 3 swings now takes 4 or now has increased poise or etc...
I would love to see a quest log. So many times I ask myself what to do now?
I recommend this game to those bored with feeling overpowered and have an extra controller laying around for when they most likely rage and break theirs.

Gone home is a great immersive story exploration game.  It will not be to everyone's taste as the game play is solely based on you moving around and piecing together the clues of what has gone on in your absence.  If like me however, you enjoy a break from big games and want a good story or puzzle game to immerse into for a short while then definitely give this a go.  The atmosphere is tense and kept me on the edge of my seat for most of the game.  Trying to figure out what had happened was interesting and for the first half of the game had 2 or 3 possible ideas.  Towards the end of the game it became obvious where the story was heading and while I did enjoy how it ended I did feel like I would have preferred the other direction the story could have gone.  The music was great in game and really enjoyed finding the tapes to listen to the next song.  Bottom line, I really enjoyed the game, the atmosphere, tension and overall story was enjoyable.  If you like games within this genre it is worth a try especially if you see it on sale as I did!

The districts are all open world and you can move about them freely and they all feel alive and breathing, and they all look beautiful.
The performance is a bit awful, I have to admit. With an Intel Core i7 4790k as 4.5GHz with a GTX 970, I was getting an average of about 50-60fps when walking around at high presets, and about 45fps in hectic fights, really needs optomising, but it was play able for me and it looks great.

I think I may be genetically predisposed to enjoy adventure games.
One of my earliest memories is sitting on the couch with my dad playing Legend of Zelda on the NES, with the guidebook map sprawled open burning every bush on every screen searching for every last trinket. With the advent of the internet, that experience boiled down to, "oh there it is." As far the evolution of the genre, I feel like they picked a winner with the Souls formula. Sure you can scour all the data you can handle about the challenges and the locations of all the cool toys, but you'll still have to contend with the twenty foot tall blast furnace wielding a gigantic spit roast like a toothpick when you get there. And shucks howdy is that cool. I know people are daunted by being pounded into the ground like a railroad tie in the first five seconds of a new fight, but every time I enter the boss arena, or a new area, or hell even an area I've been in before, I know "hey, don't stand next to that green glowing statue," cause it's going to barf poison all over you and huffing poison moss doesn't seem like the best use of your time. And those skills translate quite effectively from area to area. You can start to develop that sense of danger, that little ping in the back of the mind that whispers, beware that chest in the open area with nothing guarding it. You can even start to feel out the walls that just don't look right, or a place a treasure might be hidden in. That treasure is usually more rubbish, but hey, now at least you know.
So is it a game that is just flat out too hard, or for pros only or some crap like that? Hell no. But it is a game that isn't going to show you mercy. And if you are the kind of person that asks for none, it should fit like a glove.

In comparison to other games in its genre, Five Nights at Freddy's generally presents itself well and uses its minimalistic presentation to haunt the player further.  Beyond simply a jumpscare festival, as some would dismiss it as, all of the small details come together to create a true experience of anxiety and tension with each play.  Interestingly, it is a game that shifts from a straight horror experience into a challenge, presenting the player with more play time through the challenging gameplay that, although somewhat random, feels very rewarding when you execute properly.
In comparison with the firse Five Nights game, this game has much more polish and mechanical diversity than the old one, including the unique challenge presets in custom night, beyond simply cranking up everyone's difficulty all the way.  This game keeps the tense atmosphere of the first and adds so much more.  I fully recommend this to any horror fan, even if you didn't really like the first game.  The pacing is quicker and more frenetic in this one, so this should be right up your alley.

Have you ever played a Souls game (Demon Souls or Dark Souls) before? If you have, then you'll know what I am talking about when I say that Dark Souls II is by far the largest installment in the series so far. The vanilla Dark Souls II alone took me upwards of 30 hours to complete; now, with the Scholar of the First Sin edition, there is even more content to explore and enjoy.
Dark Souls II Scholar of the First Sin is a fantastic game. It plays much smoother and faster than both the port of Dark Souls and the vanilla Dark Souls II, and for those who have already played the original Dark Souls II, the Scholar of the First Sin edition still holds some value since it renders the game with better textures (64 bit) and better FPS. Not to mention, Dark Souls II: Scholar of the First Sin has the conveinient feature of including all of the DLC avaliable to Dark Souls II in one place (you don't have to buy Crown of the Old Iron King, Sunken King, and Ivory King seperately). Finally, as if that all wasn't enough, Scholar of the First Sin updates some of the areas of the vanilla Dark Souls II with different and new enemies (*SPOILER ALERT*: It adds a new ending too), creating a fresh challenge for those who've already conquered Dark Souls II.
Here is my Pro/Con breakdown:
Pros:
- 64bit textures
- Smooth and fast gameplay with a refined feel
- Full controller support (playing with controller is a must for a Souls game IMO)
- Includes the orginal Dark Souls II with updated areas and a new ending
- Includes all the DLC avaliable to Dark Souls II installed with it as a package
Cons:
- Souls game (Yeah, you're gonna die, like a lot.)
- For those who already have vanilla Dark Souls II and all the DLC purchased, SoTFS doesn't really have too much value
All and all, I loved this game and would definitely recommend it!

With the last homefront you felt that need to pick up a new weapon every few mins because you felt the need to try this M4 with the EO Tech, oh look a AK with a CCO, OMG a Shotgun with a ACOG!!!!!!

Warface is one of the best free fps' around.
-Is Warface pay to win?
It's definetely not. It is true that by buying kredits and tryharding boxes, you get the best guns in the game. But someone with skill and a vendor gun can beat someone with less skill and a pay2win gun. So yes, "donating" makes it easier but it's surely not necessary.
-What is the vendor system?
The vendor system is CRYTEK's F2P solution. By playing, you unlock items from three different categories (Weapons, Clothing, Attachments).
So you need to play a little bit in order to get good guns, but in COD you won't get the best guns after your first game eiter.
-Does it get boring?
As far as I know, it doesn't, I'm close to 600 ingame hours (3000 PvP games, 500 PvE games) and I still enjoy everytime I play. I would recommend using different guns and playing different game modes all the time. If you play the same gun on that same TDM map every day, you'll be bored within a few weeks.
As the game is free anyway, I'd recommend just giving it a try!

Ok so my review of verdun is, its still early access. It doesent say it is, but it is.
Frequent stuttering, and FPS drops, as well as many graphical glitches, soilders holding invisible guns, flickering scopes. When i asked someone who was a fan of the game, they replied "Every game has these issues." Or "It's just a server issue."
The gameplay could be fun, if they made the bolt action rifles inacurate at close range. They tryed with a Rising Storm styled Hold Shift to steady. But using it is pointless now. Melee weapons are pointless, In a ww1 game... Of course i think its because you dont get anything special for melee kills, for instance like Battlefield's DogTags. And they have classes in the Trench Raiders that are pretty much pointless. Because they use those melee weapons. Also the melee weapons are op, which they should be at close range, however bayonets are just as glitchy so countering a melee weapon is just useless, with a dull thunk sound is made as the club destroys your skull and the melee man goes on to get kill after kill surprising the men of the trenches because they aren't equiped to deal with it. Now thats another thing to point out, most of the loadouts arent really made for countering anything. Usally you have a class that does its own thing or counters something but these classes seam to just be rolling dice. For instance only one version of the officer class gets binnoculars, a useful tool to survey, and call artillery or gas strikes. So the fact that only one of these classes has it, kinda degates the purpose of using the other classes, unless you want to essentailly be a rifle man with the ability to call in artillery.
Also the Weapon sounds are awful, with the same sound almost seaming to be used for everything. For instance that webley sound, almost sounds like a stock sound considering you can here someone spinning the cylnder. suposedly a sound update is in the works.
The graphics in this game are awful with draw distances having to be set so low, as for the game to work well, with stuttering still. That players almost are invisible until in medium range. The use of snipers is almost useless because they are put into a squad of attackers essentially, for instance lets use the alphenjaeger. Infantry with calvary/artillery rifles with air recon, essentially light infantry, one of the units in the squad is the sharpshutze who doesent get any points, because the squad leader has an "aura" of command range, however the squad leader has to attack the trench with the rest of reguler infantry because honestly its more useful to attack with every thing you have.
Machinegunners are useful, and do what they are supposed to do, lay down fire, protect trenches, however thats only until they run out of ammo. Then well your out, you cant get any, your essentially defenseless unless you have a sidearm, but still its frustrating when you cant do anything about it.
Now that battlefield ones out, and everybodys recommending verdun over it. I have to say you have two options that can be summed up, Battlefield one has the vehicles, verdun has not. Verdun has very glitchy mechanics, Battlefield one's mechanics for the most part are solid. Verdun has the historical accuracy, uhhh well its kinda boring, Battlefield one has not. Battlefield one has the diverse gameplay while not in the style of WW1, but in the style of Battlefield. And of course game breaking glitches are few and far between however this is common in this game with every engine change which is how they attempt to fix the bugs.
The biggest issue i have is that they are moving to consoles. They arent fixing this version of the game. And apparantly its out of early access somehow.
Although i was very harsh on this game, there is something i like and that is the music, each squad gets its own musical number at the beginning of each round. Remember this was my opinion, even if it is biased against the game i feel tat a negative review could be helpful.

This easy butter chicken recipe can be made in 35 minutes and is SUPER delicious. It's rich, creamy and addictive. It's also very easy to make dairy-free!
Makes: 4 servings
Ingredients
2 tablespoons grapeseed oil (or another neutral flavoured oil)
1 lb. chicken breast or tenders (see notes)
2 yellow onions, roughly chopped
3 tablespoons chopped ginger
6 garlic cloves, crushed
1 tablespoon garam masala
1 teaspoon ground turmeric
1 teaspoon coriander, ground or seeds
1 teaspoon cumin, ground or seeds
¼ teaspoon fenugreek, ground or seeds
¼ to 1 teaspoon chili powder
Seeds from 4 cardamom pods
1 - 28-ounce can of crushed or diced tomatoes
2 tablespoons almond butter
2 tablespoons dairy or coconut cream
2-4 tablespoons brown sugar, to taste
Optional: 2 tablespoons plain yogurt
Sea salt, to taste (I like about 2 teaspoons)
1.Heat 1 tablespoon of the oil in a medium-sized frying pan over medium-high heat. Add the chicken breasts or tenders and cook, stirring frequently, until they are cooked through and no longer pink, about 12-15 minutes. Remove them from the pan and cut them into 1-inch chunks.
2.While the chicken is cooking begin preparing the sauce. Add the remaining tablespoon of oil to a large skillet over medium-high heat. Add the onion and cook, stirring occasionally, until the onion starts to brown, about 10 minutes. Add the garlic and ginger and cook for 1 minute more.
3.Add all the spices all at once, or remove the pan from the heat for a moment while you add them. (garam masala, turmeric, coriander, cumin, fenugreek, chili powder and cardamom seeds) Let the spices cook for about one minute, or until they are quite fragrant. Add the tomatoes to the pan and scrape up any stuck on brown bits. Add half a cup of water and bring the pot to a boil. Lower the heat to medium and let the sauce simmer for 15 minutes.
4.Carefully add the sauce to your blender and blend on high until it is very smooth. Add the sauce back to the pan and stir through the almond butter, dairy or coconut cream and the optional yoghurt.
5.Serve with a side of rice.

You die fast and can't craft health kits. My final score for the game would be 6/10 which is of course decent. Not recommended at full price, and don't expect to be blown away by the story. I can very tentatively and conditionally give this one a thumbs up. So let's go through what's good about it:
+ Story is not readily apparent and is told completely through artifact collection
+ Minimal yet effective sound design, including voice acting
+ Very detailed environment, often evoking the spookiness typically seen in horror games
+ Story has several threads that are intriguing both independently and as part of greater narrative (seriously, was
surprised at how hard some of the little detail hit me)
But of course, there is a lot to be desired as well
- Gameplay consists solely of walking through house, picking up objects to look at them, clicking objects to activate
them
- Very short, even if it conveys the story well in that time
- $20 is extremely steep for the amount of involvement you have in the story
- Story could have built some more mystique, but instead opted to finish in a relatively mundane fashion. Sort of a
letdown in the compared to the brilliant details you can uncover.
- Story could have been excellent layer beneath engaging gameplay, but is instead the sole layer of the experience
So yeah, it's definitely slow, story-focused, and pretty dang short. If you enjoy a solid story and exploration, you may like it, but it is by no means a 10/10. I'd personally give it about a 7/10 for what it is.

After 3 to 4 hours of playing, I finished Gone Home. Fortunately, I only paid 5 Euros for the game and in retrospect I wouldn't pay for it higher otherwise. So Gone Home is notorious for being critically acclaimed much to the chagrin of many gamers, and I always wondered whether it was justified or not.
The relationship between Sam and Lonnie comes across as clichéd but it's endearing at the same time. The more I found out about them, the more I could picture them before me and empathize with them -- but the same goes for the other residents of the house.
To me, Gone Home is more like going through an immensely big house, messing around with other people’s belongings and finding more about the lives of people by going through their private belongings (isn’t violation of privacy just wonderful – don’t do this IRL, kids or NSA for that matter), and there’s quite a lot to explore within the span of 3 to 4 hours.
However, I do have to agree with some points of the naysayers. The game doesn’t strike me as anything revolutionary or overwhelmingly great that it deserves the biggest praise. First off, the way it handles the unwritten “Show don’t Tell” rule can be a bit wonky. Sure, the game does a terrific job at integrating the explorative nature of the game within its storytelling, but at the same time we have Sam’s voice narrating the events that have occurred before, and to me, those events would have a strong impact if we were Sam herself or physically there. Secondly, I am uncertain if the ending hints to the message of the game, but if it is then I have to object to it. I don’t want to spoil anything, but to say the least the ending of the game is kinda problematic and the same thing goes with certain parts regarding the relationship between Sam and Lonnie. That said, I commend Fullbright Company for creating a game in which LGBT characters are portrayed as humans instead of problematic stereotypes or stock characters that are prone to dehumanize or demonize the LGBT community.
So yeah, summed up, I’d say Gone Home is worth the money (if it’s on a big discount) and while it has some flaws here and there in its message and way of storytelling, it’s definitely worth exploring and discussing about.

I'd rate the game 8/10.
It's a lot of fun to stalk through the house, rummaging through the stuff and reading notes here and there. Now and then you can interact with objects too and there are some small puzzle elements (finding items and finding codes)
The storyline is very nice, it is somewhat emotional too. I liked the graphics, though the game itself has a slightly haunting setting, I expected a jump scare any moment. (there were no real jump scares or horror moments).
Yet, the game didn't feel complete. There were two storylines running through eachother and only one got finished. You won't really hear much about why the place would be haunted, why there are all these secret places to visit and rummage through. It is mentioned several times that the place is haunted and that they saw certain 'activity', yet you won't see it yourself, other than an occasional dark hallway with spiderwebs or a light bulb that suddenly gives in. Oh and yes, the game is kind of short. I finished it in 2 hours. Any additional dlcs would be very welcome.

For the first ten or so hours, I was ready to defend Homefront: The Revolution. The setting and atmosphere was, for a while at least, enough to make me overlook some small bugs here and there.
But then the cracks really started showing, specifically in regards to artificial difficulty brought about by endlessly spawning enemies. As the game continued, it seemed that engaging even one enemy out in the open summoned a horde of his buddies, all of whom know exactly where you are as soon as they show up. They will continue spawning until you eventually become overwhelmed and die.
This becomes increasingly annoying when you're merely trying to make your way to the next main objective and each time you turn a corner there's a patrol that wasn't there 2 minutes ago. Yes, they just popped into existence once you looked away and back again. And now they're like some sort of reverse necromancers, endlessly summoning every living thing within a 10 mile radius to zero in on you for the rest of time.
I was willing to overlook the iffy blandness of the rest of the game and just kick back for a low budget urban Far Cry. But this is supremely unfun. Do not buy or play this game ever.

It may seem odd that someone who's played more than 200 hours of a game would give it a bad review. The truth is, I kept coming back to Dark Souls II, hoping I'd see something better in it, something that made it worthy of calling itself a sequel to one of the greatest RPGs ever made, but I never did, no matter how desperately I looked.
To make a long story (or rant in this case) short, everything you could possibly want from a Dark Souls game isn't in this. Exciting, strategic combat has been replaced. Every weapon has damn near the same speed, so PvP is entirely about trading hits and PvE is entirely about praying that the enemy you're facing doesn't start it's next combo with it's no-start-up-frames flurry. Interconnected, metroidvania style level design is replaced with straight shots, spreading out like spokes from the starting town. As for the world itself, physically believable locations, all of which could be seen from one another, are replaced with...well, you take an elevator up past a windmill and end up in a volcano.
With Dark Souls 1 already released and Dark Souls 3 weeks away (when this review was written), this isn't the kind of sequel that's going to be looked back on fondly as a standout entry in the series. It definitely stands out, but for all the wrong reasons.

Homefront: The Revolution is an underrated shooter with brisk open-world conquest, proficient weapons and engaging mechanics. Although the story is flimsy, major characters hold it together. Set in Philadelphia, the game focuses on an underground resistance group fighting the occupying North Korean forces. The Goliath vehicle (from Homefront 1) returns, but players must clumsily escort it because, sadly, they cannot command it. Story missions are rough, especially those near the weak ending.
This is a sandbox game, first and foremost. The initial world building is not as good as its predecessor, but the world design and gameplay are much better. Players will shoot and sneak their way through a few sizable levels. The basic goal is to capture ‘Strike Points’ in each level and retake America one piece at a time.
There are two Zone types—Red and Yellow. Red Zones are warzones with a heavy ‘Nork’ presence that shoot on sight. Airships slowly patrol above and you do not want to get caught in their spotlight. Stealth is encouraged initially and, after gaining sufficient ground, additional resistance soldiers make the levels safer. Yellow Zones are smaller residential locations that encourage hit-and-run tactics. These tend to use more vertical space and utilize cameras to keep civilians in line. Stealth is easier because you can blend into the crowd. After winning enough respect, civilians will riot which also reduces danger.
The difference between each area is refreshing, even though many tasks are similar. You will hack antennas, capture strongholds, recharge generators with motorbikes, and even do some basic parkour navigation. Some tasks are random, like saving civilians or killing officials. It is strange that many Strike Points can be captured while enemies are still hostile nearby, but this makes for rapid conquest. The two different Zone types provide natural pacing and satisfying conquest
Sadly, Revolution has its share of bugs. Problems include: not being able to complete side jobs, grenades falling through the ground, and enemies disappearing. My character even flew high into the air, after getting off a motorbike that was barely moving. Also, after capturing one Strike Point, the game spawned me inside a shelf. Performance is not the best—with a few late-game crashes—although it still looks good on medium settings with changing weather and a day-night cycle. The game is not technically polished, but it is quite playable.
Using CryEngine, the AI has familiar routines and similar problems. Sometimes they walk into walls, float above the ground, or forget they got shot. Fortunately, they also have many positives. They react appropriately to dead bodies, sounds, and thrown projectiles. Toss a Molotov near soldiers and survivors will search the approximate source location. Cause a large explosion and Norks will swarm that area, reducing the threat elsewhere. The AI does not cheat; they move and shoot based on your last position. The mostly-clever, partially-glitchy AI makes for decent action.
There are several effective stealth options, including a melee takedown, silenced pistol, and proximity devices.  RC cars can be driven short distances to produce chaos elsewhere; you can even drive them under vehicles undetected. There is a great selection of guns, including a powerful sniper and an excellent assault rifle. Enemies and vehicles have weak spots, so positioning and accuracy is important. The Hack grenades will temporarily turn autonomous vehicles against the Norks and these devices are also used for puzzles. It is a shame that you can only carry two primary weapons but they have alternate modes (e.g. the crossbow turns into a flamethrower) and it usually isn’t far to change loadouts.
Multiplayer is co-operative only, although this is not a bad thing. Players become a resistance soldier and complete missions across the same zones from the single player. You might escort vehicles, breach strongholds or rescue prisoners. Stealth functions well, in fact the co-op plays much the same as the solo mode. There are skills, outfits, and boosts—they could have been part of the single player to add more depth. There are only 6 missions (more are planned) that take around 10 minutes to complete. You typically buy crates to refill consumables, and the RNG Gods will dictate whether you get a useful hack device or a 10% XP boost. It’s a grind without enough content, and there is barely anybody playing just weeks after launch.
Homefront: The Revolution will provide around 15-20 hours of decent action in the single player, assuming players capture all Strike Points. What makes it successful is in how it presents the world and how it provides small encounters with different objectives. There are barely any drawn-out battles, and tasks can be completed without firing a shot. Players can progress through zones in any direction, avoiding snipers or destroying enemy patrols, and the encounter spots are rarely the same. It’s a sandbox game, so the experience relies heavily on letting you have fun in bite sized pieces. The game achieves this more often than not. Homefront: The Revolution is far from perfect, as numerous bugs, AI quirks, poor story missions, and performance issues hold it back. But damned if it isn’t enjoyable to enter a hostile sandbox and have it completely under control after an hour or two of competent shooting. 7 / 10

It may seem odd that someone who's played more than 200 hours of a game would give it a bad review. The truth is, I kept coming back to Dark Souls II, hoping I'd see something better in it, something that made it worthy of calling itself a sequel to one of the greatest RPGs ever made, but I never did, no matter how desperately I looked.
To make a long story (or rant in this case) short, everything you could possibly want from a Dark Souls game isn't in this. Exciting, strategic combat has been replaced. Every weapon has damn near the same speed, so PvP is entirely about trading hits and PvE is entirely about praying that the enemy you're facing doesn't start it's next combo with it's no-start-up-frames flurry. Interconnected, metroidvania style level design is replaced with straight shots, spreading out like spokes from the starting town. As for the world itself, physically believable locations, all of which could be seen from one another, are replaced with...well, you take an elevator up past a windmill and end up in a volcano.
With Dark Souls 1 already released and Dark Souls 3 weeks away (when this review was written), this isn't the kind of sequel that's going to be looked back on fondly as a standout entry in the series. It definitely stands out, but for all the wrong reasons.

Gone Home is an atmospheric adventure which will set you back in the late 80ies and early 90ies.
I try to explain what it's all about without spoiling anything.
Held completely in first person, you are exploring the mansion of your family .Everything is designed with love, very detailed and all absolutely true to the era it is set in. You'll discover original 90ies mags, CD's, self-help books, furniture. And I could go on and on .Just perfect. Really sucks you into the game and sets the mood completely right.
Well, you come home one day and everyone is gone. Where are they? Explore the house, read the post-it messages, hidden diaries and basically everything you could get your hands on (and that’s almost everything in the house), to find out what's going on. All the while an aura of suspense is lingering about their whereabouts. Were they abducted by aliens? Some psycho killer killed them? Monsters? You'll have to find out. And sometimes the game plays you and leads you in the wrong direction.
The music is almost nonexistent and it's very quiet in the house, all you're going to hear for the main part of the game is the squeaking/creaking of the wooden floor, the rustling oven in the basement, the wind rustling at the window sills from outside and sometimes you find MC's from the 90ies with 90ies music lying around. But other than that, nope, no music.
The first person position is very well done. You play the game with your mouse/Keypad or controller and it's working just fine with the game.
The game also has Steam Achievements, Steam Cards and supports the Steam Cloud

I began my playthrough of Gone Home ignorant of what I was about to experience. All I knew is that the game had received a lot of critical praise (including a 9.5 from GameSpot).
Once I had finished my sixty minute adventure (this game is currently listed at £14.99 on Steam) I was completely and utterly disappointed.
I felt that Gone Home misleads the player from the very start. It appears to set up a horror mystery. As Sarah you return home from a year long trip around Europe only to find no one is home and there’s a hastily written letter from your sister Sam attached to the door, essentially explaining she’s ran away, but not to worry “we’ll see each other again some day.”
It’s the middle of the night and you’ve let yourself in to this big, creepy house. Lightening can be seen bursting through the windows and the sound of thunder fills the corridors. Lights also flicker on and off for no reason (which is explained in a document later, if you find it) and when you’re inspecting clues the floorboards noticeably creek, hinting that you’re not alone.
It sets a scene that would fit into any generic horror tail and early on when you’re hearing voices down the end of a hall it sends a shiver down your spine. I did not think this was a horror title going in, I had no expectations for jump scares, the game itself made me believe it was a horror after the opening ten minutes.
Ultimately the horror theme slips away and it is replaced with a story of love. At first glance it appears a bath is decorated in blood, only to be revealed through a clue that it’s just hair dye. The voices heard are coming from a TV and the creaks of the floorboards really are just the sounds of an old house moaning and groaning.
I can understand why people really enjoyed his game. It’s a different type of story for videogames, and a nice throwback to the nineties. Also wandering around a big house piecing together what happened to your sister is fun. However, the 90s nostalgia and what actually happened to your sister really did not appeal to me.
Games where I get rewarded for suspending people in mid-air and then rewarded for shooting them In the♥♥♥♥♥seems to be where my mental state is right now…

I'll probably get a lot of hate for this, but I do not understand the appeal to this game.
There's only two things really going for it, the interesting audiologs you get each level from the phone, and the jumpscares (if you are a fan of jumpscares)
Other than that, the gameplay itself is extremely repetitive. The basic functions of the game have you checking cameras and flashing animatrons with a light. Each time you flash them they freeze in place for a few seconds, and then when they get too close you are supposed to put on a mask and they go away. At the same time you have to keep a music box wound up at all times.
What sort of annoys me, is that it doesn't really matter if you freeze the animatrons in the cameras, because they tend to randomly appear in the hallway infront of you, or start crawling in the vents, apart from that it's hard to tell how long you are supposed to keep your mask on. Sometimes you will check the cameras and then come back and immeditely lose. It's also a bit difficult to tell if the animitrons are frozen or retreating...I'll flash them in the hallway over and over again and they just keep coming back and keep getting closer which is kind of unfair in my opinion. Sometimes one will randomly be at your desk after viewing the cameras even though you checked every location moments before.
Besides this, if you are unfamiliar with the game, expect this game to last about 30mins-1 hour before you get sick of the jumpscares. It's a bit fun to have your friends / family get jumpscarred, but that's about it.
I don't think this game is "bad" i just don't think there's enough to warrent a purchase. I would likely enjoy it more if I could actually see the puppets moving around, and could actually notice the effects of flashing or get some sort of indicator that they are retreating. It would also be nice if your character could move, or at least change rooms, maybe have multiple ways to finish a level like escaping rather than just waiting for the clock.
Perhaps this game is so popular because it's so simple to play? It's hard to tell.
I'm also not a big fan of horror games, but if you want something similar, I'd suggest playing Slender The Arrival which has the same intense appeal of being stalked, but has a lot more content and more interesting challenges.
[Also, no trading card or achievements for such a popular new game? Unacceptable]

This game was a bit of a mixed.  To start off, I think after a few more updates this would be much more playable.   Even at a discounted price though, it would be hard to suggest this game, ultimately.  But, I'll take this step by step from here.
Graphics:
This was really where it was kind of all over the place.  I actually expected better from the fact that this is a CryEngine game.  Some character models were fantastic with really great animations.  Unfortunately, I don't feel like they put a lot of work into characters you don't see in cut scenes.  The people on the street were mostly Ok, but I think there is only a few character models and they are simply reused them all the time.  The world itself suffered from being all over the place.  The buildings looked good, and when you are in destroy section of Philly, you can mostly go into them and find little nooks of items.  But surrounding that may be a terrible looking pile or rubble.  I can't help but feel that if everything is going to be trashed, it's actually significantly harder to pull off.  The enemy soldiers were at best, only OK.  Some of the armored one's were really cool looking, but there is one part of the city where you basically only see guys in full hazard suits with just a repaint between silver and yellow.  The enemy vehicles looked really cool in my opinion, but there were 3 different versions of them in the whole game.
There was this lighting effect where when you were in a dark room the lit doorway would be so bright you couldn't really see through it, and conversely when you were standing in the light you couldn't really see what was going inside dark areas.  It was an especially nice tough, like this is something the developers really thought about.  There is also a nice effect as your visions adjusts to the light/dark area you were entering.
Sound:
The gun sounds were really not very stimulating.  I didn't feel bad♥♥♥♥♥when shooting any of them.  It's weird when you pull a rocket launcher out of nowhere, shoot it, blow up an enemy Humvee and you are like, "eh, at least I don't have to worry about that anymore.  The enemy sounds were sparse.  For instance, when you are near a guy with a shotgun, it makes the same yell from every single enemy shotgunner.  Most of the guys didn't talk unless you were really close and then they all basically had the same voice.
The ambient world sounds were a nice attempt, but it felt like the sound designer didn't know how to make the other inhabitants of Philly sound the same.  Sometimes there were 5 people around and their was conversaion sound that sounded more like 25 people.  Sometimes there were 25 people and it sounded like a group of 4 guys were standing around and just talking.  Other things include just sounds that were completely out of place, like they were just trying to fill an empty void with anything.  I would be running past something and I would just hear a beep, like I had just found something to interact with but there was nothing there.  I started by searching around for where the beep came from and it would be some unmanned empty console with a million buttons and nothing to interact with.
The music and the voice acting was the best part of the sound design.  The voice actors did a fine job on what was clearly a lack luster script.  They put their all into it and it really sounds good most of the time.  Sometimes there were periods where you would be doing something and some epic music would start, and other times there wouldn't be music.  But those points it felt appropriate to be listening the ambient sounds of the world.  In a nice secion of city you would see people running around, you would hear birds.
Gunplay:
Besides the off sound, the game offered an interesting collection of firearms.  Each one felt a bit different, but to me it felt like they were different for the sake of being differing.  For instance, you can get crossbow that can be alterd to be a flamethrower or a blunderbuss (of all things).  The shotgun can be modified into an automatic shotgun or a gun that basically shoots molitov cocktails.
The rub is, you can only carry 3.  That wouldn't be so bad but you were basically only allowed to select 2 becaues your one slot was locked into a handgun.  Now, that handgun can basically become an uzi, which is nice, especially with a silencer and a decent medium range scope.  But that leaves you with 2 to play with.  The third slot gets unlocked a little further into the second area and that is your RPG.  You can swap it out, but you never know when you will find a humvee or a goliath, so you will probably never remove that.  That leaves you functionally with one spot.  The issue here is that you might as well just take a sniper rifle.  The handgun you are stuck with become an SMG, you don't want to get caught fighting vehicle without rockets, and the city is over run with snipers.  At the end of the game I took the automatic shotgun because it was only then that I realized how incredibly OP it is.  Vehicle?  No problem, unload a barrel into most vehicles and you destroy them.  Ammo can be found on every enemy corpse and you get it in spades and it's always for weapons you have equipped.
Progression:
This part of the game feels completely unfinishd and hackneyed.  So, each part of the city, after you complete the obligatory Hearts and Minds quest, you basically go around and can capture enemy points (kind of like capturing a camp in the Farcry 3/4).  There are points you are clearly meant to capture first.  These are your strikepoint, they basically weaken the enemy enough for you to capture some of the more strategic points.  These net you KPA tech points.  Initially, these are used to unlock upgrades and options for your guns.  This is where it gets weird for me.  You use money to purchase guns, then you use KPA tech points to unlock the gun upgrades, and each gun and it's constituent upgrades can be upgraded up to 3/3 stars... which you use money for.  You basically use those tech point to simply unlock the guns and nothing else   I captured every single point in every single part of the city.  I had unlocked all the guns rather early.  By the end of the game I had 130 KPA tech points that were useless  Each thing I capture and even portions of the Hearts and Minds quest gives them to you.  But I think the most expensive one was actually only... 16 KPA tech points maybe.  Literally everything else cost money which you struggle to find.  At the end though, it feels like the developers knew they messed up the balance and started throwing money at me like there was no tomorrow.  You also use money for all your weapon attachments and gear with act as character progression.  It ultimately felt useless to upgrade anything.  Sure, you can carry a bit more ammo, you can run a bit faster and take a bit more damage, but you still feel the same as when you began, all that matters is the guns.  So, the progression part is a failure in my opinion.  The KPA tech points feel useless though, as if there was going to be more for them and they just stopped.  At least maybe if they had let me choose between money and tech points for each upgrade, that would have felt more worth while.

I wanted so badly for this to be good. Sadly, the title should've given it away; this is Homefront: The Revolution, not Homefront 2.
The first Homefront was a totally underrated FPS. It was linear, yes. The gunplay and mechanics were quite standard, yes. But there was a unique setting, some brilliant writing, and one moment every level where the only response I had was "Wow." Some of those moments still sit with me - in the gut, not in the brain. The same way Spec Ops: The Line still does.
But The Revolution does not have those moments. It's tutorial driven. Despite the half open world it still feels very linear. The story is worse. The writing is obtuse. The game went too cerebral. They thought about it too much and overplanned. Micromanaged. It goes to your head instead of your heart.
The graphics are ok - they weren't going to be the thing to make or break this game anyway. The controls are quite bad, mostly because there are some very important keys you can't re-assign (like holstering your weapon). Stealth is constantly suggested but impossible to actually pull off. The open world aspect felt more like a chore than anything approaching fun. The balance of money and points for upgrades is totally off: there's far too little early on and far too much later.
The whole system is buggy, especially around achievements and saving progress. The only reliable way to move forward is by sprinting back to a store to get a check point after accomplishing the optional objectives. If you don't and the game crashes while you're out in the world exploring you'll have to try to remember what you did and repeat it all.
The multiplayer is worth mentioning because I'm a sucker for co-op, especially with RPG elements. But this was terrible. The skills you unlock don't usually matter and it takes too long to get them (although it's worth noting that there are one or two that are totally overpowered compared to the rest). The different classes don't really complement each other. And finally, there isn't nearly enough content. Once you beat all the maps one time there isn't a strong incentive to keep playing.
I'm glad that they got this game out, but creating a game is very different than creating a
game. The latter is far more difficult, and requires a level of care and polish that simply isn't present in The Revolution.
Hopefully Homefront will get a true sequel one day. I'd enjoy that.
UPDATE: After playing all the DLC I can safely say that it's generally better than the main campaign experience. That's largely because they focus on telling a story and engineering some memorable moments. There's even a Half-Life 2 feel to the final one, Beyond the Walls, and that's a very good thing.

That's probably the best way to describe the game.  It's open world with a bunch of little tasks you can do... take this outpost, defend these friendlies from an attack, etc. while you have the option of following the story as closely or as loosely as you want.  So the structure of the game essentially is like FarCry in America.  Instead of open valleys, tall mountains, and little ravines... you're exploring a dense urban landscape with door to door, street to street, and rooftop to rooftop fighting in
.
If you've been a fan of the
franchise, you'll like this game.  You'll get your dose of warfare that pits you against an invading army on American soil, a premise that's usually just briefly touched on or completely ignored by the FPS genre as a whole.
The game itself, however, feels largely like a work in progress instead of a fully polished game.  The animations are passable, but not great.  For example... something simple like lifting a dirtbike up off its side and getting on it doesn't have a smooth first person animation where you lift the bike and climb on.  Instead, you press F and the bike lifts itself upright, then you press F again to climb on.  Looting an enemy for supplies shows a progress bar on your HUD, at which point when its completed you quickly pat down the body and you get your items.  Now neither of these really stand out on their own nor are they game changers, but when alot of repetitive actions have a placeholder-esque animation tied to them... they do add up.
Bullet registration on enemies can be hit or miss at times (look at me making puns and stuff), which again adds to this rushed feeling the game seems to leave you with.  Often enough you'll see a few inches of an enemies head exposed while he is behind cover, but none of your bullets will do damage until they stand up.  Similar things happen to arms and hands when they are behind cover... seeing a small sliver of them exposed sometimes isn't enough to score any hits (which you know because the game has hitmarkers).
I'm only 3 hours in so far, and while it has small things like that which I feel could have been done better... I'm still having a blast at the game.  I usually never play any game for 3 hours straight, but I just played
for that long in one sitting and it felt like only an hour has passed.  It keeps me engaged... always wanting to capture the next objective, loot the next crate, and kill the next enemy.  It's hard to put down even with its shortcomings.  It has enough going in its favor in other departments that it makes up for where it falls short.
So for people like me who want a shooter that does something different and explores new territory in more ways than one, I recommend this game.  It is fun to play.  I think it's definitely worth $40 at least, but I'm a
junkie so I was willing to pay full price because I simply didn't want to wait.
But for people who want to play a Call of Duty or Battlefield on US soil, they will probably be disappointed.  The game is heavily story and setting based, and feels unpolished as a pure shooter.  The gunplay and movement doesn't feel as smooth as Call of Duty and the environment and vehicles don't feel up to par with the Battlefield series.  The graphics are good enough, but doesn't really have the "wow" factor that FarCry has been able to achieve with each passing release.
So in the end, it's difficult to have a universal answer to the question of "Do you recommend this game?"  It depends on who you are and what you're looking for.  For me, if I want to play a pure FPS I play Insurgency.  It's an awesome shooter... even with approaching 2,000 hours in that game I don't see anything replacing it because its movement and gunplay is so spot-on.  But sometimes I want to play a game with good storytelling and a good narrative.  So for that I'm enjoying the hell out of
.
Overall I think it's a good game to supplement your other shooters.  It won't replace them, but you'll have a hell of a time in
while taking a break.
