Just finished the main story, didn't reach 100% completion however so I thought I'd offer my 2 cents.
Firstly, I'll say that I was playing on high on a single GPU, I had 3 instances toward the end of the campaign that saw my framerate drop to a crawl, but that remedied itself quickly. Other than that my framerates were fairly smooth. There was always a half-to-one seccond pause on autosave/gunsmith locker/store exiting, but I got used to that fairly quickly.
The game world -LOOKS- amasing, in my mind. Playing at 1080p, I loved it especially at night time. Fire effects look great, explosions were a little dissapointing both in visual and sound... more on sound later. NPC's look great, though some of the randomly generated combinations for resistance fighters look a little odd. I generally liked the look of the game, the details of the world especially (like the "Where to Shoot" posters all over safe-houses and such.) and the atmosphere of the world is very well realised as far as the North Korean occupation of America is concerned. Each of the districts felt unique in my mind, nothing felt over-used in terms of terrain.
The sound was a little lackluster, though weapons sound great. Explosions and such don't sound too punchy, footsteps aren't loud enough either which doesn't assist stealth, when you come around the corner into a walking KPA trooper.
The weapons were cool, they look customised/personalised like a bunch of undisciplined civillians-turned-guerilla fighters would have. ("U mad Bro?" on the reflex sight? loved it) and the Guerilla Toolkit Items like Molotovs, Pipe Bombs, Hack Tools and Firecrackers and their deployment options all looked and felt decidedly cobbled together. It didn't feel like the resistance had 'too much tech' in my mind. And the KPA forces were suitably challenging all the way through (I played on the middle difficulty) and I really enjoyed the gunplay. I especially liked the first-person take on blind firing weapons and the cover system even if I had to fidget a little to make it work sometimes.
Missions though they are simple and use the same framework, to me, felt reasonably different. "Eliminate the Snipers"  task might take different forms. The first time snipers are occupying an appartment block, the seccond time you are investigating an overwatch post that went dark, only to find snipers have taken them out. etc.
The phone is a really neat way to handle your characters quests and such, just wish some of the text messages were helpfull other than just pats on the back from the major NPC's.
Motorcycles felt great, though collision wasn't ideal and running a KPA trooper down does nothing. Would have liked to be able to turn your view more and possibly use a sidearm whilst on the bike too.
My biggest issue is the way KPA NPC's and vehicles spawn in and out almsot at random, quite often a guard harassing a citizen that I was about to shoot after I put on my pistol's supressor would suddenly vanish. Or if I see a patrol with an APC on the streets of a red zone, when I duck behind cover and prep an exlposive strapped to an RC car, suddenly when I drive it to their location, they're totally gone... not driven away, just gone.
The story wasn't great, but I enjoyed it. All in all I will be giving it another go in a few patches time on harder difficulty. Probably working to make 100% completion.

GET THIS GAME IF EITHER:

I have always loved movies like Red Dawn and games like World in Conflict and Freedom Fighter that use an invaded/occupied USA as a narrative backdrop. Homefront was decent enough for me to play all the way through a few times and dive into the multiplayer for a bit. I say all of this to emphasize how much I really wanted this game to be good.
It just wasn't. I would only recommend buying this game for more than $20 when it goes on sale some time in the future.
1) Technical Flaws: While some of these may be fixed in the future this game has serious technical flaws.  More than any other game I've bought recently.  This includes even alpha games. There were serious graphical errors and huge immersion breaking flaws in the AI and numerous scripted events fail in remarkably noticable ways.
2) A flawed implementation of a Far Cry 3 Rip off: Numerous aspects of core-gameplay will be instantly recognizable as a direct rip off of Far Cry 3's approach to open world FPS.  Even the loot of bodies looks and functions in the same way. That in itself isn't a bad thing; I love FC3's style and Ubi's trying to milk that for all its worth with FC4 and FCPrimal. But the implementation of this style in this game could have been amazing but it just didn't quite cut it. The city sections were far more limited in scope and it didn't feel so much like an open world as a series of very repetitive events. FC3 can get bland after liberating your umpteenth radio tower but this game somehow made it even worse.
3) Horrible Weapons System: It might sound cool to have one weapon that can switch on the fly into other weapons but in practice I found this was severely limiting and underwhelming.  Within a short time I had unlocked every weapon in the game and none of them were thrilling to use. This might seem nitpicky, but in an FPS your weapons are a huge part part of your experience and I didn't like how it was implemented at all. It was novel, but it wasn't good.

The hype was real for this game, at least for me that is. Love it or hate it, but I was a huge fan of the first Homefront. Even though the gameplay was a bit generic, I did enjoy the setting and world it brought you into. So naturally when watching trailers for the next installment, Homefront: The Revolution, I was pretty hyped. I preordered it and was happy to finally get my hands on it. Then I played it.
I first noticed small changes in the story and the opening "cinematic" seemed kind of cheesy at times with its obvious people standing in front of a green screen but it was fine. Opening scenes were pretty cool, I was starting to get into it, then I got to control the character. The first little city area was really nice and detailed, but I noticed some issues with animations on NPC characters and my character. For example, when I was using a tool to cut some chain on a fence, the animation was totally out of sync. Minor things, nothing to get upset about but it was noticable. So I finish this kind of tutorial mission and was on my way to the more open world section of the game. Then I notice a lot of other... Things.
First thing I noticed was this NPC character I was talking to, the most interesting thing about him is he had a twin brother who sounded exactly the same. But what do you mean? Well I guess they decided that two of the same NPCs were going to stand right next to eachother all the time. Now I understand that character models will be reused, that's normal, but when two of the same model NPC are next to eachother all the time and in a VERY small area it's just really noticable. This actually happened multiple times too, if it happened a few times sure I get it, it happens, but this was constant and just really off putting.
Now when I started entering this "open world" area, I noticed immediate frame drops. Now my PC is pretty decent, i7 4690k, GTX 970, 16GB memory, ect., and even when turning the settings on low it was still really choppy. On top of that the game just felt clunky, moving around and shooting just didn't feel fluid. I had just got done playing the new DOOM, which is a wonderful game that is just a very smooth experience, and I did feel that Homefront felt more clunky just from comparison. I know they are two different games with different play styles, but they are both FPS games and it really gives a comparison from a smooth FPS, to a clunky FPS.
Something to mention is the graphics. I'm not too picky about the way a game looks, but really this game did not look very good for something coming out in 2016 on CryEngine, even on the highest settings. They are not bad, the graphics just seemed a bit outdated. Now some areas of the game look really nice, for example the city areas. They can be very detailed, and look especially good durning night time with some weather effects like rain. However there are lots of areas that just look bland and have very poor textures.
One thing I thought was pretty innovative was the weapon system. You can unlock different customizations to turn one basic weapon into a completely different weapon, or just swapping out parts for that weapon on the spot. Like turning a crossbow into a shotgun, that's awesome. You can go in all sneaky beaky like (except sneaking is almost non-existant) and then blast someone in close quarters. Only problem is navigating the menu for swapping out weapon parts can be really clunky, and has often gotten me killed when I was trying to swap things out on the fly.
After plays a few missions the game felt kind of repeatitive, which is fine if you like games like that, I personally don't mind it. It kind of reminds me of Farcry, specifically Farcry 3. The side missions in Farcry 3 could get repeatitive, but the main story missions were actually unique and were overall fun. Homefronts side missions could get repeatitive, but the main story missions were only kind of fun... Sometimes. The biggest problem I had was when you entered a new city area and you had to "raise morale" by doing stuff that the KPA (Bad guys) didn't like. The game just slowed to a crawl. I was SO BORED at this part and it took what seemed like forever to even finish the mission.
At this point the game was running terribly with choppy frames and clunky gameplay, I was bored out of my mind, the teammates I recruited were all the same NPC model, and the game looked very subpar. I'm pretty disappointed, and this is where I stopped playing. Now I know this game went through development hell and that heavy affected the way this project turned out, but these things still cannot be overlooked. I wish I had played a bit more before writing this review, especially since this is only touching on the single player experience and not the co-op, but only after a few hours in I think I've had quite a bit to talk about.
Of course this is all just my experience and opinion on things, which I know everyone cares about and values on the internet, but I hope my insight has given you some useful information about Homefront: The Revolution. I strongly recommend watching some gameplay video of both the story and coop mode and reading more before you decide to purchase to see if this game is reight for you.

I have over 600 games in my Steam account, and the vast majority of them are still unplayed. So now I'm dedicating an hour to each of these games and writing a series of One Hour Reviews. An hour isn't very long to judge a game on, so think of this as more of a first impression, and take this review in the spirit in which it's given. Be sure to read other reviews from players who have spent more time in the game.
One Hour Reviews #47 - Dino D-Day
This is such a strange concept.  I can't even imagine where the developers came up with this idea of mixing Axis vs. Allies with dinosaurs.  What's even more strange is that this fusion somehow works.
Playing the humans is much like you'd expect from a class based shooter, which choices like playing a medic, a sniper, or an assault type class.  The dinosaurs change things up by replacing weapons (for the most part, a few dinos still have mounted guns) with abilities like melee attacks or spitting poison.
One thing I noticed though the distribution isn't exactly even.  The story (such as it is) has the Axis team responsible for bringing back the dinosaurs, so that side has virtually all of the dinos to choose from, while the Allies have only one dino (liberated from the other side).
The game offers a variety of game types, which I noticed would change based on the map I selected.  The game comes with a decent number of maps to start with, and I also saw an option for loading custom maps.  Every map seemed to have the option for deathmatch, and capture the flag was another common option.  Deathmatch plays just like I expect it would.  Capture the flag looked pretty simplistic, there were only 3 flags to capture on the level I played.  I saw where a few maps had an objective based game type, but I didn't have time to check this out in my first hour of play.  Same goes for a deathmatch variant with T-Rexes.
This is definitely one of those games that is really hard to evaluate on just an hour of play, but I had a lot of fun trying out everything.
It is possible to play singleplayer with bots if thats your thing.  The bots have a difficulty level that you can select.  But obviously the real intent of this game is to play multiplayer.   There isn't any real matchmaking going on here, you just have a basic server select, and from there you can pick a side.  There didn't seem to be a huge number of people playing, but I also had no trouble finding an active server to hop into.
Presentation wise the graphics are fine, but you aren't going to be blown away by anything.  It does have the typical options you'd expect like changing resolution, playing in a window (bordered or borderless) or fullscreen, and various other options as well.
I can't give this game anywhere near a complete review with only an hour in, but I had a lot of fun in my first hour.  And for only $9.99, it looks like a good value for the variety of maps and game types you get.  I don't know that this would be a game to keep my attention for a long time, but it definitely makes for a nice alternative to the AAA shooters that are out there.

Playing through this game designers single player campaign for about twenty five hours (deathwish or hardest difficulty setting), here is a review from an individual that has played FPS and TPS for over a decade, as well as actually having played this game. The combat of this game is very strategic, visceral, and frenetic with fluid navigation (including parkouring) providing mobility and stealth options with quality graphics and a believable immersive experience utilizing Cryteks CryEngine. As this game went through about three iterations of game designers, the completed product is a testament to persistence and the ability of these game designers to bring cohesion to a game for release to the marketplace. The subgroup of areas or yellow and red zones provide the player with unique challenges and game play styles. The start of the game requires thought and some previous FPS experience, played through the first area for five hours with only the side arm. Those with negative comments of this game might not have either the patience or skill to play this type of game, intuitive strategies such as knowing when to fight or retreat is a valuable trait during game play, this is acquired as an individual moves through the game and combat encounters. Knowing trigger points as well as upgrading abilities and weapon upgrades is vital to enjoying the game. The importance of approaching this game with the perspective of just learning to survive, to become strong enough to competently engage in combat and overpower the enemy A.I. is very challenging and rewarding, as every victory brings you closer to turning the tide against the oppression of the occupying force. In game rise of the resistance as the player completes objectives empowers the player with a sense of actually affecting the game, characters, and story. The day night cycles are very well incorporated, with night scenes immersing the player in a desolate wasteland of a nearly recognizable civilization, the amount of detail is exceptional with some clever game design such as utilizing motorcycles for generating power within the game designed world to advance, searching for resistance stashes with vertical movement through city dwellings. Every component in game has a reason for its existence, this enhances the feeling that one is truly working as part of a resistant movement to regain ones liberty. Variety of locations design is remarkable with memorable landscapes and environmental design. Weapons utilities are various with unique modifications empowering the player with about fifteen unique weapons, each upgradable and customizable for specific scenarios, including the clever utilization of weapons delivery via Remote control vehicle. Gear upgrades are very valuable, acquired through looting environmental objects and disenfranchised enemy A.I.. Pacing is important for enjoying this game, as well as a sense of awareness of your surroundings, and understanding how to effectively implement the various strategy exploits that the game designers have designed into the game world. Such as the resistances schematics throughout the resistance strongholds describing these advantages over the occupying enemy force, that these NPC have lived through this enemy occupation, and mainly in game cut scenes, all this increases the sense of immersion with this game world. The ability to travel through the world with a motorcycle adds for some exhilarating experiences, or the option to recruit up to four comrades to fight through specific objectives is vital, as these recruits actually fight with you, where some games these crew are a distraction to absorb bullets. Everyone that enjoys a quality FPS gaming experience will find much to enjoy with this game. Thank You and much appreciation to these game designers and everyone that had the determination and perseverance to bring this game to the marketplace, Good Work.

I really can't say much about this game other than... wow. Well done, Fullbright. Well done.
The game starts you off as a girl who comes home after studying abroad for a year in Europe. When you come home to an old house that is claimed to be haunted, you find that you're alone, after midnight, in the midst of a raging storm. Better than the original for mostly core game reasons: the camera is more fluid, mouse response is better, (pc) controls are better suited to using both hands in combat, dual wielding is a more viable fighting style now (except now every third enemy or so is doing it too) and humanity and stats have more bearing on play style. In general the game feel better thought out, the devs clearly had more time to focus on how the game works.
Be warned: it IS easier than Dark Souls I, especially if you've played it. Humanity can no longer be lost on death, bosses are easier, progression is easier because of despawn and the safety margin is a lot higher because of this as well.
Negatives:
Online play is based on Soul Memory; not level. Soul Memory is the amount of souls you've collected with that particular character, regardless of how many you've lost or squandered on shiny trinkets, which means someone with the same Soul Memory may be a far higher level than you in pvp, this can actually be a bonus for cooperative play. It also means if you take the time to clear all enemies from each area you pass through (and manage to stay alive through the entire process) you could end up with a much higher Soul Memory than average in the area you're in. This means that help is likely going to be hard to find in the form of other players, luckily NPC summons are still available for most bosses (at least in early game) so you're never completely alone.
Some actions are not consistently responsive using a mouse and keyboard; namely the jump heavy attack and the guard break (tap forward + heavy attack/light attack respectively). Though this could be because of the keyboard and mouse I am using. It works some of the time consistently and other times when I boot up the game I know it's not going to work the whole time.
Positives:
A lot of positives have been mentioned in the first paragraph but here's some more:
You do not have to be the same level as your friends to play with them
You can warp from campfire to campfire straight away! no more fighting through hordes of badguys to go from undead parish to quelaag's domain.
Even if you prefer to walk, do not despair! killing off all the enemies in an area until they no longer spawn will provide you with a safe (if lonely and somewhat eerie) passage through.
You will not lose humanity by dying, just souls
Higher levels are more easily achievable as the increase in souls required for each level up is a lot slower than DaS1.
Choices made in leveling have greater consequences: feel more in control of you destiny!
Interactive environment items are there for you to cause untold mayhem with, (q to interact, spacebar for action)
All in all I highly recommend this game, unless your computer doesn't meet recommended requirements; there are quite a few visual effects in this game that are lag inducing, some aren't avoidable.
Do you like grappling? Do you like REEPERS? Do you like Alienware? BUY THIS GAME

Gone Home is what I personally believe to be the single best interactive story-rich game out there. This game holds a very dear spot in my heart, and I wish I could play it again with no knowledge of the story. However, as many have stated previously, Gone Home is certainly not for everyone. This is due to the lack of action or puzzle, the short surface-level story, and the false facade it carries throughout.
Before I start my points, I recommend off the bat that if you think this game is for you, buy it now and don't read this. I enjoyed this game so heavily because I did not know what to expect at all, and it kept me guessing in a very genius way. To maximize your experience with this game, one must go into it with no knowledge of the atmosphere, the setting, the moral, anything. Let the game confuse you and then help you realize. However, if you still wish to read on, even at the cost of greatly lessening your experience, so be it. I will also state that I will be giving no details away about the actual story, not even who you play as. This review will, however, spoil non-story related elements of the game, such as atmosphere and interactivity. This review is dedicated to explaining how and why Gone Home is a thematic miracle, and why so many disagree.
This game has no action, violence, puzzle, anything. Anyone looking for a game of this nature will find it a complete waste of money, as is evident by the multitude of reviews explaining this. This game is focused completely on storytelling and atmosphere, both of which it does beautifully. If one wishes to experience a completely story-based experience, this is the game. I became personally attached to the characters and genuinely curious about the story and backstory. I do not personally understand why so many people complain about the lack of action or interactivity. First, the interactivity is there, just in another form than is commonly seen in gaming. This game will make you examine every letter, every slip of paper, every interactive object in the game to deduce on your own what happened. Second, the developers clearly state that this is a story game, with no puzzles or action. This deduction aspect of the game is key, as it refutes the second common argument, the story is too short.
This is a frequent complaint. The basis here is that, on the surface, the game is indeed short. However, it is all the elements of the game that go beyond the main story that give this game its true story. One can rush the main storyline and be fed the answers and take nothing away from this game, or they can take the time to observe their surroundings and use deduction to go so much farther. This is where the game truly shines. Only a very, very small portion of the story is given to you, the rest is left scattered around this old house for you to piece together. And it truly is no small task. As I only have 3.5 hours in this game at the time of the review, I cannot claim to have finished this. There is so much story I do not know, and have not yet found. So many sticky notes on folders and misplaced business cards to view. So many small pieces to fit together to find out what truly happened to both this home, and the people, living and dead, who live there. This is the reason to play the game again, and again, and again.
Finally, the facade the game carries is another common complaint. Stop here, please, and just play the game. This element is a very major part of the game and what I will say will take away a large chunk of enjoyment from the game. No? Fine, up to you. This facade that I speak of is the facade of horror. Everything in this game makes you afraid and on edge. Every corner you turn, every dark room you enter, makes you think something will pop out with a loud noise. Nothing will. This game was scary, and tense. Yet the developers are serious when they say it is simply story. No jump scares here. Many people felt betrayed by this, expecting a horror game. In a way, this is valid. You do spend the entire game thinking you are playing horror, yet you aren't. This was genius, absolutely genius. This atmosphere of the supernatural is the way the developers play on your nature as a gamer. The mind runs free and starts creating and telling a story that isn't there. It also takes the boredom away that would occur walking around a virtual house for 3 hours. I myself jumped probably two feet in the air at a poorly timed strike of lightning. Do not go into this game expecting to be jump scared or run away from monsters, you won't.
In conclusion, this game will not scare you, make you fight, run, solve puzzles, do twisty parkour jumps, or win QuickTime events. It will however, make you feel and make you think. I recommend anyone who thinks it sounds interesting or is tempted to try it, to do so. This game is one of my all-time favorites, and one I will come back to for a long time.

Hmm, Gone Home...what to say about this, um, title...
Well, up front, I enjoyed the time I spent with it.  However, this, to me at least, isn't even in the running for game of the year, as I have trouble even qualifying it as a game.  It leaves me to wonder why so many places gushed over what it offered
.
I'll grant it maybe most original story in a.....a game, I guess, as it covers a topic not commonly seen in the medium, but.....game of the year?
I just can't agree.
I don't think Gone Home actually does anything unique or revolutionary for being something that earns it such an award.  Silent Hill 2 did many of the things Gone Home does with far FAR better results over a decade earlier.  Slowly revealing to us the story details of a troubled protagonist as you travel deeper and deeper into the world, delivering on its atmosphere and tone with a deeply unsettling setting and characters.  Hell, it had mechanics and challenges that served to
the game's narrative.
If Gone Home earned game of the year, I feel I should have found something that makes it stand out
, but it does little in its design and almost nothing mechanically.  In some way, I feel like I'm experiencing a lesser version of Amnesia...
But it is certainly an experience.  It has a well realized atmosphere to it, there is a sense of foreboding when you enter into the house and start to unravel the events that took place during your absence.  The way in which Gone Home presents itself
well done, all the objects strewn about the house give you a real feeling of time and place, background music sets up the mood in an effective manner, and the voice acting was also done well where I could get a good sense of the character both on the surface and internally.
I started this with no expectations, little information, and was completely oblivious to what it was I would end up with when I began.  I just let Gone Home show me what it was and let it do what it did, and maybe because of that I was able to enjoy it.  I don't want to say too much more about it, as the less you know about it going into it, the better the experience will be.
But I can't recommend paying more than $5 for it, $20 is just way too high for what you'll ultimately get from it.

Dino D-Day a game about an alternative timeline where Hitler has unlocked the formula to recreate dinosaurs, and did you guess at what time period it is set ? Yep, Second World War. The most astouding thing here is that the game is being based on a pretty serious theme, but somehow changes it up, and makes it actually funny.
Graphics - Not really revolutionary, but they are quite enough to enjoy the game. Bonus points on making it look good and to run on almost every configuration possible, from the oldest to the high-end. 7/10
Music - A mechanic you won't be hearing that often, because it is mostly in the main menu and almost nowhere else. 6/10
Cinematics - None
Story - Given through the tips while you are loading, from the simple gameplay tips to the on point date and exactly who and what happened. Anything that you may know about the Second World War, won't be helping you here, as I already stated and it is written in the description by the Devs, this is an alternative timeline. 9/10
Content  - A wide variety of maps and weapons, also the characters you play as, all of them have a unique personality, some are more hard headed and some are cracking jokes, because why not. Also the game has a DlC which I have not yet bought, will probably try it out in the future. And lastly a comic issue, which I have also not yet bought. 7/10
Controls - Pretty fluent, if you have played any other team-based shooter, for instance Team Fortress or overall any source engine game, because they all run the same, mostly. Overall if you have played Team Fortress before, nothing new here, just a sprint button. 8/10
Gameplay - Great and fluent, there are the normal people, such as campers, snipers, and the people with the rocket launcher or the explosive based ammo. Those things cannot be helped, also specifically for this game, there are those little dinosaurs who just can't be shot at (Im bad). As the saying goes ''if you can't beat them, join them'' only then will you be having fun. 9/10
Another thing about the game is that it is pretty rage inducing, mostly because of exploited game mechanincs. But overall the game does more things good rather than bad. There is still plenty of the community left, but the years have surely shown, as the ageing game mechanincs and the graphical desings are being overshadowed by newer games. Still Dino D-Day was something unexpected, but certainly something worth your time.
Final Score: 7.6/10

I'm honestly a little confused about this game. Gone Home got a lot of media attention, so I figured it must be a good game, especially since it is short. The masses let me down in this case.
At the start of the game, I actually thought Gone Home was going to be a horror game. It's not, so you can breathe easy. At several points I still expected the story to take a dark turn. That might actually have been better than the ill-fitting ending that is given. It's not that the ending is bad, it is just too far removed from the tone set at the beginning of the game. The gameplay is at best unoriginal, and at worst boring. That'd be fine if the story was amazing, but it's not. The story, like the gameplay, ranges from unoriginal to boring. Yes, technically, if you combine all the game elements, this is a unique adventure game. But unique does not equate to good.
If you must play this for yourself to appease your pop culture sensibilities, it is a short enough game to do so. But if you can ignore the bizarre amount of hype around Gone Home, pass on it. You're not missing much.

The game takes up a lot of space on your hard drive. If you have a powerful PC that wouldn't be a problem, but for a casual gamer you may have to delete a couple of games. The launcher is also broken at times crashing during updating sequences. However once the game finally worked, the load times were horrible. During the time it took to load the first mission, I was able to check my Instagram, and brush my teeth. The tutorial was decent with controls that may be confusing at first, but you will get used to quickly. After the tutorial was when thing really went downhill. I started out in a easy lobby, and started the mission. The first thing that happened was my teammates ran off without me, making it impossible to do some of the tasks that require two people. Then the next thing I know, I was killed by I bad guy. The AI in this game is VERY stupid, but if you are by yourself with only a sniper rifle, it is hard to take down mass amounts of enemies. The game then prompted me to pay a "coin" to revive myself, because of course, there is no medic on my team. I then clicked yes, thinking I had some, but NOPE. I needed to pay money to get them. If you want a fun and competive FREE fps. I recommend WARMODE. Don't bother with all the microtransactions.

Verdun is amazing, although it has mediocre graphics and sound - the gameplay is amazing. As what I believe to be the only WWI FPS, Verdun does not need a competitor, unless you want a more arcadey feel, like a Call of Duty title. The gameplay is very interesting, it covers a small sector of a front, with a max of 32 players. Different squads have different weapons and abilities and are able to voice chat with each other. Some can call in gas while others call in recon planes. It is skill based and there are no OP unlocks, just weapons good if used right. A shovel or knife is great at clearing out a trench, while a machine gun can kill an entire wave of retreating enemies. One of my only complaints on the actual quality of the gameplay is how lax the balancing system is. It asks "can you please switch to Axis/Entente powers to make the game balanced" If nobody wants to switch it will stay that way the entire game. If it were up to me the squad with the fewest people on the overpowered team should be disbanded and sent to the other team. Another problem is the amount of U.S. squads, there needs to be a limit, because everyone spams the U.S. Marines, even though they're terrible and have nothing good, because they're American. Either remove one or both of the U.S. Squads or put in a system to limit the amount of U.S. squads. The British, French and Belgians won the war, not the U.S.
Overall, Verdun is a solid game with great gameplay, but with  squad and team balance issues and the graphics and sound are meh. I'd give it a 7.5/10 Definitely buy this if you enjoy WWI or want something a little new to play.

However, if you have ~3 hours to devote to navigating a well developed environment, with tons of details and a good story to tell, then this may be for you.

If you don't appreciate long movies, romantic movies, or progressive trends in video game development, this game is not for you.

Pros:
+Scary
Some will agree some will disagree.  This is why I personally believe it is scary. This game preys on one of your most natural instincts as a human when you are faced with a danger, the ability to either fight it or run from it. This game stripped me of my most sensible solutions to deal with this danger and my only option left was to just sit and delay the inevitable. Coupled with the fact that this game can create REALLY intense situations I find that all added up to create massive amounts of fear.
+The story telling
I really have to give props to Scott for this. The way the story is told is completely mysterious, and a little creepy and eerie. I find that the story telling is PERFECT for an enviroment like this. Its fun to swap theories or interpretations of the story with your peers (at least to me.)
Cons-
Boring
Note I did not find the game to be boring, however I could certainly see how someone else may find it boring.
The scares wear off after a while.
As the difficulty goes up it tends to become more hectic rather than scary. This is my personal suggestion on how to fix this. Rather than just making the animatronics faster maybe give them some abilities that get activated as their AI level goes up. Such as maybe night 1 bonnie is just basic Night 2 Maybe his pathing gets expanded/he hides better Night 3 he may be able to commence a mini jumpscare attacking the camera and taking it out for the rest of the night. Night 4/5 he can charge to your office and you have to find him on the camera and shine the flashlight on him to stop him in his tracks (Although i'm not sure if the camera flashlight feature will be in FNAF 3 and this last idea sounds like someone suited for Foxy.)
Overall If you really just enjoy action games or have seen FNAF 2's tricks before then I would say give this one a pass. Otherwise I would recommend this game immensely.

Not much of an improvement over the old version of DX9 Dark Souls II. Looked about the same when you used a SweetFX or GeDoSaTo with the older one. DX9->DX11 just feels lazy, and pretty much none of the DX11 specific effects exist. Light shafts look unbelievably cheap and the lighting itself is barely an improvement, if at all. Feels like they just held out on releasing the intended version, just to nickel and dime the franchise in every way possible. Hope they don't pull this with Dark Souls 3. Shame they charged actual money for this, since I've seen other companies do more for free.
Dark Souls II is definitely the weakest of all the "Souls" series games. Combat is imbalanced, since wearing heavy armor does not provide much benefits, due to poise being so useless. It's still the same wobbly and slippery, slow as hell combat it was in the older version, so there's not a lot of improvement. If only Soul Memory was removed, then I'd rate the online experience tolerable, but now it's just not worth the effort.
PvE is fine, and that's where I'd recommend you spend most of your time in. Lots of new summonable NPC's have been added, which is a nice touch to make boss encounters easier, but still provide the pseudo-Online experience the game is known for. Bell Keeper covenant is also probably one of the best ways to interest players into dabbling with PvP, however once you get to Rank 2 covenant, and get the "Hidden Weapon" sorcery for one of the achievements, it's not really worth it to stay any longer, since as I already mentioned, the PvP is really lacking to be engaging. No where near as interesting as the first Dark Souls was.
DLC's are also a mixed bag. While they had some interesting moments, most of them were trying to get through a level, jam packed with enemies with very little weaknesses, that are often thrown at you in hordes. Dark Souls is not build around fighting multiple opponents, and that's what you'll mostly be facing - multiple dudes in armor. Dudes in armor and they often feel like they were copy pasted with only a different color. DLC's frustrated me more, because they feel like it was just padded with artificial difficulty, so you wouldn't be able to just spend an hour on it.
As a dedicated "Souls" series fan, it just pains me to say that this game is mostly average. Level design is very flat and uninspired, enemies are mostly just guys in armor and the inflated difficulty, just because they didn't know how to make the game both challenging and interesting shows what happens when the mastermind behind the "Souls" series is not behind the project.
As I already said before, only get this if you don't already own Dark Souls II or any of it's DLC's. Aside from the Old Iron Crown, which is a ridiculously good armor piece, the DLC just feels really lacking even in the items and spells that you get. Honestly, you probably should just wait for Dark Souls 3.

To be fair, the campaign is no worse than the annual CoD - less flashy explosions, but a slightly more original theme but then again you probably wouldn't buy CoD for the singleplayer.
Multiplayer is dead, which is just as well because it's just a generic cheap "farm missions for cash to buy loot crates" Skinner box.
I didn't encounter any massive bugs other than the fact that the photographic quest didn't progress (blindly stabbing the target did work, but frankly that entire mission should have been scrapped given how utterly inadequate controls are - e.g. you cannot stand up while holding the phone, so designing a mission around holding the phone is utterly stupid).
Performance wise, FPS seemed to hover around 50 (with a few drops, including one brief case of FPS dropping 5 for no apparent reason in the prison area) in a R390, i7-6700k, 16GB VM i.e. it runs a lot worse than better looking games like Fallout 4.
IMO it is better than the base game, but I also only paid $10 for the upgrade which saved me a bit, so I get why others who paid for the DLC on release may be upset.

This game is okay; not bad, but not great either.
I loved the original
and excitedly bought the "vanilla" version of the second not long after its Steam release.  At first, I enjoyed the co-op, but soon found myself baffled and enraged by the incredibly fast rate of equipment breakage, the finite nature of humanity-endowing figurines, and the relative dearth of titanite.  The story was pretty uninteresting too.  I got sick of the game and dropped it soon after I reached Drangleic castle.
Then
came out, and it claimed to rebalance a few aspects of the original.  I wasn't in the least interested, but then I started seeing these incredible vids for
and did some googling; during my DS3-oriented searches, I incidentally discovered that the horrible rate of weapon breakage in DS2 had been a bug, now-fixed, a few story features had been added to SotFS, and that the levels had been redesigned to make them less of a chore.  Full of anticipation for the Miyazaki-helmed third game, I elected to give this new version  of the second a go.  Am I easily influenced?  Sometimes . . .
This time, I actually did finish the main game and completely cleaned out two of the DLC areas, skipping the last half of Ivory King.  Was I blown away this time?  I enjoyed this version more, but the answer is a resounding "nope!"  The story remains fragmentary and flat; SotFS fails to achieve the mythopoeic majesty of the first first game, in which enough hints were dropped to imbue the huge lacunae with a sense of awe-inspiring mystery.  The levels themselves look nice, perhaps slightly nicer than before, but as ever they are boxy and staid when set alongside DS1's rather more organic levels.  Also, the transitions between them are jarringly abrupt.  The levels
a little bit smoother to proceed through now, as some of the most unfairly frustrating aspects have been toned down a bit, but it's too bad that most of them are still about as fun as homework.  There are a lot more humanity figurines in this game, and that's good; they are still finite though, and that's lame.  For an unequivocal good, there's more titanite of various types than you can shake a stick at -- you can experiment with gear to your heart's content and that's just what I did.  The combat itself wasn't terrible, but I hated the fact that too many fully upgraded weapons are worse than useless.  A handful of the boss fights (the Demon of Song and Sinh the Slumbering Dragon come to mind) are quite satisfying, but most of them are pretty interchangeable.  The problem with this game is that it's just "okay."  Where's the sense of discovery?  Where's the impeccable art direction?  Where's the finely balanced combat in which a fully upgraded weapon of
, including a simple broadsword, can do the job and then some?
DS2, despite the beneficial changes, unfortunately remains what DS1 never was:  a fairly run-of-the-mill slog with a few high points.  It lacks the deep soul that imbued the first game with its power.  There's technique, but no vision.  Adequacy, but no truly thoughtful design.  If you have to have some version of DS2 in your life, go with this version; it has some "quality of life" tweaks and includes all the DLC areas.  It will run at 60 fps on a potato, as my rig (AMD Athlon Quad Core, 6 gigs RAM, GTX 660) will attest -- and with load times as brief as they are, the technical achievement is considerable.
(I don't rue my single playthrough, but people who play this game over and over again must be
Is fighting increasingly over-powered AI in New Game+ or invading and janking some poor, PVE-oriented sap really that much of a riot?)

Then you have the zone capturing to get on with slowly freeing the area from the KPA and if the first zone is anything to go by you might as well not bother because it will get rid of the enemies and well... there's just no point, weapons and equipment all seem tied to the main mission regardless of these zones.
Yellow zones play out a little differently as you can pretend you're a civilian in these areas and supposedly blend in with  the crowd, yet for some reason every guard instantly recognises you like you're some big shot rebel guy even after only one mission. When you're spotted in these zones you'll get an alert status meaning every guard in the area will start shooting you and actively persue you, so you'll have to hide as endless waves of enemies will spawn until the alert status has passed.
The multiplayer is kind of fun for a bit but I only really got a few hours out of it as it only has like 5 missions, you can get new gear and such from supply boxes which just give you random crap, as far as I can tell you just need to buy weapon packs until you have the weapon you want but it really is pointless because there's a really limited amount of missions to use them on.
Well to sum it up I'm just really dissapointed, I loved the first game as it felt like you were actually helping america fight for freedom in this one it just feels like you're mindlessly following the star shaped objective marker.

If you get this game expecting Call of Duty or Battlefield, turn back now. This is not a run and gun type of game. Sure, sometimes you will find yourself running into an enemy trench with your guns blazing, but not often. Employ tactics one use in most modern shooters and you will find youself dead very quickly. And even if you are super careful, you will die a lot.
You will move carefully between cover, utilizing shellholes and other defenses to make your way to the enemy trench. Any second you might be seen and shot at. You are just meters from the enemy trench, and you are preparing to make your charge in an attempt to help capture it. A shot flies past you and you duck behind the nearest cover, cowering as bullets fly overhead as the enemy tries to nail you. In a few seconds the bullets stop, and you rise again to rush into the trench. This is it, this is your chance to kill some enemies and establish a foothold for your teammates to exploit.
You rush into the trench with your rifle at the ready and are swiftly cut down by an enemy who was lying in wait. You respawn, and you get to do it all over again!
It actually is a really fun game. This isnt a game about k/d ratios. Its about teamwork. Without teamwork, your team will likely lose. Thankfully, unlike some other games, this game rewards teamwork. For example, each squad has a team leader. The rest of the team can spawn on him, so a good team leader will sneak up close to the enemy trench and then hide, letting his squad spawn in really close to the frontlines. He wont rush in guns blazing, because he will likely die quickly and not be there for his squad to spawn in on him.
If you are willing to put the team and the objective above your own stats, you will love this game. If not, I suggest moving on.

I guess i was lucky i came into this game without any expectation. As i grew up as a teenager in the 90ies, this game resonated with me. Confusing at first, i actually liked the story and the atmosphere of it. True, it's nothing exceptional, but it's for once a realistic story without game-typical concessions. No zombies, no horror, no parapsychological, no hero's journey, no fantasy, scifi or aliens. Just a story of humans, told in a convincing, non-pretentious way.
You really have to take a quiet evening to enjoy this game. It hardly develops its story in hurry. It's not for the average gamer expecting to be entertained or logically challenged. Are you a sorta voyeuristic discoverer? Do you like to go through other people's stuff? Do you enjoy drama novels? Do you have a quirk for the 90ies? Is reading several pages of various style no problem for you? Are you a girl? If you can answer several of those questions with "yes", you might like this game.
Then again: Is it worth 20 bucks? No. It's seriously too short to be priced that way. Is it the revelation the critics make it? No either. It's a well crafted story experience, not more. Is it the "walking sim" self-called gamers make it out to be? Absolutely not. My recommendation is: Get it in a deal, i know i'll get it for my sister on the next one.

I was reminded of this game about 12 hours before it came out. I purchased in haste after reading a brief overview of the Game, and as soon as I saw "Crytek Engine" I made my purchase.
I regret that decision. It's not the worst game in the world, but the fact they are charging $60 for this unfinished, buggy title is a bit dissapointing.
Graphically, not terrible, but it performs poorly even on sufficient hardware. They are supposedly supposed to improve this with upcoming patches, if so then this game is not bad in the Graphics department, but a lot of Texture work is subpar. You can tell they cut a lot of corners on this to get it out there. Lighting and overall "look" still trump CoD IMO, which still looks like the first Modern Warfare with better Textures and lighting. That series also suffers from performance issues.
Gameplay is very basic. A lot of control point missions, nothing fancy. AI isn't great. In the end you basically run around shooting stuff, taking over bases. If that's enough to keep you occupied then you aren't going to find much else to do. It's the same stuff they've been putting out for 10+ years. Also, there's 1 vehicle, and it's a Dirt Bike. Nothing special, it gets you from Point A to Point B.
I'm not going to hold a grudge against the Developers, as they were put in a crappy situation. They may still redeem themselves with future Addons\Updates, but at this time I can't recommend this game at it's current price point. I just purchased the Original Ghost Recon Series for $10 on sale and I will probably get a lot more play time from those games.
-Justin

I would just like to say before I start with the review is that Toy Chica scares the absolute hell out of me.
Scott Cawthon, you've done it again. You single-handedly managed to create a series so popular that people start pumping out videos, theories, images, and GIFs within days of its release. And now you've come out with a sequel to it (prequel in terms of story), with a third game already on the way.
As if Five Nights at Freddy's wasn't terrifying enough, Five Nights at Freddy's 2 takes it to a whole new level. Eleven  animatronics, new mechanics, zero doors, twice as hard. Along with the old animatronics from the first game (including Golden Freddy), there are 6 new animatronics to keep an eye on. And when they all start coming for you, things get incredibly hard, especially when the old trio of Bonnie, Chica and Freddy get into the mix. If you don't put the mask down the minute they get into your room, you're dead. Not to mention, there's a music box that you need to keep wound up in order to keep one of the animatronics, known as the Puppet, from coming after you. Doing that requires you to pull up the camera and wind up the music box remotely. As a result, it pulls you away from the safety of the Freddy mask. While I do feel that the game is unnecessarily hard, it's hard to say how else the game should have been made so that it wasn't so punishing.
All that aside, I would give this a 9/10, with my only complaint being the punishing difficulty.

At this point, I think you've already decided on whether or not to play this game. If your first response to that is "it's not a game," then I guess there's no point in continuing reading, but I just have to say kudos to Fullbright for doing a such a damn fine job with almost nothing at all. For something that has so little in the terms of gameplay and the like, there is so much heart and passion in Gone Home that I can't help but acknowledge that it has so many wonderful little gems of story telling done better than most films and books I've read. The narrative is spot on, and the smaller narratives kept me around, even though I already knew where the main one was going.
Caring about secondary characters is always a struggle in videogames, and their attempts at making us care about them has always been laughable to a certain extent. Little did I know that I would come to care about all of the characters introduced in this little narrative, even with the fact I never met them. Spoiler-free: you will be greatly rewarded for reading all the random memos found throughout the house. World building done at its best, and since the entire game is world building, I would love to see some bigger developers learn from the masterful construction of story done here by only a few individuals. You can go through the entire game without picking up on the stories of the mom and dad, but trust me when I say you'll be missing out on the best bits this game has to offer. To see the house open up, and with it, the inhabitants' hearts, I found myself appreciating the level design more than any game that has actual levels. Aimless this rant may be, but seriously: I remember every detail of every room, where as the game I completed before this barely stuck in my memory. Truly, this game has some wonderful design and simply from that perspective, it is a game that should be well remembered after finishing. This isn't pretentious as the likes of Dear Esther is, so while they may be both walking simulators, I feel I appreciated Gone Home immensely more than any other of it's kind for the simplicity of it's heart and messages.
I think I've said what hundreds of others have already, but this game is a remarkable example in how this medium can make something so unremarkable as a house and a love story so engaging. Also, fufilling my odd fantasy of rooting through people's stuff has been greatly appeased, so there's that. Length is a common complaint to have, but seriously, if you know what you're getting into, and you know what to expect, this game is at the very least worth it on sale. Either that, or grub it off a friend. Is that so much to ask for a genuinely great story?

There's only so much to say without spoiling the game, but it's worth a go. Gone Home does a
job building a cast of characters never actually physically encountered. Every little detail, Every object you can pick up, tells these peoples' stories. One character in particular, the sister, is so well characterized that despite having never seen her, I feel I know and sympathize with her more than a most characters in most games. Really, Gone Home is a game that simply would not work in any other medium.
You are not here to save the world, or even your family, you're just trying to figure out what happened to your family, and in the process patch together the events of the years you were gone. You don't shoot or cut or bludgeon, you just look. It's a better mystery game than most actual mystery games, because nobody helps you, you just read, listen, and discover entirely on your own.
The game is short, but that works in its favor; the content here is perfect for its length, and making it longer or shorter would have worsened the game. If the price seems too much for you, then get it on sale, because it's worth playing yourself. Basically, it's the gaming equivalent of a well-made short story, which is itself pretty remarkable. 10/10.

Verdun is a wonderfully addictive game. The trench warfare is authentic, the environments feel real, and the experience is always enjoyable. No matter how well you do in a match, it is entertaining enough to run around in the trenches of World War One. I could easily say Verdun is one of my favorite games.
Unfortunately, the game is far from perfect. The amount of glitches and inconveniences greatly diminishes the experience. Trying to join a friend's squad can sometimes send you to a seperate match. Trying to make your own squad can kick you out of the game. The leveling system is complicated and there is no explanation for it. It is hard to figure out and remember which squad does what without reading a few extensive guides. While charing across no-man's land you sometimes teleport around, ruining your advance. Some parts of the maps are angled awkwardly, causing clunky movement. The "hold your breath" system is pretty much the only way to aim well, but it hardly lasts long, is loud and annoying, and makes it harder to aim when you're done. The map rotation can send you on an endless loop of Champagne and Douaumont and never include certain maps like Flanders.
There are so many other downsides that I didn't name here, and they all become very annoying when trying to play successfully. With more improvement, and I sure hope the devs get on it, this game could be even better than it already is.

As the day dawns, you sneak a peek out of your (relatively) safe trench, to look at your hated enemy across no man's land. You feel the hate for your enemy surge as you remember all of your friends and comrades who have fallen in the battles of the past, senselessly butchered for trying to take the enemy trenches, only to fail miserably and be forced to retreat. You have grim satisfaction, knowing you have avenged them by slaughtering your enemies as they tried to overtake you, only to have the same shameful conclusion forced upon them by your hand. As the whistle blows, and you are forced to run the gauntlet once more, you scream at the top of your lungs, "I fear no enemy, for my comrades are my strength! I fear not death, for you guys can't aim worth a crap!" You evade mortars and artillery, and crawl across the no man's land, taking shots as you go to weed out defenders. You put on a gas mask to avoid suffocation at the hands of chlorine gas, which also doubles as cover for you to sneak up on the trenches. You make it to the enemy trenches, and begin the slow process of rooting them out by bayonett, bullet, and grenade. As more of your comrades enter the trench to aid you, you are stabbed by the hated enemy. As you slowly die in the trench, your NCO comes up to you and says, "Our sacrifices were not in vain, for we have taken this trench!" And to this you reply, "But we must keep this trench before it will be truly ours." And with this you die, not knowing that tomorrow the hated enemy will take back this trench, and the tens of thousands who died on both sides for this one trench were all in vain. You will die not knowing that across the Western front, the same conclusion is the order of the day, and decisive victories are few and far between for either side.

Great concept, but horrible execution. As a gamer who prefers great story, atmosphere, and/or characters to gunplay, Gone Home caught my attention for precisely that: making gameplay as bare-bones as possible to make you focus on what was happening in the story instead of what was attacking you. The downside to this approach is the story must step up to the plate and be great to compensate for the lack of combat. And that is where Gone Home falls flat on its face.
It initially sets itself up as a kind of murder mystery, since you come to your house, alone, with no one there at all during a storm. The reason no one is there is just poor timing on the player character's part, so that mystery is a bit of a let down. Beneath that, there's uncovering the family dynamic and secrets that have been accumulating since you left. And, quite frankly, that's almost as boring as why everyone was gone. Finding the clues is exciting at first, but that's nothing but a sense of achievement speaking. The clues themselves paint a picture based on stereotypes we've all heard a dozen times before in books, TV, movies, and every other medium out there. One voice throughout tries to make it better by adding emotion to it all, but trying and doing can be two very different things.
Overall, very disappointed and very confused as to why this did so well critically.

Five Night's at Freddy's does what a sequel should do in a genre and style like this. More antagonists, more things to tend to, more things to die from and more creepy easter eggs.
The positives of this game is that at first it is overwhelmingly hard to get a grip on without googling or watching videos. "How do I stop Foxy from jumping at me? Do I put on the mask?!?!?!?" you may say to your friends as you put on the Freddy head and think you're safe but oh no. You are dead. Unlike the first game, it is much harder to keep tabs on all the animatronics, especially with constantly having to wind up the music box. This game can send waves of nausea and unease upon, leaving you to jump at every single little sound, let alone the actual animatronics. The story, although filled with pages upon pages of speculation, is creepy and leaves you wondering the true story behind Freddy Fazebear's Pizza. It is a truly terrifying game.
However, all the nights are really just the same thing except with varying degrees of difficulty. Sure, more animatronics pop up on later nights, but it's just more layers to look out for. The jumpscares aren't as scary as they were on Night 1 when you're at Night 5. However, even if it stops scaring you, it becomes a stress management game and is still very, very challenging.
Pros
- Challenging and stressful
- A very sinister and creepy horror game
- A back story, although unclear, is quite disturbing and morbid
Cons
- Same gameplay, different difficulty
- Can stop scaring you
In the end, Five Night's at Freddy's 2 is definitely an heir to the first game, and I am looking forward to seeing what Five Night's at Freddy's 3 brings to the world of horror.

After playing this game for a while... It feels as if someone told this game to protect itself. It wanes and waxes as you play, ambush here, nothing there, cliff here, secret there. If you do poorly, the enemies you dispatched properly disappear, and you can continue the adventure as if you tested out of the parts you could do normally. The clothing and visual detail shines enough to make it a game that will serve as something more than just a good idea. The mechanics cater to those who will sit there and test them out.
But the problem lies with the fluidity of the game, Jumping is more tedius than fighting, falling between planks and getting blasted off ledges is actually more common than a real death, dashing forward with a bow for the first time seeing the game scroll downwards in a plummet of death. missing your jump opportunity by a hair because you didn't press the stick in time. getting stuck between enemies as you try to roll out of an ambush. And while all the pros are going to be all, git guud scrub, having a character that just steps off cliffs without even trying to stay alive is something I haven't seen since like ps1. Even the hollows hang off the side and chill there. Also, the item and spell loadout system is so mundane, running from a boss while wailing on the down button is probably some of the worst memories I've ever had in a game, as well as trying to mash out the escape branch only to see that the option is set to no for some reason... It's extremely hectic, and a smoother system would have made it a lot simpler to select items you may almost never use but still need.
After that one flaw, there's nothing wrong with the game, there's this real tomb raider type of approach where there is so much to do and get, but in your own greed, you realize you stepped over a ledge you can't go back to, and looking at the tens or hundreds of thousands of souls you have, you question your own patience thinking of if you will remember to shoot that enemy before it destroys the bridge, or that if you run ahead, four or five guys are going to whip you, OR SOMEONE WILL INVADE YOU. There are so many things that will happen, and the urge to shorten your travels or try to go somewhere with no arrows or no potions will get you killed. This is the same type of feeling you would get in the end of a cave in skyrim in the earlier levels.
The combat feels like something around  bushido blade, but flawed, hitting enemies without the proper back attack, does less damage than slapping them when they're attacking does. or when they're just plain hostile. To clarify, me power stancing and hitting an enemy does about three times more damage when they're aware of me than when not. Otherwise, combat is perfect. It's quick, unless you're surrounded, or taken by surprise, then it's hectic, it will have you running amok and hiding around corners to swig estus, and smashing two life gems for a little much needed reckless abandon. The variety and combat will have you appreciate everything more. Or wondering why they would program a zombie to run at ludicrous speed just to make an ambush situation. Combat is a staple here, and it is diverse enough to not even be trumped by games that have more fluidity to them, like dragons dogma.
I think the biggest problem though is establishing that you should always play this as if you were going to die forever. It has this monster hunter feeling where if you forget your potions or cures, you might as well just abandon the idea of moving forward, but with this heavy sense of track memory that demands you figure out how to manage with a lot less, or know when to cut your losses and not use your supposed trump card, and just come back better, or with a friend. Telling someone who has always played the hoarding type of rpg is going to lose it when they realize something they've been holding onto the entire game is gone for good, and no reload save is there to let them get that much desired redo, with all their expensive potions and buffs. Though, they are much easier to aquire than those games.
The easiest way I could describe this game, is like megaman. try to do everything you can, pick up anything worthwhile, run away from anything you can't destroy in one swoop, and then take all of those elements, and use them to beat your first boss, and after that, it's way easier than it should be because of your own efforts. Which is something I haven't seen executed this way throughout in a very long time.

Verdun is a brutal experience. The reality of trench warfare is brought to life in vivid detail, from the obliterated landscape, to the murderous modern weapons, to the disorienting gas attacks since outlawed, everything about this game feels authentic to how a real WWI front-line engagement would have been fought, and it's awesome!
Verdun abandons the mindlessness of the twitch-shooter in favor of a more tactically-minded approach. Alone, you are quite under-powered, since the sluggish weapons mean you're likely to get yourself killed if you take on the enemy alone. Only with teamwork, by multiplying your force, can you hope to overcome the enemy. Thankfully, Verdun presents players with plenty of ways to do that.
In Frontlines, the game's flagship mode, the Entente and Central powers are divided into various squads of 4. Each squad is unique and each of the 4 squad members has a unique role. Oh, and if you were thinking of picking a weapon off someone dead, forget it. You're stuck with the weapons you have. It's easy to see how players with a more competitive mindset could take advantage of the potential strengths of various squads to create a strong all-around force.
All of that would be useless if the game mode weren't as well designed as it is. You will attack the enemy line, then hold it or fall back depending on the outcome. The attack will then be stalled until the enemy counter attack has been dealt with. (This is enforced through automatic execution for desertion should you remain outside the boundaries the game has set for too long.) These attacks are desperate sprints across no man's land; trying to avoid rifle and machinegun fire. Defense can be equally terrifying should smoke or gas cloud your vision, making it almost impossible to distinguish friend from foe in the trench, (though I will criticize the lack of friendly fire, which would have made these moments feel more tense.) It's not uncommon for matches to end in a draw. Overcoming an enemy position and holding it can be difficult indeed.
As for the other modes, there is a squad defense mode where a player squad fights off endless waves of progressively stronger bot attackers, in a way that invokes my memories of Call of Duty Zombies, but without turning the enemy into bullet sponges. Players can take more hits here without dying, and with only 4 players, the battles have much less lag relative to Verdun's massive 16v16 multiplayer modes. (i recommend a strong internet connection to play the game on ultra graphics, the way it was intended, but lower options exist of course.)
There's also a team deathmatch mode, which I haven't played much yet as I haven't played enough of the game to unlock a more suitable set-up. (It seems to be exactly what you'd expect; getting kills is the only thing that matters, so teamwork is less important here.) Overall, it feels a lot more stale than Frontlines. Finally, there is rifle-only deathmatch, which is another great mode for newer players to get more accustomed with the most common weapon-type in the game. It is here I must say Verdun's weapon diversity is one of its strongest pros, and a breath of fresh air considering so many gamers believed for so long, (and so many still do,) creating a fun shooter experience in a setting saturated with bolt-action rifles was impossible. Let me assure you now, Verdun did it. Weapons feel unique, and useful in their own ways.
The only con I can think of is the steep learning curve. Considering the setting was largely ignored by developers, and that the war itself happened over 100 years ago, WWI seems completely alien today. It comes as no surprise that players have a hard time adjusting then. Some light reading on how the real soldiers fought could help, and there is an official guide covering the game on the Steam forum. However, there doesn't seem to be any in-game tutorial to speak of, unless you count the slideshow of sorts when I started the game for the first time that did little but explain the most basic details, and lasted less than a minute.
Even so, Verdun surpassed my expectations. I thought it would more or less be a Red Orchestra 2 clone; realistic to the detriment of fun, but I've had way more fun playing this than I did RO2. Take it from a Call of Duty fan (before CoD lost its way.) If you like historically grounded shooters, this game manages to feel both authentic and fun to play. Also, at the price, ($12.50 for me thanks to the summer discount,) your wallet will thank you for all the DLC you won't have to buy.

Pros:
+Every weapon in the game is incredebly satisfy and/or fun to use. Its hard to convey exactly why, but quickly snaping off a head shot with a rifle, or cutting down a squad with an MG is one of the most enjoyable things I've done in an FPS.  satisfying. Every weapon feels unique and different.
+The game is very authentic and historically accurate, without getting into the way of gameplay too much.
+The is tons of varety in maps and weapons
+The game is very imersive and can really capture the feeling of WWI at times, chargin fruitlessly at enemy trenches, your fellow soilders getting cut down around you as you dive for cover in a muddy ditch.
+There is a fairly high skill celling. Map knowledge of safe routes and vurnerable areas to attack is very usefull. Aiming, of course, takes skill like most other FPSs, but a new thing is how critically important cover is. In 'All Quite on the Western Front', the narrator mentions how the new recruits have a terrible eye for cover, and get killed because of it. This is one of the most important aspects of the game. It also takes a while to get use to the uniforms of the differnt factions so that you know who to shoot. There isn't friendly fire, but it still is bad to shoot everybody on sight for obvious reasons.
+Teamwork is very important. Knowing when the enemy is attacking from or where they're weak is essential, as is coordinating offencives to overwhelm the enemy in a certain area.
+Relativly short que times, at least in the US.
Cons:
-The game can seem very unballanced at times, and it can be very frustrighting. The german SMG, for example, seems very OP until you actually start using it and learning how situation it is and how difficult it is to use. Its still annoying to have one guy kill a squad rounding a corner my holding down left mouse button, however.
-A few buggs and lag spikes, nothing too major but still there.
Overall, the game is great, providing an imersive, challenging, and fun expirence,while most games can only manage one. If you can put up with having to be on the same team as Frenchmen :P.

There really should be two kinds of reviews - one for those who actually played the game, and one for those who didn't get to play it for any number of reasons. Of course you wouldn't recommend a game that doesn't work, but that unfair in the overall review percentage for those of us that actually played the game with ok framerate.
There's a number of techinal issues with this game, but so have a lot of games, and there's not (for me in any case) enough of them to ruin the game. The overall gameplay and visual style is really good, and if you like Far Cry 4 and Fallout 4, there's not really any good reason why you wouldn't like this as well (provided you can actually run the game).
The story is boring and uninteresting, but so were all the Far Cry games and I don't think the story is the point in this one. As good as no multiplayer game ever had a story, but since a story isn't expected, no one cares. This game is about looting for cash to upgrade and taking over bases and absorbing the post-apocalyptic landscape and atmosphere.
I see people dislike the game for being repetetive, but I can't really remember any open world game that wasn't.  If you like what you're playing, repetetiveness isn't negative - you just want more of the game. If you don't like the game to begin with, then of course the repetetiveness is like walking though Hell.
The game really feels like a Fallout reskin of Far Cry 4 (with a dash of Dying Light), and that's more than good enough for me, even with the technical issues and silly AI.
The mixed reviews is really unfair, it's a good game if you take it for what it is - a postapocalyptic FPS shooter with some minor RPG in it. And it even has a coop mode with characters and levels (although I haven't gotten around to that yet).  People tend to complain that the game is short. I'm well over 30 hours and I'm not finished yet, although I do everything there is to do. I also don't rush trough on easy. I recommend playing at Deathwish difficulty to make the game last and to have an actual challenge.
I'll leave you off with a 7/10 rusty nails and a warning: It's not really open world, it's just not linear; the levels are big and square instead of straight - that way you can choose your own entry points when taking out bases.
