Not as challenging, somewhat prettier (although I missed the worn-out, dull colour scheme of the previous game, Dark Souls 2 being more colourful) and, overall, about as enjoyable as DS1.
Those who played the previous Souls games will probably find DS2 a lot easier. Certain mechanics were simplified to make the game more approachable for casual players (warping between bonfires and quicker leveling being the most obvious differences).
There's one thing I found mildly disappointing. Boss encounters were not always as exciting as the ones from DS1. The design of the monsters is not as imaginative (and that's purely subjective) as in DS1. Most of the fights were also a lot easier than what I remembered from the previous game. I could beat most bosses in 1 or 2 tries, with only a handful proving more challenging. Some of them were completely harmless, easy to side-step or walk around. In some cases the difficulty was raised by filling the boss room with other mobs.
At the same time, there were several bosses that required some thinking outside the box but these appear later into the game.
All in all, the game was very enjoyable. It does have some really nice looking locations. While easier than DS1, it still proves somewhat challenging. It does have some lore that a player can immerse in.
The playthrough (in terms of plot and key taks) follows a very familiar pattern known from DS1, which feels a bit repetitive but not enough to ruin the game.
If you've played Dark Souls and liked it, you'll find this game interesting as well. If you haven't played Dark Souls or found it too hard, you'll probably like it even more.

A surprisingly good game.
I've seen a lot of complaints about poor optimization and bugs, so I'm going to assume it got some patches before I started playing, or my GTX 970 was simply able to grunt its way through all the performance issues.  I didn't notice any graphical problems.  The only bugs I encountered were a moment of dodgy clipping, but otherwise I've spent probably a good dozen hours in this without issues.
The game itself?  It's like an urban Far Cry game done right.
The mobility is a little restricted compared to other FC games (your vehicle options consist exclusively of a dirt-bike, there is no wingsuiting or parachuting or zip-lining/grappling), but the storytelling
is on point and is done with more consistency, depth, persistence and detail than the FC games.  The same holds true of nearly every mechanic they've cared to explore.
Weapon upgrades are varied, relatively-easily acquired, and plentiful enough that you don't acquire them all in the first hour.  Gear upgrades (for increased stealth, movement speed, etc) are similar.
Standard UbisoftGame(tm) 'collectible for the sake of collectible' fare is kept to a minimum, too.  Nearly everything you scout out and obtain has a purpose.
Taking strongholds has a real noticable effect on the surrounding environments, and sometimes comes with believable, understandable requirements that make sense and change it up.  The free-for-all shoot on sight red zones are basically discrete maps taking place in bombed-out industrial areas, and the residential centres ('yellow zones') involve a more visible and more involved civilian population with a heavier peace-keeper presence, and your guerrilla terrorist actions can really visibly change the entire mood and theme of these zones in subtle stages that are very impressive.
Standard stuff: Pros are gorgeous graphics, rich detail to the environments, solid mechanics, great pacing and difficulty. Cons are some janky UI quirks, eye-rollingly jingoistic story that hasn't done anything unpredictable yet, and rumours of bugs and performance issues that I personally haven't seen yet, so they're hard to take seriously.
Overall, it's a net win.  I'm really enjoying this game.

If you’ve played the game I’m sure most of you will disagree with my review and my thoughts, judging by all the reviews here on steam anyway, but I ask you to have an open mind, and see it from my point of view.
I'm not going to lie, gone home is definitely not for everyone. However; it’s all narrative and it's all experiential, and this is not a bad thing and it's certainly among the better achievements in the genre. I'd call it a visual novel, with a slight step beyond. It's either going to connect with you or it doesn't; with this kind of mechanic. For this kind of game to appeal to you and for it to work/make sense, you obviously have to care/connect with the characters and the setting, in such an experience as this one. So the game really lives and dies depending on you being able to connect to it in this way, unfortunately so. Understanding this it’s mostly understandable why many gamers can’t accept this kind of game or feel it’s too pretentious or artsy for them.
In this style of “visual novel narrative”: Gone Home get's it really right, where a similar game like Dear Esther to me gets it very wrong. A game like this has to have a good story. It has to immerse you into the world, into the experience. You need meaningful interactions, and you have to connect with the characters. It's pivotal you care about their struggles and find value in discovering every bit of drama and detail that unfolds along the way. If all these things are done well and are strong, then a game like this can work and can be more like art versus a casual bit of entertainment.

I have to draw some parallels between Dear Esther and Gone Home to really highlight where this game works. Dear Esther's narrative wasn’t cohesive and it was vague and there wasn't anything there that I could identify with, and by the end the whole experience felt rather pretentious. Added to that was the fact that the explorable space was mostly empty and had no real interactions. It was basically an on rails sightseeing tour, a very slow paced boring walk. Gone Home is the opposite in every regard. It explores topics we can all identify with: teen angst, rebellion, feeling you don't belong etc.... You feel sympathy for the main character whose life you're unravelling, and it’s a very intimate unravelling. Because of that depth of immersion I connected with this game heavily and was thoroughly and profoundly moved by the end. That’s saying something, because I really don’t share many similarities to the main character herself.
It really felt like you were in someone's house snooping through their medicine draw learning things about them, very personal things. All the strengths of the narrative aside, the whole story is set in a very nostalgic time for most of us, and the whole environment is full of extremely detailed items you can pick up and examine, going as far as having old VHS tapes with movies recorded off of TV with hand written labels; something that should be quite familiar to older gamers.

Like I said previously this is a visual novel, so no obviously it’s not an adventure game. It doesn’t have puzzles and an inventory, and it doesn’t need to either. Having those things wouldn’t add anything to Gone Home. Rather they would only serve to confuse the experience and what the game is and what its strengths are. It really needs to be more of a real life exploration. Would your own house have random puzzles or would you go around combining random items in your pocket to somehow craft other useful items, of course not.
So can I recommend this game? Yes, but can I recommend it to everyone? No, not really. I mean I wish I could, but I think the gaming community and the established gaming culture is too set in its ways to fully appreciate or understand what this is and what it’s trying to be. Not everyone will be able to fully grasp why this is still valid as a game, and that’s really understandable why that is, considering today’s games and the over focus on call of duty clones.

The game in a nutshell is you going home after a vacation and finding things not quite right. As you poke around you discover your sister was probably not quite the person you thought she was and the revelations about her and your family life are foremost the topics of intrigue. The other plots are there to set the mood, and I personally felt there didn’t need to be a major focus on them. If such revelations about your own family in your personal life would be meaningful and important to you, then this experience can and should connect with you if you let it.
After all of this if this game still interests you, I’d say give it a try. The game is rather short however and is a bit over priced I must say, but this kind of experience is a rather unique one. So how would you value a good book or a documentary styled biography on someone’s life? Most people are either going to hate this game or sit on the fence, but I loved it. I regard it as art and I look forward to more projects from the designers of this game. I hope this review and over view of my experience helped you. I'm sorry for the length, but after all the negative reviews I felt a somewhat more open minded positive view on the game was needed, and that needed a longer in depth look.

While Gone Home contains a well written, gripping undeniably moving story I honestly can not recommend this game to anyone. Why? Because in the (roughly) two hours it took me to complete the game I did little more than walk around the titular home flicking on light switches, examining objects and listening to diary recordings. The problem, in a nutshell, is that there is not really any actual game play.
While I am completely for games expanding the gaming medium and giving us deep, well crafted stories the fact that the medium is games requires there to be some actual game in there. Gone Home does not even require you to solve puzzles. Indeed, you need not examine any of the objects in the game at all to reach its end as simply wandering around the house will eventually lead you to the conclusion. Yes, if you did that you'd miss a wonderful story and some subtle back story on the characters but the point it is can be done.
Gone Home tried something different in being all about story and very minimum game play. However, this is to the game's detriment because (I would assume) even the most casual of gamer would expect some kind of game play element and Gone Home simply provides none.

Verdun is an excellent game. Set during the Great War, it manages to captivate the players in a setting which seems to have been forgotten by many player developpers over the years, probably because of a lesser interest by some of the biggest markets ( the USA for example where WW2 is better known ).
The maps are well designed. For having visiting Douaumont, the interior of the fort is good. The trench networks are excellent, at the beginning you will most likely feel lost in there and the enemy can come from anywhere. The factions are diverse, you can pick various types of squads from several nations ( Germany, the USA, France, the UK, Belgium and Canada ) and find a role that will suit your type of gameplay ( sniper, sneaky fellow, meat , ... ) ! Teamplay is essential. It works great when you play with random players but for those of us who can gather a good four friends to form a squad the experience is excellent.
I don't have much negative points to point out, I experienced no major bugs or issues. Someday they will hopefully add some other nations which would be great. A lot of people asked for the addition of the ANZAC. Italy and the Ottomans would be a great plus for the Central Powers side.
There is no game on the market that beat the WW1 experience Verdun is currently offering. And the oncoming Steampunk-WW1-Sci-FI Battlefield I, probably a good game for what it is, will not offer a Great War experience as good as Verdun is doing.
I hope the developpers keep working on this game for a long time ! There is so much opportunities to add things.

I have played and beat Dark Souls: Prepare to Die Edition and am a fan of the series. I have not played the original Dark Souls 2 that much so I can't compare Scholars of the First Sin to it. Anyways, SotFS is a remix of the original Dark Souls 2, with different enemy & item placements, changes to the level design and a new end boss. It comes with all the Dark Souls 2 DLCs. Controller is necessary because the Keyboard & Mouse controls are still garbage.
When starting the game you can choose different preset builds to suit your playstyle, just like the first DS game. Same different types of weapons and spells as the first game too but dark magic is now a thing called Hexes. Bonfires serve the same purpose as the first game as well except your weapons/armor are automatically repaired if they're not broken and you can fast travel right from the start. one thing that's different is that enemies will not respawn from sitting at a bonfire if you've killed them too many times, esentially forcing you to progress instead of farming or grinding. However you can burn these things called bonfires aesthetics that will make all the enemies and most treasure respawn but the difficulty will be increased in that area to a NG+ level of difficulty. Joining the Covenant of Champions will up the difficulty too but will make the enemies respawn indefinitely.
The game plays a little bit more faster than the first game, movements are quicker, enemies are too. Takes a while to get used to at first but it's an improvement. The game is not without it's flaws though. With fast travel being accessible so early in the game it's very convenient but also takes away from immersion since you don't have to play areas through from the opposite direction thus seeing less of it. That's actually more of a nitpick I guess. A lot of the enemy encounters seem to be poorly laid out and there just to annoy you but with them being able to despawn, you can just brute force your way through an area until all the enemies never come back, eliminating the challenge.
After beating it I still prefer the first Dark Souls over this one but I still think it's an awesome game.

First off: If you are looking for actual gameplay, this is not for you. It's a walking simulator that has you piecing together a story from the clues around the house; clues, not puzzles. So don't buy this expecting it to be challenging, it isn't.
That said, I loved Gone Home. It was pretty short, even for a walking simulator, just shy of two hours, so just about the duration of a feature film. And frankly, that's a good thing. Much longer would have hurt the story and its impact. In fact, as it is, the truth was revealed the tiniest bit too early.
That's not to say I wasn't moved by the story. It's short, but it feels incredibly real. The main plot is "told" by Sam, the protagonist's little sister through clues and a diary, and the subplot can be found by looking at the little things Kaitlin's parents left behind. What all that amounts to is heartwarming and -breaking at the same time.
I'd recommend Gone Home to anyone who really just wants an interactive story in a sliiightly creepy setting. If that's you, you should take a look, though maybe wait for another sale. Because while I enjoyed the game, I would've regretted paying 20€ for two hours. As it is, 8€ is what I'd pay for a ticket at the cinema, and that's a fair price for the same "amount" of entertainment (and a better story than most films have at the moment).
(Also, I did actually play through the whole game, just in offline mode, so I let it run in online mode just long enough that it would let me write this review. Silly Steam.)

To novice players it seems you could probably get the same experience running through a dirty maze with elongated 18th century dueling pistols firing, praying your shot lands, and taking 30 seconds to reload.
But that isnt the case with this gem.
When you poke your head out of the trenches (Presumming you dont get shot) you will see a strategic team based FPS with mechanics centered around historical accuracy. There isnt microtransactions. There isnt overpowered high level players. There is a simple system with each team having a set amount of squads, and in those squads are four different roles with different roles such as the heavy gunner, rifleman, corperal, and grenadier.
A good deal of the game may seem foreign, and thats because a good deal of the game is in a different langauge. (Not anything essential, just random phrases soldiers spit out, class names, and a few players, but I think that adds to the atmosphere of the game.) Combat is brutal and realistic and that too may come as a odd change of pace for some. As expected in real life, if you take a bullet to the cheat from a rifle chances of survival are slim, as is the case with Verdun. About one bullet from a rifle to the torso will drop most opponents, so you want to plan your moves carefully. When combat moves from out of No Man's Land and into the trenches, there is a entire new beast to tame. At every corner lies death, so you find yourself breathing a sigh of relief for every degree you can turn around a corner without seeing a enemy. Atop that, frags, mortor shells, and mustard gas touch down on every inch of the map making your fight for a meger few yards of ground even harder.
When it comes to performance, Verdun runs very well. I have never encountered a crash, and I get a steady framerate at all times. Sound design, graphics, and a nice gore system also top it all off for a very immersive experience.

"Your sister is a lesbian, and she left home with her girlfriend."
That's it, the whole entire plot. Now, there's no problem with this story, there is a problem in putting it in a game where you can't do anything but walk. Even the Telltale Games (which are only narrative, little gameplay) give you the ability of choices to choose the outcome of the story. Those choices make you feel like you've actually acomplished something, that's a feeling that you can't get from Gone Home.

Now, I'm not even close to being an expert at this game. The best I can hope for is competent in PVE and INcompetent in PVP. Never the less, this game is good. It holds true to a good number of the features from the original. It gives no hand outs, and you really have to work for what you get. However, there are numerous glaring graphical faults which don't effect gameplay, but are still jarring. While a good number of the changes are definite improvements to what was already there, the parrying and backstab mechanics have been changed to feel sloppier and more confusing. I do, however, approve of the guardbreak alternative to the original kicking mechanic. If an opponent is hiding behind  shield, you can knock the shield aside, and perform a critical blow. However, like the backstab and parry, it's sloppy, and almost every attempt I make doesn't land. You have to wait a set amount of time before you can actually deliver the blow. Striking too soon results in a failed attempt, which is frustrating at best. All in all, I'd give Dark Souls II, Scholar of the First Sin an 8/10. Thanks to the integrated DLC, and a number of other add-ins, the game is superior to the base game.

To novice players it seems you could probably get the same experience running through a dirty maze with elongated 18th century dueling pistols firing, praying your shot lands, and taking 30 seconds to reload.
But that isnt the case with this gem.
When you poke your head out of the trenches (Presumming you dont get shot) you will see a strategic team based FPS with mechanics centered around historical accuracy. There isnt microtransactions. There isnt overpowered high level players. There is a simple system with each team having a set amount of squads, and in those squads are four different roles with different roles such as the heavy gunner, rifleman, corperal, and grenadier.
A good deal of the game may seem foreign, and thats because a good deal of the game is in a different langauge. (Not anything essential, just random phrases soldiers spit out, class names, and a few players, but I think that adds to the atmosphere of the game.) Combat is brutal and realistic and that too may come as a odd change of pace for some. As expected in real life, if you take a bullet to the cheat from a rifle chances of survival are slim, as is the case with Verdun. About one bullet from a rifle to the torso will drop most opponents, so you want to plan your moves carefully. When combat moves from out of No Man's Land and into the trenches, there is a entire new beast to tame. At every corner lies death, so you find yourself breathing a sigh of relief for every degree you can turn around a corner without seeing a enemy. Atop that, frags, mortor shells, and mustard gas touch down on every inch of the map making your fight for a meger few yards of ground even harder.
When it comes to performance, Verdun runs very well. I have never encountered a crash, and I get a steady framerate at all times. Sound design, graphics, and a nice gore system also top it all off for a very immersive experience.

Short Review:
Pros
-Decent Graphics
-Okay gun customization and combat
Cons
-Poorly Optimized
-Short Story
-Terrible Animation
-Bad Voice Acting
-Lack of uniqueness in content
-Very small for being advertised as "Open World"
Long Review:
Intro: Homefront at first seemed like a promising game, but red lights began flashing when the original studio closed down and had to switch hands to Dambuster. Deepsilver ended up publishing the game and they have published decent titles in the past including the newest Saints Row and both games in the Metro series. Following this obvious poor pattern of development, it should already be a clear sign that the title probably won't be that good.
Pros: That being said the game itself is pretty bad. To start with the pros, I tried my best to understand what good came out of this game, but its really tough considering theres such a very very small amount of unique polish that no other game has. The idea of liberating apartments just reminds me of Far Cry 4, and the "Hearts and Minds" or morale meter of increasing the civillian morale is already stolen from other games, first that comes to mind is InFamous: Second Son. The gunplay is that of every other game except it does sort've have an interesting customization concept of swapping gun's slide and replacing it with totally different body. As mentioned in the short review, the graphics are decent, but they're really nothing to go home about, moderate as of 2016 although in a year's time they definitely will fall very short.
Cons: Now after slaying the pros I want to present the cons. For one thing, I am running a Nvidia GeForce GtX 980 FTW Edition, and I still found a lot of very poor optimization areas throughout my playthrough. Many stuttering issues that brought my FPS just because a cutscene began or a few enemies loaded on my screen. Next I want to touch on the story. In my opinion the concept seemed kind've cool and sort've unique. The execution of that said concept is very poor, the story is very cliche and predictable, Its also incredibly short, I  managed to beat it in 3 sit downs of about 3 hours. The gameplay in it is so repetitive and you just do the exact same things which include capturing small bases, finding an object and fighting KPA. After you end up beating this short but not very sweet game, you can't even return to it to complete extra side content or upgrade your weapons all the way, which punishes any player who decides to dedicate extra time towards doing the repetitive tasks. The overall production value in this game falls short of many games I've ever played. The animation is absolutely terrible. when jumping in real life I typically don't see my legs spaghetti everywhere even if I am quite thin. Also in cutscenes the major characters seem to just sink into the ground as if the KPA replaced all of America's ground with quicksand. The voice acting falls very short in the impressions that some VA's try to do. And it almost seems as if the highest produced portion of this game is the song that plays in the 35 minute long credits.
Overall: The only time I'd recommend you to buy this game is to MAYBE play resistance mode with your friends, but under no circumstances should you spend $60 on it, I'd wait until a sale marks this price down to $10-$20, because thats the absolute MOST value you can get out of this title.

This is my review for Homefront: The Revolution - 2016
I would like to first say that I like this game alot however it's not the best game in the world. Homefront The Revolution brings a new first person shooter as you play as a resistance fighter, fighting the North Koreans as they have occupied the United States and basiclly you need to start a "revolution" to take back your country.
What's the gameplay like?:-
I will be honest, it's very similer to Farcry 3 and 4. The gameplay is so much similer to it because the HUD setup is the same and the "roleplaying" elements are similer to Farcry. You do need to earn money by doing jobs in the game to buy new weapons and upgrades. I mean I am not bothered with the gameplay much myself but at least it's something I am very familer with and others to.
What's the story like?:-
I will be honest, some people are right. The story is quite Mediocre (mixed) to people and I will agree. It's not really powerful but it does have it's intense moments in the game. The stroy in this game feels it's like a action-packed movie. I mean some of the characters are really good in it but it's not enough background story.
What are the graphics like?:-
The graphics are just the same as Farcry and other games abit. I have heard that people have had problems with the graphics and Fraps but to be honest with you I get some of those's issues that it does tend to go "slow" but it does speed itself up. The graphics however like fire's blazing, explosions and world detail and the atmosphere are really good.
What other features are in the game?:-
I will be honest but there really isn't any other features much but the massive differences is from the first game is that this game is open-world. Another feauture you can do is indeed recruit resistance fighters to help you out on strongholds, police stations etc occupied by the Koreans but other then that there's no new features compared to other games. Not from what i've seen anyways.
How does this tie in to the first game?:-
I haven't really played much of the game but all I know is that this game does indeed tie into the first game but the only difference is that Homefront 2 is set in an alternative reality which means some of the events from the first game doesn't really exist anymore.
Final ratings:-
From my personal view. The game receives a favorable view from me. I will praise the visual effects, combat and the open-world features. however I am criticsizing the lack of story/backstory
Rating:- 7.1/10

I have played and beat Dark Souls: Prepare to Die Edition and am a fan of the series. I have not played the original Dark Souls 2 that much so I can't compare Scholars of the First Sin to it. Anyways, SotFS is a remix of the original Dark Souls 2, with different enemy & item placements, changes to the level design and a new end boss. It comes with all the Dark Souls 2 DLCs. Controller is necessary because the Keyboard & Mouse controls are still garbage.
When starting the game you can choose different preset builds to suit your playstyle, just like the first DS game. Same different types of weapons and spells as the first game too but dark magic is now a thing called Hexes. Bonfires serve the same purpose as the first game as well except your weapons/armor are automatically repaired if they're not broken and you can fast travel right from the start. one thing that's different is that enemies will not respawn from sitting at a bonfire if you've killed them too many times, esentially forcing you to progress instead of farming or grinding. However you can burn these things called bonfires aesthetics that will make all the enemies and most treasure respawn but the difficulty will be increased in that area to a NG+ level of difficulty. Joining the Covenant of Champions will up the difficulty too but will make the enemies respawn indefinitely.
The game plays a little bit more faster than the first game, movements are quicker, enemies are too. Takes a while to get used to at first but it's an improvement. The game is not without it's flaws though. With fast travel being accessible so early in the game it's very convenient but also takes away from immersion since you don't have to play areas through from the opposite direction thus seeing less of it. That's actually more of a nitpick I guess. A lot of the enemy encounters seem to be poorly laid out and there just to annoy you but with them being able to despawn, you can just brute force your way through an area until all the enemies never come back, eliminating the challenge.
After beating it I still prefer the first Dark Souls over this one but I still think it's an awesome game.

Counter-Strike Source is yet another game of Counter-Strike with same formula, a multiplayer match-based team FPS. The third one. It came out in 2004 and was running on Source engine, mostly to improve graphics. It also comes with bots and not much else.
Multiplayer community is as good as you expect it to be in CS games. Very lively. And very de_dust2. But that's to be expected. You can still find some lower-populated servers that play other maps.
And yea, it's mostly full of good players. But at least not crazy pros like you have in CS1.6, so it's more playable.
Well, as for bots, there is not much that I can say. They do fine. You can still tell away a team of bots from a team of real players, the way that they stick together in one or two groups. But didn't play with them enough to say anything else.
As for core gameplay itself, it stayed true to same old formula. It's still a game which has strategical part where you use grenades to cover assault. Where you need to know when to camp as team and when to move out to clear a room as team. Focusing and giving diversion. It's also still a game where you can die from single bullet before you can react. It's still a game where accuaricy and reaction are more worth than thinking. Still a game with sniper-rifle that kills with one shot no matter where you shoot and still a game where headshot bonus is way too much. Still a game where few super-players will be killing everything else. And yea, still rewards more money to buy weapons to the team that just won. And the best tactic there is to blind players with flashbang, which is no fun for those who got under this effect.
Yea, still has that core gameplay with mix of bad and good. Mostly bad.
So, let's get down to differences between original CS and Source. I can divide it into three things: Improved grenades, cover matters more and actually random spread of fire.
Grenades were improved. They are easier to throw, feeling like they have lower gravity. For me it felt that they are being thrown exactly where I want when it comes to far distance. Well, almost. Still feels better.
Each grenade also got better. Flashbang works almost same, but also makes player deaf and disables map, making player even more unaware of situation. Explosive grenade not only damages but makes player deaf for a while too. It also feels stronger. Well, or at least easier to throw at target because of lower gravity, as said. And smoke grenades become actually useful, as the smoke is fully solid now, it can actually cover up. You also can't see names of players through smoke like you could in CS1.6.
Cover matters more. Well. Or shooting through wall (wallbanging, they say) isn't as good as it used to be. While you can still shoot through some thin walls or doors, you can't shoot right through thick level geometry. So you will not get annoyed by some random bullets giving you minimal damage and slowing you down a lot because somebody is spamming through level. Oh yea, slow down isn't as huge as it was, another plus for me, can actually get back to corner despite getting shot a lot.
And the random bullet spread of weapons is actually random. Which is big for some people because in original there were only few set patterns to spread, making it semi-random. And thus the fanatics who spent 1000 hours on a game could wreck anybody by just spraying bullets and somehow headshotting everything with no care. Now you can't just do this. And so many pros whined about how much they can't just wreck things and how developers hate what truly matters - them. Because screw letting newbies a fair chance. Because they don't want competention, they just want to feel like elites.
Oh yea, and you don't have to buy primary or secondary ammo anymore at the start of round. Few less clicks on something you would get anyway.
As for graphics, I really like them. Source engine gives here a very clean nice looking image. It's not ovely detailed as Global Offensive, just something with taste. While being smooth. Outside of maybe that one spot in office map where you can block doorway for hostages with a good placed grenade with props.
Sadly, absolutely no music.
Well, I still wouldn't call it a good game. Still a mess of tactics and twitch shooting, which is punishing to majority of people outside of few pro ones. All while trying to keep you addictive with that "almost killed him, if only one more second". Even with small improvements that Source version got.

Note: This a purely narrative game. If you're expecting only action in your video games, you probably should look elsewhere (but you're missing out).
Gone Home lets you step into the shoes of Kaitlin; she's just gotten back from abroad and shows up at her parent's house. ..Except everyone's gone. As you explore inside, you find out bits and pieces of what's happened, particularly through the notes left by your sister. It's a mystery with a deeply personal and 'at your pace' style. You won't exactly have things jumping out at you, but learning about what your family has been through since you've been away is deeply satisfying and multi-layered. Even though you play as Kaitlin, the things she learns are ultimately up to you to interpret, a quality that makes Gone Home really shine. If you're looking for one of the best narrative concepts, it's this one.

While not ambitious to begin with, Dino D-Day isn't a very good game. Once it loses its unique charm, the game quickly gains dust in your library, so to speak.
What is this game? Basically, it is class-based competitive shooter which pits the Allies and the Axis against each other in an obvious WWII setting. The kicker? The Axis have dinosaures! The game feels like an awkard mash up of Team Fortress 2's classes and objective modes (with FAR less of them), and Left 4 Dead's zombies that are far less satisfying to control and devour as... but fun nonetheless. That's it, besides a DLC that I have no experience with, but I can tell you that next to no one is playing it, sadly. As for the main game, it isn't all that populated, but you will always find about 3 or so active servers.
The games gunplay is personally fine, although ADS feels a bit tacked on in the Source engine, and the dinosaurs are all unique and control reasonably well, if not a little bland. Class balance is thrown competely out the window, as you WILL NOT find it at all here. Some dinosaurs and soldier classes are overpowered and some are the opposite, which limits the potential for spicing the gameplay up while still enjoying it. The game does not have too much content either, as you will see the same maps and modes quite often, and that is the games entire extent, sadly.
As for graphics, the game is overall unpolished, but animations are up to par with other Source games, and the art style fits the game well, if not a little boring and dull. Sound is something the game gets perfectly fine, as voice work suits each class and dinosaur sounds fit as well. Don't expect anything special, however. I also haven't experienced any bugs, and the game runs fine as well.
Honestly, there's a lot of better games you can get for $10, and this game gets old really fast. It tries to imitate two games that are far better (one of which is free), and alone it isn't remarkable either. If I had to rate this game, it would be a 5/10. It would be lower if it was a triple-A title or it had a higher price, as well.
Oh yeah, you also get to kill goats. Probably the most fun part about this game.

Another part of the game I really enjoy is the stealth. Dark Souls II: Scholar of the First Sin is the "director's cut" version of the original Dark Souls II with all DLCs included. I don't think there's need to introduce the Dark Souls series as you've already heard about them before for sure. It's an action RPG where you play as a cursed character that can't be killed (is always resurrected). That leads you to Drangleic kingdom where you expect to break the curse, with help of mysterious woman, the Emerald Herald.
Whole series are well-known for the high difficulty. I think Scholar is even slightly harder than Dark Souls and for those who think it's still not enough, there are options to make it even harder. Interesting feature is the option to restart specific location to "new game plus" difficulty.
Where the first Dark Souls used to make difficulty via unique and unexpected enemies, Scholar's difficulty is more based on overwhelming you. Instead of making harder, clever and unique creatures, the game just throws groups of enemies on you. But even though the enemy placement and amount, the level design still keeps the high standard Dark Souls series are known for. Every location is made with exploring in mind, containing many secret passages and crossroads offering huge amount of playtime for those who want to see everything, and almost every dead-end or secret is rewarding you with an item (guarded by powerful enemy).
What I liked about Dark Souls II (Scholar) is that the game doesn't push you to go to specific locations. Of course, you'll have to beat every main boss through the game, but that doesn't mean you have to beat them at specific time. There'll be many passages where you'll get frustrated pretty easily but you can just ignore them for some time and go somewhere else. Until the last third of the game, you can always pick where to go, and not just follow linear location structure that you might've experienced in other RPGs.
What gets annoying pretty fast are the NPC invaders. If you play online, other players may attack you, but there are also many NPCs who will invade your world to kill you. Sadly, they aren't a big challenge (except one optional invader in the beginning of the game), they just annoy you with repeated showing up. The game in the description even praises including invader Forlorn, who just ends up being pain in the...
Dark Souls series are typical for their unique online features, and Scholar is not different. You can always see notes put by other players on the ground (secrets and hints, but also lies and troll messages), you can see ghosts of people who died at your place and you can get help with bosses from other players (and vice versa). I found the notes being most important, as it brought to me good hints and laughs many times. But it also shows something typical for Scholar of the First Sin - you'll meet pretty often notes "beware of duo" and "beware of trio" (due to the enemy design I already mentioned).
The game has also strong plan for Player vs. Player combat, as most covenants (specific groups where you gain your rank, you can join only one at a time) will require you to invade other players' games and kill them. You might be afraid of getting invaded pretty often but that's not right - through my play I was invaded only few times and it was mostly in specific PvP locations where covenants give tasks to protect the place from other players.
The environment and graphics are gorgeous. Of course, you can't expect top level graphic details, but you won't mind it for the depth and variety of all locations. You'll visit forests, castles, deadly dungeons, dragon lairs, sewers full of rats, caves full of spiders and more... and you'll love what game designers made, as they made a great compromise between technical and visual level design.
If you haven't checked through playtimes of DS players, let's make it clear - Dark Souls II: Scholar of the First Sin is a long game. It offers you tens of hours for a single playthrough considering just sticking with the main path. Add many side paths, secrets, optional bosses and DLC content, and you are getting even higher with the time game provides you. And if that's not enough and you want a bigger challenge on something you have already experienced, you can always pick New Game+, New Game++, New Game+++,...
It's not a perfect game, personally I liked more the first Dark Souls (because of better balanced difficulty and more memorable locations), but that doesn't mean it's not a great game. I've enjoyed Scholar of the First Sin and if you want a game that won't hold your hand and leaves you to the challenge, you'll love it!

Whilst I have been and "returned home" myself for a short while and should be writing my masters, I decided to take some time out to try the infamous game that replicates (but doesn't mirror) this experience, "Gone Home". It says in the Steam newsfeed from +Rock Paper Shotgun that +FullBright Games  could stretch the amount of reviews for this game to cover each day for the rest of time. Sorry, I am going to help make this game be talked about in old age.
To take a hammer to a well worn nail, I likewise cannot say very much about the game without revealing aspects of its core narrative, so I cannot say much that has already not been said (ha ha). but in summary it is a game with exceptional attention to detail, characterisation, voice acting, and writing. Without giving anything else away I approve very highly of the cassette tapes, there are some favourites in there.
So your name is Kaitlin and you have been travelling around Europe for a year and return home to see your family, but for some reason nobody is at home. You have a simple interface system of WASD, the mouse to look at a one button interaction (and one more to flip items around to look at them) which keeps the focus on the story. You will spend all of your time investigatin' items around the home to try and piece together what has happened. There are postcards from yourself, cassette tapes, newspaper clippings, bills, all sorts. Everything ranges from the mundane (soap powder) to the extremely personal (handwritten notes with doodles). The items in the game are the foundation which make the story seem uncannily real.
First of all, the game is set in the 90s (94-95 to be exact) and everything feels like it fits really well. There are bright colours, a lot of VHS tapes, vinyl, the works; it does a fantastic job in making you feel like it is that time. Some would argue that the graphics are basic but there is a high level of detail to these environments that makes you feel like a house that is "living in" with it's assortment of clutter and ornamentation. In fact if it didn't convey this feeling you probably wouldn't be so involved in the dialogue as it would be "just another game space". Secondly, the level of writing for the letters really shines through what is seen, and it is believable that you are reading about these people and that they are real. Praise where it is certainly deserved as throughout you are really wanting to know what happens to these people. The process of opening drawers and picking things up reminds me of "Amnesia: The Dark Descent" but unlike that you feel intrusive, like an invader. Everything feels so personal and real that you are embarrassed as much as the main character (and moreso) when you find things you believe you should not be looking at; that is the power of this game.
There is about 2 hours of gameplay here. That is presuming you take your time, check every nook and cranny, look at everything and read all the material that is here. It stands to reason that a gamer looking for challenge either in reactions, puzzles, or strategy might be a bit disappointed by this game. It is not a game in this sense but a well-woven story and narrative that requests that you breathe, think and care which sits alongside games like Dear Esther and Thomas Was Alone. Dear Esther is a briny, landscape spanning walk through literary passages, philosophy, and contemplation from the perspective of an older person seeking answers whereas Gone Home is immediate, youthful, anarchic and hormonal. It is the difference in perspective but no less a reflection, no less a consideration of feeling, thought and upheaval especially as it evokes these feelings in yourself, these memories. There are some twists to this story too with some excellent framing devices for these (once again cannot give away) which leave you to tip your invisible hat a few times.
In summary, an excellent game. It is another game that seeks to join the moshpit and elbow it's way into a discussion about "are games art?", because it certainly deserves to in there. It is a game for dreamers, thinkers, creative-types, and feelers, and the game celebrates this in a big way through it's design and characters. Get it now!

Homefront the Revolution is a post apocalyptic game set in the realms of philadelphia attempting to tell the story of survival and rebelion under a ruthless and oppressive enemy or so you would think. The story is very lackluster with no real sense of making a diffrence to the people who inhabit the game world, there is zero emotion to be felt with Homefront the Revolution which is a shame as again another AAA game chooses a real possible scenario as the backdrop to there game but it carries no weight in terms of emotion or caring for the person (character) next to you. The story or main campaign is easily one of the most forgettable stories i have played the only thing i remember is getting frustrated with the hearts and minds parts of the game which is very tedious and repetitive. Combat in Homefront the Revolution is very unsatisfying the game is an FPS game but has none of the fundementals of an FPS game FoV is limited to 65 i would like at the very least 90 there is no dual sensitivity for hipfire and aimed fire. There is a few bugs in the game and a lot of cut corners. You cant even freeroam after the main story is complete so if you missed things in the game like side quests you have to start the game again.
There is a co-op section in the game which was fun for a little bit but what i dont understand is why for a couple of  co-op missions there is so much in terms of character customization and weapons when there is no multiplayer, there is certain attachments for weapons like the suppresor for your assault rifle which you can only use on your assault rifle in co-op mode and not in the main game.
There is a lot of cons with this game and not enough pros to justify giving it a positive review which is unfortunate as it could of been such a great game that i could of been quite happy to sink alot of hours into but after 14 hours the main story is complete and so are the co-op missions and there is no desire to go back and play it again so as it stands its an over priced ballon that quickly deflates and i wouldnt recommend this game and would suggest either waiting for a sale or investing in another game. So sadly its a thumbs down for this one.

What can I say (the last image still lingering on my retinas): a Beautiful game.  I had previously been exposed to it via a let's plays online, but playing it myself was quite engaging.  Gone Home was intimate and cohesive, and I really found myself identifying with Sam Greenbriar.  Graphics fit the aesthetic of the story, the voice acting is on point, and the music is rowdy and weirdly nostalgic.  I cannot wait for the next game from Fullbright, Tacoma.  I expect nothing short of amazing.  Thank you for the endearing experience.  If you want an explorative yet homely story, this is your game. It's short, satisfying, and pleasantly nonabrasive.  A few things I would recommend is waiting for a Steam Sale to purchase the game as I do not think $20 is appropriate for the time you get out of it.  I say this mainly because I took my time and only spent 3 hours on it.  If you are thorough, it only takes one play through to uncover all of the details so the replay value might not be there for some.  Also, remember to keep in the mindset that this game is more passive than active hence why I use terms like 'pleasant' and 'nonabrasive'.  I loved it because I am into heartwarming stories.  It was a wonderful night cap for me, not too many challenges but genuine enough to keep me immersed.  Give it a chance.

I know many people dislike dark souls 2 and the scholar of the first sin version was just plain scummy, but I find it was a great introduction for me into the Souls series.
When I first saw Dark souls 2 sotfs (Scholar of the first sin) the only rpg's I had played were Twilight Princess, Skyward sword, and Skyrim, so all i thought of this game was that it was a difficult Legend of Zelda game with more emphasis on combat and you could change your gear. But oh how wrong I was, as with most people's experience playing a Souls game I found myself dying a lot though never really in the beginning, but somehow I never felt like giving up, soon enough I had learned the combat though I was playing with keyboard and mouse for my first playthrough.
One of my complaints is that the tutorial isn't really fun or engaging, and unlike the first Souls game it doesn't go strait up and tell you that it's going to be a difficult game that requires thought trial and error, quite the contrary actually it presents itself as easy and simple with slow yet engaging combat. This is one of my main complaints with the game, it does a poor job with the intro (Compared to Dark souls 1) despite all the beautiful environments it doesn't really prepare you much for the rest of the game gameplay-wise.
I can summarize the things the beginning teaches you into 4 things
1.if an enemy does something back away or block
2.when something looks dangerous don't go near it
3.summons help so find human effigies
4.things will ambush you, so if something looks dead hit it once
Despite what I say about the intro it is by no means terrible there are just a lot of things it could do better.
The next issue I have with this game is the bland design choices. Though most of the areas still look very nice they aren't creative or interesting With the exception of the dlc areas (I'll get to them later) and places like the dragon's aerie and the shrine of amana, in most areas the enemy designs are just humanoids of different sizes and armors. The areas feel linear and lazily done and unnaturally put together. Instead of feeling like a living breathing world it just feels like a generic fantasy world. Most of the areas though are fun to explore and have several secrets to make you go back to them.
One of my favorite things about this game though is the newly implemented mechanics (Except for soul memory and limited enemy spawns, they suck). Though I know many people will disagree with me, I prefer the rolling mechanics of ds2 and demon's souls to that of ds1, If you prefer to freely roll in any direction while locked on this game handles it very well I think. Dual wielding actually works (Though they never explain how in the game), It may not be exceptionally powerful but it can be fun to mess around with. The new gravity mechanics I find have been greatly improved with weight affecting the damage more. The new UI and durability though need to be reverted back to their original form in ds1 since they have become even more confusing than they already were.
The dlc is one of the better things in this game, though not as good as the Artorias of the abyss dlc for ds1 the dlc can provide some good fun. The areas and bosses (Except for The ancient explorer, Varg, and Cera) have cooler designs and are generally better than most in the base game (Though the enemies could still use some work) even though there are a lot of callbacks to ds1. The dlc's were one of my highlights while playing and you can definitely sink a lot of hours into them.
The story is good but the characters aren't too memorable and they all just seem depressed. There is definitely a huge expanse of lore to read in the item descriptions though they changed some in the sotfs version which was pretty scummy.
Now for a simple review i would rank it like this.
Gameplay 9/10
Design 7/10
Graphics 8/10
Story 8/10
Verdict 8.5/10
This game is good for someone who just wants to see what a Souls game is like and isn't all too familiar with dodge and block combat, or someone who has already played through ds1 and desperately craves more no matter the quality.
If you're familiar with games like these though i would skip ds2 and go play ds1.

i´m writing this in the hope of bringing a friend of mine to the souls series and of course because i really enjoyed my time in drangleic.
Actually, i´m still burning:-)
I won´t go into detail about game mechanics (edit: i kinda do) or bosses/enemies and keep it as spoilerfree as possible.
I discovered dark souls by accident while surfing online, gave it a try and immediately loved it. In many modern games, you are more like a receiver or an observer than an actual player.Often it´s just runnning from a to b in a specific order, with map markers that guide you and popups that explain everything along the way. All you have to do is act it out, watch the cutscenes that present reasoning why you ran all this way from a to b, and then continue on. I think games miss out here on their real potential of being more than mere passive entertainment , but to encourage the player to actively co-create his own unique and memorable experence. The souls games have achieved that in some sense.
Set in a world of nostalgia, desperation and long lost greatness, little is known about your fate and why you have come to this place. Drangleic reveals little of itself and that only to those who seek it. After my first playthrough, i couldn´t tell you coherently what the game was about, and now after many playthroughs, i´d rather not tell you my version of thngs, since this is a feature of dark souls that is best experienced spoilerfree. It gives you just enough information to go on your own fantasy trip if you want to, wondering what  might have happened or what will happen when you progess.What i like here, is that the game abuses no moral-heavy concepts like good vs. evil etc but it sparks your own imagination by leaving so many questions unanswered.
On a side note: It´s also possible to completely ignore the story or lore aspect and just have fun with the combat, it´s really your show!
So there you are, in a strange place called things betwixt, with nothing on you but the clothes of a stranger and your "life affirming flesh". Without any guidance whatsoever, you can only move on, eventually reaching the hut of the firekeepers. After being mocked by three charming old ladies  you will set out on a journey without rest, and you´ll probably have serious doubts about finishing the game. Will it be worth learning all these seemingly complicated game mechanics?How on earth am i supposed to beat this guy?
In short: yes it will.Man up and get in there!
Battling the first opponents you´ll soon realize that doing it like in other games won´t work, you are dealing with a buttonmash-resistant AI here that punishes mistakes pretty consistently.But the game is also not as hard as some people say, it merely follows a simple rule: Stay alert and active and you will persevere,become passive and neglectant and you will die.If you put a little time into it though you´ll notice that the  mix of rolling, backstepping, blocking and critical attacks combined with spacing and stamina management makes for a great combat system that challenges you to be at your best at all times.Try different weapons and note that every weapon type gives u a unique moveset,meaning you also have to adapt your playstyle and character developement accordingly. The same goes for armor and clothing. Heavy armor will make you slower in many actions but provide more defence and vice versa.All that together are the ingredients of an indepth rpg- experience of your own making.
As you progress, the game rewards you with a sense of achievement that i have not experienced in any other .Yes, you will die alot in your first playthrough and that can be frustrating, but if you hang in there and finally beat an area boss or make it through a tight spot, it´s one of the best things ever.Because everything is out to get you and you are under constant pressure not to let them, it makes the identification with your character more personal and direct. You really get the the feeling that you did something great and that only your own ingenuity made it happen.
The sheer amount of information on one side and also the lack of information on the other can be overwhelming in the beginning,but fret not! Here are some basic tips that will get you going:
Read the item descriptions of everything you find even if it does not make any sense at first.
Always exhaust the dialogue options with npcs you meet.
Learn what stats like endurance or adaptability actually do.
Go slow. Nobody is going anywhere, take a good look at your surroundings and try to explore every nook and cranny- there may be treasure just around the corner!
You can complete the game with every weapon you like, but your upgrade materials are finite, so use them wisely.
Messages on the ground come from other players, as well as the shades you sometimes see.They can´t hurt you:-)
The most important thing to do though, and this is really the essence of the game, is to adjust your attitude towards dying. A crazy person tries to avoid death at all costs, a sane one learns how to die right! So if you want to know something for sure in this game, like"can i jump off this ledge?" there is no safe way to get the answer, eventually you´ll have to jump.Death is in many cases also the price of knowledge.
After you complete your first playthrough you are not finished by a long shot.You can enter new game plus and test yourself again, this time the enemies will hit harder and take more damage. This continues up to 7 new games and then the difficulty will no longer increase, but you can still start a new cycle, basically to infinity. That´s another thing i enjoyed, the fact that it´s kind of a "what goes around comes around" experience instead of a straight line. Each game cycle, you know a little more.
Now the whole online side of the game could be interesting as well, battling or aiding other players is really fun once you get the hang of it. There are some downsides on the pvp part like hitbox issues and it is by no means a perfect system but since all players have to deal with it, it kind of levels the playingfield in the end. You know there´s methods to gain advantages in every game and i really don´t care if someone is doing it or not. After all everybody has the right to play how they want to.
To sum it up, i think everybody who enjoys a challenge and is not afraid of putting in some time to learn the base mechanics should play dark souls, if you don´t, you are missing out on some of the best moments in videogame entertainment.
Cheers!

An interesting experience in storytelling, but little more than that. The exploration of the house and basically walking into the unknown created an eery atmosphere right from the beginning. However, instead of ramping up by intensifying the mystery, the game loses much of the suspense about halfway in, since you quickly get used to your surroundings and it's also pretty easy to figure out where the game is going with its story. That being said, the narrative was neither "bad" nor boring. However, I think Gone Home would've served better as a genuine horror/supernatural mystery (as was teased with the whole "psycho house" setting from the very beginning).
The game mechanics allow you to interact with lots of objects (pick stuff up, flip it around, zoom in, put it back) and while that is a nice touch, it felt somewhat pointless and underused. It's only ever needed to read the back of some photo or document. Since you're only picking up mundane everyday items, there's not much else to do, which is why, again, I'd have preferred this game to actually have some supernatural elements (intricate puzzle boxes like in The Room come to mind).
Anyway, it was a short (~2h), sweet experience. Still worthwhile on its own, but also with lots of squandered potential imo. I'd never have bought it at full price, though. But for under 5$ it's worth recommending.

First, the pleasantries. The gameplay was fun, each room holding a "Where's Waldo?" game for me (Waldo being interactable objects). This may sound odd but my favorite parts of the game were the sounds of rain on the windows and roof and of thunder with its flashes of lightning. Not only were they great in terms of graphics and sound quality, they really fostered a beautiful atmosphere and sounded lovely. The rain blurring the windows was a great idea for obscuring the house's surroundings, so even from the beginning the focus is on the house and its contents.
Now, the reason why I can't reccomend the game. The story, and Sam, disappointed me but not for the reason easiest to assume. I have no issues whatsoever with Sam's sexuality, only with the journey she took to discover it. I am Katie's age and I have two younger sisters. If I came home from a year abroad and found evidence all over the house that my sister(s) had felt so alone during the transition period to the new house and school, that she had eventually started smoking, lying to our parents and sneaking out, reading graphic magazines (portraying either gender), and having sex with a kid from her high school? I would have been very, very concerned. Actually, that's an understatement; I'd have been devastated that my sister(s)--whom I love dearly--had gone through so much loneliness and then so much change and I hadn't even been there for it. And the fact that my sister(s) had run away with aforementioned sex partner, without a even a plan or idea of how to support themselves, would worry me to no end. Nevermind any kind of censure for her actions, I'd be worried about her safety and wellbeing!
The story is driven entirely on emotion, but in my experience, emotion is only a component of finding happiness. Sometimes emotion is too restrained and opportunities escape, and other times common sense is abandoned because of (even quite genuine) feelings. The story was unbalanced and Sam and Lonnie both were acting almost solely on their emotions throughout the story.
The stale parents were a part of the problem. Katie's absence was a part of the problem. Sam's heart doing all of the talking without any input from her head was part of the problem. She grew up on swashbuckling adventures and her story in the game is a pure romance, but nothing in life is purely romantic.

For such a brief, simple game, I found Gone Home extremely enjoyable. The way the writers allowed the story to develop through little fragments into this family's life was expertly done, especially the way they were able to weave in the different subplots. Also: fantastic soundtrack.
In terms of gameplay, don't go into this expecting a traditional game. It's an interactive story. There's no puzzles or action, just an exploration of a narrative presented in a fairly novel way. So obviously it's not for everyone.
I'll admit that, for the length, this game is fairly pricy; for $22 I would expect more than just a little over two hours of gameplay. That said, I'd recommend that anyone who likes well-crafted stories and feminist punk rock to shell out the cash for this when it goes on sale.

I know many people dislike dark souls 2 and the scholar of the first sin version was just plain scummy, but I find it was a great introduction for me into the Souls series.
When I first saw Dark souls 2 sotfs (Scholar of the first sin) the only rpg's I had played were Twilight Princess, Skyward sword, and Skyrim, so all i thought of this game was that it was a difficult Legend of Zelda game with more emphasis on combat and you could change your gear. But oh how wrong I was, as with most people's experience playing a Souls game I found myself dying a lot though never really in the beginning, but somehow I never felt like giving up, soon enough I had learned the combat though I was playing with keyboard and mouse for my first playthrough.
One of my complaints is that the tutorial isn't really fun or engaging, and unlike the first Souls game it doesn't go strait up and tell you that it's going to be a difficult game that requires thought trial and error, quite the contrary actually it presents itself as easy and simple with slow yet engaging combat. This is one of my main complaints with the game, it does a poor job with the intro (Compared to Dark souls 1) despite all the beautiful environments it doesn't really prepare you much for the rest of the game gameplay-wise.
I can summarize the things the beginning teaches you into 4 things
1.if an enemy does something back away or block
2.when something looks dangerous don't go near it
3.summons help so find human effigies
4.things will ambush you, so if something looks dead hit it once
Despite what I say about the intro it is by no means terrible there are just a lot of things it could do better.
The next issue I have with this game is the bland design choices. Though most of the areas still look very nice they aren't creative or interesting With the exception of the dlc areas (I'll get to them later) and places like the dragon's aerie and the shrine of amana, in most areas the enemy designs are just humanoids of different sizes and armors. The areas feel linear and lazily done and unnaturally put together. Instead of feeling like a living breathing world it just feels like a generic fantasy world. Most of the areas though are fun to explore and have several secrets to make you go back to them.
One of my favorite things about this game though is the newly implemented mechanics (Except for soul memory and limited enemy spawns, they suck). Though I know many people will disagree with me, I prefer the rolling mechanics of ds2 and demon's souls to that of ds1, If you prefer to freely roll in any direction while locked on this game handles it very well I think. Dual wielding actually works (Though they never explain how in the game), It may not be exceptionally powerful but it can be fun to mess around with. The new gravity mechanics I find have been greatly improved with weight affecting the damage more. The new UI and durability though need to be reverted back to their original form in ds1 since they have become even more confusing than they already were.
The dlc is one of the better things in this game, though not as good as the Artorias of the abyss dlc for ds1 the dlc can provide some good fun. The areas and bosses (Except for The ancient explorer, Varg, and Cera) have cooler designs and are generally better than most in the base game (Though the enemies could still use some work) even though there are a lot of callbacks to ds1. The dlc's were one of my highlights while playing and you can definitely sink a lot of hours into them.
The story is good but the characters aren't too memorable and they all just seem depressed. There is definitely a huge expanse of lore to read in the item descriptions though they changed some in the sotfs version which was pretty scummy.
Now for a simple review i would rank it like this.
Gameplay 9/10
Design 7/10
Graphics 8/10
Story 8/10
Verdict 8.5/10
This game is good for someone who just wants to see what a Souls game is like and isn't all too familiar with dodge and block combat, or someone who has already played through ds1 and desperately craves more no matter the quality.
If you're familiar with games like these though i would skip ds2 and go play ds1.

i´m writing this in the hope of bringing a friend of mine to the souls series and of course because i really enjoyed my time in drangleic.
Actually, i´m still burning:-)
I won´t go into detail about game mechanics (edit: i kinda do) or bosses/enemies and keep it as spoilerfree as possible.
I discovered dark souls by accident while surfing online, gave it a try and immediately loved it. In many modern games, you are more like a receiver or an observer than an actual player.Often it´s just runnning from a to b in a specific order, with map markers that guide you and popups that explain everything along the way. All you have to do is act it out, watch the cutscenes that present reasoning why you ran all this way from a to b, and then continue on. I think games miss out here on their real potential of being more than mere passive entertainment , but to encourage the player to actively co-create his own unique and memorable experence. The souls games have achieved that in some sense.
Set in a world of nostalgia, desperation and long lost greatness, little is known about your fate and why you have come to this place. Drangleic reveals little of itself and that only to those who seek it. After my first playthrough, i couldn´t tell you coherently what the game was about, and now after many playthroughs, i´d rather not tell you my version of thngs, since this is a feature of dark souls that is best experienced spoilerfree. It gives you just enough information to go on your own fantasy trip if you want to, wondering what  might have happened or what will happen when you progess.What i like here, is that the game abuses no moral-heavy concepts like good vs. evil etc but it sparks your own imagination by leaving so many questions unanswered.
On a side note: It´s also possible to completely ignore the story or lore aspect and just have fun with the combat, it´s really your show!
So there you are, in a strange place called things betwixt, with nothing on you but the clothes of a stranger and your "life affirming flesh". Without any guidance whatsoever, you can only move on, eventually reaching the hut of the firekeepers. After being mocked by three charming old ladies  you will set out on a journey without rest, and you´ll probably have serious doubts about finishing the game. Will it be worth learning all these seemingly complicated game mechanics?How on earth am i supposed to beat this guy?
In short: yes it will.Man up and get in there!
Battling the first opponents you´ll soon realize that doing it like in other games won´t work, you are dealing with a buttonmash-resistant AI here that punishes mistakes pretty consistently.But the game is also not as hard as some people say, it merely follows a simple rule: Stay alert and active and you will persevere,become passive and neglectant and you will die.If you put a little time into it though you´ll notice that the  mix of rolling, backstepping, blocking and critical attacks combined with spacing and stamina management makes for a great combat system that challenges you to be at your best at all times.Try different weapons and note that every weapon type gives u a unique moveset,meaning you also have to adapt your playstyle and character developement accordingly. The same goes for armor and clothing. Heavy armor will make you slower in many actions but provide more defence and vice versa.All that together are the ingredients of an indepth rpg- experience of your own making.
As you progress, the game rewards you with a sense of achievement that i have not experienced in any other .Yes, you will die alot in your first playthrough and that can be frustrating, but if you hang in there and finally beat an area boss or make it through a tight spot, it´s one of the best things ever.Because everything is out to get you and you are under constant pressure not to let them, it makes the identification with your character more personal and direct. You really get the the feeling that you did something great and that only your own ingenuity made it happen.
The sheer amount of information on one side and also the lack of information on the other can be overwhelming in the beginning,but fret not! Here are some basic tips that will get you going:
Read the item descriptions of everything you find even if it does not make any sense at first.
Always exhaust the dialogue options with npcs you meet.
Learn what stats like endurance or adaptability actually do.
Go slow. Nobody is going anywhere, take a good look at your surroundings and try to explore every nook and cranny- there may be treasure just around the corner!
You can complete the game with every weapon you like, but your upgrade materials are finite, so use them wisely.
Messages on the ground come from other players, as well as the shades you sometimes see.They can´t hurt you:-)
The most important thing to do though, and this is really the essence of the game, is to adjust your attitude towards dying. A crazy person tries to avoid death at all costs, a sane one learns how to die right! So if you want to know something for sure in this game, like"can i jump off this ledge?" there is no safe way to get the answer, eventually you´ll have to jump.Death is in many cases also the price of knowledge.
After you complete your first playthrough you are not finished by a long shot.You can enter new game plus and test yourself again, this time the enemies will hit harder and take more damage. This continues up to 7 new games and then the difficulty will no longer increase, but you can still start a new cycle, basically to infinity. That´s another thing i enjoyed, the fact that it´s kind of a "what goes around comes around" experience instead of a straight line. Each game cycle, you know a little more.
Now the whole online side of the game could be interesting as well, battling or aiding other players is really fun once you get the hang of it. There are some downsides on the pvp part like hitbox issues and it is by no means a perfect system but since all players have to deal with it, it kind of levels the playingfield in the end. You know there´s methods to gain advantages in every game and i really don´t care if someone is doing it or not. After all everybody has the right to play how they want to.
To sum it up, i think everybody who enjoys a challenge and is not afraid of putting in some time to learn the base mechanics should play dark souls, if you don´t, you are missing out on some of the best moments in videogame entertainment.
Cheers!

If you want a challenging action RPG experience, this is an excellent choice. However I would not recommend it over the first game which I feel is superior. Here is why.
Scholar of the First Sin tried something different by going for a more open and sprawling game world, but I have to say I very much miss the intricately interwoven level design of the first game. The graphics are "better" here, but somehow the overall look just wasn't as effective as Dark Souls', which could evoke a feeling of mystery and sheer dread at times. The overall art design of the first game is superior in my eyes.
The abundance of fire checkpoints had a deleterious effect on the mood too: I no longer felt the sheer relief and joy when I encountered them compared to the first game; reaching one was a moment to savour previously, but in this game it's just grist for the mill.
Difficulty wise I found it both harder and easier than Dark Souls. Some bosses I beat in a satisfying fashion, but there were a number of bosses that I had to resort to summoning, The DLC in particular was challenging, with the magic smelter demon after the Iron Passage, and the Fume Knight being particularly nightmarish for me personally.
The game has refined the combat mechanics, and the menu system is much nicer. The community element is fun although I didn't get too deep into it beyond leaving a sign at bosses and summoning for help at times myself.
Whilst the obsurity of the game is seen as a feature by many, I am not so keen on this approach to story telling. For the most part I was progressing through the game and by the end I really didn't know anything more than I won and I was now the king. The thing that I least like about both games is that it is impossible to know where to go next without resorting to the wiki. Again, others love it, but I'd prefer a bit more structure or slightly clearer in-game clues to help me understand where to go next.
It's a tighter, more polished dark souls game, which has gained in some areas (combat mechanics and online play) and lost a little in others (atmosphere and overal design). It nets out a little worse than the first game, but it is still an A+ experience.
Recommended.

Whilst people are obviously entitled to their opinions and call this game a walking simulator, I would have to firmly disagree with them on this one. Personally I really enjoyed the creepy house and the 90's settings, the way it set up a sense of foreboding that was perfectly apt in subverting expectations for the personal and moving story you eventually unravel.
My main criticism if I had to give one, would be that I wish there was more interactivity in the way you piece together the puzzle of what had happened and I appreciate that if the story didn't grab you then you may be disappointed. For me however I felt like a detective creeping around an old mansion, trying to solve the mystery of its past (much like Fox Mulder and Dana Scully, as referenced in the X-Files videos found in one of the rooms). I liked the way it didn't always give you all the information, for all the stories, but just enough to read between the lines and work out the truths for yourself.
I feel that whilst the game and its story might not be for everyone, it is certainly a refreshing look at gaming. It shows us the possibilities gaming has to expand the types of themes and ideas that it can offer insight and discussion on; the rational man with gun, things go boom approach (that we all still embrace and love) can only take us so far after all. Whilst I would not want every game to be like this, I feel that we can only gain by broadening the gaming medium to try different game play styles, embrace new (more complex) themes and appeal to new audiences, as only by doing this can our hobby develop a more nuanced world view that has legitimate things to say about the world we live in and the nature of the human condition and in doing so be considered art at more than a superficial level.
