Love is touching souls; surely Gone Home has touched mine.
People who don't like or get this game may (or may not) fall into one of three categories:
1) Anti-LGBT. I know people who don't like this game because it insults their delicate religious sensibilities. If you will play Call of Duty: Ghosts, but not Gone Home, please go home yourselves.
2) Adrenaline junkies. This game starts off feeling like a horror story, but it isn't. It's a very quiet love story. If you can't go nine seconds without shooting an insurgent, you'll hate this game like you hate non-Muricans and gun laws.
3) Un-seekers. If you're like me, you look in every corner, you search the way you aren't supposed to go before the path that's suggested, and you try to get in every box in hopes of a lucky find (yep, that's how most of my dates go, too). If you can't look between the shelves & read between the lines, this game will seem very unfinished. It's not. You just ain't lookin' right.
On a personal note, as a bisexual woman this game really touched me. I understand what it's like to be in a household and a society that doesn't understand, and they don't make the story out to be another whiny miserable self-indulgent young adult victimization. The people around her just genuinely don't know how to respond, and she's not raging at them, just regretful and hurt and frustrated. They're confused by her sexuality, and she's confused by their confusion. She thinks it's pretty clear, and always has been. I love that. It isn't dramatized or scripted, it's just a house with bits and pieces of people's histories. Thank you, developers, for making a wonderful LGBT game that isn't a parody of itself because look at us, we're so gay lololololol streamers. I look forward to a long future with Fullbright.

One of the best FPS games I've played in a while, albeit it being not too friendly for new players, because the game is fairly difficult. A keen eye is required to play this, since most of the time you scan the environment for enemies. Classes are varied and it's tied to a "Squad" system, where each squad is consisted of different country soldiers and each have their own unique traits, weapons, appearance and so on. You can also rename and create squads any way you like. Also, each squad has to have one of each class. For ex: Officer, Rifleman, Machinegunner and Grenadier. This is great, because it keeps the game naturally balanced from everyone picking snipers or grenadiers.
There's also Rifle Deathmatch, Attrition Warfare and Squad Defense, but I did not bother with them, because they have a smaller player base. Frontlines is probably the mode that defines Verdun anyway, so I highly recommend sticking to it.
Maps are fairly varied, but they are repetative, due to their nature - trenches, trenches everywhere...
Also, you will die - a lot. 8 out of 10 times, you won't know what killed you, because you die very quickly. Played this game solo, but had no problems communicating with players and even rejoining games with people I enjoyed playing with. Game has a built-in history of recent players.
Variety of weapons is crazy. So many rifles, MG's, pistols, grenades, types of mortar and even gas. Hell, you can even pick a class with 5 grenades, but only a spade as a primary weapon for smacking people.
Highly recommend playing this with "Gore" enabled, because it highlights the horrors of World War 1. Soldiers screaming and twitching in the battlefield with either their heads or limbs missing. Absolutely horryfing when your team gets shelled by a mortar that managed to directly hit 3-4 people and showers the whole area with body parts.
Graphics also look nice, the sky boxes are well done. Shadows are wonky, but the lighting itself is quite good. Do not recommend playing with a high FOV, because it reduces the size of your weapon, and also your iron sights which is CRUCIAL. Playing with 70 FOV, but it still plays and feels nice, due to it's slower nature. Peripheral vision is not the main thing here, since most of the time fighting takes place in front of you.
Unlocking new items is very easy, you get "tokens" which you can use to unlock class specific loadout ranks. Each costs 1 and it's very hard to run out of tokens. New players are not inherently at a huge disadvantage, which is nice.
All in all, a very good and solid FPS game. Would definitely recommend to anyone.

Do me a favor, though -- make sure you have someone to hug and tell they are important to you once you've finished.

I must admit I wasn't expecting much going in, considering the first one to me was a big disappointment from what others said it was, and I myself am not much a horror fan, but frankly I haven't played enough of it to find it repeatitive. I can say how it can be, but with how unpredictable some of the animatronics can be, you'll be kept on your toes.
The point of the game, and I use that word loosely, is to survive 12 AM to 6 AM. You are given a job as a night guard for Freddy Fazbear's Pizzeria. but there's a big catch. There are animatronics in the restaurant that are out for your♥♥♥♥♥ so it's a defense game in which you have to prevent said animatronics from killing you until 6 Am, in which even if they were on the brink of killing you, you go off free at 6 AM. Why they try to kill you is never explained, but the excuse is that they were never given a night mode, thus they go for where the people are, and that happens to be your office. I wonder if they kill people in other rooms during the day too, because again, why they try and MURDER you instead of sing a nice song to you during the night is never explained, but as the nights go on, through phone communication with an anonymous staff member, you are described horrific events that have went on within the restaurant. As well as that Puppet is his least favorite and Foxy is his favorite! <3~
The mechanics are simple but fun and make for a challenging and addictive expierence. There's a flashlight, which you should NOT USE FOR THE CAMERAS FOR THE MOST PART. They're only useful for actual cameras on nights 1 & 2, since you don't wanna waste any of your flashlight with how much a certain animatronic appears, and the only way to stop said animatronic is WITH THE FLASH LIGHT. The music box mechanic is pretty much the only reason to use the camera, which is...Disappointing. One of the 'major' game mechanics you never use and only need to use for one room, a similar problem in the first game with pirate cove. Scott Cawthon seriously needs to make a way to make all the cameras more significant other than just holding the animatronics in place for like 3 seconds..Sure, you could say this is pretty useful but I think it's just pathetic, considering this is probably at least what 25% of the game's data is put into. The other cameras. The death minigames are pretty cool..But there's no way to 'win' and some of them are just a chore, not even worthy of being called 'games' when you think about it. I digress, there are 3 places the animatronics can come from. The hallway in front of you, which you can press on your flashlight from within your office to check, as well as two vents on your left and right. How else to defend yourself given they make it into your office- WHICH THEY WILL BY THE WAY - well, you are given a Freddy Fazbear mask you can wear to fool the animatronics into thinking you're one of them!...Well, most of them. I will describe how I feel about the animatronics and their point in the game below.

Toy Freddy/Freddy Fazbear: I'm talking about the duo of bears that will do more than steal your precious pick-a-nick baskets, starting at the end of the hall to warn you that they're there if you flash your light down. From what I know, unlike Old Bonnie and Old Chica, these two cannot just flash in your office. Although it may be seen as 'easy to avoid' when they have stages of lurking before they actually try to attack you, it seems they catch you at the WORST time, maybe you haven't flashed the flashlight at Foxy, maybe you spent a little to much time waiting to wind up the music box, either way, it'll be these bears' fault.  Essentially, these two are saboteurs that can also kill you if given the chance.
Old Bonnie: This thing is freaking huge for some reason. Seriously, I♥♥♥♥♥♥my pants just from looking at how big he was the first time he appeared in the office. I don't even know why he's so big, or why specifically the front of his face is missing, but it makes for a frightening and formiddable foe. Similar to how he was in the first game, he appears in front of whenever he wants it seems. Just pop on the mask and if he catches you at the wrong time, similar to almost all of the animatronics, you'll be from loving them to hating them in a few deaths.
New Bonnie: Why the hell did this guy get so much significance, or like it seems to be the case. He has a special sequence from whenever you avoid him from killing you, he's always the first one to leave to stage, and he has a freaking guitar. Not to mention he's the only one with a full redesign for the second game. I don't know. Maybe I'm just not seeing how special he is, but maybe they should've made Freddy more special?
Old Chica: God this is probably the most unnecessarily complicated designs I've seen in a while, and sure, Scott captured the 'ruined and terrifying' thing perfect but...Something about is just..Too much. Maybe it's the double jaw making it look like it was from Twisted Metal, maybe it's the wires for hands, I don't know. She's just like Bonnie in terms of her behaivor, but unlike Bonnie she seems to never show up in the hallway, making when she appears even more terrifying.
New Chica: What the ♥♥♥♥ing hell. Wh-Why. Why does she look like she would work at Hooters if given the chance. I REALLY dislike the design, and something tells me it was partially fan/r34 inspired.  She acts just like Toy Bonnie except appears in the left vent with no special sequence, but something about HER design- everything about her design is just...Off for a kid's restaurant or at least compared to the others.
Foxy: This thing will be the bane of your existance and will probably kill you the most. He appears at the end of the hall and if you don't flash the flashlight at him, he kills you on the spot. I don't have the exact intervals in which you have to flash the flashlight, but I'm gonna say roughly 8 seconds. This is why all the other animatronics' appearances are sabotage, even if they don't get you. You're always stressed out by his presence, and to put insult to injury, his jumpscare is probably one of the scariest, given how he literally jumps at you.
Mangle: I really ♥♥♥♥ing like this things' design. I don't know why, but those huge creepy crawly things in games I really liked look-wise at least. Anyway, this is probably the most active animatronic in the game, having the ability to appear in your office at 12 AM, thus having the ability to end your game AS IT STARTS. Although it is one of the easier one's to deal with, seeing as it only appears in the right vent and can easily be avoided by you plopping your mask on.
BB (Satan): This thing is Five Night's At Freddy's Teemo (League of Legends) or Pyro (Team Fortress 2) essentially. Everybody hates him. Why? Well, if you let him into your office (Avoided by putting on your Freddy mask for a few seconds whilst he's in the left vent) he disables your flashlight, leading Foxy to brutally murder you. And he appears all the ♥♥♥♥ing time.
Puppet, The Marionette, The Puppo: This thing is the music box. The thing that always leads you to die. And neatless to mention the highly proclaimed scariest robot. But, the easiest to avoid. Just wind up that music box, and you'll keep that hipster satisfied. He gets♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥if you take away his music.
Golden Freddy: T-This thing is real now. I don't know his pattern essentially, since sorry to say, I haven't beaten Night 6. BUT I HAVE BEATEN NIGHT OF MISFITS, SO CALM DOWN. His jumpscare is pretty hilarious though, it's like the Batman scene switch thing, having his face just charge towards you, dettached from his body. Nothing really else to say about it.
In conclusion, I reccomend this game for anybody who can handle the spooks. Thank for readings.

Writing a review of this is possibly pointless because most people's minds are already made about this game, but if you're still on the fence here's a run down. (SOME SPOILERS)
WHAT IT'S NOT:
This is not a horror game and this is not a traditional adventure game. There are no scares (although there is a creepy atmosphere and a subplot related to a haunting) and there are no puzzles except for very simple ones that involve finding a key to unlock a door, with the locked doors only there to keep you from reading the story out of order. The gameplay is based purely on very naturalistic exploration and finding all the key objects that move the story forward. It costs $20, which I would say is possibly overpriced just based on length, and I would say wait for a sale if you're unsure. I bought it for $10, and I was very happy with that. But bringing pricing into a review of a game is silly, since if you hate it even $10 will seem like way too much and retrospectively now, I'd have been cool with paying $20 since I liked it so much, but I certainly won't knock getting it for $10.
WHAT THIS IS-GAMEPLAY:
This is an experiment in telling a story through environment, and a very mundane environment at that, namely a house lived in by a suburban family, all of whom are going through one personal crisis or another, with the teenage sister being at the forefront. You get to hear narration from the sister character when key items are found, but other than that the story is told purely through the objects that you find, from the more typical letters and notes, to the less typical riot grrl music mix tapes, board games, video game cartridges, coffee cups, book titles, etc. The idea is to give you a house that feels genuinely lived in and to give the player a sense of how the people who lived in it interacted with it, and so all of the objects are placed with care to help tell that story. It's like an interactive series of dioramas that you can explore and physically pick up and examine any of the pieces of, all of which evoke a sense of who the characters are and what they are feeling.
And I freaking love that. I've waited for a game like this for a very, very, very long time, and all the derisive reviews that dismiss it as a "walking through a house simulator" actually made me more excited to play this, and from that angle it does not disappoint. But that's exactly what it is. It's meant to be a game where when you find used hair dye and pillow forts, it's not just supposed to be for the sake of exposition, but to remind you of your own life and your own experiences, and of the symbolic importance that you remember attaching to such mundane things, and to connect with the symbolic importance that the characters attach to them. BUT you're still just finding a used bottle of hair dye, and maybe hearing a bit of dialog about it or a comment from the player character, and if the prospect of that doesn't grab you, then no, this game is very very much not for you.
WHAT THIS IS-THEMES: (spoiler-y section)
Continuing on with the love-it-or-hate-it-ness of this game, it was made by a small team, composed of, by their own description "two of us are women, one of us is gay," and it is set in a very nostalgic 1990s. The more of those intersections that you cross, chances are the more you'll get out of this and the more you'll connect with this, or at least you're closer to the target demographic for a teenage girl love story set with gay themes in the mid-90s, so, again, go into this experience with that in mind. Not that every woman or queer person or person who grew up in the 90s will love this or that every straight man who's not nostalgic for that time period will hate it, because that's demonstratably not true and because we can empathize with experiences that we haven't specifically lived by recognizing the similarities, but, to put it simply, this was clearly a labor of love made by people drawing from personal experiences, so this is a game that works on personal biases that elicit that empathy, both from the devs for the subject matter and for the potential audience. The ability to empathize is key. Basically, if you're not going into this with an active desire to be drawn in by these themes as your state of mind, a desire to enter into the headspace and see a little (or a lot) of yourself in these characters, you won't be drawn in. Like watching a horror movie, it doesn't matter how scary the movie is, you also have to *want* to be scared.
And that sense of empathy goes a long way to spackle over some of the story's flaws, of which there are definitely some. The ending is largely anti-climactic, and the story definitely slips into cliches (although occassionally on purpose in order to pull of some interesting red herrings), and with the presentation removed, it's really a fairly bare bones plot, filled with no distinctly lovable characters, so just as a straight-up story, it'd be a little hard to get into.  But again, to strip the presentation would be to strip the entire purpose of this game, which is to revel in the small details and the evocation of memory and emotion, but for all that work that went into developing this world and these people, they deserved something a little more. I would sum it up as a somewhat mediocre story incredibly well-told, one that will only be put over the top if you personally can connect to the story in some way and hit that catharsis. A good litmus test is that the main character is a whiny, melodramatic teenager, and we see a lot of this world through her eyes. She's well-written, but there's definitely no explicit attempt to make her flaws endearing. Depending on how you view her, she'll either grate on your nerves and make you wonder why the hell you're playing a game about characters you couldn't care less about, or make you smile bittersweetly rememebering how YOU were at that age, or how one of your friends was.
TO SUM UP:
This game is a good game if you know EXACTLY what you're getting out of it and are expecting nothing else.
Stripping away any personal feelings about the game, if you want the straight up "Is this a good game" review, this is an interesting, successful experiment in making a mundane location totally interactive and evocative of story, but with an overall "just ok" story to go along with it, and really not that much to do, and taken just for that, if you're purely viewing this as like a tech experiment, it's definitely not worth the money.
But to make sense of the gulf between the "OH MY GOD BEST GAME EVARRRRRR" and the "This game was terrible to the point that I think this may have been a The Producers-style scam" reviews, it's as simple as this:
If ANYTHING you've heard about this game sounded like a red flag, you're in for a grueling, boring experience. And that's ok, not every game is for everyone, and you should stay as far away from this as you can.
If EVERYTHING you've heard about this game made you excited, and you think you'll connect to the game's themes in some way, you're in for a great ride, and the yes recommendation are for those people only.
But it's a gigantic "yes." With pyrotechnics and acrobats and you can see it from space.
And for god's sake, people who hate this game, enough with the conspiracy theories already about why all the professional critics liked it. If I was going to smell a conspiracy every time a game that I thought was absolutely terrible came out that all the critics across the board gave enormously high ratings too, I'd currently be in a bunker, amidst a stockpile of canned vegetables, weapons, and jars of my own urine, poring over newspaper clippings and a frantically drawn, impossibly complex diagram on the walls by now.

The Souls series is famous for its fantastic game design. Dark Souls 1 had Anor Londo and the Tomb of Giants and Ash Lake, beautiful areas that were aesthetically aweing and mechanically satisfying in every way. Bloodborne had amazingly put together set pieces that you could just look at and be satisfied, let alone the wonderful and varied combat system. I haven't even played Demon's Souls, but just looking at it you can tell how well put together even the earliest entry to the series was.
What does Dark Souls 2 offer? Half of the bosses are reused from old games, some in parts, some just copy pasted with a different (uglier) texture. Almost all the weapons in a single weapon set have the same attacks. The level design is frustrating and best and intolerably incompetent at worst. They just throw enemies at a wall until you can't move without hitting them in areas. I just walked into a fog gate and immediately died because there was a pit of burning tar directly to my left. From the same studio that can make the entire game world a living breathing puzzle, I cannot fathom how to complete certain areas without summoning help, which the developers knew, because this edition gives out NPC summons like they were about to become illegal in 47 states.
This game is, at worst, frustrating for the sake of frustrating, unfair to the player's patience and time, and a shameless cash grab after the probable and deserved poor sales of the original Dark Souls 2. At best, it's objectively the worst game From Soft has made. Use the money you'd use to buy this and save up for any of the other games. If you need to buy a Playstation to play Demon's or Bloodborn, do that instead. Use that money to Import Metal Wolf Chaos instead. Use that money to kickstart an indie game with a souls-like levelling system. Literally any other option is better than putting up with this. If you're a souls fan, its a disgusting dissapointment. If you're not, it'll spoil the rest.
If you do not have 2-3 firends who you'll be able to summon for 100% of the game, do not bother, it's a complete waste.

Now before you think I'm biased I want to let you know that I was just as skeptical about this game as you. But believe me that this is a gem waiting to be played. This game is simplistic in design and adds a few new aspects such a sliding and using teamwork to get to normally unreachable spots throughout the intricate and tight map design. The game itself is extremely crisp and VERY reminiscent of Call of Duty: Modern Warfare. With tight map designs, fast paced combat, and a plethora of PvP or PvE gamemodes. Now a majority of negative reviews are part of the fact that Crytek made this game so graphically it was expected to be at least of par with the Crysis games which though nothing special the graphics are quite appealing. And secondly that the game itself does not present too many new features which is understandable. These two largest reasons are why so many are quick to judge this on the scale of previous Crytek games. Now the biggest question of games of this sort is, "Is it pay to win or pay to play?" The answer is neither! The game itself does reward those that are willing to put real money into the game but the beginning weapons you are given for your classes are more than capable. I have personally chosen to use those weapons over the plethora of other weapons I've unlocked solely due to it's effectiveness! Now as for purchasing new weapons or gear as per usual with these games you can of course buy a gun for a limited time or save up a lot of in-game currency (about 10,000 for a gun) to buy it permanently. Though it may seem like a lot I am fairly decent at the game and still get around 250 dollars average per game of team deathmatch and more if I play a longer gamemode like storm. So to end this review short if you are looking for a game with Call of Duty: Modern Warfare-like gameplay this is the game for you!

Gone Home is a first-person narrative adventure game about a woman coming home from college and finding out about her sister's exploits (and indeed, many of her family's problems). Set in the 1990s, the game features a fine array of 90s era memorabilia. Anyone who was a kid or a teenager at that time period will identify with at least some of the stuff in the house.
GH has received a lot of bad press, mostly because of the most outspoken (and misguided) hardcore/e-sport gamers feel this isn't a game.
What is a game? Hard to tell, really.
You'll get a lot of different answers, but the crux of their argument is that GH isn't competitive, doesn't feature combat, mostly involves you walking around the house and discovering things (hence the derisive term "walking simulator"), and the story is about a lesbian (which is why some people have referred to this game as "Gone Homo").
You'll also hear people say the entire game is pretentious and leftist/feminist or something to that effect. I've seen some people call it "man-hating." How it's that is beyond me, and I'm a 35 year-old male.
Obviously, GH wasn't made with those particular gamers in mind and that's okay. Not everyone wants to play the same types of games.
If you are interested in a story-heavy narrative focused game which doesn't have combat or stressful situations, you might very well like GH. It involves a thought-provoking story that engages your brain instead of your reflexes.
It's not perfect by any means, but it's a refreshing change of pace from the constant "kill everything that moves" tedium that are the vast majority of games.
Don't listen to the obnoxious loudmouthed idiots on Facebook or the trolls who enter into the GH forums simply to cause havoc and attack everyone. For some reason they feel threatened by this game and instead of going off to play something they enjoy, they feel the need to hurt others who like something they don't.
In short, they're bullies, and they aren't worth your time, even if you aren't interested in this game.

Hello, I am a new player to Warface, and have already decided not to play this game. I am not writing this post because I'm "a hater," I simply love games and want them to be as good as they can be. The reason I tried Warface was because of the idea of quick coop shooter missions in a free game. And to that extent, the game plays marvelously. I had a very good connection to my teammates, the game has awesome sound effects, and you can get through missions quickly, so it leaves you excited for the next one.
But everything orbiting the main game itself drags it down.
First of all, there was no character customization aside from just picking a face and moving on. It's not an RPG though, so I that's not a big deal. The bigger issue is that you can't choose between playing as a male or female. I can sort of understand, since having two sexes can almost double the amount of work put into purchasable cosmetic outfits, animations, voice work, etc. But then I learned that you can buy female characters in the shop for an exorbitant price. It cost 500 real-money tokens for a permanent skin or 1000 game money to use it for a day. After doing a mission I earned about 34 game money. So I would have to perform hundreds of missions in order to pay for my crippling addiction to play as a girl for a day. It sounds overblown but that's really how it is. It's not that playing as a female character is necessary, but i find it insulting to charge people for it. If the game had only Default Dan and Basic Betty as starting characters to choose, it would be better than picking your Permanent Male Face and then discarding it to play as The Girl, since there is only one female per class. Buying customization is fine, but offering 10+ free male options and only 1 not-free female option is pretty repulsive. That's not to say the male options were good, they were all boring, middle-aged, fair-skinned (actually maybe there was like 1 black guy?) hard-nosed, rugged "man" made out of the same grey goo as every main character on the cover of a shooter game.
After a few google searches, I found that the lack of an FoV slider is a major point of contention. That contention being that the players want it, and the developers don't. At this point, it's not okay to release a PC game with no FoV slider. It just isn't! People like me suffer simulation sickness when the FoV isn't tuned
. Similarly, the game uses red indicators for enemies and green indicators for allies, and yet there is no Colorblind Mode. Lastly, head bobbing cannot be turned off, even though this is one of the most notoriously dizzying effects in any first-person game.
It's hard to figure out where to start explaining this. First of all, your sensitivity remains the same whether you are hip-firing, aiming-down-sights (ADS), or using a scope. I've never seen any shooting game neglect to make ADS less sensitive than hip-firing. It really boggles my mind how it could have been programmed this way in the first place. This could be fixed if you allowed the player to change in the options the sensitivity for each aiming style separately like you can in other free shooting games like Planetside 2, instead of having one big Mouse Sensitivity slider.
There may be more issues with the game (and judging by how many open topics there are in the Feedback section, there probably are :lol: ) but any of these would be enough to keep me from playing the game. I hope you continue to improve the game, and I'd love to support it, if the game decides to support me.

The game turned out to be unexpectedly fun. There is a gigantic open world environment that is interesting to explore. There is a surprisingly complex weapon upgrade system, vehicles are supported and there is stealth gameplay. The game is a mess in many ways ... It is readily apparent that the details were a secondary concern in this massive, almost bloated, game. For example, when you use a flashlight, the illumination drags behind the camera movements ... to simulate a hand actually holding a flashlight I guess? The end result is that you feel seasick and disoriented from using one of the basic tools in the game.
The main missions are diverse, but the experience is very incoherent. Remember how Valve makes an effort maintain the first person perspective with free camera movements in both combat, traversal, and story beats? This game is kind of the opposite. It feels like a patchwork of disjointed parts.
Performance is a mess in large open world sections, that make up the majority of the game, even when using a Titan X.
This game reminds me of an infamous classic in the open world genre: Do people still remember Boiling Point: Road to Hell from the russian developer Deep Shadows? Both Homefront and that game are reaching for the stars on a too limited budget. The game systems are bloated and lack refinement, but they are overcompensating by providing a lot of content and scope. It kind of works, I guess? Homefront definitely feels like a unique take on the open world genre, just like Boiling Point did in its time. Just don't expect a smooth ride, because this game is full of bugs, confusion and questionable design decisions. Take it or leave it?

INFO:
-Intense, interesting single player campaign.
-Multiplayer consists of various coop missions, independent of the campaign.
-All optimization and framing issues I had-- outside of the opening cutscene-- were solved by adjusting the graphic settings to fit my system.
PROS:
-The game is difficult. It forces you to realize that you're not some COD badass, you're just some idiot with a gun and something to fight for.
-The game areas change as you play. It's amazing to see this pro-KPA zone full of collaborators and such go and turn to rioting and uprising against the KPA because of your actions.
-The guns feel real. They look heavy and slightly bulky because IRL they are heavy and bulky. You're character acts like they're heavy and bulky and this affects your ability to fight with them.
-The strike areas and strongholds are each unique and different-- no one location mirrors the next. Sure, each relief center or whatever will have similar goals to capture it, but the layouts between them make each location unique.
-The journal entries and other textual documents are actually really interesting and fill in a lot of the backstory.
-The open world is legitimately open. You have your missions, but there are numerous side objectives to make your journey easier. Even how you complete your objective is up to you. For example, if the game wants me to capture a stronghold, I have a couple options. Do I use my RC car, attach a hacking device to it and hack open the gate? Do I set charges on cooling vents and blow a hole in the wall? Do I grab a motorcycle, find a ramp and jump the wall? Once I'm inside, do I go COD style, pull out my LMG and mow everyone down, or do I move quietly through, killing when I have to and biding my time? Of course there are many more options than this, but you get the idea. To be honest, different areas require different methods to succeed.
CONS:
-Occasionally during scripted scenes, and especially during the opening scene, the audio won't match up with the video. It's more annoying than anything else.
-The "Hearts and Minds" missions are fairly repetitive. These missions are where you're trying to get the people in one of the zones to rise up and fight the KPA. The results of the missions are generally different, but the mission itself is the same.
-The motorcycles and RC cars are difficult to navigate. The accelerate too quickly and get stuck really easily.
-Once you get into your rhythm with your weapons, there's no need to buy the others. This can happen fairly early on in the game.
-The AI is sometimes inconsistent, i.e. when they'll spot you and when they won't, etc etc.

It's amazing how much loathing GH brought out of youngsters, quick to disguise it behind 'rational,' 'objective' criticism of both gameplay and writing. Players who never think twice about writing quality were flooding the corners of the 'net with either vitriol or waxed objectivity.
I adored the game. Storytelling is what I want to see focused on in video games these days, and this game delivered something truly incredible for the medium. Connections were made, emotions were felt, yadda yadda, but what I can't stop thinking about is something my friend's said for years: "Video game people are trash."
It's a minority, but it's that very loud minority that thrives on the 'net, making these angry comments a dime a dozen. In between the disgust at the themes of homosexuality, you'll find the age-old assertion that reviewers were clearly either paid off or scared of offending The Feminazi Agenda, or, like, whatever. In reality, GH is simply bad fan fiction meant for the Lifetime channel's audience to fawn over; not worth its cost specifically because you can speedrun it in 1:30 minutes; manipulative pandering to Gen-Y'ers (nefariously plotted by the developers to fool 20-somethings into thinking they like a bad game because it has a digitally-rendered trapper keeper); rubbish because Sam's a teenager and acts like a teenager; doesn't lend itself as a video game and thus should not be reviewed by the video game press, but rather should be treated as a bad--of course--novella self-published on Kindle.
Sam's side of the story treads on YA fiction tropes, and, admittedly, understanding or enjoying those tropes enhances her story significantly. (5 years ago I probly woulda agreed with the story criticism. YA fiction? Pfew, that's fer dumb kids.) Where some of the more eloquent complaints drag down on the predictable cliche, on the archetype, the simplification surrounding Sam's sexuality, and the fact that her story and hers only gets narration to, like, 'beat you over the head,' as many have so nicely put it...I saw all of this as a clear necessity of the message it was conveying and for the audience it was conveying it to. It wasn't just speaking to LGBT players, it was speaking to that sense of being an outsider we all felt and lived to some degree during our stints as dumb, selfish kids.
But then the game didn't stop with her story, it wasn't just video games' Looking for Alaska in 2-4 hours, it had a handful of other tales written for entirely different audiences, with their varying depth hidden to better fit the 'adult' audience. Add that to the game's brilliant steps in storytelling: It doesn't just match John Green at his most irreverent--in those few short hours it also affects those crustier hearts: You Can Do Better.
Will I care about what these folks said in 5 years? Nope. Will anyone? Probably not specifically, but it's depressing as hell to see this juvenile baloney so strongly and widely present in gamers.
-- Metacritic

let me tell you, I thoroughly enjoyed the experience provided by the game "Gone Home".
What began as a subtle, creeping horror, a feeling that everything you once knew is now, somehow, wrong was quickly replaced by an emotional rollercoaster that, at the end, left me feeling elated and exhausted, and wondering "what do I do now? WIll I see her again? What can I do now that this has ended?" It was as if I'd really been a part of something as huge, and exciting, and as horrifying as the experience laid out for the protagonist myself, and something was genuinely missing from my life when I finished this.
I actually felt like I connected to the characters, to their story and their plight. I felt lost without them, and I longed to see them again (even though I had never seen them).
The audio logs and music in this game made it great for me; it adds a depth to the characters, helps you glimpse their world, and how the world views them, and why the game ends the way it does.
This game is a psychological masterpiece, and should definitely be recommended to anyone looking for a depth of storytelling that can (and will) leave you blinking back "manly" tears.

Homefront is apparently a franchise I’ve never heard of. According to some reviews, it’s not a direct sequel to anything. The story is pretty easy to follow, we’re treated with a short but sweet intro sequence that tells us that the North Koreans had been selling the USA technology for decades… But when it came time to pay up, the US was in debt and collapsed… So they just moved right in and took over the country in payment. Since most of their tech was purchased from them, they were evidently able to shut down most, if not all defenses the US had.
Honestly that’s probably a better explanation than most military shooters these days. Homefront went back decades to set up the downfall rather than the quick “Suddenly the russians are here” or “some PMC did a successful power-grab and owns ALL THE GUNS”.
At the very least, it does a good job of properly suspending my disbelief. The intro does a whole timeline starting from the 1970′s with a voiceover describing how everything slowly went to hell for us during the next 50 years. Fair enough.
Reviews are “Mixed”, however most of them talk about bad optimization and how the game barely runs… That ceased to be an issue for me a couple months ago when I upgraded. As a result, Homefront runs fine. The occasional FPS drop, and even that went away once I tweaked my graphics settings - Most of which are on High (Though not on Very High).
Mechanically, the game has its ups and downs. It’s a sort of psuedo-open world that is comparable to the Far Cry series. Indeed, one could sum this game up with “Like Far Cry? Play this”, because it’s the usual tower/base/zone control where you assault a stronghold or radio and that zone suddenly gets littered with resistance fighters, which in turn, helps you traverse the area a little more safely.
I say “psuedo” because there’s not a whole hell of a lot to do while running between base-controls. Every now and then a dynamic event pops up (Such as five snipers pinning down a squad), wherein you get some money and resources for completing it but they’re skippable if you have your sights on a mission - which gives you a lot more money and resources.
There’s only one mechanic so far that I despise - Driving. There are bikes littered throughout the zones and sometimes you need to take it into a building and park it on a sort of wheel-generator, hold down forward for a bit to “charge” a generator, then you’ve captured the base. The problem is, as it kind of was with Far Cry, is that vehicle driving in first person is a huge pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ I tap D and it turns a full 45 degree angle when I’m just trying to inch away from some rubble. At least Far Cry gave you a large open world with fields - This is Philadelphia. There’s rubble EVERYWHERE. In my six hours of gametime I’ve yet to go thirty feet without ramming straight into something. So I'm screwed if there’s ever a mission where I have to drive one through a siege.
So far that’s been my only source of annoyance. A less annoying but still irritating issue, some of the bases are hidden in buildings where you have to find a secret ‘entrance’ in order to get into it. I’ve had to resort to youtube and walkthroughs twice to directly point me to where I need to go because I once spent ten minutes circling a building and climbing around the stairs, only to find out there was some blue paint on a bookcase that I never even saw. I walked by that bookcase a dozen times but that damn paint was never in my field of vision.
I also left a safehouse to be stuck in the “leaving” animation, where a Korean shotgunner was right there unloading into me. Some safehouse, right?
Beyond that, I’ve run into a couple of bugs but nothing has been directly gamebreaking, except one broken base that I can’t control… Hopefully restarting the game will have fixed that.
So I’ll just sum up with “Like Far Cry? Are you a 100%-er? Then you probably won’t mind this.”

This games biggest issue is not many play it, scratch that, almost none play it.
For starters, it is better than TF2 (but that's not hard to do) or at least very similar. which where the issue is. Just like TF2 this game has odd bots (The skill level of the bots is all over place. sometimes they don't know how to melee other times they never miss a single shot.) But, people play TF2 so you never notice it.
For example, there is no playing raptor with normal level bots.
The raptor is played similar to the spy from TF2, minus the cloack.
You HAVE to get behind them or you get picked apart. Some of the maps it's easier said then done, but doable. But, with bots, it doesn't matter. The moment you come in line-of-sight of the Allied forces, they instantly snap to you, no matter where you are, and rain death onto you. If you're actually able to close the distance on them, they instantly swap to their melee and take you out before you can even land a blow.
Game currently favors the nazi's. The allied forces have a decent group with some okay specials. (Not counting the medics, they're basically the same person, just pick male or female.) but the Nazi's have pretty much every advantage, which is historically accurate, but in a game where dinosuars walk around with Assult-rifles strapped to their back, Historical accuracy shouldn't be the name of the game.
Examples, The allied forces have one dinosaur named trigger which is... Not going to lie, didn't see a point behind the little guy. Felt like he was just there so the allied forces could have a Dino, even if he is just a reskin of arguably the weakest dino.
Haven't played the DLC yet, I think it's odd they make you pay for Co-oP considering the fact that so few actually play this game. That being said, Really wish the Goat was apart of the allied forces in the base game, even if just for the sake of giving the allied force some degree of a point behind playing.
It's more team focused than TF2 (Example, in TF2 the engi can lay down a dispensar which heals and restores ammo with the engi being there. In this game the allied forces have two classes that do the same, one for health, onr for ammo, but they have to physically be there, which demands a greater sense of teamwork.) So for Comp teams that are looking for a fight, this game is a decent enough pick. If you can get a full match together.
The rounds typically don't last very long, I chalk that up to imbalance between the factions and only a handful of game modes that rarely last long in other Team based shooters.
If this game had a greater player base, I would instantly reccomend it over all the others. It's a great game with a interesting concept, which is the reason I'm giving it an Up vote. It's not bad, it's just few play it.

If you explore every inch of Gone Home's mansion, it will take you about 3 hours.  Not once during those 3 hours will you solve a puzzle, combine inventory items, be chased by a monster or interact with NPCs.  The story is told through rifling through the nooks and crannies of your family's home and uncovering the skeletons who lurk in the closets of your parents and your younger sister.  Virtually all of the dialogue is voiceover narration by your sister in the form of audio logs which chronicle an intensifying relationship with her friend Lonnie.  Gone Home is bursting at the seams with details, the gradual discovery of which slowly patch together a narrative and setting that a man of my age found very easy to relate to.   While some of these details require too far of a stretch of the imagination (love notes or evidence of a possible affair left lying around for anyone to happen upon) and the ending thuds pretty hard, I found Gone Home to be overall enjoyable and the perfect length.  Recommended!

TL;DR – Not a "game," but a novel approach to storytelling. Worth experiencing.
If you're interested in this title, please keep the following in mind: THIS IS NOT A GAME (in the traditional sense). Much in the vein of "Dear Ester," this is a form of interactive storytelling. Rather common in 90s PC "games," this title is aimed at exploring a story by piecing together a narrative from the environment around the character. It's titles like these that are going to either be engrossing to some or uninteresting to others. Frankly, calling all interactive media "video games" is a bit of a misnomer, just as much as it would to be to consider a rap mixtape the same as a classical opera: they share a similar medium (and possibly, even, many common elements), but are vastly different and have different appealing qualities.
As for the title itself, just like any story, the appeal of the story will depend on your own preferences and persona. That said, avoid just watching a "Let's Play" and give it a try. If you're interested enough to want to experience this story, you should try it for yourself. The atmosphere has been artfully constructed, the resulting effect then of wandering through an empty home is chillingly quiet and intensely intriguing. I found the characters interesting, the stories sad and wonderful, and the little Easter Eggs fun. Still, it will all depend on your preferences.

By now, I'm sure you know that the hype surrounding Gone Home was a bit misleading. Google any game news feed if you need more of an explaination.
This isn't a "game" as much as it is an "interactive experience/story". So, establishing that fact up front - this exprience is "meh". Gone Home starts by setting an erie and unsettling environment as a young woman whom just got back from an extended period of time to her parents empty home (on a dark and stormy night). Your "task" in this story is to search for clues as to why everyone is gone and what happened while your character was away. The concept is interesting, but ultimately the pay off is lackluster. The story seems as if it may take a supernatural twist and become intense, but it never really does anything memorable, and the conclusion just kind of made me wish I hadn't wasted an hour and half searching for a great story that never really solidified.
I'd skip this one unless you're really into erie settings and clue-finding first person experiences. Even then, It's still hard to recommend.

Let me get the bad parts of Gone Home out of the way first. There is no challenge present in the slightest, it's hardly even a 'game' at all. The runtime for me was barely over an hour, and I read nearly every piece of story to be found. That being said, very few games I have played have had an emotional impact on me the way Gone Home did. You play a girl named Katie who has spent the last year abroad and has finally come home to visit her family, only to find the house completely empty. Every little detail in the house has a purpose, and while there is an overarching 'plot' to the game, there are actually several subplots that are equally as powerful as the main story. I highly recommend a playthrough if you find the price is right and you are looking for a welltold story that can only come from the gaming medium. I personally got the game in a Humble Bundle so I don't feel 'ripped off' in anyway, but buyer beware, you are getting only a hour of entertainment from Gone Home. It might be one of the best hours of gaming out there, though.

Dark Souls 2 is an action role-playing game set in an open environment. The game evolves around the player character who begins with a human who is cursed to always resurrect after dying. To break the curse, the undead travels to the fallen kingdom of Drangleic and is tasked by the Emerald Herald with obtaining four Great Souls from other powerful undead.
The game's plot is minimalistic, and varies based upon how much the player explores. There is little guidance and lack of direction given. The player must come to his/her intuition as to which path one must take, which can ultimately lead to a dead end, desired destination or even branching paths. Despite all this however, the plot is deeply ingrained in the essence of light and dark and how one cannot survive with the presence of one another.
This game is not just an ordinary casual RPG. It is an intense RPG for hardcore players who seek a challenge, as dying is frequent and bosses are abundant. To add to that, enemies deal a lot of damage and players must learn to time their blocks/parries, attacks as well as dodges rather than hack n' slashing. Save points (bonfires) are limited and scattered far from one another. The game evolves around the concept of using deaths to teach players to learn from their mistakes, as well as how to react in almost relentlessly hostile environments. From experience, there has not been many RPGs that has challenged me the way the Dark Souls series has. I must reiterate: this game is EXTREMELY difficult.
The button mapping and camera controls for keyboard is messy. If one were to consider buying this game, it is a PREREQUISITE to have a gamepad/controller or you will be in for a hard time. The graphics is not the best, but it is made up by the deep gameplay and non-stop action.
Overall, Dark Souls is a quality RPG game that challenges players to a new level. It's gameplay may be minimalistic and feel like a lack of direction, but it was designed in that manner to allow the player to unravel and uncover the deep story plot through thorough exploration. It is matched with sheer happiness and relief upon progress and completion. If adventure is to surprise and mystify you and invite you to uncover the secrets of a forgotten world, then Dark Souls is a great game for you. If entertainment is fun without failure and progress without pain, you'll have to find another game.

Well, besides the pointless argument about "this is not a gaem" this is mostly what says on the tin. If you don't like reading Steam descriptions before buying a game and feel wronged, you are at fault.
That being said: This is a really good storytelling experiment. It manages to make a house that for most part feels realistic and lived in, which is great and can get you wondering about how much can you learn from someone through their personal belongings and the way things are arranged in the house. If it is not the sort of stuff that you might find interesting, please don't buy this game. It might be something interesting for a game designer to play, specially if you're concerned with environmental storytelling. The story told isn't really extraordinary and characters are flat and borderline token lesbians, so I wouldn't give it points for "daring" to have gay characters, because for most part it isn't really what defines the characters. Instead they are defined by teenage romance tropes and 90's nostalgia.
So in short, don't buy this game if:
a) You think regarding something as "not a gaem" makes it inherently inferior.
b) You don't like games without somebody to kill or a " " "challenge" " " (Can't put enough scarequotes around that word)
c) You can't be bothered with descriptions on the Steam store.
DO buy it if:
a) You have 20 dollars to throw away (because the price mark is really one of the least lovable things about this game)
b) You want to see how much can be told about a character just through the space he/she's lived in.
c) You want to learn things about environmental design.
d) You are in need of increasing your gaming hipster/connoisseur cred.

Bought this on sale for 11,49€.
Played it for 75~ min.
Returned it after.
Why? ->
While the game plays rather realisticly as you die once you get hit by a rifle round, with how your characters movement is played out, how you aim and such things this is sadly more of a hinderance in actuall gameplay due to the poor netcode. While on top of it, it encourages people even more to just camp as they allready do, due to the nature of this game.
It does not help when my movement & aiming is realistic if the netcode is so bad, that a guy who just a second ago had turned his back to me, while crouching, does a 180° in less than half a second and instantly shoot & kills me.
It does not help when people at bigger distances are rather warping than walking - (kinda like its the case in BF3/BF4) - just in this game the distance this starts to occur is way, waaay less - If you ever played Battlefield 3/4, you know what I mean with warping players at distance. Imagine the map Noshar Canals on BF3, the all loved TDM mode map. From the train yard respawn to the crane, thats the distance players would allready start to warp-run in Verdun, its just bad. In fact you'd still have a very good chance of hitting & killing them, if they would not warp that is... and since not everybody warps, thats even more of an annoyance.
Could be only the players with bad connections warp, could be its random, I dont know, but it does not really matter since w/e the reason may be, its entirely & utterly stupid, gamebreaking and in this game also totaly ambiance-destroying.
Sadly this game also kinda feels like a free2play game the first time you start it. Once you level up you get, lets call them "unlock points".
You have 4 classes you can choose from, well classes, they have somewhat different guns but thats it pretty much at the beginning.
You need to unlock just everything, its like the new players are ment to be cannon fodder until they somehow manage to get enough unlock points to unlock the good stuff, like Grenades, Scopes, (presumably) better weapons....
In the 60~min I did actually play I got 3 unlock points, everything you unlock costs 1 point BUT now we have weapon attachments aswell, like bajonets & scopes (scopes are a must have pretty much). To get those you need to unlock one after the other, for every gun. So you need to buy the gun for 1 point and then spend 1 point for every attachment. The trick here is attachments unlock after each other, so lets say you want the scope, you still need to unlock the bajonet first to even be allowed to unlock the scope and so forth. It is just stupid.

And that unlock system is right where the next issue starts, you have no idea whats good, what the stats on any gun are, ROF, ammo capacity, damage ... You know it once you unlocked it and even on google I could not find any proper Verdun fansite that would list gun statistics or such. I guess you could google for the historic weapon names but that wont tell how they act in the game, at the most you'll know the amount of ammo they can hold.
So yea, obviously I'm aware that other FPS games also use those, imo, just ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ "unlock ingame content by gaining XP" or simular, but Verdun chose to implenet it just extremly badly overall.
Another "issue", more of a performance problem, when you die you can watch other players untill you respawn. However for some reason watching those players maxes out your GPU. I have a 970 @1400mhz, when playing Verdun maxed (apart of AA. I had on the second highest option), it never went above 75% GPU usage from what I've seen. Once I watch somebody when I'm dead, 99% GPU usage instantly, 55 - 60FPS
Its not necessary a big deal, or anything gamebreaking, but it does not really speak for the performance quality of verdun either.
If you can, somehow, look over all of these issues, dont have a problem with camping & holding positions - like it legimately was in the trenchwarfare in WW1 - and dont have an issue with only seeing one enemy every 30seconds or so (unless they/you actually play the objective and attack-charge), you might get something out of this game. Otherwise, I would not bother. Honestly Verdun looked extremly promissing, but it fails to deliver.
Don't be intimidated by people who are saying the game is super hard. It's really not, it's just a huge circlejerk. Unless you're a filthy casual of course.

Edit: I've now ran an entire playthrough and have successfully completed the game on the standard difficulty so I figured I'd revisit this as I intended.
This might be the end of the Homefront franchise as we know it, if not forever. A disappointment I'll never get over. I wanted to love this game. Instead I tolerate it.
Initially I was scheptical about the jarring day one complaints and number of proposed bugs and issues many people seemed to be having that I simply wasn't. However after playing without issue for a few hours before taking a long break (a week or two) to allow some patching and otherwise cleaning up of the overall experience, I found that little had changed aside from that rediculous saving bug that occured every few minutes, forcing frames to drop to near zero as the game autosaved. I still experienced choppy visuals and framerate issues as well as god awful bugs like repeating or broken sound clips, xbox and PS4 controller prompts for buttons I'd recently seen a keyboard shortcut for, the usual tripe. There was nothing that prevented me from proceeding through the main campaign or the flashpoints but they were still everywhere.
Gameplay is thoroughly average, you capture bases and take territory, you kill some norks, you ambush some more norks, you use resistance boobytraps to launch norks thirty feet into the air, the game truly is just a run and gun affair with some not so nice stealth mechanics thrown in.
The gun play might feel floaty (I have aim assist off) and the recoil might seem excessive if you're used to current gen shooter mechanics- I'm looking at COD here, not ARMA3, so prepare for a vague learning curve on how weapons and the very basic cover system work together- though as a shooter it flops around like a fish out of water by comparison to superior releases in the genre.
The cut scenes and key character models are marvelous, but seem wasted when you look at the sub-par AI and the repetitive skins used for some of the civilians or non-essential fodder. Though I've not had any of the issues with people witnessing enemy vehicles simply not reversing when they hit walls etc, I have seen some less than stellar combat where enemies don't flank, they don't seem to adapt, they don't seem to think at all. They shoot at you, they duck, they run somewhere else thirty yards away, duck and shoot, and lets not forget the charging blindly at you around a corner deal. They sure like to rush you. Just like real combat! Not.
I'm getting a little ranty but I felt like given how hard this game has been nailed to the wall, I have to give it some credit, it went through a terrible development process and an even worse development cycle and it certainly shows on the rougher edges- but I DID have fun, and where the visuals are nothing ground breaking for 2016, I'd gladly say they're keeping up with many current shooters whilst not establishing any really new trends of their own.
TL;DR? Proceed with caution, read the reviews, check out up and coming patch notes and maybe try and grab this one on a sale. I don't feel it warrants a negative review but just barely earns a positive one. When you waited as long as I did for this game, only for it to get squeezed out of the digestive tract of a series of less than stellar studios or developers and handed on for someone else to clean up? Well it more than pains me to say it was thoroughly average.

I played through, and completed 'Gone Home' and was left with massive disappointment. This is no game at the end of the day, it feels more like a tech demo of sorts.
Graphically, it does the job that it sets out to do I suppose, with nothing awe-inspiring to be found within. Everything is presented as you would expect with most 'home' locations in games these days. The rooms are very well decorated and do feel very realistic in their layout.
Audio-wise, there's not a lot really besides a fair few audio dialogues throughout the game. They tell the story of why the house is empty, mainly through letters written by the protagonist's sister. She gives brief details on the father and mother but mostly talks about what's been going on in her recent life and ultimately, reveals nothing of significance to the person playing the game. There's nothing found within the storyline laid out before you that actually impacts upon what you're experiencing in the house and as a result it feels a very dis-jointed experience. If anything, it's extremely mis-leading as what sounds and feels like a horror game of sorts becomes... nothing. A simple traipse through an empty house.
It's hard to say how the game plays when there's really no game to be found within. It's like a 3D version of those mind-numbing hidden object games, except you aren't exactly given clues in 'Gone Home' as to what you need or why.
Reviewers apparently went crazy for thise game, and awards were bestowed upon it. I just don't know where the hype and praise came from because deep down, it just feels like a more advanced version of HL2's 'Lost Coast' mod, or 'Dear Esther'. If you have come to 'Gone Home' expecting some kind of survival horror, or heck, even just a game with a beginning and an end, you won't find it here.
In a word? Dreadful.

I thought Gone Home was absolutely fantastic. It was beautifully atmospheric, the thunder giving me a fright every time it thundered. I absolutely love unravelling a story when I play a game, and that's what this is. It's an interactive story, with every note that you read placing another piece to the puzzle of where are your family. I didn't know what to expect when I played this game, and I think that's the best way to play it. I think you have to want to play a game with no action. It's wonderfully crafted with thought going into your character and her relationship with her family. I felt at home in my character's body, I felt scared for her, and I felt happy for her.
Perhaps the price is a little high, I bought it for £4 or so on a sale, but I think £8 is an appropriate price point. It took me 2 and half hours to play, offering very little replayability. Except perhaps in a few years once I've forgotten what has happened. But that playtime is the equivelent to watching a film. And I pay £7 to go to the cinema, or £10 to buy a new DVD.
I loved this game and would definitely recommend it if you enjoy unravelling a story. And perhaps it's on sale.

I wish there was a neutral rating I could give this game.
It's obvious that Warface was built around Co-Op. The missions which you can play with 4 other people are fun as hell. You actually have to coordinate to get through them. If you don't have a capable medic in your team - you're screwed. If you rush ahead and don't wait for your teammates - you're also screwed.
Even the bossfights require cooperation between teammates. In moments like these is where the game really shines with potential.
However, the Competitive PVP modes don't feel right. They feel tacked-on and too fast-paced. And the reason behind this is that the gameplay itself just isn't designed for such Call of Duty-esque run and gun fast-paced multiplayer. The gameplay concentrates on details - it has lots of animations which make the game feel rather sluggish and slow-paced - kind of like Battlefield. This kind of gameplay would be perfect for larger-scale PVP combat, and NOT the tightly packed maps which we have here.
It's like the game developers themselves couldn't decide whether they wanted to create a slower-paced realistic type of FPS, or a fast-paced twitch shooter. And what we get at the end is a weird, inconsistent mixture between the two. Fast-paced gameplay just doesn't work with Warface.
Now, of course since the game's free people will have suspicions about whether or not it's pay to win. I'd say that it kind of is, but not by a lot. The awful weapon rental mechanic is here, but thankfully, there is a way to unlock permanent weapons by earning XP specifically for them. The only problem is that once you've selected you want your XP earnings to go towards the unlocking of a certain item, your XP progression only matters for this item only.
In other words, you can only work towards unlocking one item at a time.
And of course this unlocking requires quite a bit of grinding, so brace yourselves.
All things considered, it is a pretty high-quality shooter. If you feel like cheaping out on Battlefield, feel free to try this one.

This is a unique take on a WW1 FPS. Not only is the game beautiful to look at, the movement and game play are tons of fun. The weapons are consistent with the WW1 era which makes for some interesting variety. Another aspect of the game I find appealing, and unique to Verdun, is the terrain. These guys were in trenches, sometimes in hilly regions, other times mostly flat. There is rain, mud, smoke, haze - all these things make navigating the battlefield, without losing your head, a challenge. This is, in most cases, a one-shot-kill game. So, rushing, taking a couple of hits, then ducking to regen your health is not an option. The only aspect of the game I've found a bit frustrating is there is the concept of deserting. At different times during play, parts of the map are playable, while others are considered out-of-bounds. Entering the non-playable area and not leaving very quickly results in your death, due to desertion. I understand why the mechanic is there, but feel it could use a bit of fine tuning to be a bit more fair.
That said, Verdun is a beautiful, well crafted game offering hours of raw, head-popping fun -- I definitely recommend it to others. Hope to see you in the trenches!

To be honest, I don't understand why this game has so many bad reviews. It is an excellent release, worth every penny. What they accomplished, being in the shoes of the resistance fighter, was done extremely well. This is not Doom or Call of Duty and even thinking about comparing to those is plain silly. You will not be fighting waves of enemies like Rambo. If you attempt to do so, you willl die very quickly. You are supposed to be adopting guerilla tactics, which involves a lot of hit-and-run, outsmarting the enemy, etc. It is an FPS in its own right and big props to the devs for getting it right. Also many concepts were borrowed from later Far Cry games, such as visibility indicators and take-downs and having played all Far Cry games, starting with first one, I can't say this is a Far Cry clone.
I hear many people are having performance issues. I am running it on MSI GS60 pro gaming laptop with 970 and it runs very smoothly, with the exception when the level has just loaded. I don't see any framerate drops and run on the high settings.  Graphics are pretty good as well, not the best though.
The only complaints are NPC animations, which look a little clunky, especIally of other resistance fighters. Maybe also having an ability to drag bodies away would help, especially in yellow zones. AI can be stupid sometimes, where you can corner them in a small hallway with nothing else but a knife. In one of the yellow zones I managed to slice up about 15 or so soldiers with a little health damage. In an open firefight they are generally pretty good, hiding behind covers and flanking more often than not.
Would I recommend buying it? Hell yes! If you are concerned about price, you can get an activation voucher in other places for less.

Dark Souls 2 is an action role-playing game set in an open environment. The game evolves around the player character who begins with a human who is cursed to always resurrect after dying. To break the curse, the undead travels to the fallen kingdom of Drangleic and is tasked by the Emerald Herald with obtaining four Great Souls from other powerful undead.
The game's plot is minimalistic, and varies based upon how much the player explores. There is little guidance and lack of direction given. The player must come to his/her intuition as to which path one must take, which can ultimately lead to a dead end, desired destination or even branching paths. Despite all this however, the plot is deeply ingrained in the essence of light and dark and how one cannot survive with the presence of one another.
This game is not just an ordinary casual RPG. It is an intense RPG for hardcore players who seek a challenge, as dying is frequent and bosses are abundant. To add to that, enemies deal a lot of damage and players must learn to time their blocks/parries, attacks as well as dodges rather than hack n' slashing. Save points (bonfires) are limited and scattered far from one another. The game evolves around the concept of using deaths to teach players to learn from their mistakes, as well as how to react in almost relentlessly hostile environments. From experience, there has not been many RPGs that has challenged me the way the Dark Souls series has. I must reiterate: this game is EXTREMELY difficult.
The button mapping and camera controls for keyboard is messy. If one were to consider buying this game, it is a PREREQUISITE to have a gamepad/controller or you will be in for a hard time. The graphics is not the best, but it is made up by the deep gameplay and non-stop action.
Overall, Dark Souls is a quality RPG game that challenges players to a new level. It's gameplay may be minimalistic and feel like a lack of direction, but it was designed in that manner to allow the player to unravel and uncover the deep story plot through thorough exploration. It is matched with sheer happiness and relief upon progress and completion. If adventure is to surprise and mystify you and invite you to uncover the secrets of a forgotten world, then Dark Souls is a great game for you. However, the game is clunky and I feel more like playing an unfinished project: AI navigation, Hand-to-Hand combat, animations aren't smooth at all. Disclaimer: Despite that I have 77 hours on Steam, I actually have over 200 hours logged into the game, as I've been playing this game before it came to Steam, in fact I've been playing this game when it used the GFACE web launcher, and I have the in-game banner to prove it. Also, skip to the end for the TL:DR.
---------
-Introduction/Gameplay-
Warface is another example of the "Great Idea, Flawed Execution".
Warface is a "squad"-based near-futuristic FPS set in Africa, China and other generic locations. The developer, Crytek, being the same company responsible for Crysis, would make this game follow in line with their pass games. While it does to a lesser extent, the innovation of Crysis is only marginally being used in this game. The key feature being the ability the swap weapon attachments at will. That is literally it. The only other "innovation" (I use innovation pretty lightly) is sliding. Needless to say, this game falls more in line with Call of Duty ripoff shooters than it does being a Crysis clone, which in my opinion, would actually be better.
For PVE content, the game has 5 maps on different difficulties. 2 normal, 2 hard and 1 "insane". However, the game suffers TREMENDOUSLY from Artificial Difficulty. On Insane, your team can get wiped very easily, either through a charging one-shot kill CQB unit, a Demoman, a Spec-Ops, a Sniper that can fire faster that you or someone threw a grenade "accidently". On some maps, there literally is no strategy, if there is, the "strategy" comes from simply camping in a specific spot in the map.
The "bosses" are truly one of the most hilarious things I've seen in a while. There are three bosses: Heavy Gunner, the Mech and the KA-50 Helicopter (which is actually Mi-24 gunship). Considering the broken nature of the game, these "bosses" can be taken down relatively easily if you know what you're doing.
For the Heavy Gunner, find cover, wait for him to reload and just shoot his back. Or if you're brave, you can actually spin around him until he reloads, however only medics can do this trick effectively.
Depending on the Map, the Mech can be easily taken down by having someone camp in a specific part of the map, while letting other players get rocket launchers to destroy the Mech. If the map doesn't a specific camping spot, the Mech doesn't have an effective strategy to defeat.
For the Helicopter, if you have the Aquatic Assassinator, it can be taken down in less than a minute if all of your shots hit. Despite being a WATER GUN, the game treats with explosive splash damage. However, if you do not have the water gun, there is no strategy on dealing with the copter.
Both the Mech and Helicopter have INFINITE ROCKETS WITH NO RELOADING. Needless to say, you can seen how frustrating this can be on Insane maps.
-Business Model-
I will give credit to the game for not being P2W, but then again, it's hard to make a Co-op based game actually P2W.
You need to complete missions to earn rewards, which is pretty standard. HOWEVER, the rewards you get from completing missions (talking about PVE) is very low. Not including the First Mission Win bonuses, the amount of money you get is $160 (for Normal maps). This is a huge problem because money plays an important factor to your loadout and dare I say, the way you play the game itself.
I jugde rewards based upon monetary gain rather XP. As money is the most crucial currency in the game, when honestly, it should'nt be this HARD to actually earn money without the use of VIP Boosters, which can increase your rewards to a maximum of 255%.
You see, this game uses a "Repair" system in the game. If you've been playing F2P for quite awhile (especially those Aeria F2P games), then this should easily turn you off. All items in the game (being weapons, armors, items and consumable) can be bought with in-game money. However, oddly enough, smoke grenades are timed exclusive and only white smoke grenades can bought in in-game money. All the items are separated by "tiers". Being Common, Rare, and Ultra-rare. Do not be fooled by such a thing, as the rarity only shows you how expensive it would be to repair the weapon or item. One of the most useful item(s) in the game is the Warlord Armor Set. However, it is literally the most expenisve things you'll get in the game to repair.
The repairing system is actually time-dependant rather than being dependant upon how frequently you use it. So, let's say you joined the match with the wrong class or the wrong loadout, when you leave, you will be punished regardless. Due to this fact, people tend to rush games so they can keep thier repair costs to a minimum.
Since because the real meat of the rewards is the first win bonuses, you'll only play the 5 PVE maps, wait until tomorrow to refresh, and do it again.
-Playerbase-
Throughtout all my years of playing games since kindergarten, I've NEVER seen a playerbase so........ asinine. The playerbase in the game is truly dreadful. Not in terms of toxicity, and in terms about how really stupid these players can be. It also does not help in your favor when the MAJORITY OF PLAYERS SPEAK SPANISH OR PORTUGUESE. (Despite playing on the North American server). As a result, teamwork communications is obviously non-existant if you don't speak the langauges.
On Insane Maps, the common team is 2 riflemen, 2 medics, and a sniper. However, considering the playerbase is full of morons, sometimes it's only one medic (that being me). Everyone loves to blame the Medic for their problems, even though it was anything but their fault (being the Medic).
What these idiots fail to understand is that, you are supposed to bring 2 medics on Insane maps, not 3 snipers, 1 rifleman, and 1 medic. But, IF YOU DO NOT REVIVE THEM, they are going to attack you regardless if it was (not) your fault. These idiots also fail to understand that the defibrillators for the Medic have a ~15 second recharge time, which basically means you cannot revive multiple teammates in a row. But they do not care, and are still going to insult you for not reviving them.
To be honest, I've had FAR MORE bad experiences with the players in this game, I could tell you but the reviews have a character limit.
-TL:DR-
If you question yourself whether or not you should try this game out, or if you're lazy to read the review and skipped here, then the answer is no. You very much are only going to be playing this game for a few hours before you get easily bored of it.
