I absolutely love this game. its not like call of duty (and youll find a lot of the people complaining about it are big fans of call of duty), you have to take your time but also sprint into the trench as fast you can. primarily its one shot kills apart from the odd handgun, this can get very frustrating if you're new as while you are trying to figure out the game you also keep dieing.  you will get better and you will start to see how the game flows.
My personal tips for new players:
-pick a non vital role. play as a rifleman until you've figured out how the game flows and how some of the other classes use their weapons to its best abilites.
-be prepared to die. lots. like a said, its primarily one shot kills, and if theres a well placed enemy machine gunner then everyone will be dieing on regular basis.
-don't worry about reloading or saving grenades. you most likely will not live long enough. this will change, just wait till you have a moment when you realized you survived an encounter that you usually die in.
-even spread defense. it works in rugby, its works in verdun. spread out and cover the sections of land in front of you, if theres a weak spot, the enemy will find it. also if theres a spot on the trench no one wants to defend because theres constant machine gun fire and bombing, thats the spot they'll be invading.
-watch your mini map. defending: watch for areas with weak numbers. attacking: if you see a teammate(s) in the trench infront of you then theres no enemy there, charge in and give em a hand.
-communicate with your team. if theres a camper, if you see a mass charge, if the enemy has just killed you and are invading that side of the trench, let em know. make your reports short but detailed. again youll see the flow of the game after a while
- last but not least. GET IN THERE!!- rifles are the most common weapon in the game. if you have a single shot rifle that does not make you a sniper even if you can peg a guy or two from 150+ yards. snipers have scopes. if your rifle has a bayonet then your role is to charge, and keep charging. we only win if we're in the trench we're attacking.
But seriously, a great game at a fair price.

As stated many times previously if you are looking for a "game"...of any description...move on.
What "Gone Home" creates is a compelling short story where the reader (player) creates the narrative themselves through exploration.
I found this deeply compelling, beyond the main storyline there are subplots that are not handed on a plate. Read everything. Every letter. Every scrap of paper. Understand what narrative is being played out in the scene before you. How have the rooms been left?
The commentary points to "My So-Called Life" as an influence, and this completely hits the nail on the head. It captures the time and place of the 90's more than anything else in the medium and certainly takes me back to my own teenage years. I felt a definite emotional connection through the entire story (Although the consumed rum during play may have added to this), the final conclusion felt rewarding, and I was so pleased that the writers did not ultimately betray the characters.
I heartedly recommend.

(I'm going to attempt to keep this as spoiler-free as possible, but that's kind of hard, since some of the reasons I love this game so much are kinda spoiler-y.)
Where do I even start with this? I was pretty skeptical because of all the negative reviews this got, but I picked it up on sale anyways. I was already pretty aware of how part of the story goes, thanks to some spoiler-y things online, so that was a bit of an incentive. What I wasn't aware of, though, was the actual ending. Watching this entire story unfold was great! No, this is definitely not the game for you if you're expecting enemies, combat, bosses, or jumpscares. This isn't a horror game. It's definitely got a spooky feel to it, though, which is really nice.
On the topic of the story, I really saw a lot of my friends and myself in this game. The strong teenage emotions, the parents that just don't understand, the feeling of needing to rebel against how ♥♥♥♥♥♥ society is. You basically get to unfold how the sister, Sam, dealt with all of this. It's hard to be more descriptive without giving away a huge plot point.
Okay, I'll just come out and say it, if you're in the LGBT+ community, you'll probably at least somewhat appreciate the story in this game. Even if you're not, there's still a good chance that you'll enjoy the story.
The main reason I see people♥♥♥♥♥♥talking this lovely game is because of how the media handled it. Apparently it was overplayed, oversold, given reviews that were "too good." Honestly, if you're just bitter because of politics and/or "game journalism," you need to get that♥♥♥♥♥♥outta here. Let people praise this game if they want to.
Do I think it's worth $20? Ehh, that's debateable, which is why I played it safe and picked it up while it was on sale. If you happen to catch this for like ten dollars or less, I'd say go for it. Give it a try. Just don't go in expecting hardcore action or anything spooky happening or whatever. This is a game about exploration. It's a 3D interactive storybook. If you know that before getting into it, you'll be much more satisfied.
TL;DR: Good exploration game with a lovely story that gave me butterflies. Price is meh, so you might wanna grab it on sale.

i absolutely love this game, and even though i havent even gotten to ng+ on either of my two characters, i have become pretty op(if i wanted to be) with my first one, a strength build.
even though i find a certain amazement in this game and role-playing games like it, there is one very bad experiance i had just TODAY. ill get to that later, though, right now ill state the pros and cons. just after stating my personal opinion of this game lol
this game is just simply amazing, hands down! i just cant hate it for very long at all, regardless of what happens. i have a very interesting playstyle, mainly running around and taking advantage of the short moment of invicibility you gain when rolling(its so short by the time you recover it ends, make those frames count!), and even though the total weight of your equipped items will put a serious hindrance on the more, "mobile" play styles, i managed to cram all my needs for this play style to make me light, AND still pack QUITE the punch. and for that i am very deadly against most NPCs, although my actual play style usually involves swiveling around to a small enemies backside and stabbing them in the back, and hammering the larger ones real hard before they can recover. and the game is still fun :D
NOW for the pros and cons.
pros
+this game can support and even encourages variety in this game, i recommend swapping play styles or at least creating and designing different characters(you can have many characters) for different play styles and equipment layouts.
+the graphics are very pretty, i recommend standing at the edge of the cliff in majula. the water is amazing!(water is quite hard to design in games, fromsoftware did a very good job)
+there are so. many. items. you can try out all the different items and see how they would help you, if you should equip and use them, etc.
+there arent as many areas as i would like to admit(although some of them are rather expansive), but each area is either unique from all others or blends very well with its adjacent areas.
+a good few bosses, most of the areas in the game have their very own bosses, with a few exceptions.
+phantoms and invaders can now finally use their own estus flasks! :D
cons
-unlike the original Dark Souls, you CAN be invaded while hollow, which is unfair in my opinion because you still cant summon support while hollow. also, human effigies are harder to get then its Dark Souls equivelant(humanity) and doesnt heal you when consumed.
-the bonfires themselves now have absolutely NOTHING to do with the amount of estus in your flask, you must now find estus flask shards hidden through out the world and return them to the person that gives you the estus flask itself. you start off with 1 charge of estus(!) when its first received, and every shard only increases it by one charge.
-i very much hate the fact that, unlike Dark Souls, Dark Souls II gives rings actual weight and durability, activating a rings ability degrades it and the weight of just one ring can mean the difference between life and death.
-this con ties in with the bad experiance at the end of this review. certain bonfires, and i have no clue which ones(i can safely confirm "kings gate" bonfire as one of them, though), are not in secure locations. by "secure", i dont mean there is an enemy right next to it, that would be stupid... what i mean is other players can invade you as you rest at that one bonfire, which would immediately kick you off said bonfire and make it unusable for the rest of the invasion.
now for my "bad experiance". i was basically screwing around with my layout, i didnt really care whether i ended up as a light or heavy class, since im skilled with both. in pve. im actually fairly bad at pvp(and my layout wont help) in any area but a certain, open area in "doors of pharros" where the entire floor is flooded, hindering movement speed and tipping the tables in my favor. anyways, i was playing with my equpiment to see what two weapons would give me all 5 types of damage(physical, magic, fire, lightning, and dark) when powerstanced. well, i had both my normal weapons unequipped and in place one very, very bad weapon. and just then, i was invaded by some chick with a curved sword. i was standing at the "kings gate" bonfire, which resides at a very cramped section of "drangleic castle", and my best option was fighting her in the room that had the bonfire in it, which was a very bad environment for pvp since its a very small room and it has the bonfire(which counts as a wall and therefore cant be moved through)right in the middle. we were both forced to move and roll around the bonfire and therefore in the same redundant circle. i managed to get one of my main weapons on before the fight, but than she got so many cheap shots she cast a pyromany called warmth that heals anything(including enemies and bosses) adjacent to it. this made the fight more interesting, and longer, and i managed to do decent damage, but she ultimately killed me very easily. i was and still am very angry because of that, since i was by no means ready. of course, the game wouldnt just hit you in the face and scream in your ear "HEY! YOUR GON' GET INVADED!", but there are moments when you cant do pvp, such as afk time, and that time is usually spent at a bonfire. oh wait, fromsoftware forgot to make certain bonfires secure from invasions! way to go, devs.
i would normally give this a ten out of ten, but knowing that in certain areas(and i have no clue which) i can be invaded while afk really makes me mad, so i'd give this an 8/10 just for that.

I loved this game so much the first time, I replayed it a year later.
This was a shining example, in my opinion, of a 3D short story. While the bulk of the story consisted of exploring rooms and counting doors, I never  found myself bored. This is because the story, to me, was so compelling.
Yes, it was a cliché angsty teen romance, but it's the one I wish I had when I was a kid. I hate to say I loved this story more because it was a gay romance, but it's true, and you have to give it that credit. I sincerily hope that this game helps out some LGBT teen out there in these situations we've all been in.
Novelty aside, the story was pretty cute. The two main characters are quite a pair; the silly, cool, devil-may-care girl we all knew in high school, and the oddball, punkish girl looking for somebody that understands her. For a 90's kid, at least (I'm pretty sure there's some translation there, for others out there) I found myself really pulled in by their personalities.
Those last few pages, as you trek back across the house, nothing to explore, left only to listen, were some of the most emotional moments I've experienced in a video game. I'll fully admit I was bawling by the end of it. Especially once I got to the attic.
I guess, in closing, I say take this story for what it is. If you like a teen romance story, you're set. If you're gay, I'd really really suggest checking it out. And if you're a crybaby like me, have some tissues ready.

i absolutely love this game, and even though i havent even gotten to ng+ on either of my two characters, i have become pretty op(if i wanted to be) with my first one, a strength build.
even though i find a certain amazement in this game and role-playing games like it, there is one very bad experiance i had just TODAY. ill get to that later, though, right now ill state the pros and cons. just after stating my personal opinion of this game lol
this game is just simply amazing, hands down! i just cant hate it for very long at all, regardless of what happens. i have a very interesting playstyle, mainly running around and taking advantage of the short moment of invicibility you gain when rolling(its so short by the time you recover it ends, make those frames count!), and even though the total weight of your equipped items will put a serious hindrance on the more, "mobile" play styles, i managed to cram all my needs for this play style to make me light, AND still pack QUITE the punch. and for that i am very deadly against most NPCs, although my actual play style usually involves swiveling around to a small enemies backside and stabbing them in the back, and hammering the larger ones real hard before they can recover. and the game is still fun :D
NOW for the pros and cons.
pros
+this game can support and even encourages variety in this game, i recommend swapping play styles or at least creating and designing different characters(you can have many characters) for different play styles and equipment layouts.
+the graphics are very pretty, i recommend standing at the edge of the cliff in majula. the water is amazing!(water is quite hard to design in games, fromsoftware did a very good job)
+there are so. many. items. you can try out all the different items and see how they would help you, if you should equip and use them, etc.
+there arent as many areas as i would like to admit(although some of them are rather expansive), but each area is either unique from all others or blends very well with its adjacent areas.
+a good few bosses, most of the areas in the game have their very own bosses, with a few exceptions.
+phantoms and invaders can now finally use their own estus flasks! :D
cons
-unlike the original Dark Souls, you CAN be invaded while hollow, which is unfair in my opinion because you still cant summon support while hollow. also, human effigies are harder to get then its Dark Souls equivelant(humanity) and doesnt heal you when consumed.
-the bonfires themselves now have absolutely NOTHING to do with the amount of estus in your flask, you must now find estus flask shards hidden through out the world and return them to the person that gives you the estus flask itself. you start off with 1 charge of estus(!) when its first received, and every shard only increases it by one charge.
-i very much hate the fact that, unlike Dark Souls, Dark Souls II gives rings actual weight and durability, activating a rings ability degrades it and the weight of just one ring can mean the difference between life and death.
-this con ties in with the bad experiance at the end of this review. certain bonfires, and i have no clue which ones(i can safely confirm "kings gate" bonfire as one of them, though), are not in secure locations. by "secure", i dont mean there is an enemy right next to it, that would be stupid... what i mean is other players can invade you as you rest at that one bonfire, which would immediately kick you off said bonfire and make it unusable for the rest of the invasion.
now for my "bad experiance". i was basically screwing around with my layout, i didnt really care whether i ended up as a light or heavy class, since im skilled with both. in pve. im actually fairly bad at pvp(and my layout wont help) in any area but a certain, open area in "doors of pharros" where the entire floor is flooded, hindering movement speed and tipping the tables in my favor. anyways, i was playing with my equpiment to see what two weapons would give me all 5 types of damage(physical, magic, fire, lightning, and dark) when powerstanced. well, i had both my normal weapons unequipped and in place one very, very bad weapon. and just then, i was invaded by some chick with a curved sword. i was standing at the "kings gate" bonfire, which resides at a very cramped section of "drangleic castle", and my best option was fighting her in the room that had the bonfire in it, which was a very bad environment for pvp since its a very small room and it has the bonfire(which counts as a wall and therefore cant be moved through)right in the middle. we were both forced to move and roll around the bonfire and therefore in the same redundant circle. i managed to get one of my main weapons on before the fight, but than she got so many cheap shots she cast a pyromany called warmth that heals anything(including enemies and bosses) adjacent to it. this made the fight more interesting, and longer, and i managed to do decent damage, but she ultimately killed me very easily. i was and still am very angry because of that, since i was by no means ready. of course, the game wouldnt just hit you in the face and scream in your ear "HEY! YOUR GON' GET INVADED!", but there are moments when you cant do pvp, such as afk time, and that time is usually spent at a bonfire. oh wait, fromsoftware forgot to make certain bonfires secure from invasions! way to go, devs.
i would normally give this a ten out of ten, but knowing that in certain areas(and i have no clue which) i can be invaded while afk really makes me mad, so i'd give this an 8/10 just for that.

As a 3-year veteran at rank 31 (which is actually really bad), I have over 500 hours on this.  When I first starting playing it there were very few game modes to chose from.  The coop screen had only three difficulties; easy, medium and hard.  The versus (I don't really remember what everything looked like) had maybe team death match, plant the bomb, and free-for-all.  Special Operations were included in coop originally, but several additions to SO were put in, which made it stand out as one separate mode.  The original SO had just tower raid, which was 18 floors of increasingly more difficult AI's attacking you with shotguns, knives and other explosives; and just MAYBE Cold Peak.
With the doubling of coop missions (now Easy, 2 normal, 2 hard, and one insane), tripling of versus (now free-for-all, team death match, plant the bomb, bag-and-tag, storm, capture, and domination), and tripling of Special Ops (now tower raid, Cold peak, and cyber horde), this game has been my most played game for over 2 years.
There was just a recent update called "Operation Coliseum" which I haven't played yet (cuz I'm writing this review), I don't know if it's Special Ops or not yet.
Coop missions start with your team (consisting of between 3-5 players depending on which difficulty your on) entering the map in a chopper, rather than just spawning in the map randomly.  After leaving the chopper and walking a bit away, it will fly away far beyond the map's exterior and not show up again until the end of the section.  Once in the map, players much work as a team to complete the mission by killing all enemies (called "Blackwood), including regular, on-ground fighters, snipers, shields and machine gunners.  There is a mid-map boss called a heavy gunner which can only be killed by shooting him in his back with heavy fire.  One good way of killing him is by flanking him and waiting for him to have his back towards you.  Once he starts to reload his machine gun, the sniper and medic can reek all havoc on his back and kill him.  I have been in games where 3 or 4 veteran players automatically, without thinking, go into strategic battle alignment and kill him instantly.  It is POSSIBLE to kill him yourself (I speak from 2 experiences), but you need to be patient and resourceful for a long time.
Towards the end of most games, there is a boss called a "mech", which is very hard to kill.  You have to use bazooka-like guns to shoot him in his belly several times before he falls.  When he is down, you must shoot the top of his head until he dies.  Repeat several times.
Only 2 maps have an enemy chopper to destroy at the end.  To destroy them all you have to do is shoot it with bazookas like 10 times.
I know I'm going on and on about this game without really REVIEWING it.  So here's my opinion.
One of the pros to warface are the games modes.  There are 15 possible games to chose from (listed above), and dozens of maps to play them on.  My favorite modes are storm, plant the bomb, capture, insane, and easy.  I can complete easy by myself so I usually just find 2 or 3 noob players to carry them through it.  On the dark side I usually need 3 or 4 veteran players to carry ME through the insane maps lol.
This game needs two things: A single player campaign (or better yet a campaign where a team of 3 or 4 friends can play through several hours of Blackwood enemies and missions, all in one big "story") and a decent voice chat.
One con to this entire game are the hackers.  In EVERY SINGLE MAP there is at least ONE hacker who has an outrageous KD who no one can kill.  Luckily Crytek has implemented "fair-fight" into Warface, so every few days I get a worldwide notification that "so-and-so" got banned for life.
That's all from me, I highly recommend this game for anyone who likes immersive coop missions and severely intense special ops.  Its free and only takes 2 hours to download.  HAVE FUN!!!
Almost forgot, most of the original coop maps aren't available thanks to the new updates and maps that come out every few months.

Verdun is ambitious...
Verdun is a game that explores a setting that only strategy games have gone into. It has you duking it out in trenches in a 'king of the hill' esque gameplay mode. You'll fight as various armies from WW1 as you take turns attacking and defending with each. This game lives in dies in trenches with you following NCO's and working as a team to take objectives. On paper this sounds amazing but unfortunately it's not. This game is not well optimized and doesn't look that great, the gameplay itself is a snooze as you either move through the trench getting shot at for not knowing what to do or just run around blindly. Verdun expects you going in to know what you are getting into. It does little to explain itself and get you adjusted to the controls and mechanics. I can't recommend this game to anyone except those looking for a wonky "realistic", "historically-accurate" shooter that doesn't deliver. Red Orchestra is a better blend between the casual and the realistic setting this is going for. Pick that game up instead it's got a few hundred people less than this game and is cheaper. Don't buy this unless it's on sale or from a grey key site.

LATEST AND FINAL UPDATE: I finished the game, 30 hours all told, and I really enjoyed it. I had one lockup after 27 hours, but that was it, otherwise it was great and mostly glitch free, one small bug that prevented a minor side mission from being completed, but nothing that effected the campaign. So, as before, I give the game a definite thumbs-up.
UPDATE: I now have over fifteen hours in and I'm still enjoying the game. The game world gets even more interesting when you reach the Ashgate Yellow Zone (which is the third Yellow Zone, if you include the first one you see at the start of the game). There is color and a whole different looking environment than the first couple of Yellow Zones.
And in those fifteen hours no crashes, no glitches and most smooth 60fps gameplay. It has slowed down at times, but the only way I knew was via the Steam fps counter, otherwise I never would have even known it's was doing 60fps. And damn, it's a really pretty, very detailed game.
ORIGINAL REVEW: I have in just under eleven hours on the Steam version and I’m really enjoying it. It does have some rough spots, but it’s a lot of fun to play. I like open world games and Homefront scratches that itch. I think combat is a lot of fun and the modular weapon system works great and is a nice change. The plot is rather thin, but really so was the plot in Watch_Dogs and it didn’t bother me. The game map is fantastic. I don’t have any issues with the “greyness” of the Red Zones, there is a lot of color and objects around all that concrete. And there are tunnels and high catwalks and all sorts of paths to use.
I do have issues trying to access some of the harder to reach locations, the game doesn’t make them easy. However the designers included a clever system of using blue paint or flags to let the player know that there really is something to find and gives hints on how to reach them.
Some people have faulted the AI, but I’m finding them a challenge. They do seek cover when fired on, call in reinforcements and will flank you. And in the Yellow Zones, your stealth techniques really do get a workout.
It’s not a perfect game, but it is fun. And if it doesn’t break new ground in some areas, it’s better that the recent Assassin’s Creed games and as interesting (in a different way) as Far Cry 3 or 4. Fair warning however; it does take a good half-dozen hours before you really experience the complete gameplay.

Games for a very long time have been about fun, enjoyment, a leisurly pass time that people use to escape the harshness of reality, or to acheive something great and experience something unique to them. Recently, though, a lot of game journalists and critics have started to talk about the need for less violent, less action-heavy, and more original games focusing on things we've never seen in games. As a result, games like Gone Home were created to fill the niche people have been looking for. What should have been (and would have been) bottom-of-the-bin indie story games have since become critically acclaimed classics. I'm not one to bash any game, since the creation of more unique games is never a bad thing, but to praise this game among others in the same genre who did it better, is ridiculous.
This game was basically the almagamation of the perfect parts to create a game that appeals to exactly everything critics were looking for at the time; 2 parts visual novel, 1 part taboo story, and 99 parts contrived. The phrase "oscar-bait" really comes to mind when I think of Gone Home, almost as if it were a paint-by-numbers on how to create a game critics will love for that year. It delivers nothing we haven't seen already, while delivering it in a way that we've seen more than a handful of times, but it was released at just the right time and played by just the right people to get it major acclaim from journalists and critics, something alot of the other games in this genre didn't get.
Gone Home is an interesting beast in that it delivers all of it's gameplay in a way that we've seen before, and is still not interesting in this format either. There is no gameplay other than picking up letters, cassette tapes, random household items, and keys (to name a few) and observing them or adding them to your inventory to advance the plot. While observing these objects, you can read the text on a note, or rotate the objects to observe all sides a la L.A. Noire, and sometimes find information like lock combinations and secret locations on the map. In that respect, the game does the minimal investigation very well, but then it faulters over it by placing a million objects in the game that serve no purpose. Since the game has no direct way of really determining what is important, it's just as likely that a three ring binder could have valuable information than a book with some information on it. You could spend a lot of time picking things up hoping to get something important only to find out that everything is pointless to interact with, and only a few key elements are there for any real reason.
Ultimately, it's a game that lacks any real interaction, and real mechanical substance, and leaves the player feeling as though they're not being engaged and have 0 agency in the game world they're a part of. All of these facts can be a great way to present an interesting story to the player, one they have no control over and have to experience no matter what decisions they make. Sadly, though, the game doesn't take that opportunity and just creates a bunch of hoops the player has to jump through to experience the rest of the narrative. You have to work for the narrative by way of abitrary hoops, but the game hands you the solutions, then you can continue and "experience" the rest of the narrative. Had they simply added some challenge, some actual thought, something like piecing together clues instead of just having the clues handed to you, there would be a very interesting mechanic in the game that would have really pushed this closer to being a game than a "jump through the hoop to advance the plot" story.
Gone Home is something that got stuck between being a movie and being a book. As a movie, it would've been terrible since it has nothing of substance for the person to experience other than seeing the character experience something. As a book, it has very little build up and is nothing more than just reading about someone reading some notes with very little internal dialogue and character devleopment outside of the few audio/text logs given by the sister. It delivers it's narrative in a way very few games have before, but is in such a way that no game (or any narrative) should
be delievered. The story is presented entirely through narrative set pieces, naration by the sister of the main character, and notes scattered through-out the game. As far as I'm aware, story writing 101 is to not give the entirety of your exposition by way of indirect narrative (i.e. something the audience can't actually see occuring). If the game was you playing as the lesbian sister and seeing all of the consequences and making the choices and experiencing the hardships, this could have been a perfect story, and something we truly had never seen in video game format before.
In terms of atmosphere, this is barely at "visual novel" levels. It has set pieces and locations that can be interpreted as showing off the mood and personality of different characters. Other than the maybe two or three set pieces that really evoke this emotion, there is
little to help visually tell the story other than creating a set-piece to something mentioned in a note or audio log. Something that really broke the immersion (or lack there of) for me, was the fact that there were a million notes scattered through this house that's supposed to be somewhat realistic.
. It's almost as if the house is just a big collection of "ooo look, something from a classic movie that realistically makes no sense"! There's trap doors, walls that just seemingly open up for no reason, and a totally stable cavern under the house that also makes little to no sense in reality. The atmosphere of the game is completely broken when you take the few poorly implemented "gamey" elements that the game tries to include, and apply them to the serious narrative the game tries to put across.
My biggest gripe with this whole game, and the biggest flaw in it, is the fact that it sets up so many possible scenarios and gives a really tense, almost horror-like feeling. A lot of people have attested the feeling of constant tenseness to the feeling the character has when they arrive home to see a life they know very little about anymore. That would be acceptable if the game was invoking a sense of anything other than tenseness/anxiety. Creating a constant tenseness or minor anxiety for the sake of making a narrative point is just annoying, and results in the player feeling mentally exhausted and getting little payoff for it. Ultimately, the game taking an approach that was the exact ending it seemed to be setting out the whole time seems lazy since it doesn't match up with the eery atmosphere the game was evoking the entire time
What it all boils down to is a game that, if it were released any other time, would've been extremely niche, and avoided by a lot of people. It's passable at best, and presents nothing we haven't already seen done better. The atmosphere is confused, the narrative is boring and presented in an extremely unengaging way, and the lack of gameplay leaves the player in an empty "jump-through-the-hoop" scenario to just advance the plot to see if anything interesting ever happens. If you're looking for a game that is a visual novel, I'd aim more towards a game like Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons or any Telltale game since they deliver in all of the aspects this game fails to (plot progession by more than arguous tasks, real character connection, a feeling of agency, and a real plot that is more than just some "cute" dialogue between characters). If you can guess the plot of a story game because you've seen the exact same elements in other mediums, then there is something inherently wrong with calling it the game of the year.

Well I am going to absolutely honest here I have accessed so far the 4th part of the city into the game within the 2 hours (slightly over 2 hours actually) of gameplay I have actually played in this game.
I firstly must say I been looking forward to this game since it was first announced and I played the first Homefront. I have read the reviews from others and other major sites. I can honestly say the only negative thing I can personally find in this game is optimization.
Gameplay and graphics were spot on in my opinion and even though I set my expectations low because I didn't expect it to even release after waiting so long with no news. I am extremely appreciated of the fact they brought everything I honestly expected in the game. Story is pretty good so far and I have no complaints and the gameplay and the feel of the game is very good.
Optimization as I mention is the only downside of this. I did update to the latest drivers in hopes for SLI to work with this game since it was provided in the latest drivers by Nvidia, but it seems SLI does not work for this game. So I am only able to get on high settings across the board (nearly maxed settings, but not quite there) and I achieve a stable framerate around 90 FPS constantly through my playthrough of the game. Of course when I attempted max settings the frames were so unstable and plummeted to nothingness when it is maxed out. This would be the only downside, but the game only just released so I am not going to gripe about it because of that and will wait and see for future updates.
As for other negative reviews and the reviews from IGN, etc. I honestly would suggest others to take it with a grain of salt. I would honestly give this game an easy 8.5 for the quality gameplay, story and experience this game has given. Which I personally find very enjoyable right now and I like the game and for those who enjoyed Far Cry or any type of shooter game this is great.

I personally find this game a good successor of both it and the Homefront series and hope to see more like it in the future (with better optimization and graphics).

Verdun is ambitious...
Verdun is a game that explores a setting that only strategy games have gone into. It has you duking it out in trenches in a 'king of the hill' esque gameplay mode. You'll fight as various armies from WW1 as you take turns attacking and defending with each. This game lives in dies in trenches with you following NCO's and working as a team to take objectives. On paper this sounds amazing but unfortunately it's not. This game is not well optimized and doesn't look that great, the gameplay itself is a snooze as you either move through the trench getting shot at for not knowing what to do or just run around blindly. Verdun expects you going in to know what you are getting into. It does little to explain itself and get you adjusted to the controls and mechanics. I can't recommend this game to anyone except those looking for a wonky "realistic", "historically-accurate" shooter that doesn't deliver. Red Orchestra is a better blend between the casual and the realistic setting this is going for. Pick that game up instead it's got a few hundred people less than this game and is cheaper. Don't buy this unless it's on sale or from a grey key site.

I had some hope for this game but nothing unrealistic.
Graphics - fairly okay graphics, nothing anyone that's played shooteres hasn't seen before, decent night lighting, and using the flashlight at night actually illuminates like a flashlight. NPC character models are just okay copy and pasted NPCs with maybe a duifferent weapon or helmet.
Sound - Okay sound quality as well, voice acting is okay. Actual voice from characters in the game is wonky, Sometimes too loud, too quiet, some times screaming at your face and then whispering to you.
Gameplay - The meat and potatoes and I'll sum this up to be quick.
- A to B Ultra linear progression,  example, you start off in a district, and then follow story points, rinse repeat. The only difference is that there are some side stops you can make on the way and loot. On that topic, you have an EXTREMELY simple craft and loot system, nothing crazy just 5-6 ingrideints to make a grenade or two, or a couple of devices.
- Side missions, pop up and repeatable usually the Same AI's in the Same exact area doing the same exact thing.  There are other Side missions to do that arent repeatable.
- The AI, is weak at BEST, most don't engage you, and if they do all you need to do is find a corner or doorway preferably, and then simply wait as they single file rush the door one at a time, if they even manage to find the doorway pathing. Most will stand in the open waiting to shoot at you, some take cover... very few react to seeing you, unless you let yourself get scanned. Friendly AI is even weaker, there's a half parkour system, the AI does not use any of it, and won't follow you unless there's a walkable path.
On top of this the enemies here are pretty much actual robots, they take upwards of 2 headshots to 6 nody shots to bring down,  unless your using sniper so if your expecting realism this isn't going to be your sauce.
AI spawn points are pretty terrible too as it's possible to clear a building or containers and have enemies spawn where you just cleared. even if you were undetected.
attacking enemy walled strongholds is a joke, the enemies attempt to leave the stronghold or buildings to come kill you, or simply run arund ground level in the middle of it. Instead of using cover and tactics to try and fight you.

I've had a great time with this game so far. I've seen all of the horrid reviews describing this game as terrible, but personally I can already tell this will be one of my favorite games of the year. The story is quite intriguing to me, I love the revolutionary aspect. The environments are beautiful, even though I run the game on low due to a bad computer. It runs at a solid frame rate for me as well. The gameplay is amazing, too. The guns each individual different recoil kicks and sounds make them quite distinct from eachother and gunfights feel amazing. The weapon customization is one of the best things about this game, as every gun has 2 other sub-types. For example, the battle rifle, my personal favorite weapon, comes off the shop as a DMR, but it can also be turned into a semi-auto sniper rifle and even a "freedom launcher" rocket launcher! Every gun in the game including the basic pistol has 2 other weapon convertions available for it, adding even more variability and possibilities for strategy. In my setup, I use a shotgun with the "incendiary launcher" conversion with a marksman rifle as my other weapon. The game will remind you a lot of Far Cry, as it is open world and has different zones with activities to do inside, like capturing outposts. Except, this game takes that Far Cry formula to the next level. The outposts to capture have variability and are fun, instead of the Far Cry outposts where I'd get bored and find them just as tedious chores to do. The world around you feels alive as while you walk around, some citizens may support you, but others may be "Nork" sympathizers. This game is truly a diamond hidden in the rough. The only problem is the sub-par optimization. Frame drops aren't too common but they happen sometimes and it's a bit of a inconvienence but I can get past this as I enjoy the game a lot. The game is actually rather difficult, too. I played it on normal difficulty with aim assist off and I found that stealth was a requirement unless I did some hit and run. You might want to go guns blazing right off the bat but patience is the key as you really feel like you are a revolutionary due to the KPA outnumbering and outgunning you. The multiplayer is actually very fleshed out and really makes you feel as if you are a revolution. You can do some amazing things when you work together in this co-op mode. Now, for the final verdict. I reccomend buying it on sale due to those optimization errors and bad AI, but wait a while and that will be fixed (hopefully). I give the game an 8.5/10 due to stellar gameplay and story, only limited by bad AI and a below-average launch.

To be honest, this game really isn't special or worth it's asking price. Just go watch one of the bazillion walkthroughs and you'll get basically the same experience from playing it.

I have to admit, this game wasn't as bad as many of the reviews said it was. Goes to show you can't trust any reviews except your own. However, this game wasn't for me as it probably was for many other players. Although I only played the game for approximately two hours, here's my opinion on how well Homefront: The Revolution did in standard categories.
Some notes to keep in mind:
-Average shooter skills
-Played on hardest difficulty
-Avid FPS player
-Average system spec (i7 4790k, GTX 660TI, 16GB 1866MHz ram)
Now onto the review...
Graphics: 7.5/12
The graphics are what you would expect from a CryEngine game, it is definitely higher end than most games. The city looks very realistic and almost Division-like although it has a more scanty and poverty driven erosion rather than abandonment. Rain and water on the ground reflected somewhat accurately albeit I see random white spots in buildings indicating small puddles, even when it was night time. Graphical glitches are present like many people have seen; so far I have seen enemies caught halfway between walls when they die, friendly AIs with no guns, and quite frequently a floating dead drone. Overall, the graphics was not the problem for me, even with those funny glitches.
Audio: 2.79/5.58
Sound tracks were okay, but the voice acting wasn't very smooth and there were many bugs with my playthrough. If you press esc or alt tab while an npc was speaking, their speech was gone completely. Only the animation would remain. Not even the subtitles would continue if the speech disappeared. You would think the sounds of the weapons would be closer to the real thing, afterall we live in 2016 and effects are pretty accurate and realistic nowadays. Instead, this game chose to focus on its cutting edge graphics and just kind of toss the audio in the blender and hoped it mixed well, which it didn't.
Performance: wtfwhy/2
Why did the developers decide to waste money on denuvo? Dunno, but one thing I do know is that wherever Denuvo is, performance issues will come. It takes a moderately high to high end pc to continuously run this game at 60fps. For me, the game only took a dip to about 35-40 FPS but that was still enough to make the shoddy gunplay in this shooter somewhat hard to control even with controlled single shots from a decked out assault rifle. Changing settings didn't do anything: I restarted the game with low, medium, and high settings (minus AA and VSync for all of them) and didn't see any change in FPS. The controls were somewhat easy to understand but not as customizable as you may think. Only the basics were allowed to be changed, however things like replacing the holster button to something more convenient than 0 (zero) was not possible because it wasn't even in the keybindings.
AI/Difficulty: lol/420
Enemies and allies were all hit or miss on the hardest setting. There's a 50% chance you run into a convoy that does the right thing and defends it with their lives, taking cover and moving up when neccessary. The other 50% you have either every KPA in the block and their mothers bumrushing you as they spawn close by or wall huggers. Yes, wallhuggers. Doesn't even matter if they are shocktroopers, assaults, or even vehicles. They will pick a wall, they will run to that wall, and they will hug that wall. Outside of skirmishes when its time for stealth, you can't rely on your pistol because they won't go down with a single headshot. Takedowns are reliable but the stealth mechanics in this game makes it so easy to be spotted unless you are taking a lone soldier down. On the hardest setting I managed to secure all of the first zone when you are ambushing a convoy by just taking cover and popping headshots which you should be doing anyways, cause ammo is limited. Given the fact that Dambuster guaranteed Dark Souls-like difficulty... can't say they properly did that because the AI is bad.
Overall: meh/5
This game is okay; it isn't as good as Far Cry 3 or Crysis, but it is a hell of a lot better than the first Homefront. Weapon customization was a big plus, story was also much better as you aren't stuck with the same 3 ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s the entire game, and just being able to freely choose if you want to gather materials or do missions makes this game a whole lot better than what I expected. However, in my opinion Homefront: The Revolution doesn't make the cut with triple AAA games... You can't just slap the words CryEngine on a game and then expect people to pay $60, we want more than just graphics. Not only that, but to take away the multiplayer PVP and then leaving only COOP was a bad idea. If this game was released at $30 then maybe I might have bought it, but for now I'm taking my $60 and going to Overwatch

Gone home is an interesting game for me to review, as it isn't a typical game that I would play. In fact, nothing about it is typical. Gone Home is a mystery adventure game where you play as a college age woman returning from a year in Europe to find her families new home empty. If you look at Gone Home in terms of it's story, it's great. I would say brilliant, but the ending left something to be desired, as well as leaving Oscar's story a tad bit cofusing. The gameplay itself is nothing speacial. You wander through a huge, empty house, picking up and discovering anything and everything you find, hoping it will lead you to the next chunk of story.
If you pick apart Gone Home, it isn't a particularly appealing game, but as a whole, the experience is unforgettable. The story along with the gameplay, just works. Every picture, soda can and post it note is part of the grand story, that you get to put together. You're excited to find a note book, a scrap of paper, to open up the next door. You get attatched to the characters based on the things you read, find and hear. The gameplay alone couldn't do that, and the diary entries alone couldn't either.
Gone Home is a perfect example of what interactive story telling can really do. It can effect you in tons of different ways, something a movie or book just can't do.

An absolute immersive experience of a war that occured 100 years ago between two lands in Europe. The sound of gunshots in the distance and the screams of your fellow mates suggests a horror element of the Great War,and the impact of that on your personality as you don't see wars the same way ever again.
If you love old time Twentieth-century warfare in Europe and the immersive and realistic aspects of a war that impacted those around it and the generations up to today. Verdun is a game for you old school lovers as you will use your trusty rifle and your dirty equipment in Trench Warfare, facing the threat of enemies,the environment,and worst of all: barb wires.
This game has some content worth mentioning:
Pros:
-Gameplay, feels great paced between running and fighting in a FPS genre
-The Environment depicts the wars in Europe greatly, leaving a vibe to it.
-The classes and the teams add a living element to who was involved and what they'd offered.
-Guns and weapons feel great but somehow they one-shot kill everyone.
-The horrors of War update feels alive even more with new content and the option of Gore to add that survivial aspect.
Cons:
-No tutorials, you just have to figure out the controls and the classes because the game doesn't inform you what does this do.
-The lack of teams in the Entente powers and the Central powers makes it that the Great War feels short and uninterested like where is Australia,Russia(in the first half, left in 1917),Italy(first on Central Powers then the Entente),and Serbia.
-Trying to figure out where the hell that shot came from.
The Verdict:

There's a reason why I have almost five times as many hours in Verdun as any other multi-player FPS in my Steam library, and double any other such game I've ever played.
It is, quite simply, that good.
And in a sea of many such games, it is Verdun's uniqueness that sets it apart. Not just the WWI setting, where the devs have been trailblazers, but in the deliberate pace of its combat dictated by the predominance of the bolt-action rifle.
I once joked that the bolt-action rifle was--to borrow a line from Star Wars--"an elegant weapon from a more civilized age", and while no one can rightfully call the Great War civilized, there is an elegance to the pace of combat in Verdun. There is very little of the "spray and pray" that typically characterizes on-line shooters, and attempts at it are typically quickly silenced by a single, precisely aimed shot across No Man's Land.
The squad system, while perhaps counter-intuitive to new-comers, is genius--rewarding, as in real life, people who play together and learn to function as a team. What many complaints about Lvl 100 squads being "OP" miss is that it's not the  special abilities of such squads that make them powerful. It's that the players in them have played together long enough to often function like a well-oiled machine--and that wins battles.
That brings me to the community, which is great, in my opinion. More mature on the whole than many other such shooters, and a place where I've made a lot of good friends. I highly endorse forming (or joining) a casual clan to get the most out of the Verdun experience.
10/10, Highly recommended to any serious shooter fan.

First, I would like to say that I think all the hate for this game is a bit misplaced. To many reviewers base their reviews solely on how well the game runs. I think that it is an important factor yes, but people should review on content as well.
Does the game stutter, or suffer from graphical problems. Yes. Slightly. I am used to running Fallout, skyrim, MGS:TPP, Killing Floor 2, Elite Dangerous, basically everything I own on high or max settings with 60fps. Currently I am running about 47-50fps on the "High" settings. There was some tearing and choppiness, but turning on V-sync helps.
There are complaints about lip syncing being bad. My answer to that is, "Have you played any video game, ever?" I don't think I have ever seen a game with perfect lip sync, or even what I would call great. Mouths are hard to animate. Get over it. If you really care so much about lip syncing, that that kills the game for you, you need to lighten your standards.
Now, IN TERMS OF ACTUAL GAME PLAY AND CONTENT!!!
I would say this is definitely worth a purchase. Try it. I found the whole Koreans invading the US a bit Red-Dawn esque, but if you can get by it, the story is not half bad. I am only in about an hour or so, but everything has been pretty solid so far.
MOVEMENT/GUNPLAY: Movement handles pretty much how you would expect from a CryEngine game. It can be a bit blocky. Yes, your character moves slow, but what you have to realize is that this isnt Halo or COD where you just run around and shoot people in turbo mode. You are outnumbered, outgunned, and outclassed in about every way, so moving slow is essential to make sure you dont run smack into a patrol and die.  The gunplay is crisp and rewarding, and it feels good when your bullets find their mark. I think people have gotten too used to being super soldiers, and expect too much flashy gunplay. While it doesn't suffer the "cap gun" feel of COD and some other games, the gun sounds could use more "oomph" to them.
AI: While I have only had about an hour to examine the AI, I will say that I have been more impressed with other games, but that being said, I have definitely seen much worse AI, in more popular games. Have the people complaining about the AI ever played a Bethesda game, like ever??? The enemy AI seems pretty keen, and I have deliberately fired shots just to see how well their "search" mechanic feels, and I think it is pretty good. You definitely feel like you are being searched for, rather than the AI just going through the motions.
Is it worth 60 bucks? I think so. To the rapid-fire, ADD-like, spastic pewdiepie generation, it might bee too slow for you. I am playing on the normal difficulty, and I have died several times in firefights, but never have I felt cheated or gypped. You will die after being shot a few times. Welcome to real life pal. No BS overshields, no health regen that babies you. Preparation and thoughtful execution of your objectives will give you satisfying payoffs and make you feel like you really worked to liberate that stronghold, or find those supplies.
TL:DR
Bottom line; Don't let the negative hype decide for you. Buy it, put an hour into it, and decide for yourself. You can always refund.

Well well, after spending over 560 hours of my precious lifetime on this game it's time for a fitting review.
This one will be a long read so skip all the way down for Pro's and Con's, or get yourself a nice cup of coffee, lean back and read through all of it.
If you never played a Souls game before, note that these aren't meant for people with little patience and anger issues (trust me, you'll lose your soul in real life just like in the games).
I started with Dark Souls 1, not knowing anything about it apart from the reputation of being "difficult" and having a medieval setting....oh and 'cause I thought it was a Skyrim/Two Worlds-like RPG (enjoyed the heck out of these as well).
Boy, oh boy was I wrong..
Many reviews have already covered that part though, so I'll just describe how Dark Souls changed my perspective on combat based RPGs and video games in general: I can't say I'm a gaming veteran or have played many RPGs for that matter. Went through Morrowind, Oblivion, Dark Messiah etc. just to figure out one day that these type of games were my thing...or so I thought.
Challenge was the one thing all of these games were lacking (dead? just reload, man!) and that changed when I got my hands on the Prepare to die-Edition of Dark Souls.
Over a 100 hours on Steam and I'm pretty sure about 4 times as much on the 360 made me forget about all the other games (at least made some cash at Game Stop). So much about Dark Souls 1.
When I started DS2 SOTFS (let's keep it short, right?), the character editor, much like in DS1 didn't really impress me...no great variety of hairstyles, beards (but at least some weird tattoos you can have right in your face). Didn't matter to me though...DS1 has left a huge impact, following that came huge expectations of course (go play Saints Row if you wanna play as a bearded lady!).
So why on earth would you spend money on a game, that slaps you harder than a 13 year old girl, you just snatched away the cellphone from?
Why spend money on a game that's graphically not as impressive as so many games nowadays and that doesn't help you get through all the stages with a fancy mini map and quest logs and the like?
Let me tell you why, young Padawan...
Every time you die, your life bar shrinks and you'll become more and more hollowed (meaning you're gonna look like an old cucumber with white eyes), making death a serious thing, as you're not able to save and reload manually, unless you make your mom pull the plug (more about PvP later). Therein lies the challenge, which, combined with the demanding combat system makes you actually cautious about your enemies' attack patterns and surroundings.
So many have mentioned it already and they're absolutely right: patience is the key.
Also, the Boss fights in the Souls series are an absolute highlight, although SOTFS makes you fight the same (or similar) bosses in some areas
,
but that's just a grain of sand compared to the amount of bosses with all 3 DLCs, from complete pushovers (how did I die to Prowling Magus, though) to bosses that will leave you with trauma and eye bags.
That leads us to the biggest feature: Online Multiplayer.
Starting with Co-op, you can just skip the part with trauma and eye bags by summoning up to 3 friendly players (in SOTFS, previously 2 in DS1 and DS2) who will help you finally beat
that annoying boss who keeps killing you with only a sliver of HP left.
Or you could use those friendly Phantoms™ (available in White™ and Gold™) to clear an area before a boss fight, send them home and face said boss alone or with less phantoms (recommended on the first playthrough, the more phantoms you summon, the more HP has the boss).
And now to the dark side of Dark Souls (heh):
PvP
I wish I could tell you about the horrors I have experienced during this part of the game, but this review is long enough already and you're still reading it.
Once you get out of the cozy, welcoming place called Majula and visit a new area, you'll sooner or later get invaded by another player. These phantoms don't wanna help you beat a boss, rather make you cry and enter midlife crisis earlier than you might have planned (well, a portion of them at least).
Other than that, beating another skilled player, landing your first parry, or beating a group of gankers (no one likes gankers) is just as rewarding as beating Sir Trauma of House Eye bags.
I could write so much more about PvP but that part is best experienced on your own, after a few fights you'll know if it's your thing or not, anyways.
TL;DR
Yeah...I guess that sums it up pretty much. Would I recommend that purchase? Yes!

A simple and engaging story which rewards immersion and contemplation. The exploration and atmosphere are superb, with an intriguing mystery. For such a small team to create an epistolary coming-of-age story, in which the main characters never actually appear.
The setting is excellently chosen to give both the atmosphere and story credence - the mid 90s allow for a lack of cellphones and communication, the punky teenage angst and lone discovery. Whilst Washington State allows the house where the story takes place to feel isolated and stuck in time, a sprawling mansion with secrets left unfound by its current residents.
I would recommend this game to a wide variety of both traditional gamers who enjoy story, secrets, collectibles (the lack of achievements appeals to me, driving personal goals rather than competitive, pre-defined ones) and reading text as well as to those who may not normally play video games, but could be shown how the medium can be used to tell a story; totally violence free and deeply moving is not usual in gaming, but very refreshing.

From my playtime of the sequel to the popular game Five Nights at Freddy's, I could say this game isn't good or bad. Just eh.
The gameplay changes compared to the first one. The lack of doors and new animatronics made me curious at first. The trailer for the game got me hooked.
One faithful day, a friend of mine purchased me the game, and I took some of my time to play it. I was excited but at the same time anxious. I had no idea what to expect.
I managed to get an hour of playtime from it, and I lasted up to Night 4 before leaving due to frustration and boredom. But from my playtime from it, the game was kind of neat, but felt very similar to the first game. Check on the animatronics and hope you don't die.
In the original game, there were 5 animatronics (including Golden Freddy). In this game there are 10. The two I managed to notice the most were the Puppet and the Balloon Boy. The Puppet forces you to wind up a music box to prevent him from going to your office, while the Balloon Boy takes away the ability to use your flashlight, thus getting you killed by Foxy. These two kept me on edge, which fits in perfectly.
But, this game seems more like a DLC pack or extra map rather than a sequel. It felt like I was playing the first one with a few new mechanics.
Do I reccomend this to you? Only if you enjoyed the first game. If you are willing to take some time out of your day (or night) to give this game a go, go for it. But it might get a bit boring or tedious at times. But if you aren't aware of the first game or the franchise in general? I don't reccomend it, play the first game.
Overall for me at least, this game recieves a 5/10.

This is a humble game. In a forum where bombast is the norm, it's easy to write this game off as meaningless and/or boring. But that said- Gone Home is a story that from the start promises no grandeur, no epic struggle, nothing but a simple tale about people's lives told at a whisper- the kind you need to lean in close to hear- intimately close. You need to want to catch the subtlety, otherwise it won't be crammed down your throat. The game plays more like a book- if you don't like where the plot is going, you can't change it like we've become so accustomed to doing. It's just /there/, willing to let you explore but seemingly just as content if you choose to pass it by. It's also "short" by universal game standards, but the depth of story and character is well worth $10 to the average consumer when it's on sale. I have to say one thing is worth mentioning: I raise an eyebrow at anyone who says they finished in 2 hours. If you take the time to explore the game and really immerse yourself in the house, you should get 4-5 hours out of it.  Skyrim can be speedrun in less than an hour for ***** sake. GH is not a speedrun game.
So if you choose to listen, to lean in close. I hope you won't be dissapointed.

I read the reviews before I began to play and thought to myself (oh crap, another assassins creed unity fiasco) I mean every game has bad reviews the first couple days or even weeks because of reasons that many new releases suffer for that usually get patched within a couple weeks, but people were seriously hammering down on this game like it had reset the cure for cancer back to 0. I reluctantly started playing it after a long days work expecting to be disappointed by another crappy AAA title, and then you know what happened next? I sat in disbelief and confusion in what in the actual hell everyone was complaining about! I have an amd 8350 cpu and a GTX 760 (not massively high end) and I play this game on all high settings with NO PERFORMANCE ISSUES AT ALL like seriously, I can't say I understand how people with I7's and 980s are having performance problems when I can run at high with a steady 60fps no problem.
I havent encountered a single bug and the game plays exactly as I wished it would, open world style fps with a challenge, I would say this game is almost like a combination between farcry & Mercinaries 2, it has the rpg aspects that everyone expected with the epic gun customization and crafting, and keeps to the promise of guerilla warfare over run and gun tactics.
I find it ironic that I followed the division for 3 years only to play it for less hours than I've already put into this game which I only knew about a few weeks before launch. The story so far is amazing, some parts funny some parts really dark (pretty much exactly what I expected from a sequel to the original storyline)  but in all seriousness I can't put my finger on why people hate this game so much, its like people are just aching for the next game to blame and follow the band wagon.
Hopefully the reviews dont stay the way that they are because if so then I know a lot of people are going to be holding back on this purchase which is a real shame since it's actually quite solid of a title.
All things considered I could give this game a solid 7.5 personally, mainly because the voice acting is pretty poor, but the gameplay and story more than make up for some interlapping lines and such.
EDIT: So I havent beaten the story yet, but I have dabbled in the multiplayer to see what they have going on there since it was a pretty big part of the game. Firstly to anybody whos wondering, there's no competitive multiplayer, all of the focus was put into the coop which I personally prefer. The characters customization is pretty varied, male and female characters and a crap ton of gear that you unlock using currency and exp from playing in coop matches. roughly 25 or so items for each part of the body, head, arms, legs etc. and then a wide variety of skills that don't make any appearance in the single player portion of the game. It has a very similar feel to the single player, for example if one player decides to be loud and proud it doesn't mean that you have to be as well, you can remain silent and unseen by the enemy even if they are blasting their converted LMG into the heavens. Speaking of which the gun customization is all the same in the multiplayer but the system implemented makes it take far longer to unlock all of the guns, conversions, gear etc. because you unlock them via crates and don't directly choose what you want to unlock (although you can choose categories to unlock like attachements, vanity, weapons and such, but you just cant choose precisely what you want)
All in all im happy with the multiplayer, very good if playing with friends since you truly do need to rely on your allies to win since the game can be unforgivingly difficult, but that's not to say that randoms are no good, but obviously with no in game voice chat it's nice to have people you can talk to directly via TS or other means. Anyways with that being said I can confidently give the game a solid 8 now for very nice and replayable multiplayer.

Verdun has excellet gameplay and graphics and all that, but what I don't see people talking about a lot is how Verdun goes beyond the screen.  The gore, for example, is not really meant to awe at.  When you shoot someone and blow their arm off, or you shoot someone in the gut and have to listen to their screams for a minute or so, you actually kinda start to feel responsible.  Seeing all the explosions, experiencing suppression, seeing the gore, and experiencing the dark and depressing atmosphere can really sort of open your eyes to what the war was.  It's not like killing evil nazis or crazy zombies.  It makes you realize that you're killing a living, breathing human being, and that's something that no game has ever made me feel.  It can make you realize that people were actually doing and seeing all the same stuff in real life.  Verdun is the most respectful and accurate portrayal of warfare that I've ever experienced.

I wish there was an in between for yes and no reviews. I guess I'll simply say I recommend it "conditionally" and I'll explain what I mean.
I have always loved dinosaurs since I was a kid... and as a teenager/young adult I also developed an interest in WWII history. This game meshes the two together and I find it quite interesting and funny. The game itself has some humor to it and some pretty crazy unrealistic stuff but it makes for some great gameplay. Playing as T-rex can be fun if you know what you are doing and don't just stand there in the open while everyone pelts you with grenades and rockets. Conversely, taking on a T-rex is also quite fun if you use the right strategy (the Hardgrave berserk strategy tends to be the fastest and most effective.)
There aren't always many players online so some servers have bots. Depending on the class they are, the bots can be somewhat tricky to downright stupid. It can be pretty fun facing off against bots for practice, but after a while it can become too easy. If this is your first time playing, I recommend playing with bots to get a handle on the controls and character abilities, but don't expect actual players to act as bots do.
I got this game completely free. I think $10 is an okay price for a game like this, but I've seen it often on sale for $0.99 so I recommend waiting for a sale. It might not be worth buying right away for most people.
The amount of servers with people on them and the amount of people playing total tends to fluctuate (highest on weekends) but generally there is only a few servers and maybe only 1 or 2 that are actually full. Because of the small player base, chances are you will run into some of the same people a lot. I often see a few players who are either extremely good at this game or are hacking and this definitely changes up the game for people who are not on their team. If you play for a while you'll notice these same people always playing.
Now... I'm not saying that the game is completely UNbalanced, nor am I saying that it is DIFFICULT to learn, but the classes can definitely take some getting used to and you might play a while without realizing the full potential of some of the characters or maps. As for balance, it is definitely debatable. The combat is asymmetrical, even for deathmatch. Each team has completely different classes except for maybe sniper and medic but even those classes have different guns and abilities. It can be argued that each team has a class to counter a class on another team. For example Nigel (bazooka/flamethrower) is a great anti-raptor character and Hardgrave (rifle and berserk mode) can easily bring down a T-Rex given the right circumstances. I find that the tide of the war greatly depends on the skills of the players. Sure, Axis dinosaurs seem OP at first, but the Allies can win easily if they know what they are doing and use the correct abilities. I find that the team that wins right off the bat tends to be the team that keeps winning regardless of alternating from Allies to Axis each round, and as I said there tends to be one or two players who carry the game. If they are on opposite teams, this will make for some tense gameplay. If they are on the same team, then you will steamroll the other team and it might be fun for a while until it gets repetitive or if you get tired of those carries taking all the kills.
This game can be either really fun with money well-spent or a boring complete waste of time. It depends on what you are looking for. However, if you want to try something that will make you laugh and is fun to mess around in, I recommend picking this up if it reaches $0.99 on sale again.

I wish there was a "neutral" option, but I chose to recommend because I think people who enjoy games in this genre will like this one.
The only other "walking simulator" game I've played is Dear Esther, which really colors my view of this game and the genre altogether. Like Dear Esther, Gone Home has some gorgeous surroundings, a background story that unfolds as you progress, and a slightly spooky atmosphere. I like all of these things, until I realized that being in an unsettling environment (in Gone Home's case, a haunted mansion) is just a gimmick to keep you awake. There is no actual danger, there are no enemies, and there is no way to be harmed or die -- so why play on fear at all? I understand that the atmosphere has to do with the story, but I felt like it was added just to keep things from feeling too dull while you uncovered the real meat of the plot. I can see where spooky atmospheres come with the territory of being alone in an abandoned place, but is there no other way to keep people engaged, or am I misjudging the entire genre based on two of the most popular games in it?
That being said, I really liked the story. I *wanted* to uncover more things to hear more about it. I thought the teenagers were very accurately portrayed -- in a good way -- and that includes the paranormal things they engaged in. I value story over gameplay, but I wouldn't have finished the game if I didn't want to hear the ending. Finishing the game for that one sole purpose, without the added enjoyment of the experience, was unfulfilling.
So, this game is probably great for those that enjoy the genre, or are looking for a cute story with amusing details drawn out into an interactive experience. I tried to like it, but it wasn't for me, and it's disappointing enough that I'll be steering clear of future titles in the exciting world of walking simulators.

Playtime/replayability: I believe most people will play through the game once. It took me around 1 hour to finish it. You can get more out of it (an hour more or so) if you read all the notes, which I did not.

Oh no! There is a DIFFICULT tag in the steam store page! This can't be good! You cannot be more wrong than that. The game is not hard by itself, it just punishes you greatly for making mistakes and dumb decisions. And I mean GREATLY. A normal enemy taking almost 1/4 of your health in 1 hit? That's normal. No pause? Normal. No difficulty changing option? Casul. EVERYTHING mentioned above is a normal mechanic of the game. That's why we love it.
Graphics, compared to the first game, are astounding. Really impressive enviroment, great ragdoll psychics (except from the flying weapons) and CAAAAAAAAAAAAPES make this title really good. For the gameplay, the plot is really serious and it allows the player to choose it's own way of progressing through it, without the quest system. As for the mechanics, they are a little bit different. More opportunities, (at least to me) increased difficulty, more viable arsenal of armor and weapons is the strength of Dark Souls 2. The community and mods really depend on the situation. There are hackers, of course but the SOFTBAN system deals with them quite good. Sadly, it also COMPLETELY SHUT DOWNS MODDING IN ANY WAY. You cannot even change the look of something just for you, because it looks nicer that way. The game will recognize it as a change in the code and "punish?" you for it. I can't really count that into the overall rating, because the game DOESN'T need the mods to be viable and nice looking.
For a casual player, the game might feel a bit unfair. That's only the first impression. When I got into DS1 for the first time, when my friend was explaining everything about it, I didn't feel the point in this. But then, I fell in love with the Souls series.
Dark Souls 2 is quite different than it's father however. Only the basic mechanics are the same. Even though I was playing this game with 100 hours+ into DS1, I was still learning. A lot.
Remember, this game is unique because of the way it puts the player in its world. You progress and learn by trying new things, and as a result - dying. Thats a basic mechanic. Dying. Death. DONT BE AFRAID TO DIE. It's even better if you died during a new boss fight, because now you know the moves, the area, weaknesses and powers of the boss, and you can be more prepared.
Maybe it wasn't a proper review, more like my experience of the game. But still, even though it's not the easiest of games available, it's definitely the best one.

This game is as unbalanced as full of hackers, aided by poor hit detection and connection and strong support by microtransactions (it's not pay2win, but you'll struggle). While at first it seems quite the opposite, only the hackers are consistent throught the ranks, once you get to rank 13 (you unlock the professional servers, up to level 80 I think), you'll see all the flaws in this game. It's as unballanced as a one legged chair, with the early unlocked weapons and armour (specially weapons) being unable to compete with the more advanced arsenal present in professional servers. This is expected, and I know that, but this is where the microtransactions start to be tempting. But the worse of all is the poor detection and connection. Allied with the early, less powerful weapons, and you will rarely finish a match with a positive k/d. The slide function, while a relatively nice addition, in the hands of more skilled players and coupled with the afforementioned poor hit detection, and a shotgun wielding slider will take out your entire team, over, and over, and over, ... , and over again.
You are probably thinking, "This looks like more of a rant of a terrible player", and while it's true that I'm rubbish in this game, I used to have fun in it. The Co-Op is rather nice, but one only can complete the same missions so many times. It gets tiring.
Since these problems have been on the game since ages ago, I don't recomend it, there are cheaper alternatives (paid ones even, because this game has cost me a bit of sanity, there are only so many times you can call other players... not very friendly names, because they only kill with the grenade-launcher, another thing that is OP af), and to be honest, I would rather just play CoD Ghosts, because the problems that Ghosts have are nothing compared to this game.
Play it to see for yourself, after all, it's free, if you don't like it you can just uninstall it, no harm done, and if you do like it, even past the early professional ranks, well... kudos.
I used to like it. But after time I started to hate it. And I'm very sorry for that.

Your pistol can act as a silenced air powered assassin tool, a 9mm handgun, AND a .45 cal smg. You don't need to be at a workbench to change them up, you can do it during battle. Like your shotgun? Who dosen't, right? Well now you can turn it into a napalm launcher once you buy the upgrade. The versatility of weapons reminds me of the Resistance franchise on PS3 (which was known for it's insane weapons).
Hows the sound? I'm not a huge sound critic but everything sounds balanced
How does it look? One of the best I've seen
How is the story? As I said, i'm not far in. But the KPA is obviously a metaphor for alt-history China in this Homefront (the last HF the KPA had no similarities to China).
How are the controls? If you're using a m&k I couldn't tell you. I am using a 360 gamepad because the BetterDS3 program bugs out in game, making my PS3 gamepad useless. I hope that gets patched. The 360 gamepad works fine.
Is it stable? It hasen't froze or CTD'd yet.
Should you buy it? That's up to you.
