- They released a patch today that is supposed to change how the game saves graphical settings, but other than that I did notice that the game does not stutter when the framerate drops below 60, and the devs have repeatedly acknowledged that many are having performance issues. It's a great sign for the future that the game will improve.
- They look good, but it's also a Cryengine game, so it's hard to screw that up. Perhaps a bit rough on the eyes sometimes, however. General texture quality is acceptable, sometimes fantastic, and character models look generally detailed enough to please the majority of the graphically perceptive players. Shadows range from passable (general environmental shadows) to blobby messes (character shadows, small objects) and they do have some heavy impact on performance it would seem. Knocking them down from "Very High" to "High" gave me a pretty noticeable boost in performance.
Lighting in daytime looks really good, however fails to impress in any of the nighttime segments that I've played so far. The only time lighting sources that are not from the daytime look impressive is in smaller indoor areas where there's a lot of artificial lighting going on at once.
The world itself really does have a very nice amount of detail, and it really does feel like a real urban environment, at least so far. There are some woeful oversights however, such as ocean water not only being entirely flat, but also hardly even existant. Now I understand, maybe swimming plays absolutely zero role in this game, but for me to get a "leaving mission area" warning the second my feet touch the water, and to have my character literally walk on top of the water as if it was completely solid and then just suddenly fall into it when I "get too far out of the zone" seems really unpolished and a little lazy. At least use some stock Cryengine water or something.
Animations overall are average. I can't say I noticed anything too bad, but they don't standout either. They do flounder pretty signifigantly when there are a lot of NPCs in the same spot all trying to out manuever each other, and they glitch out and spaz as they continue to waltz in each other's way.
Graphic options are pretty basic. If you've played a Crytek game before, it will look very familiar. Simple labels with simple settings. There is an FOV slider, but it doesn't go very far and it seems to be using Vertical FOV rather than "standard" horitzontal, so the label only goes up to 65, which using a conversion calculator says should equal about 95 horizontal FOV. Probably the largest offense with this however, is that not only does it not really look like the FOV is quite that high, but there are some serious clipping issues with the first person animations when set this way. I also have yet to find an open configuration file that lets you change this further, but I'm also not the most observant with the files.
- Not too great. I'm running a 980ti and a 4770 CPU, and I am having trouble keeping it at 60, and when it drops, it stutters. It doesn't drop signifigantly however, generally only falling between 50-58 FPS, but it makes the game hiccup a bit (Vsync doesn't make a difference).
Again, turning the shadows setting down seemed to help a bit, but not enough to make it stable. I'm curious if it's a symptom of the game loading in assests as I'm moving around, as it does even out smoothly when I stay still or at least in the same small area of the map, but there are a few times where framerate drops regardless. The "Objects" setting also seems to help, but very minimally. I'll toy around with these settings further, but I'm not even that upset that the framerate drops, I'm more offended by the fact that the game stutters so badly when doing so, especially when it's only dropping by 5 frames at most.
- I'm a bit let down with this one, sadly. You can hear most things just fine, but the mixing does sound slightly off. A few voices do seem to be too quiet or drowned out, and environmental sounds seem passable at best. I also can barely recall the music (though again, I haven't played too much yet), and what I can remember seemed rather generic.
Voice acting is also disappointing. I've certainly heard worse, dear god, have I heard worse, but I've heard
better. In the opening scenes, none of the voice actors caught my attention and truly tried to draw me into the experience. They just played the part and that was it. If I had to describe their performance, I'd say it sounds like most of them honestly have real talent, but not enough experience to truly deliver it. Other voices actors are pretty bad though, at least to me. Maybe I'm spoiled after playing a bit of Uncharted 4, but I don't feel engaged as a player with the voice acting.
- This is where some things get pretty positive. For example, the gun customization. The first weapon you get is a standard pistol. However, you also are told to buy a conversion kit. This plays an interestingly detailed animation of the weapon being taken apart in your hands, and then put back together as a sub machine gun. I have no idea the realism of this mechanic, but it does look really, really cool, and I genuinely look forward to trying out other gun conversion mods later in the game.
Guns that I've used so far also feel okay. Not amazing though. There is some recoil to them, and a little impact, but they could have been much better. What's interesting, is that you can steady your aim with every weapon as far as I can tell. You can of course aim traditionally down the sights and fire away, but the recoil (even with a mouse) will throw your aim off. However, holding shift while aiming will make it more steady and allow you to hit the target better. It's a neat addition to the gunplay I think, and makes it a little more challenging.
Controls feel very Crysis-like, if that makes sense, as in, they are a little weighty, and you can see your characters shadow and body when looking downward. You can walk up to some surfaces and mantle them, giving the game some slight verticality (which will likely be expanded upon later in the game, I imagine) and you move at a decent pace. There are vehicles in the game, or at least a motorcycle so far. On a keyboard, I didn't have any trouble controlling it. The mouse sensitivity shoots up when using it, but otherwise drives just fine, and it a rather fast way to get across the map. I haven't found out just how large the game's "open world" is yet, but it seems quite big, at least from my own perception.
There is a looting system, ostensibly leading to some more complex crafting, but so far I've only crafted molotovs.
Should you buy Homefront: The Revolution today, right now? Perhaps not. Despite any praise I've given the game, honestly, nothing about the game as a whole feels very polished. It feels like it really need a few more months of development. And maybe patches will iron out the performance issues and tweak the gameplay for the better, but that's never an excuse.

So, after 262 hours of playing this game I think it is time for a better, more comprehensive review in english:
This game is different from other shooters and that's what makes it so fascinating.
As many others reviews state, you are lucky if you even get to fire a shot in the beginning. If you stick your head out the trench the first time, some level 100 guys will sure be trying to blast off your head trying to compete for medals, rank and honor.
This brings us to the point you will first encounter in Verdun - These are the ways you will probably uselessly die in the beginning:
Being...
... struck by Artillery or Mortar.
... mowed down by some psycho MG.
... choking your lung out in a mix of different gasses.
... bleeding to death in barbed wire.
... executed for frantically running away from your trench.
... yet again killed by a psycho guy, this time stabbed or naded.
... killed  by drowning in the muddy water.
It is quite frustrating in the beginning and takes a while to get used to, however every kill is a worthy lesson on how to do it better next time. Vedun sure isn't the classic egoshooter: Everything is dark and muddy meaning you can barely spot a thing (These maps are sure not visually attractive, just tactically.), you will be distracted by screaming buddies in the mud that just lost their limbs to a mortar (This it of course if you choose to turn on blood and gore... ) and you really need to spend time finding a good position: Either you get blasted away immediatly or, with a little bit of experience, mow down tons of players passing by nearly being impossible to be killed.
Also, teamplay is manditory here. If you just wildly call for gas, you may even give the enemy cover to come. If you just place your MG without having cover, a sniper will probably blast you away. However, in the counterpart, this also means good teamplay and a high troop rank (You'll get it higher if you play with the same people often) will make you benefit big time.
And this brings us further on to the battle types:
Frontlines is of course pure classic WWI gameplay, you will run for the enemy trench thousands of times and will probably still rarely be the first to make it there, no mans land is a widow maker.
Deathmatch is probably the best to test and show off your skills if you don't have any of the legendary guys there, then you need to become legendary first too. :p
The Troop Battles are basically deathmatch with two teams, it is a good place to train and learn how to be deadly and not dead in the beginning.
However Troop Defense (Waves of more and more AI trying to exterminate you and your troop) is probably the best to learn the game, AI is quite predictable and you will have time to get used to your weapon and learn the map, knowing where you are and how the game (AI) works will really help you later on.
Regarding the weapons: There are tons of them and they are very characteristic in their usage. For example, trying to fight off a guy with the Luger pistol running towards you in the distance is nearly as effictive as throwing a potato at him, thus I named the Luger "Kartoffelkanone" with love. :p
Same thing for MGs, if you spare the ammo and have a good position they're a delight but if you try to storm a trench - R.I.P.
To sum it up:
If  you looking for a real challenge, willing to invest time to feel the often useless but therefore ocasionally really rewardning emotions and learn how to survive from the masters, this WWI simulation is definatly right for you!
See you in the trench mate! :)

The kicker here are the Dinosaurs, which I think are a fantastic addition to a FPS. It definitely forces you to change characters to counter your enemies. For example, lots of tiny dinosaurs rushing you? Go shotgun and flamer. There are some neat new items unique to the game to, my favourite is the Jack Rabbit. It forces your opponent(if they are a Dinosaur) to stop and eat it. Basically a stun. There is a sweet pistol sized single shot shotgun that the soldier with the BAR uses.
I mean, there isn't much here besides 24/7 multiplayer.
The best part though, Compy ( : He has the most beautiful model I've ever seen for a Dinosaur and he is an absolute blast to play! He is a super tiny extremely fast Dinosaur. You need to go sneak around, but be aware you're very pretty blue tail will stick out from around corners! The best part! You have a grenade strapped to your back which you explode with RMB. More kills make it more powerful. I haven't had so much fun in a FPS than with Compy. I <3 Compy.
Honorable mention, I was at first in love with the Microraptor. Super awesome character, one of the best. He flys and spits acid, what more could you ask for? Well I'll tell you what, you're stuck in first person view ): He needs third person mode so I can see his model as a fly around. This is the main reason I main Compy instead, watching him run is HILARIOUUS! I love it. Team Compy!

Verdun - the best game about First World War since... ehm... hmm. This game proved that "boring" and "monotonous" trench warfare can be bloody fun. War is hell. You hear your commander whistle, you jump off the trench, you see your buddies run straight into chlorine cloud. Your squadmate tries to put on gas mask and misses the barbed wire, gets entangled in it. Your other friend turns to him, looks, thinks about helping him, but gets nailed with an enemy bullet. French, British, American, German, Canadian, Belgian... No man's land is just a giant mincer, chopping off your lives short. You see how people in front of you get mowed, running straight into machine gun crossfire. You have a split second to decide: do I crouch and turn back? Maybe I can get through? You are wrong. You will never get through. And even if by some miracle you make it to the enemy trench, you'll get ambushed by a rifleman, hiding behind a barrel. As the time goes, you'll see young soldiers become veterans with waxed moustaches, ready to die for their Fatherland. But is it really worth fighting?
If you start thinking about it all, you might miss the command to retreat. The next thing you see is your lifeless body flying away, while the mortars hammer your position. Unless you affix your bayonet and charge your enemy, how dare you claim to know anything about true dirt and pain of virtual warfare? Get immersed into this painful world of war, and remember lads: It's a long long way to Tipperary

If you're looking for a dungeon crawler/RPG that will literally have you crawling your way through to progress, then this is the definitive choice for you -- probably. Maybe its part of human nature to be unreasonably masochistic, or perhaps we tend to find pleasure in defeating what many deem insane to even try. Its not necessarily for everyone, but once you've broken through that barrier and embraced how immersively fun this game can be; you'll enjoy every brutal moment and every unforgettable triumph.
The online community is extensive, with hundreds of guides that will help newcomers understand the mechanics (the tutorial is far better than DS1 but still hard to follow for those unfamiliar with the series). On top of that, I find this game a lot of fun to play with random phantom players helping you out - Taking down some of the biggest bosses in a group of four is up there with one of my favourite gaming moments in recent memory. Just be careful that not every phantom in your world is here to help you...
You will die a lot, thats something you need to come to terms with. If you're not one who is up for trial and error or being patient/trying new strategies then I would turn a blind eye to this one - which would be a shame considering how much this game has to offer. In my opinion the satisfaction of progressing more and more each time you play, learning more about the enemy tactics until you've practically mastered the combat and navigation, is something that only FromSoftware can offer.
The story is more focused on the player instead of the world this time around, which is a shame since I always liked the vision of being a lone pawn in a grim and dying world... don't worry, you'll get the same feeling each time you walk into each gigantic castle or every time that you clamber further down into the depths of The Gutter and The Black Gulch (the latter areas are actually scary). Put simply, you need to kill four lord bosses, each located in areas around the world. With them you'll be able to fight the King and become a new monarch. I think. 30 hours in and halfway through my New Game Plus playthrough and I still doubt if I understand any of this. Don't worry though, you'll find it more fun to make your own story as you go along.
You can play this game pretty much any way you want - to a certain degree of course. You can play the game as a nimble yet fragile warrior that dodges, or maybe as an armourclad knight that uses greatswords to dish out damage. You can even play as a mage, using sorceries to do a wide variety of things (I do find that the mages are the cheap way to play, and they're the most annoying thing ever in PvP). Whatever you prefer, you'll be able to pick and choose as you play and finetune it through levelling as you go along. You can even reassign your points by talking to the old hags at the beginning area by using a Soul Vessel, if you feel inclined to make a major respec to your character.
Overall: This game takes the difficulty of older games and mixes it with triple-A standard game design, featuring some of the most memorable bosses and areas that I've come across. You'll find it hard to finish everything, considering how much content is packed into this special version of Dark Souls II. The game will almost never feel easy, but that doesn't mean that it's never enjoyable (though sometimes you'll feel like breaking your PC). No matter how hard it gets, just remember that the payoff will be all the more sweeter with each drop of undead blood you spill...even if that blood is yours.
TL:DR; if you want a real challenge that you'll struggle to complete and strive to master, then get this game. It does difficulty and actual game design better than any other RPG that I've ever played. Praise The Sun.

Normally, I'm a big fan of the Souls games, however, one thing I am not a fan of is FROM SOFTWARE's inability to be reasoned with. I was accused of cheating for using a few mods that made the game playable for me. In particular, I was soft-banned for using DS2Fix and x360ce. These two mods do the following:
-DS2Fix: Fix a glitch in the game that causes the durability of your weapons to decrease at twice the normal rate when playing the game at 60 FPS.
-x360ce: Allows you to use directinput gamepads in Dark Souls (in other words, most older gamepads before the XBOX 360 controller).
I have written a request to Bandai Namco to have my ban lifted after admitting that I used these mods (I later bought myself an XBOX 360 controller after finding out about soft-banning), and FROM SOFTWARE told me that since I violated the EULA (even if it was only so that I could play the game the way it was meant to be played), that my soft-ban will not be lifted.
Since a lot of the achievements in the game are a lot more difficult to obtain without any sort of online interactivity, this ruined the game for me in a lot of ways. That is not to say that the achievements and the game are impossible to beat solo, but it will be a much less enjoyable experience as a whole, considering that several bosses are, for the most part, large mobs, as opposed to the much more interesting and creative bosses found in Dark Souls and Demon's Souls respectively.
The game also puts a lot of emphasis on ambushing and surprising you in inconvenient locations just to make sure they get a couple of extra deaths out of you, which in my opinion is just cheap. After being ambushed and dying as a result of said ambush, it becomes pretty easy to figure out what to do in subsequent attempts, but it just seems blatantly unnecessary. The game is not terribly hard, but you will die simply because you're not ready for every single ambush and surprise the game has in store for you.
Another thing I would complain about (but kind of seems moot, considering that I'm soft-banned anyway), is the concept of soul memory. Every single soul you collect is added to a stat that matches you up against opponents (and potential allies) with similar amounts of souls. For novice players, this can be troublesome, considering that a lot of souls that are collected will inevitably go to waste, either through the purchase of items, inefficient leveling, or simply through permanently losing souls. Demon's Souls, Dark Souls and Bloodborne do not utilize this system, and in my opinion, it's better that way.
Lastly, another thing I don't particularly like is the concept that enemies can disappear. Permanently. If you play through a stage enough times, and keep killing the same enemies over and over, they will eventually stay dead, making soul farming more difficult, unless you have plenty of bonfire ascetics onhand. The only problem with using those is the stage that they're used on is raised one more difficulty level and EVERYTHING is reset for that level, which compels you to have to redo the entire stage (it would be foolish not to), and fight a stronger version of the same boss at the end of the level.
Therefore, soft-banning aside, I consider this entry in the Dark Souls series to be the weakest entry in the series. It does a lot of things that makes it ever-so-slightly less enjoyable than other FROM SOFTWARE gems.
All in all, I would recommend this game only if you're a die-hard Souls fan, if you're very careful not to use any sort of mods whatsoever, and if you don't already have all of the original Dark Souls II and its DLC. Remember, ANYTHING other than the what the game originally came with can result in a soft-ban, and you will NEVER get unbanned ever again.
If you want to be safe, you should probably just stick with the PS4 or XBONE versions. FROM SOFTWARE, like a lot of other 3rd party console developers are not particularly good at releasing PC Ports.
TLDR:
-Don't use mods.
-Make sure that you use an xinput gamepad (for example, the XBOX 360 controller).
-Don't purchase if you have DS II with all of its DLC already.
-Not as good as other Souls games.
-Might want to play the PS4 or XBONE versions instead.
Overall:
4/10 - PC Port
7/10 - SOTFS (in general)

The lack of mechanics is not what I dislike about the game, I have no issues with games that is narrative driven, my biggest issue is that it's simply asking for too much for too little. It's not even as long as a movie, hell it might not be as long as an episode of your favorite show, yet it cost more than a movie ticket to an IMAX showing.
I feel Gone Home came out during a time where indie darlings were still some thing special, and those who raised it so high on a pedestal only saw the superficial value of Gone Home and never considered consumer value in it's praise.
Gone home is ONLY for the most curious, or at a heavily discounted price.

So, I just passed the 10 hour mark, and while that is not nearly enough playtime for me to give a comprehensive review. I thought I'd give a short rundown of my experience so far.
The pacing of the game is slow compared to the big AAA games, like Battlefield and Call of Duty. Unfortunately, this mere sentence might put someone off from trying this. Slow, does not mean that it is boring or easy. Neither does it mean that you can't make plays. In the trenches, your reflexes and aim will determine whether you'll survive the encounters, and if you succeed, the encounter will leave you satisfied.
As much as I love the pacing. It does have some issues. While you do walk slower than other games, do not underestimate your ability to scale walls. Many times have I while in a firefight, managed to walk up the trench wall, only to get shot in the head by the enemy. This problem does not seem to persist when prone (I find it unsportsmanlike to go prone in the trenches), though crawling into a rock, or sandbag, will leave you levitating over the ground, which does make you an easy target.
The maps are good for the most part. I like fighting in the trench, but you are not necessarily restricted to it. As mentioned earlier, you can easily get out of the trench and then perhaps flank the enemies. Be wary, as this makes you stick out and likely to get shot.
The only map I dislike, is the map called Aisne (The forest map). This seems to heavily favor the team with the hill, as it is easy to defend. The only time I managed to win against a team with the hill, was when we continuously bombed the hilltop with mortar strike, and with a few close calls, we actually managed to hold on to it too.
Other issues is that on some maps, it is possible to get killed pretty quickly after spawning, because some spawn are set in the open, though this has only happened to me on Aisne.
It is pretty late, and I wanted to get some words out about this game. Feel free to share your input on where I am mistaken, or share your own thoughts about the game. Might update this "review" later.

The original Dark Souls II was a great and challenging game! Scholars is also a very good game but there are many things that just don't work right. It feels too easy in some locations, while it feels pretty unfair in others. Many locations feel unbalanced compared to their setup in the original.
There are some nifty additions there that just don't work. For example placing an enemy on an elevator that should trigger the floorplate to make it move again to surprise the player from behind. Most of the time the enemy doesnt trigger the floorplate. Some other times the enemy leaves the elevator but gets stuck. Enemies get stuck in many places or their pathfinding bugs out.

I have been following this series since I first got introduced to it by Markiplier's playthrough of the first game. I bought the first game and LOVED it, so I was excited when the second game was announced, and was surprised to see it come out early. Regardless, I bought the sequal almost immeidietly after it came out.
This game is easily the best in the series thus far. Sure, the first FNaF is a good game, but FNaF 2 took the concept of the first game and expanded it ten fold. For starters, there are no doors in this game, just vents and a large main hall. Now, this may seem like cheaply added difficulty, but Scott made sure to fix that by 1: limiting power to only the flashlight, 2: adding a defense mechanic with flashing the light at animatronics, and 3: adding the music box. The music box is what creates the challenge in this game; without it, you could just sit still and flash the lights and put on the mask, making it rather easy. However, like Foxy and Freddy in the first game, the music box is what requires you to check the cameras, this time with more urgency and fear involved. Urgency in that if you let it go for too long, you're dead, and fear in that the animatronics (especially the vent-dwellers and old animatronics) will stop at nothing to keep you from winding it. Vent dwellers are the worst offender for deaths, since you have to keep your mask on for about 6 seconds before they leave, making a window for Foxy or the puppet to strike. Trust me, in the later nights it gets VERY nervewracking (NIGHT 6 NIGHT 6 NIGHT 6, I'll leave it at that).
What also makes this game better is the animatronics. There are 9 in the main game, 10 in the optional nights (11 total if you count the puppet, but he doesn't have a changing AI or difficulty). The new toy animatronics, which were heavily advertised, have the easiest pattern, with Chica, Bonnie, and Mangle going to the vents, and Freddy going down the hall. They are the easiest to spot even before they attack. The older versions, minus Foxy, are a bit less predictable. Sure, you can see them in the vents, but their attack pattern is randomized, and you only have a second to put your mask on when they arrive. Any more than that and they get you. Foxy can be heard via the rythmic beat similar to most Slender games, as he usually appears first. Foxy is the ONLY enemy you need to flash the light on, as he is the only one aside from the puppet that can kill you even with the mask on, so using the light is mandatory when he arrives in the hall. On a personal note, it would be REALLY cool if Foxy had frames for getting closer to you in the hall like the other animatronics do. Balloon Boy is essentially the light jammer from the first game; if he gets in, your lights are disabled permanently, making it impossible to lure Foxy away. He can be seen in the vents before he attacks, and even has his own approaching sound effects, so you can be prepared for his arrival.
Overall, this game is great. Would I consider it a SCARY game? No, not even close. Sure, Foxy always makes me jump when he attacks, but there's no consistent scares after the first couple of nights/deaths. However, I will give this game credit that I was ALWAYS stressed in every session, as I was always concerned of who would come at what time, since the AI is randomized. It's for that reason that I consider this one of my best games this year, and with Scott hinting at a THIRD game coming soon (and by hinting, I mean putting up neon lights on the internet saying FNaF 3 COMING SOON), I'm looking forward to what he plans to do to top this.

Verdun is a first person shooter placed directly in World War One on the Western Front. I must say that overall it is a very solid game, but it does require a powerful computer. Each game consists of one side that attacks the other side's trench, and if successful, captures it, and now must defend it; however, if they fail, then the defending side counter-attacks, and et cetera. People connect in squads of four; the leader of this squad can call down gas and mortar strikes. The graphics are high-quality, and the game itself follows true to the actual events of World War One. However, I must warn you that if you aren't very good at sniping, this might not be the game for you if you are the one playing defense.

Gone Home is almost all story and atmosphere and no gameplay, and that is totally fine. It's an entertaining couple of hours of exploring a house and figuring out what has happened to the protagonist's family, both during her now-finished year abroad and before that as well. Teen issues, love, writer's cramp and relationships are all themes that feature prominently in this game. From the minute you arrive on the doorstep and notice that the entire family is missing you'll be intrigued and rush around looking for clues. It's a bit like Myst albeit with near-to-none puzzles.

Gone Home is what it would be like if you were to bring a theme park walk through attraction into a game.
It’s a linear story experience like any other theme park attraction. It begins with the story when the character returns home, finding out that her sister isn’t home to greet her. Instead there’s ominous voice message left on the answer machine. You then go onto an exploration journey, finding oddly diary journey pages sprawled across the house.
It went into fair amount of details to recreate the sense of the 90’s with references to old popular pop culture references and songs. Being a child of the 90’s it does bring back some fond nostalgic memories. But, I can’t imagine how it’ll hold up for someone who hasn’t experienced growing up or living in the 90’s. While the main story still hold some significant social discussion for our time, it might quickly become a footnote in history.
The game guides you through its puzzles with hints, items and notes scattered around the house. This is playing it as it is intended, without changing the game settings to unlock all the doors. You slowly unveil the story through each note you pick up. There are only a few key notes which prevents you from progressing into the next story arc, while the rest are optional additions to the story and easter eggs.
As a final note, this is a linear story with no variations to it. The only thing you can do is omit parts of the story by not finding the optional notes. With that said, it provides a mediocre exploration experience, which could enormously benefit from VR sets such as oculus rift.

Having come home to an empty house full of clutter and messily written notes to and from members of a family... you get this amazing sense of feel of what the life in this family was. In this review of Verdun I will be covering 5 catagories of gameplay (Which includes game community)
*** Preformance ***
Although the graphics aren't that of the new Battlefield 1 coming out, Verdun is a beautiful looking game for its content and context. If there is one annoyance I have it is the optimization of the game, I run a GTX 750Ti and I can run everything at high and some ultra, and I get about 40-45 FPS when I play, but I have read where some people with higher grade cards experiance lower or even wors frames, but for me it was fine with some drops in FPS the lowest I have had being was 20 FPS but that was at the beginning of a map when everything renders. One other annoyance that ties into community and preformance, some players turn landscape and foliage quality off or too low to get an edge on players, where as if you were hiding in bushes on your screen, on another players with no foliage you would be laying in open ground. Over all preformance out of 10 would be a 7.5, due to the time it has been out and has been repatched time and time again.
*** Gameplay ***
The key factor Blackmill was going for in this game was realism and authentisity, and I think they hit that mark to a certain degree, which it is real and fun for both sides fighting. The guns are authentic and so are the squads and languages spoken. I understand if they really wanted to make it realistic by taking out UI and making friendly fire a thing but Blackmill I am assuming wanted to make new players feel welcome without being too harsh in gameplay. Over all score would be a 9 out of 10, the gameplay is spot on with the weaponry mechanics and realism.
*** Mechanics ***
The mechanics and such for Verdun are average for me. Running is a little clunky and the default keys to crouch and sprint with are assigned in a very weird place, so I rebound crouch to CTR and sprint to SHIFT. However aside from movement mechanics, the bullet mechanics are well made for a 32 player trenchwarfare FPS, there is bullet drop at long range and if you want a kill while the enemy is rushing toward you at an angle you gotta know how to lead your shots. Over all I give mechanics a clunky but not too shabby 7 out of 10.
*** Realism *** (In a sense of immersion)

In this review of Verdun I will be covering 5 catagories of gameplay (Which includes game community)
*** Preformance ***
Although the graphics aren't that of the new Battlefield 1 coming out, Verdun is a beautiful looking game for its content and context. If there is one annoyance I have it is the optimization of the game, I run a GTX 750Ti and I can run everything at high and some ultra, and I get about 40-45 FPS when I play, but I have read where some people with higher grade cards experiance lower or even wors frames, but for me it was fine with some drops in FPS the lowest I have had being was 20 FPS but that was at the beginning of a map when everything renders. One other annoyance that ties into community and preformance, some players turn landscape and foliage quality off or too low to get an edge on players, where as if you were hiding in bushes on your screen, on another players with no foliage you would be laying in open ground. Over all preformance out of 10 would be a 7.5, due to the time it has been out and has been repatched time and time again.
*** Gameplay ***
The key factor Blackmill was going for in this game was realism and authentisity, and I think they hit that mark to a certain degree, which it is real and fun for both sides fighting. The guns are authentic and so are the squads and languages spoken. I understand if they really wanted to make it realistic by taking out UI and making friendly fire a thing but Blackmill I am assuming wanted to make new players feel welcome without being too harsh in gameplay. Over all score would be a 9 out of 10, the gameplay is spot on with the weaponry mechanics and realism.
*** Mechanics ***
The mechanics and such for Verdun are average for me. Running is a little clunky and the default keys to crouch and sprint with are assigned in a very weird place, so I rebound crouch to CTR and sprint to SHIFT. However aside from movement mechanics, the bullet mechanics are well made for a 32 player trenchwarfare FPS, there is bullet drop at long range and if you want a kill while the enemy is rushing toward you at an angle you gotta know how to lead your shots. Over all I give mechanics a clunky but not too shabby 7 out of 10.
*** Realism *** (In a sense of immersion)
Verdun is spectacular at immersifying me into the trenches of World War I. Sometimes when the artillery is soaring over head i'll take a second to look up, as I hear the yelling of other soldiers in the trench next to me, and there is a certain type of peace as well, looking at the whistiling wizz-bangs overhead. But me gawking usually ends with a German putting a Luger round throught the back of my head, pulling me back to reality, "Oh, I died. Damn."
A solid 9/10
*** Community ***
The Verdun community is very welcoming with most people, even to noobs at the game, dont be afraid to ask questions in all chat, usually a few people will tell you the answer to put your gas mask on. But the unfortunate part about Verdun is the size of the community, its fairly small for such an awesome game, but I am seeing more people playing because of the recent announcement of Battlefield 1, which is good and possibly bad for Blackmill, but Verdun will always hold a place as one of my most favorite games ever. I am veering off track but, the Verdun community is spectacular, if you see Kaiser Wilhelm in game, he's cool as well nice guy. Rating for community 10/10

I had fun playing this game alone, and with a friend. It runs very smoothly in 1440 on medium graphics with a GTX660. Not sure what all the robot futuristic pics are about in the game's slideshow here on Steam. I don't think I saw any of that in the game. The last few pics in the slideshow that have soldiers with a present-day appearance is what I saw when I played. I tried the first co-op mission with my friend. Co-op has a very present arcade feel and the enemies glowed red making them look more like a target in target practice. It was extremely easy but fun nonetheless. I did not try the spec ops game mode. In versus mode my favorite choice would have to be Free-For-All or "Bag and Tag" which is a dog tag collection mode. Storm was a neat versus mode too which is kind of like the Rush mode in Battlefield 4. Some of the maps like the desert map in particular really stood out and seemed unique to me, while other maps were so cliche I could have sworn that I saw them elsehwere before. I did not see much point to the game's system of slow item decay. After a while you have to repair things like weapons (other than the starting items) with in-game cash, but the cash is awarded after every round played. I seemed to have an overabundance of cash, at least plenty for any repairs. So, in my play time that appeared to be a pointless system. I liked the sliding maneuver that you could do. I really liked the hit indicators. Music was cool, nothing crazy. Sound effects seemed pretty decent. The playing field always seemed balanced no matter what level people were. One thing I did not like was if people started leaving your team (for example if it becomes 1 vs 6), there was no auto balance mid-match. You'd have to get your♥♥♥♥♥kicked and wait for the match to end. Or just leave, but the game says that you lose some exp and in-game cash if you exit during a match. Overall I'd say the game has a few unique traits but offers nothing that will blow you away. It can be a good time though, especially for it being free. If this game were to cost money then I would not recommend.

Mothers are women who inhabit or perform the role of bearing some relation to their children, who may or may not be their biological offspring. Thus, dependent on the context, women can be considered mothers by virtue of having given birth, by raising their child(ren), supplying their ovum for fertilization, or some combination thereof. Such conditions provide a way of delineating the concept of motherhood, or the state of being a mother. Women who meet the third and first categories usually fall under the terms 'birth mother' or 'biological mother', regardless of whether the individual in question goes on to parent their child. Accordingly, a woman who meets only the second condition may be considered an adoptive mother, and those who meet only the third a surrogacy mother.
The above concepts defining the role of mother are neither exhaustive nor universal, as any definition of 'mother' may differ based on how social, cultural, and religious roles are defined. The parallel conditions and terms for males: those who are (typically biologically) fathers do not, by definition, take up the role of fatherhood. It should also be noted that mother and fatherhood are not limited to those who are or have parented. Women who are pregnant may be referred to as expectant mothers or mothers-to-be, though such applications tend to be less readily applied to (biological) fathers or adoptive parents.[1][2]

Not sure what all the robot futuristic pics are about in the game's slideshow here on Steam. I don't think I saw any of that in the game. The last few pics in the slideshow that have soldiers with a present-day appearance is what I saw when I played. I tried the first co-op mission with my friend. Co-op has a very present arcade feel and the enemies glowed red making them look more like a target in target practice. It was extremely easy but fun nonetheless. I did not try the spec ops game mode. In versus mode my favorite choice would have to be Free-For-All or "Bag and Tag" which is a dog tag collection mode. Storm was a neat versus mode too which is kind of like the Rush mode in Battlefield 4. Some of the maps like the desert map in particular really stood out and seemed unique to me, while other maps were so cliche I could have sworn that I saw them elsehwere before. I did not see much point to the game's system of slow item decay. After a while you have to repair things like weapons (other than the starting items) with in-game cash, but the cash is awarded after every round played. I seemed to have an overabundance of cash, at least plenty for any repairs. So, in my play time that appeared to be a pointless system. I liked the sliding maneuver that you could do. I really liked the hit indicators. Music was cool, nothing crazy. Sound effects seemed pretty decent. The playing field always seemed balanced no matter what level people were. One thing I did not like was if people started leaving your team (for example if it becomes 1 vs 6), there was no auto balance mid-match. You'd have to get your♥♥♥♥♥kicked and wait for the match to end. Or just leave, but the game says that you lose some exp and in-game cash if you exit during a match. Overall I'd say the game has a few unique traits but offers nothing that will blow you away. It can be a good time though, especially for it being free. If this game were to cost money then I would not recommend.

Gone Home is an absolutely beautiful game. Not in terms of graphics, or gameplay, but “feeling”. Your character -Kaitlin Greenbriar, is returning home a few days early after a yearlong trip across Europe. The year is 1995, and Kaitlin’s family (Mom, Dad, and little sister Samantha) have moved into a new home, in a new city, while she was away.
The home is a large mansion willed to them by her paternal great-uncle. It’s just after midnight, and a violent storm is raging. After retrieving the hidden spare key, Kaitlin enters this strange new environment, only to find it empty. Soon enough she finds a somewhat alarming note addressed to her, written by her younger sister “Sam”. The entire game consist of Kaitlin exploring the large and strange house piecing together what’s happened to her family while she was away, and solving the mystery of Sam’s alarming note.
The game perfectly captures the feeling, and alternative culture of 1995. Kaitlin often stumbles across Sam’s mix tapes featuring kick♥♥♥♥♥rock from two of the greatest “Riot Grrrl” bands of the period, Bratmobile, and Heavens to Betsy . If you’re into that type of music, as I most definitely am, you’ll stop just to listen as it plays. The voyeuristic nature of the game- exploring every room, and going through Kaitlins family’s things- adds, along with the raging storm and excellent use of lighting, a strong sense of tension. While the games overall story isn’t particularly ground breaking, or even original, it is incredibly sweet. In point of fact, the whole game could be described as “short and sweet”, and that’s what many have a problem with.
Many people object to a two – four hour game (depending on how you play it), having a normal price tag of $20. My personal guess is that the cost is to cover the licensing fees for the music, and the music is an integral part of the game. Regardless, the game is often on sell for 50, or even 75 percent off. How much you pay for it, is up to you. If you’ve never played this type of game before (explorative walking simulator), then you should definitely wait for the lowest price option. Like every gaming genre, it’s not for everyone.
One word of warning, the original soundtrack being sold does NOT feature the music of Heavens to Betsy, or Bratmobile, it’s the background and atmospheric music from the game. Whether or not you think it’s worth purchasing –I don’t- is up to you.
While there are those out there who don’t consider going home an actual “game”, I most definitely do, and I loved it. For me, it was a short, sweet, and wonderful experience. I eagerly look forward to the developers next effort.

Yet another undifferentiated shiny Counter-Strike knockoff. On the plus side, this game is not Counter-Strike. On the negative, it is yet another game to get bored of for exactly the same reasons. It is not glaringly objectionable in any element of its execution. It just completely fails in all aspects of innovation or imagination, right down to its use of obsolete non-ballistic hitscan weapons. Battlefied 4 is no poster child for engrossing tactical dynamics, but at least its bullets actually fly through the air in an arc.
In terms of stuff that the game doesn't even do as well as Counter-Strike; it doesn't have much world-penetration mechanics (though it says it does), nor does it render decal textures on players, nor on the world with any significant persistence. This would be minor if there were other things to differentiate the game in any way, but there aren't. It is just a piece of uninspired, formulaically conceived Counter-Strike redux.

I think, to a certain extent, you either like it or you don't. But I would say that it lacks what it needs to carry most people, or at least myself, into the "like it" zone.
If you don't know, Gone Home is a game where you walk around a house and explore, listening to a character's diary of sorts to find out what's happened while you're gone, and while the gameplay isn't particularly engaging, it's very atmospheric, and the house is so detailed it's easy to get immersed in the story.
The problem is, the game puts all of its focus on the story and, in my opinion, fails to deliver a good story.
I read reviews before I played the game, and was upset when all everyone got out of the game was "It's lesbians," partly because it's a mild spoiler (I guess, although it's a lesbian love story so it's slightly vital for the premise), but it really seemed like the general opinion of those who didn't like the game was that all it had was lesbians.
But the thing is, remove the homosexuality, make one of the characters a guy, and there's absolutely no substance. The story doesn't really go anywhere for a while, and it doesn't really offer anything. It even feels like the characters don't have much personality most of the time.
As immersed as I was, I was really disinterested in the plot and the characters as it played out, and I really wanted to like it. It does suck, because the story is the main draw of the game, but I also feel it's its biggest weakness.
Now, I want to talk about what I DID like about the game.
For one, the house is really cool. It was big enough (almost a mansion) that there was a lot to explore, but small enough that it would be realistic to live in, under the right economic circumstances (ALMOST a mansion). And it was filled with such meticulous detail that if you like exploring environments in games, you'll apreciate this. With the detail, and the soft sound of rain outside, it really sets a cool, relaxed mood.
The voice acting was really good. It helps that there was exactly one voice actor, but man, did they cast well. Paired with the intamacy of the diary entries, I was so immersed that I actually became really uncomfortable when she talked about when she discovered she was gay; I felt like I was intruding. This is actually so good it's bad, but I'm sure that was just me, and most people won't have that reaction.
The "put back" ability. THIS. You can pick something up and throw it around like a lot of first person games (Amnesia comes to mind), but this is the first game I've played where you can place something back exactly as you found it. This should be in every first person game from now on! I spent probably about 15 minutes just doing that and enjoying it.
As a side note, that also adds to the atmosphere, as if you want to take the game seriously, it doesn't quite seem realistic for the character to be walking around, throwing everything she picks up. Good game design!
The 90s nostalgia is strong in this one. Seriously. It's really well done.
Overall, this game did a lot right to put you into it, and I didn't actually find anything tedius like others did; as long as you know what you're getting yourself into, you'll enjoy the "gameplay." But, unfortunately, I think the game failed to deliver on its main goal. It had a lot of potential, and I don't think the game is "bad," and in fact I'd love to see more games work like this. But those games' stories are going to have to have more substance for them to work.

While I like what improvements this game has received over the first, I am astounded that Scott would allow your success in the later nights to be dictated entirely on luck.
The first game, at least if you made a mistake, You knew it was YOUR mistake, and you felt responsible for your actions.
But in this game the animatronics can bombard you making you incapacitated and have no chance to wind up the music box, so if you have an unlucky streak of attacks, it's game over, not because of your mistake (you've done everything right up until that point), but you failed because of luck.
There is no reason why the player should be punished for doing everything right. It makes the game laborious for a completionist, and gives a false sense of accomplishment when you do make it through the night, because you know you got through not because of skill, but because you got lucky that you were graced with the appropriate amout of time to wind the music box.

Warface is a fun game, and a good free to play for people who want a shooter without spending money. It's simple enough that everyone can get the hang of it pretty quickly. My second match I went something like 25/9. The medic is actually useful in combat, the shotgun has a range better than 1 meter. The climbing system is a little buggy, but encourages team play. We need more things that encourage that in today's games. On the fly customization of your guns is very interesting, and it's not so fast as to give ridiculous situations, but not so slow to just wait to die and respawn. Guy a little too far to accurately hit from this range and he's pinning you down? Hunker down, spend 3 seconds or so putting a magnification optic on your rifle, bam, fight back. Not a AAA game by any means, but good for a free to play.
Now, this is the part where I explain why I won't recommend this game. First few matches were fun, and a blast. However, a few matches in, I came across my first hacker. Now, finding one in a game isn't too terribly condemning. What was condemning was that there was nothing we could do about it, and after that one left, more took their place. LMG user getting 4 headshots on 4 guys rounding a corner with 4 bullets before we had even trained sights on him. We couldn't kick him, because the game doesn't allow you to vote kick someone on the other team. I can understand why they would do this, so that you don't kick the best player on the enemy team, but what about situations like this? A quick search found no report option, but I could very well have missed it. It wasn't super obvious enough that I could find it when I needed it though.
They very quickly had us pushed into our spawn, and we couldn't leave because of the LMG hacker on the left, the multitude of people on the right (non hacking, it was just 75-80% of the team) and a sniper watching the climbing paths. Spawn protection was not enough to stop the impending slaughter. It wasn't even a fun fight back, because for every 1 kill we got, our entire team got wiped.
Until the devs do something about the hacking, I can't recommend this game. If that's fixed, then by all means, try this game. It's free, microtransactions exist but are not needed, and it's a fun little game if you don't want to slap down $60 on a AAA shooter.

Verdun is best described thusly:
"Tug of war, but with rifles and mustard gas."
It's a fun game, especially with friends, the hit detection is good, and the game is based on skill, ability to work as a team, to the point where you can level up your squad's abilities, the more you play with it, not only on an individual level, but as a group level, for example, one of the squad could unlock a kit that gives him a machinegun, but you are unable to sprint while holding the machinegun. If the squad levels, they will be able to sprint within range of the NCO, and eventually even if they aren't in range of the NCO.
The combat is at times, slow, based on patience and accuracy, and the ability to spot a target over a long distance, rewarding accuracy and good hand-eye co-ordination, but at the same time it can also be fast, and reflex based, especially when rushing a trench. Most of the weapons in the game are Bolt-action rifles, so obviously, every shot counts, so far as I've played the second most common weapons are pistols, be they revolvers, or semi-automatics.
One member of the squad is the NCO, they are the commander of your squad, giving orders, giving certain buffs in an area around them (the command range) and each squad's NCO has a different ability, ranging from recon planes, to Mustard gas and mortar support.
Overall the game is enjoyable, good fun, and great for having a laugh with your friends.
One last thing: Be prepared to die a lot. It happens.
8/10

It's 1995. You've just arrived back home from a long trip in Europe to find your home deserted. Through a series of notes and a brilliantly atmospheric environment, you puzzle together the fate of your missing family and learn precisely what happened to your sister while you were away. I cannot recommend it highly enough. It manages to pack more pathos into its 2 hours than Skyrim managed in 60. I laughed I cried, I cringed and I felt for characters you never actually meet.
Video Games may not have had their Citizen Kane yet, but if there is any justice in the world
will certainly be remembered as it's Battleship Potemkin.
A trendsetter and a sign that the medium is maturing.
Pros
-A deep and engaging story
-Incredibly Atmospheric
-A true interactive story
Cons
-Its short, 2 hours is enough to max the game and it has very little replay value.
-The "gameplay" is weak. There are a handful of puzzles but otherwise there is no "gameplay" to speak of.

I don't know where to start with this game. Not saying it in a bad way, but in a very good way. Gone Home is very unique unlike the first-person games now-a-days. If you were looking for a first-person shooter with limbs flying everywhere... This is not a game for you, which I am sure you would know that probably because you have seen a trailer or two of the game. Gone Home is a story based adventure-ish? game that ttakes you back to the mid-1990's. Although you play a different character in the game, it is a story about your sister Sam, who narrates about the few adventures that she had while you were away on your trip. But the one main adventure that runs through the rest is her friendship with a girl named, Lonnie. It is quite a lovely story, some parts happy and funny, some are drenched in sorrow and sadness. I wish I could go more into detail with the story line, but I am not a spoiler. Throughout the exploration of your house (A big house I might add) you find many neat things around every corner. Letters, (Which you will see a ton of) cool items that most 90's kids would understand, (Recommened for 90's kids!) and tons of soda cans. Some items that you pickup push the storyline forward. I wanted to get to each key item as fast as possible to see what the next part was going to be about (Gripping story if you ask me!). A lot of the things you think you can't interact with, you actually can, so search every part of each room. Also, a few of these items are pretty funny. Plus, the kick♥♥♥♥♥cassette tapes rock! Mainly the only thing that I thought was bad, was the shortness of the game. If you have read more reviews about Gone Home, one of the things you will hear is, "Its too short!" or "Very short game!". I have no problem with the game being short, maybe if they could just put an extra 20 (30?) minutes into it. If you dont like short games... Dont play it. I reccomend buying it when it is on sale (Holiday sale, Summer sale, etc.). Overall, it was a touching game. I loved the story that was pulled you in with curiosity and adventure. It was heart-warming, wishing that something like this could happen to me as well, seeing that this storyline very much relates to many people who have been in Sam's shoes.
Pros:
-Graphics
-Interaction
-Storyline (Loved it!)
-The secrets... 0.0
-Everything else!
Con (Thats right, only one!):
-Wish it was a little longer
Recommendation to:
-People who love a good story
-Exploration
-People who enjoy non-violent games
-90's kids!

This game is a true masterpiece. It is set back in the days of World War 2, and is an exquisite display of the true hardships the citizens of Nazi Germany had to overcome to thrive in their world. It's emotional yet heart-warming story-telling of the views on political corruption in both the Nazi and the Jews' perspective.

The gameplay is spectacular, just like any modern fps should be, but it gives this unique feeling of actually being in the game and part of the whole experience. It is a form of gameplay even rare to this day. At parts I felt as if I were one of the Nazis, and in some others I felt as if I were one of the Allies fighting for freedom. Overall the gameplay was truley astounding.
The music was spot on. Every single tune throughout the game came at the perfect timing. When something tragic happened (and a lot did, but I don't want to give away any spoilers), slow and depressing music was played. When the game was a little more light-hearted, a nice, happy tune was played. Overall the music was perfect and very well-suited for the game and its emotional moments, and I would buy a soundtrack instantly if one ever were to come out.
This game has an extremely high replay-value. It's main selling point is obviously its multiplayer, and it is great. There is a tremendous variety of characters and weapons to choose from. The game runs very smooth with a descent enough processor, and its dedicated servers allow you to always find a smooth match. The online multiplayer game modes are all fun and creative, such as a conquest mode, a team deathmatch mode, and more. In the end this game will keep you playing for hours on end.
Overall, I highly recommend this game. Its value is way above its small asking price of $9.99. I hope you have considered purchasing this game for yourselves or your friends because it is definitley worth picking up.

I got this game in a bundle awhile ago and finally got around to playing it.
For a simple exploration simulator it isn't bad, the attention to detail is actually pretty amazing with all the little things you can interact with around the house. The detail on all the little notes, even the ones you might miss completely encourage thorough exploration.
Unfortunately the game has some pretty major issues which prevent me from recommending it.
1. Your character basically has nothing to do with the story, there's very little information around the house about your character and your character provides very little commentary on the whole situation so for the most part you could be a playing as a random stranger who ended up on the front porch for all I know.
2. The story has all the setup for some kind of horror/thriller, but ultimately ends up being a sappy (and I thought frankly stupid) teenage love story.
3. Short with no replay value. I exhaustively explored the house and you can see from my steam playtime how long that took. There are no randomized elements of any kind and no real puzzles to solve so for me there is really no reason to go back and play it.
4. Price. I got this as part of a bundle so I wasn't aware of the real price, but on coming here to write this review I had sticker shock. $20 for a game this short with no replay value is highway robbery. Even on a 75% off sale I couldn't recommend it with how many other excellent games can be had for under $5.

There are HOURS of fun to be had in this game. I dare you to 100% it. The extensive open world map has impressivly fluid graphics. It consists of smaller areas such as military bases, large airports, cities, and small villages that can be 100% completed if you collect all boxes scattered within and destroy obviously marked structures (water towers, fuel towers, power stations, gas lines, etc.) though this attracts attention. This progress leaves you with upgrades and cash that can be spent on helocopter drops including weapons and vehicles. Once a place is descovered you can fast travel to it from your map.
Of coures there is an arsenal of fun weapons (that can be expanded with DLC) though an FPS this is NOT. The weapons combat has a more arcade feel and there is apparently no such thing as stealth. Tuck yourself away with a sniper rifle to pick off the bad guys and you'll find one shot and everyones guns are instantly fireing at you. There's also no real reward for killing them. In the end you will find yourself almost always having to evade their infinte numbers and waiting for the cooldown before walking back in front of them like a different guy on the island in the same outfit as the guy just shooting them.
The grapple and parachute make traversing the map extremely fun and easy. The grapple also serves a melee attack and can string together two objects including vehicles, humans, and unmovable serfaces. aah, good times. As mentioned in another review this would have been amazing to see in Farcry 3.
As far as the story it's more or less just there to move you around the island for yet another mission and to unlock challanges.
The story doesn't do much to deepen your experients with the game so don't expect The Last of Us story line action movie style. The misions and challenges are still fun and do well for breaking things up with different types of action.
I don't want too sound too negative in my review but i won't gush over it either like another greatest game ever. However, I would highly recomend this game to any PC gamer (especially if you can get a deal) if only for the kicks and giggles. If it was missing something before it was multiplayer. But as of the date of this review the multiplayer mod DLC was released on Steam. Happy Gaming.

When I played the game, I knew nothing about it. I had never heard of it. All I knew was the cover art from my steam library. The game came in a humble bundle.
At first I thought it was a horror game, the ambiance of the beginning just seemed to give it, but after a few minutes I started to realize it was something entirely different.
Along the lines of Dear Esther, the game is an interactive story of sorts, a game about exploration. You look through the house and find little bits and pieces of a story. The story is beautiful and just plain adorable. It was a treat to explore.
There is only one other game I have kept my steam trading cards for, and I hold it as one of the highest pieces of art in gaming, this is now the 2nd game I will keep the cards for.
As a note, this isn't a "game" in the traditional sense. People are giving it poor reviews because they are treating it like something it's not. This is a short story, with an interactive delivery rather than ink and paper. It's about the experience, not the entertainment. This is an example of art, not just some passtime piece.
If you take nothing else from this review, take this.
Play this game.

Warface! Been out for a couple years but I only recently gave it a try. First off, do I recommend it? Overall, yes but its not perfect it has some annoying aspects bugs and shortcuts that drag down the overall quality.
What does Warface do right? Fun. Its like a low budget Call of Doody but they dont encourage you do sprint none stop or wall run like a bad Kung Fu movie. You have three different modes, co-op which is basically up to five players vs bots on maps of varying difficulty that cycle daily - some of these are kinda cool such as pitting your team against a badass mech. Versus is your standard selection of player vs player maps so youve been here done that. Lastly is a mode I havent tried yet  so im not going to try and describe it other than it seeming to be something akin to co-op with more meat on its bones.
Guns are a pleasant suprise in that they dont try to hash over and rename obvious weapons, Most of the weapons, not all, are either real ones or closely based off real ones to the point that they use the originals name with some special tags or extra digits. The way the grindy items are unlocked is odd but not exactly bad, unfortunately it relies on RNG to get you to some of the items - basically you select either weapon armor or attachements to progress along and as you complete missions you progress along the current selected group/item untill it unlocks. Once it unlocks you can use or buy it (depending on the item) to use another locked item in that catagory takes its place and the progress starts over again so you can grind through that one as well.  Unfortunately its not class specific so while you may like to play just snipers weapons that pop up might not be a proper rifle for awhile.
Downside of Warface seem to mostly be in the catagory of 'lazy developer shortcuts' and are most obvious when your playing PVE oriented matches. On normal difficulty grunts are pretty much dumb as a bag of rocks and will readily let you shoot them full of holes, to balance this out the devs included shield guys who are utterly impossible to avoid or stop once they start charging no matter how far they are from you or what weapon your using you cant prevent them from knocking you over (though a team mate can shoot them from the side/back) and then suddenly the shotgun grunts grow a brain and hone in on you.
Bots also will jump on stationary turrets that are absurdly accurate and understandably devestating,  if you dont get the right angle or a good grenade toss on these things they can be a bother especially because they never ....ever...ever miss even on normal. Enemy mini bosses (Heavy Gunners) move around slowly, but instantly turn towards the closest target and always knows where everyone is which isnt the worst thing in the world but its really obnoxious to see in action.
The cash shop stuff is predictably pricey for this sort of game, though with the exception of revive tokens (which you can technically gamble free cash to try getting) none of it is vital go gameplay and tends to mostly be for cosmetic stuff such as skins or banners. They need to take a page from CS:go on this one and take their own spin on it, if they were to implement weapon skins you can straight up buy for small prices or gamble with free cash to try getting  it would be nice.
The Steam DLC pages for these are a pretty good investement sorta, you get a respectable weapon and an assorment of gear for one class. However the problem is, your rarely if ever play just one class outside of PVP unless you are playing with a clan with everyone taking specific roles ahead of time.

First, the game took me about 3.5 hours to complete and that was me going over every inch of the place, I mean EVERYTHING. I mention this because people tend to put a dollar amount on game length; not that there is anything wrong with that. Second, this game is all about exploration for the purpose of telling the story; and it's an excellent story. You won't be solving puzzles, getting into combat of any sort, or thinking really hard at all; like I said it's all about being told a story. Last, the graphics are not amazing by any means, but they're not bad. When playing this type of game I tend to want top notch graphics, i.e. The Vanishing of Ethan Carter type graphics. It just helps you get more immersed in the story. Anyway, the graphics don't take away from the game at all. The developers do a good job of having you care about, and feel for, the characters. Well at least two of them, but it's enough (in my opinion). So, if you're in the mood to hear a good story but dont feel like watching a movie, I recommend picking it up. If you have a nice headset, I recommend wearing it; helps with the immersion!

Verdun is an interesting concept of a game based on back and forth trench warfare, assaulting from one trench to another. It's a pretty novel idea and has some pretty cool concepts. But in it's current state it's definitely not recommended.
Verdun has several problems with bugs, bad matchmaking, poor netcode, and it constantly crashes. The map design may be authentic but it's very constraining, making gameplay not really about flanking, more is it about your ability to flood the map with more bodies than your enemy or your ability to quickscope the enemy. Of course, teammate will dominate- if you use voicechat you're sure to have an edge, but you're going to have a hard time playing with your friends considering the squad matchmaking will constantly give you error 101 (did not reserve you a spot on the server) if you try to connect with a squad of your friends.
It's a novel idea, but unless you're really in love with the western front of WW1, it will quickly grow to be a frustrating experience as you die from latency, falling through the map, and are forced to play in random squads, time and time again. If they fixed the bugs Verdun could be great, but they haven't and it isn't.

This one is a hard call. It not a bad game -- I played all the way through and didn't regret it. It's just that for everything that went in to it, I felt I got very little out. It's scope is too large for the genre and the playtime is too long for the payoff. Despite that, the game is very well put together, engaging, and quite capable of evoking a range of emotions.
If you know you like narrative walking simulators, then this is a no-brainer. For everyone else, I'd say pass.
[Spoilers follow; don't read before playing, but do afterwards for my justification for not recommending]
The thing that really bothered me was that this game effectively builds up all kinds of tension - the stormy night, the dark rooms, the abandoned house, the ghost hunting, the uncle's dark secret - and yet failed to capitalize on any of it. At first, it heightened the experience. Later, it became trite and annoying; I was just waiting to be scared. In the end, when I found that tension was all for nothing, it just left me with a bad taste in my mouth.
I was also disappointed that none of the side-stories resolved at all. We never found out what the uncle did. We never found out the status of the parents. We don't know what happens to the runaway. We never find out about the dad's career. Finding the details was really fun, but then finding out that they were meaningless in the end (the daughter was mostly oblivious to all these facts) again left me with a sense of incompletion and frustration.

At first, I didn't really know what to think, as this game was unlike any other FPS I've ever played.  The attention to detail was superb, the graphics top-notch, the music evocative of the time period... Not really understanding the strategy of this game, I ran headlong into No-Man's-Land, charging the enemy trench much like I've done in several other FPS games.  Then brutal reality hit me as I died again... and again... and again...  I realized that the devs of this game have done their best to accurately portray the brutal reality of trench warfare in WWI by making sure that any one person cannot be OP.  This game relies heavily upon the squad-based model of play, with each member of the squad occupying a specific role that is key to operating effectively as a team.  There are no lone wolves in this game.  You either play cooperatively or you're all smoked.  For that reason, I think you'll find a better community within this game than in many others, as it rewards you working together than alone.
Also, as someone who has deeply studied WWI history in and out of college, I can vouch for the historical realism of this game.  The devs have gone out of their way to create the most accurate, realistic recreations of the environments along the Western Front ever seen in a WWI game.  Also, you have to give them props- they sought to make a WWI shooter, which many argued would be impossible... "how can you make trench warfare exciting?" etc.  Well they've done just that, and this game is anything but boring.  I've played some truly thrilling matches.
I do hope that in the future that they release more DLC, with new maps and nations like the Austro-Hungarians, Italians, Russians, ANZAC, Turks, and possibly colonial troops like the Indians, Sikhs, French West African troops, etc.  It would be neat to see the entire war portrayed, and not just the Western Front.  Having future DLC releases that feature each front of the war would be ideal- one DLC for the Italian Front along the Isonzo River and Trentino, another DLC for the ANZAC at Gallipoli in Turkey, another DLC for the Russians and Austro-Hungarians/Germans along the Eastern Front, and heck, maybe even another DLC for the Middle Eastern Front with the British, Arabs, Egyptians, and Turks.  All of that would be superb, however, the game is definitely complete as it stands.  I just think those additions would truly make the game that much better.
I would heartily recommend this game to anyone who loves realistic, gritty, difficult FPS shooters. So, I really love the 90's atmosphere; the house + its ton of details. I felt like I took a trip back to the mid-90's and got lost into a time-wrap of some kind. Everything is pretty much not nailed down here. So - it can be picked up, locked at, examined, and moved around.
And the way the story unfolds, is just great - whether by narration, from through the actual objects themselves, finding certain areas, solving some puzzles, or whatever the case might be. You basically return to an empty house and you're to find out where everyone is + why you're actually there, as everything feels up close + personal in the first-person experience. I won't go much further than that, as that could actually ruin the experience itself.
Do yourself a favor: don't spent full price on this. I certainly didn't. It's a very, very short game. B/c it is so short - that could be a worthwhile reason to replay it, in case you missed something in the game, want to check the Commentary out, to know the game inside + out, want to re-explore the game, or whatever the case might be.
Compared to most games on the market - Gone Home is a very different + interesting adventure game focused on exploration, loaded with a unique + ordinary 1990's atmosphere for a game that will make people that were alive in the 90's - especially those who were teens or children, during that era - relate to very easily. It will feel like you've....Gone Home, naturally. With the way the story unfolds and the way it's presented to the player - this is a trip definitely worth taking, if you don't spend the farm on such a short game.
But, oh - what a grand, short little game this is!
Final Grade = B.

Think Red Orchestra, but WWI.
If you're looking for a fresh take on a shooter, fun squad based combat, and absolutely intense and cutthroat close quarters fighting, this is an excellent FPS. The trench fighting makes the game in particular. It's quick, vicious, and there's several ways to approach a situation. Maybe you just start lobbing grenades as the grenadier, maybe your officer takes point with his pistol or he calls in mortars or gas to push the enemy back. Maybe you send a rifleman up the trench side to flank around and shoot the opponent in the back from above. You'll become very paranoid whenever you're in a trench and constantly be checking your back. It's more fun than you'd think, especially given that your choices for weaopns are either weak early semi auto pistols, bolt action rifles, or horribly unwieldy LMG's.
On the flip side, The weapons are deadly accurate in this game at range, and after you've played for a few minutes you'll find yourself regularly shooting at enemy troops over open sites at distances that would be inconcievable in most modern games. Some of the maps allow for some seriously long range shooting and you can pick off pesky MG gunners from very far away. Rifles are almost always one hit kills if you hit center of mass so accurate shooting feels solid and rewarding. Thankfully there's a lot of cover but long range sniper duels are not uncommon.
Overall an interesting and different FPS. If this on sale for even $20 or less don't even think about it, just go ahead and get it, you'll enjoy it.

This game is strictly multiplayer and doesn’t have any official servers like Counter-Strike: Global Offensive so expect players with bad behaviour and a relatively good amount of spawn camping.
