Gone Home is an interesting game, that tries to make a full game out of Bioshock's characteristic environmental story-telling. Made by some of the same people, it simply tells the player the story of a 90s family, with a focus on a tennager's social/emotional life.
To achieve that, the game uses everything at its disposal to display the scenery in a way that feels natural, and as if you were back in that era. I'll say that this was very well made, and I believe that they've achieved what they intended, for the most part. The overall experience, however, may not have quite hit the mark, for some people. I'll simply try to break it down to major points, as there is lots of different analysis on this game, due to its 2013 impact.
Everyone seems to have taken a very personal stance with Gone Home, and many people have looked deeply into what meaning this game may have had, and claim that is what made it great. They also seem to overlook that many games employ this. They have subtle references and sidestories. However, since those aspects rarely get major attention, and few people look into that, it ends up being novel. Sometimes, it's not about the game itself, but the whole ambient created around them.
There's a lot of different perspectives around it, and most were made by people far more intelligent and experienced than I am, and with a lot more research. But hey, this is just a game, and people look too closely into it, at times. I've beaten the game in 3 hours, with virtually everything explored, and spent the rest of the time alt-tabbed, reading reviews, and watching videos. Then, I took a week off of the game, and am now writing this review with a fresh-er mind.
Anyway, that was just context! Here are some of my thoughts.
Gone Home is simply about exploring a house, mechanically. You pick up objects, rotate them looking for clues, read lots of notes, books, receipts, everything you can find, really. The only
present in the game is in the form of locked doors, or numbered-locks. You'll usually find the keys fairly close to where the lockpads are, and the doors are simply a way of
. I don't think it feels very forced. Or maybe that's my
at work. Regardless, there isn't much to it, in way of mechanics and challenge. It's mostly reading, listening to diaries, and slowly piecing the different stories in your head.
This is a weird one to write about, since it did not affect me at all. However, since Gone Home is a game that doesn't focus on being a game, but a different way of telling a story, I have the impression that it will affect people who don't normally play video-games. This is simply put because they will not find it natural for these elements to be present.
These elements are the locked doors, that seem to be locked arbitrarily, as a way of gating progress, and the most important one, how notes are literally everywhere.
Notes are spread around all over the place, some being decades old, hence having no place under a bed, or in a table next to the telephone. Again, I can easily overlook this, but it is certainly a flaw when it tries to transcend video-games.
Now, as I said, the game was set in the 90s, and felt like that 90s. And it does it in a very similar way to Bioshock, which I loved. That is, by representing the era with music cassettes, magazines, tv show posters, old VHS with recorded movies, etc. There's a whole lot of that. And the game is also well put together, in the sense that everything seems coherent with the tendencies of the time.
It's a very nice way of presenting a setting, and I think they've certainly nailed it. The music cassettes were especially cool, since they were set up for you to find a play them in a room while you explored it.
This is a highlight for many people, but a low point for me, personally. The stories revolve around a single family. It has marital issues, teenage emotional struggles, old parent relationships, the story of the house, etc. I really like the way its told, but I don't care. At all. Maybe I like empathy, but I couldn't care. The notes were very well placed and written, for the player to get the story bit by bit, without it feeling incoherent, or with too many words. However, it was simply not engaging to me. Contrast that with Bioshock's failed Utopias and progressions therein. Or Zeno Clash's strange worlds, Fallout, and I could go on...
I like games (and books, series, etc.) that take me to new places, and ask some question that would never come in the real world. That's far more interesting to me. I can't be bothered with these mundane stories (sorry if I sound arrogant haha! It's not the intention), because it's not what I play games for. But this is very subjective, of course.
This is a very important point I want to make. It's the 90s. Most of the positive reviews I've read/seen, were from people that were very aware of this era in their lives, and they related with the characters, as a result. I'm not saying this is a bad thing, but it must be considered. I haven't lived the 90s, meaning that I had very little connection with the game. Sure, I had some very vague memories, but it's not the same.
Overall, I think there's a lot of the game that is supported by that familiarity, and that's also why it's often hit or miss. It was well executed, but it's only going to be truly meaning-ful, for the people who are nostalgic about all of the references, and general ambience that Gone Home gives.
This is also something I find important, and the game took full advantage of it. In a book, or a movie, there's hardly a time to think, without pausing it, especially in the latter. You're constantly receiving information, and need to process it instantly.Quite a bit that can be lost in this way.
If you start thinking about a certain scene, you'll probably lose a few other pieces of dialogue or another scene, etc.
With Gone Home, due to it being a game, there's a lot more time to process that information, and also to relate to it, without compromising. It's interactive, in more ways than are obvious. I'm not talking about stopping exploration to think about it. I mean the seconds you would otherwise
between actions. Even between picking up a note and putting it back down. Perhaps turning on the light, or opening a door.  All of this could be
time. However, it's time for you to think about the new notes you've read. What could have happened? Why did the character think that way? How does that relate to you?
This is a very nice aspect inherent to the pacing in video-games. You can have the information spread around, and still be able to easily connect everything while you're playing, without making any compromises. And Gone Home uses it neatly.
I think that's all I wanted to add to the discussion. Overall, I think it's an incomplete experience. What it tries to do, it does wonderfuly! However, I think it relies too much on its theme and
subjects to make an impression on the player. It's a one-trick poney. All it does, is to apply the concept of environmental story-telling.
There's also very little interactivity. You're merely a witness. You never actually do anything. And there were opportunities for that. Some scenes that look like the player could interact with a discover some neat secrets. Nope. None of that, missed opportunity.
I was interesting to play, and read around it. For 20$, though, no, unless you
a different take on games, regardless of the 10/10s. If you just want something to play, this is definitely not for you.

Dark Souls II is a good game let down by the fact that it's merely good, when it is the successor to an incredible title. The biggest weaknesses as compared to the original are the easier gameplay and the smaller scale story. To put it simply, the game is easier. Partly this is because the game explains things a lot more at the start than the first one did. This I don't have a problem with. While Dark Souls holding back information from the player was often great, early on the game this is just infuriating, because basic aspects of gameplay are made far too mysterious and vague.
Dark Souls II clears that up, which is nice. However, the game itself is simply easier. There is no single thing that can be blamed for this. Everything just feels...easier. There's still some tough parts, but overall the game just isn't as tough. This took a lot of the motivation from me. In the first game, after my millionth death all I could think was "I AM♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥AND I WILL SHOW THIS GAME WHO IS THE BOSS!" The difficulty made you want to prove that you're a bad enough dude to take on Dark Souls. DSII...not so much.
The other big problem is the narrower focus to the story. In theory the idea behind the DSII story is actually good. You play an undead, cursed to die and come back to life until you lose all your memories and become a mindless monster, and so you journey to distant land searching for a cure. The problem is that for this to be done well is that it needs a very personal focus. This is a struggle that deeply affects an individual. However, the protagonist to any game in this series is a blank slate. You never say anything. You have no name. You are the classic silent protagonist. This worked in the first game, because the story was your journey discovering the world you were in, and ultimately deciding its fate. It was about you, but solely in the context of the world as a whole. DSII instead is about your personal struggle, but without a strong protagonist to carry the story. There's still the exploration from the previous game as you discover the history of Drangleic, but it just doesn't feel quite as grandiose or interesting as in the first game.
Yet as much as I've written about this game's flaws, I do actually like it. Frankly, the game mechanics are still great. This series has always had phenomenal combat, and that is still here. PvP has especially been improved, with a lot less focus on backstabbing than before. Much of the world still looks beautiful. Levels are a delight to look at and the enemies have interesting aesthetic design. Though it is easier than the first game, DSII still has plenty of challenging areas to♥♥♥♥♥♥you off.
So if you want something of the same quality as Dark Souls, you'll be sad. But if you're willing to have a merely good game, then go for it. It's still a Souls game, and unlike anything else.

Gone home is a procedural storytelling "game" in the loosest sense of the word. It tells it's story through incredibly minimalist interaction with the enviroment and through the discovery of hints of the past, while listening to the "journal of sam". The story is entirely around this person, and not about the player character at all. And while the story is genuinely touching and heartfelt, It's not enough to make a game upon.
This is a game made by people who do not truly understand the medium of video games. This story could have been told better through more interactive means, have more to do, and simply put. make it more of a game than a walking around touching and looking at things simulator. You are a passive observer, looking at things, opening a door and the most imput you ever do is putting a key combination into something. It's entirely linear, it's stupidly easy and it tops out at maybe 2 hours total.  That's less than the length of a feature length movie on average.
Overall, Gone Home's story is a touching hearfelt nostalgia heavy tale that is well worth experiencing, but it is completely wrong for the medium and is ridiculously overpraised. the 20 Dollar price tag is stupdendously overpriced for such a shallow experience. Video games are not cinema, and this is an example of why it does not work. For a game with such a touching story, to be so shallow, so short and so ...boring, it's almost criminal.
Stay away. Stay as far away as you possibly can.

Can't figure out if this game is for you? Let me help you!
ABOUT:
This game is the sequel to the heavily praised game, Five Nights at Freddy's. Five Nights at Freddy's 2 is a psychological indie horror game. As I had stated in my review for the first game, it is not like Silent Hill or Heavy Rain in the psychological aspect, where every choice you make effects the game in some way. You actaully have no choice but to sit in an office as a nighttime security guard for the new and improved Freddy Fazbear's Pizza, a restaurant where kids can have a grand time! Pizza, songs, and cute animatronics that are more kid-friendly now, like Chica the Chicken, Bonnie the Bunny, Foxy the Pirate, and Freddy Fazbear himself! Kids love these things! But when it gets dark and it's closing time, it's up to you to watch over the animatronics. But why would you need to watch over the animatronics if all they do is stand there? I'll give you a hint: after closing time, standing there is not all they do.
GAMEPLAY:
Five Nights at Freddy's 2 is notably more difficult than the first game. You sit in an office with open air vents to your left and right and a dark hallway ahead of you. You also get a flashlight to light up the hallway and, if you pull up your screen that shows you what various cameras in the building see, to light up the dark corners of the room you are viewing. Instead of doors to keep animatronics out, you have an empty Freddy Fazbear head to disguise yourself. This way, the animatronics will think you are one of them and leave you alone. At least for now. There is now also a music box that you must wind up periodically; if you fail to do so, there will be consequences.
REVIEW:
As I had previously mentioned, this game is much more challenging than the first one. I cannot even get past night two. I'm not sure that I like the new animatronics. With new Chica having a more (for some odd reason) feminine appearance, new Foxy/The Mangle having a white face and red painted cheeks, and new Bonnie having a more toy-like look. Flickering my flashlight at Mangle and the old animatronics (the old animatronics are very creepy looking in this sequel) seems to do nothing for me. The Puppet is quite annoying sometimes. But it is a good addition to the game. The game is kind of difficult to hop into and get the hang of. However, it is a fun game and very scary. Sound, like the first game, plays a major role in the game. It's very important that you listen carefully, so I highly recommend using headphones (as much as you probably don't want to with a game like this). I would recommend this game to any gamer who enjoys a good scare. However, I do think somebody looking to play this should probably play the first game first, just to get used to how the Five Nights at Freddy's franchise works. And, in my honest opinion, I like the first game more.

Not everyone will appreciate Gone Home. It's not about shooting, leveling up, or even solving puzzles. Some may even be put off by the story, so it's definetly not for everyone. That being said, however, if you're an open-minded person who enjoys a good story-driven game, then you owe it to yourself to play Gone Home.
It's 1995. You arrive home after spending a year abroad. There's a mysterious note on the door from your sister who seems to be missing. Your parents are nowhere to be found. The house is eerily empty. What are your sisters whereabouts? Where are your parents? Your questions will be answered as you explore through the house and interact with the enviroment. There are letters and notes to read, books to find, and journal entries left from your sister to listen to. The game does an excellent job providing a sense of mystery and even fear as you explore the house, not knowing what may be behind the next door you open. The background music also sets the stage for a gloomy but yet sometimes hopeful atmosphere. As the story unfolds, you may find out that there isn't much to be afraid of.
Your adventure is, unfortunately, short lived. If you spend time exploring through every room, you can complete the story in about two hours or less. After you complete the game, I recommend playing through it a second time and listening to the developer commentary. It's great to hear what goes on behind-the-scenes, and you come to realize that the developers are people just like you and me who enjoy making video games.
Overall, a 9 out of 10. It's not for everyone, but Gone Home is an experience like no other.

Overall, I'm extremely impressed with this game. The developers really did a good job mixing together interesting historical elements and innovative gameplay features. Unlike CoD-type FPSs where you can get by with spraying and praying with automatic weapons, or you can survive a few body shots, Verdun forces players to rely on their skill to win battles, as most weapons used are bolt-action rifles or pistols that only work up close. On top of that, squad-based strategy is huge in this game as the unique abilities of squad members synergize with each other and prove extremely effective in taking/defending trenches when used correctly. Another impressive feature of the game is the fact that the developers' coherence to historical accuracy actually adds to the quality of gameplay. The countless times you get killed out in no man's land, or blasted away in your trench by unpredictable artillery barrages really gives you an idea of how much of a ♥♥♥♥♥how trench warfare was. This forces players to constantly update their strategies and listen to the commands of their NCO, who generally has his eyes on the whole map.
Improvements needed:
-Use of "career points" in the Frontlines game mode to upgrade loadouts/abilities in a similar fashion as the Attrition game mode. I'd like the opportunity to diversify my loadout within a squad so I'm not stuck using the same weapon for the duration of my time in a squad.
-Decrease the zoom on binoculars, or allow for variable zoom/focus. The only thing binoculars are currently useful for is seeing all the way across the map, which doesn't provide a view of any sort of strategic position.
-Add squad member descriptions to the in-game "Squad" tab. If I'm ever in a new or unfamiliar squad, I have to spend 5 minutes accessing the game guide, finding the proper squad in the squad menu, and reading enough of the description to understand what I'm doing. Meanwhile, my team's getting reamed and I'm likely getting kicked for inactivity.
-Add a Red Orchestra 2-type tutorial so players don't have to research the game guide to understand how to play the game properly.
-Campaign/career mode would be cool if the devs could figure out how to pull it off. Although, in their defense, if it was to be historically accurate, the campaign would consist of your character sitting around in a trench, maybe shooting a few enemies, and then getting blasted by artillery or mowed down in a charge across no man's land, and the character's army would've gotten essentially nowhere by the end of the campaign. An interesting story could probably be told somehow though.

Dark Souls 2: Scholar of the First Sin is basically a remake of the original DS2 content.
This enhanced edition comes with many great features, this game is also the same price as the original.
Changes:
-SOTFS comes will all the DLC's of the original Version, so basically you get the full package in one.
-DX9 vs DX11, DirectX9 has poor lighting and Anti-Aliasing. It was a shame that the original DarkSouls 2 came out with DX9 and didn't decide to update it to DX11. DX11 offers sharp and crisp visuals, making the game more atmospheric and gives the game a better re-play value.
-Bugs, YES BUGS! most of the bugs have been fixed, there's no wall-clipping, it's basically a super polished version of the original.
-64bit, Finally this version actually supports 64bit! - **** YEAH!.
-60FPS, that's right, most of PC Gamer's wet dreams for this game has become true! Making rolling, and monsters polished!.
-Monsters actually have a 'brain' as they're been polished, some have new attack styles, some are just more fluent.
The changes made the game harder, I still cry when trying to defeat that ******** King's pet. Damn the DLC's are hard! Goodluck!

This is an extension of my "normal" Dark Souls 2 review.
The DLCs are just more Dark Souls, they're worth the money if you appreciate the base game.
Scholar of the First Sin itself is basically a remix of game mechanics and enemy spawns, and plays like a version 2.0 of Dark Souls 2. It seems this was the intended balance and difficulty of the game originally. However, I would have appreciated if the "normal" Dark Souls 2 would have remained at its original balance. It's affected by the release of this content, and I can't imagine why. The versions are very different. The truth is that the base game doesn't improve from only /half/ of the changes. There's an experience lost to history as well I feel, and that's a shame. In a short sentence, they ruined the "normal" version in favour of this one.
They split up the player base a bit, but since the player base is rather large, I don't really see it affecting much. This is coming from playing the already owned "normal" version and buying the SotFS edition both in December 2015 to compare them. This is obviously going to get worse with time so take this with a grain of salt.
This is the final iteration of the game -finished- as intended for the player to get into. If you haven't played it before, get this. If you feel like you /really/ want to revisit Dark Souls 2 but you're not sure if you want to go through some of the same old stuff just to play the DLCs, get this version instead to mix things up.
The added DX11 is icing on the cake and is a noticeable difference immediately.
Do I like their monitary model for previous owners? No. It could be worse, but it shouldn't be this much. I paid $10 on sale and that's still slightly too much to pay for this, after owning DS2 and the DLC already. Remix and DX11 aside, it's not worth $10 for that. $7.50 is my fair price point for that, $5 is too low, $10 is stretching it. I don't even remember what the non-sale price is, but it's ridiculous.
But do I recommend this version to fans of the series? Yes. If the game is worth playing twice, it's worth remixing it to play it as a somewhat new thing. Enemy placement has completely changed. If you had a "system" of how to make a new character and an order of what areas to go to, to pick up certain things or progress, that's changed. There might be more backtracking, yes. But there's new enemies to fight that for damn sure weren't there before. (As a NG+++ player in the "normal" made me double take) And to me, those changes with a few other big ones keep it fresh instead of making me upset. To you? That's gonna depend.

Dark Souls II is a well known old school action RPG that has earned its reputation from more than just masterful fighting mechanics, wonderful graphics and fledged out world, but also for its notorious difficulty. This review will cover both Dark Souls II and Dark Souls II: Scholar of the First Sin. The latter is essentially Dark Souls II with a portion of extra content, varied enemy placements and some entire new enemies. It also contains all standard Dark Souls II DLC content.
Even at a glance at this game you will immediately notice how visually stunning it is. The in-game textures are eminently crisp, even the backgrops are particularly realistic; from mountainous volcanos to vast oceans. With that said, the actual textures are not even the star of the game's visuals, the actual level design is probably the most breathtaking part. The way developer From Software has laid out these magnificent landmass is a sight to behold. At no point did I ever feel lost during my journey through this winding scape of land. Bonfires, (essentially the game's checkpoint system,) are set apart strategically throughout the world and there is always a large segment of content to explore between each. For the most part the world feels like it has been created apace with enemy placement. Enemies are, (for the most part,) well situated as well as expertly modelled, well textured and competently animated. Finding a new enemy is always a pleasure due the clear-cut quality and effort put into each.
Gameplay wise, Dark Souls 2 is all about the combat. Traversing through the enormous world all to unlock that next boss, that next challenge that you know is going to be difficult but oh so rewarding. Reigning triumphant over bosses never gets old. Killing a boss in Dark Souls is up there with the most rewarding feeling I've felt playing a game. You always feel like you have accomplished something. Being able to tell your friends you've beaten a Dark Souls game is a fulfilling feeling. That said, for those players that don't care about bragging rights, it is entirely possible to summon other players into your game to assist you with the game's tougher content. There is even a way to summon your own friends using a special in-game item which means playing through the unabridged game with a friend is achievable.
Whilst a lot of focus of the game is on the enemy mechanics, there is also a lot of other features in Dark Souls, including player vs player combat, lore and probably most importantly, gear collection. Aside from overcoming well designed bosses, Dark Souls II is largely about unlocking and obtaining gear to wear, use or otherwise hoard. From unlocking boss souls to be traded for legendary items, to finding items to enchant your weapons, to finding that amazing set of armour you've always wanted, Dark Souls II always gives you the feeling that there is something amazing hidden around every corner. Chests, hidden passageways, enemies, corpses. All of these things may potentially contain the armour piece you've been waiting for and attempting to collect every item in the game will drive you insane. (In a good way.)
The PvP in Dark Souls is by no means one of the highlights but it can create some memorable moments. If you are playing online, other players may potentially invade you at almost any time, and it is terrifying. The enemy player is able to roam around the level and hide amongst monsters to attack you; they are essentially an aggressive NPC except far smarter. And sometimes much laggier. The moment I got invaded whilst attempting to clear a room full of spiders was both frustrating and exciting, but what really killed my excitement was when he one-hit-KO'd me by stabbing me in the back. While I was facing him. Sure, Dark Souls may have some lag issues but I still feel that the multiplayer is a welcome feature in Dark Souls especially for those out there who are more interested in PvP, (player vs player,) than PvE, (player vs everything.) That said, I would not recommend this game to someone who is only looking for PvP chiefly due to how lag is compensated for, but also because to have any chance at competitive PvP, you will also need to defeat many bosses to unlock gear strong enough to fight other players. You will also need to obtain a high enough level to even get matched with interested parties.
Once you have officially "completed" Dark Souls II to a degree you're happy with, whether that be by simply defeating the final boss, or by defeating every optional boss, collecting every item, and full upgrading your favourite weapons, and completing the very well made DLC From Software has released, the game offers you New Game Plus. "NG+" for short. Each time you finish the game you are offered the opportunity to restart the game with all of your items, gear and stats. In this mode there are a number of changes to the game that will make your experience far more intense. Perhaps the most noticible amendment is that there are amplified numbers of foes added throughout the game, even new enemies you may not have even seen before. Even the beginner's zone is absolutely riddled with aggressive enemies giving you a hasty feel for how the game is going to be from then on. As well as new enemies, some bosses have obtained powerful new abilities and increased health that will make defeating them a second time a much larger challenge than it was the first time through. Finally, NG+ will add a large number of new items that were not available in your first playthrough, including some new boss souls obtained by the milestone bosses throughout the game. New Game Plus also allows you to obtain items you perhaps missed or accidentally lost in your first run. New Game Plus can be activated every time you defeat the final boss so replaying the game infinitely is entirely feasible.
One of the least talked about features of the Dark Souls series is its lore. The lore in these games is extremely subtle, leaving a huge portion of it to the beholder's imagination. Although From Software never blatantly tell you what the game is about or what the story is, they allow you to discover it through a mixture of your own logical conclusions and the NPC character's fully voiced stories to do the work for them, and I must say it is an elegent addition to the game. It is a wonderfully different style of storytelling that not many other games have attempted much less succeeded at. It is yet another reason Dark Souls II is so compelling and addictive.
The leveling system in Dark Souls II ties in with its currency system. As you progress through the game you will obtain souls. (Hey, it's in the name.) Everything you kill will reward you with a number of souls. These souls are able to be spent at numerous merchants around the world for spells, weapons, armour and usable items. As well as this, souls are also used to level up. You read correctly. You have to resolve between using your souls on leveling up or buying well needed gear and items. This mechanic means that you are always weighing up your options rather than just blindly leveling up each time you hear a ding. You could go through the game focusing all of your souls on leveling up, sure, but you would be missing out on new weapons and armours and you'd be too destitute to upgrade them at the blacksmith. I feel that this constant balance is interesting enough to keep even the newest RPG fan attentive throughout an entire playthrough.

Five Nights At Freddy's 2 is... interesting. While I certainly liked this game, there are definitely some things I noticed quickly about it that left a sort of bitter taste in my mouth. The biggest gripe I'd say I have with this game is that it feels a bit rushed. The game was originally scheduled to come out in 2015 but certain Let's Players on Youtube received early acces to the game. Fans cried out that they wanted FNAF2 now and Scott agreed and decided to extend the early acces version of the game, release it to the public and call it a day and this really shows in the final product (though this is more to blame on the fanbase than the creator). It's not particularly worse than the first game, but it does feel less polished. Another complaint I had with the game was that cameras are essentially useless in the sequel. In the first game, they were absolutely VITAL; you needed to check them for Freddy and Foxy but with the new game, all of the animatronics will come at you, regardless of how often you check the cameras. One final complaint I have with the game is that it definitely feels less tense after the first night, once you start to get a feel for how things work. In the original game, I couldn't do more than one night per sitting because once I made it to 6 AM, I was on my knees, thanking God and was COMPLETELY mentally spent but in FNAF2, I did night after night and made it to night 5 in only an hour and a half (which also shows the games very forgiving difficulty).
All the negatives aside though, it still is a very fun game. I felt like a master, coming up with new strategies, figuring out what each sound meant, how to react to what, etc. and the story and lore of this game are DEFINITELY better than the first one. The parts where you're looking through Freddy's eyes actually had me shaking at times (which has never happened to me before). Something about how the others look at you just really makes you feel like you don't belong in a very unnerving way. It's hard for me to NOT recommend this game to someone, it's very fun, has a more interesting lore to it than the first game and is way less chance oriented and more reliant on player skill, this time around. Still, there ARE some flaws with it. Flaws that I think Scott will do well to learn from if he makes a third entry in the series (which I'm sure I'll buy too).

Gone Home... an appropriate name, taking so many of it's players straight back to childhood memories of the wonderful 90s. And, it gets it oh so right. From the moment you show up on the front porch and start looking at the ceramic decorations, all the way to the last homeade mixtape, Gone Home is a pitch perfect time machine, and a story of heartwarming and sometimes heartbreaking family discovery.
Playing the role of the oldest daughter in the family come home to an empty house, it's your job to Nancy Drew your way to truth. There are no puzzles besides locked doors, and frankly the game has more in common with a seek and find game in it's mechanics. Don't be fooled though, the atmoshpere manages to take you from checking out each object, straight to being immersed in the life of this family - you reach a point where you really step into the role of the older sister. The story telling sticks to a main arc concerning the younger daughter, but through careful discovery and contexual clues, multiple interwoven sub-plots emerge and both sadden and delight.
That's about all I am going say. It would be a crime to spoil a single bit of this game, and it's a shame that playing it twice won't yield the same sense of discovery and that the reveal at the end won't be nearly as emotional... but still, it's worth at least one dedicated playthrough, as this is sincerely one of the most moving video game experiences I've ever had the pleasure of immersing myself within.

So, I'm assuming you've played Dark Souls, and you enjoyed it. Dark Souls 2 is, more or less, more of the same. If you don't want more Dark Souls, then don't buy this. If you're a newcomer to the series, buy Dark Souls. It's a classic, cheaper, and a better game.
What's new? In terms of core gameplay, very little. The controls are almost identical (jump is now pressing the right stick while running, but this can be easily reverted in the options), which is good because they didn't need to be fixed. There is still all the usual medieval weapons and armour, and a fair amount of overlap in terms of spells and magic rings (of which you now get to wear four, instead of two). Expect the same, excellent, rewarding, challenging gameplay that you're craving, and for that reason alone, Dark Souls 2 is more than worth the recommendation.
What you do get, of course, is a new world, populated by new creatures, new bosses, filled with new lore (still similarly inscrutable). The world is simply gorgeous, moreso than Lordran ever was. The view from Majula, the new safe zone, is utterly breathtaking. The areas are well designed as usual, making excellent use of the 3D environments. There are plenty of unlockable shortcuts, one-way passages, and opportunity for ambushes. In this respect, Dark Souls 2 does not disappoint.
In terms of enemies and bosses, Dark Souls 2 suffers somewhat from a lack of innovation. There are, of course, the obligatory hollows and dragons, but so many of the enemies are humanoids, or come from Dark Souls. Even one of the bosses is more or less a direct copy of Sif, and many of the others are simply large humanoids in armour. One of Dark Souls' strengths was its varied (and often creepy) bestiary. Dark Souls 2 still has its share of interesting designs, but it is content with being merely adequate in this regard.
In fact, Dark Souls 2 suffers generally from sequel-itis. The enemies aren't the only thing that feel a little lazy. The other day, I was marveling at the detail of the debris scattered around the crumbling fortress in the Forest of the Fallen Giants, and how the walls and the ground appeared to be so individually broken and crumbled, not just the same textures copied and pasted ad nauseam. Then, I looked over at a space blocked by large chunks of debris, and instantly realised that I was not able to walk over there. Why? Because the ground had no debris, no interesting characteristics, and had the same small square of mossy texture copied over and over again. After that, I kept noticing it: every piece of ground/wall that I couldn't reach, was boring and covered by one small texture. It was such a tiny thing, but it sometimes destroyed the immersion.
But that said, even a lazier Souls game is a Souls game. It is still better than 90% of the AAA games being released at the moment. For that, I give it a recommendation. 9/10
(PS: If, like me, you were worried about how Dark Souls 2 spawns its enemies a finite number of times, then don't. There's a simple way to farm souls and items from enemies: simply join the Company of Champions covenant, by talking to the Victor's Stone at Majula. It will cause all the enemies to become infinitely respawning, but more difficult, while in the covenant. You can then farm indefinitely, and simply abandon the covenant when you're ready to resume adventuring.)

This game was an amazing experience, if you allow it to draw you in. I loved it, and I was moved by a truly well crafted slice of simulated reality. If you're the type of player that rushes from objective to objective not really caring about the bits in between this game will be short, perhaps a bit overly cliched and unfulfilling.

You can find a surprising amount of information not at all important to the main conclusion of the story, but it provides context. It's an almost voyeuristic view into a family over a period of time which you were not privy to.
Some factors are only hinted at, while others are quite blatantly overt. I feel though that this just helps to culminate in the overall impact of the story, but you definitely need to key an eye out for small details. The atmosphere tends to be quite claustrophobic and anxious at times, it seems counter-intiutive once you reach the ending, though it does work in the scenario. Just imagine yourself arriving to a new family home you've never been to before, old and creaky, seemingly abandonned in a rush, I'm certain the slightest noises wil disturb you.
In short, live your character, if you don't, you will not have the full experience.

I'm a huge Souls fan and this game was a great playthrough. I do have a couple of issues with the second installment but overall I enjoyed it and look forward to playing through it again some day. I suppose I'll break it into pros, cons, improvements, and even areas I felt were a step back from the original DS1.
Improvements:
Combat feels more fast paced thanks in part to the higher framerate cap and binding the iFrames to a stat.
The facelift to 1080p from 720p definitely helps bring the world into a crisp new view.
Dual Wielding system was modified to be more viable and useful with Power Stancing.
Covenants served more of a purpose and directly affects your experience in the world.
Story and Lore are a far bigger aspect of the gameplay, helping to guide you through the world.
Pros:
The game has the same brutal learning curve and difficulty the series is cherished for. Even if you're a souls veteran, DS2 has it's own learning curve to bust your♥♥♥♥♥on.
The Durability system plays an important role in your travels and requires you to strategize and plan out your movements from bonfire to bonfire. Many players felt annoyed by this new hinderance, but I like it.
Another added gameplay element is your humanity. In DS1, running around hollow did not offer too many disadvantages. in DS2 it not only penalizes your maximum health, it continues to do so until you hit a hard cap, which can cripple you. It forces you to become smarter and less likely to power through the game via attrition.
Cons:
The story carries less mystique than it's predecessor, offering a clearer glimpse into the events of the world. While it is a plus in some regards, it dampens the ability to take away what YOU want from the world as you explore.
The finite amount of souls and respawns can cause the world to become barren given enough time farming. Though this is unlikely to happen to most, idiots like me usually do a sweep and clear of each area, exploring every nook and cranny. Another problem is I use bonfire respawns to learn how to defeat creatures, and usually by the time I've mastered the way to kill a specific monster it has only a few respawns left.
The Magic system still feels like something they wanted players to focus more on for utility than viability as a primary weapon. It can be done there's no doubting that, but the "wind up" period for mages is staggering and you'll always be hindered by casting uses, much more so that weapon durability which is also something you have to worry about.
The story is great, but giving you a glimpse at a set back story can take away from who you want your character to be, or rather who you wanted them to have been in life. It takes away from the "Sandbox" of it all.
Areas they Took a Step Back (IMHO):
The Finite Enemies is equal parts challenging AND potentially crippling if you're not careful.
The PvP based covenants that guard certain parts of the game are a serious hinderance when they force themselves on you. They take too much from you for being an uncontrolled event. It forces you to drop your souls and that's brutal enough if you say lose a mass of souls you were attempting to recover, but it also hollows you. When souls and more so effigies are at a premium in the game, nothing is more infuriating than some prick walking into your world and using the less than acurate hit box system in PVP to back stab you with a rapier from six feet away, killing you in one shot.
As I mentioned before the PvP can range from a fun challenge to an exercise in frustration. If invaded it appears that the game takes your opponent's (The client) hit box locations over yours (The Host), this seems extremely counter intuitive as it can give your opponent a ridiculous advantage over you, able to hit you after you've already stepped away from a swing.
The world feels less like a "World" and more like a "Series of Maps". Sure the game is still seemless in it's transitions (mostly) to new areas, but the areas don't FEEL connected at all. One exception of this is the DLC areas, which I could tell were designed by the original DS1 team before I looked it up.
Final Thoughts:
With all this in mind, I highly recommend this game so long as you're not expecting a prettier DS1, you'll be sorely disappointed if that's all you want. This is a different game entirely. It's a great installment in the SOULS series, but it has taken more steps back than I felt it put forward. But that aside as I said it's a great installment and if you're a SOULS fan it's worth a playthrough.

This game is seriously underrated! The story was very engrossing and I like the concept of progressing through the story by finding environmental clues. It's a new way to approach narrative in gaming and it made me want to find out more about Kaitlin herself, her sister (who's probably the protagonist) and her parents.
It's an intimate and believable story about love and adolescence told beautifully through audio narrations that's well written and voice-acted. It may be something we've seen before in teen dramas but not in video games and there's nothing else like it. The fact that Sam is a lesbian isn't gimmicky. It would've made no difference if it were about a straight couple, and funny enough, this game has more character development than a lot of mainstream video games (with gameplay) that has character models.
The notes, drawings, photos and other things you find in this game shows how real these characters are. I love exploration games and I like the dark atmosphere in the game that anchors the story perfectly. That being said, you can complete the game within a few hours and then you'll know how to complete the game in 47 seconds after that. If you can appreciate story-driven games with little gameplay (like Stanley Parable or Telltale's The Walking Dead), then I recommend you give this game a go. Most people probably don't so that's probably why there are a lot of negative reviews. Apparently, casuals aren't "real gamers".
Though I recommend this game, I don't recommend it at it's normal price (£15). There's no incentives to replay the game again but the story will stick with you forever. Knowing Steam, this game will go on sale all the time (much like every other game) so pick it up when the price drops.

Gone Home is a game of free exploration. (Free enough to gain the popular tag "Walking simulator" on Steam.) It isn't as much a game as a story, and after a playthrough I feel more like having been the main character of a movie or a book than having played a game. In Gone Home, you return to your parents' home after trip abroad just to find the house empty. Why you don't know, and you walk through the house trying to figure out what has happened.
So, how is the story? Good, yet predictable, and I like the concept of exploring in my own pace by turning household things around in my hands and reading through letters and newspapers. The game is, unexpectedly, not scary at all. Instead it is relaxing and piques my interest. The sound is atmospheric and contributes to a nice overall feeling. The experience is probably best a rainy autumn evening accompanied with a cup of tea.
Other than that I don't have much to say. You walk around in a house, open doors, read notes, look at objects, and build your idea of what has happened.
Even though the Gone Home is fun, its biggest problem is that it's far too expensive. I finished the game after 80 minutes, after taking my time and not rushing anything. The price on Steam is 20 EUR, so in the end the hourly rate is much higher than a visit to the cinema. If you like a good story and want an hour and a half of entertainment I recommend buying this game on a sale.

So I've put this as recommended but this is a tad misleading.  If there was a "sort of" I would choose that.
Firstly the game is fun, easy to get to grips with.  It's pretty generic in the multiplayer pvp modes, the maps are very detailed and quite fun.  The coop mode is where this game becomes unique, they update it quite often and there's a couple of different game modes and 4 skill levels which can really test your ability.
So anyway I'll do some pros and cons:
Pros:
1)  Easy to get in to, the initial match making puts you with rookie players (more on this later) so everyone is of a similar skill level, this is great as you aren't constantly getting destroyed and eases you in to the game.
2) It looks pretty great.  Obviously as it's Crytek.
3) LOADS of weapon/loadout options, and you can get all of it without spending any money.
4)A lot of maps for different game modes.
5) Coop mode, this really is what makes this game stand out and why I continue to play.
Cons:
1) Spawn killing is one of the worst parts about Team Deathmatch.  Most maps it's laughably easy for the other team to get the upper hand and just camp outside or even in your spawn and pick you off.  Almost nothing you can  do once this starts.
2) There are lots of weapons and it is all free HOWEVER.  Getting enough in game money to buy anything takes ages and you also need to be certain levels for certain weapons, levelling up is not a quick thing.
3) After level 12 you're no longer considered a rookie.  You're autmotically put into the "professional" rooms.  This was incredibly frustrating as you now play with everyone from level 13 all the way up to 79!  As a casual player I am no where near as good at this game as 95% of the people who play pvp.  They really need a wider variety of match making, e.g. levels 13 - 29 or something, when playing against the higher ups you really don't stand a chance.  It goes from similar skill level to these players who are constantly going prone, crouching, standing, jumping and sliding whilst simultaneously getting headshots, it's as if they're dancing around and for me personally, really ruins the game.
4) Pay to win.  Whilst people say it's not pay to win, when you enter the professional rooms it definitely becomes closer to this.  There are way more players with the elite temporary items (Which are just so much better than the standard items).  It took me a few hours of grinding to buy a new weapon which still isn't that great compared.
So overall I do recommend you try this game, just be aware of the leap in skill level needed for PVP.  Also the community online is quite funny.  The only time people take the time to chat is when they're complaining about another player hacking or that a new player isn't very good and we should kick them for that reason.
(On the hacking note, I don't believe it's widespread.  I do believe however that some players have really perfected the art of getting headshots almost all of the time whilst sliding along, it's bloody ridiculous)

As I loved The Stanley Parable and Dear Esther and read some detailed reviews (without spoilers) I felt like I had to play this. In a vacant mood tonight, I thought it would be a great time to begin a game that I expected a lot from, especially storywise.
Lets see what we have here... The character we play as is gone for a year and comes back to her home to see her family is simply gone. Great, we already have the feeling of suspense so why would you try to increase it with some plain ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and cliche a newly bought (although in this case, it's not bought but essentially the same thing) mansion with a ghost in it? Although I'm pretty sure that it's just a reference for that cliche, making fun of it but a simple question comes to my mind: why? This cliche has been used plenty of times, parody of this cliche has been done plenty of times even the parody of the parody of this cliche is worn out today. So why did the devs had to take this kind of path, because it's new in gaming? As a relatively new artform, gaming has to create original ideas or remake the classics (by the way I would love to play "The Birds" or "Les Miserables" or any of Poe's stories) before hopping onto the easy and comfortable parody train.
It is possible to see the evolution of art, a background of thousands of years, when you look at The Stanley Parable and Dear Esther. You can find the traces of Jonathan Swift in The Stanley Parable and Philip Sidney in Dear Esther but when you look at Gone Home, you'll only find Stephenie Meyer. Considering that Dear Esther and Gone Home revolves around the similar theme to some extent (loss of beloved people) it's surprising to see how one achieves to be a masterpiece that will survive for years and how the latter achieves to be a game that no one will remember in 5 years.
Soundtrack is the only positive I can mention here, great stuff there at least.

War face is ... Generic in most aspects.  It does not bring anything new to the FPS genre, but yet I still play it ...  It has 4 classes which you can choose from and each their own weapons and play style.  Rifleman uses assault rifles LMG's with the ability to resupply ammo to themselves and team.  Medics can use shotguns and can heal and revive the team.  Engineers use SMG's and they can place directional Mines while repairing armor for themselves and team.  Lastly Snipers dont have any unique traits but the only thing is that they can deal high damage over long distances.  The game is set-up for Cooperative gameplay right as soon as you login. You get to choose from 6 co-op missions that change everyday, 3 'Special Operations' which give really good payouts and a random item upon completion and lastly PvP mode which has 8 games to choose from.  If you have friends it asks you before you join a game if you would want to invite them.  The Devs update things every once in a while.  The rotate new missions in and out and bring in newer Special Operative missions which are longer, much more difficult, and a drastically higher payout with unique rewards.
To unlock weapons/armor/attachments in the game, you have to earn VP which is won by completing missions and/or PvP matches.  Once you unlock them, they are yours. In some instances you buy them with in-game currency, no biggie.  Others are unlocked by level and you can buy them for 1 day, 7 days, or permanently.  There are unique weapons and armor sets that require 'Crowns' for purchase.  Crowns are earned by completing co-op missions.  These are the 'elite' sets mostly recognized by their Orange color.  They add stat and other bonuses to your character which gives a slight edge to your gameplay.  Certain 'Special' weapons/armors are awared by completing the Spec Ops missions and they can have awesome advantages and perks.
Some of the main flaws with the game are that everyone is selfish and/or point ♥♥♥♥♥s, with the occasional hacker-central here or there.  What I mean by selfish is that the majority of folks you play with dont adapt to the team.  For example, everyone is either Assault or Sniper.  There are barely ANY medics, besides myself.  Another issue is poeple dashing or running super far ahead of everyone and getting themselves or the team killed.  They would then blow up the message box telling you to 'rush to the next checkpoint' or 'just go' because they just want to be dumb and watch everyone die like they did. This normally occurs if you play the harder or Insane difficulty missions, and sadly even the easier ones.  No one has a sense of Unit Cohoesion or cooperative play, hell let alone tactical prowess when you do missions or spec ops which makes you wonder why do you play as the supportive roles.  They rush into danger and get themselves killed and ♥♥♥♥♥ at you to get shot at to revive them.  Not alot of people play their class roles and there are only a small few people who have a tactical sense and work well with a team.  It gets infuriating trying to heal or repair armor and the person youre helping just runs around like some CoD junky.
There are hackers here n there and its the main reason I stay away from the PvP elements.  I dont call folks newbs or whatever because I know im not that great at PvP and my K/D spread is at a 0.9, I dont really care. But its when I get killed from a headshot by a dude across the map who is in a random corner shooting through walls.  Or in a Domination game, they capture all posts instantly without moving an inch.  Its things like that that become irritating to engage in PvP.  There are very few that Ive noticed in the PvE portion, but I dont see anyone complaining.  The matchmaking is unbalanced for new players.  Youre thrust into any room or any game with people who outrank you with better gear.  I understand the debate with skill vs gear and I did rock some people with just basic stuff but it gets kinda obvious that it takes quite a bit more hits to take down some people.
In my honest opinion... It gets a 6/10.  I recommend it to people who want a quick taste of 'team FPS' other than dirty bomb... or TF2.  I do like that the game is updated and changed frequently its great.  The devs still have not made changes to playing a supportive role.  You just get♥♥♥♥♥♥on by everyone for not being a rambo dumbass with no sense of tactical prowess.

I find Dark Souls 2 to be an incredibly divisive game. Even within myself, I go through periods of thinking it is an incredibly poorly realised sequel that lacks some of the fundemental principles that made the original such an amazing game, and then switch to feeling as though the game is pretty amazing.
The Bad:
The invasion PvP is based upon a consumable item. When the game is built around the risk of having your game invaded by someone out to kill you, adding a cost to every attempt to invade someone feels like a nonsense
Many of the enemies aggro to you in groups, which doesn't fit the 1 v 1 feeling that the dark souls combat is built for
Many of the enemies feel like they cheat - big enemies swinging their weapons seemingly infinitely without needing to regenerate stamina, enemies hitting you when the graphic of their swing misses, and more.
Movement feels floaty and imprecise in comparison to the first game
The game work doesn't make sense as it progresses - there's a great deal of dissonance when it comes to where areas are in relation to each other.
The story feels like a nonsense, washed aside with some suggestion that the player will end up progressing "without really knowing why".
The Good:
The organised PvP is really fun and easy to find
The variety of weapons is really cool
The weapon movesets are very fun
The fashion souls is alive
The menu updates are really effective, and a general tidy up of the UI
If you've not played Dark Souls, then I'd recommend that over this. If you have, I'd say to pick this up. You'll have to grit your teeth

As I loved The Stanley Parable and Dear Esther and read some detailed reviews (without spoilers) I felt like I had to play this. In a vacant mood tonight, I thought it would be a great time to begin a game that I expected a lot from, especially storywise.
Lets see what we have here... The character we play as is gone for a year and comes back to her home to see her family is simply gone. Great, we already have the feeling of suspense so why would you try to increase it with some plain ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and cliche a newly bought (although in this case, it's not bought but essentially the same thing) mansion with a ghost in it? Although I'm pretty sure that it's just a reference for that cliche, making fun of it but a simple question comes to my mind: why? This cliche has been used plenty of times, parody of this cliche has been done plenty of times even the parody of the parody of this cliche is worn out today. So why did the devs had to take this kind of path, because it's new in gaming? As a relatively new artform, gaming has to create original ideas or remake the classics (by the way I would love to play "The Birds" or "Les Miserables" or any of Poe's stories) before hopping onto the easy and comfortable parody train.
It is possible to see the evolution of art, a background of thousands of years, when you look at The Stanley Parable and Dear Esther. You can find the traces of Jonathan Swift in The Stanley Parable and Philip Sidney in Dear Esther but when you look at Gone Home, you'll only find Stephenie Meyer. Considering that Dear Esther and Gone Home revolves around the similar theme to some extent (loss of beloved people) it's surprising to see how one achieves to be a masterpiece that will survive for years and how the latter achieves to be a game that no one will remember in 5 years.
Soundtrack is the only positive I can mention here, great stuff there at least.

Dark Souls II: SOFTS is a very similar game to Dark Souls, but it's more refined, despite a few design choices that are not well received by many fans. The port is a lot better than the original game, for which I highly recommend dsfix. I have yet to play the third, so I cannot compare it to the first two.
This game can be difficult for newcomers, and that's a very good thing, as it makes victory much more satisfying than in some other games with strikingly similar combat systems, such as The Witcher 3. It's almost never unfair, the sole exception to which is far enough in that it doesn't detract from the game too much (The location in question is a pretty big hurdle due to the sheer number of enemies, especially on the first playthrough). There are far fewer locations which solely rely on the player having knowledge of the area than in Dark Souls I, which, while some may contest is offset by the number of scenarios where the player must fight several enemies, is a vast improvement to the extent to which battles feel fair. The main way I have found that the game can be made less fun for the player (and the main thing I would advise newcomers to avoid) is if a greatshield is relied on too heavily after it is acquried in the early game, which takes much of the excitement out of almost all fights, as the difficulty ceases to exist until a few sets of circumstances (a few bosses that require the player to actually learn to play) are encounted, making these particular sections of the game much more difficult for these skill-less players who have used a crutch to scrape by than the whole experience would be if the player learned to deal with threats in a better way.

It's important to note what this is, and is not. In my view it is NOT a game, it is interactive fiction. You're being told a short story, with the exploration of the house simply adding to atmosphere. It is NOT going to challenge you, it is NOT going to take more than three hours or so  to complete (apparently it's possible to do a speed run in 30 seconds!). It is creepy but by no means horror. It's not worth full price (£15 in the UK), but would be worth £5 of my time I guess.

I find Dark Souls 2 to be an incredibly divisive game. Even within myself, I go through periods of thinking it is an incredibly poorly realised sequel that lacks some of the fundemental principles that made the original such an amazing game, and then switch to feeling as though the game is pretty amazing.
The Bad:
The invasion PvP is based upon a consumable item. When the game is built around the risk of having your game invaded by someone out to kill you, adding a cost to every attempt to invade someone feels like a nonsense
Many of the enemies aggro to you in groups, which doesn't fit the 1 v 1 feeling that the dark souls combat is built for
Many of the enemies feel like they cheat - big enemies swinging their weapons seemingly infinitely without needing to regenerate stamina, enemies hitting you when the graphic of their swing misses, and more.
Movement feels floaty and imprecise in comparison to the first game
The game work doesn't make sense as it progresses - there's a great deal of dissonance when it comes to where areas are in relation to each other.
The story feels like a nonsense, washed aside with some suggestion that the player will end up progressing "without really knowing why".
The Good:
The organised PvP is really fun and easy to find
The variety of weapons is really cool
The weapon movesets are very fun
The fashion souls is alive
The menu updates are really effective, and a general tidy up of the UI
If you've not played Dark Souls, then I'd recommend that over this. If you have, I'd say to pick this up. You'll have to grit your teeth

A cupcake (also British English: fairy cake; Hiberno English: bun; Australian English: fairy cake or patty cake) is a small cake designed to serve one person, which may be baked in a small thin paper or aluminium cup. As with larger cakes, icing and other cake decorations, such as candy, may be applied.
The first mention of the cupcake can be traced as far back as 1796, when a recipe notation of "a cake to be baked in small cups" was written in American Cookery by Amelia Simmons.[1] The earliest documentation of the term cupcake was in "Seventy-five Receipts for Pastry, Cakes, and Sweetmeats" in 1828 in Eliza Leslie's Receipts cookbook.[2]
A Hostess CupCake, showing the typical "snack cake" style of cupcake.
In the early 19th century, there were two different uses for the name cup cake or cupcake. In previous centuries, before muffin tins were widely available, the cakes were often baked in individual pottery cups, ramekins, or molds and took their name from the cups they were baked in. This is the use of the name that has remained, and the name of "cupcake" is now given to any small cake that is about the size of a teacup. While English fairy cakes vary in size more than American cupcakes, they are traditionally smaller and are rarely topped with elaborate icing.
The other kind of "cup cake" referred to a cake whose ingredients were measured by volume, using a standard-sized cup, instead of being weighed. Recipes whose ingredients were measured using a standard-sized cup could also be baked in cups; however, they were more commonly baked in tins as layers or loaves. In later years, when the use of volume measurements was firmly established in home kitchens, these recipes became known as 1234 cakes or quarter cakes, so called because they are made up of four ingredients: one cup of butter, two cups of sugar, three cups of flour, and four eggs.[3][4] They are plain yellow cakes, somewhat less rich and less expensive than pound cake, due to using about half as much butter and eggs compared to pound cake. The names of these two major classes of cakes were intended to signal the method to the baker; "cup cake" uses a volume measurement, and "pound cake" uses a weight measurement.[3]

Gone Home is a lot like some of the older adventure titles of many years past. However, in place of expansive and crazy settings and mysteries, the likes of which you saw in the Myst series, or other point and click puzzlers, we are presented with a very contained and compact story about a woman and her sister, and her sister's love story. There is no puzzle to be found here, but a digital connect-the-dots form of story telling.
Simply put, if this story hooks you. really hooks you, then all the other flaws of the game can fade away into the background. If it does not, then the game has nothing else holding it together. It is derisively tagged "walking simulator" on Steam, and gameplay-wise, that is frankly about the extent of it. How this shakes up is frankly up to how forgiving you are.
The core story of the game is a sad and sweet tale, but somewhat clumsily delivered. Calling it an attempt to "tug the heartstrings" is a bit too subtle. It's also quite difficult to feel the story is as grounded as they want, when some of the little set piece moments used to deliver it are so ridiculous. I am referring to a specific table later in the game. This is a sort of tonal whiplash of sorts for what they clearly intend to be a very serious piece. Player engagement and empathy is a tough sell in any title. Many games stick only to very well-worn themes such as romance, fear, etc, for this very reason. A few have ventured into the realm of parenting recently, which has generally well received. However, the love story, and the persectution here, are simply too on-the-nose in trying to force empathy. Perhaps if the game were longer, and provided more of a chance to internalize this.
It suffers, of all things, from a show-don't-tell problem that occurs too often in film as well. It is difficult to invest when all you have is text, and is even worse in the gaming medium, where you cannot control the score and camera as entirely as one can in film. You need to convey these emotions through the work. I would point to the flash game dsy4ia as a great example of attempting to convey a concept this way. The best of the horror genre in games also excel at this.
Mechanically, the game is fine. The environment is pretty well detailed, with plenty of nooks and crannies hiding a bunch of notes to collect and items to examine. Which is good as it is the primary game mechanic. The main character moves at a relatively glacial pace however, which while it serves the convention of making the player experience the narrative slowly, also feels artificially limiting as it does in any other title.
Overall, Gone Home is a digital poem, or a parable, about a girl learning about her sister. As a game, it's as simple as they come. As a story, it has some heart. But this game had aspirations well above their skill to deliver unfortunately. Were it extended to a slightly more fleshed out title, it could have been something bigger. As it is, it will be memorable to some who can invest themselves, but a completely forgettable experience for others. Which I find unfortunate. I think this would have been a fantastic machinima, or animated short actually, given slightly more control of pacing, and ability to interleave the story more. But in form of a game, it just felt like walking slowly, and having a sad story preached to me. This is a fault more of the delivery than of the content, but I just wish this one had more play testing with people outside of the dev team.

A cupcake (also British English: fairy cake; Hiberno English: bun; Australian English: fairy cake or patty cake) is a small cake designed to serve one person, which may be baked in a small thin paper or aluminium cup. As with larger cakes, icing and other cake decorations, such as candy, may be applied.
The first mention of the cupcake can be traced as far back as 1796, when a recipe notation of "a cake to be baked in small cups" was written in American Cookery by Amelia Simmons.[1] The earliest documentation of the term cupcake was in "Seventy-five Receipts for Pastry, Cakes, and Sweetmeats" in 1828 in Eliza Leslie's Receipts cookbook.[2]
A Hostess CupCake, showing the typical "snack cake" style of cupcake.
In the early 19th century, there were two different uses for the name cup cake or cupcake. In previous centuries, before muffin tins were widely available, the cakes were often baked in individual pottery cups, ramekins, or molds and took their name from the cups they were baked in. This is the use of the name that has remained, and the name of "cupcake" is now given to any small cake that is about the size of a teacup. While English fairy cakes vary in size more than American cupcakes, they are traditionally smaller and are rarely topped with elaborate icing.
The other kind of "cup cake" referred to a cake whose ingredients were measured by volume, using a standard-sized cup, instead of being weighed. Recipes whose ingredients were measured using a standard-sized cup could also be baked in cups; however, they were more commonly baked in tins as layers or loaves. In later years, when the use of volume measurements was firmly established in home kitchens, these recipes became known as 1234 cakes or quarter cakes, so called because they are made up of four ingredients: one cup of butter, two cups of sugar, three cups of flour, and four eggs.[3][4] They are plain yellow cakes, somewhat less rich and less expensive than pound cake, due to using about half as much butter and eggs compared to pound cake. The names of these two major classes of cakes were intended to signal the method to the baker; "cup cake" uses a volume measurement, and "pound cake" uses a weight measurement.[3]

Gone Home is a exploration, point and click game. Your character has just come home from college, in the UK, and you’re visiting your family, but when you get there, the house is abandoned, with only a note on the door from your mom. You start exploring the house for any more clues or signs of anything abnormal. You start finding journal entries from your sister, Sam. She explains her life, without your character, Kate. All the stuff that she hides from her parents and what she does, her new friend and her secret relationship. The whole story is Sam’s new friend Lonnie and her, get to know each other very well, and start dating. Her and her friend have their things that they hide, for example, they like to sneak off and watch punk rock concerts, and the fact that they are dating each other. They’re enjoying life, but of course they have to hide everything. So you explore the house for more clues, more journal entries, and more secret areas to find out more about the story. It’s a really nice story, really sweet and really sad at the same time. I like these games, where they are just relaxing, just story. This is one of the point and click games I will play. I loved it, it relaxed me. I randomly played this game and I loved it actually. The story of your sister who has a secret little life, and relationship.
The atmosphere of this game fits with the story. An abandoned house, told by one person, who’s just explaining what they missed while they were at college. I imagine if the house was actually full of life, it wouldn’t have been as good. You can move items and inspect them. You find little cassette tapes that play a song by the punk bands that Lonnie and Sam listen to. The game does have some puzzles or hidden areas. If you listen to the story and follow it, you won’t get lost, but I can see people that don’t listen to the story and follow it, will quickly quit and never try it again. The game also takes place during the night, while it’s raining, so you can hear the thunder and lightning around you while you explore the house.
Honestly, play this ♥♥♥♥ing game, it’s amazing. The story flows really well, the ending is great and it’s satisfying to know what happens to them. If you want to know what happens, you gotta play that game, I’m not going to tell you. Best game I ever impulse bought. 10/10

This isn't the easiest game to describe, let alone review.
Some nitpicky people will even try to tell you it's not a game at all, since there's no way to die/fail/lose.
There's only one level, only one thing you work towards, and then it's over. A mere 3 hours in (for me personally).
That can't be good, can it?
It is. It so is.
The player controls Kaitlin Greenbriar who, after a year of travelling abroad, has Gone Home.
Her homecoming isn't quite as she'd planned it though, since nobody appears to be there to greet her.
What follows is an exploration of a large house, its history, what your family has been up to in the year that you weren't there, and why nobody is there.
This exploration is done very literally, you roam through the house in a first person perspective and look at things that you find. Almost everything can be picked up and analysed, most of it won't progress the game along (should you choose you can spend half an hour looking at a pack of toilet paper from all angles). What this accomplishes is that the house you wander around in feels very real. It's not laid out like a videogame level (mostly anyway), it actually feels like a home.
Some objects spark memories, either Kaitlin's or those of her younger sister, Samantha. The protagonist's are displayed along the bottom of the screen, but Samantha's are fully voiced, generally taking the form of diary entries. The voice acting is believable, emotional, endearing.
The game tells you a story, primarily Samantha's, of how Kaitlin being away has impacted her life, what she's been up to, how she handled moving to a new house, how she's making new friends. Endearing is a word I've used already in this review, several times maybe even, but that's what the game makes you do. You care about Samantha, and every diary excerpt you uncover makes you care a little bit more.
By the time you've finally made your way to the last room to explore (game progress is generally non-linear except for two or three segments where you have to know a trick that is only explained in Samantha's diary entries to gain entry to a new part of the house) you'll be hooked and want to know the conclusion.
And I
the conclusion. The entire game builds up to it so well, both foreshadowing and alluding, and it's amazing feat of storytelling.
Treat yourself and play this game, but expect to be told a story and explore a house, not to have your reflexes challenged.
Definitely, passionately and endearingly recommended.
