**EDIT**
You can read my original review down below, but obviously with close to 100 hours into this game, I'm not playing because it isn't fun, but I still wouldn't recommend playing it without some sort of walkthrough or guide. To sum up this review in one sentance, I liked Dark Souls because it was challenging with ultra tight combat and a world that invited you to explore it as much as you can; Dark Souls 2 isn't challenging, it's cheap with horrible hit boxes
, poor level design, and the exploration aspect has been replaced with copious ammounts of enemies that you must tediously kite over one at a time to beat. The original review I posted is now below.
___________________________________________________________________________________
When I am writing this review, I have clocked over 65 hours across 3 characters, and obviously I'm still going to play it, but it's only because I'm so damn stubborn. Also, my only experience with From Software is Dark Souls, I haven't played Demon Souls, Bloodborne, or any of their previous games, but Dark Souls is by far the best game ever made in my opinion, and then they threw it all away with this.
I liked Dark Souls because of it's interconnected world, its fairness to let you explore and unlock secrets, it's genius design and enemy placement. It was difficult because of it's tight combat mechanics which forced you to time hits perfectly and know when to strike. Enemies never swarmed you to the point where you simply cant outrun them or roll past them if you want. The levels were designed with the idea that you had to pay attention, but paths were usually straight and didn't' have precarious ledges that it forced to you go past. Also, environments themselves were rarely punishing (except for Blighttown) and didn't have weird traps or holes that were designed to kill you and do it all over again. I bought both Dark Souls 1 and 2 on the same day, and I spent close to 100 hours playing Dark Souls before I decided to try the second.
Without going in to too much detail about why I hate Dark Souls 2, let me sum it up with these points.
*Enemy agro range is WAY too far making it very easy to get swarmed.
*Paths are crooked with holes everywhere  and enemies close to ledges so you fall when trying to hit them.
*Elevators are too small and falling off randomly is common when you are riding with other people.
*Only 1 Estus Flask to start, and it doesn't even give you full health, making initial exploring too risky.
*Over abundance of enemies with slow combat makes kiting and fighting one at a time such a chore.
*Environmental traps that allow online trolls to kill you when you summon them for help.
*Soul Memory that prohibits you from getting help if your level is too low because you die and can't retrieve souls.
*A very disconnected world with at least a dozen dead ends that force you to travel back and figure out where to go.
*People invading you when you are Hollow and trying to get your souls before you die again and lose them.
*Boss fights which obviously require assistance from others.
*Invisible enemies you cannot lock on to but they can you.
*Items breaking over and over again.
*Snipers that shoot you mercilessly across the level while you try to melee.
This game would be fun, but they took the idea of making a game difficult and ran with it too much. One example that comes to mind is the Undead Crypt. One spot in there has bricks you have to attack to break, you can't roll and break them, but there are bells everywhere that when struck with a weapon summon about six ghosts that come to murder you. You would think you are the only one who can stike these bells, but no, zombies that spawn infinitely behind you without your knowledge can hit the bells and agro the ghosts; just to pour salt on the open gashing wound, even after you kill the ghosts, ringing the bell again brings ALL of them back. It seems they wanted to make a faster paced game with slower combat mechanics too, I can't understand why this game receives such great reviews. This just isn't fun anymore. So many times I die from a cheap thing like poor level design or an enemy that I didn't mean to agro comes out of nowhere and gets a cheap shot in that I found this too frustrating to enjoy. I have died and then lost over 100K souls so many dozen times that my characters soul memory is so high I can't summon for help when I need it the most.
I honestly don't know if I even want to beat this anymore; and what is really bumming me out is I know that I can beat this game, I have the skill and patience to master any video game, but I'm coming to realize that I just don't want to even humor this one anymore. Dark Souls 3 better make this a little more fair.

This is one of my favorite games of all time. The sole reason I made a steam account was to attempt to play the demo on my pc. I first jumped into the demo on my playstation 3, and was instantly hooked. I went back and replayed the demo dozens of times. In that small, tiny, free slice of the game I got at least 15 hours of gameplay. The actual full game has dozens of times more content than the demo, and all of it is just as fun, if not more fun, than the demo.
At first look, it just looks like any other action shooter, but this is so much more. The brilliant idea of including a grappling hook that can pull you to any location was pure gold. Whoever thought of that should get a very large cut of the profit. Combining the grappling hook, parachute, vehicles, combat, explosives and tons of other things is simply said, some of the most fun I've ever had playing video games.
Vehicles and driving are fairly solid, but I would prefer better controller support on the pc since there are sensitivity issues while driving cars, but everything else is fine. Especially helicopters. There are few things as fun as flying around high above danger, shooting miniguns and rockets at enemies below while simultaneously hijacking chopper after chopper as enemy pilots attempt to take you down.
Not only is the gameplay solid, but the graphics look amazing (on pc at least). Panau island is a beautiful place, and I sometimes just decide to jump into a jet and fly across the massive, beautifully detailed island. And that's another thing, did I mention the size of the game? Panau Island has over 400 square miles of glorious sandboxy goodness for you to do whatever the heck you want. Whether that be taking over enemy bases and strongholds, blowing up everthing in sight, finding creative ways to kill enemies, just admiring the scenery, playing evil knievel in all the possible vehicles, or all of the above, Just Cause 2 is possibly the most fun you can have while gaming.

I would just like to say that I've only played Dark Souls 1 once, I think I had a whole hour to it, no idea why I didn't finish or contunue playing, however Dark Souls II is a game I can pick up. I loved it since I went from the get-go. It's a difficult game, without a doubt. As the game loves to tell you, you will die, a lot. But there's a certain charm with the difficulty of the game. Due to the hardness of the game, it somewhat elevates and extends the actual playtime of the game. This isn't an arcade RPG that's going to take you 6 hours to finish "the main quest". You will most likely be commited to a 20 - 30+ hour  playthrough. I'm at my 22nd hour while making this review and I believe I'm half way through and about level 105.
This isn't a game that will hold your hand, I'm not going to lie - the game will tease you and kill you for your curiosity. Some may find this disconcerting as they are usually used to the game telling them where to go and what to do. It shouldn't be a problem as you sort've understand and just know when and where you should be in relativity to your level and gear. If you're not in the right place, the game will let you know, straight away, the hard way. However, if you would prefer the game/a experienced person to tell you what to do or where to go, there are many guides on Reddit/IGN - however I wouldn't recommend this, it just breaks how you should play the game.
Bosses are extremely well thought out and are a hell of a lot of fun to fight, I have always had a problem with games nowadays in which they never seem to have any kind of classic boss fights with the whole, big massive health bar and huge damage and tactics to kill them. Should you find them too hard, the game offers a summon feature in which you can summon up to 3 other players in the same level bracket, which off the top of my memory is -5 your level to +5 of your level, and this works really well as it doesn't seem to scale the boss to how many people you have.
Having an Xbox/PS3/PC Controller is extremely recommended - it feels a hell of a lot more easier to play than a keyboard and mouse - that much is clear.
All in all, buy it, My primary games that I play is Counter-Strike: Global Offensive, Skyrim, The Witcher 2, Rocket League and World of Warcraft - so I'm not a full RPG dryhumper. However I'm sure those guys will enjoy this game greatly.

Gone Home is an unusual, quirky piece of interactive storytelling... Less of a "game" than I expected, but no less enjoyable for it.
Wandering around an empty house, reading notes, documents, and crumpled letters is intriguing, and slightly unsettling: you don't know this place (neither does the character you play), and you're never quite sure what's going to be around the next corner or behind the next door. Maybe it was just me, but entering darkened rooms with a storm thundering away outside gave me a constant sense of unease and foreboding, and I was genuinely nervous about what I might uncover as I flicked each light switch. Whether or not that was warranted, I'll not spoil.
As the clues unravel the story and the voice of your sister, Sam ("speaking" to you via her journal), shares details of inner turmoil and intimate secrets, a genuine concern to uncover what has happened to your family slowly builds and drives you onward. It won't take you long to reach the conclusion (a friend did it in 2 hours, my experience was just over 4... but then I do have a tendancy to poke into every nook and cranny and examine every object available to me), but I'd be surprised if you didn't feel some emotion at the revelations.
This is due in no small part to the beautiful voice acting of Sarah Grayson as Sam - honestly, I've never felt such a connection to a character that doesn't appear on-screen before. The ambient audio also works very well, and there's some kick♥♥♥♥♥girl punk music to be enjoyed by sticking various cassettes you find into nearby players.
Visually, it's not groundbreaking - but it does the job. There's lots to look at, details to uncover, and some sly humour hidden away if you look for it.
Definitely a game to try if you like to deviate from the mainstream, but once again: be prepared for a short experience.

PROS:
1. Authentic WW1 gameplay. It's all there, from gas to the snap-crackle-pop of a round going by your head.
2. Fun with friends. Squads have 4 slots.
3. Varied maps.
4. Wide arsenal
CONS:
1. Servers desync terribly sometimes.
2. Community now as opposed to alpha (see below).
COMMUNITY
I recently started playing the game again due to the new update adding US and Belgians. My very first impression was this: the community is cancerous. When I first started playing Verdun, the community was very helpful and team-oriented. People would call out targets, provide situational awareness, cooperate on assaults, etc. It was very fun to be part of a team that worked together. The community today is a far cry from that. The chat is a bunch of COD kiddies arguing about how they ♥♥♥♥ed eachother's mother. Nobody uses teamwork to complete the objectives; it's all about "OMG I JUST GOT 20 KILLS WITH MY MACHINE GUN." Said MG gunner neglects to pay attention to the fact that his squad is getting slaughtered as they try to cross no-man's-land with no covering fire.
I recommend this game if you have three other friends to make a full squad. Otherwise, you will find no enjoyment in working with others in this game, which is unfortunate because it's a team-based game.

Fantastic game with a great community. The setting and atmosphere is perfect, all the weapons/outfits are historically accurate, and even the use of language is impressive. When you can't see them, you know the nationalities of your allies and enemies by their shouts. If you're a German and you hear French and English in your trench, you'd better get ready to fight. It's a small detail that I personally find very immersive.
Brutally simple gunplay. Most weapons are bolt action rifles, and you die in one shot most of the time. I think the setting and mechanics of the game turn away cancerous "COD-kiddy" type players who crave killstreaks and fast paced gameplay, ludicrous guns, etc. You can usually spot them whining for 2 or 3 matches in the chat, and then never see them again. I really doubt this was intentionally done, but having these players naturally phased out dramatically improves the community. Good job, Devs!
Speaking of which, the community is full of proper gentlemen, the type of guys you feel proud about capturing a trench with. The overwhelming majority of players are friendly, helpful, and non-toxic, Something nice to see in a modern FPS game.
This game requires patience, and you will probably die a lot when you start playing. It plays very differently than shooters like COD or CSGO, and therefore it won't appeal to everyone. Having an interest in history also improves the experience, but definitely isn't necessary to enjoy. I think many FPS fans will appreciate this game because frankly, it's just a lot of fun.
It's clear that the developers wanted to create a proper WW1 shooter, something that many people, myself included, have awaited for years. Thank you for fulfilling this wish.
TL;DR: Amazing game, don't buy if impatient or diehard "COD kiddy"

A satisfyingly more frantic take on the original formula. There's more multitasking to be had as the increased number of animatronics can come from three places versus two, and a Puppet character replaces Foxy as the mechanic to keep you invested in the camera instead of spamming the halls and mask. With multiple animatronics able to be around you at the same time, the game comes down to split-second decision-making in deciding whether or not to placate the Puppet, fend of an animatronic in the hallway via flashlight strobing, or abandon everything to duck into the Freddy mask and hide. Scarily enough, the latter decision will sometimes be made for you. The movement is nicely faster and lights turn off upon mouse release, almost making the original seem a bit clunky in comparison, and all of the micromanaging that must be done makes the game wonderfully hard as nails. Couple that with increased graphical fidelity and animation, and a sensibly expanded take on the series' lore that paints the animatronics in a new light, Five Nights at Freddy's 2 is a genuinely great sequel worth every penny!

Although it is not a worthy succesor to DkS 1, it is still a good game if you're yearning for more Dark Souls.
While Dark Souls 1 had a great first part and a terrible post-lordvessel part, DkS2 is just mediocre throughout.
+ Greatly expanded gameplay, with addition of power stances, making dual wielding actually viable; archery is also better as you can move around this time. Reworked poise so that it isn't as ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ as it was in DkS1.
+ Tons of customization - there are lots of armors and weapons. Feels a lot less restricting. Boss weapons also pretty much all have a unique attack.
+ DLC is great all around. Best bosses, best soundtrack, best level design, interesting lore that shines a new perspective upon the vanilla game; great items as well.
+/-  Level design is all over the place. Some areas have some good vertical elements that adds variety with some cheeky hiding places for items - particularly Drangleic Castle and Earthen Peak
However, most areas are just a straight corridor, extremely horizontal (almost to the point of being straight corridors) with no shortcuts or anything interesting going on like alternate paths.
- Story (or lore) is very disappointing. It's basically Dark Souls 1 with different names. Plus it has a lot of references to DkS1 (every boss soul basically contains "this soul is reminiscent of a being from another time..." clearly hinting at DkS1 characters. It's just a nostalgia trip. There's nothing new here if you're looking for story.
- Soundtrack isn't all that good. Only theme I remember is Majula and that's because it plays everytime you go there.
- Enemies are placed to ♥♥♥♥ you in the mouth and frustrate you in some areas, instead of providing some challenge. Expect some unavoidable 1v3s (versus powerful enemies, not hollows) or worse.
- Terrible world design manifesting in its disconnected world, to the point where it doesn't even make sense. You're in a swampy poisonous area, take an elevator up and you're suddenly in a burning lava covered castle.
If you're looking for more Dark Souls, it's worth picking up. It's more of a "filler game" cashgrab than anything.

Reminds me a bit of Rising Sun / Red Orchestra 2.  If you like that type of game play, it will be fun to play, but set in WWI.  If you're not a fan of "mystery shots" or the occasional random air strike kill, this game will probably annoy you.  Honestly, I find it to be a delightful mixture of both.
I feel that there is still a lot of work to be done for this game, but the developers, as of May 2016, seem to be pretty interactive and consistent with the community (for the little time that I have owned it).  Assuming they continue to put fourth their best effort and improve some of the minor clunkyness of the game (watching people run up ladders, some of the double-breathing sound effect when holding your breath and wearing a gas mask, etc.) I would recommend checking out this game.  I also think that it has a lot of room for improvement as far as making it clear how the points system works, and where you need to go to unlock weapons.  Currently, it is impossible to unlock weapons with points you have earned outside of a match.  This isn't a huge deal, as once you find a particular country/position you enjoy playing you will concentrate mainly on unlocking those weapons, but if you are attempting to 100% all of the achievements the game has, you'll quickly grow to find this setup a bit tedious.
Overall, worth a purchase if you like WWI, and defiantly worth a purchase if you've played Rising Sun RO.  Otherwise it might be best to wait until the next steam sale.

Verdun takes you away from what you seem to find in modern shooters and puts you back in good old trench warfare where you must rely on your squad-mates and teamwork to survive. Rather than gathering kill streaks for care packages and loading yourself up with perks you'll simply pick a position in a squad, adjust your loadout accordingly and you're thrown right into the trenches. Instead of an every-man-for-himself approach to things Verdun keeps the focus on teamwork and it achieves this by appointing an NCO (essentially a captain) to every squad who can issue orders throughout the game.
The main gamemode of Verdun (and my personal favourite) is Frontlines where you'll find yourself and your squaddies playing tug-o-war for a long stretch of land, periodically pushing and attacking or retreating and defending. You'll find yourself dug into your trenches when you start and your first objective will either be repelling the enemies attack or attacking their trenches yourself. The attacking team will have strategic points along the enemy trenches which they must assault (the other team will be defending these points during this time). Your job as the attacker is to clear out the enemy trench claiming the land for yourself and once you do your enemies will be forced to retreat to a trench further back and hold that ground instead. On the other hand if the defenders succeed at repelling the attack they will keep hold of their land and immediately be able to launch an assault on the opposing team. This will continue back and forth until one team has taken all the land from the opponents and captured their HQ or until the time runs out in which case the win goes to the team holding the most land.
Instead of rushing forward you'll have to plan your attack carefully, following any helpful commands your NCO may issue you along the way. Frontlines (like the rest of Verdun) rewards you for taking your time and scouting out your enemies and if you try to take a kamikaze approach to things you'll likely find yourself dying quickly and repeatedly. This is a major advantage to the game over many other FPSs as you'll find yourself learning to play properly and focus rather than hoping that a huge amount of luck will be on your side.
There are other game modes besides Frontlines and these include: Attrition which is a team deathmatch style mode where you each have tickets which are lost upon someone dying. Once a teams tickets have been depleted the opposing team wins. Rifle Deathmatch is a free-for-all upon which you choose your weapons when you enter the game and can level those up by killing other players unlocking things such as bayonet attachments. The player with the most kills at the end is victorious. The last game mode is Squad Defense where you play single player in a squad and must defend against waves of oncoming AI enemies until you are eventually wiped out. Each game mode has it own allure but Frontlines is the most popular and you'll find the majority of players spend their time in that mode though you'll not have trouble finding games in the other modes.
Squads are one of the main features of Verdun and there are 12 of these to choose from (if I'm correct). Squads have different perks and abilities which are unique to that squad and the same goes with the 'classes' you'll find within each one. Each squad is made up of four different 'classes' some of which include the Oberjäger or Guide, Scharfschütze or Tireur d'élite, Überwacher or Observateur and the Aufklärer or Éclaireur and each of these squads and classes have their own load-outs and play-styles. For example the Scharfschütze is a marksman class and prefers lots of distance between him and his unlucky targets, whereas the Aufklärer excels at melee and needs things to be up close and personal. Choosing which squad and class you play will greatly affect how your outcome so it'd recommend giving each squad/class a try until you find what is right for you because they truly all do play very different. Each squad will also have an NCO who will appoint attack and defend orders for the rest of the squad to carry out. Attacking/Defending these targets and/or remaining within your NCO's command range will award you with extra points and will help your squad level up unlocking various different things for you such as perks and even some additional classes. Although the desire to do your own thing can be strong the gameplay really is geared towards teamwork and you'll find very few situations where going solo reaps a better outcome than going as a group but the choice is still yours and you are not forced to follow orders.
I think one of the graphics of Verdun are amazing and I find myself admiring them every time I play. The attention to detail and sparce placement of objects adds to the immersiveness in-game and together with the artillery bombing and rifles sounds going off creates a perfect war atmosphere.
Also the in-game community seems to be refreshingly nice which is a rarity in most first person shooters I've played so that was welcome. Rather than abuse there seemed to be a lot of friendly interaction between people and players were willing to help when a question was asked.
My only issue with Verdun is the fact it can be very difficult at first and some may find that offputting. It took me a good few games until I really felt comfortable and at first  it was frustrating feeling like I couldn't move without being killed. This quickly changes though if you're willing to take a game or two of hardcore defeat and soon you'll find yourself playing as well as you would in any other FPS.

Oh boy,
I got this game soley because it was the first World War 1 FPS game i have ever found.  I liked it because this time in history is virtually non-existant in the gaming world.   Seeing this was a nice change of pace.
The best part about this game, is the community.  They are helpful, and unlike most FPS fanbases, they think.  When I was mulling over the idea of getting this game, I checked the reviews, like you are now.  What I saw a lot of was "you are gonna die a lot, but don't let that discourage you."  They were right, but I kept trucking along.  I got better, and it was fun; then everything changed down the road.
With the new updates coming out, Verdun fell into the trap that nearly every FPS fell into: Catering almost exclusivly to the marksman/sniper class.  I made a discussion about it on the community hub, and they told me just to keep practicing.     I did, but there were still some major problems.
The biggest problems facing this game and two things: 1) spawn system is a mess.   Too many times have I spawned only to IMMEDIATELY get a mortar thrown right on top of me and have my head blown out my backside.  2) As stated before, catering to the marksmen class.  In some maps, like Duramount for example, I REFUSE to play that map as the allies.  It is such a sniper's nest.  Your game play is literally nothing but spawn, die, spawn, die, spawn...die.  To test this, I had a friend watch me and time how long it took me to die when i respawned.  I didn't move forward, all I did was spawn and immediately crouch down, and then died.  My life time?  0.83 seconds....I WISH I was making that up.
This game has(had?) a lot of promise, but so far I am seeing a bunch of wasted potential.  The devs are working, but are they doing the right work?  This game needs a lot of polishing.  As it is now, I cannot recommend it, but I hope that will change.

Let's start with the obvious drawback that has everyone balking : This exploration game is extremely short. I finished it in little less than two hours - and I took my time reading everything, listening to audio tapes, the works.
Is it worth its price ? In my opinion, yes. 20 bucks is something you could pay for a Blu-ray, and that's exactly what this game is term of gameplay : an interactive movie.
Not an action movie packed with cinematics, though - the entire game is spent walking around the house, discovering secrets, picking clues, and hearing the voice of your sister (the voice acting is spot on, by the way) telling you what happened with her during your absence. Plus some other side stories - your sister isn't the only one with a story, though hers is the most developed.
All of this contribute to make you feel engaged about the characters - you want to know how the story end. That's the whole point.
And that's the problem with this game, like all story-driven games. It's pretty much hit or miss : either you like the story or you don't.
SO - if you like a well-delivered love story, with excellent acting and character developement, then go for it. You're going to love it. Otherwise, don't bother.

I bought Gone Home on its release day after following the Fullbright Company's blog for several weeks. Early 1990s aesthetics with queer themes and a riot grrl soundtrack? Of course I’m in!
It's been more than a year since then and I still count Gone Home as one of my favorite games.
Backstory:
Gone Home came out at the beginning of my Junior year of college. I'd just moved into my own apartment (as opposed to the cramped dorms of the two previous years) and I was reveling in my newfound adulthood with utility bills, cramped bus stops, and a probable case of scurvy.
Gone Home also came out in the same period that I did.
Blah blah blah. Long story short: It was a challenging time in my life that I’ve navigated through slowly and with much consideration on what’s truly important -- not unlike in Gone Home.
(Slight Spoiler Alert)
I won’t say my circumstances mirrored Sam’s. I wasn’t a teenager in the 1990s -- Hell, I was still wearing neon stirrup leggings and plastic animal barrettes by the time Y2K was supposed to bring the world to its glorious robot-driven end (or something like that). But in listening to Sam’s audio diaries and sorting through her notes throughout the game I was overcome with this intense nostalgia and sadness that I’m sure all kids who have ever struggled with familial approval will recognize.
I’m not quite sure I can put into words what Gone Home did for me on an affective level.
Playing it was like coming home early after middle school and sneaking into my parents’ room to search through their bedside drawers for proof of vulnerability. It was humanizing and wonderful and very, very uncomfortable at some points (I’m referring to the game here mostly -- my own explorations were more a lesson in the “better left unknown” category).
After the game ended (no spoilers I swear!) I curled up on my couch and cried for a good 20 minutes. Partly for the Greenbriar family. Partly for my own family. Partly because it was 3AM and I had a legal studies power lecture in four hours. Mostly because I found something special in Gone Home that I’d been looking for -- a LITERAL exploration of what it means to make a family out of individuals.
Despite what I’ve said about my own personal connection to Gone Home, I truly don't believe you have to identify as LGBTQ and/or female in order to enjoy the game.  I'd actually really encourage people to try and broaden their horizens with narratives that may not be familiar to them. Spice of life, amiright?
The narrative itself explores relationships among individuals with secrets and flaws (like in real life!) which is certainly a universal theme and as such can be appreciated by many. (((Though I will admit that having a queer female major character is, imho, awesome and definitely something I'd like to see more of.)))
On a purely visual level, the graphics and the continuity of the mid-1990s aesthetic are outstanding. Like, EVERYTHING is so much fun to look at.
Gameplay itself is intuitive and smooth with regular WASD movement controls and left/right clicking for further exploration/picking up/putting down objects. ALTHOUGH it should be noted that this game doesn't play particularly well with integrated graphics -- specifically on Windows 8 for reasons?
The soundtrack is hands-down one of my all-time favorites as far as video games go (I even put it above Schyman’s Bioshock score) with Bratmobile, Heavens to Betsy, and The Youngins providing most of the Riot Grrrl ambiance. Even if punk or Riot Grrrl music isn’t your thing it just goes SO WELL with the narrative that you’ll find yourself bouncing along with it.
All in all, I honestly believe Gone Home more than deserves its critical and public acclaim.
THAT BEING SAID -- it should be noted that Gone Home has suffered majorly from certain segments of the gaming population who have specifically sought to discredit/negatively warp public reviews both on Steam and other public gaming review sites. This is most clearly visible in that while there are an overwhelming number of positive reviews versus negative reviews, the "most helpful" review section has been bombarded with massive numbers of thumbs up on the minority negative reviews.
People who don't own/haven't played the game come to the Gone Home store page for the single purpose of voting down the positve reviews and voting up the negative. That's just a fact.
Why?
It's messy.
And childish.
And ultimately irrelevent to the fact that Gone Home is an excellent experience for those who are open to taking it as such.
If the price is a bit steep (the one criticism I can agree with) then I suggest picking it up during a sale or borrowing a friend's library.
And have fun for frack's sake.

If you've already played Dark Souls, Demon's Souls, and/or Bloodborne, you needn't read further as you already know what to expect.  But let's assume you haven't or you'd like to know if this is worth picking up if you already have Dark Souls 2.  Well, this is a sort of "remix" version of Dark Souls 2, with slightly different and more devious enemy placement.  It also seems to have all the DLC intact and is fully optimized for 64-bit systems and as a result, it runs PERFECTLY at max settings on this PC.
Alright, so let's assume you're new to all of this and have no idea what this game is.  So imagine Ghosts n Goblins, but as an action RPG.  Dark Souls 2 can be painfully tough, but extremely rewarding.  It's ridiculously addictive and a refreshing change of pace from most mainstream titles that strive to handhold and pander to more casual audiences.  Will you beat it?  Probably not, but you'll definitely enjoy it, especially if you enjoy a more retro style difficulty that puts the skill of the player more to the test rather than your willingness to just grind in a given area until you're overleveled, which can't really happen anyway as you are limited to how many encounters you'll actually run into in a given area.
Dark Souls 2 is not for everybody, but those that do play it swear by, and at it.

The voice acting is great, and you can feel the emotion in Sam's voice as she tells her story.
If you're interested in a good story, and want something casual but engaging, I would definitely recommend this game.

This game, contrary to how it might appear, is certainly not about the story or plot, or even about gameplay. It's more a really personal account of a reasonably mundane (as in normal, not boring) lives of an American family, with a focus on the younger sibling via her notes. Because does this so well, I definitely recommend this; it was two days ago I played this and its still stuck with me. You can see my play time is around 3 hours, and that's all it lasts: I suggest playing it in one sitting, preferably by yourself and sat somewhere comfortably.
I think the experience you'll get from Gone Home will be something very personal to you, so I won't presume to describe what you'll feel. Myself; I felt like I'd got to feel inside someone elses emotions and life for a few hours, like people watching but better. Afterwards, I felt that I needed to know the characters better despite the awareness that they were imagined by the designers of this game.

Dont let the negative reviews deter you, but at the same rate do not pay more than 5$ for this!

I see a lot of negative reviews for this game, and a these reviews seem so completely wrong and totally misunderstand the point of the game, that I felt I had to write my own review.
If you're going into this expecting gameplay and a riveting story, well I guess turn around, stop reading this, the game isn't for you. The gameplay consists of walking around a house, clicking on stuff, and reading things. It's not even an adventure game, in that there is no challenge, everything is rather linear.
The story is also lackluster. It's a story about a family going though rough times. But it is the emotions that this simple story, in it's tone and delivery, elicit that make it worth it.
There are slight spoilers ahead, but they are needed to bring across the point. If you've ever been a person confused about your own life and sexuality, or as is my case, an older sibling who graduated high school, went off the college or whatever, and left younger siblings behind to fend for themselves, you'll find yourself identifying with either Sam or Kate.
I found myself identifying with Kate, as the older sibling who had also left a younger sibling behind with mom and dad. That older sibling in me came out, wanted to make sure that Sam was alright. I almost picture myself coming home from college to a similarly deserted (but MUCH smaller) house, and finding writings from my own younger sibling, discussing her problems in school, her issues with love, and with mom and dad.
Yes, the story is a simple, "girl meets girl, girl discovers her sexuality, girl runs away with girl, family is left to pick up the pieces" story. But it is the tone and delivery (the voice acting is top notch) that make this an experience that should be experienced first hand, at your own pace, not at the artificial pace of someone doing a Let's Play.

Although not as great as Demon's Souls or Dark Souls, this game holds up rather well.
Lets go over some areas mkay..
Combat - Combat is great in this game as it feels more smooth and natural thanks to much better animation.
Gameplay - Improved thanks to the animation once again, movement is nice and smooth and overall feel is generally nice.
Story - If you know the Souls series then you should know what to expect. For Souls veterans you can expect a very vague but somewhat at the same time an interesting story. Drawn to a kingdom for practically no reason other than "I got this hunch ma". For newcomers, if you're expecting a blockbuster story or a Bethesda-esque story then you will be disapointed. The story is vague like I have said but it's quite interesting and builds up in the later stages into a quite epic ending.
Performance - One of the best PC ports I have ever experienced. When I completed it I had the AMD FX-8350 and an R9 270 and it handled the game at max with 60fps easily, no drops in the entire playthrough I can gaurantee.
Atmosphere - FromSoftware know how to get this right, it's dark and moody and sets the tone of the game well.
Difficulty - This game is quite difficult but that depends on what you're playstyle is, when people say it's the hardest game ever I gaurantee that they play it like a Call of Duty game. To live long you take your time, watch your enemies movements and respect them at all times, if you underestimate them you will learn very quickly.
Overall - This game is worth a look if you enjoy an Action-RPG romp and this game will keep you busy for roughly 40+ hours.

As a 50 year old English man Gone Home really worked for me. It reached my emotions, it touched me, it resonated with me in a realistic way (I married an American) and it brought other emotions too, but enough on that as I don't want to give spoilers.
I related to all of the characters in one way or another, It brought back feelings from my youth which was very fulfilling on a personal level.
It also introduced me to Riot Grrrl music. It is a genre that totally missed me by. Surprisingly in my mind as my musical tastes are rather obscure. For example Guided By Voices were on an in game poster, and I listen to them a lot. Many of the other bands mentioned I am familiar with too. I am a particular fan of punk (from all decades). So yes Riot Grrrl passing me by is a surprise.
But enough about me, back to the experience.
It took me a couple of hours to complete, which I find for an experience/art style game is a comfortable time which feels about right. I played through in one sitting, which is how I like to play through these kind of experiences.
The mechanics although simple work very well. I used a Xbox 360 wireless controler.
I went through the game blind, so the sense of discovery was immense for me. I highly recommend not finding out much about the expeience before you start.
So for me Gone Home is way up there for me as a great experience.
So if you like experiences like I do then I rate this 92%.
But if you prefer action, adventure and horror and hate "Walking Simulators" then it is a 12%

Just Cause what?
I heard frequent talks about the game being a great and fun action shooter with lots of random stuff blowing up and unrealistic, yet amusing mayhem. I kinda imagined it like being a Saints Row focussed on grappling hooks, aerial stunts and a jungle surrounding.
Oh boy, was I mistaken.
The first thing coming to my mind: Jep, console-port. Technically there isn't an issue with console ports, I know quite a few that belong to my list of favourite games. But if 'HEY I'M A CONSOLE PORT' jumps into your face just by looking at the game's menu and said menu's handling, that's one minus. When navigating said menu feels tedious and not geared towards utilizing a mouse at all, that's another.
And then the game starts, dropping you right in without anything remotely resembling a story. If I say that the first Duke Nukem had a better intro story, then that's not an overstatement. Well, we're here for the action, smooth combat and stylish grapple hook slinging, not the story, right?
I was literally baffled once I got my hands on the first few guns, started using the grapple hook and fought a couple of enemies. But not in a positive sense. I mean, the game is built around the grappling hook, right? Then why does it look like glitching, crappy animation made in a hurry whenever the character grapples upon something? Why does jumping look like it was importerd straight from CounterStrike (No, neither Source, nor 1.6, I'm referring to the original first release)?
At this point, all the other minor-medium negative points, like ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ enemies, malfunctioning physic, extremly plain and unintuitive gunplay  or the fact that the left mouse button fires the right firearm and vice versa, barely playmuch into the rating of this game being terrible.
Admittedly, it might have some great moments or content later on, but that's of no concern to me when the first hour of play already makes me want to puke at whoever deemed the animation engine of the game acceptable for modern play.
Result: 3/10, because hey, at least it doesn't look extremely bad and it got grappling hooks.

This game is very vehicle driven - if you want to hijack a plane in mid air you can. If you want to have dogfights with jets this is your game. However, the truest mode of transportation you'll find is Rico's grappling hook. This thing is like spiderman and his web; It'll take you everywhere and anywhere across miles.

i haven't recommended this game before? shameful. it's my favorite game.  i love it. there's nothing else like it and no proper way to describe it. the dark souls franchise is my favorite of all my years of gaming, so anything i have to say on the subject is going to be heavily biased.
despite that, i truly think you should try this game. whether you've played dark souls or demon souls or even standard dark souls 2, this is by far the best of them all. bringing back the dual weilding for dark souls 2 was a smart idea and the level design changes alone are worth the money. not to mention dark souls has the best online community out there. (again, i am biased, but i stand by it.) very few RPGs have been able to effectively blend the single and multiplayer experience in the way the dark souls series has. you can play for hours by yourself and forget you're online and then stumble into the wrong area at the wrong time and get invaded by someone out of nowhere. the game of cat and mouse and the combat between a real life oppenent in this game is unmatched by any other out there. every kill and death online has meaning-was earned. hard fought. the fights are tense and i love it. the iron keep bridge fight clubs are a huge attraction for me. levelling up your character by testing your skills against other players in a 1 on 1 duel-it's such a blast. and i haven't even really mentioned the enemies. scholar of the first sin is filled with tons of nasty enemies that will punish you for every mistake you make. the bosses even more so. it's another thing i love about the dark souls games. it's that feeling of hitting an obstacle that seems insurmountable until you step back and looks at it, study it, and then finally, conquer it. the dark souls game, and this one especially, capture that feeling in a way no other game has. the feelings of accomplishment are always that much more meaningful when they're preceeded by tons of feelings of failure and frustration at one's own mistakes. i especially enjoyed learning each enemy's moves and attacks and learning what weapon/spell/tactic it would take to defeat them. skill has always been sufficiently rewarded in the dark souls games. and the more of it you have and the better you are at the combat mechanics, the more you are rewarded. dark souls 2: scholar of the first sin is my favorite game...i just wish i could do more than recommend it.

Verdun is a great first person shooter that is more on the casual side. Nothing like COD but not as competitive as CSGO. If you are looking for a great shooter than I cannot recommend a better one right now. The game is set in World War One that is instantly known for is trench warfare. Verdun takes inspiration form World War One but this is far from shooting across trench lines. You will find yourself navigating no mans land to launch intense trench raids.
I would say the game play is 80% fighting in the trenches close quarter (not from trench to trench). 20% navigating no mans land. Since most fighting happens very close the game is well balanced in weapons. Pistols and Submachine guns do not feel overpowered compared to rifles and machine guns. The game works within squads so fighting close to your squad is beneficial but not required by any means. The maps feel great as they lend to lots of different tactics.
There are several nations available to play as British/Belgium/Canada/France/Germany/US. Each faction has  unique weapons that bring different game play to the battlefield. The uniforms as well are all different from each other and Germany can have many different uniforms per squad. Weapon unlocks are done manually with points that you get very generously. Only the first couple matches will you have problems unlocking weapons after a couple matches you will have built up enough points to unlock any weapons you choose to.
The only downside right now is that sometimes with all the uniforms it is hard to tell friend from foe in the hectic battles within the trench lines. The developers have not abandoned the game and gets a steady amount of updates. Despite the numbers playing I was always able to find a match that had plenty of people playing. I would recommend this to anyone looking to find a new FPS experience.
Even though BF1 has come out. Verdun remains to be the best WW1 shooter on the market

Let's get this out of the way: Gone Home isn't worth $20. That's the cost of 3 to 4 very good books containing 3 to 4 very good stories--the primary element that Gone Home utilizes to drive its appeal. This interactive story is, however, well worth the $5 I paid for it.
If you like shooting or antagonists or running or violence, this won't be a good purchase for you. In fact, I actually turned to Gone Home in my hiatus from Borderlands; I wanted to think hard about subtle details, to read between their lines and discern truths about life through them.
My favorite element of Gone Home is that every questions IS answered, despite what other reviewers have written. If you take the time to find the answers to the questions, it's abundantly clear where Katie's parents are, where her sister is, why she's in a strange mansion, why the lights sometimes flicker, and why it is June 7th, 1995. There's an intricate story arc--all details worked out--that runs behind most of the trinkets Katie picks up, and it's the players' challenge and pleasure to identify it.
In short, people who don't enjoy Gone Home aren't looking to sort through the details of the game, and I dare say that it is impossible to really complete this story in less than 2 hours. Maybe someone much more clever than I could exhaust it 2, whereas I spent nearly 4 in my leisurely enjoyment of the experience. I'm glad I bought Gone Home rather than a Wendy's burger or a pack of cigarettes.

Remixed, revised, and Master Quested; Dark Souls 2: Scholar of the First Sin is an interesting piece of work. The bulk of my DS2 experience has been with Scholar, and I'm still not exactly sure why that is. Naturally we always have to play the latest edition of a game, especially if it's multiplayer-enabled. That's what everyone else does right?
---------------
Before I go any further, I should point out that this review is actually the conclusion to my huge Dark Souls 2 write-up. If you absolutely positively must know what I think, then have a look:
Part 1 -
Part 2 -
Part 3 -
Part 4 -
---------------
With that out of the way, let's focus on Scholar of the First Sin. This edition of the divisive sequel offers numerous changes to the world. Many of the areas have been made more difficult. There are now more enemies to contend with, additional NPC invaders, and exploration has seen some slight revamps. Ultimately, these changes create a "different" Dark Souls 2, and that's not necessarily better. It's still a great game, but let's focus on the specifics.
The first really noticeable change is in Heide's Tower of Flame. There are Heide Knights everywhere, and they're still sitting around. Upon defeating the Dragonrider, these lazy knights will make your life miserable. In DS2, the tower was a rather bland area, with its plethora of giants just standing around waiting for an Undead to fight. This area now all but forces co-op. Only the Dragonrider is required for progress, so you can always come back later. This change is IMO a good one. It makes the player pause and consider options.
A number of other areas received enemies in places there weren't any before. I was shocked when I revisited DS2. It's practically barren by comparison. However, sometimes SotFS fills that void with Pursuer appearances. Now I liked The Pursuer the first couple times I fought him. He's a dangerous foe early on, and a pretty solid fight. When you fight him several times in a single area, he becomes that clingy weirdo you met through an online dating website. He sorta gets the hint after you leave the Lost Bastille, but then he shows up in the tutorial area and it's just... Why? Go away already!
Then there is the prevalence of NPC Invaders. Early on these folks were intriguing. Now? They're just a nuisance. Claiming victory over an NPC Invader is the hollowest victory imaginable. None of these clowns are ever as good as a human opponent, but they show up frequently, hoping that you'll care. I will admit that Armourer Dennis was a hurdle, but that's because he shows up very early on (in an optional area). Everyone else is a bum that exists solely to fill space.
There are a few other enemy re-arrangements that definitely improve on the original game. That hallway of turtle knights in Forest of Fallen Giants? Replaced by a few skeletons (Praise the Sun!). There's no exploding undead rushing for you and Straid as soon as you teleport to his bonfire. Amana's Shrine is a little bit more dangerous. Aldia's Keep is busier than before, and the Dragon Shrine is really well-done. The Undead Crypt seems to have gotten a few more ghost-spawning statues. This can create some nasty pincer attacks if you let things get out of hand. Earthen Peak doesn't feel mostly abandoned and...well I think you get the idea by now.
While I don't appreciate all of the changes Scholar brings to the table, I think that overall it's my preferred way to play Dark Souls 2. Keep in mind though that this is just my view. If you spent a long time with vanilla DS2 (100+ hours), you might not be too enthused by Scholar's changes. Then again you might also find them to be invaluable. That said, these changes also aren't substantial enough to make someone who hates DS2 turn around and love Scholar (or vice-versa).
-----------------

Okay so there's a few disclaimers here.
1. I've been wanting to play this game since before it was released, so needless to say I was kind of excited to get it on sale. If you don't have that deep desire to play this "game" it may not turn out so well for you, like most of other reviewers would tell you.
2. I wouldn't necessarily call this a "game" so much as an "interactive story". No shooting. No zombies. No real puzzles. Just click, observe, read, find combination, read some more, and feels...ohh the feels.
The bad:
- Incredibly short. Could have been developed on further, but would have proven detrimental to the story. This isn't about the gameplay, it's about the story, and any added puzzles or interactive nonsense would have taken away from that.
- For some, the lack of "gameplay" is irritating and disqualify this as a "game". I say pish posh, different strokes for different folks.
- Price. Luckily, I picked this up for $5, but I don't see how anyone could justify paying the full $20 for this game.
The Good:
- Story story story story story. The story, albeit a slight bit predictable and not really surprising, is still amazing and heartfelt. Trying to unravel this yarn while dealing with the creepy dark house on a stormy night with this overwhelming sense that something terrible has happened to your family and then finally finding out what's happened is a sensation that my words can't describe. Just know that there are feels of many shapes, sizes, and colors, and there are oh so many feels. So many. gah.
- Very interactive. You can spend 10 minutes just looking at stuff in a living room. Belive me, I did.
- Immersive experience. Throughout the game, I could imagine being in this situation and how it would feel coming home to an abandoned house and nothing seems right. That sense of urgency when looking for a light switch in a pitch black room knowing good and well there shouldn't be anyting in there but can't bring yourself to believe it until the light comes on. That sense of relief when you find out that what you think has happened is just you jumping to outrageous conclusions. An experience like that is something I have seldom felt in all my years of gaming.
- Have I mentioned the story is awesome?
All in all, I loved it. I hoped my expectations would live up to reality and was pleasntly surprised they did. This is a great interactive story that you won't forget if you're willing to take the chance.

I bought into the hype around this game.  It's not aweful, but it's boring and entirely predictable.  I kept waiting for whatever was going to make this game so special and I never really found it.
Being a child of the 90s I had nostalgia for all of the pulp culture references in the game and it deffinately nailed the time period.  I felt like I'd been there.  On a personal level, only in a way most of us remember our teenage years.  The feeling of isolation, like no one understands you.  Parents either being way too distant and  self absorbed, or controlling and indifferent to how you'd like to live your life.  Or, as in the case of the family depicted in the game, yo-yoing back and forth between the two as it suits them.
The game deffinately captures the feeling that it was a time where everything was changing and none of us really new where we as a society were headed. I guess that says something.
If capturing a setting and time period accurately and filling it with lots of stuff to look at was all it took to make a great game I would think it deserves all the hype around it.  However, in a game where all you have is the setting and the story, I would expect the story to be a bit more original and actually go somewhere.

TLDR
A simulator game that tries so hard to be realistic that it misses the point of a game. May have worked better with a larger playerbase and if the mechanics were thought out a bit more. Can't reccomend in its current state.
I was excited about this game at first because I had enjoyed WW1 RP server in Gmod and had studied the period a bit in school. I felt it would be a unique take on a FPS, taking the fast paced action of a stereotypical shooter and tossing it out the window for a slow, gritty, you're-flat-out-gonna-die feel. I loaded this up for the first time and squadded up with my brother and it was fun. Kind of in the way that a cool toy is fun and then as you play with it more you notice flaws and build contempt.
For starters, there is really no sense of "progression" in the sense of an incentive to log in everyday. Kit unlocks or whatever they're called accumulate way too quickly and before you know it, you have nearly every kit you could care to unlock unlocked. This isn't inherently a bad thing, but with everything handed to you so easily, there is really nothing to work towards. Now there is a squad progression thing where if you stay in the same squad for a long time, you unlock better perks such as more lethal gas or buffed command auras. But the issue is, THIS RESETS WHENEVER YOU LEAVE THE SQUAD! That means that if you cut off the game and come back tomorrow, those hours you spent unlocking that stuff will be gone. This would make more sense if it didn't take so long to unlock or if you just retained it, like if the squad was permanent or something, I don't know. Anything except what currently happens.
Now, I know that this problem isn't a game's fault directly, but there's just no playerbase here. Like I'm lucky to get a full team in a game and sometimes the teams are heavily stacked whether by numbers or experience. The game just seems to quiet to be a game about a war where there was constant artillery and sniper fire and gas attacks. And again, with no people to really play with, the whole progression system in place just doesn't work.
Another thing that isn't inherently bad is the realism. Realism in games is great. That being said, I think this one tries too hard to be realistic. Things like artillery being an instant kill mostly is fine by me. 1-3 shots to kill on every weapon. ehhhhh sure fine. Red Orchestra does that and that game's great. Standing in barbed wire for about 5 seconds causing you to bleed to death? Ok, I'm drawing the line there. There are just too many instances of where this game attempts to be realistic and ends up being unrealistic in the process. This goes back to the squad progression system where it's supposed to show the "advancement in technology through the years of the war" or something like that. I think that's pretty cool personally, but does time reset itself everytime you go to sleep? NO! It's issues like these that make it so hard to like this game.

Now that I've finished this PC version of this game as well (had played it on the console before) I thought I'd write a review with what I like/dislike about this version/the game in general.
The SotFS edition adds some DLC areas/bosses as well as changing a few existing locations/monsters. Instead of finding some rather easy water trolls in the area before a certain bossfight, instead you'll find a smaller version of the 2-bodied flexile sentry down there which, if you don't expect it, makes for a small 'help' moment. I wouldn't say it made the game harder (like some reviews claim) but just a bit different. While on that topic, I still don't think Dark Souls 2 (or SotFS) is a difficult game. The bosses rarely use tactics that can't be dodged (which you'll learn right from the start to do properly, more so by normal enemies than bosses) and you'll become a dodge master before you've even finished the game. Sure, some bossfights take quite some time when playing with a different class (I've had more trouble with some of the earlier enemies than bosses or later game normal enemies) but overal it's not a 'hard' game. Difficulty doesn't come from giving enemies more health/let them do more damage, that just makes fights take longer. And once you get the hang of it, you'll learn to only take 2 swipes at a boss and roll away after the second hit instead of being cheeky and try to get a third off as well. Patience is the key with any fight.
So, if it's not an incredibly difficult game, why do you hear so many people (including me) become rather upset about it?
For pretty obviosu reasons; it's a poor console port. Sure, you don't need to install mods (and risk getting banned from online play) in order to play on 60FPS, which is a blessing, but they haven't thought about a lot of useful things.
For starters, the key mapping. Yes, I've played this game from beginning to ending with a keyboard and mouse. Yes, I do own a controller and yes, I do know that makes some things easier, like pickign between a power attack and a normal attack (which when using a mouse means double clicking, which ofcourse doesn't work 99% of the time but instead you swipe a normal attack twice). That's more of an annoyance, but furthermore, a lot of keybinds cant be properly relocated to the keys you want meaning you'll have to use either your movement hand towards the arrow keys or you're aiming/attack hand in order to change spells/items, leaving you vulnerable to incoming attacks, which is critical duing PvP fights.
While on that topic, those don't work. At all. On consoles they used a steady server and for some reason the invaders always had a stable connection when fighting the host. On PC, 9/10 times it can't connect to the DS2 servers (aafter clicking 'ok' 3 times it sometimes managed to get a connection after all, which usually disappears after 15 minutes of playing and you can't reconnect without exiting the game) or you'll be fightingagainst someone that is either missing all their hits when they clearly hit (which is very nice for the invader but not so much for the host) or magic spells will go by you on your screen but still take away health as if hit. Making for a 'rather frustrating' Mirror Glass Knight battle.
So, with all these annoyances, why do I still thumb up this game? For its price you're not likely to get a more satisfying title. Yes, you'll only swear to punch the invader in the face if you ever see him in real life a few times and yes, you might smack your desk leaving you with a hurting hand but still, that satisfying feeling when you beat a boss, solo, after a bunch of tries is like no other.

Now, before we start I want to get a few things out of the way: I HAVE played it all the way through, and I'm a sucker for story driven/ exploration walking simulator games. Yume Nikki and Stanley Parable are both in my top 100 list and I don't regret playing them. That said...
Gone Home is basically interactive fiction - and there is nothing inherently wrong with that -, but it does everything a story-driven game shouldn't. The atmosphere is fantastic, and the 90s vibe is pretty cool, as well as the sound design which is great as per usual with this sort of game. While it has been described as story rich/ deep, the story seemed to me as cliche and under-developed, with several interesting drama points not being explored by the writers. Another obvious problem is the shortness of the whole experience, which makes it hard to really relate or connect with any of the characters, especially since the most interesting ones are under-explored.
Summing it up.
Pros:
- Great atmosphere
- Amazing sound design
- Pretty cool 90s feeling all around
Neutral:
- No bugs found in my playthrough, minor or major
- Definitely overhyped
- Interactive fiction. Stay away if you don't like these types of games. (Or, in my opinion, even if you do like them)
Cons:
- Storyline is too short, under-developed
- Can't really feel any of the characters
- The "big twist" is cliché'd and really is nothing special.
- Unjustifiable price tag. (I guess you can get it on sale, though)

Gone Home is centered around Kaitlin Greenbriar who comes home from a long trip around the world only to find a mysterious note left by her sister on the front door. The entire family is gone and your job is to discover what happened to them and for this you have an entire home to explore at will, but there is much more to see in here than you may think at a first look. The story is believable and touching as for the entire time I was expecting something bad to happen like in a cheap horror movie, but the story is grounded in reality and the game delivers one of the best written stories in recent games. The best thing about Gone Home's plot is that you'll never see it coming, as the game constantly has that haunted house feeling, mostly because it is empty and left upside down as everyone left in a hurry, but in the end you'll be surprised to see how each clue you've found along the way will piece together the plot in the end.
The gameplay in Gone Home is simplistic but it fits perfect in the atmosphere of the game and in the first-person adventure genre. Unlike most of the games, Gone Home trusts your intelligence and doesn't give you any kind of hints, letting you explore the world in any way you want, but it also lets you understand the story from your perspective, which is great since the main focus of this game is effective storytelling and on that front this game definitely delivers. The house is huge and as you explore more of it you will discover new hidden paths and everything you find along the way will complete the story bit by bit, uncovering more of the plot as your play through the game, making everything that you find relevant to the story in a way or another, and by the time you reach the end of the game it feels natural to be like that, but it certainly leaves you with some questions which may help understand the game in your own way, something that makes it a different experience depending on how you see those things.
Gone Home looks good and the house feels organic especially if you grew up in a similar environment or time period. Every detail of the house is rendered with detail and the light/shadow effects are incredible since the game managed to creep me out simply because it was too dark in a room. Compared to the games of 2013 this game still looks good; there's nothing too shiny, but it's definitely a decent looking game and for the theme and the story it wants to tell, the art style definitely suits the background of the game.
Given the fact that Gone Home is a short game with only one voice actress I was pleasantly surprised how good it was because usually in a small game you don't get to hear good voice acting, however this isn't the case as Sam's voice is flawless and you will venture in a roller coaster of emotions and feel her pain and her struggle throughout the game. The music is a nice addition and the tapes that you will find and play have some good songs, but the most important part in the sound department were the natural sounds like the rain or the thunder effects which are so good that they gave me chills and made this game feel like a horror experience.
Unfortunately there is nothing else you can do once you complete your first playthrough, so apart from replaying the story to gain a better understanding of what's happening around the house, there isn't anything else to keep you occupied once you complete the campaign which is about 2 hours long if you really take your time and explore the house.
Gone Home is not a typical game, it's a unique experience, so you either love it or hate it, but unfortunately it's a little bit more expensive than it should be so you are either a fan of this kind of game and buy it now or you else you'll probably just have to wait for a Steam sale big enough to justify the purchase of such a short, yet amazing game, but either way you should definitely give this game a try once you found the perfect time to get your hands on it.

I was excited about this game at first because I had enjoyed WW1 RP server in Gmod and had studied the period a bit in school. I felt it would be a unique take on a FPS, taking the fast paced action of a stereotypical shooter and tossing it out the window for a slow, gritty, you're-flat-out-gonna-die feel. I loaded this up for the first time and squadded up with my brother and it was fun. Kind of in the way that a cool toy is fun and then as you play with it more you notice flaws and build contempt.
For starters, there is really no sense of "progression" in the sense of an incentive to log in everyday. Kit unlocks or whatever they're called accumulate way too quickly and before you know it, you have nearly every kit you could care to unlock unlocked. This isn't inherently a bad thing, but with everything handed to you so easily, there is really nothing to work towards. Now there is a squad progression thing where if you stay in the same squad for a long time, you unlock better perks such as more lethal gas or buffed command auras. But the issue is, THIS RESETS WHENEVER YOU LEAVE THE SQUAD! That means that if you cut off the game and come back tomorrow, those hours you spent unlocking that stuff will be gone. This would make more sense if it didn't take so long to unlock or if you just retained it, like if the squad was permanent or something, I don't know. Anything except what currently happens.
Now, I know that this problem isn't a game's fault directly, but there's just no playerbase here. Like I'm lucky to get a full team in a game and sometimes the teams are heavily stacked whether by numbers or experience. The game just seems to quiet to be a game about a war where there was constant artillery and sniper fire and gas attacks. And again, with no people to really play with, the whole progression system in place just doesn't work.
Another thing that isn't inherently bad is the realism. Realism in games is great. That being said, I think this one tries too hard to be realistic. Things like artillery being an instant kill mostly is fine by me. 1-3 shots to kill on every weapon. ehhhhh sure fine. Red Orchestra does that and that game's great. Standing in barbed wire for about 5 seconds causing you to bleed to death? Ok, I'm drawing the line there. There are just too many instances of where this game attempts to be realistic and ends up being unrealistic in the process. This goes back to the squad progression system where it's supposed to show the "advancement in technology through the years of the war" or something like that. I think that's pretty cool personally, but does time reset itself everytime you go to sleep? NO! It's issues like these that make it so hard to like this game.

Before I begin, I'd like to remind everyone this game is twenty dollars.
I beat this "game" in 90 minutes. Does that sound like it's worth the price? Gone Home has been sitting on my hard rive for more than a year, and today I learn why.
I'll start with what I liked, since the experience was more like a template to fill something much larger and far more intriguing. The set design was good, as were the object locations. Strange that I should comment about that, but everything makes sense as to where you find it.
On that note, they do a fantastic job of making this house a home. You really understand people live here and their little quirks and habits are present everywhere. The argument between mother and daughter on the cork board was a nice touch.
The sound design is also very well done for the atmospheric touch and constantly had me listening to every little bump and creak in as I made my through the house.
I can tell this is a character-driven drama and one that takes the writer's heart and soul, so I'd heavily recommend the writer adapt this to a screenplay or short story. A short film would be a much better use of a subject matter that clearly means so much to the designers.
Thus it pains to have to say what I'm about to say.
This is worth ten dollars, and that's strecthing it. There's NO payoff at the end. The whole time the story is building to something, but the overwhelming majority of all the interesting bits turn out to be mostly red herrings. If I may compare this to Alone in the Dark: the New Nightmare for a second. In that game, there were books worth of story detailing the history of the island, the Morton family, the Abkanis culture and religion, Carnby himself, and even the corrupt Bureau 713. Little of it was actually necessary, but to gain a full understanding and context for the events of the story, you needed to read all of it. In Gone Home, all but one of the characters are dropped, and everyone else had equally interesting stories. The biggest letdown comes about an hour in after you've been expecting a turn to some type of survival horror or even suspense. Instead, I'll give you a nice spoiler I noticed as soon as I started: there is no "run" key.
I'd probably understand who was who better if I had more frequent exposure to character's faces. Instead, I have to fumble with names, and I'm terrible with names alone.
As you traverse the house in a fashion similar to Castlevania but far more contrived (it's called "padding" ladies and gents) you'll notice the art style actually changes. Later, you'll stumble upon half-eaten potato chip bags with fresh-lock clips. The clips look like they're from a different game altogether with a notable drop in textures and model detail. One thing that threw me on characters was how portraits and photos supposedly showed the people, but each time it was like a different artist rendition. When you first start the game, go to the left side of the stairs and look at the family portrait. Notice how the girls appear to be in a completely different style from the father?
I spent most of my "investigation" wrestling with god-forsaken controls. I ended up spinning several times and getting hung up on doors. Navigating becomes a pain when you need to worry about boxes, which are EVERYWHERE. The game flat out tells you when you need to use certain commands in a given room, almost remosing the need for player input. In order to sift through the multitude of ultimately meaningless documents, post cards and notes, you need to select them on the tables or in the drawers. The "crosshairs" to do this are so specific, you WILL need to hold the little four-pixel dot in the center of your screen over absolutely everything just to make sure you don't miss anything. The "Scooby-Doo Effect" cherished by classic horror fans that told you something was usable is absent, which means opening a drawer does not make it obvious if something is in there you can use or read. You have to 1 be close enough, and 2 carefully move your pointer over every single scrap of paper in the jumbled mess of things in the drawer.
That's another thing. When you open a door, cabinet, or drawer, you, the character, can actually block the door from opening all the way, creating the illlusion of a jammed door when all you really need to do is step to the side. And here I thought Slender: the Arrival's click-dragging doors was annoying.
There are no puzzles, minimal characters, about a half-dozen dropped side stories, controls that basically fight you with with a combination of OCD and ADHD, and an ending you see coming a mile away. This game is not worth the price tag and I'm happy I got it on sale last year.

The gameplay is basic, walk around the house and find clue, read personal letters, find keys, and overall explore every nook and cranny of the house.
The game unfolds through in game narrative instead of usual cutscenes and this compliments the atmosphere of the game tremendously. Not much can be said about the story without spoilers, but once you get engrossed and invested into it, you'll more than likely just keep playing until the very end.
Gone Home isn't a game for everyone, but if you like exploring every area, a very interesting story, and a very moody atmosphere, you'll feel right at home.

A beautiful story beautifully told.  This game fits into the more experimental side of the narrative genres; it's the exact oposite of what a videogame is stereotyped to be, and has therefore recieved a certain amount of rejection from certain members of the gaming community. It is my firm belief that videogames are as viable a platform for art and literature as any other, and if you share my conviction (given, also, that you are an open minded-accepting person, in regaurds to the subject matter of the story) you will find a new, interesting, and, in my opinion, masterfully executed expiriment in storrytelling. Do not expect a gaming challenge in any way, shape or form - there are no puzzles, and the house really does invite itself to be explored - but instead a storrytelling expirience unburdoned by these things. On a final note, regaurding the story itself, it is utterly refreshing to find a narrative supporting the LGBTQ community in an industry so often downtrodden with outdated and oppressive views of gender as a whole.

50 hours in, I am not having a good time.
I have been playing PVE co-op, and it is incredibly frustrating. You will run into one of two scenarios:
1: You end up with one or more obvious hackers on your team who will run around headshotting everything they see. You'll barely be able to get any kills yourself, let alone accomplish any of the mission's challenge objectives (such as accumulating knife headshots or grenade multikills). Normally, I would consider this frustrating and bad enough on its own, if not for the following scenario which happens more often.
2: You end up with people on your team whom you'll swear are mentally defective, under the influence of narcotics, or both. You know the type: The ones who think it's hilarious to run around in the spawn knifing their teammates or wasting all their ammo shooting the inside of the helicopter, then decide the best strategy is to charge straight towards the enemy and attempt to defeat them by bludgeoning them with their own face.
Then, when they inevitably die, they scream insults at you, call you a noob, yell things like GOGOGOGOGOGOGOGOGOGO, or quit, leaving you to try to complete the mission with only one or two people, far less than the mission is clearly designed for. These people actually make me glad to be paired up with cheaters, because those runs are about the only ones you actually successfully complete.
Being paired with players who are both not cheating and not intolerable idiots is a fairly rare occasion.
This latter case wouldn't be so bad (after all, nearly every fps suffers from this to some degree) except that this is an MMOFPS with item rental and repair mechanics. And so not only are they wasting your time, they actually make you lose progression once you start to use weapons and armor that need to be repaired, which defeats the purpose of trying to get those items in the first place. Why would you spend hours trying to unlock cool gear just to have it become a tax upon your further attempts to acquire more cool gear? What's worse, I suspect that if you actually played long enough to get a full set of high-end equipment, it would not be sustainable. Your repair costs would be so high that you would be taking a loss on every match even if you won. Wtf?
Because of this repair mechanic and the awful community I really can't recommend this game to anyone.
