text:
Trigger warning: may contain observations and opinions that hurt feels.
Updated almost two and a half months later after playing again recently.
Also the comments section is not there to waste my time discussing every little detail. This review is there for potential customers who have never played Verdun. Enjoy being ignored if you feel like flamebaiting or trolling.
TLDR: 6,5/10. Good, but not great. Very atmospheric game with lots of undeveloped potential that has issues. So a red thumb because Steam forces me to be black and white like that.
I feel strongly about this game and I really used to like it, so that is why I write this as a warning for potential buyers and as constructive criticism toward the developers. The positive reviews show many people "want" this only WW1 MP FPS available today to be good and so do I, but I am at a point where the bad outweighs the good. This game has tons of atmosphere and potential but it is being dragged down by some of its flaws. You can read several reviews citing poor optimisation, no spawn protection getting you in a loop of being spawnkilled over and over again, clunky controls etc. that are also correct. But these are my personal five reasons that mar my enjoyment of this game to the point of not being able to really recommend it anymore in descending order of annoyance.
- glitchy weirdness, exploiting or worse in PvP: in a significant portion of sessions I have played, for instance an invincible guy around level five with two hours on the counter or with a similar profile joins and starts killing people who are hiding wherever they are on the map, not a single shot missed at high rates of fire. They end up with K:D scores like 55:0 against people level 80 and above. This game also lacks vote kick options so you are left with people who use exploits or such cheats for as many matches as they wish to stay. One option that does not explain everything my regular squad of four has seen is that these people are using low graphical quality settings and terrain clipping exploits. One example of the other mysteries that remain unsolved to this day is how players who are perfectly hiding at the bottom of a trench with no enemies around get shot from far away through ground and sandbags.
Update: friend with 275 hours showed me footage of aimbotting (immobile player making stab kills in the distance) post-summer sale...
- nonsensical spawns: I am not even talking about the lack of spawn protection, rather there are circumstances where you have to defend a trench and the game decides to spawn you about a 100 m away from it and you have to run through a stretch of no man's land that has no cover whatsoever to attack the trench you are supposed to defend. That is not what defence or holding your ground means. Yes, that also means GG because the opponents can mow you down with impunity.
- classes and weapons: some are clearly meant to be under- or overpowered. The German side has very few portable MGs that take too awkwardly long to set up and to be effective except for heavily prepared and dug in defence scenarios, and all of their rifles have only five rounds (Entente usually eight to ten). While this is historically correct, it is very annoying to see there is no balance when confronted with Entente soldiers that can fire basically all MGs like the Lewis, Chauchat and BAR while running, they have an OP semi automatic rifle and do not need to reload as much. Reloading can be deadly because it is an awkward procedure that is harder to interrupt than in other FPS I have played.
Some classes are not even assigned a firarm which I feel is a poor choice. A source of minor annoyance is that you cannot pick up dropped weapons or restock on ammunition (but you typically do not live long enough to run out of it).
- silly suicides: instead of invisible walls some games have added a warning system with or without a timer to return back to the zone the game wants you to be in. In Verdun not getting back to the zone in time instantly kills you and the game says it is a suicide that costs you XP. I have noticed these timers often are too short to get back to the map. I have also charged at the beginning of matches into the right part of no man's land only to discover I am getting suicided.
- bots in coop: they teleport. One moment they are thirty meters in front of you, the next they respawn next to you in the trench and stab you. Obviously at this point the coop mode is relatively new, in general has very rough edges and needs work.
Update over two months later: flying, teleporting, invisible bots and invisible weapons galore. This mode still needs work unfortunately.
Positive bit:
- We can hope these things will change because the game is still actively being supported and expanded.
But for now if you ask me with the things I have mentioned: thumbs down for the current state of the game which tends to annoy or frustrate just a tad too often.

I will review this version and not the regular DS2. This game is amazing. Despite what all the people who want to whine about it and suckle at Miyazaki's (the director of Dark Souls 1 and Demon Souls before it)♥♥♥♥♥♥as the greatest thing to ever happen to game creation, this game is absolutly awesome. ESPECIALLY the newest Scholar of the First Sin edition. As it fixes nearly all the problems with vanilla DS2. Many also do not know the story as to why the original version was moderatly poor and the DLC so good. The director of DS2 suddenly left one day and never came back partway through production and near the end of their timetable so they pulled one of the head guys off of Bloodborne to finish DS2. He did the best he could with the resources and time he had left. Then he was in charge of the DLC from start to finish. See where this is going? After being put in charge the DLC turned out amazing. Enter Scholar of the First Sin. Put in charge of this edition our savior rebuilt the game from the ground up. And while he obviously couldn't just change every little thing he made it into an absolutly AMAZING rework. Moving enemies to places they make sense being, making farming items not the biggest pain in the♥♥♥♥♥♥ and just overall taking everything I originally had complaints about in the vanilla game and brought it up to the DLC standard. If you have never played DS2 dont bother with the original. Get this version. If you were dissapointed with DS2, pick this up on sale and give it another try! If you still enjoyed the original for what it was, grab this version and you will feel like you entered into some magical new game plus version right from the start.

I'm reviewing this game merely because it's user reviews are "mostly positive" at the moment. It really wasn't very good and I got it in a humble bundle thankfully. If I had actually paid for this, I would not be at all happy. The game starts out with lots of tension, suspense, and mystery but ultimately boils down into a sappy, under developed story that was hardly worth the time it took to bait out. I enjoyed the atmosphere of this game, which was kind of creepy, but that is about all it has going for it.
There is literally zero gameplay, all you do is walk around the house. You can pick up items and inspect them, but this is hardly even useful and some of the plot points are redundant enough that you don't even need to inspect items, just read letters.
At first I thought the tags were a joke, but honestly, this isn't a game, it really is a "walking simulator". And that is coming from a guy who absolutely loved little inferno (another game with less developed gameplay elements).
All in all, you would be wise to skip this one, it is really a snooze fest. I actually regret spending my 2 hours to finish it. 2 hours for such an abysmal game is inexcusable. It would be different the game was impactful and deep and visually beautiful like brothers a tale of two sons (which was also very short), but this game has absolutely no redeeming qualities to make up for its short duration, lack of gameplay, $20 pricetag, and lackluster story.

Although I might argue that Gone Home is more an exercise in story-telling than it is a 'game' in the true sense, that doesn't exactly do it justice - it was really fantastic game.  It doesn't set the world on fire with new ideas- just takes a few things and does them really well, and with very little waste.  There's nothing that doesn't either further the plot or tell the player something about one of the characters, and it really has a lot to say about them, if you're astute.  That said, I wouldn't recommend it to everyone.  If you're a patient person who likes a good story and can get into a character, and you have an emotional connection to the mid 1990s, (no matter how hard you may have tried to bury it) this one will hit pretty close to home.  Bonus points if you completely missed out on some of the underground culture of the period and would like to experience it an- I'm loath to say "authentic" way.  The re-creation of a period and the impressions it left on the people who lived it is another of the game's themes, and it does it lovingly and without pretensions.

The story happens every few years. A parent attempts to sue some family establishment (like a theme park or a restaurant) because a child was traumatized when he saw a wandering mascot not wearing its massive cartoon head. Those kids are lucky. At least there's an actual, live, profusely sweaty human under Mickey's cool exterior. But imagine if there weren't. Imagine that underneath Mickey Mouse's exterior was nothing but a soulless, poorly programmed automaton, and that it might toss the first person it sees into an empty cartoon suit full of grinding metal and gears.
Now imagine your job is to watch over those creepy mascots at night. Five nights, in fact. And instead of having all of Disney's power and money to shut down any attempted Electric Parade uprisings posthaste, you're working at a second-rate Chuck E. Cheese called Freddy Fazbear's that has just enough electrical power to keep the desklight and the security cameras running between the hours of 12 a.m. and 6 a.m. (And that's if you decide you're safe enough to keep open the metal doors that you can lock down if you detect any threats.) This is Five Nights At Freddy's in a nutshell, but even that explanation doesn't begin to express just how nerve-wracking an experience it is.
It's nerve-wracking even before the real terror starts. The game is well aware of just how unsettling the bright multicolored fantasy objects we hoist onto children on a regular basis are in the right light, and your first look around at Freddy Fazbear's Funtime Palace--empty, dimly lit, and derelict--is a little chilling. Before anything out of the ordinary even happens, every synapse in your brain is sending the message that you do not want to be here. But for a few minutes, all is well, thanks to a recorded message left for you each night by your predecessor, a guy with a business-casual midwestern lilt who gives you a basic rundown on your duties and the morbid history of the place. And even then, this man's reasonable tone when talking about people being stuffed into the metal suits, or when describing a disturbing incident called "The Bite of '87," puts you on edge.
But then his message is over, and the real game begins. Your job is to flit back and forth between the security cameras, ensuring all the wacky animatronic characters are where they're supposed to be, which is in the back room. When they're not--and the fear instinct that comes with realizing that will serve you well here--your job is simply self-preservation. Close the doors, turn on the lights outside your office, and wait for Freddy or one of the others to wander away. The trick of it all is the battery bar at the bottom of the screen. Every action you take drains it, and drains it quickly, so keeping the lights on or the doors closed for half of your shift means the power to the whole place gets killed about 20 seconds before you do, in one of the most sudden and terrifying jump scares ever executed in any medium. Survival is a matter of conservation, observation, and timing.
This is fine. Everything is perfectly fine. Nothing to worry about here.
Five Nights at Freddy's may not seem like much of a game, and indeed, aside from the appearance of Foxy, the animatronic beast that awakens on night three, there are no real surprises once you've mastered the particulars and have died frequently enough. Only one of the animatronics actually moves while you are directly watching it, telling when you need to be on the ball, and hitting the lights or doors is easy until the later chapters. But the devil is in the details. Five Nights At Freddy's works its terrible magic because of contrasts. The part pizzeria's daytime atmosphere is replaced with desolate, looming shadows at night, rending the happiness with an ominous pallor. There's no music outside of the main menu, so anytime the oppressive silence is broken by footsteps, or random humming, or a sudden sting when one of the animatronics is right outside your door, is cause for sheer panic. In addition, while most of the story is imparted by the nightly phone call, if you're observant, you might notice how a particular sign you see changes its message from time to time. It starts with a warning against running or pooping in the pizzeria, but later morphs into a newspaper clip reporting on dead children. The print is so small that you have to squint to see it, which means ignoring your actual duties. And hello, you're dead. Being observant might save your life in Five Nights at Freddy's, but being too observant will get you killed.
The real miracle here is that the game communicates its gut-wrenching horror without a single drop of blood, yet still belongs in the upper echelon of horror games. You could describe Five Nights at Freddy's as consisting of mostly still pictures, but it's that stillness that causes you to sit there, hands shaking, with less than five-percent power left, praying the clock ticks over to 6 a.m.

"Welcome to your new summer job at Freddy Fazbear's Pizza!"
A familiar voice over the phone welcomes you as you settle once more into the dark halls of Freddy Fazbear's Pizza. However, this time around, the experience is far from what you remember from the original.
No doors to hide behind. The Animatronics you know and fear will be up and close with you, wandering in and out of your Office sanctuary. Your only defense? An empty Freddy Fazbear head and quick reflexes.
This time around, more of the grim story behind the Animatronics and the Pizzeria is revealed and the terror-factor of the game is ramped up a great deal more than the previous game. The traditional five night story is back again, along with the bonus Sixth Night, which also factors into the story, unlike the first game.
One other unique addition is the multiple challenges of the Seventh Night, each one granting an aesthetic reward upon completion.
All in all, this game is still worthy of the title of "Scariest Game Ever" and has once again proven that this series and developer Scott Cawthon are ones to watch in the future. Easily worthy of a 9/10. Buy this game now and challenge yourself to face your fears!

Gone Home is more of an experience than an actual game. There is little in the way of puzzles, no combat or action to speak of. Hell, the only actual character in the game is you and the house you return to. The thing is, the story doesn't revolve around the protagonist at all. Searching the empty home you're told the tale of your sister and her relationship with your parents and her girlfriend. Through interacting with the environment you're shown and told her struggles to overcome what some people might consider unnatural and to come to terms with her burgeoning love for this other girl. For anyone who's grown up as LGBT or knows someone who did you should really do yourself a favor and pick this hidden gem up. There may not be much to it, but the emotions conveyed throughout more than make up for any shortcomings.

Gone Home is an emphatic example of a developer showcasing how games as a medium can be more than they are often perceived or designed to be.
Not because it's mechanics are superb, simple and clumsy as they are. Nor because it crafts a grand and extensive world, instead content to set itself entirely within a normal home somewhere during the mid 90's. It's noteworthy almost for the fact that it's so ordinary and simplistic, intended not as an epic adventure, an adrenaline pumping blockbuster, or a deep and intricate journey to build up your character before the final battle.
Gone Home is merely the story of a family, flawed and broken in places but held together by an intrinsic bond they're unable or unwilling to break, and thus are forced to come to terms with their own internal issues or watch as their world begins to fall apart around them.
In this you are little more than an onlooker; an intruder even. Rifling through drawers, reading through letters and diaries; looking in places people aren't supposed to be looking and the private affairs contained within. It creates an almost uncomfortable intimacy between you and these characters, who despite being nothing but fictional creations feel very real and relatable.
And that is where Gone Home's "boring" premise proves its brilliance. In creating such an unremarkable setting it presents itself with an opportunity to tell a story that feels almost biographical, centering largely around a teenage girl on a personal journey of self discovery as she makes her way through adolescences with a familiar naivety and passion. It's a narrative that exists almost more for discussion and contemplation than simply a piece of fiction to be taken in and then discarded like so much other enjoyable yet shallow entertainment we absorb, nuanced and deeply personal and demanding of further dissection and analysis than I'm likely capable of providing.
And not everyone is going to appreciate it for what it is, writing it off as "not a game", overhyped, and no doubt "pretentious" and "preachy", and that's fine. Gone Home isn't a game designed for the larger gaming audience; the people who would rather play an online match with some friends or ponder over stat choices than spend time discussing a narrative that's so close to home (pun not intended) and fulled by larger societal issues and contexts.
Gone Home is here as more of an example that games have the ability to exist as more than a bundle of flashy mechanics and visuals; that they can inspire topics of debate and interest beyond their immediate selves as a more thoughtful voice amid so much noise. I hope its not the only one I'll be hearing in the future.

I admit, it wasn't really cool when From Software decided to charge people $60 for a game that already existed, except they changed things around / the improved edition add on. However for those who already owned Dark Souls 2, got a huge discount and only had to pay $19.99 instead to upgrade their game.
I'm just pointing that out before giving this game the actual review, because although I am a huge fanboy of Dark Souls, I won't be biased and ignore the bullcrap stunt From Software pulled. With that said, let's begin shall we?
I feel it's highly important to point out what the differences are. After playing a good 120+ hours on this game, trying out different builds and getting 100% achievements for this version... it's safe to say I know the major differences are, between the first version and this one.
Looking into the game itself, the gameplay is solid, replayability has always been a strong point in the Dark Souls series, bosses are fun (too many are humanoids though, and a few are not memorable in the slightest), characters / stories are weak, PvP is really addicting to take part in, mechanics have dramatically improved in comparison with the first Dark Souls game, and the DLCs are entirely worth completing for they offer a lot of rich content.
For $60 ...? No, i'd rather stick with the first Dark Souls II game. While this is better than the first version, I don't believe it's worth buying it as another game entirely. Is it worth getting for $20 if you already own Dark Souls II? Yes, I agree that is a legit price. Deep inside, I want this to be a free upgrade to those who bought their game, but From Software decided their biggest patch was worth charging people money.
Dark Souls 2: SotFS as a GAME gets a 8 / 10 score from me, because the game as a whole is freaken great.
SotFS Edition gets a 5 / 10 ... not enough content added to Dark Souls 2 to consider it a whole new game. In fact i'd go for a 4 out of 10 if it wasn't for the enemy placement and tweaks being such a huge impact to the experience. I again feel it's worth it, ONLY if you already own Dark Souls 2. Otherwise don't bother unless you really want a Dark Souls 2 game but at this point, i'd wait for Dark Souls III to come out this April 16th.

An extremely touching, sensitive, and affecting portrayal of an American family experiencing more drama than most. A short game, but the quality of the writing more than makes up for the lack of length. A refreshing break from the normal kill-or-be-killed mentality of many games today.
Positives:
+ An extremely well-written story, with interesting characters, and an intriguing plot.
+ Not overly long - doesn't pad the game out with unnecessary filler.
+ Open-ended enough for you to feel like you have choices, closed enough to ensure you don't miss out on anything.
+ Cleverly plays on several horror stereotypes.
Negatives:
- Slightly irksome graphics; for instance low-fidelity windows.
- No replayability, as the game is completely story-based
Rating: 86%

Five Nights At Freddy's 2. To be completely honest, this game is MUCH scarier than the first. When you saw the first game for the first time there was this feeling of not knowing anything about the game, and not knowing what to do or how to do it. And then you got used to the first game so that it wasn't as scary or hard anymore. But then this one comes out. And it brings that feeling back. But this time on another level. You notice the feeling, and you're really confused because it should be just like the first game and because you are so experienced with the first game, but Scott actually changed/added a lot more things to this game. There is now 10 animatronics that you have to worry about (11 if you include Golden Freddy) which makes the game a LOT more stressfull. A wonderfully paced and written interactive story. Or is it a snooping simulator? This is a game in which every drawer, cabinet, closet, and cubby that you'd expect to find in an American home can be opened and rummaged- and you will need to in order to reach the end of the game. This mechanic grows weary but is offset by the amazing story that unravels through investigative discovery.
This game is best enjoyed if you have not spoiled any aspect of the plot before going in, as the plot's impression changes expectations on a regular basis. What is this game? A murder mystery? Supernatural thriller? A tale of spousal betrayal and professional ennui resulting in the destruction of the American middle-class family? The imagination churns when presented with the setting of a young woman returning home to a large, empty, and dark house during a rain storm. The developers take advantage of the player's expectations, challenge them, and twist them in a satisfying way.
Despite being fully voiced and rendered, the most interesting aspect of this game is what you don't see or hear; making it as thought-provoking as a novel. In a game where the pace revolves entirely around the player, i found my heart racing to reveal the finale. This is a pinnacle of the "non-game" genre that i'm finding so appealing lately for its fresh ideas and defiance of modern convention.
This game ruined my life. Buy it now.

I admit, it wasn't really cool when From Software decided to charge people $60 for a game that already existed, except they changed things around / the improved edition add on. However for those who already owned Dark Souls 2, got a huge discount and only had to pay $19.99 instead to upgrade their game.
I'm just pointing that out before giving this game the actual review, because although I am a huge fanboy of Dark Souls, I won't be biased and ignore the bullcrap stunt From Software pulled. With that said, let's begin shall we?
I feel it's highly important to point out what the differences are. After playing a good 120+ hours on this game, trying out different builds and getting 100% achievements for this version... it's safe to say I know the major differences are, between the first version and this one.
Looking into the game itself, the gameplay is solid, replayability has always been a strong point in the Dark Souls series, bosses are fun (too many are humanoids though, and a few are not memorable in the slightest), characters / stories are weak, PvP is really addicting to take part in, mechanics have dramatically improved in comparison with the first Dark Souls game, and the DLCs are entirely worth completing for they offer a lot of rich content.
For $60 ...? No, i'd rather stick with the first Dark Souls II game. While this is better than the first version, I don't believe it's worth buying it as another game entirely. Is it worth getting for $20 if you already own Dark Souls II? Yes, I agree that is a legit price. Deep inside, I want this to be a free upgrade to those who bought their game, but From Software decided their biggest patch was worth charging people money.
Dark Souls 2: SotFS as a GAME gets a 8 / 10 score from me, because the game as a whole is freaken great.
SotFS Edition gets a 5 / 10 ... not enough content added to Dark Souls 2 to consider it a whole new game. In fact i'd go for a 4 out of 10 if it wasn't for the enemy placement and tweaks being such a huge impact to the experience. I again feel it's worth it, ONLY if you already own Dark Souls 2. Otherwise don't bother unless you really want a Dark Souls 2 game but at this point, i'd wait for Dark Souls III to come out this April 16th.

At the time of release, weapon durability was mistakenly tied to framerate. This meant that at 30fps, your weapon decgraded as usual. At 60fps, your weapon broke twice as fast. FROM Software took over a month to patch the issue.
Meanwhile, a number of people (including myself) used a mod called "DS2Fix", in order to fix their broken system. Later it was revealed that FROM Software "soft banned" all users of DS2Fix, SweetFX (graphic enhancement), ReShade (graphics enhancement), x360ce (lets you use other controllers than an Xbox controller), and many more, without informing any of us and giving no recourse in lifting the ban.
So I'm stuck with a game I paid for, not being able to play with anyone else, for trying to temporarily fix their broken game.

An absolutely nightmare for an obsessive compulsive. I spent several hours trying to clean up a digital house because the digital family that lives there apparently doesn't believe in putting things back in drawers when they are done with them.
But that being said, Gone Home is really great narrative experience. I'd love to see more games that are interactive fiction with this level of fidelity. I especially appreciate how you will get as much of the story as you are willing to put into it. There's a main narrative that you'll get as you enter various parts of the house and will conclude the game, but there are several sub-plots that you only get through examining artifacts your family has left behind. You can skip right over all of that if you want, or you can find every note and scribble to piece together a broader picture.
I do have one complaint about the game, but it gets into spoiler territory so I wont discuss it here. All I'll say is that my biggest issue still didn't detract from the overall experience and I still highly recommend the game. Can't wait to see the developer's next project.

Verdun is by far the best WW1 FPS I have ever seen. The Uniforms and Weapons skins are highly accurate, and you can tell that the developers have put in a lot effort into their research and have the utmost respect for the historical aspects and environment that they are trying to recreate (with one exception, see below). Game play is fairly free flowing which honestly was a big surprise when I first experienced it for myself, this is due to the very clever game mechanic of re spawning on the NCO - it's a very clever idea and works almost perfectly to maintain the momentum of the game (well done Leo). Now unfortunately, there is one HUGE negative to the game within its basic game format - there is ZERO friendly fire (in non private games) this massively detracts from the games realism and frankly makes their statements of 'Realistic World War Game Play', 'True Trench Warfare' and 'Authentic World War 1 Setting' completely mute and void - it's a huge negative on the integrity of the game, and undoes so much of their great efforts. Unfortunately there is no other way to say it.... 6.5/10 without friendly fire, 9/10 with friendly fire.

You'll likely get assistance from other players. Or, on the other hand, they'll try to kill you too. Be wary - all the time.

option with a yellow, wiggly, indecisive hand for its icon 'cause that's how I feel right now.
I've got no objections to the gameplay (or lackthereof) in
. In fact there was something about being left on my own in such a detailed environment that I rather enjoyed. Rather than having puzzles in the traditional adventure game sense, the challenge of the game comes from piecing together the jigsaw-puzzle of a plot from the environment. Despite not having any mechanics to enforce progression (such as conventional puzzles), it still
like you're accomplishing things.
Naturally this comes with a trade off: if you aren't interested in the details, then you're not gonna enjoy
.
But I think my biggest problem with
is that the atmosphere of the game just doesn't match the story. You arrive home late one night to find your house empty. There's a distraught message left on the answering machine, a note from your sister pleading your character not to "go snooping like [she] always does", and a turned-on TV playing a severe storm warning on repeat. All in all, it feels like the setup to a horror story, or at least a tragedy. I thought that something happened, something terrible, and caused whoever was at home at the time to leave in a hurry.
In reality, nothing even remotely tragic happened. The reality of the situation was a teenage romance story that, for me at least, bordered on
.
...Admittedly, I am not in the target demographic for love stories so I might be biased in that regard. But moving on.
builds up a tense atmosphere, then doesn't do a whole lot with it. Presumably the "worst-case scenario" buildup was meant to make the main love story plotline feel like a relief, but it just doesn't work. Sam's narration throughout the game also detracts from the mood. Her stories contain very little conflict and are, to be honest, pretty sappy.
The entire narration mechanic just baffles me, honestly. Why bother letting Sam narrate her life story when you're just gonna rifle through her journal anyhow?
That said, the game is not totally without its charm. The object tooltips ("Grab Cup", "Read Note", etc) often changed to more personal observations ("Sam had this when she was like four" for a folder, "Gosh, Dad" for a dirty magazine, etc), which was a touch of detail that I absolutely adored. Even though the protagonist was silent for most of the game, it still felt like I was playing as a character with a personality. But these moments were few and far between, and the main character might as well have been faceless for what a pitifully tiny role she played in the plot.
TL;DR: this game is... somewhat enjoyable, but there's just not enough good parts for me to be able to recommend it.

Some people actually hate this game because they see it as cheap jump scares, the dumbest and oldest way in an attempt to scare someone. Those people are missing the point of 5NAF2.
What makes the game is not the death, but what leads up to the deaths. The new electronics have this friendly design that seems like they won't hurt you, but end up being just as buggy as the originals. The originals end up looking so ♥♥♥♥ing scary that it makes the previous game look cuddily by comparison. All the world you work in just lies on top of you, choking you with a horrid enviorment where nothing is your friend no matter how friendly it looks. If you mess up your swing, take too long checking the cameras, don't flash the light enough, don't wind the music box fast enough or long enough, don't pay attention: the bots are going to punish you for it. They might kill you, or might make you panic, or make it so you aren't paying attention to another threat. The fact that its you against everything and just hoping time ticks fast enough paints a horror experience that very few recent games have gotten (I'm looking at you Resident Evil 6 and Dead Space 3)
The game even has a twist, given the game play and the first one is not as subtily woven in but still hits just as hard. And is a hell of a lot more then we expected.
Where the game lacks, although maybe I haven't found it, is some subtile things that really make your hairs stand out on edge. An example would in the first game would be the subtile death moans the robots gave when they snuck in. They don't seem to have that and seem a bit more in your face (sometimes pulling the monitor down when they're in the room). granted there are still creepy things about the game, but they're a little more public and evident then they are in the first game.
Think of it like Portal vs Portal 2, or Dark Souls vs Dark Souls 2. Where there is more of the game, and while it doesn't appear as deep as the original or explode in the same way, it can still pile drive you and make you♥♥♥♥♥♥yourself with the experience.

I got this as part of the recent Humble Bundle and figured I should finally get around to playing it. I'd read many, many glowing reviews, as well as some of the more rabid hate pieces it managed to generate. I don't think it deserves quite the level of hate it gets, but it certainly, in my opinion, did not deserve anything higher than a 6/10 anywhere. There isn't much to this, clocking in at just over 2 hours with zero replayability. There is no branching decision-making, there's no mystery left after that initial time through, nothing but a relentless boredom, actively draining fun out of the world. This game should not have been a game. It would have made a decent short film. Maybe an okay novella. A $20 game this is not.
I started my playthrough mostly neutral. It had good atmosphere, there were lots of objects to interact with, and the start of the story was strong. Then, a journal entry starts being read at you, seemingly out of the ether. I didn't find anything that seemed like it should trigger this exposition. It just sort of happened. As a way of delivering the story, random voice-overs from a character who is not present from a book you never find does not seem like a particularly inspired option. The voice work was well done, but the way to access it felt lazy. Touch some random object, get a chung of story read at you. If this was the way they were going to deliver the story, I could deal with it. Maybe I'd find the diary later, making the fact that Kaitlin seemingly knows the content more palatable. Alas, it was not to be.
This leads me on to the story. It was a sweet love story that was well told for what it was. It was not particularly original and it did not make good use of the medium. The side-plots for her parents were particularly dull, feeling more like some badly presented teen drama. The subplot for the uncle started off interesting, and then just fizzled. It felt like everything not related to the standard teenage drama was thrown in to make the game seem less shallow.
Now, on to the "gameplay." In this game, you walk around, pick up objects, read letters, throw things around, and that's about it. Sometimes, they'll get added to your inventory for no real reason other than to justify the fact that you have an inventory. You can't do anything with what's there, really, other than to look at the items again. You click around, maybe cause as much mayhem around the house as possible (This is about the only reason I made it through the plot: destroy everything her family once held dear), and discover the "secrets" of her family through the random letters detailing her father's failures and her mother's indiscretions left strewn about the house in a rather haphazard and entirely illogical manner. If I had secrets to hide, I wouldn't leave them sitting out on the table in the foyer. It all devolves into fetching some key or combination from some container unlocked by another key or combination in a tedious scavenger hunt around the poorly laid out house.
Finally... That house. Their seemingly normal home is riddled with secret passageways, random compartments, and bizzare room connections that make you wonder who in their right mind would ever have built this place. The house is also riddled with Sam's garbage, strewn throughout in a manner that implies that it was not a natural occurrence and was merely contrived in such a way as to force one to explore even more, despite it making no amount of sense whatsoever. It also implies that Sam's supposedly overbearing parents were completely detached from what their daughter was doing while trashing their home. This makes even less sense when you consider that all signs point to her father essentially working out of the home office. Lastly, and this is a minor but rather jarring thing I found, is that Katie has no room in that house. They mention they were going to make up the guest bedroom for her visit, but she has no permanent room. I understand she's supposed to be a college student, but presumably she's coming home for the summers and other breaks.
To summarize, this would have been an ok movie or short story, but not a game. I cannot in good conscience recommend it to anyone, as it is too short with too many glaring issues. This is a game, despite what some reviewers say, but it is not a particularly good one. Very little in the way of gameplay, and the story truly is not revolutionary or unique in any sense of the terms. If you really want to know how it plays out, watch a Let's Play and save your $20 for something that actually deserves it.

Gone Home might have been an enjoyable experience if it were a very small piece in a much larger game. As it stands, this walking simulator desperately tries to force the whole "90's" ambience within the house while trying to force us to care about players that are never introduced.
The game finalizes the nail in the coffin by never even really "introducing" the protagonist. Yes, you learn all about the character you're controlling, but those bits of trivia are lost by the fact that she has no significance. Her journey is completely linear, and everything is so sterile and unapproachable that it makes the player feel indifferent to her fate.
Finally, the main "story" of Gone Home is rubbish. Yes, you learn about the family, and you learn what happened to your sister while you were in Amsterdam. How do you do this? By finding little snippets of paper that cue voice-overs, and letters addressed to different members of the household. But here's the thing- we have NO reason to care about these people, nor does the pitiful inclusion of their details evoke any emotion. It's just fodder to make the game feel longer than it should've been.
I bought the game for around $6 and it still felt terribly overpriced once I played it. Watch a Let's Play- it'll be more entertaining than anything you can do with the game by yourself.

Excellent and thought provoking game.
One has to enter Gone Home with the expectation of experiencing an intimate and deep story. This is not for min/maxers out there who want to get to the credits as fast as possible, is for people who enjoy coming through every area with a fine tooth comb. Lots of reading required and a lot of thinking about what's been read.
Both the writing and the voice acting are absolute genius. Is not really a very dramatic story, nor is it original, but it's told with so much heart that it brought tears to my eyes. Fullbright managed to tell this small story about small people with a sense of weight that trumps every epic battle between good and evil. Is not about a wide ranging plot that will change the face of the Earth forever but a small chapter in a family’s life; but that doesn’t mean is any less tragic, dramatic or important for the player.
I’ll love to play more of this kind of game in the future.

I love the Souls series. Loved Dark Souls Prepare to Die edition and thought it was a fantastic game. DS2 is the first dark souls game I ever played (only played dark souls 2, 1, and demon's souls), and with that being said, I have to say that it's not as good as demon's/dark souls. It's a great game but has some clear flaws, while also doing some decent things that are an improvement from Dark souls 1.
Pros -
- Improved combat
- Better visuals (Ds2 SOTFS is only slightly better in terms of its visuals than DS2 vanilla)
- Lots and LOTS of gear
- Lots of weapons
- More viablility in multiple builds (faith is a lot better, sorcery still decent, pyromancy still good, strength and dex builds still great)
- Fashion souls
- Some great boss fights (will mention this in the cons as well)
- Definitely challenging
- Overall better PVP than ds1
- Runs much better on PC than dark souls 1
- Scholar of the First sin comes with the crown dlc's, which are all pretty awesome for the most part
- Each New Game + added makes the game way harder than many other souls games, where the game adds new enemies and even more phantoms. Along with new items/boss souls.
Cons
- The story is pretty bad in a lot of cases. Won't spoil, but it's nothing in comparison to Dark souls 1's narrative.
- The run system is changed. Not that it's worse, but it can be a bit offputting to players who are use to running from ds1
- Immersion is often broken in terrible areas such as the beginning of the game where you are a classless, genderless undead, but you're then able to remove your gear to show you're male.
- Game has some of the worst ambushes and ganks in any other game in the series. Makes the game artificially hard to many, including myself. Game has areas that are often hard based on a game of patience rather than skill.
- Although some of the bosses are pretty fun to play against, most are fairly unoriginal or just lame. Most are human-like sword weilding bosses, and the monster/creature ones tend to be absolutely terrible. Way worse than most of the bosses in dark souls 1 and demon's souls
- Game is challenging, but isn't as hard as dark souls 1 or demon's souls (or bloodborne). Familiar soul's players will find this game very easy.
- No reason to buy this game if you already have dark souls 2 with the dlc. SOTFS doesn't offer much in terms of new content. DX11 isn't worth the cost. Only purchase if you either don't have the DLC, or don't have the game at all and want to try it out.
- The areas in the game often make no sense or are just original. No spoilers, but you'll essentially end up on top of a large tower that leads to a lava based sunken kingdom.. WAT?!
- Hitboxes are a little funky
This game has its issues that holds it back from being great. This is probably to do with B team for FromSoftware working on the game. But the game is still good. It's easily the worst in the souls series but that's not saying much, since the series is filled with great games, and even though this game is the worst, it's still good. If you liked Dark souls 1, bloodborne, demon's souls, or just wanna try the series out for the first time, this isn't a bad start. If you have vanilla dark souls 2 with the DLC, do not get this game. It's not worth it. The changes with DX11, the texture updates, and enemy placements aren't worth it.
I give this a 7.5 out of 10.

Verdun is a World War One multiplayer game, that is set in a realistic World War One setting. This game offers a very unique, immersive battlefield experience, this including some very intense battles of attack and defence really make this game one of a kind.
This is a multiplayer trench warfare game, that focuses on obviously trench warefare and how to use that to your advanatage throughout the game. The war of Verdun was fought from 21st Febuary to 18th December in 1916 against the German and the French armies in france I do believe. The reason why I point this out for this game is that this game is basically that event that was in actual history. So knowing this knowledge of the actual war, does the game replicate that from history into the game? Yes they have captivated that in a fantastic way in the First Person Shooter. Now on with the gamemodes, there are 2 gamemodes that you can play on this game. Dynamic Frontline & Rifle Deathmatch, I will explain each of these game modes verbally. Rifle Deathmatch is basically a team deathmatch in the trench warfare. This did seem a bit generic, and didn't really pull me in as much as Dynamic Frontline did. On Dynamic Frontline you have two teams, defensive and offensive which sides switches all the time between each of the games. The objective of this gamemode is for the offensive team to push forward to get to the defensive teams trenches. The offensive teams have a certain amount of time to get to the other side and push forward. Then after the match ends the two teams switch over and they go through the match again. This gamemode in my opinion is definatly better than the Rifle Deathmatch. There are a few weapons available for you to use, but since this game was set in the actual Verdun war then there aren't that many. You have your Pistols, Bolt action rifles and LMGS. I haven't used any of the LMGS yet, so I will just explain the other 2. The Bolt action rifles are basically a one shot kill, if you can mark them and then shoot them anywhere on the body they will go down in a single shot of that weapon, although keep in mind that after each shot you will have to reload. They are a very authentic type of weapona dn very suitable for this type of game. Pistols are quite good as well, but unfotunatly they aren't as accurate in range and their reload speed are fairly long, so be careful when using pistols in this game.
The graphics of this game looks extremely realistic and play out well with the World War One type of genre that the game is going for. It has some nice shadows and lighting throughout the game that really bring this game to life. It does have motion blur, which has the option to turn it off which is always good for those people who don't like to play with motion on.
+ Nice graphics and atmosphere
+ Decent guns
+ Matches can sometimes last for a hour or two
+ Trading Cards & Achievements

The guns in Verdun are all real true-to-life guns, which work in the same way as they did in the time. Verdun also gives war facts in the loading screens about the map you are about to play (which by the way, are all also real places, reconstructed in a way which makes them look a lot like they may have looked at the time!). So when your 7 year old son says that he wants to be a soldier, direct him to Verdun, where he could learn some facts, as well as probably change his thoughts about soldiers.

It's no secret that Dark Souls II is an inferior game to Dark Souls, yet I'd much rather play DS2 than almost every other video game that exists. It's still outstanding how good the combat feels and how well the obtuse way its story is told works in this atmosphere.
This particular version, which at first glance looks like a DX11 upgrade, is actually the right and best way to play this game. If you already own Dark Souls II, but haven't touched the DLC, I very much recommend this upgrade, because let me tell you that the DLC areas in this game are incredible. They have some of the best bosses in the game (In fact, THE best boss in the Dark Souls series is in one of the DLC areas in my opinion)
It doesn't fix any of Dark Souls II's obvious problems, yet it adds great content, while making the game look a smidge better and turns Drangleic into a more lore-friendly contitent with enemy and item placements that make more sense than the vanilla game. There are still more two-handed sword wielding giant humanoid bosses than there should have been, the torch is still useless, there's still impossible geograpy... But it's still Dark Souls.
I can't however recommend a paid upgrade for those who have already purchased and played the DLC, unless it's super cheap.

Firstly I should state that I honestly wouldn’t believe that this is actually the first text you would read about Gone Home. Considering that I will focus mainly on proving how everyone’s wrong and I’m right about it, because I’m the smartest guy around.
Common complaint about the game is stating that it actually isn’t a game. Now, you see, it is okay that it’s the game someone wouldn’t like, but it doesn’t stop Gone Home from being one. Yes, it has a rather simplistic gameplay that can be described as walking around, looking at things and, well, listening to audio-diaries of a questioning teen. And deciding that it isn’t enough is virtually the same as reducing complex form of art to a tiny fraction of it. Experience points, health bar, combat, puzzles, possibility of losing the game — all of it is nothing more than a method you can use to entertain the audience. Without them Gone Home still has a story to tell, has a path of progression organized inside a mansion in a metroidvania-esque kind of way. And these are the methods and means, too. Now, are they enough is a separate question. The fact that you can actually get the end credits in two minutes knowing the right path, doesn’t all of a sudden make the process of discovering this route less meaningful. Actually that’s all this game is about. Telling a fairly simple story with unusual means; not completely unusual, right, because a concept of hiding backstory in in-game objects isn’t something new for video games. But Gone Home takes one more step into empowering this particular method of organizing game structure and story.
Rotating Street Fighter SNES cartridge while listening to Heavens to Betsy wouldn’t count as a universally appealing thing. Nostalgia about being a teen in early 90s isn’t a feeling you can force yourself to feel. In a similar way, feeling satisfied from re-constructing a story in your head with no visible on-screen results may be a concept that’s just too imagination-oriented for everyone. How to be sure that you didn’t fail, that you didn’t miss some things? Maybe there is more to the story than the main bulk of it that just auto-launches in audio form when you reach next “story point”? Well, yes, there is. And no, you can’t detect whether you’ve seen it or not, unless of course you’re a sentient human being and have an ability to google things on the internet. The game though won’t acknowledge the fact that you solved some mystery in any way. This makes it a more intimate experience, if you’re invested in story of course.
This leads us to the second most common complaint about Gone Home. It states the following: the game would receive far less attention from the media and gamers in general if it didn’t have teenage lesbians as main protagonists. This leads to a conclusion that the game’s story is not interesting, that the game itself is terrible. While the premise is actually true, funny thing is that it is so only due to a high amount of people posting all along the internet, that if Gone Home didn’t have young teenage lesbians it wouldn’t get as much attention and, of course, concluding that the game isn’t worth anyone’s attention. What’s really amusing here is that the game doesn’t really imply anything with its story. It’s like a modern short realistic novel: unusual but nevertheless possible. Despite your abhorrence to anything, if it exists — it exists. There’s no moral in here. Teens really did have a problem coming out to their parents about being gay. Gone Home crosses the line of comfort zone for story-driven video games. There isn’t an awful lot of them which use a realistic setting. I doubt that anyone sane enough would call military shooters realistic speaking of their plot. All that’s left are historical strategies and various simulators. You can find sci-fi, fantasy alternative history, hyper stylised noir stories any day. And, well, telling stories about ordinary humans is just as important for an art form, for its development. In short summary: it’s a love story, and it’s actually quite good. And having trouble with it because of a bigotry is massively stupid. If you really have a problem with someone’s sexuality… I thought about writing that I’m sorry that I couldn’t change it, but came up with a different one You can go ♥♥♥♥ yourself.

So this was an interesting experience. I bought this game as a friend of mine wanted to see how it was since on the surface it seemed sort of like a horror game. It's not tagged as such so I figured it wasn't but anyway. This issues I found with this game were rather simplistic but very glaring.
The first is the setting, being in the house all alone in the middle of the night during a storm seems like the perfect atmosphere to scare even the tightest of jeans off of young hipsters. It's not the atmosphere for this kind of game. Moving about the house has an ominous and eerie feeling to it. One that just screams "supernatural stuff" but never decides to deliver. There are A LOT of "secret" (and I use secret sparingly) passage ways that lead to dark and creepy hidden sections of the house. A place where you would expect a horrible secret to discover. This brings me to the story and it's pacing.
The game takes place in a house owned by your main character's parents. You are immediately greeted to a letter stating that "Sam" who must've lived here is no longer there and that you should "not dig through the house." Immediately this is a good start. It draws you in with the thought that there is something terrible and evil within the house. Enough to push someone away and to warn others to not go snooping around. By the way SPOILERS. I'm not sparing any detail with this review. As the story progresses you learn more about the parents. Katie, your main character, her parents both HAD successful careers. The father was an accomplished writer and you find evidence of this everywhere with books he's written and attempted screenplays. The mother was a very successful park ranger and recieved lots of promotions in her career. You may notice I am speaking in past tense. As if something horrible had happened and caused them to disappear, or flee the house pointing back to the letter at the beginning but nope. I wish this game was that smart. The mother was having an affair and it kind of screwed up thier lives so there's that. Getting more into the other girl, Sam. As you explore the house you read letters detailing journal entriues of hers telling you about her life as your main character had been away. That is when you find out that the house they lived in belonged to a psychotic killer named Doctor Oscar Mason or something along those lines. This again, builds tension towards a supernatural element in the game. You also learn of her friend Lonnie. As she is first introduced her character seems odd and very untrustworthy. Acting rather stange and distant. As you read more journals you expect some sort of decent into madness. Maybe Lonnie is more than she seems to be. Well she is, because she is a lesbian, and she wants to have a relationship with Sam. Now I don't judge in anyway. I believe anyone should be with whoever they want but I do know some people react to such a discovery poorly and that they may be some huge reveal to other but to me it was about as impactful as throwing a twinkie at me. All the suspension in Lonnies introduction was completely lost and reduced to detailed explanation of their "hidden secret". The story shifts focus a well to sam and her relationship with Lonnie. Detailing the adventures they had as well as the aforementioned poor reaction from her parent's when coming out to them. This shift in story was unexpected, most of the beginning builds up the supernatural aspect and then it's dropped and forgotten. It doesn't help any that multiple times they try bringing it back in long after the relevance has faded and the atmosphere has lost it's touch. Including a weegee board and notes from the doctor saying "I wish to com ba-" and even a cultist pentagram that looks like a summoning ritual. After all of that the story abruptly ends with Sam leaving to be with Lonnie and me feeling completely ripped off. I think this took me what, 2 or 3 hours? $20 is extremely too high of a price to be expected to pay. $5 seems like a good base price and then maybe get it on sale.
As far as gameplay goes the tags get it spot on. It's a walking simulator, you walk around, search through some stuff and discover the plot as it unfolds. What you're suposed to do next is never 100% obvious though it has it's moments so I could classify it as a puzzle game but not really to the extent of something like Portal. A weird thing that takes a lot of getting used to is the awful idea the dev had to make the mouse move like a hippopotomaus every single time you highlight something. It's extremely awkward and very stop and start. The zoom in feature is also not all that helpful or at least it wasn't for me and just seemed to be there to be there. Walking around is at a decent enough pace but I have no idea why there wasn't at least a "brisk indoor walking speed" button when the backtracking starts to get tedious later.
If I were to give this a score I would give it a 4/10 heavily carried by atmosphere and the first half of the story as well as some aspects of the gameplay.

Note: I want this review to be as helpful as possible. If you have something to say that would help me improve it, please make a comment.
Summary:
It's a game about exploration, in a very non-standard way. In fact, it is only a game because there is some interaction, with minimal thinking required to go forward. You are back to your house after a long time being abroad, but nobody's home.
Gameplay:
The gameplay consists of looking for clues about what happened to your family, and the game succeeds partially by being able to tell a story using bits of text, pictures, and audio diaries from the main character's sister.  The fun part about the gameplay is exploring the house and discovering each family member's story, and there are several items and songs to discover in the house that will appeal to people who, like me, have lived as a teenager in the 90's.
Story:
The game kept me wondering what happened to the family, why there was nobody home. Due to some elements in the game (sound, music) and in the story that had something to do with the supernatural, I kept thinking something very cool and surprising would appear at the end. Some people will relate to the drama that is being told in this game, but to me the story was not interesting enough and
. I will describe most of what happens in the story below:
So I felt that the game was a wasted potential due to the lack of a great story to tell.
For your reference, I am a very experienced player, and a fan of Interactive Fiction games, with or without graphics, as well as Point'n'Click games in general. So yes, I like playing games that are more about the story than the gameplay, and this one disappoints because there is not enough drama, only a regular soap opera story.
Sound
The sound effects are really good, and the soundtrack is amazing. In fact, I recommend buying the soundtrack for this game if you can!
Value
I got this from a bundle, so it was not a big deal. If you are like me and, despite negative reviews, want to see this for yourself, get it on a sale but be aware that you might be disappointed with the fact that the game promises too much, and gives too little. As a side note, you'd spend your time and money better playing games like "The Novelist" and "Richard and Alice", where you are actually given interesting characters and both are also about real life dramas, and both actually make you think about life and the choices we make.

Okay so this game is a 1st person 3D point and click adventure.  It is a fairly unusual game.  Short too, I completed it in 3 hours.  If you're going to buy this game don't read much on it, I wouldn't even want to see the trailers and am glad I didn't.  It's all about the discovery of what has happemed in this game.   I found myself wishing I could jump in the game but that isn't needed.  Yeah, so, no shooting either.
I tried to play it in Ubuntu 14.04 and I could not get the controls to work right, but I didn't mess with it for very long either.  I am able to get most linux games to work no problem on my system.  It worked no problem in Windows 7.
It has detective/mystery type overtones.  It's creepy in a way because you are looking through other people's personal things, and that is also part of what is compelling about it.  There are secrets to discover both about the story and also in the physical space of the game.  Discovering things about the house were probably what I liked best, touching on those childhood dreams come true type stuff.  Also worth noting that the basic premise of the game is unrealistic and doesn't always quite make sense but that didn't bother me.  The story made sense, just some of how it is presented is unrealistic which might bother someone who is a stickler for that kind of stuff.
So I recommend this game because it is different and I appreciate games that stretch the ideas of what we commonly think of as games.  I woulldn't want to play another game like it probably.  Just glad I could experience this.  Then again maybe if the theme of the story was different I might.  I found myself getting board near the end once I figured out what was going on, but then it was over shortly after that anyway.  It certainly isn't for everyone.  If you are interested in games from the perspective of exploring new types of gameplay then you will probably want to get it.  Point and click types would really like it I would think, just keep in mind it is a short one.

The Epic Sequel to the popular First Person Shooter Four Nights at Freds. In this game, play as Larry Daley, a security guard at the popular Pizzeria, Starbucks. Your goal, just like the last game, is to stop minorities from stealing the Pumpkin Spice formula. Unfortunately, your budget has been cut AGAIN, and you no longer get Military Grade weapons. Instead, you have to fight them off with your fists. This makes the game much more challenging, as you have to get up close and personal. The only problem is, that every now and then, you have to deal with Kermit the Frog. Kermit will come out every time you forget to turn on the Singing Fish on the wall. Other than Kermit, 5 other minorities have been added to the game as well. There is Better b4nny, or Dyrus as people call him. There is also Captain Falcon, Call of Duty Ghost, Bubble Buddy, Batman, and of course, as hinted in the previews, Hatsune Miku. Now, with 11 minorities to worry about, no guns, and Kermit bugging you every time you take a♥♥♥♥♥♥ you must survive through the night by wearing your fursona suit. But don't think I didn't forget about the multiplayer! During the game, you will find various Pokemon within the tall grass, which you can capture and collect. Then, you can battle with friends over the Nintendo Wifi Network. They re-added all the original guns from the first game for these Pokemon Battles, and they added new guns, such as the Halo Pistol, and the Gravity Gun. This is the best multiplayer since Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2, and I can't wait to see where the CoD series goes next.
The creator of the game ever worked with the makers of Dead Rising to create the new Zombie mode, where you can play as Paul Blart, Larry Daley, Tony Montana, and Captain America to fight off the alien invasion of Weeaboos. Okay, time to talk about Warface, is it good or is it bad?
First, Warface is a FREE TO PLAY First Person Shooter. Yes, its free no need for membership to play or anything, the only thing you need to play is an account and thats it, once you have an account you can play now.
But...by being F2P, does it mean its a bad game? The answer is no. Warface offers 3 modes to play, CO-OP, PVP and Special Operations. So you like to play missions? You can do it. You like deathmatch? You can do it!. You want to fight against an horder of robotic zombies? You can DO IT!.
Warface offers a great experience without the need to spend real money!. To unlock weapons, attachments and armor for you character, you need to play missions, fight in PVP or complete a special operation. Everytime you complete a mission, a small % bar appears on 3 items, you choose 1 and play several missions until you unlock it, it takes a while....but hey....you are playing to get that item, instead of paying X dollars to get it.
Warface is Pay to Win? No, even though it has an option to buy a special cash, still it offers you: revival coins (for COOP),  several skins or weapons only available with that special cash. The coins are helpful, but you get several after login into the game some days.
In the end Warface offers a great FPS experience, you can do what you want! if you only want to do coop missions, you are free to do it, the character customization is minimal, but who cares about that? So if you are looking for a military FPS that is F2P, I recommend Warface.

I can't say I'd recommend this game to play, but might be a game worth experiencing. That is whether you watch someone else play it or just try it yourself.
I say that because I'm not really a big fan of linear games. I can tolerate them, but only to a point. Gone Home has advertisted itself as a 'Story Exploration Video Game' and it just that. You explore your environment while they take you on a ride. It's vaguely similar to theme park attractions where they shuffle you along room to room to tell you a story. Such as the peculiarly perfect placement of breadcrumb notes to lead you along the story.
The problem is, the part of the thrill of theme park attraction is buying into the experience and thrill of the environment. Gone Home tries to capture but doesn't quite reach it, at least for me. Perhaps with Oculus and some additional VR gear, it might bring the experience more to life, but until then it is nothing more than a movie you could simply watch.
Being a kid who grew up in the 90s in the suburbs with one sibling, I can say that this did tickle my nostalgia. It gave me fond memories of my own childhood. Of my friends and classmates who have I grew up with come out of the closet. Of a time where acceptance was only starting to become the popular belief. And I have a odd fondness to narrative storytelling, but even with all that Gone Home doesn't have the full experience it needs to make me want to play it again.
Gone Home is a growth in the lines of experimental narrative walking games, such as Dear Ester and Stanley Parable, and is worth a look.
...But what you might hear as a large complaint is the full price tag of $20 USD Gone Home, while the original Dear Ester and Stanley Parable were both free game mods. I can't fully dismiss that the price tag was a deterrent since I didn't jump to grab it at full price. I've grabbed this in a Humble Weekly Bundle Leading Ladies for $15 USD, which included a pile of other games I wanted to play. However, price tag isn't something you're really reading the review for anyways, since each individual already have an idea of how much they are willing to spend on a particular game.

Dark Souls II: Sotfs is...well, it's a game. If you're looking for gameplay and storytelling similar to Dark Souls I, you're probably better off buying a PS4 and Bloodborne. If you're looking for an active PvP/Co-op community, you'll most likely find it here. Save for the occasional Bad Apple and/or hacker, the PvP/Co-op community is quite good. Would I reccomend Scholar in general? Yes, yes I would. Would I reccomend it for a hardcore Souls player? Probably not. Anyone that has played Dark Souls I for any extended period of time and has experience in handling it, you'll probably struggle at first, saying things like, 'How did that hit me?', or 'I was nowhere near that!' when dodging attacks. Quite an experience. Don't be dissuaded by the negative, snarky, vaguely-homophobic reviews.
It's not "exciting", it's not "action-packed", and in fact, it's probably not like anything you've played before. Do yourself a favor and check this one out. You'll be glad to have it in your mental archives.
Barely-enough lighting, haunting music, genuinely creepy ambient noise, and great voice acting.
Not an entirely original story, but a well-done one at any rate. This will probably sit best with the slightly-older crowd -- the children of the 80s, who are old enough to look back on their highschool days and feel that distant sting which somehow still brings back a smile.
Some might dismiss the story as thin and predictable, but I'd encourage you to judge for yourself. It kept me anxious and guessing until the very end, and wrapped up in a way that I didn't quite expect.
It's not a true puzzler but there are enough "ah-ha!" moments to keep up the suspense. It reminds me of the classic Zelda games in that the map is quite small, but it's also very non-linear. You'll return to previously-explored areas with new information and discover them all over again. It's a cleverly-designed experience.
For those like me, who avoid (and miss out) on some entertainment for fear of jump scares, I feel I ought to mention that you can enjoy this one without worry.
A few reviewers cite the high price/entertainment-hour ratio as a turn-off. (Even taking your time, you'll still complete the game in under 2 hours.) Watch for a Steam sale or Humble Bundle and you can get a real bargain. I believe I picked this up for about $3-5, which is right on point.
Wait for a rainy weekend night, turn out the lights, put your phone on airplane mode, grab a drink, and enjoy this thing.

Dark Souls II: Scholar of the First Sin is the second draft of From Software's Dark Souls II. It's absolutely gorgous, and its variety of landscapes and enemies is stunning. But aside from how freaking beautiful this game looks if you're a long time Souls fan you're going to notice something different about Dark Souls II and SoTFS.
Is this game good? Yes, it is. Even for all its ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t it's easier than Dark Souls or Demon's Souls. Is it better than Dark Souls or Demon's Souls? No, it's not. If you're a Souls fan you'll take any bit you can get. If you're a newie to the franchise looking at picking this game up because it's newer and prettier, trust me, Dark Souls: Prepare to Die is going to be far more satisfying and is going to frusterate you less.
----------------------------------------------------------------------------
What is that difference? It was made by a different team. And it shows. While From Software markets the Souls series as brutally hard, "pepare to die" and so on the actual game design is very free of what I call "♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t". The older games were far better designed than this one, SoTFS showed they were learning (the DLC is actually really good for Dark Souls II) but Demon's Souls and Dark Souls don't have this ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t like Dark Souls II/SoTFS. It's still a good game, but it sucks the creators didn't understand the design principles of the original team until the DLC.
What is this "♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t"? You'll fight against larger groups of enemies, you'll fight against large groups of minibosses. The previous games in the franchise made it easy to judge what was coming up, the enviornment gave clues. You see burn marks and burned bodies on the bridge? Remember the dragon from earlier? Yeah, when you cross that burned section a dragon is going to breathe fire at you. In Dark Souls II you'll often find enemies jumping from the ceiling or out of hiding places that you never could have seen coming. Dark Souls II also has some forced death sequences, something the Souls series NEVER does (other than Seath's fight in the first one). You'll open up a door and have the entire wall collapse ontop of you, something you can't avoid nomatter what you do.
----------------------------------------------------------------------------
TIPS FOR NEW PLAYERS
#1, be patient. The Souls games will test you. Dying isn't as punishing as you will first believe. You loose your souls, and if you're human you switch back into your hallowed state unless you recover your bloodstain. Those souls can be used to upgrade your equipment and stats, but your stats are pretty useless, people beat the game easily without leveling once; it's more useful to level your equipment and that doesn't cost many souls.
#2, summon help if you need it. Playing the game with other players is a lot of fun. Getting invaded in Dark Souls II while traveling with some other players is really satisfying. The AI is very good too, you'll play against an NPC invasion and you almost wont be able to tell the difference between them and a real player.
#3, DO NOT LOOK AHEAD! Knowing what's coming makes the game a lot easier, but the most satisfying part of Dark Souls is overcoming the challenges (bosses, hard areas, other players) and exploring the world. I used a video guide for Dark Souls 1 and I regret it because its a lot more fun to play blind. PLAY IT BLIND. If you like the game, you'll like it a LOT more playing without any help (unless you're really stuck, or need to know where to go next). If you don't like the game, and you've put 10 or 15 hours into it then Dark Souls probably isn't a game for you.
#4, give it a shot. Dark Souls can be hard to get into. You don't know the mechanics, you don't know the rules, but you'll learn. Don't quit because you don't know how to lock on to an enemy. Don't quit because you did something foolish and died and feel intimidated by that weakly enemy whom killed you. TAKE A BREAK IF YOU'RE HAVING A BAD DAY, COME BACK AFTER SOME NETFLIX.

This is one of the most overrated games of recent time. Just because a game is controversial and nostalgic doesn't make it stand on its own. If it was released as a free project, then I would think this was an achievement. So many people praise games and movies when they do something out of the "norm" in the story or otherwise. This game has great voice recordings, the texturing and the modeling are also good. I found my self smiling and almost giggling with memories as I went through the house for the first 5 minutes. But after that, I lost it. I found my self just needing to complete the predictable game just becuase I had heard it was short and I figured I might as well see the whole thing.
One thing that really bothered me is that even though it is supposed to be an open exploration game, it is extremely linear, so much so that it takes away from the whole point. How am I supposed to feel like I am exploring a house, when I have to unlock sections of the house by completing certain "find the key" sections of the game. And to explain why this was such a bother was because so many of the plot developments (notes) about the family progress in a chronological manner over a year, in notes that are already in the correct order as you find them. Why are notes that are more recent near the end of the game, and notes that start at the beggining of the chronology are found at the beggining sections of the house? Did the mom live in the closet during the 6 month mark and then move a month later to the kitchen so she could leave behind another piece of paper. I know there needs to be a fine line of guiding the player, but I felt the devs missed it. I understand why to an extent, but at the same time It didn't take me long before I figured out I was being spoon fed a story in a faux-exploration manner.
All though this game was short, it was a time consuming very short story that overstayed its welcome.
I would say go though this game once because some of the few 90s references are great for anyone who grew up during that time. But it is not as great as people say it is. The house is huge, but just feels empty, and I don't mean devoid of people, just that it feels lifeless by itself. Everything feels structured in its layout and there are not that many props, just a few striking 90s references, and then a bunch of light switches, toilet paper, towels, and coffee cups. In so many ways this "coming home" experience could have felt more powerful. This game can't survive on the narration of a journal for the whole 15min total of narration for almost 2 hours of walking from lifeless room to lifeless room.
Maybe I'm spoiled, I just finished the Vanishing of Ethan Carter and I had my self pouring over every item I found, all the while being emotionally touched by the way the story actually came together in my mind alongside the actual plot, and not just as the naration dictated. In this game I got tired of hearing the whiny sister talk and explain while I looked at glass coasters with a fern on it. Thing was I never felt like I was involved in this game, and the character you play seems just as distant. There are so many better ways to tell a story and create a depth of feelings the player can sense in the visual medium of video games, other than to just put a bunch of objects in front of me and then tell me about the objects as I chronologically come across them.
Nostalgia: + (for about 5 minutes but somethings are really cool, like the inclusion of magic eye papers)
Voice Recording: + (even though the subject annoyed me like someone elses slowly released fart in a small room, to me it was still very tenderly and emotionally delivered)
Atmosphere and Sounds: ~ (okay, but mostly bad, good lighting, the house is lifeless though and doesn't feel like anyone could ever be home even if the game put them in there, and the thunder claps seemed really off and badly recorded.)
Story: - (bland, slightly intriging for a second, and then it turns into, walk here, unlock this, walk there, while narration complains and explains)
Gameplay: - (It's hard to have an exploration game where exploration really matters if I have to go through the story in chronological sections anyways, I never felt like I was figuring anything out)
