Is this game good? Yes, it is. Even for all its ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t it's easier than Dark Souls or Demon's Souls. Is it better than Dark Souls or Demon's Souls? No, it's not. If you're a Souls fan you'll take any bit you can get. If you're a newie to the franchise looking at picking this game up because it's newer and prettier, trust me, Dark Souls: Prepare to Die is going to be far more satisfying and is going to frusterate you less.
----------------------------------------------------------------------------
What is that difference? It was made by a different team. And it shows. While From Software markets the Souls series as brutally hard, "pepare to die" and so on the actual game design is very free of what I call "♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t". The older games were far better designed than this one, SoTFS showed they were learning (the DLC is actually really good for Dark Souls II) but Demon's Souls and Dark Souls don't have this ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t like Dark Souls II/SoTFS. It's still a good game, but it sucks the creators didn't understand the design principles of the original team until the DLC.
What is this "♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t"? You'll fight against larger groups of enemies, you'll fight against large groups of minibosses. The previous games in the franchise made it easy to judge what was coming up, the enviornment gave clues. You see burn marks and burned bodies on the bridge? Remember the dragon from earlier? Yeah, when you cross that burned section a dragon is going to breathe fire at you. In Dark Souls II you'll often find enemies jumping from the ceiling or out of hiding places that you never could have seen coming. Dark Souls II also has some forced death sequences, something the Souls series NEVER does (other than Seath's fight in the first one). You'll open up a door and have the entire wall collapse ontop of you, something you can't avoid nomatter what you do.
----------------------------------------------------------------------------
TIPS FOR NEW PLAYERS
#1, be patient. The Souls games will test you. Dying isn't as punishing as you will first believe. You loose your souls, and if you're human you switch back into your hallowed state unless you recover your bloodstain. Those souls can be used to upgrade your equipment and stats, but your stats are pretty useless, people beat the game easily without leveling once; it's more useful to level your equipment and that doesn't cost many souls.
#2, summon help if you need it. Playing the game with other players is a lot of fun. Getting invaded in Dark Souls II while traveling with some other players is really satisfying. The AI is very good too, you'll play against an NPC invasion and you almost wont be able to tell the difference between them and a real player.
#3, DO NOT LOOK AHEAD! Knowing what's coming makes the game a lot easier, but the most satisfying part of Dark Souls is overcoming the challenges (bosses, hard areas, other players) and exploring the world. I used a video guide for Dark Souls 1 and I regret it because its a lot more fun to play blind. PLAY IT BLIND. If you like the game, you'll like it a LOT more playing without any help (unless you're really stuck, or need to know where to go next). If you don't like the game, and you've put 10 or 15 hours into it then Dark Souls probably isn't a game for you.
#4, give it a shot. Dark Souls can be hard to get into. You don't know the mechanics, you don't know the rules, but you'll learn. Don't quit because you don't know how to lock on to an enemy. Don't quit because you did something foolish and died and feel intimidated by that weakly enemy whom killed you. TAKE A BREAK IF YOU'RE HAVING A BAD DAY, COME BACK AFTER SOME NETFLIX.

I have very mixed feelings about this installment in the series when compared to DkS1. It's had many improvements, but it also suffers from many steps back.
Pros:
- Graphics are much improved.
- More weapons, armors, spells... Variety!
- Customization! You can reroll your stats now using a semi-rare item!
- Co-op is enhanced. More coventants to co-op, more "revive" items to allow co-op. Who doesn't like friends?
Cons:
- Level design... It's nowhere near as intricate and interconnected as DkS1 or even Demon's Souls (or Bloodborne for that matter). It's quite a shame. The transitions from zone to zone is bland and unnatural. The levels feel like game levels as opposed to a large believable dark fantasy world.
- Controls... They are much more "floaty" and there is an ever so slight delay between input and action. It makes the combat feel much more clunky than DarkSouls1. And the change in controls for 2H weapons is very annoying to me personally. I preferred the lock on targeting in DkS1, but in DkS2 you will swing the direction you are facing, regardless of lock-on. While this in theory offers more flexability, it also leaves you open to easy errors and swinging at air instead of your intended target. Walking backwards and suddenly want to swing infront of you? You need to stop walking for a split second before you swing, or else you'll just swing behing you, missing your enemy, and leaving you WIDE WIDE open to get shanked. There's no option to turn this on or off, which is frustrating.
- Story. While it has a lot of backstory and lore bits to be found if you really want to dig, the overall story as it's presented tends to fall flat -- lacking likeable characters and leaving a lot of things unexplained, even moreso than DarkSouls1, which is saying a lot. This is a controversial con, but I stand by it as my opinion.
- Bosses. Can you say reskin? There are repeat bosses... Quite a few. Looking at you Smelter Demon, the most obvious of them all. And most of the bosses are generic humanoid of some sort. In this crazy world of Dark Souls, I expected more creativity and variety in the boss encounters.
Pros AND Cons(Flip a coin):
- More PvP. This can be good and bad depending on your feelings about PvP. You can be invaded at any time, no matter how dead or hollowed you are. Are you online? Yes? Prepare to be invaded.
- More online interaction in general, especially with covenants. While this can be GREAT for day 1, month 1, or even up to month 6, eventually people will stop playing this title online. This will result in a lot of the games content being effectively locked away from you. Do you want to rank up in this coventant to reap the rewards it offers? You can't, because there's no one to invade or co-op with, and you need invasion wins or co-op wins to recieve tokens to present to your covenant... Oh well... I guess I can never, ever get it...
OVERALL; TLDR;
Good game. Recommended. Flawed, but fun, if it doesn't make you rage.

Ugh... god... another ♥♥♥♥♥♥ Unity game that puts more importance on the story than the actual game. Well I'm not going to grade it based on it's merits as a story. That would be like rating a scientist based on how colorful his shoes are. Nope, I'm grading it based on how it plays a video game, and as a video game, it sucks! It's not even a game. You walk around an empty house, knocking stuff off of shelves, digging through people's underwear drawers and randomly wiping boogers on dishes while some annoying teenage lesbo runs her mouth about some crappy relationship with another lame pretentious teenage lesbo. The objective seems to be finding as many poorly written notes as possible and trying to read as many as you can before you have an aneurysm from the overwhelming, relentless amount of boredom this game creates.
If you can some how manage to stay awake while you play this boring, mind-numbing sack of♥♥♥♥♥♥ you'll find clues telling a smaller story about some kids' interactions with a ghost that may be haunting the house, named Oscar. They didn't even bother giving an ending to this little sub-story. So why is it there? I guess to help add some content to this very thin, exhausting, piece of crap. Said irony is that it puts so much importance on story that all it ends up doing is hurting literature in video games. Now, as much as a lot of people sings the praise of the Counter Strike name alone, I for one don't buy it. I do not entirely understand why people call it "fun," persay. As you're probably noticed, I don't like the game.
Now, don't call me a hater yet. First, I'll explain what I think it gets right. In my personal opinion, kills are satisfying in this game. That feeling you get when you successfully kill someone is brilliant. That is... if you do.
The main issue I have with the game is just how unforgiving it is in almost every combat scenario. Far too often to I find myself spraying my gun towards an enemy at close range, not even getting close to killing him before he kills me with the same stunt. This doesn't just apply to that. This happens almost every time I tried shooting someone. More then once, I felt cheated out of a kill due to some reason I wasn't grasping.
The fact that I can't seem to get any good amount of kills with any gun doesn't help matters for me. So, more often then not, I'm at the bottom of the scoreboard with a K/D of 0:5.
Now, I realize that this game isn't all about the guns. Leave Call of Duty to that. It has actual objectives which, for the most part, work out fine. You got hostage rescues, bomb defusals, and a variety of other custom gamemodes like Jailbreak and GunGame.
I also do like the majority of the blood effects for some odd reason.
But with all of this games positives, I can't help but get turned off by the games unforgiving and sometimes borderline unfair gameplay for me. So, I do not reccommend.
(This review is purely subjective.)

There is some important info you need to know before buying "Gone Home"
1. It is not a game. "Game" implies that there is gameplay and some kind of goal. This is an interactive story. There are no boss battles, no power ups to collect, and no end goal besides having the story told to you. If you thought "Dear Esther" was boring, DO NOT BUY THIS.
2. Gone Home is short. You can easily finish it in 90 minutes. If you think 20 dollars is too much for a 90 minute experience, DO NOT BUY THIS. (I know I have spent 20 dollars on 90 minute movies that were much worse than this)
3. Story, story, story. Gone Home is about the story. The story is a drama. If you are not someone who pays attention to detail, you will miss a lot in this game. Everything in the environment is meant to service the story. If you are not a fan of serious drama, DO NOT BUY THIS.
If you are still reading then this game may be for you. Mild spoilers ahead. If you do not want to read spoilers I will just say that this story is amazingly well crafted. The characters are more real and believible than any other game I have ever played. And you should buy it right now.
MILD SPOILERS HEREAFTER:
In Gone Home you play a girl who has just spent a year abroad on vacation. You come home from your red eye flight expecting your parents and little sister to welcome you home. Only to find a note on the front door from your sister saying she has run away for reasons unknown and your parents are nowhere to be found.
What follows is your exploration of their new house (they moved into this house while you were away) trying to figure out where everyone is.
The story is told through the environment and also through journal entries from your sister. These are recited to you by an excellent voice actress. Your exploration uncovers the trappings of a standard upper middle class life.
The story is engaging, and very moving. By the end you may shed tears of sadness and of joy. (The story is very bittersweet.)
Gone Home is an incredible example of video games as Art. This story could not have been told in any other medium and because of the way it is told it becomes even more emotionally powerful.
There is a twist in the story, that is fairly obvious to spot for anyone paying attention, but that does not detract from the quality of the narrative.
If you like Dear Esther buy this immediately. If you are on the fence wait for it to be on sale.
There is an aspect to the story that warrants discussion but to give it away in a review would be a disservice to the game. I'll just say there are some mature themes in the game. And by mature I mean emotionally mature not porno mature.
If you like your games to be full of explosions and awesome action, this is not for you.
If you want a thought provoking and amazingly well told narrative Gone Home is highly recommended.

Gone Home is not so much a game, as a way of
. It weaves together superb stories and characters with a narration/("gameplay") that works remarkably well, fells natural and is simply well done. Therefore thumbs up: Buy this game if (and only if) you are into exploring well written stories, and do not mind lack of traditional game elements.

, prospective buyers should be aware that this game will likely take around 2 hours to complete and has little replay value. If you think 20 quid is too much for that, I would recommend waiting for a sale.
As a further recommendation, I suggest considering to turn off the audio diary in the settings. What this does is play pieces of an audio diary when you discover related pieces. The diary provides much more explicit information than the items alone, and therefore considerably reduce the amount of own deduction you need to unpuzzle this story line. Personally I found it useful and engaging, but if you want to be a bit more hardcore you might want to disable it.

While this game can be easy to criticise for the the lack of common gameplay elements expected to be found in a game, it's not less true that its narrative structure is among the best in any game I've played.
The game mechanics are somewhat missing in depth, the puzzle elements are too shallow and one would appreciate if the developers could have been more creative in that regard. But on the other hand, their simple approach allows for an amazing story flow, and that kind of balances the final outcome.
But ultimately it would be utterly unfair to point fingers at the developers for being too lazy to build a more complex game. I say this because almost every aspect of this independent game has been given enough attention to be on pair with big budget games. The voice acting - although being just one character - is just stellar, same as environment sounds and soundtrack. The graphics are simple but very well polished. And the whole world creation is vibrant with detail, being fundamental in the main narrative building, while at the same time going out of its main path to give you a richer context on a background narrative. Also the recreation of a 90s vibe it's almost worth on its own.
Story wise don't expect a very complex structure, but expect a very Human story that will resonate within you. I, as an heterosexual male, find completely irrelevant the sexual orientation aspects, as I could easily identify my self with many of the struggles portrayed here.
All in all, Gone Home it's a good game that will take you just a few hours to finish, or less depending how invested you become in it. But it isn't a game for everyone, first because it deals with a subject that some people are just not in a mind set that allows them to play it without being too judgemental, and secondly - and above all - it's a game that embraces its gameplay elements in a way out of conventional methods.

Sometimes you catch Bonnie staring deep into the lens of a camera, and think, "Where are the others?", you quikly switch to camera 12! AND NOTHING IS THERE.
SUDDENLY ALL OF THEM ARE ON THE LOOSE BUT WAIT!....there are more who want you. There's Foxie who can't be found anywhere but the hall...there's Old Bonnie...who is now near faceless.

Horror: 7
Psychological Anxiety: 8, 9 and sometimes, at a crucial moment, 10.

Replayability: 7

A thorough playthrough of Gone Home will take you about 1.5 - 4 hours, depending on how thorough you are, and it doesn't star a protagonist who wanders around the world looking at things over the barrel of a gun. If for you, those two qualities constitute a poor game, you will not like Gone Home. Fortunately, there are plenty of other games that allow you to walk around shooting things for 40+ hours. Go play those games, and know they are in no danger of extinction.
Gone Home can also exist. It's not about violence, but instead about teenage rebellion, little family dramas, and the subtle ways that ancestors continue to haunt their living descendents. The story is told entirely by exploring and observing your environment. It allows the player to connect personally with the setting with a degree of specificity that would not be possible in any other storytelling medium.
At one point, you find a school-preparation list with all items checked off except for "a positive attitude." This kind of attention to detail will allow you to discover secrets and emotional truths from these characters organically. I love it when game designers include these kinds of touches, and am thrilled that someone with a good story to tell has made a game built entirely from the sort of subtle cues we too often rush past on our way to complete some hollow objective.
Gone Home is full of voices and objects and set pieces I am not used to seeing in games. I am glad that I have been able to encounter them here. I am saddened that those who prefer the more prevalent gameplaying paradigms feel threatened by the fact that this game got made, and that some are playing and enjoying it.
It is possible for many different kinds of games to exist, and Gone Home is a rare sort of game. It deserves the critical acclaim it has received, and is too good for the ludicrous scorn that some member of the gaming community have felt the need to heap on it.

Consider buying it if it goes on sale. It might be worth its default price, if it came with a large popcorn and soda-but it does not, because this is not a movie theater.
Get it on sale, if you get it at all. Do not expect exciting gameplay, but do expect some interesting narrative tricks.

Monmonstar’s Review of Five Nights at Freddy’s 2
!!! MINOR GAMEPLAY SPOILERS!!!
A fantastically amazing sequel to the first game which scared the♥♥♥♥♥♥outta me! 12 animatronics each with their own AI and ways to get rid of them (and not be killed by them). FNaF 2 is hard and when I say hard I mean hard! I feel like I'm Vishnu! Having many pairs of arms and having to do SO MANY THINGS AT ONCE!!!
However it is scary but not as tense as the last one, the problem is with FNaF 2 is that the animatronics constantly come at you, rather than a build up to the actual scare in the original, at first the jumpscares can be extremely predictable and after a while the jumpscares are just plain annoying rather than scary!
New Mechanics...
THE FREDDY HEAD
You have to do a lot to stay alive in FNaF 2, you have a new Freddy helmet mechanic where when an animatronic enters the room you have to hide being it in order to 'trick' the animatronics so it simply replaces the doors. But this is flawed in a way. While the head does provide some immersion and you can’t use the cameras or the new flashlight (I will get to that later) when the withered animatronics enter the room (The ones seen in the trailer) it’s extremely unfair towards the player, if you are 0.000000001 milliseconds early in taking the head off they will kill you without a chance and a frustrating robotic scream and one huge gaping mouth in your face to see you off to your static-screen doom!
THE FLASHLIGHT AND THE HALLWAY
This was one of the mechanics I liked the ability to light a black abyss (One huge dark hallway) in front of you to illuminate the hidden animatronics chillin' in the hallway. Foxy plays a huge role in the flashlight mechanic where as if you don’t "flash your light at him from time to time" he will jump in your face! However you don’t need to worry too much as he goes away after a while (and comes back every now and then). To replace the power usage from the original game you have flashlight battery, you are given 4 bars (5 counting the outline) using the flashlight too much will drain power from it, drain all of your power (or a certain little ♥♥♥♥♥ of an animatronic getting into your office!) then foxy or Freddy can get you!
Summary...
FNaF 2 is harder than the first but less scary I found, don’t get me wrong this is break your chair scary! But the original had a more eerie ambience and scarier events (I'm never going to forget the first time I saw an "ITS ME" hallucination or all the animatronics’ parts staring at me in the repair room!)

This is primarily Sam's story, so if you don't like teen drama, I'd advise you to stay away.  I found myself more interested in the side characters instead of Sam, to be honest, and Sam was portrayed realistically.
This may be peculiar to my computer, but the graphics were extremely dark, even on the highest brightness setting.   The game could have use more lighting - maybe have Katie pick up a penlight so rooms aren't pitch black.
The real flaw of this game is that there is no replay value at all.  Once you have gone through the game, the mystery is gone, and examining the items only tells you so much.   Only buy this game if is on sale, and I will be cautious about any future Fullbright games.

1,500 hours in CSGO. Thousands of hours in the Battlefield franchise. A few hundred hours in Call of Duty games.
The Warface maps are small--smaller even than Counter Strike, which is criticized for small maps. I'm not impressed with the Warface maps. They don't lend themselves to holding angles like CSGO. They aren't big like Battlefield. They aren't even tactically as good as COD. I struggle to understand the map design. They don't promote skill based play.
So if we're not holding angles and have precision based shooting like CSGO. And we're not dealing with a larger, tactical map like Battlefield. What are we doing in Warface?
You can do these unrealistic, arcade style slides? 9 times out of 10, I easily kill the arcade slider in close combat.
The other terrible game mechanic is toggling rapidly between laying prone and standing up. You can switch so fast that it looks like a
In medium to close combat, expect the prone toggler but its not that hard to spray them down.
I enjoyed playing the game, but the maps and gameplay options just get old. The prone toggling and arcade sliding, while fun at first, don't lend themselves to long term game play.
You can pay for better weapons. Some claim you can get these weapons for free by grinding XP. Yes, you can.
But you can't afford to use them afterwards! Try using some of the best weapons, armor, boots, etc in the game. You will pay HUGE repair costs after each mission. You will pay more for the repair costs than you made on the mission. Forget pay to win. It's pay to play.
Think about it. It's a free game. Repair costs are there to force you to pay to use the weapon. The whole game mechanic is designed to force you to spend money (or the game can't exist). Or not be able to use the weapons you either purchased or unlocked through grinding levels and XP.
: If you have played other FPS games, you know there will always be hacks. Rather than a real anti-cheat that detects when the game's memory has been compromised, they opted for Fair Fight. Fair Fight is a performance based anti-cheat, where if you play substantially better suddenly you can be banned. There's other factors as well.
The problem is hack sites that sell wallhacks and aimbots also provide guides for getting around Fair Fight. A lot of it is common sense about doing better slowly, not following people through walls, not following people who can't see you, etc.
I've seen more wallhacks in Warface than I saw in CSGO, Battlefield, and COD combined. It's infested. There's even people in game advertising hack sites. It's easy (but not always reliable) to scream aimbot in any game. The truth is, any aimbot shot COULD have been made by a skilled player. It's easier for me to spot a wallhacker and in Warface, there's always going people who ALWAYS know where everyone is.
I have seen dozens of people Fair Fight banned. I just think with the guides out there for getting around Fair Fight, many are getting around it.
Develop a real anti-cheat that detects when the game has been hooked.
If you want a Battlefield type of game, with super small maps, less tactical options, and prone togglers, then play this game.
If you get beat in other FPS games, just spend money on this game. You can buy super fast boots that make you run much faster. You can buy health regenerating vests that will take you from near death to 100%. You dream it--you can buy it. And maybe even win, assuming you find a game without a wall hacker. ;)

Review: Counter-Strike: Source is a late predecessor of current generation First Person Shooters that has adopted and retained mechanics that are reminiscent of its former titles in the series. The level of skill required to master the game is in most aspects to a higher difficulty than that of other FPS games. Accompanying the base game, community made modifications including maps, skins or game modes can be found in the server browser. Unlike other common games however, Counter-Strike does not award players constantly with rewards or achievements nor does it have a leveling system. For a game made 10 years ago, the quality in development and execution is tremendous. These characteristics are reverberated throughout each of the Counter-Strike games and thus makes it one of my most favourite series of all.

SoFS is basically "Dark Souls 2: Remastered Edition". Which means better graphics, tweaked monster/item placement, some improvements from original Dark Souls 2.
For those who played DkS2 before: worth if you didn't lost interest in this game first completion. Improved PvP (lags are rare these days), additional summon, better enemy AI, all you need to boost your experience.
For newbies:
If you like games that demand dedication to play (don't be fooled by those who say that it's a game for masochists, all you need in Dark Souls 2 is patience and caution... plus some time to learn how to roll and parry :roar: ) that force you to learn it, you will have LOTS of fun here. If you like to explore the lore completly by yourself (remember old Final Fantasy, first one? This is basically this lore-wise, but hella improved) this is the game for you.
If you like Mass Effect/Fallout style dialogues, hollywood-like epicness and arcade-style playing, maybe some romance with big-boobed chick... You'll be dissapointed. All you can meet here is Washing Pole slicing through you like warm knife goes through butter.
Thanks to its uniquess, this game (or should i say... whole series?) is one of best in todays gaming industry. You'll miss alot if you skip it.

Review: Counter-Strike: Source is a late predecessor of current generation First Person Shooters that has adopted and retained mechanics that are reminiscent of its former titles in the series. The level of skill required to master the game is in most aspects to a higher difficulty than that of other FPS games. Accompanying the base game, community made modifications including maps, skins or game modes can be found in the server browser. Unlike other common games however, Counter-Strike does not award players constantly with rewards or achievements nor does it have a leveling system. For a game made 10 years ago, the quality in development and execution is tremendous. These characteristics are reverberated throughout each of the Counter-Strike games and thus makes it one of my most favourite series of all.

Good source of entertainment for 2 to 3 hours depending on your pacing. If you're not into story driven games then you won't enjoy it because the gameplay consists of walking around, picking things up and unlocking combination locks.

There are a few other side stories that you can figure out by reading notes. It's definitely not the "best video game love story ever told" but it's entertaining.
The design of the house you explore is very interesting and the only low res textures were inside drawers, which is probably to save RAM.
The voice acting is good and sounds genuine. The ambience is always mysterious and I got jumpy a couple of times from the odd sounds coming from the house and the constant storm outside.
The 90s setting is interesting; not something that is done often, if at all. Seeing video tapes and noticing the distinct lack of modern technology is pretty nostalgic.
I wouldn't pay $20 for it considering a lot of eBooks are cheaper and accomplish almost the same thing, since the game is 95% story. I did get it with Humble Bundle which was a good deal with 9 other games for $10. If you want this, wait for it to go on sale.

I don't know where to start.
Even with a small amount of playing time, I noticed the following things. Warface is a game, where the graphics do not exactly shine through compared to nowadays content, but the gameplay is a classic first person shooter, where your goal is simply to take out the enemies. Sure the best guns might require a bit of the "real money" and still those can only be rented, but the free-2-play character can still do the same thing as the pay-2-win person. All the pay2win person achieves, is maybe a better accuracy on the snipers, a bit more damage on the pistols, some shotguns, but nothing major. I can still do the same as the pay2win people do. Now the snipers are not exactly accurate, sometimes the bullets miss when they should hit, which is annoying most of the times it happens, but you have to live with it. The game is not at all realistic, accurately shooting while sliding, and sliding overall with tons of heavy weapons maybe falls into the "not realistic" category, but that's what makes it fun! Nothing is more entertaining that shooting someone while sliding, and getting those extra points.
Overall the game is very solid and the gameplay is entertaining, few annoying game features, and a couple ones which are maybe a bit overpowered *cough* shooting while sliding *cough* but it is definitely one to check out if you like CoD or Battlefield, not for the ones who want the most realisitic gameplay like CS:GO, and for those who can spare a buck or two will have a heck of a fun time with the game.

To start this off, Dark Souls 2 is not Dark Souls 1. It wasn't trying to be, and it never will be. Nor, in my opinion, should it have tried. There are some things I dislike about Dark Souls 2, but on the whole it's an excellent game.
I will lead with the things I dislike:
-Invasion mechanics in DaS2 are dumb. Basically, it's either horribly unfair to the invader (because it can be incredibly easy for the invadee to summon 2-3 helpers) or horribly unfair to the invadee (related to my other problems), with very little room in between for good invasions outside of fight clubs.
-Soul memory is dumb. I like the idea of trying to prevent twinking, but the way they did it is terrible. SM is the total number of souls you have ever collected, and this includes the souls you have lost in blood stains you have failed to reach. With multiplayer matchmaking based on this, it's extremely punishing to new/inexperienced/bad players, because the more souls they lose, the less their SM reflects their "skill" at the game.
-I strongly dislike the hollowing mechanic in DaS2. Losing max health when you die is, in my opinion, just bad gameplay. It makes it so that instead of needing to improve (or git gud, as the saying goes) to progress, you have to improve just to reach the same spot you were at before. On top of that, it just makes the game easier for people who don't die much. Both of these points feel counter to the philosophy of Dark Souls as it is, but to make it worse, you can now get invaded while hollow. It's a bit easier to go human for when this does happen (you don't have to rest at a bonfire), but it's still pretty stupid for someone to have to do that just to fight on even footing with the invader (and I say this as a red phantom).
-Some enemy placement, especially in Iron Keep and Shrine of Amana, is bad and the designer should feel bad. Don't get discouraged by these zones (or any zone, really; these two just felt like their difficulty was gimmicky). You will likely hate them and yourself by the end of each.
-Reusing bosses. This was something that bugged me a bit in Dark Souls 1, too, so I don't count it as a strong negative, just something that From tends to do that I dislike. Not a big deal in the end, though, especially since they have done it less than in DaS1.
Woof. That ended up being a bit longer than I intended, and it may paint a bad picture for the game, but I assure you the rest more than makes up for it. Speaking of, now we get to the good parts:
-Generally smoother gameplay than DaS1. A lot of people have complained that the controls feel looser or slower than DaS1, and I would have originally agreed. However, having gotten used to the changes, I find the combat to generally work better.
-Overall, a much better port than DaS1, and it has 60 fps. Not a huge count in its favor, but the game is definitely prettier and runs better.
-The world is huge. Yes, this was the case in DaS1, and no the world of DaS2 is not as interwoven. But I'm okay with that. The levels are large and sprawling, giving me a great sense of progress with just how far I've run since the last time I was in Majula.
-The lore is, in my opinion, just as good as DaS1's was, but with a different feel. Don't go in expecting DaS1 lore; while definitely a sequel, DaS2 is still its own game. In a way, I actually enjoy its lore more. You get to know the big players in DaS2 in a way that you never did in DaS1, and you learn the progression of Drangleic better than you did Lordran. You still have to piece it all together, you still have to talk to all of the NPCs, and you still have to read item descriptions.
-Magic is, in my opinion, much improved in DaS2. I didn't mess with it much in DaS1, though, so take my word with a grain of salt here. Regardless, the different styles of magic feel unique and distinct from each other, and the way magic scales is nice.
-Weapons in PvP have wonderful variety, though a bit less in PvE. Due to the changes in scaling, Dex weapons tend to be inferior to Str weapons in PvE, but both are quite solid in PvP. For PvP, it truly depends on your favorite playstyle, whether you want to be light and fast, or heavy and strong. For PvE, bleed and poison (which scale off of Dex in DaS2) are nigh useless (they either applies too late to be useful, or the enemy is immune anyways), which takes away one of Dex's biggest benefits and makes it feel lackluster compared to Str. Other than that, both styles are enjoyable and viable.
-Enemy/boss variety is great. A lot of people complain that the bosses in DaS2 were boring compared to DaS1; however, I think there are a couple of factors here that play into this. First and foremost is that these people were already quite experienced with DaS play from their time in the first game, so they are going to have a much easier time with DaS2 on their first run than they did with DaS1 on their first run. Secondly, there are simply a LOT more bosses in DaS2, which can make some of the ones that you had an easy time with less memorable. I personally feel like the bosses are thematically excellent, both in terms of boss arena, aesthetic, and attacks, especially in the last half of the game (including the DLCs, though they have their crappy fights, too).
On the whole, I tend to agree with the general sentiment that DaS1 is better for PvE and DaS2 is better for PvP. That being said, I also find DaS2 to just feel more replayable than DaS1 was. There is a lot more to the game in DaS2. Both are excellent games, however, and I don't think DaS1's greatness subtracts anything from DaS2's greatness, or vice versa. So if you like the dark fantasy genre, and are looking for a challenging game to pick up, I cannot recommend DaS2 enough. As with the first, prepare to die -- a lot. But pick yourself up, and don't you dare go hollow.

To start this off, Dark Souls 2 is not Dark Souls 1. It wasn't trying to be, and it never will be. Nor, in my opinion, should it have tried. There are some things I dislike about Dark Souls 2, but on the whole it's an excellent game.
I will lead with the things I dislike:
-Invasion mechanics in DaS2 are dumb. Basically, it's either horribly unfair to the invader (because it can be incredibly easy for the invadee to summon 2-3 helpers) or horribly unfair to the invadee (related to my other problems), with very little room in between for good invasions outside of fight clubs.
-Soul memory is dumb. I like the idea of trying to prevent twinking, but the way they did it is terrible. SM is the total number of souls you have ever collected, and this includes the souls you have lost in blood stains you have failed to reach. With multiplayer matchmaking based on this, it's extremely punishing to new/inexperienced/bad players, because the more souls they lose, the less their SM reflects their "skill" at the game.
-I strongly dislike the hollowing mechanic in DaS2. Losing max health when you die is, in my opinion, just bad gameplay. It makes it so that instead of needing to improve (or git gud, as the saying goes) to progress, you have to improve just to reach the same spot you were at before. On top of that, it just makes the game easier for people who don't die much. Both of these points feel counter to the philosophy of Dark Souls as it is, but to make it worse, you can now get invaded while hollow. It's a bit easier to go human for when this does happen (you don't have to rest at a bonfire), but it's still pretty stupid for someone to have to do that just to fight on even footing with the invader (and I say this as a red phantom).
-Some enemy placement, especially in Iron Keep and Shrine of Amana, is bad and the designer should feel bad. Don't get discouraged by these zones (or any zone, really; these two just felt like their difficulty was gimmicky). You will likely hate them and yourself by the end of each.
-Reusing bosses. This was something that bugged me a bit in Dark Souls 1, too, so I don't count it as a strong negative, just something that From tends to do that I dislike. Not a big deal in the end, though, especially since they have done it less than in DaS1.
Woof. That ended up being a bit longer than I intended, and it may paint a bad picture for the game, but I assure you the rest more than makes up for it. Speaking of, now we get to the good parts:
-Generally smoother gameplay than DaS1. A lot of people have complained that the controls feel looser or slower than DaS1, and I would have originally agreed. However, having gotten used to the changes, I find the combat to generally work better.
-Overall, a much better port than DaS1, and it has 60 fps. Not a huge count in its favor, but the game is definitely prettier and runs better.
-The world is huge. Yes, this was the case in DaS1, and no the world of DaS2 is not as interwoven. But I'm okay with that. The levels are large and sprawling, giving me a great sense of progress with just how far I've run since the last time I was in Majula.
-The lore is, in my opinion, just as good as DaS1's was, but with a different feel. Don't go in expecting DaS1 lore; while definitely a sequel, DaS2 is still its own game. In a way, I actually enjoy its lore more. You get to know the big players in DaS2 in a way that you never did in DaS1, and you learn the progression of Drangleic better than you did Lordran. You still have to piece it all together, you still have to talk to all of the NPCs, and you still have to read item descriptions.
-Magic is, in my opinion, much improved in DaS2. I didn't mess with it much in DaS1, though, so take my word with a grain of salt here. Regardless, the different styles of magic feel unique and distinct from each other, and the way magic scales is nice.
-Weapons in PvP have wonderful variety, though a bit less in PvE. Due to the changes in scaling, Dex weapons tend to be inferior to Str weapons in PvE, but both are quite solid in PvP. For PvP, it truly depends on your favorite playstyle, whether you want to be light and fast, or heavy and strong. For PvE, bleed and poison (which scale off of Dex in DaS2) are nigh useless (they either applies too late to be useful, or the enemy is immune anyways), which takes away one of Dex's biggest benefits and makes it feel lackluster compared to Str. Other than that, both styles are enjoyable and viable.
-Enemy/boss variety is great. A lot of people complain that the bosses in DaS2 were boring compared to DaS1; however, I think there are a couple of factors here that play into this. First and foremost is that these people were already quite experienced with DaS play from their time in the first game, so they are going to have a much easier time with DaS2 on their first run than they did with DaS1 on their first run. Secondly, there are simply a LOT more bosses in DaS2, which can make some of the ones that you had an easy time with less memorable. I personally feel like the bosses are thematically excellent, both in terms of boss arena, aesthetic, and attacks, especially in the last half of the game (including the DLCs, though they have their crappy fights, too).
On the whole, I tend to agree with the general sentiment that DaS1 is better for PvE and DaS2 is better for PvP. That being said, I also find DaS2 to just feel more replayable than DaS1 was. There is a lot more to the game in DaS2. Both are excellent games, however, and I don't think DaS1's greatness subtracts anything from DaS2's greatness, or vice versa. So if you like the dark fantasy genre, and are looking for a challenging game to pick up, I cannot recommend DaS2 enough. As with the first, prepare to die -- a lot. But pick yourself up, and don't you dare go hollow.

Some people utterly trust each other, some people don't, some people shouldn't, but none of it is explicitly referred to. You just discover evidence of the various family members' lives.
It was a brief but unique and memorable experience for me and I enjoyed it immensely.

Let me briefly summarize the experience you will likely have with this game.
1) The game starts, and it feels like it is going to be a great narrative driven adventure/horror game.
2) Scary and mysterious atmosphere keeps it interesting, and you're trying to figure out why your family isn't hom!
3) Your thoughts are racing - are they dead? Are they tied up in the basement?
But then...
4) You realize that the entire game is basically just you finding out in the most ineffecient way, that your sister is homosexual.
Oh, and your parents are just out of town or something - no biggie.
5) No really, that's it. Shocking, isn't it? Yes. Homosexual. Ain't that just wild? How will we live with this startling revelation. It isn't like we live in the 21st Century, and people have been coming out of the closet left and right since the '80ies.
6) So, you're probably thinking, that surely, if that's really it, there has to be some sort of oppressive agenda behind the parents and that's why it was so difficult and all that, right?
No - it's literally just that. Some girl, still in high-school, has come to the conclusion that she's into other girls, and now she's run off with her pretty friend with oddly-colored hair.
I mean really... There's just no story here.

This is the only "walking simulator" (I guess it's an official genre now) I have played so far.
You arrive to the house of your parents, it's night and rainstorm outside and you just walk around the house, which keeps making these creepy noises like squeeking wooden floors so you feel like you are not quite alone, which I found rather scary (would recommend playing at night, with lights off and headphones for best experience) but I'm an easy guy to scare to be completely honest. Within the house you find different clues like newspaper clippings, letters, phone messages, diary entries from your sister or cassette tapes and slowly (or actually rather quickly, the game is only about 2 hours long and that's only if you take time to read all the stuff you find) uncover what happened between your younger sister and parrents while you were gone in Europe for a year.
And I will admit that even though the story is quite generic and very predictable, the game still managed to draw me in with it's creepy atmosphere and excellent (at least in my opinion) voice-acting.

The walking around, looking for stuff is literally all you do though, there are no puzzles
or any other kind of gameplay features so some people might find this game rather overpriced and I wouldn't blame them at all. In fact I too think that 20 euros for a game like this is absolutely ridiculous but if you got it the way I got it, that being a part of the humble bundle, this is definitely worth playing.
So I will give this a recommendation even though I really don't think the price-point is right at all.
*Also it runs at 120 fps without any drops, which I can't really appreciate with my 60 hz screen but I'm sure it will make some people happy :D

If you love causing wide-spread destruction, Just Cause 2 is a fun time. Looking for something other than a massive collect-a-thon, like maybe a decent story and some meaningful collectibles? Nah. Just Cause 2 doesn’t give a damn. And that’s perfectly fine. A grind-y B-movie adventure in a (still)glorious island sandbox.
Total size on my hard drive (with all DLC): 5GB
+ Great graphics, even for a game from 2010. Crank the sliders and enjoy.
+ Lots of weapons. You can also dual wield a few different combinations.
+ Lots of vehicles. Planes, trucks, cars, sports cars, bikes, APCs, attack helicopters, fighter jets – if you see it, you can drive it.
+ Inventive uses for the grapple. You might have seen gifs of two airliners grappled together. The grapple works on anything and everything, creating some very funny possibilities.
+  Geographically, Panau has a little bit of everything. Deserts, jungles, cities, towns, vacation resorts, snow-capped mountains, naval yards and airports. Then you can dive into the water and see what is beneath the surface...
+ Satisfying audio design, especially explosions.
+ There are upgrades you can take to ease the strain of the combat, but the endless hordes can get challenging. Don’t try to hold your ground, you won’t survive. AI is predictable, but aggressive as well.
+/- Story. We’re secret operatives in the fictional island nation of Panau because Panau has got oil, and that’s something that ‘Murica wants, y’see. Yeehaw! Over-simplifying, but not by much.
+/- Characters? We don’t need no stinkin’ characters – not when the standard adventure stereotypes will do. You’ve got your standard evil dictator, a crafty CIA boss, a pair of beautiful secret agents, and (of course) Rico Rodriguez himself, who possesses all the traditional action-hero traits. Local Panauan gangs? We’ve got your standard Communist gang, your religious fundamentalist gang, and your regular gangster gang. Not a negative because it’s clear this is all intentional.
- 100%-ing the game requires a high amount of patience. Half-way through, there are no new techniques to learn; it becomes a repetitive grind.
- Grind is essential anyway. Upgrades, for instance, are acquired by finding hidden weapon parts (collectibles). Much of the story is hidden behind “chaos levels.” Cause chaos by blowing stuff up, reach the desired level of chaos, do the mission, then cause more chaos to unlock the next mission.
- Stronghold takeovers do provide some change in the monotony. Except they use the same mission patterns repeatedly.
- Want to highjack a vehicle or hack a terminal? Quicktime events.
Overall, Just Cause 2 is a fun if shallow ride. Sometimes, though, it’s cool to drive or fly around a nice sandbox destroying stuff without worrying about things like characters or story. Sometimes its good to just have fun.

Having been a diehard fan of the Original Dark Souls' PvE and PvP, I couldn't wait to get my hands on DS2: SoTFS edition. I have to give FromSoft props for their improvements in the Graphical and Optimization departments. The combat is Fluid, and feels substantially more fast-paced than in the previous game.
I hear you ask
It's very simple, really.
It's the PvP.
Granted, I don't have an excessive amount of time clocked in the game thus far. The farthest I've reached is Huntsman's Copse (before I realized that in a half asleep state I borked the stats on my toon when respeccing), and so far all I've seen in PvP is these ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ twinks that run around and invade people at low levels who could barely stand a chance. A fine example of this is an experience I had just recently in Heide's Tower of Flame. I was simply trying to make some progress on my lonesome when I was invaded by a twink wielding some fast lightning sword and a greatbow who somehow managed to hit me despite being directly behind him. Despite my blocking his attacks, I had over half of my health drained in 1 hit through my shield. Another example, also in Heides, was someone at my toons current Soul Memory (145,710, Level 50) running around/fast rolling in Havels armor with two swords.
The main point of my rant is the function with which you're matched with people in Co-op and PvP, the Soul Memory stat. If you're looking at this game as a potential purchase, Soul Memory works by keeping a record of how many total souls you've collected on that character. I feel that despite the greatness that this game has inside it, that this obnoxious of online play measurement far, FAR outweighs it. I cannot in good faith recommend this game simply because this method of grouping players for Online play makes an already arduous, sometimes frustrating game 100x worse.

I started playing Warface, during the summer of 2015 at the request of some clanmates from another game as a break. Having played this game for a full year and having spent a good chunk of money on the game, I feel quailfied to speak on it honestly and openly.
While fun for a time, you shouldn't invest your time and definitly money.
This f2p shooter, developed by Crytek, while good is just plauged with too many issues and has too little going for it to be worth it for you to invest a sizeable about of time in it.
The Cooperative and Special Ops missions are good but their is little strategy to to them and the become repetive and boring quickly as its the only way to make money without dropping actual money on the game.
Multiplayer, is good and slightly addictive but is plauged with issues. Laggers and hackers, players from Asia, South America and other areas of the world who have horrible connections that make them impossible to kill and Cryteks inability to to address the issues for whatever reason. Whats left of the community from the console versions and current players is active on the North American and European Teamspeak servers and they are a nice addition to the games dynamic. Also, while Crytek is actively trying to work on the game and improve it, the issues that have been unaddressed since the game was first put out condemn it.
Overall this is a fun shooter to pick up for a few months or weeks to just play for grins if your sick of Call of Duty or Battlefield but please don't invest too much time or any money into it or you'll regret it.

Five Nights at Freddy's 2 is a great example of how game sequels should be done. It introduces new elements while still keeping familiar ones from the last game. The game includes the original five characters (including Golden Freddy), and definitely maintains the intense atmosphere from the first FNAF, but also features newer characters (some still pretty familiar, others not so much) and new scenarios.
FNAF 2 is definitely more difficult than its predecessor, though, like the first, the behavior of the characters begin to get a little predictable. However, that doesn't mean that there aren't any surprises in store.
In fact FNAF 2 contains a lot more easter eggs than the first, and some are pretty creepy.
That being said, FNAF 2 tells more of a story, unlike the first one. The original FNAF was incredibly mysterious and didn't explain itself much (reading all of the fan theories was extremely fun). Don't expect that here. FNAF 2 has more of a story, and the way it tells it will send chills down your spine.

You look around your trench, at the mud and filth you are told to defend. Spindly toothpicks, which were once trees, stick up here and there on the edges. The sky is an oily black, whether from clouds or from smoke, you aren't sure.
"Hold this position lads!" The NCO screams, crouching nearby a small slit in the barbed wire and sandbags of your battered fortifications. He clutches a Webley six-shot pistol in his hand, and despite his proper attire (cap, coat, and all, like a proper British soldier), he is covered in filth, and his eyes are sunken into his skull by weeks of unbroken horror. He cares not what happens to him anymore—he is simply concerned with preserving his men through what is about to happen.
There's artillery fire. You hear it, distinctly closer than usual. You look up to see the shells streaking across the black sky, hanging in the air for what seems like minutes... then the first ones fall. Short of your trench, in no-man's land, churning up the corpses of horses and men, kneading the dough for the ovens of hell. The next ones hit closer. Five meters. You huddle under the limp overhang above you, simply hoping you are spared.
BANG! BANG! BANG! Your ears ring and vision blurs. Then silence—the barrage is over. Which means the attack is about to begin. Nary a hundred meters out, their whistles ring out, and you hear the officers scream, with shrill emotionlessness, "ANGRIFF!" just before there is an eruption of gunfire.
The Frenchmen on your left open up with their chauchat machine gun and Berthier rifles. There are already screams all around you; some of emotion, anger, fear, and others of blind pain as the lives of young men are stolen away.
Your faithful NCO stands up, baring his pistol, and empties all six rounds downrange, just as you see a German drop into the trench beside him, his Stahlhelm glinting in the faint light of the distant sun. You raise your Enfield rifle, ready to fire, but alas, too late for your comrade, whose abdomen is run through by a Gewehr 98 bayonet. You fire, and your aim is true. One German falls, you snap your bolt back, then forward. Another man is in your sights, and, heart pounding, you just barely manage to catch him in the chest.
More whistles, and a cheer from your trench. They're retreating!
Only a moment does your joy last, for the words "prepare to attack" are uttered before the enemy have even reached their side again. As you and your comrades step over the eviscerated corpses of your friends to launch another futile raid into the hellscape of Western Europe, circa 1918, you may wonder how man could bring himself to fight any more wars after such a thing took place.
These things described here all happen in a typical Verdun match. The combat is dynamic and visceral, the models and animations are excellent, the sounds are snappy and dense, and the community is full of friendly, yet serious players. The developers are dedicated, fast, and updates (and recently, expansions!) are FREE. GRATIS.
If you are at all interested in history, or warfighting in general, do yourself a favor and experience Verdun.
If only to remember the war to end all wars.

The premise is simple, you have arrived home from abroad to an empty house and a note from your sister telling you not to try find out what happened or where she has gone. I won’t spoil any more of the story as remaining uninformed of the plot I think is vital to this game.
Gone Home manages to generate an oppressive and foreboding tone from the outset and sets up a mystery for the player to be solved. The sound design, although limited to the sounds of an empty house in a storm, are very effective and help to make you feel as though you are lost in your own home.
The aesthetic style is simple stylised and effective, with a lot of care and detail going into the everyday objects around the house that you can inspect to gain a better idea of what happened while you were away. These reveals more often than not take the form of journal articles being narrated by your sister Sam, these are very well voice acted and convey emotion well.
Gone Home is very light on gameplay. The presence of mechanics to occupy the player are minimal. This may switch off many people but it is quite impressive how engaging this uncovering of events and getting to the bottom of the mystery can be without the need for further game mechanics.
In fact it is when more traditional game mechanics that Gone Home experiences issues. Most of the time the player has free reign to gather clues around the house and piece together the story, but areas of the house are locked. The key hunting for progression is problematic because although it is presumably there to ensure that discovery happens in a linear fashion, the end of the game can be found prior to experiencing much of the story found behind these locked doors. This leaves a skeletal version of the story without the depth that all of the journal entries provide, something which routing of the game through locked areas would ostensibly be there to prevent.
Perhaps my biggest issue with the game surrounds the finale, which I don’t feel carries sufficient resolution to the dread and foreboding that the game sets up within the first few minutes. It feels as though the emotions the game wanted to elicit from the player were inappropriate and misplaced in light of revealing the whole story.

That said I think it was a good experience and worth playing. It is an experiment in subtle environmental storytelling which I felt was very effective and worth exploring. It is very short (I found everything the game had to offer within 2 hours) so it pays to keep this in mind as I don’t think the game is very repayable.
In short, Gone Home is to games what short stories are to books. An opportunity to explore unique and interesting concepts that can be powerful, but are short experiences which would not benefit from extension.

You need to know two things upfront about Gone Home:
1.) It is less of a "game" of much more of an interactive story.
2.) It will last you four hours or so, after which there is very little reason to play again.
That said, neither of those are inherently bad things. The game is incredibly well detailed, keeps you a bit on edge the entire time (don't worry, there are no real jumps or scares) and tells a solid little story. Besides, if you grew up in the '90s, Gone Home will play hard on your nostalgia. It's fantastic.
Enjoy it for what it is, take your time, and go along for the ride. If you do, you'll end up with a good bit of enjoyment from Gone Home. Honestly, my only real knock is the price. I got it for a few bucks during a Steam Sale, and felt great about my time with it (side note: there are a couple tiny Easter eggs you can go after post-story, but again, not much). But, had I paid $20, maybe not as much.
Next time it's on sale, give it a ride.

'Gone Home' should be thought of more as an interactive novel than a game, per se. There are no mechanics to learn, no fail states, and the only puzzle is following the threads of the story to figure out where everyone has gone. While the game ends once you have uncovered the reason behind your sister's disappearance there are a number of sub-plots that you may be compelled to dig into concerning other family members.
It won't take long to get through - I clocked just under two hours on a fairly comprehensive run through - and the storylines won't win any literary prizes, but what 'Gone Home' does do is take a huge step forward in the field of interactive novels by shedding any pretence at being a traditional game.
If, like me, you think that story is a hugely important part of any game, I urge you to take the leap and try a "game" that is nothing but story. Given the short play time maybe wait for a sale, but it is worth some of your time and money, and the developer deserves the support.
If you think a game needs action or complex puzzles, look elsewhere, as you'll only be disappointed.

A World War I game, "could never be fun" they said, it could never be "dynamic" due to the endless waves of machine guns and infantry. They were wrong.
This game is a product of a passionate community backed by a benevolent development team that focuses more on improving the game than lining their pockets. First off, look at the price, $25 for content that will last you 100+ hours. I've had this game since January of 2014 when it first entered early access and if you are the least bit interested in history, first person shooters that require actual skill, and dynamic squad and team play, then this game is definitely for you.
While playing solo is rewarding in itself, once you grab a few friends you can level up your squad to gear out with all the late-era swag armor and higher squad perks that makes you almost feel like a god. Not only that, unlike other FPS games, the game as a sort of weight if you can appreciate the historical aspect.
For example, you and your squad/team charge an enemy trench as artillery pounds the earth beside you. Your commander blows his advance whistle and the machine guns are all the while are opening fire from both sides... Then, what's this cloud of smoke? GAS GAS GAS! You put on your gas mask and into the dark fray of the enemy trench you go, firing haphazardly to defeat the enemy in a last ditch effort to keep the momentum of your attack going, lest you fall back and fear an overwhelming enemy force breaking through your own lines of defense.
Hundreds of weapons and attachments, multiple styles of play and squad type variants. Endless hours of fun. 10/10 would die from barb wire again.

__________________________________________
The 'Soul' series is known for harsh difficulty and rewarding gameplay in which dying is mostly the players' own fault for making a wrong move at the wrong time.
In difference to many modern RPGs the lore is kind of hidden as well as it's neither presented in amazing cutscenes nor illuminated from every perspective.
The player has to actually read dialogues and item descriptions, revealing piece by piece of the backgrounds and the story.
In 'Dark Souls II' the main recipe of the series stays the same: A lonesome traveler in a kingdom (haunted by an undead curse) starts a journey full of fighting, exploring and dying. The player will get crushed by hammers and axes, pierced by spears and arrows, cut by daggers and swords, melted by fireballs, cursed by hexes-... there are definitely lots of ways to die and you have to face all of them if you want to survive and see the end of your journey.
There are many negative aspects that stick to 'Dark Souls II' since its release. Many of them are still somewhat present but with the three DLCs, the 'SOTFS' edition and several patches many aspects have changed. I don't want to make another huge review about the game's content (you could easily fill several pages about lore, characters and stuff), so I'll make it 'short' (well okay - it's still quite long) and focus on some main points that bothered me in many reviews.
__________________________________________
The changed enemy positions in the 'SOTFS' edition and the great levels of the DLCs shall provide some nice challenging experiences for anybody. From my point of view the difficulty level has the right balance between 'challenging‘ and 'frustrating‘. Sure there are some annoying parts, some ganking and some cheap deaths, but it never feels too easy or so hard that I think I may never be able to do it. Even the 'Fume Knight' and the 'Frigid Outskirts' are manageable. And for players who still think it's a piece of cake: Fortunately there is a convenant for you mad ones that increases the overall difficulty even more.
__________________________________________
The 'Soul' series was never known for the best graphics of the generation but all the time the overall picture was great and the 'charming' atmosphere made you forget about some of these muddy textures. 'Dark Souls II: SOTFS' is not breaking with this 'rule' but the improved graphics of the 'SOTFS' edition are definitely a good improvement and especially armors are now very detailled. (However with texture modding and ENB and stuff you were able to get nearly the same results out of the original 'Dark Souls II')
The varied landscape in combination with huge buildings and massive monuments of the past (and several nice particle effects) really creates some admirable places where you are able to forget the hopelessness of your journey and immerge into Drangleic – at least until an invader stabs you.
__________________________________________
They say it's no real 'Souls' game, just something else. Sure it’s neither Allant nor Gwyn, neither Boletaria nor Lordran. However Drangleic has several memorable moments, names and characters as well. The story and the lore are atmospheric and well done and I get nearly the same feeling as in the other games. Especially the DLC stories and areas are totally brilliant. They could be imagined as different Archstones and small parts of the world that create an exquisite overall picture, be it the Brume Tower or Frozen Eleum Loyce.
__________________________________________
I'm a huge fan of the 'Souls‘ series and I've spent several hundreds of hours in the different games: I‘ve visited Boletaria and fought with King Allant, walked in the Valley of Defilement and felt like a demon myself after killing Garl Vinland and the Saint Astraea. I’ve travelled through the holy city of Anor Londo, met the former Lord of Sunlight and brought peace to the legendary knight Artorias and the darkness known as Manus in a time and world long forgotten...
The 'Souls' games were always full of memorable moments and from my point of view 'Dark Souls II' is no exception in this category: On the top of the castle I fought the Mirror Knight under a rainy sky, I’ve challenged the proud samurai Sir Alonne in a duel and travelled to a castle sunken in a sea of fire - At the end I was finally able to meet a king who has lost everything.
It was definitely a remarkable journey.
__________________________________________

In comparison to the precursors some decisions and changes aren't entirely positive, like e.g. the high amount of bonfires, the immediate teleportation ability or the simplified upgrade system. Some parts of this old 'gloomy desperation' and helplessness that haunted you in the other games are missing - but there are also positive changes that improve the gaming experience: The 'SL1 invader twinks', the 'Dark Wood Grain Ring' rolling (a.k.a. the Ninja Flip) and the lag-stabbing insanity of 'Dark Souls' are nearly gone, respecing your character is now possible and the sheer amount of different weapons, spells, armors and items (Fashion Souls!) is simply amazing and enables many different builds and styles. In addition some of the items that had to be farmed for long hours in the Original 'Dark Souls II' (e.g. Visible Aurous Set) can now be aquired more easily in chests and treasures.
And above all... since 'Dark Souls II' the game finally features beards - praise the sun for this milestone! \[T]/
__________________________________________
From my point of view make the changes of the 'SOTFS'-Edition the games' atmosphere and lore more coherent and provide challenging new fights and changed enemy positions.
The DLCs of 'Dark Souls II' are simply amazing and provide exactly what Souls veterans are looking for: fantastic levels with shortcuts and hidden paths, new interesting stories with remarkable characters and challenges from which even the toughest veteran may burst into tears.
Still 'Dark Souls II‘ is not perfect and overall more a Titanite Chunk than a Titanite Slab. However it’s still damn good and keeps me interested even after over 100 hours. It’s probably an 8.5 out of 10 - well at least if your nerves and your will are strong enough.
So in the end… it is time to meet your fate Bearer of the Curse. Take a last look at the bonfire, your last anchor in this sea of darkness. Pick up your sword and your shield and move on into the unknown. And never forget your Estus flask…
...you’ll need it. Trust me.

Just Cause 2 is an amazing sandbox game. After the first two cheesily bad missions, you're dropped right smack in the center of Panau, a small totalitarian country of islands, with few guns or grenades and all cities occupied by the government. As you gain in strength, upgrading weapons, vehicles, and your health, you become stronger.
As you work with 3 different criminal factions, the government loses territory. There are 3 factions: The Roaches, a mafia of sorts with a leader who speaks in medical terms; the Reapers, Panau's own branch of the Communist Party; and the Ular Boys, strong traditionalists opposed to all foreign customs.
There are vehicles galore (though too many Tuk-Tuks and motor scooters) and lots of collectibles and destructibles. Much of the world is empty, but when you steal a tank and go on an explosive rampage, you tend not to notice these things. Overall, worth the price whether it's on sale or not.

As the nations march bodily to war, springing from their age-old places in the rich, civilised continent of Europe, the clock ticks downwards for those on the front. Swept in a wave of excitement and fervour, the gullible and hopeful grab their best clothes, train tickets, pocket watches, running to jump into a place in the new armies... those wary, those intellectuals and pacifists those who thought differently, beaten up, trodden down, bullied by their own families into taking an ill-fated place in one of the most horrific, brutish and uncaring moments in modern human history.
We know the outcome now... how many of them knew?
You say you'll "never forget". I think you already have.
At this moment, 17:11 GMT on the 23rd March 2016, the gigantic free DLC "Horror's of War" has just been released. Dozens of new players that I have never seen before have crawled out of the woodwork in a flurry of excitement. Over the last nine months the developers of
have teased weekly snippets of information, details on mechanical changes, new features and optimisation patches. A quick ruffle of clothes, digital shouts of excitements, and this Wednesday evening has been long awaited. Time to settle some old scores.
It's also my one-year anniversary of playing the game.
The number of squads has almost doubled, with the addition of US Marines, Doughboys, Belgian troops, German schutzen sentries, and German pioniers, in addition to the previous German Stosstruppen, Landsers, Alpenjaeger, British Tommies, French Poilu, Canadian Assault teams, and more. Forty new weapons have been added, including the "Wex" flammenwerfer, the G88, the Mauser C96 "Broomstick" pistol, the BAR automatic rifle, and the T-Gewehr with hide-out penetrative bullets. New squad abilities have been added, including Big Bertha, 340mm Railway cannon, smokescreens and White Phosphorus barrages.
Almost all of the animations in the game have been renewed; overhauled, they are smoother and more realistic than before; death animations have been added, each nation now has it's own unique gasmask.
The most anticipated part of the update is the key "Horrors" expansion, replete with and stuffed with savage gore. This includes dismemberment, improved ragdoll physics, death animations, screams, bloody pools, skin melting, and more corpses. This is, however, purely optional; if you have little interest in such a grotesque paradigm, then the toggle button is in the options menu.
A new map has been implemented; in addition to the recent Fort Douaumont map, the night-time Champagne region, the most ambitious map yet, complete with underground tunnels, sandbags and trench walls is here to stay. Expect high volumes of shrapnel, machine-gun fire and keep your ears open for the sound of spitting fire.
A new fourth gamemode has been added, a co-operative wave-assault online mode, "Squad Defence", where you and some sullen survivors of a forlorn assault attempt to survive against dozens of AI opponents rushing your position. They're pretty dim, and a bit buggy at this time, but they're still difficult to defend against.
With all these gigantic changes, it's easy to miss out on the smaller things. Ten new gramophone songs have been added, rifles now eject spent cases, textures have been fixed.  New loadout descriptions, you can no longer sight down your rifle and jump, buffs for the terrible French Chauchat, an extra bullet for the Ruby in the name of historical accuracy, gas blinds faster, is less slightly less visible, slightly more lethal and makes a sounds upon impact...
Oh, and it's on a new and updated Unity version too.
With this nine-month in-the-waiting free expansion pack,
is no longer the game it was; in a digital renaissance it has become much more, building anew on the ruins of the old.
Verdun is the realest, dankest most bomb-diggity Great War game on Steam. So buckle up bros, grab your Chauchats chums, strap on your helmet homies, roll up your kitbag kiddos and "Avec moi", monseigueurs, 'cause swaggity swooty, we're going for all kinds of booty.

Just Cause 2 has the following going for it:
(a) it takes place in a huge and varied world full of stuff to grapple onto, jump off of, hop into, steal, shoot, maim, and just generally wreak havoc with,
(b) the game controls well, so that you shouldn't ever feel like the controller is coming between you and your desire to do the above, and
(c) it is frequently on sale with rock-bottom discounts, such that you can likely pick it up for a couple of bucks.
These things. in combination, make it worth buying and playing for a few hours (or even a few dozen hours). This is a sandbox game -- if you try to follow the main story arc, eventually the lack of a discernable plot, the painfully bad voiceacting, and the "explore every crevice of the enormous world to find every practically-useless collectible" gameplay will probably test your patience. Fortunately, nothing in the game requires you to do those things -- there are plenty of hours of fun to be had in finding the nearest military base, commandeering a fighter jet, and causing untold trouble with your new toy.
LEGEND

Gone home is an interactive story - in game terms, it is a first-person exploration game with a few puzzles, but it is deliberately designed to pose no challenge to anybody. Instead, all interactive mechanics serve the goal of immersing the player in the character they control, and discover the stories of the people that live - or lived - in the house the player is exploring, most of them being immediate family of the player character.
After some 2-3 hours of game play, the game will end on solving the last of the puzzles and the player will come away quite familiar with the unseen occupants of the house, their relationships and their lives - and lots of references to 1990s US mainstream pop-culture to either remember or research.
A review of the game-parts of this piece of software is necessarily short: The visuals are adequate, but not special - the focus is on the story-carrying items, which are all lovingly designed to a noticeably higher standard than the rest of the assets that only serve to build the backdrop of the house. The sound design is flawless, the music pleasant and mostly concerned with carrying the mood - with the exception of certain pieces that are actually part of the story. There is occasional voice-acting, which is great and effective. As mentioned before, despite the existence of puzzles, there is no challenge to Gone Home. All puzzle parts, such as closed doors or missing items, purely serve pacing purposes and to keep the player from rushing past things they are meant to find.
What about the literary part of this game then? If this were a novel, it would be in the genre of literary realism, and - and this is where the choice of medium and the unconventional way to tell the stories contained in it really shines - it would be young adult and mainstream literary fiction at the same time. The inspired choice of setting, a family home, makes this experience ideal to be shared between generations - real families should play this, each member on their own or together in front of a shared screen. That said, the setting, the stories and the characters are too detailed and specific in their cultural, historic and social background - white, latter-half 20th century suburban middle-class - to be universally understood by and identified with by any player from any possible background.
Consumer advice: At undiscounted listing price, this felt bad value for money for me. Wait for at least 50% discount, strongly consider buying at 75% or better discount.

Gone Home is a game that is difficult to talk about, especially to those who without an M4 AR would be inherently bored out of their tiny minds. The immediate question is the genre. After seeing only a few screenshots, the phrase “horror FPS” springs to mind, but in reality Gone Home is none of the above.
It is the mid-90s and you have just returned from a year long trip travelling around Europe. When you return home, the house is empty and there is one hell of a storm raging outside. In hindsight, the obvious question is “Where is my family?”, but the game is bracing enough to have no clear goal and is simply an exploration. You can pick up and examine pretty much all the objects in the house which help tell the story about what your family got up to during your trip and before you know it, you are stuck right in the heart of an immersive tale.
And it is scary in a way. Even your own home looks eerie in the dark, and I was playing this a week after I’d just moved into my new uni house. Give it a go to find out more, but not for the current £15. The game will be finished in under two hours and has absolutely no replay ability, so wait for a sale before being charmed by this gem.

The description for the game says "You arrive home...expect family to greet you...somethings not right...unravel the mystery...". The devs expect you to draw your own conclusion at the end with giving you pretty much no clues as to where the family went and why they left. You get a small idea of where the sister went but even that is shrouded in mystery and left unsatisfied. One second you have the answers then the next second the story changed and not in a cool twist kind of way. Some people online have drawn up conclusions and most of those conclusions can be debunked from facts and plots within the game.
