Just Cause 2 has the following going for it:
(a) it takes place in a huge and varied world full of stuff to grapple onto, jump off of, hop into, steal, shoot, maim, and just generally wreak havoc with,
(b) the game controls well, so that you shouldn't ever feel like the controller is coming between you and your desire to do the above, and
(c) it is frequently on sale with rock-bottom discounts, such that you can likely pick it up for a couple of bucks.
These things. in combination, make it worth buying and playing for a few hours (or even a few dozen hours). This is a sandbox game -- if you try to follow the main story arc, eventually the lack of a discernable plot, the painfully bad voiceacting, and the "explore every crevice of the enormous world to find every practically-useless collectible" gameplay will probably test your patience. Fortunately, nothing in the game requires you to do those things -- there are plenty of hours of fun to be had in finding the nearest military base, commandeering a fighter jet, and causing untold trouble with your new toy.

Despite the praise (presumably from over enamoured fans of the excellent original) after having played around with it for a little while I'm having trouble coming up with any conclusion other than Five Night's At Freddy's 2 is not a particularly good game.
Fundementally the problems stem from the redesigned features the player uses to keep themselves alive. In the original game you had a mere two doors with two light switches with rapidly draining power reserves. You had four animatronics, the intention of the game was to look through the cameras identify their location and prevent incusion. The tension was palpable and the atmosphere was tense. The sequel goes ridiculously overboard much to its detriment.
Effectively now you have to deal with more than double the number of animatronics, who move more randomly and have three points on ingress, also they teleport into the room you're in near instantly giving you 1/2 a second from sighting them to react with the new freddy head item. Which due to said head being unlimited the fear of running out of power is non-existant even with the new flashlight item. Ultimately what it comes down to is you no longer have time to view the cameras instead the game practically forces you to idle in the control room rotating between the lights and triggering the new music box item (a less interesting Foxy). It's not fun and it's largely the only way to deal with games massive difficulty hike. Gone is the atmosphere and dread, replaced with a dry and dull robotic cycling of actions to avoid instant and frequent game overs.
Even the graphics seem to have taken a hit with several of the environments seemingly appearing to be more cheaply put together, lacking the little touches that made them feel like real places. Also for whatever reason one of the new Animatronics seems to be deliberately not blended into the enviromnents and it looks particularly poor. Also the individual animations seem to be stripped down and less interesting, not to mention the goofy fly over the robots perform when you're wearing the Freddy mask.
While it's not all terrible, the new micro-game elements included are an interesting diversion albeit deciedly random inclusion and the other new additions like the flashlight and music box could have made for an interesting game, they just fall flat in the worst ways. Which really leads to the overall problem here, nothing new is better than FNAF and infact it's pretty much all worse. If you're looking for artifical difficulty, cheap deaths and lazier jump scares you'll find something here (and this will no doubt be another hit with the youtube gamer crowd) but it honestly lacks the clever design and atmospheric potential of the original game, which at least for me personally is enough to not recommend it.

Five Nights at Freddy's 2 is a pre-sequel to the original Five Nights at Freddy's.
It takes place in 1987, like last time, you're a security guard in a pizzeria. A haunted pizzeria.
Unlike in the last game, you don't have doors to hide from the Animatronics, instead you get a Freddy Fazbear mask, and a Flashlight. You need to use both of these new gameplay elements, in order to protect from the animatronics. If you see Foxy in the Hallway, you need to flash at him every few seconds, in order to stun him, because the mask doesn't work on him.
When you see any of the new animatronics in the vents' blind spot, you need to put on the mask, and wait until they leave the room.
The storyline explains many mysteries from the first game, such as the missing children accident, in which the 5 kids got kidnapped, and stuffed into the costumes of Bonnie, Chica, Freddy, and Foxy. The phone guy calls you every night, telling you hints and what is currently happening, such as the theft of the Golden Freddy costume (The costume of the kidnapper) and how the animatronics are malfunctioning. When you die, there's a chance you get a Atari minigame, which shows what is happening. In one of these, it tells you to "Give Gifts" in which you control Freddy, to give gifts to the children, after you do that, it tells you to "Give Life" and you need to... Stuff the kids into the animatronics' suits.
The game is a lot harder, and a lot more scary than the first game. This time you need to look for 10 ANIMATRONICS. In 12 rooms! That's a lot more than in the first game, oh I almost did forgot to mention this: There's a music box in the Prize Corner camera, where you need to wind it up from time to time, otherwise the Marionette will get you.
The game has a lot of new mechanics, its a lot more scary, it has a lot of new animatronics, a fitting tension soundtrack when something happens, it's definitely worth the 3 extra dollars.
If you liked the first game, get this one definitely. You'll be scared.

a really interesting premise, and a really well done game, if you're willing to call it that. I'm more likely to call it an interavtice story than anything else, but as it still has some game-like elements (and because its a lot easier to call it that) it's probably easier to call it a game.
But enough about semantics, let's get to the game itself.
You are Kaitlin Greenbriar, and you just came home to an empty house and a note taped to the door. This is where the player starts their journey to find out why the house is empty and where your family has gone. Powered by this curiosity, you explore the house. The mechanics of this game are really simple, and the house, however large, is relatively easy to navigate. The main meat of this game, however, is this story. It's hard to talk about it without much spoilers, but basically, things are a little turbulent in the Greenbriar house. There's a distinct sense of intimacy felt between the player and the the various members of the family when exploring the Greenbriar household, especially when reading through the verious missives between gossiping wives, bickering authors and teenagers falling in love for the first time. In any other format, this story would be a little cliched, but with the added layer of interactivity and the non-linear method of advancing the story, it creates a whole different experience that hasn't been done well before. The ending is satisfying, if nothing else.
The one critisim that I can give this game is that it is essentially a one-shot title. It lacks the type of replayability that even some of the most basic games have, but, considering its format, I feel like replaying this game is more akin to rereading a book. Like finding more and more little things that one would not have noticed the first time around. I certainly tried my best to touch and explore every little object, but I'm pretty sure that there were a few things that I didn't bother with.
Overall, I will recommend this game to anyone who wouldn't mind trying something new. That said, whether you like it or not is completely up to your tastes.

So, after a year since the release of original Dark Souls, we are treated to a remake known as the Scholar of the First Sin edition. Now, what does it offer? Well, it doesn't offer anything new to the original concept. Dark Souls II is still the same souls game we've played and loved. Still the epitome of rogue like game with a high rewards and high consequences principle. But this time with newly arranged enemy placements, improved visuals and 4 players co-op for the ultimate souls experience.
The combat feels much fluid, the game flows better overall and enemy placements certainly suprised me a couple of times. The structure of the world also seems to change quite a bit and you will find yourself arriving at new places in different order.
The 4 players co-op can certainly be entertaining but some times chaotic with random invades and group pvps. The game seem to cater more towards co-op play by introducing new NPC phantoms to aid you in battle. Needless to say Fromsoftware also added invading phantoms to torture you.
With the SOTFS edition come bundled with all three previously released DLCs, players are treated with vast new environments as well as new contents and challenges to overcome. It is especially nice for people like me who have not purchased the season pass for the original game and for those returning veterans who wants more replayability and value for money.

This game is really polarizing between those who think it's a masterpiece and those who hate it because it has little actual gameplay. I went into it knowing exactly what kind of experience I was going, but also a little skeptical, and I was surprised to find it really well-executed.
I wasn't surprised to discover that the devs had also worked on a Bioshock 2 DLC, as Gone Home is basically the "explore, and find audio logs & read letters" experience of the Bioshock and System Shock games, without any of the combat or RPG elements. The game takes place in June 1995, after your character has spent a year abroad. You arrive to an empty house with all of your family members mysteriously gone. Most of your time is spent exploring the house to try and unravel what exactly happened during the year you were traveling.
The "A" plot is a fairly predictable coming-of-age story about your sister Samantha. But while the story is somewhat mundane, it's improved by the high quality of the voice acting (almost all of it done by Sarah Grayson as Samantha), writing, and the production design. The handwritten pages you find scattered around the house believably seem like notes that a teenager might pass to her friends during class, and the samples of Sam's creative writing were hilarious.
Each of your parents also get their own subplot. Your father's is the more compelling of the two because while the other two stories are pretty clearly spelled out, this one was a little more subtly written; it ties into a dark family secret, and how this affected his own writing career and marriage.
A lot of mid-90s riot grrl culture is used as flavor throughout the game, and while some of the "pointless interactivity" (as they themselves refer to it in the commentary) could get tedious, I appreciate the devs' commitment to this worldbuilding philosophy.  The creepy atmosphere adds a fair amount of tension, without being overwhelming, and the house is pretty fun to explore, with its secret rooms & passages.
Recommended, especially if you can get it on sale or in a bundle (as I did. Thanks Humble Bundle!) When you're done with the game, don't forget to explore the Greenbriar house again in Commentary Mode.

To start off, this game does almost nothing to improve or hone the design of the original. What it does do is completely forego atmosphere and a genuine sense of dread and paranoia that embodied the first game, with jumpscares as an auxillary aspect of what made it so tense and frightening, and try to cram in as many jumpscare opportunities as possible, to the detriment of any sense of pacing or atmosphere.
Even from night 1, I got the feeling of playing a game of spinning plates. Or playing a Bop-It. (Seriously, on higher levels you can get attacked every 5-10 seconds and it basically becomes like a really weird, awkward rhythm action game.) The tight, insidious design and gradual introduction of different enemies in the original feels thrown out the window. Losing generator power by doing things in order to defend yourself or simply calm your jangled nerves is gone. It was that interplay of different danger elements in the first game that made it so difficult/brilliant. Now, you need to flick your wrist downward in less than half a second if an enemy gets in your face. That's it. You need to do that over and over and over again. And occasionally flicker the flashlight down the hall for Foxy, who's now tied with the music box as the most dull and predictable game element. Also, adding more animatronics didn't make the game scarier or more interesting, since the lot of 10 actually have 5 different behavior modes between them. Another thing that's disappointing: the animatronics feel so samey now.
This is FNaF 1's hyperactive, sugar high, immature kid brother. It's pure Youtube jumpscare reaction video fodder, and one gets the feeling that was Scott Cawthon's intent in churning out such a lazy, sloppily designed sequel within just a few months: Cash in on the original game's current status as an internet phenomenon. I think he could have put out a much better effort if he worked on it until 2015 like he said he would, but I also don't blame him for getting while the getting's good. In short, it's disappointing that the weakest and laziest part of the first game's design -- jumpscares -- got such a field day here.

Gone Home was an awesome little adventure. Upon arriving at her parents' new home, the PC discovers no one is home. A dreaded creepiness surrounds the house as you explore to find clues hidden within. This is what got me the most into the story, I couldn't wait to figure out what happened to her sister, and what else was hidden in the creepy house.
As you can see, it took me 3 hours to beat the game, so it's not worth the full price of it. But I got it in the current humble bundle for 9 bucks along with a lot of other games, so way better deal. That having been said, the game was designed to be a couple hours long and I wouldn't have wanted to play it much longer. You explore your entire house, and you discover what happened to your family, it's tied up nicely and definitely worth a playthrough, especially if you're not used to this type of game.

After about a solid 100 hours in the game and im still rather a new comer to the title I feel like I can write a solid review about verdun. If your looking for a flashback of simpler times where your skill, accuracy, and timing were rewarded this may be the game for you. Growing up I would spend countless hours on cod, cod2 and all the medal of honors. Although this game is set in ww1 the core mechanics of playing verdun seem very familiar and almost nostalgic to me. The weapons are simple, upgrades make sense, squad work is essential, and everyone has their role. Objectives are very simple and are a constant tug and pull style frontlines that are pretty realistic for the time period. Maps are well designed and balanced for the most part and utilization of cover and map placement is the key to sucess in the frontlines. Graphics are impressive and youll only have a few glitchy textures at far distance but that varies from rig to rig. Sounds are pretty good aside from a few stale sounding explosions (artillery and grenades will kill you alot) but im sure theyll add more. The Historical accuracy of this game was a thing the developers took seriously and it shows, Im a huge history buff and I haven't really noticed anything a miss. The thing that is this games selling point is literally its price at only 22.99USD you can't go wrong with this game and its still in beta with a steady supply of new content. The only real downside is the games small player base or community. Late at night you'll often find it difficult to find full matches even when changing servers EU, JP, ASIA, AUS.  But im sure the games community will only grow from here.

TL;DR: A beautifully presented love story.
This game is an exploration-driven story. You arrive back from holidays to an empty house, expecting someone to be home. What awaits you is an eerily empty mansion vacated by its owners (your family), and you are tasked with putting togeather the story of how and why no one is home. This is done by reading notes, letters and other tidbits of information scattered around the house, as well as "journals", which tell portions of the story in audio form when discovered; arguably the most important parts of the story.
Personally I thoroughly enjoyed this game and would recommend it to people who enjoy games with nice (albeit slightly cliche) stories; it helps if you're able to appreciate love stories. There is no action in this game, so if you are thus inclined this game is not for you. This game is for the patient, the meticulous and the thorough, as racing through this game will only result in a poor experience.

Do you often find yourself rolling your eyes at having your hand held through a game? Do you feel like sometimes you want a game that won't just spell every detail out for you explicitly? Do you feel like a lot of games just don't trust you to "do it right" on your own?
Do you like the investigation parts of L.A. Noir but would like to be trusted to notice minor details on your own and have to really digest the meaning and context in your mind?
Do you want a game that believes in you? Then this game is worth your attention.
In one single map, albeit large, Fullbright has managed to fill it with impeccable detail.
While the main story is spelled out to you gradually through the course of the game, to only listen to the exerpts from the journal is to only have a fleeting glimpse of the full story. Every character in this game has a detailed story arc and absentee characterization, but to get the full story, you have to take your time and really digest the clues you find. You have to consider the context of each one.
Fullbright has taken a relatively small game map and filled it with so much meaningful detail, the home itself can tell multiple, interlocking stories mostly without having to explain anything at all explicitly. It's as if someone took the small wordless stories found in many Bethesda RPGs and made an entire game out of them.
It is worth noting however that while this game lacks most mechanics we are used to, it is very much still a game. The mechanics are just harder to quantify. This game works different mental muscles than most games use. You might feel frustrated or fatigued or even bored with this game at first, but that is not because of any specific fault with the game itself. It just requires a mindset not typically used in games. Keep in mind that the game is primarily about investigation and reflection and that there are no waypoints or quest markers to do the thinking for you.

Just before you continue with my very wordy review, I have noticed that ALL of the negitive reviews of this game are being thumbed down just because they're negitive. Please keep that in mind when looking through any negivitive review for this game.
Five Nights at Freddy's 2 is the sequel to the massively successful game: Five Nights at Freddy's. From the trailer, it looked like it could be x3 scarier, x3 more challenging and have many more interesting mechanics than the first. There were many thoeries that suggested that the Freddy mask would only work on the old animatronics (which do make a return) and the new ones were trying to disable the old ones. All of this was very interesting and very exciting and the huge FNAF 1 fanbase (me included) was more than just a little hyped for this game. It was set to release early next year and I was very, very, VERY pumped. So here wer are. It's out about 2 - 3 months before it's release date. So the question is: Is it better than the first? Answer: Nope. Well, is it as good as the first? Answer: Not even close. So... is it a terrible game? Answer: Not quite.
So what went wrong? In a horror game, less is more. This is something that Scott seems to have completly forgotten about in this game. The first game had just 4 animatronics (5 if you include the easter egg Golden Freddy) 2 of them worked in much the same way (Bonnie and Chica) One of them needed constant attention or it would sprint at Sanic speeds down the hallway to destroy you (Foxy) and the final would sneak into your office if he was close enough and you were careless enough (Freddy).
Now, Five Nights at Freddy's 2: 6 of them are indenticle. Yes, you read that right: 6 OF THEM. So what about the others? Well there's Foxy who appears at the end of the hallway and jumps at you if you don't flash him with the light enough. There's Baloon Boy who attracts foxy and disables your flashlight if he gets into your office and there's and you can do F*CK ALL to stop him once he's there. Yup, he's just a massive game over screen that instead of reading game over reads: "Ha Ha! F*CK YOU!". Then there's mangle who works in much the same way as Baloon Boy except he goes away if you wear the Freddy mask. Thankfully.
Bonnie 1.0, Chica 1.0 and Freddy 1.0 all kill you by appearing in front of you and if you don't wap out that Freddy mask and smash it RIGHT into your facial region quick enough (as in 0.05 seconds quick) then they dissapear, only to reappear seconds later and murder you brutally. Freddy 2.0 just needs to be flashed at a bit with the light and he'll f*ck off. Bonnie 2.0 and Fan service Chi- Sorry, Chica 2.0 both appear in the right and left vents and will go away if you plonk on the Freddy mask for a bit. Except after night 2 ALL of the 2.0 models never really come out of the stage area. Then there's that f*cking puppet. That puppet single handedly managed to give birth to a slue of sh*tty fan theories, defeat the point of the camera system AND make multiple people rage quit. He is by far the most pretentious one as he needs to have the music box reset evey once in a while and if you don't do it then he insta - kills you. So while it does add a layer of tension to the game, it's also REALLY f*cking annoying at times. The death animations are also quite a bit worse than the previous game, as is the death sound effect altough I personally think the new game over screen is more disturbing than the first one. Oh yeah, and the atmosphere and sound design is not where near as good as the first game, with the exeption of the sound that plays when a nasty thing is nearby.
So is their even anything good about this game? Yes! There is! The puppet does indeed add a layer of tension and the old animatronic look creepy as hell. The overall graphical quality of the game is a little blander but otherwise just as good as the first game. Mangle also looks very creepy and the first time playing through the first night is horrifyingly scary to say the least, although that fear wears off VERY quickly. I do like the addition of the flashlight stopping the animatronics from moving even through the cameras and it does give you a decent reason to actually look for them, but the fact that you need to keep winding up the  music box and the fact that 94.98734689% of the time there's something down the corridor really doesn't give you enough time to look for them. Another very creepy thing is seeing the animatronics crawling through the vents. Bonnie 1.0's redesigned look really shines when it's in the vents, same with Chica 1.0. The addition of the mini games at death as also quite cool and very creepy.
So, is it worth the money? Not really. It's a couple of £'s more and it's got the same amount of content.
Verdict -
If your a massive fan of FNAF 1 (Like me): 7.50/10
If not: 5.85/10

Ok, before I write anything about the game itself, I have to say four words.  Go.  Play.  It.  Now.
Done that?  Great!  No?  Ok then, here we go.  "Gone Home" is a compelling work of fiction in and of its own right.  Narratives in games have only just begun to scratch the surface of acting as dramatic pieces of art.  For years we fought that battle, however, this is the first game I've played in twenty-five years of gaming that I feel has met that edge and surpassed it.
Granted, this is not gaming's "Citizen Kane", this is a modern Indie film set as a game, something akin to "Juno", "Cloud Atlas", or "Blue is the Warmest Color".  So far though, most of our games have been more "Rambo", "Star Wars", or "Apocalypse Now", and while none of those is by any means a bad thing, they're all largely set around action pieces, with story ranging from almost non-existent to only linking those fantastic action pieces to all about the nature of what those action experiences says about us.
"Gone Home" breaks this trend though, by not relying on action, but conflict in other ways.  This is not the first game to not deal with combat or competitions by any means as it's source of conflict.  Notably, simulation titles of all sorts have done it for years.  What this is though, is the first game to combine a non-conflict based game setting in a first person point of view, to tell the story of someone else.
Frankly, if your character does nothing, the story still happens.  The only difference is for you and the player character, Katie.  The story is actually about Katie's family, who she has not seen in over a year, specifically, her little sister, Sam.  If this had been a film or a book, it would have been largely from Sam's point of view, just as "Juno" was from Juno's point of view.  This being a game though allows for something more.  It allows for you to react to the story.  Katie is, in all honesty, a blank shell for you to project yourself on, save for two things.  One, periodically you will trigger "Letters" to be read by Sam to Katie.  These are largely what tell the story.  The other, at one point, you'll find another writing by Sam of a rather graphic nature, of which, depending on your speed of reading, can be illuminating, however, Katie, not wanting to know that about her sister, immediately puts it down and will not pick it up the rest of the game.
As such, how you feel is how Katie feels, you have just come home from a long trip, late at night, no one is there.  Now it's up to you to figure out where everyone is, learn how your family's life has changed, and worry and have hope for your currently missing family.  Your experience will be totally predicated upon you feel.
As far as story, that's all I can tell you.  On the flip side, the game play is sluggish at best, and finicky at worst on older machines.  I survived it because the story is so compelling.

This game perfectly captures the various aspects of World War I in a manner that is both realistic and fun.  The graphics, while not the best, are quite good for an indie game, and while the UI might not look impressive, it does its job well.  All the different classes and weapons are very well balanced against one another, and the maps offer as much variety in scenery and gameplay as is possible given its setting.  It's gameplay mechanics recreate the back and forth of trench warfare in a manner that doesn't feel forced, and gameplay offers a stark contrast in engagements, either sniping across no-man's-land, where machine guns and rifles dominate, or the savage close quarters trench combat in which pistols and grenades excel.  The only real problem the game suffers from is optimization issues, with lower framerates and higher ping that is to be expected.  However, the developers have done quite a bit to fix this issue, reducing its severity and scope to the point of a minor, occasional annoyance.  In my opinion, this is probably the best shooter obtainable for $20 on Steam, and is well worth its asking price.  I wholeheartedly recommend this game, but feel free to look at more recent gameplay videos to assess its character, and make sure to read the Official Steam Guide to ensure that you understand some of its less-explained mechanics.

Wow so many bad reviews there. I can understand why people would not like the game but still.
It is a good game, but it's also a niche genre: narrative.
If you like visual novels or games like that, which are strongly bound to the story and narrative you will like the game. If I were to compare this game to a VN or Anime genre that would be 'Slice of life'.
It's hard to talk about Gone/Home without spoiling.
So let's talk gameplay.
It's an FPS without the S. You explore in first person view. Since you are exploring you gotta be curious and look around a lot. Finding certain objects will give you a narrative talking about that object or related event associated to it. So your goeal is pretty much to touch every item here and there.
During my first 30 mins I was like "damn that's starting to pïss me off, hope it's not a lame joke like SURPRISE! HAPPY BIRTHDAY! We were all hidden in them johns! Woohoo!"
But no, the story is simple, but solid. Once I got up to the second floor I got intrigued and became more and more curious about that whole mystery. It's all a puzzle; try and find what happened.
At some point I was really starting to think a lot. I poped-up the map and... I saw something weird... So I investigated and found a secret passage lol. You were supposed to discover the passage from its other end actually :) /me proud
In the end I grabbed a key near the game completion that I didn't use: that's really an open game for you.
Graphics are quite good. But it's the amount of details that is impressive. You can grab pretty much everything that is lying around and examine those stuff. In 3D. Made me remind of Shenmue a little bit. Some piece of paper are useless but most will give you background story on... on the story. You can be interested or not, it's freebies.
The SFX are awesome. Even though there is no music at all (unless you insert some music tape in a tape player) each object has specific sounds. Closets, drawers, papers, pillows, etc. Crazy, really crazy. All of this is useless to the game of course. But this adds an atmosphere. And damn, that must have took a while to record and design all of those props. Incredible really.
At the end of the game you will discover an object that you will know is the final step. Using the object will end the game. Everything you have heard through the narration is actually heard there by the main character :)
Very nice. Well okay, that was a little spoil, but I think few people caught that little detail that closes the story and makes it whole.
All in all, a nice game with a peaceful pace. Explore, read and try to understand the characters depicted throught those drawing, letters and photos. I found myself having some feelings during the gameplay. But not as much as a good old Ever17 or Clannad of course :)
Note that once the game is over there is zero replayability; like a book if you will.
Recommended for a lower price though. The game is worth the high price for it's expensive details and overall mastery of story telling. But, as the game is quick and you could skip pretty much every details and all, and just focus on the story itself... well... in that case I'd say it's worth less.
Anyway that's 3 hours of gameplay, top. I looked at EVERYTHING in the game, every single props and took my time to read and stuff. Guess you could complete the game in 5 minutes (speed running lol) or an average of 1 hour being less attentive to details than me.

I know a lot of people don't care for this game or this story (and honestly, it's more or an interactive story than a game) but I actually enjoyed it. Granted, it is expensive for what it is (I'll admit that I got it on sale,) I'm not a female, nor am I gay, but despite that, I do know a few gay folk, some of which are family, and I do believe that the story depicted here speaks volumes. A lot of LGBTQ folk experience descriminitation, which may, in fact, come from their own family or "friends," and I feel that this story helps to highlight their struggle to accept who they are, and for their own friends/family to accept them in return. I know people who are are gay or transgendered, and have been shunned; either by friends, family, community, or a combination of those, and realize that it's difficult for them to try and juggle who they really are, and a version of themselves that they feel will be accepted. I think that everyone should play this game to learn of the struggle that many people face. There's no reason that these people should experience the hatred of a community, or, indeed, their own family, for feeling that they weren't born into the body they should have been, or because they love somebody that shares the same gender as them. To quote a very old phrase/chiche, "Can't we all just get along?" I feel that this game should be played by all demographics, to perhaps experience a bit of the descriminitation that many people are subjected to each and every day, and perhaps to learn that, no matter who we are, we all feel things the same way, and that love is no exception.
TL;DR: Don't be a narrow-minded, yeasty, fen-sucked canker blossom.  Have some respect for a fellow human being who, while they might feel or love differently than you, has just as much of a right of a right to it as you do. After all, this world has enough hate in it already, don't you think?

This game mostly falls flat on its lack of design focus and lack of polish. It starts with a cute and clever concept and the solid Source foundation and then trips over almost every amateur game design pitfall in the book.
There's 9 classes per team unique to each side for a total of 18 classes, but none of them are well-defined enough to provide any sense of depth; they're all about as complex and nuanced as a TF2 Pyro with default equipment and no air blast. The game would have been immensely served by folding the classes into about half as many with clearer combat roles. Despite this, learning what all the classes do is still daunting due to the complete lack of a tutorial and each class's description being muddled with mostly flavor text rather than a clear and immediate idea of how to play, as with TF2's bullet points.
There's a lot of other conveyance issues that make understanding what you're doing or where you're going pretty difficult, such as a lack of clear descriptions, popups, or tooltips about objectives. You might never know that you're trying to PREVENT explosives from going off if you're on the Nazi side, because the UI doesn't imply it. Even if you did, you might never know that you can defuse explosives rather than just run for cover - a "Hold 'E' to defuse" tooltip when looking at a bomb at close range would have been extremely welcome and easy to code in, but again: this game skimped on polish and clarity. Even the killcams could have been adjusted to improve clarity; as it is, they zoom too fast, too close, and too-poorly-framed for you to even see the opponent and where they are. If you don't know the map, 80% or more of the time you will have no idea where the opponent is, ruining the point of a killcam. I suspect that they just took Valve's implementation and didn't touch it, and it doesn't work because the model sizes and dimensions are more variable.
So, once you start getting the hang of it, what's past the learning curve? Well, not much, to be honest. As mentioned before, the classes are watered-down, spread too thin for any one of them to keep your interest for more than 5 minutes, at best. Almost all of the weapons are pretty much the same, with variations only in rate of fire, bullet spread, etc. And there's not a lot to distinguish different gun types the way that TF2's minigun requires slowing to a crawl or how a machine gun in Battlefield has the necessary magazine size to easily inflict the Supression effect at will. The most distinctive bullet weapon is the scoped rifle, and even that has only the intricacy of a Counter-Strike AWP, with none of the satisfying boom, versus significantly faster (and often smaller) targets.
The visual design is also "one and done". Good luck having any idea where your own grenades are landing if you throw them while moving around. Everything suffers from that familiar "realism clutter" you get when detailed textures intersect with a lack of solid art design, color scheming, or effective use of light and reflection. It's a look that gamers who played 15 years ago will remember all-too-well from the medium-high-budget games of that era. The aforementioned scoped rifle's zoom overlay is just a black mask taped over the screen; no sway, no blurring anywhere, no love, no soul. It worked, so it was time to move on to the next piece of content and never look back.
Finally, the netcode is pretty bad, and although that was quite familiar for Source games made around its time (2011), and although it's lag-corrected so everything is pretty fair, it's still unsatisfying to fire a low-rate gun and have your enemy drop dead well after you've pulled the trigger.
If this game had cut its ambitions in half and spent that extra time improving what was already there, this could have been a genuinely fun game. As it is, I only get two feelings when I'm playing: frustrated and confused when I don't understand something yet, or bored at its simplicity when I do. It's an example of kitchen-sink design that throws a bunch of characters and weapons at you and says, "here, I'm sure you can find something in here that's fun" rather than taking the time to make sure that only fun things are in it.

I was a bit skeptical about playing Verdun. I thought that possibly the servers were empty or that it would be filled with only people who are so good that it wouldn't be fun. I was wrong. Verdun is what I think to be an accurate representation of trench warfare; confusing, muddy, and filled with death.
The game feels good, although a bit clunky at times (trying to run from prone or being unable to run from a grenade in the middle of the reload animation). The graphics look very realistic, the textures of the clothes, mud, weapons etc all have a very gritty and real world trench warfare vibe to them. The little details in this game make it great, things like random gear and dead horses scattered all over the battlefield give you the sense that a front has been established and you are a part of the on-going war.
I'd have to say I'm slighty dissapointed in the some of the community. While many players work together (somewhat) and are respectful, there is a handful who call names and slander other players. This is upsetting because it is the very reason I never will play COD, I don't want to get on a game only to have chat filled the terrible and un-original insults of what appears to be an immature playground bully. That being said, that is a small percentage, most players are respectful.
As far as there being people too good to have fun, it does happen where a few folks are just excellent at killing from across the map, however because of the era, technology and layout of the battlefield you still have a chance.
Overall Verdun will take some time to get into, be patient with yourself and just accept that you WILL die. I say you shouldn't miss this one and we need good people in our community to go over the top for your country.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing

To summarise this game quickly, Verdun is a fun, intriguing and cool experience.
Now, one of the most iconic concepts in the game is the genre itself, it takes place during the Great War (First World War) from 1914 - 1918 during the battle of Verdun. This is very unique because VERDUN IS THE ONLY SHOOTER GAME THAT TAKES PLACE IN THE GREAT WAR! There are way too many World War II games that i've lost count and barely any at all for the First World War. The only WW1 games you will find is either this and some strategy games. It's such a forgotten about idea and I hope that this will start a new line of WW1 games.
Now there are some things that aren't so good about the game. The fact that this is a FULL RELEASE doesn't make it feel like one. There should be more maps spanning across the French/Belgium border however there are still enough maps for the state the game is in. Another thing is that the gameplay itself doesn't feel finished and that there should be more too it, the graphics are great but the GUI needs tweaking. Arial white, red and yellow text on the screen doesn't suit the way the game looks. Make the text look old fashioned.
I've played only Trench Warfare as that is what WW1 was all about so I don't really have much to say about Team Deathmatch but its probably just the usual shoot-each-other concept. Also add some animations for the player deaths. The way the dead body just goes to this floppy ragdoll as soon as he takes a bullet makes it look kinda unusual, maybe show the dying soldier with his hand covering his wound whilst slowing falling back and then dying, kinda like in GTA but were not comparing a game like that here!
You play as three different nations. The French, the English and the Germans. Remember that the game takes place during the battle of Verdun so the Italians, Greeks, Russians and Americans arent invoved here. The thing I don't like is how the make the nations look kinda silly. The English and French with the curled moustaches and monocles made me cringe a little bit. The teams are still realistic and great though.
The maps and the artillery are coolest parts. The developers took the trench warfare and mapping seriously. It seemed so immersive to be running across no-mans land holding a Kar98 bolt-action rifle with mortars blowing up all over the place, trenches and barbed wire all over the field. The developers executed the progressive action of the trench battles really well. Having to use the trenches to the advantage, dangerously running across no-mans land in massive teams while getting shot at, sniping and using machine guns from the trenches, planes and bombs flying across the sky and silently waiting for the right moment before charging to the other trenches was just so fun!
The combat consists of bolt-action rifles, machine guns, pistols and explosives. The combat is long range because you would be hiding in your trench, picking off the enemy one-by-one on the other side of the map unless they're running through no-mans land like an idiot. The gameplay is not as ridiculous as games like CoD or CSGO because teamwork is a must to claim the battlefield. People will the hiding in MG spots, other will be sniping with their rifles. Some will be firing mortars at the enemy and others will be spying on enemy activity with their binoculars or the recon plane will fly above. All while working together like a big happy family (except it's not happy) and waiting for the right moment before charging through no-mans land in a team to claim the enemy areas. It gets hectic when the enemy charges into your trench and all you can do is keep your gun out for any enemy that will pop around corner, unless you die and you have to retreat.
Overall, M2H and Blackmill Games have executed the concept extremely well and will potentially start a new line of WW1 games. The game is a realistic, intriguing and fun experience and is a must buy. Although the game should've stayed in Early Access for a longer time, the game is in a very playable and completed state.

If you've played the original Dark Souls 2 (with DLC) and are wondering what Scholar of the First Sin added, then the answer is... well... not a lot, honestly. A few enemies are rearranged and certain areas that didn't make sense before (i.e. Hiede's Tower of Flame) are now upgraded to be a bit more interesting. There's also an NPC added who tosses out a whole bunch of lore every now and again, along with a new boss fight and ending. But other than that, it's essentially the same game.
On one hand it's cool because I can safely say that all of Scholar of the First Sin's changes are for the better. The little tweaks to the enemies make the game flow a lot better and the added lore makes the game make much more sense than it did before while still retaining its mystery.
On the other hand, it's still pretty much the same game. The enemies are still placed roughly the same as they've always been and the new boss isn't even particularly difficult. And nothing's really stopping you from watching the new ending on Youtube.
So what I'd say is that if you've been contemplating another Dark Souls 2 playthrough, then this is worth buying. But if you weren't thinking of that already, then give it a pass.
And if you haven't played DS2 at all, then buy this immediately.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing

Pros:

- The gameplay is fast paced and challenging (at least if on the german side)
- The maps are widely varied and really offer very different combat situations
- A lot of attention is paid to historical accuracy, you can really see the effort and love the devs put into this
- Even with the balancing problems it is loads of fun to play
Cons:
- There is only one con for me at the moment, and that's the balancing of the game. It's pretty much non-existant at this point, with almost every map and definitely the weapons and other equipment being completely in favour of the entente. Even the maps favour Entente heavily. Basically playing Entente is like playing a game on easy mode, while playing for the German Empire is oftentimes a frustrating challenge. So if this is a big point for you, then this won't be much fun for you. Honestly I barely play this anymore due to this problem, it's pretty much game breaking for anyone not playing the entente faction.
Also the Devs seem to have to philosophy of "let's add new content but never fix anything about the game or its' balancing"
I'll update my review as things change, but this is it for now.

If you like games with poor combat systems, clunky mechanics, terrible systems (ie: currency system), no tutorials to help you through the fact that the game still thinks you're on an Xbox, and the worst implementation of coop multiplayer I've seen to date, then you will absolutely LOVE this game. It LOOKS like fun, and then you play it and realize you were robbed. Having played it, I now know I wouldn't have willingly paid $5 for this. Devs slapped it together half heartedly after the console release and had the audacity to charge full price for it all the same. I've heard defenders of the game say that it's "super hard" or that it's just "incredibly challenging and not for everyone". True, but not because it seems that it was intentionally designed that way. Instead, it's difficult and you will die repeatedly because it just simply isn't designed well. Your challenge will come from trying to work around poor game mechanics and the stupid situations the game will inevitably place you in.
All that being said, the idea of the game is really quite good and so are some of their systems. The multiplayer for example, where in order to add a friend you have to summon them via a spell of sorts on the ground that they see in their dimension and once activated, they join your physical world (as opposed to just being a ghost that you glimpse at times, like so many other players). It's actually quite a good and original idea, but in order to reach that ability, you must first grind for about 2 hours or more like it's an MMO. And even then, you're not necessarily guaranteed to find your friend's "invitation" as there are so many other players' invitations on the ground. Supposedly there is a ring you can buy (assuming you didn't lose all your soul currency getting gang♥♥♥♥♥♥♥by the AI) that makes joining a friend easier, but I couldn't stomach the game long enough to go grind for more currency to buy the damn ring.
So, good concepts, but poorly executed in my opinion. While I certainly recommend against buying this game, maybe keep an eye out for the third one? Hopefully they've put some more effort into making it playable. 3rd time's the charm, or so they say. Don't buy this one unless you hate yourself and your money.

There's very few gaming experiences that transcend the perceived notions of what makes a game and totally immerses the player into the narrative itself. Gone Home is one of them.
It's unfortunate a large majority of gamers can't comprehend the intent of Gone Home. They strive to min/max and rush through asking "where is the game?". Doing this is a disservice to Gone Home and the story it tells, and makes you part of, over the brief couple hour experience it provides. The chills, the surprises, the sadness, the nostalgia, the empathy, and the perversion of peering through relics and stories of other people's wants and desires. But it soon becomes your life. It becomes your sister, your mother, your father and your story because of the level of immersion and realism in the narrative.
While there is little choice in your actions and your goals, the roller-coaster the game sets you on is masterfully crafted and designed to string you along, piecing together clues and stories to help you ultimately figure out all the questions you are asking yourself as you play. While the progression is somewhat transparent, everything wraps up beautifully, and rather unexpectedly (for me anyway, as I was seeing a much different ending).
The game also expects you to have some memory of the 90's. Ideally, you will want to be born sometime in the 80's to get the full effect of the emotions and connections to increase the immersion. This is not necessary, but I think these connections are what fully drove this home for me. While I wasn't a female growing up in the 90's, the artifacts and objects peppered throughout the game all hit those nostalgic buttons for me and made me connect further with the story and characters.
Besides the faults, In the end, I felt heavy; choked up. After a couple of minutes of contemplation and wrapping my head around my experience, I breathed in deeply and snapped back to reality, my reality. I don't care if it's a "game" or not (a common complaint) but why can't more games do that?

If you have played and enjoyed wide open sand box style action games, then you will love this game. At first a couple of the controls were a bit weird, but after a couple hours it began to work well. It also has a story you can follow, with segways into random mayhem as you build up enough rep to progress. Its a free for all rampage to get the rep, pretty fun. Huge island game world too.
My only realy gripe is that when flying, it goes into a high up 3rd person view, which is very difficult to control a fast plane through ravines, under bridges, and trees to do some races. The trick I found was to always hold down the right mouse button and pull the camera down level with the plane... while flying those races, as it prevents camera-auto-snap to that bad angle. After I figured that out, I was able to complete 100% races. Actually I have 100% completion of the entire game and achieves. Yes. this game is that fun I actually wanted to do 100%!
So, grab this game on sale. You will love it if you like open world action flicks with driving, boating, flying, sky diving, and crazy action.

A solid 3/10 texture pack, 5/10 improvement in online play, but 2/10 purchase value, story improvement 2/10.
Where to start with SotFS....I swore I would never get it, but did as my curiosity overwhelmed my doubts and hate of "exclusive" titles...in short, my doubts were right.
Scholar of the First SIn is clearly an attempt to keep the PC/Xbox souls fanbase occupied until DS3 given that Bloodborne was "exclusive" to PS4...THis also probably nicely kept some more revenue flowing in from the series which you just have to look at how Darksouls 1 is still averaging 1000+ players online versus about 2000 for this game to realise how committed the player base are.
Is it worth it? Well it's debatable, for me though, no.
Should you buy? Well yes I guess if you want to play DS2 as the original has 25% of the player base. Ths is exactly as many were prophesysing, it split the fan base...Good job FromSoft....This has for the most part menat if you want online play you are forced in to SotFS version.
So the game itself....It's effectively dark souls 2, just with an enhanced texture pack, and some rearrangment of content so that there are some different enemy placements, with expanded and improved online play.
Firstly the textures...a disappointment, truly. To see this you need only go back and look at the original videos for what was promised for the graphics of Dark Souls 2 pre-release, but which werent delivered for hardware technical reasons, ie hardware wasnt sufficient to deliver a decent frame rate, well it's a year now since then the hardware has improved dramatically, given they wanted to charge an almost full game price for new buyers for SotFS version, probably could hope that perhaps delivery on that original promise would be made....But no. So as a texture pack does it seem richer compared to original DS2....no.
Regarding the enemies, not many make sense although it was described as being to make more sense....go figure that Heide knights are found everywhere except in Heides tower...because, makes sense reasons. New 'red phantom' enemies which are slightly tougher but not really anything to call "new enemies" are found around the zones now, but their density is high in the startingzones and just thins out toward the end...a reflection of the effort put in overall. Many of the zones are "harder" due to being more filled with enemies thanks to this, but this is false difficulty, much like tossing 50% more hp on a boss and saying, "look how much harder it is!". I have heard terms like "reinvigorating" thrown around to describe the effect this has....It's not. Instead it seems fatiguing. Zones become either a sprint through scenario, or a wait at the department of motor vechicles to slog through the queue of enemies.
Online play is improved a bit with the new version, more online slots exist so you can have more allies/enemies in your world simultaneously. Unfortunately this doesnt scale well with bosses where most co-op happens as often overpowered characters co-op bosses and with more overpowered people on a boss....the decrease in challenge generally seems greater than a linear decrease. Nicely though the netcode is a little bit improved too so it doesnt seem so sluggish, and FromSoft are on top of cheaters a bit more which is great. Unfortunately as said previously, the player base is split, so where most people play this, there is still a chunk who play the original. If you want online you are pretty much now forced to buy the SotFS version.
Story expansion is pretty thin, the Aldia character doesnt shed a great deal of light on anything, or anything that Vendrick didnt already make clear with his story and the four crowns plot.
Final verdict, I have to recommend it, begrudgingly because ti really isnt worth the asking price. Unfortunately so much of the spirit of darksouls revolves around the community and online play factors, so if you arent playing this version you are stuffed for it. As a total package I would give it 3/10, people who owned the full original game got all the story and some of the non-online improvements free, or paid a small price for something that wasnt worth it by buying the SotFS version. People buying the full game werent getting content worth the price asked given the game is over a year old.

"Over the wall, boys! Go go go!"
We ran as fast as we could through the hail of gunfire, muddied boots stomping on scorched ground. The landscape was filled with craters made from weeks of constant artilery fire. I heard the familiar rattling of machine-gun fire up ahead as xKITTYSMASHERx fell dead in front of me. I leapt over his body into the crater that he almost reached. Gripping my rifle, I peeked out of cover to see the familiar shape of a German helmet, grey and rounded. A constant stream of shots rang out through the air followed by an explosion that blasted inside of a crater not far from mine. My gaze was steady on the helmet, as I was fighting to not think about the ever growing number of fallen comrades. Taking aim, I pulled the trigger and felt the familiar kick of recoil, only to miss the shot. There was yelling in the trench up ahead.
Cursing, I ducked back into cover for a brief moment as bullets whizzed past my hole. Eventually, mustering up the courage to try again, I took one more peak. The helmet was still there. I cocked my rifle and took aim once more, being extra careful to line up the ironsights properly. I held my breath to still my pounding heart if only for a moment.
Time seemed to slow as as my rifle spat out a flash of rage. Just one of many. I hit my mark and saw blood spray out into a shadowy mist in the distance. But the helmet didn't move at all. More yelling. Another explosion off to the far right. As the blood spray settled, I came to to the realization that the spray wasn't blood.
The death whistle of artillery flying through the air grew louder as it descended on my position.
I was shooting a rock.
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
Verdun is a historical WW1 era FPS that offers a fresh perspective on the genre. This ain't Call of Duty. On loading screens, instead of some quote from Sun Tzu or something, you get a little piece of real history, which is pretty neat.
The game emphasizes squad-based teamwork by putting players in groups of 4, with each player having a unique role in the squad in terms of their armament. Squads have their strengths and weaknesses. Some are great at assaulting trenches, armed with grenades and bayonets. Others are fantastic defenders, providing machine-gun support. Some are equipped for reconnaisance and surgical strikes, with binoculars, mortar fire, and rifle scopes.
The main mode is the Frontlines mode, where teams alternate between attack and defense in hopes of capturing trenches/territory. There's also a free-for-all deathmatch mode.
This game is ruthless in terms of difficulty. Most everyone dies in one hit with a few exceptions, which really creates a sense of danger when running through no-man's-land as you desperately sprint through artillery fire in search of some hole to hide in for a moment. This game requires methodical and patient offense. If you run around taking potshots you'll just end up waiting to respawn for most of the game. If you don't work with your squad, it's hard to be effective.
Gameplay aside, the community has a brand of humor of it's own, making fart jokes when someone drops gas, and coming up with squadnames such as "Squadward" and "A Gentle Caress of The Inner Thigh".
This game falls under a solid B+/A- range due to it's innovative perspective on the FPS genre, as well as it's charming community. The developers care about the game as they release updates on a regular basis.
It's worth buying.

In this game you are Katie, a 20 year old girl who was on a tour trip. After one year traveling around europe, you finally come back to home, but you can't find your parents and your younger sis Sam. So the game is you walking in a mansion, interacting with documents, letters, and other stuff that will give you information about your parents, your sis, their relationship and how your younger sis feels about this new place. The focus here is your sister, who just find out she is in love with a friend. Now your sister is gone, and you don't know why.
Some people will tell that the game story is very clichè, and despite it is true, it is still very deep. The story happens in mid 90's, so if you was born before that, you will remember many old stuff you used to have. Prepare to drop some tears, since this game can be as good in evoking emotions as To The Moon.

"I have Gone Home and I have gone home but I am not home." -  Robert Yang from PC Gamer
I was slightly interested in Gone Home. It looked like some sort of creepy exploration game, that slowly builds the tension as you discover more and more. However my interest disappeared more or less when I learned it was hardly a two hour experience for the price of 20 dollars. I watched a video of the first few minutes of the game, it seemed to have that atmosphere I liked yet I still just lost complete interest. No way I was gonna buy that for 20 dollars for such a short amount of time. Of course, I, like everyone else saw the sharp difference between critics and players. Which more often than not, I agree with the players. I know how current video game critics are, and I have disagreed with most of them and their rave reviews of the latest innovative indie game or the latest flashy AAA game. Regardless, I went in with an open mind, I could easily enjoy the game. I didn't expect much, I suppose that gives the game a better chance to impress me.
The story was lacking, it didn't surpass my already nonexistant expectations of the game. The story just happens as you collect the various items, you slowly find out about how your sister was shunned by everyone at school and eventually found love with another girl. That's really it. Sure, you get some more detail about how her family denies her love for another woman, and some nice tidbits about the activities they do together and the ideas of their future, yet it all fell flat. It happened, and I felt no substance. Nothing truly interesting, nothing that made me enjoy each journal entry. It felt bare, maybe even forced; each journal entry is quick and useless. I'm not one for love stories, yet I have enjoyed love stories in various non-romance genres; this is just a story of your young sister falling in love with another girl and then running off with her. I saw the twist coming, which shouldn't impact the quality of the story but yet the story had nothing going for it anyway. The characters aren't bad, the setting isn't bad, their struggles aren't bad, it just wasn't interesting; it had not a single thing going for it. It just happened, and then it was over. Story is certainly the primary focus of the game, the experience finishes before it even starts; Full Bright's narrative will leave a lackluster taste in your mouth, it's clear that the story wants to be meaningful yet never works for it.
The game's atmosphere is one of the few things I think game does fairly well with. It's a nice flashback to the mid-90s. From Street Fighter to Pulp fiction, every little reference fits perfectly. It was nice seeing the details over the CD/LP player. Even the cover art of the textbooks scream 90s. They nailed making the house feel like it belongs in the 90s. The house itself feels creepy, not a soul in the home that seems both alive with knit-knacks everywhere while dead with some barren rooms filled only with boxes. The few places that feel they have life to them are both refreshing and creepy. The darkness certainly adds another edge to the creepiness yet all this creepiness and potiental terror soon washes away when you realize the game only cares about the light exploration; adding no depth to the atmosphere. While the game has an eye for detail of the era, it lacks detail in everything else. The house is lifeless in the wrong way possible, there were no extra details provided to the experience. Add some occasional random ambient noise, some creepy squeeking of the boards, a more complex engine that gives some realism to the world instead of everything you grab feeling like the lifeless assets that they are, etc. Hell, in the game you find your sister's book that goes on about her hunting ghosts, that could of been a really nice trigger to have some more creepy things happen in the house. Perhaps some creepy noises as said before, or an object making a strange shadow in a room. Yet all that potiental isn't used at all. The game's details begins and ends at the recontruction of a 90s home. The house provides no other purpose other than a lifeless realm to find some details about the family, with the sound of the thunder storm outside looping again and again. For such a short game that the developers pride in an immerisve experience, I expected the home to be leagues more complex.
Graphics weren't anything impressive. In fact, the most impressive thing visually is the background of the main menu; I would of vastly prefered the game used that style instead of this vaguely realisitic style. The characters in the photos look strange and unintentionally hilarious with the aesthetic. These photos even clash with the celebrity photos that were obviously ripped from real pictures instead of applying the style used with the family photos. The textures letters, books, and anything else with text are impressive; it's nice that you can read the words even without selecting the pictures when most games would have them be a pixel mess until you select them.
Sound design is minimal and lacking. I didn't expect some amazing audio but I expected something leagues more immersive. Again, the atmosphere could of been built up much better with the right use of sound design. Even some footsteps would have been nice.
Voice acting is nice. I wouldn't say it was anything amazing, it was simple and nice. I got no feeling that the actresses were trying too hard, they fit their roles nicely.
Level design isn't terrible nor is it good, it's always interesting to discover little short cuts or areas you didn't notice before. Gone's Home length ultimately hurts the level design for its only meant to be gone through once. The game is straightforward, if you go from room to room properly, there is no need to visit a room twice. You can just finish the game within 30 seconds if you remember a specific hidden room. The level design offers a possible "oh wow" moment that only works once. There is no lasting appeal for the level design because of the limited style of its content.  The house is small for length and content standards, ruining all lasting appeal.
The gameplay has you explore the house and read messages and sometimes listening to them. That's it. Point and click games have mastered with variety in the gameplay way before Gone Home was in development yet Gone Home didn't even try this. Exploration is limited and utlimately wasted in such level design.
Ultimately Gone Home feels like a prototype of a game, meant to wow potiental investors with a basic guideline of the game compressed into a lengthy demo. While in reality, Gone Home is a complete game sold for 20 dollars filled with potiental yet is outdone by any other point and click game that has come decade before it. Full bright prides Gone Home as a immersive, engaging tale told by the exploration in a seemingly dead home while in reality it is a game with a empty storyline that wants to engage you but never does, a house designed to immerse you yet gives up five minutes in, and gameplay that doesn't attempt anything new after the first room.
This game feels like critic bait, critics went crazy over it apparantly because it offers a meaningful story. It instead feels like they are going crazy over it because it's a minimal game in a industry filled with complex games, a minimal game that concerns a plot about two girls falling in love. The story has no substance but the fact it concerns a story about characters that are not in the forefront in games, it gets rave reviews. Or even more simply, reviewers being paid off or pushing an agenda, as video game journalism has frequently been subject to. Love stories have been done better in games that don't concern love stories, hell I find KotOR II did a better lovestory with Handmaiden and that's completely optional.
Don't believe people that say Gone Home isn't a game, it certainly is a game, it's a bad game.

Any fans of the first game are surely in for a treat with Five Nights at Freddy's 2. Bumping the animatronic count from 4-11 (12 if you count the puppet) turns up the game's stress levels to 11, one minute you may be tasked with fighting back an eager Foxy whilst trying to trick bonnie or chika into leaving your office. Anyone would believe that the game would be rushed, seeing as a mere 3 months after the original the sequel is released, but story sequences in the style of Atari 2600 games show that some love and effort has gone into the final product.

First, the caveat: This game is not, by any stretch of the imagination, worth $20. That said, I got this as part of a Humble Bundle (Still going on as of 9/20/14) as an afterthought, and as it turns out I enjoyed it immensely.
The story was engaging, if somewhat cliched and melodramatic. The atmosphere was fantastic. More than once I felt rising anxiety as the sound effects, lighting, and locations implied the potential for horror. The lesser narratives that play out in the background are fairly nuanced and interesting, and you feel like you're learning about the family's dynamics.

Dark Souls II is an epic fantasy rpg set in an undead medieval world. To clarify, Scholar of the First Sin is the remastered version of the original game. It comes with all the DLC bundled, as well as having some minor changes to the game itself. This review will first cover the game itself, and then the enhancements added by Scholar of the First Sin.
As a disclaimer I am a huge Dark Souls fan; I had already played Dark Souls I & II on Xbox 360 before playing this.
This is a fantastic game. It is easily one of my favorite games of all time. Artistically, it differs slightly from the first Dark Souls; the first game is more gritty and realistic, this one is more fantastical and surreal. But both games are a masterpiece in their own right. The core gameplay elements are pretty much the same as the first Dark Souls, so returning players will feel at home.
+Epic plot that subtly builds as the game progresses. While this game is not very "story based" in the most traditional sense (cutscenes, dialogue, etc.) it has an overwhelming amount of story and lore hidden away in the game. People who liked Lord of the Rings for all the excess lore that the series had hidden away will love Dark Souls.
+Excellent characters. This game is mostly a lonely game where the main character travels and fights without speaking to anyone. But whenever you meet an npc they are almost always an interesting character. Like in Dark Souls I, the player will slowly understand more of the story as they reach new places and meet npcs.
+Artistically beautiful game. This game takes advantage of atmosphere to make important moments in the story leave a greater impression on the player. The setting always feels new and unique in different areas. The most important plot moments are always highlighted by a setting desgined to create a specific look and feel. This game tells a story with few words, and that is its most impressive quality.
+Addictive gameplay. I found Dark Souls II to be even more addicting than Dark Souls I. And I was pretty addicted to Dark Souls I. The gameplay follows a simple system where the player can either block with a shield or dodge by rolling. Doing either of these actions or pressing the attack button consumes stamina. This simple system makes for unexpectedly deep battles. Positioning the character in relation to the enemy is crucial, because the player has to plan where the best spot is to deal with different attacks.
+Loads of hidden weapons and armor, with reinforcements and elemental infusions available.
+The silly ragdoll physics in the first Dark Souls where dead bodies stick to you and can be kicked around like a soccer ball have been removed.
+Even more extensive multiplayer than the first game. Lots of covenants available. Summoning and invasions galore. You can also play the game cooperatively or alone, like in the first game.
+Extreme amount of replayability. I have never played any game series with as high replayability as Dark Souls (both I & II). There are secret areas to explore. There are loads of hidden weapons/armor sets. There are hidden, optional bosses. There is an extensive array of background lore and plot detail. Most importantly, there is New Game plus, ++, +++, and so on. The game will keep growing more difficult with each replay all the way through the seventh replay, and the player keeps all their equipment and leveling each time. But that isn't even the beginning of the replay value. One of the most impressive things about this series is that each weapon type has a whole different strategy. You can go longsword, greatsword, ultra greatsword, katana, spear, rapier, halberd, scimitar, curved greatsword, hammer, great hammer and lots of other things. You can also learn any of the four supernatural skills: pyromancy, miracles, magic and dark. Depending on what you choose, you may have to level the character differently, and your strategy/play style will have to change. This game has the power to take over your life. Be warned.
+Brutally difficult, yet manages to be fun despite this.
+If an enemy drops an item when they die, it shows up right away. In Dark Souls I, it wouldn't show up until their death animation had fully ended, so for every single enemy you had to wait and watch them die to see if you would get an item or not.
+One of the trademarks of the Dark Souls series is that the multiplayer elements are fully integrated into the story. In most games, if you want to do multiplayer of any kind, you select an option for it in the game menu. In Dark Souls, the single player and multiplayer are integrated into a single experience. Multiplayer elements are activated by finding in-game items that have to be used in special ways to invade "other worlds" or perform summons. When I played Dark Souls I for the first time, the game's whole multiplayer element was a mystery that I had to discover the workings of while playing.
+You have some options to reallocate your characters' levels if you screw them up, unlike in Dark Souls I.
+The DLC is fantastic. If you liked the main game it's definitely worth purchasing.
This game is a masterpiece. There are no cons.
As far as the upgrade goes, I personally was very pleased with it. The biggest benefit is the graphics, but there were also some gameplay changes.
Pros:
+Graphics upgrade. I am coming from the Xbox 360 version of the game, and I was absolutely blown away by the upgraded graphics. So beautiful... *sheds tear*
+Bundled DLC. The DLC in this game is fantastic. It is gorgeous to look at and as epic as the main story. No Dark Souls II fan should go without playing this DLC, even if they don't play the remastered version.
+Gameplay updates. So I am listing this as a pro, but it will really be up to the player to decide if they appreciate the changes. Originally, I didn't like that they changed the original game, because in my opinion the game was already perfect. But after playing it I can say I was pleased with almost every change they made. Here's some of the biggest changes:
***The Ring of Life Protection can no longer be abused by repairing them at the blacksmith upon every death. Not only are less of them available, but repairing them costs some exhorbitant price. Repairing them upon every death is no longer practical. I think this is a great change. I don't think abusing the ring is in the spirit of the game.
***Lots of enemy spawns have been adjusted. Some of the adjustments are artistic (e.g. having the Heide Knights actually appear around Heide's Tower of Flame, rather than scattered across the world) and some of them are for gameplay. Also, there were a couple parts in the original game where suddenly the non-boss enemies got extremely difficult. For me one example of this was the enemies you fight leading up to the giant old dragon that gives you the ashen mist heart. Another example would be an area before the third bonfire in the Shrine of Amana where there were just way too many enemies. These parts have actually been made easier.
***The keys to the DLC areas have to be found rather than just magically appearing in your inventory.
***In No-Man's Wharf, you can actually kick a bridge over in the area right before boarding the ghost ship, so that you get a shortcut to the bonfire. Maybe I missed it before, but I didn't see this in the original Dark Souls II. I was thrilled to see this, because without that shortcut available the pressure to kill the boss on attempt one is pretty high.
Cons:
-You cannot use your save data from the original Dark Souls II.
In the end, if you have never played Dark Souls II, I
recommend purchasing Scholar of the First Sin over the original edition, especially if you liked Dark Souls or Demon's Souls. If you already played the original Dark Souls II, then it depends on how much you like the original game.
