Holy crap. How does a company that makes the masterpiece that is Dark Souls make this garbage?
Remember all the things that made DS1 actually enjoyable to play? Gone. Intutive level design that lets the player feel like they are actually making forward progress? Gone. Enemy AI that was challenging yet fair? Gone.
Remember the Estus Flask? Your best friend in the world of DS1? Remember how the game MADE IT A POINT that you get the flask within the first dungeon? Yeah, good luck finding it on your own without a guide.
And do not even get me started on the whole losing a chunk of your max HP when you die. IDGAF if it was in Demon Souls. IDGAF how it ties into the lore. It was a crap mechanic then and it's a crap mechanic now. Actively punishing the player for failing whereas in DS1 the biggest fret about dying is losing your souls and having the refight some enemies with far superior AI than in DS2. And don't get me wrong, death still stung like a ♥♥♥♥♥, but it never put you worse off than you were before you died.
And seriously, removing the ability to level up at bonfires? We seriously can only level up at the Emerald whosafudger? Yeah, take away that feeling of bliss and respite bonfires gave us in DS1 and MAKE US TRAVEL ALL THE WAY BACK TO MAJULA OR WHATEVER AND LEVEL THERE? I don't care if you can warp between bonfires at the beginning of DS2 it's still unnecessary tedium.
And battling, oh man battling. DS1 felt tight and responsive. DS2 just feels sluggy. Like there's a huge delay between pressing the button and actually swinging your weapon. And the lock-on system SOMEHOW GOT WORSE FROM DS1 TO DS2. HOW DOES THAT EVEN HAPPEN??
DS1 was a masterpiece in progression and how it introduced the player to the world. Undead Asylum IMHO is up there with Super Mario Bros. world 1-1 in how it introduces the player to the mechanics of the game. But DS2?? "OH HEY HERE'S YOUR INTRODUCTORY LEVEL IT'S JUST KINDA TREE ROOTS WITH NO REAL CONNECTION TO HOW YOU'RE ACTUALLY GONNA BE PLAYING THE GAME."
And I cannot believe I am saying this, but I seriously miss the simplicity of the UI in DS1. It was a mess, yeah, but it was freaking readable and understandable and INTUITIVE.
That's really what it comes down to. DS1 felt intuitive. DS2 does not. DS1 felt like it was rewarding to play. DS2 just feels frustrating. Everything that DS1 was DS2 isn't. And that's not a good thing.

Alright first of all from what I played thus far, it is the most terrifying game I've ever played in my life. This WON'T LET YOU BE CALM OR COLLECTED. It is difficult that's for sure, and this game constantly gets you stressed, worried, and always fumbling about the cameras, flashlight, and music box, so many times I literally minimize the game by accident sometimes when an animatronic is at my office, like Old Bonnie and made me flip out so much. That's what clinches this game over the first, in the first, after awhile you'll get a strategy down and after awhile you'll find it less scary. In my opinion, this game doesn't have that luxury. Due to all the animatronics after you, there are so many things on your mind you'll never be calm and be constantly worried by the presence of the animatronics.
The gameplay of this game is very similar to the first, so of course it's easy for old players to jump back into, but of course the most obvious changes come that there are at least 10 animatronics after you by the end, which includes:
-The New Animatronics
-The Old Animatronics
-Balloon Boy
-The Puppet (or Marionette)
That enough is already a handful to deal with, but also you're responsible for rewinding the music box, in which everytime I do so I literally flippin out since I know someone's in the hallway or something's in the vent, and it's stressful   as crap since you'll have to do it fast (but it's so god dang slow). And also, no doors. Yep, that enough got me terrified. I find myself most of the time wondering when to put it on whenever I saw something in the hallway as I worry when they'll get into the office. All of this alone, to add with the same mechanics as the first, feels like a different game, although it shouldn't. You're just too worried about everything after you, that you just think of it as a new experience.
I really only have one minor complaint, and that is with a no "Options" tab, mainly to level audio or to maybe configure a different key for the flashlight. I found "Control" as the flashlight button a bit annoying only because for some keyboards using Windows computers, it is right next to the Windows Start Menu button, so you may accidentally exit the game, or if you are recording this like I am, it'll end the video. It's a minor annoyance, but the game has me regretting me ever playing because it's so scary.
Now I won't say that everyone will find it as scary as me, but I think most will agree it has the horror right on. I do highly recommend it for any fan of the original, newcomers, or really just the general horror fan. Just be warned of heart attacks while playing, Fazbear Enterainment is not responsible for death or dismemberment.

I just looked at my gameplay hours ad thought it would be time for a review xD. It's one of the best FPS out the in the moment in my opinion, you can choose to pay to get items (like weapons, armor and skins etc.) but you can get all this with ingame currency (only takes a little longer).
CLASSES:
You begin with a few weapons for each class (yes they have a class system in this fps :P) (you have an engineer which uses a smg and can restore armor for teammates he can also plant an claymore, then you have the medic which ofcourse can revive and heal teammates he uses the shotgun, then you have the rifleman which uses a rifle/mg he can resupply ammo for his teammates, last but not least you have the sniper which ofcourse uses the sniper he has no extra teamfunction) btw you don't level the classes separately and you can switch classes ingame.
WEAPONS:
Some of the weapons ingame you have to unlock with experience just like your armor (head, gloves, footwear and bodyarmor) and attachements (these you get all for free, you have to keep repairing them tho). Some stuff you can buy directly for 1 day, 7 day's or permanent, and then you also have the box system (buy a box and get a weapon and other stuff usefull and just plain rubbish). You can which i like alot, customize your weapons ingame like change the scope grip etc..
MODES:
You have different game modes in this game you have Versus like: the team death match, free for all, search and destroy, capture the flag (to name a few). You also have co-ops and special operations these 2 let you play as a team (max 5) vs bots with different difficulties, which require you to work as a team where you need every class in your team depending on the difficulty. The co-ops change every day from difficulty and maps (you get to play 6 different co-ops every day) there are 30 (give or take) different co-op missions some take you on a boat, some on a cable railway etc. (a wide area of environments). The special operations are somewhat the same only the missions take longer and are much more difficult (a sinlge co-op missions takes 5-20mins where a special operation takes about 30-60mins). Most of the special operations work with hordes/waves of bots which get harder every wave with different enemies they also have objectives just like the co-ops (defend a tank etc.).
Small summary:
There are almost no hackers at least not above level 12 (you change to the profesional server after that level so i don't know before that level), level 12 only takes about a few days with a few hours every day. The community really depends on the clan you're in. You can slide in this game!! :P. The game has frequent updates with events which gives nice bonuses (weapons, boosters etc. etc.), the game also got a few graphic updates lately. The versus maps a little small compared to other shooters except for the bag and tag game mode which is huge O.o.
-Almost no lags
-no russians (they got their own server ^^)
-you can go crazy with a Katana in some maps :P
-alot of different weapons (like 30 for each class so do the math :P
-just pick up that AK and shoot no crazy chopper kill streak or whatever (god i hate those)
-only thing i hate is the repair cost with high quality armor weapons etc.
It's an immersive experience which I absolutely recommend, but don't spend more than 5 bucks for this 1 hour-long game.

Really interesting game, actively developed, with a new free expansion coming soon. Recommended.

I'm surprised by the near unanimous praise this game has received from the game critics. There is, essentially, nothing to really like about this game. At its core,
a simplistic means of giving a story, one that is pieced together through wandering around a spooky house and retreiving keys to open locked doors, revealing letter fragments, postcards, and magazines which inform the player on the story at hand. Specific items will cue voice-over readings from "Sam's Journal" (Sam, being the player character's younger sister) which are the essential bits of plot. So, it's an explortion, plot-driven game dealing with societal issues. Sounds like a winner, right?
In theory, I suppose so.
The game starts off well enough, with an eerie introduction to the "psycho house" and the first 15 minutes or so are pure exploration. We see the reamains of the father's book writings and the mother's job as a park ranger. It's interesting to slowly learn about this family's life... until you go upstairs. (a light spoiler or two may follow, so be warned. Nothing serious, just conceptual stuff). The plot begins its course, revolving around Sam, and her love life. What began with such a promising opening becomes a series of "pseudo-exploration" journeys (you're really just looking for the next page to move the damn plot along), while Sam delivers an incredibly sappy and cliche love story through her diary pages. And my, how saccharine it is. Just because you change the gender roles of those involved does not automatically make a stroy like this "innovative and unique." Sure, it's a change in perspective, but it follows the same beats, the same events that drive nearly every other teen romance ever. All the creepy atmosphere and dark undertones are completely wasted by the end. It really is unfortunate.
A few other minor gripes plague my view of
. There is no player marker on the map (which, admittedly, isn't used
often), which had me lost a few times. Thankfully, the house isn't too complex so the confusion wasn't a huge deal. Another downside is the game's runtime. It can easly be beaten in under an hour, and the maximum amount of time one can spend in this game cannot be more than 2 hours (assuming they just play through the story once). There's little reason to return, and no interesting plot threads to keep you thinking. Such a short runtime has had me wonder whether this would have worked better as a short film, or a music video or SOMETHING other than a game. Although, in that case, it would probably be worse than it already is, because the story would be given directly, as opposed to the more "vignette-esque" presentation in the game. In any event, the game is too short to be a game. If it had to be this short, and the story could not have been told in any other format, I would argue the game should not have been made at all. I don't want to spend money on a game that will only keep me entertained for one hour, and it's even worse considering this is not a particularily good one to begin with.
In short,
is a lackluster title that showed brief glimmers of promise. It was rather disappointing to essntially watch a game crumble before my eyes.

This game is hands down the most mind-blowing I’ve ever played. Calling it like GTA would cheapen the experience, since it takes the open-world concept to the next level, so much so that GTA feels 2 dimensional and slow in comparison. There are ZERO boundaries, you can fly, drive, shoot, bomb, and grapple to your hearts content across a staggering variety of landscapes, building styles, and even on moving vehicles. The latter situation in my opinion is critically under-utilized as a mission type, since it involves some of the most gloriously satisfying gameplay moments. For instance, using the splendidly variable double-grapple, you can tether a pursuing car to the side of a bridge, resulting in the pesky pursuer tumbling end over end right into the water, out of sight and out of mind. Or, for a more conflagrant approach, one can grapple onto a henchman’s car, plant a bomb on the front, then jump away while detonating the explosive, taking out a whole group of them! Although a good portion of the missions are of the “run, shoot, defend” type, one can quickly find one of the myriad of badass, death-dealing vehicles or special weapons to spice it up.
It truly is the open-world element that shines on this game, so much that it feels as if the storyline is an add-on. You can play for hours upon hours upon hours and never feel a single tickle of boredom. There’s always a new sight to see, a new vehicle or weapon to upgrade so that you can take it for a spin, and a new method to creatively grapple your way into badassery, so download this and start playing!

Firstly, this is more of an interactive story than a point-and-click adventure. Also, despite its looks, it's not a horror game either. Neither of these are bad things in my book. The game is more centred around discoverng a narrative of the player's sister, and other miscellaneous information about the family.
There is a large focus on looking through anything you can open, and reading anything you possibly can. Some of these will have a voice-over to go with it, which can seem out-of-place to begin with, but will make more sense in time.
Areas are also blocked off to begin with, and can only be accessed through backtracking and discovering keys to unlock doors. While this can be frustrating at times, it's an understandably necessary game device to use in order to guide the narrative in the proper order.
I completed this game in a little under two hours over the space of two days, and I found myself drawn to this small, enclosed story world when away from the game. For it to stick with me even outside my play time speaks for some well-crafted story-telling. The additional information and minor storylines for the other family members makes the game setting more believable - the house is populated by real people, with real personalities, instead of place-holders. Everyone has their own life stories, and as one of the daughters in this family, you gain a candid look into that of each family member.
In terms of value for money, I picked this up for ~$3 during a Steam sale, and I am quite pleased with what I received for that amount. While I would say it's worth maybe $10 for the engaging story, the length and format the game takes doesn't lend itself to a $20 price tag.
While this game may not appeal to everyone, I believe it is worth picking up during a sale if you enjoy a more story-driven exploration game.

I love this game. The PvE and PvP are very fun, and of course, INCREDIBLY challenging. This Dark Souls is a lot more keyboard + mouse friendly, unlike the first Dark Souls which if you tried playing with Kb/m, you would surely rather kill yourself.
The graphics are VERY beautiful, and all the enemies, NPCs and bosses are very unique and strange. And can also be, pretty freaking creepy! Now, guides are strongly recommended if you've never played this game, or any Souls game, for that matter, because let's face it. Without one, you'll wander aimlessly, be severely undergeared/underpowered, and you'll probably just wander into the toughest enemy right off the bat and first thing you'll experience is a very, very swift death.
Not to say that happens anyways... dying is INCREDIBLY common in this game. You WILL die. A lot. Like.. A LOT, A LOT. Unless you can mangage to make your character incredibly overpowered!
The customization and builds for each class in this game are really great. I think it's one of my favourite things about this game, because there are literally HUNDREDS of different ways to build your character, whether they're suited for PvE, PvP, or both! It's a very unique system in my opinion. In most RPGs with classes, you never would expect to be able to play any kind of caster/mage class and be able to use sword/shield, 2 handed weapons and or big heavy armor, but in this game, you can build  your characters however you please. You can make a Sorcerer that uses incredibly heavy armor, a giant tower shield and a staff to cast very strong offensive spells and still have some defenses so you don't die right away, as Sorcerers are VERY squishy. Or, you can build one that just wears light armor, have a strong shortsword and a Pyromancy so you can roll around and dodge quickly, and get close enough to your enemy to incinerate them in flames and hit 'em a few times with your sword before rolling away. Anything is possible!
Now, the thing about the Souls series of games that EVERYBODY knows them by, is the difficulty. From Demon's Souls (Or even King's Field if you wanna go way back..) to the up-and-coming Dark Souls III, these games are hard as ♥♥♥♥, and you WILL die over and over and over again, and you WILL lose all your hard-earned souls forever, over and over again, and you WILL get stuck at certain enemies or bosses and will spend hours upon hours trying to get past them. This game has NO mercy, and all I can say is: Prepare to die. Get ready to smash your controller or mouse/keyboard, punch a hole in your monitor and go buy a gun to contemplate shooting yourself with, because this game will♥♥♥♥♥♥ YOU. OFF. I would recommend having a pillow nearby to grab and scream bloody freaking murder into whenever you get angry. It helps a whole lot.
But yeah. that's my review. It's an incredibly fun and rewarding game, and I recommend this one, past installments, future installments, and even Bloodborne.

Gone Home is a first-person walking simulator from the same team that brought you the Minerva's Den DLC for Bioshock 2. You play as a girl who just got back from Europe. She enters her parents house at the dead of night only to find it completely abandoned. The only clue of your family's whereabouts is a note on the door from your sister asking you not to look for her.
First off, let's get the positives out of the way. The house looks pretty good. There's tons of clues, little notes to read, objects to interact with etc.It looks very believable, almost as if people actually live there unlike most video game mansions you find. I almost felt nostalgic while exploring it. It reminded me of the times when you were kid home alone at night and you were so scared of your own house, then you turn on the lights and wonder why you were even afraid to begin with. It's very silly to think about, but that's what I thought about the first few minutes of the game. There's plenty to just mess around like inserting casette tapes in a radio. So much to discover in your first playthrough. In fact, this sole element was what made me really get into the game for a while. There's a lot to discover about the family which sadly takes the backseat from the main plot. It's almost a flaw seeing better plot points being almost completely dismissed in favor for an average love story that really has nothing interesting about it.
Unfortunately, those are the only aspects I can give this game credit for. Gone Home has very little gameplay to it. You need find three specific codes which is pretty much the only thing you need to make progress. Alternatively, you can skip it and beat the game in 47 seconds.  I even find it hard to classify this as a point and click as even though it somewhat resembles the genre, it doesn't involve the brainteasers and puzzles its known for. There's no depth to be found here. If you know what you're doing and with the right settings, you can easily beat the game in seconds. It's not that I have anything against the so-called "walking simulator" type of games as I love The Vanishing of Ethan Carter, but even then Gone Home just feels empty and shallow. I understand that the game wants to tell a story. Fair enough, but if there's nothing interesting going on and I discover everything that needs to be discovered on my first playthrough then what's the point? The note on the door you find within seconds of starting up the game has all the answers you really need. A normal playthrough will only take you one hour. It's almost insultingly short compared to any other visual novel or walking simulator I've ever played.
So if there's no real gameplay, Gone Home needs to fall back on its story. That aspect is obviously the focus so I'll cut it some slack and say that if the story was good, this game would have gotten a pass. The way it depicts said story is awful though. Once again, I have to remind you that it's a mystery game with no mystery. You find out through voice recordings which is basically an excuse to have the game take place in 90's so the whole thing can be narrated that your sister is in love with another woman. First off, this begs the question, why couldn't this narrative be told through environmental storytelling? That's what the game seems to be designed for and the development team even succeeded in certain area's with their previous project on Bioshock. It would certainly make me think more highly of this game, but that's not how it's done and as a result, it feels more like an audiobook than anything else. The story itself isn't anything to write home about either. Some argue how earthshattering it is to feature a lovestory between two women and how it breaks norms, barriers or something. While it's true that this is mostly uncharted territories for video games (not that lesbians are never depicted in video games), there are millions of books and made for TV movies structured exactly the same way. Replace a few names here and there and you've got Gone Home Part Deux. There's nothing new here at all. Not to mention that the characters are so bland that they might as well have been anything else. They could have been a straight couple in a different decade and the story honestly wouldn't have made a difference. At first, I thought the timeperiod was going to be used to show how homosexuals were treated back then, but it does not take that direction. The prejudice from the parents isn't serious enough  to make me feel anything about these characters which creates a second problem. Their romance is so perfect and happy that you have to wonder what the conflict was supposed to be or why they even bothered telling this story, because as it is, it did nothing for me and considering how it doesn't tackle a lot of problems LGBT-people deal with on a daily basis like prejudice or maybe show us flashes from how much worse it was back then from a historical point of view, it probably won't do a lot for them either.
If the developers didn't think that Gone Home was worth the 20 dollars asking price and it was free to play, then I would just deem the game a failure and move on, but this is not the case. They certainly must have thought highly about this game when I can find books or even films for less than half the price with the exact same story. Did I mention it took me one hour to beat this game? That's why I advise you not to buy it. Please understand this. I'm not complaining that it is not a "real video game". Some of my favorite games are essentially visual novels though admitedly still more of a reliance on knowledge and skill. I'm also not saying that it is bad to have women and/or LGBT-characters as your main characters in games nor am I saying that it has to feature combat or something, but this is not the way to do it. Writers take note: when you write a character who is homosexual, don't make that their only personality trait as if that even counts for a personality trait. Most people are you know, people with a developed character. There are much better story driven games on many platforms including Steam.

I entered Gone Home with very few preconceptions. I knew nothing about it apart from what I could see from the first few screenshots and tags on the store page. As such, I assumed that it would be a simple exploration game with a few basic puzzles thrown in, expecting the experience to be on the slightly boring, possibly drawn-out side. While I wasn't entirely incorrect, to leave it at that would be a huge disservice to the narrative, which is the singularly most compelling part of this title.
Gone Home puts you in the role of Katie, who has returned home after a trip to Europe. Upon arriving, she finds no trace of the rest of her family. Most notably, her sister, Sam, has written a note requesting that she not be searched for. This is when the experience opens up, allowing the player to begin exploring the rather sizeable house in earnest.
The narrative unfolds in a somewhat unconventional way. Rather than having every plot point delivered through cutscenes, conversations or other exposition, the player learns about characters and the environment largely by reading written notes and letters scattered throughout the estate. Most of these simply serve to provide some background details to Katie's family and the house itself. Those that are related to Sam are often accompanied by a brief voiced anecdote that eventually build up to the reason that she is missing. One particularly nice level of detail with the notes is that they vary a lot depending on who wrote them, varying from cursive handwriting to typewriter print to childish scribbles, further adding to the impression of the writer.
You learn about Sam's growing friendship with a delinquent from her school, a seemingly stereotypical anti-authoritarian character who would rather play video games and attend concerts than classes. This seems to clash with Sam's personality, who is more creative and academic.
As you may have gathered from the above section, advancing the story is a simple matter of exploring and finding notes, but it also involves occasionally hunting for keys and codes to unlock doors and containers. While this may sound like a way to artifically extend playtime, these objects are often found in the vicinity of important notes, so they do not require any particularly extra effort to get. Some notes will also reveal hidden areas, but even these are conveniently marked on your equally-convenient map of the house. It's apparently so big that Katie has to carry one at all times.
One nice feature is the ability to closely examine and rotate any 3D object that you can pick up. Do you want to get a closer look at what that book is about? Turn it around and read the blurb. Do you want to know the nutritional information of that can of soda? Spin it around and turn your head. While certainly not necessary to get through the main story, this allows you to better immerse yourself in the environment, and it is needed to fully understand the characters' backgrounds.
On the other hand, the vast number of interactive objects in the world has the potential to obfuscate what is significant and what is not, especially in the initial few minutes. It can be hard to tell whether that book on the shelf will provide more clues to the whereabouts of Katie's family, or if the pack of cards in the drawer will. While this is not an objectively bad thing, some players might prefer that interactivity be restricted to objects of importance.
This game, which I hesitate to use as a label, is played from the first-person perspective. Anyone who has had any experience with this mechanic will feel immediately at home (pun totally intended). The controls are as one would expect: move the mouse to look around, WASD to walk, Ctrl to crouch and click to interact. Additionally, there is a field of view (FOV) slider that allows you to adjust how wide your view of the world is. This will help if you are prone to simulation or motion sickness in first-person titles. Apart from that, there isn't much else to say here; everything works well.
Gone Home employs a rather clean aesthetic, going for a simple and relatively realistic look for its environment. This makes almost every object in the world easily recognizable, whether it be a lamp, a magazine or a bag of frozen spinach. Lighting is also used to great effect. Unexplored areas are usually difficult to explore due to being unlit, making lamps serve two purposes: making things easier to see and acting as a marker of places that you have been without needing to refer to the map.
In short, the visuals do not detract from the experience. If you are bothered by HUD elements such as a reticle/crosshair and highlights on interactive objects, they can be easily disabled.
The ambient soundtrack of Gone Home, while certainly effective in creating an ominous atmosphere, is, I feel, nothing particularly amazing. It is one of those cases in which the music works fantastically within the given environment, but falls somewhat flat if listened to as standalone tracks. However, there are a few particular songs that bear mentioning.
Scattered throughout the house are cassettes containing music which can be listened to. The songs contained within simply ooze an aura of the mid 1990s, the period in which the story is set. Anyone who was born in the early 90s (myself included) should feel an immediate wave of nostalgia, regardless of whether they like the music or not.
If you are someone who can appreciate a strong and emotional story revolving around a teenage girl's emotional and sexual development delivered to you at your own pace in a realistic setting, then I would very strongly recommend Gone Home to you.
If the prospect of exploration and a bit of reading put you off, I would still tentatively say to give it a try. The story might still be enough to keep you interested. Besides, getting through the game should only take about two hours, give or take how much of said exploration and reading you do.

You're likely reading this review wondering whether you should get this game or not. Sadly I probably cannot answer that question but I can give you my opinion about the game. If you're interested in that then read on.
As with all sequels there are always two kinds of potential buyers: those who played the original and those who didn't. Chances are that whether you're new to this or not you've already heard, read or seen something about DS2. One thing the Souls-series shares is a very passionate community and they are very vocal about the games. I personally see this as a positive sign; it means people care deeply about these games.
Unfortunately for DS2 a lot of negativity takes center stage. This personally strikes me as being somewhat unfair and it's easy to dismiss the game outright because of the naysayers. However what often seems to happen is that many people pass off what is essentially just their opinion as if it is a solid fact. I wouldn't say you should dismiss those people - instead try and read between the lines; perhaps what they consider a bad thing is something you'd like or don't really mind that much. One very interesting thing to keep in mind though: it seems that the majority of the people who greatly dislike DS2 are people who played DS1. Perhaps it is a question of perspective then? I personally know many people who started with DS2 and later played DS1 who greatly dislike DS1. I also know people who played DS1 and later DS2 who prefer the sequel. Personally I still play both games and love them - each for different reasons.
FOR THOSE OF YOU WHO NEVER PLAYED THE ORIGINAL:
I'd actually urge you to read any of the reviews of the first game first to get an idea what these games are generally like. The main reason I suggest this is that DS2 doesn't deviate much from DS1 in terms of general gameplay. But of course you might be here because you are wondering whether you should start with DS2 instead of DS1? Or perhaps you've already decided to completely skip DS1 completely? Both those things are completely fair points.
Let me start out by saying that I believe DS2 is actually harder in the beginning for new players. You're given less Estus flask uses (healing) than DS1 and you loose a fraction of your max health each time you die (down to 50% max health). On top of that DS2 likes to throw more enemies at you at once compared to DS1. All these things combined can easily make for a frustating start for a completely new player - each death compounds your difficulty and the means to restore your lost health are limited at first.
It also depends on why you might be interested in playing a Souls game. If you are really interested in the lore/story I'd absolutely recommend you check out DS1 first. Although knowledge of DS1's story is not really needed to appreciate DS2's story it naturally builds on DS1's lore because it's a sequel to it. And a word of warning: the Souls games are known for their obscurity. Few things are explained to you - most of the story has to be pieced together by yourself. And even then not everything is ever completely clear. Keep that in mind.
If you're here for the gameplay (and by extension PvP) I'd probably recommend DS2. From a mechanical point of view DS2 is more solid with regards to its controls and systems. I can't comment on the balance of PvP (and that's always a great debate) since I personally don't take part in it but this is the general vibe I get from the community.
FOR THOSE WHO PLAYED DARK SOULS 1:
I find it really difficult what to tell you. Not that I find DS2 hard to recommend - I'd say chances are good that if you liked DS1 you'll like DS2. And if you didn't like it DS2 might not be different enough to win you over. But as with so many things in life it depends entirely on your expectations.
If you essentially expect DS2 to be exactly like DS1 in a new package you'll probably be disappointed. Mechanically I'd say most changes are for the better although the introduction of weapon durability and how it is handled on PC is a matter of great debate. The upgrade system has been changed and requires less titanite but is harder to come by early if you need extra, as you can't immediately buy unlimited amounts. Infusions (elemental damage upgrades) has been expanded to include things such as bleed and poison effects.
World wise Dark Souls 1 was a smaller, more compact experience with areas that connected with each other, cleverly looping around with shortcuts you could open along the way. Dark Souls 2 in comparison is bigger; more open and sprawling, spanning a larger area and losing some of the interconnectivity from the first game. One major change, probably due to being the world being larger, is the ability to warp between bonfires from the very beginning of the game.
For as far as difficulty goes: that's a tough one to talk about. If you're a DS1 veteran who could dodge-roll his way easily through the entire game with an SL1 character then perhaps it might not be that difficult for you. Whether that's the fault of the game or the fact that players (you) is now familiar and experienced with the system is probably open for debate. Where DS1 often had singular enemies (or pairs) DS2 often has you fighting groups at a time. The same concept extends to bosses where a fair share of encounters has you fighting 2 or even 3 enemies at once.
Whether any of this appeals to you as an experienced Souls-player is entirely a question of taste. As I have tried to emphasize: these things are often a question of perspective and expectations.
There are things I greatly dislike about DS2 compared to DS1 but there are also plenty of things I think DS2 did better. But as I already said: I love both games and enjoy them for what they both did right - not for what one game lacks compared to the other. You might disagree of course and that's completely fair.

TL;DR: Verdun is a beautifully executed team-based, first person shooter that accurately represents the first World War, and trench warfare.
Detailed Review:
Verdun, at it’s heart, is a first person shooter based in WW1. That alone is merit enough to take a look. It’s gameplay is refreshingly objective based for the genre, and focuses, of course, on the trenches, with squads of players attempting to take and hold the trenches of their opponents. This is the very heart of Verdun, and all aspects of the game orbit this.
Verdun features squad based gameplay, with 4 men in each team. Each squad plays a different but significant role in the battle, with 4 different roles in each squad. Each squad is led by an NCO, who directly controls the squad’s unique ability, and indirectly controls where the squad goes. Unique to Verdun is the resounding emphasis on this squad gameplay. Many of each squad member’s abilities require the NCO nearby to function, pushing squad members to stick together. Not only this, but the longer you play with the same group, the better your abilities get (eg: better artillery, recon plane bomb runs, machinegunner able to sprint… The list goes on). You also get nicer uniforms. Because historical accuracy.
Speaking of, the weapons are true in style for the era, and the game’s focus on historical accuracy is as much a balancing factor as it is a selling point. Most weapons are bolt action rifles, with a few squad members getting either a pistol, melee weapon, or machine gun. Some squad members get access to weapons with scopes or bayonets on them, with a few more having access to grenades. The actual loadouts of the individual squad members varies based on the squad’s role. Only downside is the lack of customization for loadouts. Each squad member has three loadouts to choose from but there is no play inside of these loadouts. Mind you, this is forgiven for the sake of balance as well as making each squad feel unique and impactful.
The final item I want to touch on is the squad progression system. This feature is, to my knowledge, entirely unique to Verdun, and a highly rewarding one. The concept is simple: the longer you play with the same group of people, the better your squad gets. Better artillery, recon planes that drop bombs, allowing your machinegunner to sprint with the squad, uniforms with metal helmets, etc. The idea is entirely novel to me, and it’s my favorite part of Verdun.
Verdun is a great game. It’s an excellent FPS, it’s emphasis on team work and objectives are as refreshing as they are wonderfully executed, and I would definitely recommend this to anyone who's tired of CoD and clones.

Soaking in a story in an interactive way that feels very smart and genuine.

The concept is simple: you come home after a year of traveling to find no one has come to greet you, no one is home, what happened?
The gameplay simpler: move around the house, pick up objects and subtle clues as to what had happened in the past year.

The main story arch about the protagonists sister is told through audio diaries (of which the voice acting is superb). All the characters in the story though, you get to know through several objects riddled all around the place. Connect it all together and you'll genuinely be enjoying yourself. If you're smart enough, you'll figure it out half way through. The compelling atmosphere and soundtrack just strengthens it all. It's 1AM, rainy outside, creepy old house in the woods... goes hand in hand with a story about missing people.

There can be arguments made that this is not a game due to the lack of the "failure state" but in all honesty, that was the last thing running through my mind while playing it. The characters feel genuine enough that you become interested in how it all ends and forget about any other gameplay elements it could have included.

Generally I will recommend this game but only at a reduced price. The original full price does not feel fair to me as it is just the product of its own hype. For 3 hours of content, no. If you are looking for something unique and easy on the mind, wish to discover colorful characters and like to investigate the scene to understand whats going on - look no further, this is the best it's going to get.

You're likely reading this review wondering whether you should get this game or not. Sadly I probably cannot answer that question but I can give you my opinion about the game. If you're interested in that then read on.
As with all sequels there are always two kinds of potential buyers: those who played the original and those who didn't. Chances are that whether you're new to this or not you've already heard, read or seen something about DS2. One thing the Souls-series shares is a very passionate community and they are very vocal about the games. I personally see this as a positive sign; it means people care deeply about these games.
Unfortunately for DS2 a lot of negativity takes center stage. This personally strikes me as being somewhat unfair and it's easy to dismiss the game outright because of the naysayers. However what often seems to happen is that many people pass off what is essentially just their opinion as if it is a solid fact. I wouldn't say you should dismiss those people - instead try and read between the lines; perhaps what they consider a bad thing is something you'd like or don't really mind that much. One very interesting thing to keep in mind though: it seems that the majority of the people who greatly dislike DS2 are people who played DS1. Perhaps it is a question of perspective then? I personally know many people who started with DS2 and later played DS1 who greatly dislike DS1. I also know people who played DS1 and later DS2 who prefer the sequel. Personally I still play both games and love them - each for different reasons.
FOR THOSE OF YOU WHO NEVER PLAYED THE ORIGINAL:
I'd actually urge you to read any of the reviews of the first game first to get an idea what these games are generally like. The main reason I suggest this is that DS2 doesn't deviate much from DS1 in terms of general gameplay. But of course you might be here because you are wondering whether you should start with DS2 instead of DS1? Or perhaps you've already decided to completely skip DS1 completely? Both those things are completely fair points.
Let me start out by saying that I believe DS2 is actually harder in the beginning for new players. You're given less Estus flask uses (healing) than DS1 and you loose a fraction of your max health each time you die (down to 50% max health). On top of that DS2 likes to throw more enemies at you at once compared to DS1. All these things combined can easily make for a frustating start for a completely new player - each death compounds your difficulty and the means to restore your lost health are limited at first.
It also depends on why you might be interested in playing a Souls game. If you are really interested in the lore/story I'd absolutely recommend you check out DS1 first. Although knowledge of DS1's story is not really needed to appreciate DS2's story it naturally builds on DS1's lore because it's a sequel to it. And a word of warning: the Souls games are known for their obscurity. Few things are explained to you - most of the story has to be pieced together by yourself. And even then not everything is ever completely clear. Keep that in mind.
If you're here for the gameplay (and by extension PvP) I'd probably recommend DS2. From a mechanical point of view DS2 is more solid with regards to its controls and systems. I can't comment on the balance of PvP (and that's always a great debate) since I personally don't take part in it but this is the general vibe I get from the community.
FOR THOSE WHO PLAYED DARK SOULS 1:
I find it really difficult what to tell you. Not that I find DS2 hard to recommend - I'd say chances are good that if you liked DS1 you'll like DS2. And if you didn't like it DS2 might not be different enough to win you over. But as with so many things in life it depends entirely on your expectations.
If you essentially expect DS2 to be exactly like DS1 in a new package you'll probably be disappointed. Mechanically I'd say most changes are for the better although the introduction of weapon durability and how it is handled on PC is a matter of great debate. The upgrade system has been changed and requires less titanite but is harder to come by early if you need extra, as you can't immediately buy unlimited amounts. Infusions (elemental damage upgrades) has been expanded to include things such as bleed and poison effects.
World wise Dark Souls 1 was a smaller, more compact experience with areas that connected with each other, cleverly looping around with shortcuts you could open along the way. Dark Souls 2 in comparison is bigger; more open and sprawling, spanning a larger area and losing some of the interconnectivity from the first game. One major change, probably due to being the world being larger, is the ability to warp between bonfires from the very beginning of the game.
For as far as difficulty goes: that's a tough one to talk about. If you're a DS1 veteran who could dodge-roll his way easily through the entire game with an SL1 character then perhaps it might not be that difficult for you. Whether that's the fault of the game or the fact that players (you) is now familiar and experienced with the system is probably open for debate. Where DS1 often had singular enemies (or pairs) DS2 often has you fighting groups at a time. The same concept extends to bosses where a fair share of encounters has you fighting 2 or even 3 enemies at once.
Whether any of this appeals to you as an experienced Souls-player is entirely a question of taste. As I have tried to emphasize: these things are often a question of perspective and expectations.
There are things I greatly dislike about DS2 compared to DS1 but there are also plenty of things I think DS2 did better. But as I already said: I love both games and enjoy them for what they both did right - not for what one game lacks compared to the other. You might disagree of course and that's completely fair.

This game is a lot of fun to play and the progression is pretty great.
The system as it is setup is one that leaves the player feeling accomplished when achievements are made.
Naturally, it's not perfect and given the DEVS are working with limited resources (compared to major studios) they have come a long way in a short time and should be congratualted.
That said, I'll offer an opinion on improvements that I think would improve the game.
1) There really needs to be a general class.
- once a player reaches lvl 100 they can have access to the general class
- this class has a map upon which they can display markings that NCO's can see
- given the selected NCOs, the general can suggest where to best execute their abilities
- say, for example, the general issists that certain sqauds defend certain areas and could coordinate the use of the NCO abilities for maximum effect. Upon the map, the general can place a marker for each NCO ability
* drop gas here, shell this area, call in recon, and perhaps draw lines in no man's land for route guidance
* similiar to switching teams and positions, NCO's should be given a prompt to agree to the general's suggestions
something along the lines of "press H to comply" and has 30 secs to issue the command, or they can ignore
- moreover, the general should have their own abilities like refreshing an NCO's cooldown, or placing an aura that adds defensive/offensive capabilities (it's no secret that the presence of a general on a battlefield has an impact on moral of both sides).
2) There absolutely has to be bullet drop. As much as I enjoy sniping from across the map, the fact is, the bullets fly like lasers and the lack of relying on skill cheapens the experience. Yes, it's fun stopping whole pushes with a clip, but, I'd rather earn it than shoot laser beams.
3) The Machine gunner class should be able to leave their gun. This way when sawrmed, the MG class can still retreat with a pistol and then perhaps return to their spot when the push is over. Just the same as in real life.
4) the Bomber class, once reaching a certain lvl should be given an arc displayed on their screen for grenade tossing. Yes, an argument can be made that the player should develop a feel for the class, however, at higher lvls, players should be given advantages in taking out the guess work.
5) Tooltips should be displayed for each class up to lvl 5. An example being bullet points displayed on the bottom for snipers reiterating that they should be looking for MGs and other snipers first. Finding concealed cover etc. This should be the same for every class so that new players can understand their role in the group better and get in line with cooperating.
6) there should be a medic class and killing the medic when healing should give other players negative points ( much like how in WW1 and 2 soldiers on both sides would often avoid hurting or killing medics. Some say the african campaign was the last of chivalry in war, this however is WW1 and it was definitely frowned upon to kill medics in the field)
7) If your servers ever get up to spec to handle engineers building temp defenses, that should be implemented as well.
TL;DR
-Firefights are great, intense, and when won, definitely worthwhile
-Sqaud mechanics when followed are awesome and players cooperating is a must
- NEED to add bullet drop
- NEED to add additional classes

The game focuses on the idea of the mercilessness of world war 1.    It is merciless.  There is no tutorial and you are thrown into batlles with highly skilled players. It is the type of game that is punishing to everyone who wasn't playing it from the very begninning when all the players were learning and starting out at the same level. It is very hard to develop any skill in this game when you generally die a few seconds after you pop your head out of the trench in which you have spawned.  95% of the time you will not get any clue as to where the bullet came from, nor will you see any movement or indication of the person who shot you.  Much of the time you will die while prone behind cover or only crawling up just enough to be able to see above the top of your trench or hill, which you have to do if you ever want to take a shot at anything.  Keeping your head down will not reduce constant death and respawning.  It may give some sense of the futility of the war but I don't feel it makes for an enjoyable game or even a game that I feel compelled to try to slog through.

I never felt like I was part of a big battle, which was  a hoped for experience that was a key draw for me.  It felt more like a handful of people playing deathmatch in trenches, with you as cannon fodder for the master players.
The game performed reasonably well and I never had any stability problems(running the linux client).
If you are the type of gamer for whom this sounds challenging and fun then by all means purchase the game. It will most likely satisfy your expectations.  I purchased the game, with reservations,  after reading the reviews and fearing that it would be a frustrating experience.  It was and I regret buying it.

You know an exploration clue-finding game is gonna be good when your first instinct is 'hey lookit that blue cup, lemme see if I can pick it up. I can! Do I have to put it back where I found it or can I fling it across the room? I can fling it across the room!' That is to say game-mechanically it is sound and engaging, for y'know a 3d point-click. That sounds mean... No it really draws you in, or at least it did me because I spent my childhood in the 90's and this game really does everything to bring you back. Every little detail of the environment pulls you back and hits you with nostalgia. From the style of music on the cassette tapes, the cassette tapes themselves, the posters, VHS, everything is there. Even those raindow-from-hell Lisa Frank binders!
Aside from all that, the story drew me in and I became invested in what the hell happened to Katie's (who you play as) family and particularly her sister, who is the main focus. The story is sad, it's sweet, and if you're someone who really tries to jump into the character's shoes and can emote from this form of stimulus, then you are in for one hell of a ride.
I have to say that this game is not for everyone. I can see a lot of people being bored with Gone Home; if you need action in your games than move on, and likewise if you didn't live through the 90's you won't get a lot of it and the nostalgia factor will be wasted. But for everyone who enjoys exploration, clue-finding, and stories about family and growing up; do I recommend this game? Yes, wholeheartedly so.

At first glance, I thought this game would be a pass. It had nothing I would typically be interested in: I rarely play MP or co-op because I find the competition/survival aspect stressful, I tend to avoid historically-based war themes (especially involving Nazis), and while dinosaurs are cool, they haven't been a draw for me since I was a kid.
But as Dino D-Day was free for a weekend, I figured what the hell, I'd give it a shot. The dinos+WWII aspect was at least enough to make me curious.
Lo and behold, by the end of the weekend I had sunk over 14 solid hours into the game, half in online MP matches and half messing around in SP with bots to get the hang of classes and mechanics at my own pace ("dinomon" difficulty mode is a hilarious godsend). The fact that achievements unlocked for me even though I didn't own the game yet was pretty cool too.
As for my dislike for WWII themes, it was surprisingly a non-issue. While in a match the Axis/Allies thing kinda dissolves into the background and simply becomes red vs blue. It helps that they don't flaunt or overuse Nazi-related imagery or buzzwords. There's the occasional themed comment from a character after a kill, but otherwise any blatant "historical" references are primarily in the menu text and voiceovers.
I really like how you can seamlessly switch classes or sides at any point (, and . keys respectively). It's not something I'd abuse if a match/team is working together really well of course, though the game sometimes auto-balances teams and swaps you unwillingly. Not really a biggie, but less fun if you get saddled with teammates who don't know what they're doing. You can always switch back when a slot opens though. :)
What sold me however, was how laid back MP matches were. Not at all like your standard CS:GO/Halo-type level of stress and hair-pulling: it didn't feel like there was a competitive urgency in matches, the voice chatting I did hear was free of gratuitous cursing/whining/trash talk, and "newbie abuse" in text chat was very, very minimal. I think the absurdity of the dinosaurs is a big part of all that, honestly. It's difficult to take the game as seriously as one with a completely human cast, so "failure" becomes either amusing/inconsequential or just simply a temporary annoyance till you respawn.
Parts of the game
more frustrating, but mainly the class-balancing issues, like how much of an edge Compys and Raptors have over humans based on their size and speed. Being pounced to death over and over can get annoying - especially when you know the people playing the small dinos are just using them because they're easy
OPed, and require almost zero skill to rack up kills. (Obviously that's not always the case, as good players do play small dinos, but you can tell when someone doesn't quite know what they're doing. I'm more impressed when I get sniped by someone from across the map.) Either way, it's still not even close to the amount of stress I expected.
Dino D-Day, despite boasting themes and genre/play-styles I wouldn't normally even take a second look at, managed to enthrall me so much that I bought it. (The 90%-off sale was also a factor, but I actually did want the game.) I even considered the 4-pack, but that kind of requires that one a) has friends, and b) they would even be interested in the first place. I guess I'll stick to making friends in-game for now. :P
Btw, if anyone needs a buddy for some of the trickier two-player achievements (Nigel/Microraptor, Ilona/Raptor, etc), I'll gladly assist.

Gone Home relies on your passion for exploration and investigation. It attempts to conjure feelings of fear and apprehension from your childhood days where a dark passageway was the road to hell itself. At the same time, it gives you life whilst forgoing interaction and gameplay via mementos and hints about its characters' lives.
Whether you will enjoy the - fairly minimal - time spent exploring the house is determined by your personal investment into the story. Are you interested in deciphering the lives of a messy Portland family? Do you enjoy games that are relatable or give in-depth characterization and insight? This game is for you. (Buy it on sale, as $20 is a little steep)
However, are you more of a guns and guts person? A gamer that thrives on fear and thrill? Hold a preference for button-mashing, screen-staring, and long hours? This game, even if it somehow dipped below $5, will not be to your liking.
Gone Home is so incredibly polarizing. Many love it, and many hate it; and to me, that itself says a product just might be interesting enough to take a look at.

This game is a lot of fun to play and the progression is pretty great.
The system as it is setup is one that leaves the player feeling accomplished when achievements are made.
Naturally, it's not perfect and given the DEVS are working with limited resources (compared to major studios) they have come a long way in a short time and should be congratualted.
That said, I'll offer an opinion on improvements that I think would improve the game.
1) There really needs to be a general class.
- once a player reaches lvl 100 they can have access to the general class
- this class has a map upon which they can display markings that NCO's can see
- given the selected NCOs, the general can suggest where to best execute their abilities
- say, for example, the general issists that certain sqauds defend certain areas and could coordinate the use of the NCO abilities for maximum effect. Upon the map, the general can place a marker for each NCO ability
* drop gas here, shell this area, call in recon, and perhaps draw lines in no man's land for route guidance
* similiar to switching teams and positions, NCO's should be given a prompt to agree to the general's suggestions
something along the lines of "press H to comply" and has 30 secs to issue the command, or they can ignore
- moreover, the general should have their own abilities like refreshing an NCO's cooldown, or placing an aura that adds defensive/offensive capabilities (it's no secret that the presence of a general on a battlefield has an impact on moral of both sides).
2) There absolutely has to be bullet drop. As much as I enjoy sniping from across the map, the fact is, the bullets fly like lasers and the lack of relying on skill cheapens the experience. Yes, it's fun stopping whole pushes with a clip, but, I'd rather earn it than shoot laser beams.
3) The Machine gunner class should be able to leave their gun. This way when sawrmed, the MG class can still retreat with a pistol and then perhaps return to their spot when the push is over. Just the same as in real life.
4) the Bomber class, once reaching a certain lvl should be given an arc displayed on their screen for grenade tossing. Yes, an argument can be made that the player should develop a feel for the class, however, at higher lvls, players should be given advantages in taking out the guess work.
5) Tooltips should be displayed for each class up to lvl 5. An example being bullet points displayed on the bottom for snipers reiterating that they should be looking for MGs and other snipers first. Finding concealed cover etc. This should be the same for every class so that new players can understand their role in the group better and get in line with cooperating.
6) there should be a medic class and killing the medic when healing should give other players negative points ( much like how in WW1 and 2 soldiers on both sides would often avoid hurting or killing medics. Some say the african campaign was the last of chivalry in war, this however is WW1 and it was definitely frowned upon to kill medics in the field)
7) If your servers ever get up to spec to handle engineers building temp defenses, that should be implemented as well.
TL;DR
-Firefights are great, intense, and when won, definitely worthwhile
-Sqaud mechanics when followed are awesome and players cooperating is a must
- NEED to add bullet drop
- NEED to add additional classes

If you enjoy artsy, story-based games like To The Moon or Dear Esther, you would probably like Gone Home.
You wander around an old mansion, reading notes and examining objects. You learn about the characters as you do so, following their lives through old papers - letters, stories, school assignments - left on desks and such. You find the evidence of their lives and personalities in the form of their possessions, decorations, etc.
The game takes a few cues from the adventure game genre, in the form of locked areas that you gain access to conveniently in the same place you find an important piece of story.
By the end of the game I almost feel like I got to know a real person by digging through her stuff.

The game focuses on the idea of the mercilessness of world war 1.    It is merciless.  There is no tutorial and you are thrown into batlles with highly skilled players. It is the type of game that is punishing to everyone who wasn't playing it from the very begninning when all the players were learning and starting out at the same level. It is very hard to develop any skill in this game when you generally die a few seconds after you pop your head out of the trench in which you have spawned.  95% of the time you will not get any clue as to where the bullet came from, nor will you see any movement or indication of the person who shot you.  Much of the time you will die while prone behind cover or only crawling up just enough to be able to see above the top of your trench or hill, which you have to do if you ever want to take a shot at anything.  Keeping your head down will not reduce constant death and respawning.  It may give some sense of the futility of the war but I don't feel it makes for an enjoyable game or even a game that I feel compelled to try to slog through.

I never felt like I was part of a big battle, which was  a hoped for experience that was a key draw for me.  It felt more like a handful of people playing deathmatch in trenches, with you as cannon fodder for the master players.
The game performed reasonably well and I never had any stability problems(running the linux client).
If you are the type of gamer for whom this sounds challenging and fun then by all means purchase the game. It will most likely satisfy your expectations.  I purchased the game, with reservations,  after reading the reviews and fearing that it would be a frustrating experience.  It was and I regret buying it.

I haven't played a game like this before.  It's very difficult to categorise, so in my Steam library I have placed it under Adventure, Visual Novel and Miscellaneous.  I came into the game with some trepidation, as it presents itself as if it may be a horror experience.  Those bothered by this can stop worrying; aside from the slightly nerve-wracking storm effects, this is not a horror game and is not designed to scare you.
With it's wonderful message and story and immersive sound and controls, It's an easy game to praise.  However, it currently costs £14.99, which is a LOT for any game of this length.  It took me around three hours to complete.  Bearing in mind that you can get many, many games with higher production values and many times the play time and replayability for far less cost, it is unlikely that you will find many to touch you so strongly emotionally.  There are few games so powerful in this regard.  However, there do seem to be multiple stories at play here, some of which are sadly not resolved.
It does have its issues.  The otherwise beautifully detailed setting can be jarred by the sheer number of repeated objects; no real house has so many tissue boxes, for example.  It's hard to see why this is the case since so much care has been taken with most other objects.
I also felt that I would have got more out of this game if I were American.  Certain themes and maybe objects probably represent a culture a British person like me will have missed out on, despite being a 90's kid myself.

So what has changed in this version?
Enemy placement and item placement. Some NPC locations have also changed. These changes are enough to surprise an experienced DS2 (vanilla) player. There are new NPC invaders and new NPC summons. New NPC summons are greatly improved and are more humanlike now. They even do gestures. Also there's a new final boss who is worthy of being a final boss. Some graphical improvements, mainly lighting effects. Dark areas actually require a torch to navigate now. Also all the DLC content has been integrated into the core game.
So is this worth buying?
If you haven't played Dark Souls 2 before, absolutely worth it.
If you have played Dark Souls 2 but not the DLC content, absolutely worth it.
If you have played Dark Souls 2 and the DLC content, consider the changes and decide yourself.
Overall a superb game and one that is worthy of the Dark Souls name.
P.S:- Just make sure that your graphics card support DirectX 11 before buying this game.

This is not a game, it's not a challenge, it's barely even a mystery.  It is, in fact, an exploration of a new mode of storytelling.  It's been compared to Dear Esther, and while I might say the two are in the same medium, I'm not even willing to say it's the same genre.  Gone Home tells us a story where more than half is told purely through the detritus left behind as photos, notes, cassettes, and thousands of little pieces that come from living your life.  It's a very effective medium for immersion and I found myself emotionally attached to the characters and their stories by the end.
If you're just looking to play a game, you won't find one here.  If you are interested in reading a short story in a wholly new way; Gone Home is for you.

Warface is what I'd imagine free to play Call of Duty would be like. Just like CoD, it's fast paced on relatively small maps with few spacier exceptions. Unlike CoD though, weapon physics in this game still require some sense of aim and there is no unbalanced killstreak bs, so that's good. The game is surprisingly poorly optimised though, considering my PC was able to run Crysis 1 and 2, yet it isn't able to handle Warface, even though it certainly looks worse even on high details settings.
Game feels fairly balanced, especially for free to play shooter - though it's fair to say many people tend to use AUG all the time, so you get the idea… overall the gameplay is just okay - nothing special, but nothing bad, but considering this game is absolutely free, I guess it's a good thing. I liked enviromental effects that change the way you play on the map for a a minute or so. However, as it always is with free to play games, it's easier to run into loud children and cheaters.
Overall, I think the game would be worthy of 10 € pricetag or something around that. If you don't feel like buying new CoD every year, and don't like the hardcore feel of CS, this is your way to go if you want close quarter combat game. Solid 7/10 I'd say.
+ Map design
+ Weapon customisation system (like in Crysis)
+ Fast paced, but not overly chaotic - teams have set spawns, which is great
+ Sliding is fun
+ Good graphics for free to play shooter
+ Kind of well balanced
+ Also provides COOP modes against AI
______________________
- Poor optimisation
- Somewhat laggy
- Sliding is somewhat OP
- Somewhat childish community
- Hitmarker is ugly as hell (seriously)
- Painfully long load times, even on SSD

For a Unity-based game it is an incredible piece of work though, if not highly optimised.

Let me first say that I really enjoy story-driven games, I have no problems with short and to the point games if the experience is worth it, and I don't buy all of this "it's not a game" crap about interactive story videogames. Still, I did not like Gone Home as I feel it fails even as a interactive story game.
Although I sympathyze a lot with the issues about homosexuality that Gone Home addresses, I don't think the game manages to get its point across very well, nor to establish any sort of emotional link with the player.
I have two major complaints about Gone Home.
First, the narrative device used for telling the story. Basically, you explore the home while hearing your sister's diary read to you as you discover clues. At the end you find the actual diary, which is everything you've been listening to during the game.
Being this a first-person game, the expectation is that anything you hear is going to be from the point of view of the main character, so when I heard my sister's voice I was expecting it to be some sort of audiolog or registration I found, instead of an extra-diegetic narrative device. Unfortunately, that wasn't the case and it ruined a lot the immersion.
Second, the sister's story is overly saccharine and completely irrealistic, as if out of a badly written light romance novel, to the point that I actually wasn't able to be involved at all in the issues the game was trying to address because of the horrible writing.
SPOILER ALERT
At the end, you discover that your teenage sister has escaped with the "woman of her life". I guess the game expects you to feel happy about this, happy that she found love, but all I could think of was "this girl is a dumbass, her love is going to fade eventually and she'll discover she's thrown her life away."

So what has changed in this version?
Enemy placement and item placement. Some NPC locations have also changed. These changes are enough to surprise an experienced DS2 (vanilla) player. There are new NPC invaders and new NPC summons. New NPC summons are greatly improved and are more humanlike now. They even do gestures. Also there's a new final boss who is worthy of being a final boss. Some graphical improvements, mainly lighting effects. Dark areas actually require a torch to navigate now. Also all the DLC content has been integrated into the core game.
So is this worth buying?
If you haven't played Dark Souls 2 before, absolutely worth it.
If you have played Dark Souls 2 but not the DLC content, absolutely worth it.
If you have played Dark Souls 2 and the DLC content, consider the changes and decide yourself.
Overall a superb game and one that is worthy of the Dark Souls name.
P.S:- Just make sure that your graphics card support DirectX 11 before buying this game.

Five Nights 2 is a somewhat mixed bag. It's certainly a lot more ambitious than part 1, but at the same time it feels a little less intense. Visually the game has improved significantly, as well as the variety of places there are to see in the pizza joint. There's also a lot more animatronics to keep track of, which keeps you on your toes. The story continues on and is, in my opinion, as well told as in the first, letting players (and the community) piece things together the more its played, and the *SPOILERS* mini-games are a welcome addition which break up the monotony of being repeatedly mangled, leaving the (frequent) deaths much more welcome than before.
Freddy's 2 is not without it's faults, however. Past night 2 the game became a somewhat exhaustive process of switching between the music box, the hall light and the mask with no real good opportunity to actually use the cameras, which unfortunately takes a lot of the tension out of the game for the sake of ramping up the challenge. Sadly, too, without the slow build up of tension that the first game had, the jump scares are considerably less effective, and while Freddy's 1 still manages to creep me out, Freddy's 2 has already lost that ability. It's also a bit sad that after Night 2, the heavily teased 'Toy' versions of the characters stop making regular appearances.
Overall, I heartily recommend this game, but here's hoping that Part 3 (come on, we know it's coming) moves a little more back towards horror.

Gone Home is a completely narrative driven title which I thoroughly enjoyed. However, I would like to stress that the primary reason for playing this game is for the story, NOT the gameplay, of which there is very little. I couldn't help but notice that there are several poor reviews on Steam that are laregly negative, which I fail to understand, although that may simply be my opinion. I can only conclude that those people either do not enjoy an interesting story, or do not appreciate a story that involves romance.
Essentially, the description of this game effectively portrays the situation. You play as Katie Greenbriar, a girl who is returning to her family's home after a lengthy overseas trip. Your family is not home however, and there appears to be numerous clues suggesting that your sister is involved in some sort of intimate relationship. You discover that your sister is supposed to be home, as she did not accompany your parents on their vacation. It's your job to learn where exactly your sister went, and precisely why she left without waiting for your arrival.
The way in which this story progresses is not unlike that of the Bioshock series, where rather than being presented with several cutscenes that pull you out of the action, you are prompted to find various journal entries that your sister has left around the house, and listen to them, not unlike the Voxophones in Bioshock. The more entries you discover and listen to, the more emotional the story becomes, and the more absorbed I became. It succeeded in interesting me so much to the point where I actually completed the game in one playthrough, without taking any breaks, as the game was both engaging and considerably brief.
This game successfully creates an atmosphere. The year is 1995, so you are confronted with various tapes and casettes as you explore the house, searching for clues. I found myself listening to each and every one of Lonnie's tapes in their entirety, as they so effectively reflected Lonnie's 90's punk-rock persona. The voice acting was additionally superb. Sam conveyed pure vulnerability as she explained her feelings and thoughts in each journal entry.
The only issue I had with this game was it's length. Despite it feeling intentionally short, I desired for more development in the overall story. In one playthrough (again, without taking any breaks) I was able to complete it in a grand total of two hours, which obviously is not long for a video game, or interactive story, whichever you prefer to call it.
9/10 for Gone Home, which may seem a bit generous to some, but it is what I believe to be a near-flawless game if it weren't for a short narrative and little depth.
