Dark Souls is one of the most amazing games I have ever played, I would even go as far as to call it a masterpiece. The game was dripping with atmosphere, spectacular world design, interesting characters with heart touching stories, and tight gameplay with some interesting online features. Now this review isn't for Dark Souls, this is for Dark Souls II: Scholar of The First Sin. Scholar of The First Sin of SoTFS is a re-release of Dark Souls II which was released in April 2014 (For PC.)  The game introduced improved graphics and gameplay, a new world to explore with new enemies and new weapons to fight them with. So here is my opinion on Dark Souls II: Scholar of The First Sin.
The Story in Dark Souls II is about you, an undead who has ventured into Drangleic to find a cure for you undead affliction. I won't continue on as this would spoil the game and chances are; if you're reading this review you have no played the game yet. The story is interesting, and not directly told to the player. One of the greatest part of any souls game is the way the story is presented; the story is hidden in item descriptions and in dialogue with the NPC's. The Dark Souls community has done a great job of uncovering the lore and story of the game.
The gameplay in Dark Souls II is a great improvement on the first game. The movement is made to feel much more fluent and easier to control, the combat is dramatically improved. Dual wielding is now much more viable in the game as dual wielding makes much more sense; R1 and R2 will use the object in your right hand and L1 and L2 will use the object in your left hand, a new power stance feature has been added to the game. The power stance feature allows for a player to activate a whole new move set exclusive to a set of weapons. The way this works is by holding Triangle or Y on the controller when two of the same weapons are equipped. Magic and ranged weapons have been improved by allowing the user to move when using them. One major issue that I have with the game is that the difficulty feels forced, the main way the games attempts to make things difficult is by just throwing more enemies at you. Upon death you are reverted to a hallow; this means you are unable to summon other player to assist you and the players maximum health is lowered, this is rubbish gameplay in my opinion as it negates the desire to explore the world. The player’s maximum health can be restored with the use of a humane effigy but these items are finite if playing offline. One huge downside is that a controller is highly recommended to play. This is due to the poor control scheme that has been implemented into the game. I use a Dualshock 4 controller to play Dark Souls.
The characters in Dark Souls 2 are not really all that interesting. The characters lack what made the characters in Dark Souls 1 enjoyable; the characters in Dark Souls 1 were interesting and had motives of their own. The characters in Dark Souls 2 are boring, for lack of a better term. The emerald herald is the closest thing to an interesting character but she has the personality of toast.
The game uses online features in unique ways; players are able to leave notes on the group which other player are able to see, this would be helpful if 99% of the messages did not say “try tongue, but hole.” Bloodstains show how another player has died, usually warning players of a dangerous area. Ghost are able to be seen at times, these are other players in their own world. The multiplayer works like this: You are able to summon or be summoned into the world to assist in defeating the environments boss. Upon doing this the player is rewarded with souls and human effigies. A player is also able to invade another player’s world and fight them in an honourable dual, or a not so honourable 1 vs 3. The online gameplay is quite fun but isn’t required to complete the game.
This is where I have one of my biggest problems with the game, the world is often bland and makes no sense. In one instance you are at a windmill surrounded by barren wasteland; you beat the boss of the area and continue onwards. You take an elevator upwards and find yourself at a castle made of iron; the castle has sunken into the ground reaching lava. This makes no sense and ruins the player immersion. Dark Souls handled the environments of the game so much better as the world was beautiful to look at with great landscapes to look at. The whole world loops back in on itself creating all these short cuts which just give the game an overall fantastic feeling to it. Dark Souls II is nothing like this as most areas will end in a dead end forcing you to fast travel elsewhere and take a different path.  While the DLC has improved on this and provided much more interesting locations the rest of the game is still a disappointment with much to be desired.
Dark Souls II: Scholar of The First Sin is an amazing game with fun and challenging gameplay, the story is interesting and the online gameplay is very pleasant.  Although I recommend that you play Dark Souls before Dark Souls II: Scholar of The First Sin. You will have a much more enjoyable time with that game, but I am not saying that this game isn’t worth your money. If you enjoyed Dark Souls then this game is worth your money, even if it leaves much to be desired.
Should you buy Dark Souls II: Scholar of The First Sin?
Yes, yes you should.

Gone Home fits right into the category of games people love to hate. Yes, it's a walking simulator. Yes, all you do is unravel a story. Yes, it's short and a bit expensive but the price is the only real negative I'm going to give to this game, although I got it for less than that on a Humble Bundle.
I find it sad how many people don't seem to be accepting these new narrative games, dismissing them as mere curiosities at best. Like Dear Esther before it, there have been countless discussions about the nature of these games, with the argument that they're not real games since they don't have complex mechanics, rulesets or goals. To which I say, so what? Why shouldn't videogames go beyond their comfort zone and explore new ideas and concepts? Traditional videogames aren't gonna go anywhere and it's a good thing that developers are expanding videogame technology into new ways to tell the stories they want to tell.
Personally I'm thrilled that people are using this medium to tell stories that players can experience at their own pace and I want to see this genre get more more mature and more accepted by the community.

(Warning: Minor Spoilers Below)
Gone Home pushes the boundries of what we as consumers would define as a "game". It has more of an interactive visual novel feel to it but doesn't sacrfice any of the hands-on approach one would expect of such a game style.
Stepping into the role of Kaitlin Greenbriar, you return home from a trip abroad to find that your family members, (Mother, Father and Sister) are nowhere to be found. A hastily scrawled note on the door from your sister Sam tells you not to go looking for her.
The entire opening segment sets the mood for what I had assumed would be some kind of haunted house ghost story, and the game itself uses that feeling to its advantage, setting the stage for further exploration.
Once inside, the majority of the lights in the house are off. You proceed to traverse room to room, turning on lights, searching through cuboards and cabinets, opening drawers and glancing over forgotten grocery slips and half-read letters.
The background music is simple yet at times eerie, setting the player on edge and reminding them that something grusome may wait just around the next corner.
Instead of horror though, we find humanity. The characters that this home belong to, although we never meet them, are just as real and fleshed out as if we'd seen them face to face and held a conversation. With Sam, it's easy because we have the letters as narrative that tell her story overall. But it's the underplayed subtle suggestions of the rest of the game that tell us about Same and Katie's parents. We know that Katie's parents are having a rough time, we know her father is a struggling author, we know that her mother may have had an affair. We aren't told these things outright, but we are shown them and allowed to make our own decisions based on what we've seen.
To wrap this up, If you're looking for gun fights and jump scares, you're looking at the wrong game. But if you're in search of an intriguing, well-written and artistically told story about a family and its secrets, then look no further.

Fun game with a bit of a steep learning curve.
Your first hour or so is going to be brutal. The game is unforgiving, chaotic and a little bit confusing. As you begin to understand the gameplay meta a bit and understand how the guns handle, you'll begin to see a bit more of what Verdun has to offer. On one hand, you have a very competitive marksmanship dueling game here, even if you are not using a scoped weapon, a lot of the gameplay is moving in and out of good cover, finding a target and landing a perfect shot before moving again. The game can get brutal too, with up close and personal trench warfare gameplay that completely changes the pace you were just playing at. One moment you're picking off heads that peek up from a trench or a crater, the next you're rapidly firing off a clip into a squad pouring into your trench and bayoneting the last ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ standing.
Verdun also has an interesting progression system. Your personal progression is pretty straight forward, as you level up you gain more points to unlock alternate versions of the four classes in one of seven different squads (soon to be more) which can help adapt a class to your personal playstyle. The other side of progression is squad progression. The more you play with squadmates, the higher level your squad will be. HIgher level squads get passive bonuses that might affect reload speed, mortar strike impact, point capture speed and a few other things of that nature. Playing with buddies will speed this process up quite a bit, but it works by playing with random players as well, while helping to forge a sort of casual familiarity with them. From the main menu, the game will show you active squads with familiar players in them, helping you maximize this squad progression whenever possible.
Very unique game that really got it's hooks in deep on me. If any of the gameplay I described interests you, I'd suggest grabbing it.

There is little "game" to Gone Home. There's no combat, there aren't any puzzles, and there's no way to fail. The thrust of the play is picking up objects and examining them.
However, Gone Home is beautiful. It's essence is a strongly emotional experience, made more sympathetic through experiencing it as a story told to the player character. The connection is strengthened, not only by allowing the player to control a character's actions, but also through incredible attention to detail. The house feels like a real house, transported through time from the mid-90's. All of the objects manage to tell a piece of the story, whether by offering details on relationships, or by simly not jarring the player out of the time period presented.
I cannot recommend this game highly enough.

SETTING/VISUALS
As someone who is really interested in WWI history, I became addicted to Verdun the moment I stepped into the detail-packed trenches. They are a perfect recreation, filled with bunks, medical tents, and even cramped cooking stations. The maps in this game look like they belong in a museum, and in fact they brought in historians (I have no idea how an indie team managed this) to make sure the game was as historically accurate as possible. You can play as the Central Powers or the Allies. Each squad picks a faction, and it feels awesome to play with your friends as a Canadian squad and hear the French squad down the line shouting in French as they get blown to bits by artillery (everyone is always being blown to bits by artillery or poisoned to death with mustard gas).
The graphics are clearly not from a top-end studio, but are actually pretty gorgeous and really immerse you in the environment. However, the animations aren't very good, and until the game becomes more popular and gets more funding, I don't think they will improve. They are wooden and only do exactly what they have to, and they really feel like placeholders.
GAMEPLAY
If you like casual run-and-gun gameplay, you are going to hate this game. You will feel frustrated constantly and impatience will lead to you spending most of your time respawning. There currently doesn't seem to be any bullet drop, and wind resistance would be a welcome change to increase the difficulty of aiming at long range, which feels a little too easy right now.
However, if you like having a realistic damage model (one shot to the head or torso kills you), and like a game that forces you to work with your team and think before you act, this is the right kind of game for you. In Verdun, positioning is everything. You can die over and over again without getting any kills, and then figure out a way to flank the enemy force and mount a machine gun behind their lines, and go on a 20 kill streak.
Verdun is also very chaotic and exciting, with artillery explosions all around you and your allies crumpling to the ground as you run across no man's land, and the next moment you're doing a trench run with a revolver, piling up enemy bodies as they come around the corner.
This is the only WWI multiplayer game that exists, and I really hope it gets more recognition and funding so we can see it's full potential (they are about to ad all the factions and dismemberment and gore, and ultimately they want the whole multiplayer to work as a dynamic world where factions gain and lose ground, which you can see being implemented already). I'm hoping anyone who plays this and loves it will help spread the word.
Overall, this is a game for history buffs and harcore players.

Very impressed with the graphical updates (the lighting especially looks fantastic), the remixed enemy positions are a welcome change for those of us that have played through dozens of times, and invasion matchmaking happens much more quickly (or not at all, but at least it will immediately tell you). If you already own the DLCs, I'd recommend picking it up on sale for the best value.
Here's an example of some of the interesting remixing From has done (very minor spoilers ahead): Heide's Tower of Flame is no longer as simple as "run past everybody, grab loot, attack boss". First off, the two handed mace and sword knights are buffed by the Dragonrider's presence. They attack much faster, and more aggressive (sword and shield knights may be buffed too, but I didn't notice much of a difference). Once the Dragonrider falls, they turn into the same old slow dudes we're used to. Also, Heide knights are no longer scattered around the world; they're enemies that hang out in the tower. As before, they don't aggro until you hit them... Unless the Dragonrider is dead. On repeat trips to the tower, the Heide knights that previously chilled out peacefully will aggressively pursue you, aggroing from long distance. This is particularly difficult to deal with when approaching the cathedral to go after the Old Dragonslayer. Oh, speaking of the cathedral, that isn't all. There's a fire drake waiting out front.

This review will not be covering many specifics of the game, mostly only basics.
Warface is a free to play, tactical first person shooter. It is developed by Crytek, which is probably most famous for its Crysis series. It has very nice graphics and it runs very smoothly; my computer can't run Minecraft at sixty frames per second almost on minimum settings, but I play this game and run a comfortable forty to fifty frames or more the majority of the time. I personally believe that if you tricked out your grandma's old Windows 95 computer, it could run this game (but don't actually try it). This game has four different classes: The Rifleman (which uses AR's/LMG's and ammo), which is the most balanced class of all, and in my own opinion, the best; the Medic (uses Shotguns, Health packs, and defibs), which is the close quarters monster of the game, especially with the new automatic shotgun in the game; the Engineer (uses Submachineguns and armor kits), which is balanced out between CQC and medium ranges, and effective for being on the run with; and the Sniper (Marksman/Sniper rifles), which is very difficult to use but when you learn how to use it very rewarding the same.
Gameplay
Like mentioned before, the gameplay is incredibly smooth, although loading into matches is very slow. The games you play, whether it be Versus, Co-Op, or Special operations, revolve heavily around teamwork, although it may not seem like it at first glance. If you like the lone wolf feeling of the Call of Duty world, I don't honestly think that you will progress far in this game, and even if you do, it won't be a smooth ride.
About the Teamwork
If you are playing with a full team of players that have no clue what they are doing and have complete disregard for you, the teammates, then you'll probably be butt♥♥♥♥ed, very, very hard. I find it beyond obnoxious when I play Storm, Plant the Bomb, or Capture especially when I see a team that does not work as a unit, when they run into battle like headless chickens. They're timber for the fire, beef headed for the meat grinder. I understand that it can sometimes be hard to, say, if someone has been shot, to put yourself in a position to heal them if you're a medic, but it's simply rediculous that you play most PvP matches with no restored points at the end on either team. Assisting teammates to spots, staying in a group, reviving/healing, and repairing armor or restoring ammo are most of the examples of a teammate being useful; it's not that hard to do any of the above. Even covering teammates from a secluded location with your sniper rifle can potentially save the game, but these are things that many players don't seem to care about. I ask of you reading this review, please, please, PLEASE at least try to support your team. It is beyond important in Insane or even Hard missions, namely the mission HQ. There are certain missions that are quite literally impossible to beat by yourself; teamwork is the only way. To give a little bigger vision as to how important it is for this game, I once played a Storm match with six other players on my team. There were exactly three players on the enemy team, all of which were higher levels than my teammates. What followed was absolutely rediculous. In five minutes of gameplay, the enemy had accumulated well over thirty kills, and our team had about four or so, most of them coming from me. We had about one twentieth of the objective captured, and the enemies all had found superior positions on the map and utilized excellent teamwork. I ended up leaving the game because my teammates were doing nothing but spawning and running forward, in such diluted numbers that none of it was to any avail. Now, one time, in Team Deathmatch, my entire team was working as a unit, even reviving and restoring health and armor and ammo. We stomped the enemy team into the dirt because we all played as a squad, even though we were outnumbered by one, and we conquered, with a victory over fifty points over the enemy team.
All in all, I think Warface is a great game based on tactic and teamwork, and over the months that I have played it become a far better game than I could have ever hoped for it to be.

So I never played the original internet takeover, that the original Five nights at Freddy's was. Mainly because I'd watched so many playthroughs on it, that I went from being scared with the youtuber to laughing at how adorably lacking they are at knowing the strategies. Since this only just come out, I decided to give it a go myself, completely unaware of how many times I would want to shove Foxy's face inside a blender.
Here's the main question you probably want an answer for. Is it good? Absolutely. Is it scary? Kind of.
Chances are, you probably know everything about the original FNAF if you take interest in this, so let's talk about the new animatronics.  We have the new Bonnie with his more innocent makeover, who I find scary until Night 3, when he becomes completely tame compared to everything else that is going on. Easily, the least likely to fly in your face.
The new Chika is basically a slightly better version of Bonnie, and likes to appear in the hallway with a birthday present and a stripper outfit. I wish I could make that up. Then we have the balloon boy who starts in cam 10, then flies off the face of the earth, only to randomly appear in the left vent. I have absolutely no idea where he goes.  But think of him as Nelson from the Simpsons; he's coming for you, with the intent to point and laugh at your failure until you inevitably die. But never actually attack you.
I'll save the rest for you to find out, because finding out is half the adventure. A painful adventure, where you will spend an hour figuring out how to deal  with each enemy.
The feature with this game that everyone was staining their pants with bleach over, is having no doors to protect you when Chika stands outside the window, gasping at how erect your nipples are. Or at least, that's how I pictured it. She's gotta have that shocked expression for a reason. But who needs a powerful door, when you have the most amazing flashlight, mankind has evar created?
If you have a friend who is dying from some incurable disease, flick the flashlight at them a few times and they will be skydivng into your mother's bed while holding the olympic torch. At least 4 of the animatronics will come for you from the hallway, to which you can respond by flicking at them for a minute, and they will probably be gone. Which results in the first hour of every night, being a game of red light green light with Foxy. He just loves to join the party early.
Which brings me to my next point about this flashlight. You will not run out of power. Like evar. One of the most intense parts of the original, was trying to find every animatronic who was trying to kill you, while saving power so you don't have to listen to a small classical piece, then get given a hug from Freddy for the 765th time. Use the camera and flashlight all you want, this time. You have 4 bars of battery life, and they really take their time in going away.
And if that doesn't work, then you have the Freddy disguise which really makes me question how Bonnie reacts when he sees a human and then suddenly sees his boss. If anyone comes through the vent, wea the mask and you'll be fine. At least for the most part, but I'll get into that dumb mechanic in a moment.
And lastly, we have the music box, which you can just tell was put there just to give the player a reason to check the camera. So with all of these pieces of equipment to use for so many enemies, you're always put on edge with not a moment to rest. Sounds like a formula for a scary game, to me.
And it sure is. Most of the people who play this will be sweating like a teenager who is playing pin the tail on the donkey, with the number 1 female student from yoga class. Never a dull moment.
Or at least, that's how it starts off. Point being, this game is hard. And when I say hard, I mean the hard that starts off as frustrating, before quickly downgrading to an expected annoyance. You will die in this game. A lot. Which gives you plenty of time to learn how the mechanics of each animatronic work, and by the time you do, the game becomes as scary as a mansion with a swimming pool made out of jelly. By the time I got to night 4, I knew when every jumpscare was gonna happen, so I just laid back and stared at the screen, waiting for death.
"But Hedgy, if you understand how everything works, then it can't possibly be hard." Well you'd be right if it wasn't for 3 walking, scrawking problems.
Old Bonnie
Old Chika.
And Old Freddy
Chances are, if you have looked at the discussion section of the FNAF2 community, you will find a lot of people stuck on night 3. And these two are exactly why. Sometimes when you put the camera down, you'll see Bonne in front of you with his mouth hanging open, or Chika practicing her part for the scarecrow in the newest drama performance. You have a grand total of less than a second to put the mask on, or you're dead. And you will be doing this a lot. It will probably end up being the only thing that kills you for a while, and since it's so easy to see coming, it doesn't feel like it's there for horror.
On a really good day, you'll get all three in a row without a break, giving you no chance to wind up the music box, and hearing the heartwarming sound of the 3 animatronics giggling because of it.
Which means that night 3 onwards will probably go like this. Flip the camera, wind music box, flash in the hallway, check the vents, occasionially put on mask, repeat until you realise you weren't quick enough, then insert a broken piece of glass through your eye socket. And since there are so many sound effects that tell you where everyone is, you really have no motivation to sight see.
Lastly, we have the minigames that sometimes appear after you die. These have you take control of an animatronic, and walk around in a format that reminds me of hotline miami, before getting jumpscared and going back to the main menu. These exist to tell some more of the story, but I'm guessing that Scott didn't realise you would die so much, which makes these easter eggs get old. And fast.
Looking back at this review, I notice that it sounds like I hate this game. I don't, it's great. And still really fun, even though I know when every scare will happen. There is a great challenge that comes with each night, making it feel very satisfying to win. And at first, you do feel legitmate fear. But after a while, it just becomes a challenge to get through the night, the fear having long passed away.
So, to summarise. It's great, but not as scary as the original

Alright instead of going into the pros and cons of the game, I will just specify whether or not certain groups of people I think will enjoy the game.
If you have not played Dark Souls 1 OR Dark Souls 2 yet, do NOT buy this game. Despite being called 'easier', I would recommned starting with Dark Souls 1 since it is the prelude to Dark Souls 2 and has solid gameplay and a story that makes the game enjoyable to people who play it first. The playerbase is still close to Dark Souls 2: Scholar of the First Sin so don't worry lack of online features.
If you have bought Dark Souls 2 with the DLC, I would recommend not buying this game unless you think you can gain many more hours out of a very similar game or if you are interested in participating in PVP quite a bit.
Alternatively, if you bought Dark Souls 2 without the DLC, I would suggest buying this game if you enjoyed Dark Souls 2 and are interested to see the new DLC along with what has changed in the base game. It is a great deal if you were thinking of buying the DLC since it costs $30 alone while Dark Souls 2: Scholar of the First Sin costs $30 if you already own Dark Souls 2.
If you own Dark Souls 1, never played Dark Souls 2, and feel like you want more, then I would recommned getting Dark Souls 2: Scholar of the First Sin. While people constantly say that Dark Souls 2 is generally a worse game than Dark Souls 1, Dark Souls 2: Scholar of the First Sin improves on a lot of the things that Dark Souls 1 feel short on but also fails to implement certain aspects of gameplay and story properly. Dark Souls 2: Scholar of the First Sin is by no means a perfect game so it does have its weaknesses and strenghs just like any other game. In the end I think it is worth a try and with the steam refund system you can refund the game if you feel like it is not for you. (Casual) Just be sure to not play over two hours if you are on the fence about buying since it can be difficult to stop if you get absorbed. My only exception would be if you are interested in using mods or cheats in the game. Dark Souls 2: Scholar of the First Sin cracks down heavily on cheating and any form of modding so if you want to mod the game at all and are not interested in saving $30 on the DLC, buy Dark Souls 2.
All in all I think Dark Souls 2: Scholar of the First Sin is an amazing game worthy of being the souls franchise. It does have noticible flaws, but it does all the things that you want a souls game to do. It's a great game to play until Dark Souls 3 comes out. :)

The game does appeal to players both new and old to the series itself and the original Dark Souls 2, but personally I feel the former are more likely to really enjoy Scholar. Why? Because the latter cannot help but be reminded of the fact they would have to spend 15€~ on what basically amounts to an elaborate patch; spending more money on what the game should have been from the very beginning.
Bearing in mind what I said about it being an elaborate patch, one could argue it does not solve a lot of real issues. The game is, like the original, still more or less requiring a controller if you do not want to feel like going cycling without pedals. In addition to this, the complete joke that is Soul Memory remains only this time you are allowed to purchase a ring to gain some measure of control over it - great idea right? WRONG. We are back to the "issue" that Soul Levels posed for PvP matchmaking in Dark Souls 1 while still more or less requiring you to forego items in order to play at maximum capacity for a given Soul Memory tier, because those souls would be better spent on improving equipment or leveling up.
Is Dark Souls 2: Scholar of the First Sin a good game? Yeah, it is, in spite of a few glaring issues. For new players I heartily recommend it. If you however already own a copy of the original Dark Souls 2, I would ask you think hard on whether you want to support this kind of greed before making the purchase.

Hello, hello? Uh, well, if you're hearing this, then chances are... you've made a very poor career choice.
Five Nights at Freddy's 2, the sequel to the highly praised Five Nights at Freddy's, brings a lot of new stuff to the jump scare filled table. With more animatronics to fend off and zero doors to use, Five Night's at Freddy's 2 knows how to make your horror game horribly hard. Compared to its predecessor, Five Nights at Freddy's 2 has a lot more tricks up its sleeve, with random death mini-games and a ton of easter eggs. But the question still remains, is Five Nights at Freddy's 2 still as scary as it was before?
Five Nights at Freddy's 2 brings some new gameplay mechanics, as stated above, there are no doors and there is no power generator that can run out. You now depend on a flashlight and a Freddy Fazbear mask. The flashlight is your new power generator in this game. Once you're out of batteries, Foxy will be more than happy to munch your face off. You'll also need this flashlight to shine into the hallway outside your office, and lighten dark corners on the camera feed. The Freddy Fazbear mask is very interesting and works a lot like the old doors. Once an animatronic is in the air vents or in front of you, you'll need to put on the mask to make them go away. If this is not done fast enough, a load jump scare will scare the bejesus out of you. Next to the load of animatronics you have to deal with, you also have to check on the music box every once in a while. If you won't wind up the music box, The Puppet will take good care of you. All these things combined can make some tense scenes, but also a lot of cheap deaths.
Five Nights at Freddy's 2 is a very fun and jump scare filled game. For the story gamers around us, there is a lot of background story to uncover, the forums are full of predictions and theories! But like i said, there are a lot of cheap deaths in the game. Night five and six are mostly based around luck, and make you do the same strategy over and over again. But really, who hasn't heard about Five Nights at Freddy's now? If you're a horror fan who can take a lot of jump scares and fun but sometimes unfair gameplay mechanics? This is your game. This is a quick intro for those who want to get into the franchise but actually haven't played a souls game. I know I needed this when I started.
-You can build a character around a variety of archetypes, want to be a reaper complete with scythe and dark magic? What about a shield and spear hoplite? Maybe you feel like beating people to death with an anvil-on-a-stick while wearing stone armour. You can.
-Fighting isn't just swapping out weapons with different numbers, you get invested in your gear. You've chosen to be a reaper? Well you'd better learn how to reap with that build. No matter your setup you will learn to use it and you will have to behave differently for each. No more "New weapon, I'll just hit bad guys until they die. Now I'm bored with this weapon".
-When you're on fire it feels like being Neo dodging bullets without the slow mo. It could all come crashing down in an instant but for a while you're untouchable.
-Not holding your hand is a selling point but when you don't have a clue about certain game mechanics you're pretty much boned unless you find a guide. Read up on effigies, game progress routes and the Emerald Herald.
-"It's a game that too often sacrifices fun, replaces it with tedium, and tries to defend that choice by calling it a challenge" I'm not proud of quoting gamespot but this was always stuck in my mind. As newcomer, aggroing one enemy at a time, cheeseballing, and even waiting for hp to regen before moving on (I know, I know, but gotta hoard effigies) seemed to be the only way to play. All to avoid having to repeat a section, lose my souls and lose precious max hp.
-Tongue but hole
Summing up, you will have to be persistant. If you can accept that it might take a few dozen deaths to clear an area and let your rage go then it's a rewarding game.

Verdun has come a very long way. It has always been fun but the game has never offered as much as it does today.
- The game has territory capture modes, team death match and free for all
- territory mode is the main game type
- has some things in common with Red Orchestra 2 and Insurgency, but has its own brand of capture and defend
- capture and defend gives teams a chance to attack, counter attack, and if the attacking team doesn't take the objective then the other side gets to attack -- good balance
Criticisms:
- the rifles are modeled well, but we need a training mission to help with how to shoot: judge target distance, we need adjustable sight elevation... it would be good to know how many inches to hold over if your weapon is zeroed at 100 yards but the enemy is 250
- we need better and bug free in game communications
- shifting between standing/crouching/prone is clunkier than it is in real life, this needs to be optimized
- if concertina wire is going to play such a big role then we need classes of soldiers to clear/cut the wire
- the artillery system is a bit hokey and the recon aircraft don't play a realistic role -- in real life they delivered pictures and drawings (YES, DRAWINGS!) to division level leaders
- hit detection suffers and becomes frustrating
- map performance seems to degrade with every map
Remember the game is in pre-release, but it's already fun and the developers have shown their willingness to develop this further. Recommended.

I really enjoyed this game. There isn't much traditional gameplay. It's more like an interactive story that unfolds at the pace you want it to.
The story itself is endearing. I started playing it, and couldn't stop playing it until I got to the end. If I were to put this game into book form, it would make a very short book. It's more like a playable short story.
There's an incredible attention to detail, both in the items and things you find and examine, and in the environment. You're home alone in an old house, and you notice every little creak that the house makes.
I sort of understand the $20 price tag, given the amount of detail and thought that had to go into this game. However, I can't say that the price is worth the experience. It pains me to say that, because I think this is worth experiencing, but had I spent the full amount, I would have been disappointed.
At time of writing, (September 14, 2014) it's part of the current Humble Bundle. It's worth beating the average to get this game, so go do that.
I've heard some call this game scary. It's not. It invokes some small, primal dread that you're not alone in this big empty house, but overall, it's not scary. It did make me feel lots of feelings, and not all of them were good. But that's okay, a game story doesn't have to be good all the time.
Definitely pick up this game if it's on sale, or if you're reading this during the aforementioned Humble Bundle. Just don't expect any agency or choices. Your only choices are how you explore the story.

Imagine Myst, with all of its mystery and wonder, the excellent story telling and strange interactions with the environment.  Now take away everything that made Myst fun and interesting.  Put it in an everyday house and have the script written by someone with a social agenda.
This game was a waste of time, had no real pay-off and had so much potential to be great.  It felt like someone was just telling a story better fit for a half-hour special on the Oprah network.  I wanted there to be some development that took me out of the sludge and made the game worthwhile, but nothing happened.
Pros: Atmosphere was well done at the start.  Sound and voice acting was professionally done.  Controls were simple and the interaction with an empty house gives impressions of thriller games like Slender.  Oh, and the game was blessedly short.
Cons: There was no pay-off.  The story was trite with an obvious social message that got more club fisted as it progressed.  The tension goes away when you realize that this is not a thriller but a drama.  The simplicity of the controls only emphasizes how boring the game is after a while.
Bottom Line: Potential wasted.  Don't waste your money and if you get it free, I recommend reading a good book instead.

Let me say that the criticisms against Gone Home are valid: it's too short, and too pricey for what it offers. DO NOT buy it at full price. I'd say half price is good.
Having followed it during development, I knew what to expect and so I didn't have the wrong expectations: it's a game based on exploring one intricate space, absorbing the story through the detailed objects you come across. It's a very focused experience.
In that regard, Gone Home succeeds. For the two hours (ugh so short) I was in that house, I really was immersed. It felt really lived in, like a real home.
You get to know the characters - your player character and her family - through various items strewn around, and while it's all very in your face and void of subtlety, it's still well made, and endearing. Especially the little sister; I want a kid sister like that.
I've been looking for a game like this. Ever since Tex Murphy: The Pandora Directive, I've been waiting for another game that lets me search premises and detailed rooms in first person, examining objects and looking for clues.
So, how does GH fare? It's... a start. Everything's too easily found, the path through the house is pretty linear. The main story is too simple, and boring. It was the side stories that were more interesting, the ones about the secondary characters, the history of the house... all that.

Game is pretty awesome, highly recommend it. Not for run and gun shooter fans, this game takes patience, intelligence and team work. Each match plays like King of the Hill with a series of trenches, where one side defends and the other side attacks. If attackers take the defenders trench within the time limit (I think 5 minutes) then the timer is reset, and defending team has to retake their trench, if they fail to do so then they retreat to the next trench behind them.
Eventually one side is either pushed too far back to their last trench, or the overall game timer runs out and the side who captured to most trenches win.
The Squad system is pretty interesting, but with some issues. There are multiple squad types each having different rolls, and thus having different soldier types available, but most people play using the German Landers, French Poilues, or British Tommes squad types because they have the most streight forward soldier types in their squad; An officer who uses a pistol by default but can level up to have a rifle and can call in artillery, a Rifleman who can upgrade to be a sniper, A machine gunner who can use a machine gun (go figure), or a Grenadier who carries a lot of grenades.
Apparently the squads themselves level up but from my experience once you create a squad there’s no way to find it when you stop playing and come back later. Usually I find myself joining free spots on existing squads anyway, so take this bit with a grain of salt.
Overall a pretty cool Objective FPS that you can play with friends or by your self.
Pros:
-Great First Person Shooter, very tactical heavy requiring teamwork, brains and patience.
-Straight forward role system that unlocks as you level up.
-Various maps that have different challenges as you try to fight through them.
-Non Toxic player community that is actually pleasent to banter with in the chat.
Cons:
-Player population very, sometimes its hard to get into a server, other times its deserted.
-Wonky Animations, but they're still working on it.
-Some LOD issues with terrain where you can sometimes see players through objects like sandbags or obstacles that are far away.

Alright instead of going into the pros and cons of the game, I will just specify whether or not certain groups of people I think will enjoy the game.
If you have not played Dark Souls 1 OR Dark Souls 2 yet, do NOT buy this game. Despite being called 'easier', I would recommned starting with Dark Souls 1 since it is the prelude to Dark Souls 2 and has solid gameplay and a story that makes the game enjoyable to people who play it first. The playerbase is still close to Dark Souls 2: Scholar of the First Sin so don't worry lack of online features.
If you have bought Dark Souls 2 with the DLC, I would recommend not buying this game unless you think you can gain many more hours out of a very similar game or if you are interested in participating in PVP quite a bit.
Alternatively, if you bought Dark Souls 2 without the DLC, I would suggest buying this game if you enjoyed Dark Souls 2 and are interested to see the new DLC along with what has changed in the base game. It is a great deal if you were thinking of buying the DLC since it costs $30 alone while Dark Souls 2: Scholar of the First Sin costs $30 if you already own Dark Souls 2.
If you own Dark Souls 1, never played Dark Souls 2, and feel like you want more, then I would recommned getting Dark Souls 2: Scholar of the First Sin. While people constantly say that Dark Souls 2 is generally a worse game than Dark Souls 1, Dark Souls 2: Scholar of the First Sin improves on a lot of the things that Dark Souls 1 feel short on but also fails to implement certain aspects of gameplay and story properly. Dark Souls 2: Scholar of the First Sin is by no means a perfect game so it does have its weaknesses and strenghs just like any other game. In the end I think it is worth a try and with the steam refund system you can refund the game if you feel like it is not for you. (Casual) Just be sure to not play over two hours if you are on the fence about buying since it can be difficult to stop if you get absorbed. My only exception would be if you are interested in using mods or cheats in the game. Dark Souls 2: Scholar of the First Sin cracks down heavily on cheating and any form of modding so if you want to mod the game at all and are not interested in saving $30 on the DLC, buy Dark Souls 2.
All in all I think Dark Souls 2: Scholar of the First Sin is an amazing game worthy of being the souls franchise. It does have noticible flaws, but it does all the things that you want a souls game to do. It's a great game to play until Dark Souls 3 comes out. :)

The game does appeal to players both new and old to the series itself and the original Dark Souls 2, but personally I feel the former are more likely to really enjoy Scholar. Why? Because the latter cannot help but be reminded of the fact they would have to spend 15€~ on what basically amounts to an elaborate patch; spending more money on what the game should have been from the very beginning.
Bearing in mind what I said about it being an elaborate patch, one could argue it does not solve a lot of real issues. The game is, like the original, still more or less requiring a controller if you do not want to feel like going cycling without pedals. In addition to this, the complete joke that is Soul Memory remains only this time you are allowed to purchase a ring to gain some measure of control over it - great idea right? WRONG. We are back to the "issue" that Soul Levels posed for PvP matchmaking in Dark Souls 1 while still more or less requiring you to forego items in order to play at maximum capacity for a given Soul Memory tier, because those souls would be better spent on improving equipment or leveling up.
Is Dark Souls 2: Scholar of the First Sin a good game? Yeah, it is, in spite of a few glaring issues. For new players I heartily recommend it. If you however already own a copy of the original Dark Souls 2, I would ask you think hard on whether you want to support this kind of greed before making the purchase.

This is a quick intro for those who want to get into the franchise but actually haven't played a souls game. I know I needed this when I started.
-You can build a character around a variety of archetypes, want to be a reaper complete with scythe and dark magic? What about a shield and spear hoplite? Maybe you feel like beating people to death with an anvil-on-a-stick while wearing stone armour. You can.
-Fighting isn't just swapping out weapons with different numbers, you get invested in your gear. You've chosen to be a reaper? Well you'd better learn how to reap with that build. No matter your setup you will learn to use it and you will have to behave differently for each. No more "New weapon, I'll just hit bad guys until they die. Now I'm bored with this weapon".
-When you're on fire it feels like being Neo dodging bullets without the slow mo. It could all come crashing down in an instant but for a while you're untouchable.
-Not holding your hand is a selling point but when you don't have a clue about certain game mechanics you're pretty much boned unless you find a guide. Read up on effigies, game progress routes and the Emerald Herald.
-"It's a game that too often sacrifices fun, replaces it with tedium, and tries to defend that choice by calling it a challenge" I'm not proud of quoting gamespot but this was always stuck in my mind. As newcomer, aggroing one enemy at a time, cheeseballing, and even waiting for hp to regen before moving on (I know, I know, but gotta hoard effigies) seemed to be the only way to play. All to avoid having to repeat a section, lose my souls and lose precious max hp.
-Tongue but hole
Summing up, you will have to be persistant. If you can accept that it might take a few dozen deaths to clear an area and let your rage go then it's a rewarding game.

I'm a sucker for good music, love stories, and mysteries and this game provided all of those things. The game lasts a little over 2 hours if you take the time to explore like I did.
9/10: The story is about love and rebellion and coming-of-age. There are a couple side stories you can find if you explore. The main story is really well done and the pacing is great. Some of the side stories leave something to be desired, but that's kind of expected.
10/10: The lighting and the feeling that everyone just vanished is genuinely creepy. The house looks like everyone left in a hurry. Drawers and cabinets are left open, things are broken, empty pizza boxes are all over the place. Plus the lights flicker and that's always spooky.
4/10: I wouldn't say this is a walking simulator like one of the tags says. It's more like an exploration simulator. Sure there's a lot of walking, but that's not all there is. You can pick things up and read them and turn them Amnesia-style, but there's no real reason for it. I turned over every object looking for clues or something cool. Nothing. You do find things if you look around though. There are little notes and objects hidden everywhere.
6/10: The characters and their stories are handled a little weird. You know basically nothing about the person you play as except that she likes traveling. The mom's story requires you to explore A LOT. The father is kind of lackluster, but the parents as a whole are alright. The meat of the character development and the story are the main character's sister and her love interest. The minor characters like the uncle and that neighbor kid get name drops like once and are pretty pointless.
2/10: This isn't very well optimized. Like a lot of people have said, there are frame rate crashes all over the place. It puts a lot of stress on your computer for a game that doesn't have a lot going on visually. Maybe there's a patch somewhere but I haven't found one. The lag doesn't make the game unplayable, but it's just frequent enough to be annoying.
10/10: The atmospheric/background music is on point with whats happening in the story and there's cassette tapes (good ol' 90s) laying around that add some pretty good music to the mix. All of the audio is superb.
: 7/10: As much as I loved the story and the music, the performance issues broke the immersion. It's a short game and it's not worth $20. My suggestion is pick it up in a Humble Bundle or wait for a Steam sale. This game is awesome for people who like good stories or for anyone who wants to take a break from fast paced AAA titles. It has very little replay value (maybe one or two more runs after you beat it), but it's a good title overall. Definitely not as bad as some of these reviews make it out to be.

With some time spent both in Dark Souls 2 and SotFS, here are my two cents on both games.
First off, the differences between both games from the top of my head:
Dark Souls 2 had a few paid DLCs that are included in SotFS.
Console players got SotFS for FREE, PC users have to pay for it.
SotFS includes additional enemies (some of which will revisit you a few times);
Some items and bonfires have been relocated, so if you've played Dark Souls 2 before, you might want to comb through each area and make sure you aren't missing anything.
NB: Dark Souls 2 characters will NOT work on SotFS and vice versa!
Pros:
- Way better optimized than Dark Souls, The game runs a stable 60 FPS. Even with the nearly mandatory dsfix, Dark Souls has certain areas that lower your framerate significantly. I do not recall such performance issues to happen in SotFS/DS2 (I might be wrong, however).
- Fluidity - the combat feels a lot more fluid when compared to Dark Souls, animations seem improved, invincibility frames when rolling depend on a certain stat. You will often get hit even if it seems like you would've dodged the attack unless if you invest levels in said stat.
- Fresh start - New areas to explore and a new story to learn.
- Additional enchants - Can enchant your weapon in effects such as poison, without the use of rotten pine resin.
- Warping between bonfires - you can now go from one bonfire to the other without acquiring a certain item.
Cons:
- Soul memory - One of the biggest turn-offs in this game. The more souls you spend on leveling and purchasing items, the higher your soul memory becomes. There is no way to reduce the same. It would at least make sense if the soul memory used for temporary/usable items would not count or would be reduced upon their use. From now on, your character's level will not matter, and what initially seemed like a good idea unfortunately is quite a bane for most players.
- Frustrating areas - Just like Blighttown from the old game, there are certain areas you just want to get over with as soon as possible.
- Invasions - you only get cracked blue and red eye orbs, which cost a lot.
- Hollowing - hollowing works so every time you die, you lose 5% of your total HP, and the effect stacks. While you get a neat visual change with each of your deaths, your health is permanently lowered, down to 50% HP. To revert this, you need to use a human effigy, which restores your human form. Alternatively, you can become a white or gray phantom and successfully assist the host - upon doing so, you are returned to your human form along with some goodies and souls. NB: You can still get invaded while you're a hollow, however you cannot invade others unless you're in your human form.
- Design - the game can feel very linear and unlike in Dark Souls, Miyazaki who's work is revered by the Souls community has not worked at all on Dark Souls 2, nor on SotFS.
- Hitboxes - Infuriating. Example:
Verdict: Dark Souls 2: SotFS is a decent game, however I would personally strongly recommend buying the first one. Why get Dark Souls? Because it's more fun, has a much better story and doesn't feel as linear.
If you have Dark Souls 2 with none of the DLCs just get SotFS when it's on sale (if you don't mind starting over).

is such an insanely rich and expansive game; FromSoft could have released two separate games. Which is kind of what they did.
Back when
was first released people considered it a hollow and bleak follow up to the original
, me included. However it wasn’t without its high points and strengths. FromSoft took much criticism to heart and released three DLC packs with an incredible amount of content in each to offset some of the lacklustre areas from the main game, as well adding several elements that pad up the lacking story somewhat. They wrapped it all up in a new graphics package, slapped a full price tag on it and flung it back onto the selves. A gutsy strategy, but the game is better for it. The game is an immersive role-playing monster that keeps sucking you in. Furthermore, it has an insane amount of options and content to explore and exploit. Finally, it retools and refines many of its predecessor’s aspects.
is a behemoth of a game that merits any self-respecting gamer’s attention.
picks up thousands of years after the original
and continuously throws you down a well of unyielding challenges and adversity with the express purpose of hardening you for the next battle. The original world of
is gone and in its place is a dilapidated, nearly abandoned kingdom called Drangleic. You are an undead, who ventures to this land to find a cure for your, and your family’s hollowing condition. The game sets of off with the bare minimum, as is a staple of the FromSoft narrative style. You’re forced to discover the bulk of the story for yourself. This is where the developers went overboard. Instead of hiding plot and infusing it with delicious lore, they now provide you with the bare minimum of plot and nearly drown you in lore. Admittedly, the lore of
is incredible and novels could be written on its depth and enriching character. However, the lack of apparent plot rather withholds you from thoroughly exploring it. You, as the player, are not motivated to investigate items, characters, or world as explore. The only thing you’re told a few minutes in is to “seek the king”. When you eventually do find the man in question he’ll tell you to seek adversity. Finally facing the final boss is punctuated with a resounding “what the hell was that?”
The thing is, that when you finally discard the narrative’s notions, and do explore on your own accord, you’ll be rewarded immensely. It seems almost as if FromSoft did not just want to make the gameplay difficult, but also the story. The Scholar of the First Sin edition provides some context to the ordeal, but you’re mostly left to your own devices in terms of plot direction and interpretation.
While the story may not be too captivating, the general gameplay is thoroughly addictive. It is common knowledge at this point that the
series are difficult. The difficulty spike from other games requires you to learn and to invest effort. The eventual successes after many a loss will feel monumental. This risk reward structure is enthralling to say the least. Not only do you earn valuable progress, but also experience and valuable items to customise your character and playstyle.
is a genuinely personal experience, and the game offers you near countless tools to differentiate and customise your experience. While the game does force you to picks a class at the very beginning, you easily deviate from your initial resume. From the starting area the world lies open at your feet. Hundreds of weapons to try. Dozens of armours to wear. Loads of magic spells to learn. Zounds of monsters to slay. The game lends itself to all manners of play. You can play a buffed out tank and brave hordes in plate mail. Or stay lithe and swift and put out ludicrous amounts of damage. Physical matter not your thing? The try the magic arsenal. We have lighting, darkness, fire, and poison; even this blue stuff that just kills things. You can have it any way you want, and hardly any play through will be the same. There are even special weapons that combine the styles. The insane degree to which you can adjust, mix and match makes for some incredible fidelity. It is therefore good that the game also has a respec button to mulligan your build when you see fit.
However, it is important that your stomping grounds for your personal build is well tilled, and unfortunately, that is not always the case in
. While character tools are amazing, the level design is somewhat lacking. Rather washed-out areas and straight corridor stages make up the majority of world. A true shame, because the original
and its predecessor
all had environments that were maze like and harrowing to traverse. Making it to the short cut in the old games was a relief. In
it’s just a convenience. This issue is mostly resolved in the three DLC areas that send you into completely disorienting maze like tombs, towers and cities to fight even deadlier enemies, but also find even more and better loot.
From a technical standpoint,
addresses many complaints from its predecessors, but also introduces some new, and unwelcome changes. Praise be to the sun when the backstab got nerfed. Praise be to Vendrick when the online connection now takes place via dedicated servers instead of P2P. Hail to the crowns for the new dual wield animations that allow for the amazing samurai, ninja and berserker builds that flay and destroy the many bosses.
has taken care to make good on several sigmatic issues with the original, and FromSoft has succeeded in most cases. The result is a more playable and durable system that is more manageable to use.
On the flipside though, the game introduces a stat called soul memory to govern the interaction between players. It basically changes the thresholds for cooperation and invasions from level based to purely experience based. This skews to balance to nearly ridiculous levels where proper online play becomes extremely hard or downright non-existent until you manage to reach a later section of the game where you may or may not fit in. Furthermore, boss design, the Souls’ series great pride, has taken a hit. Most bosses are souped up guys in armour with broken tracking and disjointed hitboxes. The number of monstrosities that do show up are hardly a challenge. Some fights against these blood knights are extremely amazing, but the majority is forgettable. Once again, the DLC bosses fix this issue to a great extent.
In general, enemy design is based on “guys in armour.” What is even worse is that FromSoft decided to just go for the horde approach when it came to enemy placement and difficulty tweaks. When you die it’s either due to a horde of cheap, enemies, or one enemy with infallible tracking on its weapon. The Scholar version addresses this with amended enemy placement, but the damage is already done.
Despite some shortcomings, the overwhelming amount of content, immersion and options ultimately make
a main course on any video game dinner menu. The meaty length and beefy options allow for a multitude of approaches that can fit anyone’s playstyle. While the story doesn’t flavour the dish too much, the underlying textures provide a distinct taste that will have to dig in a little deeper. Although the chef’s final changes may divide the guests on what wine goes best with it, at the end of it, you’ll be satisfied and well fed.

You will actually find it more enjoyable to play the game with someone, and I mean someone actually sitting next to you, so you can endlessly speculate what really did happen in the house. Gone Home actually makes for a great game(?) to play(?) on the couch.

"Gone Home" is NOT a game. It's more of an interactive experience in the vein of "Dear Esther" (although with two more puzzles to solve than that title). You play a student who comes home after a year abroad only to find your parent's house empty and it's up to you to find out why. The mystery is slowly revealed to you as you explore the house and discover notes and letters written by your sister.  I won't reveal anymore than that because well, I don't want to spoil it for you. Gone Home does a few things very nicely. The house is well designed and even though this isn't a scary title, there is a lonely and forboding atmosphere to be found. The sound design is also nicely done and the story is nicely told, even if it may not be everyone's cup of tea. Gone Home is a true interactive experience as there is no right or wrong way to go. You are left on the front porch of the house and the rest is up to you. You can pick up and examine anything and everything in this house which is both a blessing and a curse. Due to the non linearity there are times you'll literally be picking up everything because there might be a note there to give you some extra story points. Gone Home  is also very short. The first game was an excellent horror game, perfectly giving a feeling of stress, dread, and fright to many who played it. However, after a while it became to predictable and therefore not as scary, making it less enjoyable to play. The only thing that could revive my interest in the game was a sequel. And that is exactly what Five Nights at Freddy's did. Not only did it up the difficulty by doubling the number of animatronics, but it also made the patterns more erratic and less predictable, giving the game longevity. It brought over and intensifed the same feelings that FNaF had given to the player so it is a better scare in general. However, there is another thing that FNaF2 did that FNaF did not: Add depth. In the first game it was simply sit in a Chuck-e-Cheeses and try not to die, but in this game the between nights cinematics, the minigames, the  puppet, and even the phone calls added a layer of story and eerieness absent from the original. It leaves the gamer with questions about the story, and even throws in hints suggesting things that seem impossible (like the puppet being the ringleader of the first game). The last phone calls in the game are especially eerie and that last phone call even has a plot twist which answers questions then raises many others. This mystery floating around the game makes it much more enjoyable to play, making it not only a good scare, but a great game as well.

The only reason I own this is because it was part of an indie bundle that contained some good games I liked the look of. £15 for what amounts to a short novella is a ridiculous price really so even though I am the sort of person who wants to give everything a fair go that initial price barrier is what stopped me.
So I finally got around to seeing what the fuss was about and while I wouldn't call it terrible at all, it's certainly not GOTY material. I started off looking at everything I could (highly recommended to lower mouse sensitivity). Even though I had known about the hidden room with the key to the attic I left it til last since I felt I was going to explore this as intended. Interaction isn't heavy, you can pick up things like cups and specifically placed books but not everything else. There was a letter that lampshaded the whole "spooky flickering lights" trope that could lead you into thinking this is a horror game. It is not. It is much like exploring the ruins of a building in Fallout as you read old notes, follow along the corridors and come across the remains of the people and what happened to them. However since there is no combat, travelling outside the house or interacting with other people they had to ramp up the effort they put into the story and "level design".
The game is teenage lesbian love story with a heavy dose of rebelion. Girl meets girl, girl ends up becoming punk and rebelious like other girl, parents don't like what is going on, other girl has to leave, ect. While the summary may make it seem rather tripe, it's not that bad, it's just not that amazing either. The short story format probably hinders the kind of story they are trying to tell here since you don't get to know the characters long enough for what you find out about them to have much of an impact. While there are a few members of the family the story doesn't touch much on anyone else besides the youngest daughter. In fact you may forget you are playing as the eldest due to how little use of this character is taken. Despite this I actually was disappointed that I heard so little about the mother and father compared to the daughter. Pretty much everything in Gone Hom revolves around the youngest daughter and her girlfriend.
Set design is pretty good for the most part. There are places where thought is put into why certain objects are where they are, you can tell what happened there as a result. There's the rejection letter close to the alchohol, the pillow fort in the TV room, the opened clothes drawers in the parents room and the bottle of hair dye in the bathroom.
The last of which brings me to my next point, the journal entries. As you explore the house you will come across various letters and items. When you pick up certain ones a narrated journal entry of the star of the game is played. I assume that these are all from the book you pick up at the end. Of course the problem with telling the meat of the story through this journal is if you don't tear the pages out and spread them across the house then you have to leave them intact and the player spends most of their time wandering around not knowing much until the end where they spend 5 minutes reading up on a large percentage of the story.
So instead you get this story fed to you though intangible "audiologs" that are attached to what appear to be normal items at first glance until you put them down and cue the narrator. This isn't bad per se but it's clear that the developers had more focus on this being a story told through traditional means than they would have liked. They wanted the story to be told through exploring the house and picking up bits and pieces but they ended up relying a bit too heavily on the audio logs.
I smiled a bit at some points where nostalgia was used for audience hooks. There's a bunch of nostalgia spread around which seems to be one of the things that got critics hooked. The other is the lesbian romance.
Had the star of the show been a boy or the girlfriend switched with a boy then I'm sure people wouldn't have given this anywhere as much praise as it has gotten. While the VA for the star of the story delivered her lines brilliantly and with emotion, she was still voicing an average short story. The story was too short for the characters to properly hook you at all and the plot of it was rather standard life. I wouldn't be surprised if critics praised this because anything less would have possibly risked them being labeled as homophobes.
A book I read, The Lovely Bones, is somewhat similar to this in ways. Besides dealing with mature subjects it essentially features an outsider viewing their family unseen and how they live their lives. However the differences are plentiful. Besides being a written novel it benefits from it's medium and allows you to connect to the characters in the way that Gone Home didn't manage to do. The Lovely Bones also focuses on various family members including that of the outsider rather than mostly on a single one. You get a better sense of relationships as a result too.
Had Gone Home instead had the main character be a ghost viewing their family it could have really told a far more immersive story. You could have the family members actually be in the house interacting with each other rather than reading letters in an empty house. The story could have gone on a lot longer as a result allowing you to connect with the characters more. Why you could even affect at least the progression of the story by interacting with objects to influence the family members to do certain things. Though this would require far more writing, modeling and even animation to do this.
-----
Gone Home is an average story where the focus is clearly on one character and the others just serve support roles. Exploration is looking around a room, finding objects and letters that trigger story points and finding hidden rooms and passages because spooky inherited house reasons. There is a little thinking at some points to find and uncover certain points of the story but not much else.
All in all it's a risky buy even at 75% off. Not at all deserving of it's praise but it tries some interesting things that will hopefully inspire better people to have a crack at something great. Ask yourself, "Am I the kind of person that is drawn to cheap pandering that it can make me like an average story more than I ever would rather than feel somewhat insulted at the attempt". If Yes you might like Gone Home, if no then think about it before trying this because that teenage lesbian romance and rebellion story is the selling point here, not the exploration aspect.

is such an insanely rich and expansive game; FromSoft could have released two separate games. Which is kind of what they did.
Back when
was first released people considered it a hollow and bleak follow up to the original
, me included. However it wasn’t without its high points and strengths. FromSoft took much criticism to heart and released three DLC packs with an incredible amount of content in each to offset some of the lacklustre areas from the main game, as well adding several elements that pad up the lacking story somewhat. They wrapped it all up in a new graphics package, slapped a full price tag on it and flung it back onto the selves. A gutsy strategy, but the game is better for it. The game is an immersive role-playing monster that keeps sucking you in. Furthermore, it has an insane amount of options and content to explore and exploit. Finally, it retools and refines many of its predecessor’s aspects.
is a behemoth of a game that merits any self-respecting gamer’s attention.
picks up thousands of years after the original
and continuously throws you down a well of unyielding challenges and adversity with the express purpose of hardening you for the next battle. The original world of
is gone and in its place is a dilapidated, nearly abandoned kingdom called Drangleic. You are an undead, who ventures to this land to find a cure for your, and your family’s hollowing condition. The game sets of off with the bare minimum, as is a staple of the FromSoft narrative style. You’re forced to discover the bulk of the story for yourself. This is where the developers went overboard. Instead of hiding plot and infusing it with delicious lore, they now provide you with the bare minimum of plot and nearly drown you in lore. Admittedly, the lore of
is incredible and novels could be written on its depth and enriching character. However, the lack of apparent plot rather withholds you from thoroughly exploring it. You, as the player, are not motivated to investigate items, characters, or world as explore. The only thing you’re told a few minutes in is to “seek the king”. When you eventually do find the man in question he’ll tell you to seek adversity. Finally facing the final boss is punctuated with a resounding “what the hell was that?”
The thing is, that when you finally discard the narrative’s notions, and do explore on your own accord, you’ll be rewarded immensely. It seems almost as if FromSoft did not just want to make the gameplay difficult, but also the story. The Scholar of the First Sin edition provides some context to the ordeal, but you’re mostly left to your own devices in terms of plot direction and interpretation.
While the story may not be too captivating, the general gameplay is thoroughly addictive. It is common knowledge at this point that the
series are difficult. The difficulty spike from other games requires you to learn and to invest effort. The eventual successes after many a loss will feel monumental. This risk reward structure is enthralling to say the least. Not only do you earn valuable progress, but also experience and valuable items to customise your character and playstyle.
is a genuinely personal experience, and the game offers you near countless tools to differentiate and customise your experience. While the game does force you to picks a class at the very beginning, you easily deviate from your initial resume. From the starting area the world lies open at your feet. Hundreds of weapons to try. Dozens of armours to wear. Loads of magic spells to learn. Zounds of monsters to slay. The game lends itself to all manners of play. You can play a buffed out tank and brave hordes in plate mail. Or stay lithe and swift and put out ludicrous amounts of damage. Physical matter not your thing? The try the magic arsenal. We have lighting, darkness, fire, and poison; even this blue stuff that just kills things. You can have it any way you want, and hardly any play through will be the same. There are even special weapons that combine the styles. The insane degree to which you can adjust, mix and match makes for some incredible fidelity. It is therefore good that the game also has a respec button to mulligan your build when you see fit.
However, it is important that your stomping grounds for your personal build is well tilled, and unfortunately, that is not always the case in
. While character tools are amazing, the level design is somewhat lacking. Rather washed-out areas and straight corridor stages make up the majority of world. A true shame, because the original
and its predecessor
all had environments that were maze like and harrowing to traverse. Making it to the short cut in the old games was a relief. In
it’s just a convenience. This issue is mostly resolved in the three DLC areas that send you into completely disorienting maze like tombs, towers and cities to fight even deadlier enemies, but also find even more and better loot.
From a technical standpoint,
addresses many complaints from its predecessors, but also introduces some new, and unwelcome changes. Praise be to the sun when the backstab got nerfed. Praise be to Vendrick when the online connection now takes place via dedicated servers instead of P2P. Hail to the crowns for the new dual wield animations that allow for the amazing samurai, ninja and berserker builds that flay and destroy the many bosses.
has taken care to make good on several sigmatic issues with the original, and FromSoft has succeeded in most cases. The result is a more playable and durable system that is more manageable to use.
On the flipside though, the game introduces a stat called soul memory to govern the interaction between players. It basically changes the thresholds for cooperation and invasions from level based to purely experience based. This skews to balance to nearly ridiculous levels where proper online play becomes extremely hard or downright non-existent until you manage to reach a later section of the game where you may or may not fit in. Furthermore, boss design, the Souls’ series great pride, has taken a hit. Most bosses are souped up guys in armour with broken tracking and disjointed hitboxes. The number of monstrosities that do show up are hardly a challenge. Some fights against these blood knights are extremely amazing, but the majority is forgettable. Once again, the DLC bosses fix this issue to a great extent.
In general, enemy design is based on “guys in armour.” What is even worse is that FromSoft decided to just go for the horde approach when it came to enemy placement and difficulty tweaks. When you die it’s either due to a horde of cheap, enemies, or one enemy with infallible tracking on its weapon. The Scholar version addresses this with amended enemy placement, but the damage is already done.
Despite some shortcomings, the overwhelming amount of content, immersion and options ultimately make
a main course on any video game dinner menu. The meaty length and beefy options allow for a multitude of approaches that can fit anyone’s playstyle. While the story doesn’t flavour the dish too much, the underlying textures provide a distinct taste that will have to dig in a little deeper. Although the chef’s final changes may divide the guests on what wine goes best with it, at the end of it, you’ll be satisfied and well fed.
