POSITIVE: The Content is outstanding!!!!!! There are mini-bosses after mini-bosses and the world is massive which is a treasure-cove of awesomness! I have clocked many hours of this game and I still think I have a long way to go. In each area, you are stopped possibly by a door that needs to be opened. It is ok, you can move on to another area where you can continue exploring, which is suppose to be Dark Souls main objective: "making" you explore other areas rather than the specified path. By using this objective, the game is not linear, it is an "open-world". If every game would follow this method, it will leave an insurmountable time of fun!
POSITIVE: The Visuals in Dark Souls II: SotFS is A-MAZING!!! I love standing in Majula and overseeing the sea. The work in other areas is also amazing I must say because it brings you into the game whereever you may be. Words cannot describe but if you are to buy this game, you will put your controller down and stare at the beautiful scenery before your eyes. There are even mods that will enable you to have a gloomy and dark atmosphere like the original Dark Souls game.
POSITIVE: The weapons upon weapons upon weapons!!!! There is a variety of weapons to choose, dual wield, cuddle, spells to cast, and dominate with. It is in your hands to combine and absolutely dominate the field. This, right here, is the best of what SotFS can provide to anybody playing this game. ENDLESS AMOUNTS OF COMBINATIONS AND ENDLESS FUN!!!!
POSITIVE: What saved this game from my sour taste was the DLC. My God the content was phenominal! Every area you enter is a beautiful yet skin-crawling experience. Ivory King is by far my favorite area as well as story when you dive into it more. The content can be finish in 20-30 hours all-together, but it mostly depends on the individual. (I'm experienced with the DS games so I knew what I needed to do.)
NEUTRAL: The Music is beyond clarity compared to the other Soul games. It brings out areas with melancholy and forboding environments that leave either you scared for your life or pleasantly happy to be in that specific area. Nevertheless, the music "tried" to make itself dark but everywhere I went seemed not an eerie place to be. (The last song at the ending is a pleasure to listen to!)
NEGATIVE: Covenanats (or online multiplayer) are awesome to be in now rather than Dark Souls (it was good but not as frequent when it came to invasions.) The basis of SotFS is the premise of multiplayer so most of the covenants would be used quite often right? No! The only factions that are mainly played are Blood Brothers, Blue Setinals, Bell Keepers, Dragon Bros, and Sunlight Bros. The others have a little love but it is a tedious task to join the rat covenant since you have to wait for players to enter your dungeon. I cannot immerse myself in these covenants unlike the original DS. In DS, whichever covenant I joined "meant" something. It was kill for the dragon, kill for humanity, or uphold justice to the weak. But with SotFS, we are brought to an atmosphere of kill for pleasure kind of idea which should hold true to what covenant you enter.
NEGATIVE: The Lore and Characters are terrible compared to Demon's Souls and Dark Souls. The previous Soul games have boundless backstories to each and every character you meet that makes you feel sadness, despair, grief, and empathy. You want to help them like any person would but nothing will help them, no matter how much you want to. (Maiden Astrea--*tear*.) Every character you meet "tragically" has a heart-wrenching ending that will stick to your mind forever leaving you hopeless. (Artorias, do I need say more?!) As for Dark Souls II, the characters are not memorable in anyway. Yes, you speak to them where they talk about their dark past but it does not even compare to the dark atmosphere of the previous games. Honestly, why take out the most vivid and memorable moments of the Dark Souls Franchise and make it in to a full-fledged difficult game (which is honestly not hard at all???) With SotFS, they tried to bring back the lore for each of the bosses but in the end it was a slap to the face for us fans; for instance, the headless snake girl's lore is a princess loved her, ditched her, she wanted to look like a babe forever, and was sucummb to it and messed everyone up. THE END! WTF?! Also in the previous games, you have backstories to the enemy bosses (by reading their equipment or when you talk to NPC's.)
NEGATIVE: The Bosses in Dark Souls II are, do I have to say, TERRIBLE!!!! If you are a veteran of Dark Souls and Demon's Souls you know what I am talking about. Almost every boss you meet is humanoid and has the same technique which is applied by easily moving around in a 360°. It tears my heart in how simple the bosses are. I do not know what the developers from From Software were thinking but the only thing that they implemented during this game was to make it as difficult as possible, and to do this is by pitting you against more than 2-3 more bosses or to include mini-units to make your life miserable. Basically a gang-bang of bosses and mini-units to pummel you. This is not difficult anymore. The only thing this game will train you to be is the most patient person ever! Nevertheless with the updated version of SotFS, Glass Knight actually looks like a whole different guy! He ACTUALLY raises his sheild when you cast spells and is ACTUALLY a challenge now! I was so happy when they did this. Honestly, he was a complete mess with the base game of DS II.
Closing Statement:
I really do not have anything else to say, but if you are expecting a game that is better or up-to-par with Demon's Souls and Dark Souls, this is not the game. Even though I have played Demon's Souls and Dark Souls (countless hours) I must say, sadly, that this game lacks the essence of what made the Soul games a unique playing experience. I believe with the hype the original Dark Souls received with "prepare to die". From Software's focus was to make our lives as miserable as possible by creating a game where "difficulty" was to throw as many enemies at you as they can. But in truth, they forgot the most valuable asset to their game: memorable characters and their mysterious lore.
SCORE---85

Gone Home is a personal thing. If I were to answer the question "Should I buy this?", it would depend on who you are.
1. Are you patient?
2. Do you like to drink in your environment, explore and discover a good story rather than being hand-fed it?
3. Do you like "games as art"?
4. Do you enjoy "walking simulators"? (No action or puzzles)
5. Is this game on sale at the time?
6. Are the 90's full of childhood nostalgia?
If you agree with all of those, then yes, it's worth your time. I don't recommend paying full price simply because it's far too short for what is asked for and there really isn't much content. It is a one-time experience that'll stick with you in memory, and you may not even consider it to be a video game. It is something indescribable. I found myself in tears more than once due to the introspection and empathy this little gem put me through.
Don't let the outpour of negative reviews deter you from at least giving it a look.

I lay in the trenches of the german first line listening to the mortars drop and the machine gun bullets wizzing by over my head. I take brief pod shots at the enemy line but have a hard time seeing anything through the grime and smoke. Then I hear an all too familair sound.....Für das Vaterland! Attacke! Attacke! Our NCO had just ordered us to charge the enemy lines and seeing that spreading cloud of chlorine gas on the horizon sure dident help puersuade the descision. I briefly considered shooting myself in the foot or hiding behind our line somewhere but what real soldier would do that?
"Screw it" I thought, and with that I bounded up out of the trenches and proceeded to run for my life hearing noise of war and whistle of bullets all around me. Knowing if I hesitated now, even for a second, I would most likely end up facedown in the mud. Reminding myself of the noise variances akin to bullets, A hiss means its close but a snag means its a near miss. If you hear the latter then you better hit the ground like a fat man chasing a doughnut.
Needless to say the next several minutes are a blurr of mud, screams, and smoke. Seeing several of my comrades fall in front of me and not get up again, knowing I might soon be joining them I close the bolt on my Grewher 98 as I get close enough to the enemy line to see heads moving about. Several of my fellows in a foxhole beside me raise up to run into the enemy trench which lay devestated from artillery fire, I notice movement in front of me. Several brits had rose up to take shots at my allies. I expose myself out of my fox hole and pick them off using 3 of my 5 shots earning myself 4 kills, as one of my bullets had went through my enemies neck and into his NCO behind him,  I see my friends scramble into the trench all safe from the horrors of No Mans Land. Then I see more movement on my right and turn to see the barrel of a MG sticking out amonst the sandbags. I close my eyes muttering a curse under my breath and accept my fate as I hear the sound of the machine gun open fire.
I reopen my eyes and find myself back in the trench I had just fought my way out of just to do it all over again. Except now the enemy was charging us.
9/10 would die for my friends again
P.S. Listen to a Sabaton playlist while playing this, its OP as ♥♥♥♥ >:D

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

Tread with caution. If you are open to a narrative the requires sympathy and honor for an experience that is often difficult and tragic for people who actaully have to live it - then this game is brilliant. If you are looking for standard-fare fast-paced excitement, then keep moving.
That being said if you are open to the former but have exerience with the latter - this experience is worth it. You will be teased with the occasionally standard tropes of an atmosperic horror to discover instead warmth and heart. This game acknowledges the expectations that gamers bring with them and instead delivers a human experience in place of simple thrills.
It is understandable that many object to not being served what is usually expected in what is traditionally defined as a 'game' but even those who object have to admit that Gone Home is attempting something authentic. For those who can apprecite this, Gone Home  is worhty of respect.

Writing a review for the best game you've played in your life is a really challenging task, it's even harder than finishing Dark Souls II without dying. I'm not sure what to say, every aspect of this game is better than perfect. Dark Souls II is as good as a video game can possibly be, every person in the world should play this not just hardcore gamers.

I can't believe I haven't left a review for this game yet. It is a awesome WWI shooter. Don't expect to survive more than 2 hits and most of the time it is a one shot kill. Expect to die.  A LOT. When you first start out you are gonna want to go gunho as most shooters will let you.
When defending, everyone lines up on the trench to drop anyone charging forward to stop them from capturing. Expect to sit in a trench for a long time killing people as bodies fill the trench.
When attacking, expect the same treatment from your enemies. You need to hop from crater to crater to make it to their trenches to capture it. If you fail to capture it in time, you will need to retreat in time so you aren't executed. The game has a system that are basically killzone if you are in them for to long. Each side has different squads you can play as with four people per squad. Each squad has different roles and different weapons. Then, each role has three levels or upgrades they can have.
I highly recommend this game if you want more than a run and gun shooter where accuracy is key.

From there it progresses with a strong sense of foreboding - I often had to look around quickly just to see if I was being watched by someone...

Play it in one go. It's basically like walking around in a book.
I wouldn't call it a game as such, there's nothing to do really apart from scrutinize everything and read, so I wouldn't buy this for the game quality - but definitely for the story. Oh and obviously not for anything more than what it's worth - a fiver at the absolute max!

I'm a big fan of Five Nights at Freddy's, so I was pleasantly surprised to see the sequel release much earlier than expected. But is it just a lazy cashgrab that takes advantage of the wild popularity of its predecessor, or is it a worthy sequel?
I won't go into the story too much, because if I did I would simply give away the unexpected twist at the end. All you really need to know is that you play as a night guard at a family restaurant called Freddy Fazbear's Pizzeria, a Chuck-e-Cheese rip-off, where the animatronics go loopy during the night and try to rip your face off. You have to do whatever you can to stay alive from 12 PM until 6 AM. The game tells its background story in very subtle ways. The reason why the mascots are so violent, or possibly even sentient to begin with, is open for interpretation.
The basic concept is the same as in the first game; you are stuck in the security room and can use the cameras to survey the rooms in the restaurant. When the mascots get too close or decide to attack, you have a simple method of defending yourself. Since there are no more doors to close this time around, you have an empty Freddy Fazbear head you can wear to temporarily fool the animatronics. You also have a flashlight to check dark areas, and vent lights to check the two vents in the room. Also new is the music box that needs to be wound up regularly. If it stops, it spells inevitable death. It's another thing to manage, and another source of stress.
Five Nights at Freddy's 2 bumps up the amount of hostile animatronics to 11 in total (as opposed to 4 in the original game). Not all of the characters are active in the early nights though, and the game does a pretty good job at easing you into it. In the last nights however, it throws everything your way, and you have to use everything you've learned so far to survive.
Five Nights at Freddy's 2 is NOT an easy game! It requires fast reflexes, a lot of practice, strategy and a bit of luck. It consistently challenges you throughout all of its nights, forcing you to adapt and learn the new mechanics. You're going to die, a lot! When all the animatronics are coming after you, the gameplay becomes extremely hectic and nerve-wracking.
I feel that Five Nights at Freddy's 2 is in fact too difficult for its own good. When you are forced to replay the same night over and over again, the scariness wears off quickly. Jumpscares lose their effect and simply become an exclamation point on your defeat. The randomness and sometimes cheapness can be frustrating, but not so much that you don't want to give it another shot. It's addicting and fun, and immensely satisfying when you finally survive the night.
If you somehow survive the nightmare that is night 6, you unlock the 7th night, which allows you to customize the AI of all the animatronics except for 1. This was a neat addition to the first one, but here it's probably one of the best things about the game! With such a large line-up, there are so many possibilities to play the game the way you want to. Want to face off against one super powered animatronic? You can. Want to see what it looks like when you get killed by Mangle? Just put her AI on 20 and deactivate the rest. You can make it as easy or difficult on yourself as you want, and it adds so much to the game's longevity and replay value. If that wasn't enough, there are a bunch of preset challenges that, when you beat them, unlock cute plushies that appear on your desk.
There are a few things that bother me about FNaF 2, however. For some reason, the mask button won't work (or even appear) immediately after you put down the cameras. Since the timing to put that thing on is so unforgiving at times, it's a frustrating problem that can be solved with a patch. (So hop to it, Scott!) Also, Foxy seems a bit OP. He's very active, even when his AI is set to 0, and a complete jerk on the higher settings. Finally, the mini games. Every now and again when you die, you play an Atari 2600-esque mini-game that tells a bit of background story. That's all fine, but they can't be skipped. After dying, I want to try again immediately, but I can't skip the mini-games so I have to sit through them first. I found that quitting the game and starting it up again is actually a faster solution.
To wrap it up, Five Nights at Freddy's 2 offers revamped game mechanics that are fun but hectic. It loses its scare factor rather fast due to its high difficulty, and it doesn't have the creepy atmosphere that the first one does in my opinion. None of that means that it isn't tense, however, and your heart rate will increase frequently. It's a solid sequel, be it with some flaws, that just happened to be finished sooner than expected.
Don't forget; in case of Foxy, mash ctrl!

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

Ok so I'm well aware of the controveries. The LGBT stuff, the fact that it sells itself as a horror game initially and then isn't one, etc.
But that's irrevalent in my case, for I am going to rate this solely on what it is: A Walking Simulator and Visual Novel.
And it does those well. It describes a story of love in an era when such love would be frowned upon. And yes, it is a political point, but the idea people have with that game that it has a political agenda seems a bit far-fetched in my opinion.
The story is compelling, at least in my opinion. Picking up journal pieces and slowly piecing them together leads to a strong narrative.
But most people aren't willing to buy a story for $20 when they could buy another game.
So do what I did. Buy it via Humble Bundle. Or get it on sale.
Cause at those points, the sappy narrative will be worth your while.

The Good: This isn't your normal first person shooter where you can run around on your own and rack up the points. Sure, you can do that in Verdun, but it won't get you anywhere very far. The gameplay is based around solid team work and good communication, something you don't normally expect to see worked into fps games often. It makes for an enjoyable and satisfying gameplay in a time setting that is not explored through games very well, but the sounds, guns, and different maps really put you feel like you're in the Great War, hunkering down trying to avoid bullets and artillery, and then sprinting to the enemy trench to take out the enemy.
The Bad: There isn't really anything terrible that I have encountered yet in Verdun. I suppose one improvement I can suggest for the developers, however, is to somehow implement a tank or two on the battlefield, a major part of the war. You are able to use a lot of new "modern" weaponry in the game like grenades, machine guns, submachine guns, gas, and even planes, but no tanks. The team balancing sytem is a nice and welcome touch, but sometimes the game is too lopsided and things can turn south every game. Not sure exactly how to better that.
In summary, it's a fun and creative WW1 fps. If you're looking for a different type of shooting game, I'd recommend this one.

The game lays itself out very clearly from the get-go. It's not an action game. You're not going to get the crap scared out of you. This is not amnesia. It's an interactive story in which you find yourself in an empty house and figure out why, exactly, the place is so damn empty.
Picking up scraps of evidence about who, exactly, your family are. It's like being thrust into someone else's life without knowing the first thing about them - but by the end, I felt that I intimately knew the protagonist's family.
If you're not a fan of reading, you're going to have a bad time. If you'd rather blast the heads off of all who oppose you, you might want to skip this one. Think of it as an adventure game light. There really aren't a ton of goals or puzzles to find in a concrete sense - sure, finding items will unlock more information about the family and more rooms to the house, eventually, but the big puzzle is finding out who you are, who your family is, and what, exactly, is going on with your sister.
Really though, I can't for the life of me figure out why all of these people giving the game thumbs down bought the game in the first place. Do they just rush into purchases without at all knowing what they're getting into? Did they see FPS and think that they're going to be fragging ghosts or some crap?
All in all, I'd totally recommend this game. Just know what you're getting into.

It's rare I find a first person shooter I like as they sort of all seem similar to me. Although Verdun is simplistic with it's guns (it is WW1), the terrain and the way they organized the classes is what makes this game very peculiar.
The setting is WW1. The battlefront is eastern France. It's you and your squad trying to push the front lines. Well, only if you choose that game mode. Verdun boasts three game modes for the moment : front lines (where it's a defend/advance territory tactic), offensive in which your constantly pushing back defenders to take control of new areas and lastly, last stand where you and a few other players have to hold back hordes of opposing players. The guns themselves are simplistic and depending whether you're playing as an Entente soldier or Central powers soldier, will determine the type of guns you use. Some guns have more ammo than other guns but (speaking specifically about rifles) each gun is relatively the same. Each player is given a rifle and a pistol. The squad leader is stuck with a pistol and cannot holster a rifle. This player has binoculars instead. With this, the squad leader is able to tell the squad where to advance as well as launch mortar/artillery fire to his choosing. The class system is a little bit different in Verdun than other games. You are not actively allowed to jump from class to class as it may be occupied already by another player. This player has to accept your offer to switch classes. This is important as this game is highly based on team work. It is near impossible to advance or defend without the help of your team mates. Most of the guns offer a one-shot kill but head shots do count for extra points. Some classes even have some high powered machine guns if you rank up enough! I should also add there is a ranking system in place where after each match you will be given experience points to unlock further arsenals.
The maps/terrain are what really set apart this game from other shooters. You can't simply start running and gunning. Everything is a calculated move and no-mans land is really dangerous. You never know whose peaking from their trench waiting to pick you off. You can however, move slowly and try to remain undetected. Moving slowly and moving with squad mates really increase your chances of winning. Some action players may not like this "look-then-move" strategy but it's what really distinguishes the game. I'm a personal Halo fan and love the running-gunning-blowing up sort of stuff. This gives me a little break in that and also forces me to really work on my aim. It can be quite the thrill trying to advance and sneak behind enemy lines. Don't go too far though or you may be killed by the game for staying out of the playable area. All basic controls are here. WASD provides for basic movement while the mouse let's you point and shoot where you want. "G" throws a grenade (when you get one) while "V" is melee. I should add some grenades are gas grenades in which you will need to equip your mask to avoid further damage. A great feature in this game is the ability to crouch or prone when necessary. Space will stand you up or allow you to jump. Holding "shift" (or sprint) while aiming down your sights will make your player hold his breath for a better shot.
The
aren't too bad at this stage. Their up there but I think they could do a little better. I have a brother (whose really into WW1/WW2) also mentioned some of the trenches are way too clean. I understand the game has to look neat to a point but some realism would be appreciated. I wouldn't mind seeing mud being slapped up by a player as he's running, or even mud pits that can slow players down. The
are okay at the moment and aren't extremely immersive or over the top. The basic sounds are there but adding a few more things may take the player to another level. Hearing shots skimming over your head can't be beat.
Overall, this game has some huge potential. I'll be keeping an eye on it to see where it goes. I'm hoping down the line they add a few more perks and add a few more options for players to play with. I know it's world war 1, but even adding a "radio" that let's you "report" enemy positions may be cool! Luckily, there is a system now in place that takes care of this.

Putting aside the fame/infamy of this game and going into it skeptical and with an open mind, with the sneaking suspicion that I probably wouldn't care for it, I actually got engrossed immediately and couldn't put it down once I started. I see that all the reviews on the store page are negative, but yes, I really rather enjoyed this game. I didn't even think I would, but I did. I feel like the press made a bigger deal of this game than it probably deserved, and that the reviews I see here seem to be backlashing against that. People should just take it for what it is. Nothing more, nothing less. And what it is is an enjoyable little game. So with that said, here's why I like it:
It's a personal and touching story presented in an interesting way. I myself like to examine every little object in every little room in whatever game I play, so the gameplay happens to tailor to me in that way. I found it appealing to be alone in this empty house examining every little thing and getting some little details into the story, a glimpse into this family's lives and personalities and flaws and desires. It's all pretty intricate, and there's a lot that can be missed. I think it was pretty cool to see the story of this family unfold before my eyes without any of them actually being there. It's a personal experience for you, and the character you play as, since you are the only one there in this empty house, and to figure out what the ♥♥♥♥ happened here you just have to poke around and look at all the ordinary little objects in each room. Just about every mudane little thing in the house tells some sort of story, and that's what was so fascinating about this whole game. That, and the lonley atmosphere and realism. Although, the ineraction of the characters via notes may be a little strange.
And on that note, I feel like it would have worked more in the game's favor if there weren't voiceover journals. I think you should have just read them; that really would have drove home the whole indirect, subtle storytelling thing. Granted, the voiceover brings you closer to the character, makes her more relatable and adds some dramatic flair. But it would kind of take me out of it when it happened. Like, how am I hearing this right now? And it breaks the silence.
But anyway, even though I liked the game and am recommending it, $20 is honestly perhaps asking a little too much for it, considering that it's pretty short. It's worth experiencing though, and I enjoyed what I played. I got it in a Humble Bundle, so I certainly feel like I got my money's worth. And I feel like $20 might actually kind of be worth it anyway, considering a new DVD costs around $20 and typically takes like half the time to complete. In terms of sheer quantity of entertainment by length of time, I think $20 is fair. That is, if you think buying a new DVD is (and this has the added benefit of being interactive, and thus more personal to you). Maybe you don't. Maybe you should wait for a sale. Or maybe you shouldn't buy it at all. As for me, I liked it. Maybe you will too. ♥♥♥♥ all these other ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s, be openminded and judge it for yourself if you really are curious. I mean, $20 isn't even that much money anyway, and I happened to like it. There are worse things you can spend $20 on. I thought this was pretty good. Sue me, ♥♥♥♥♥es. I ain't a part of yo system.

Okay, after a lot more playin the game, my opinion on this game has changed.
Is it scary? Well, for the first few nights, yes, I think it suffered that I played with friends, but it did make it more fun, and that I knew a lot about the game from watching videos from Markiplier.
Is it a good sequel? It does do some things different despite having the same principle, if you haven't played the first one, this will be a very fresh experience, but if you play them back to back, then it might get a bit more boring.
Is it a good horror game? Sort of, it'll naturally scare you at first, but as you go on, you'll probably only get startled by the jumpscares
Is it difficult? Yes, this game is indredibly difficult and frustrating, and that's it's major drawback, since it's so frustrating, you get frsutrated rather than scared!
Overall, can I recommend this game? Yes, can I give it a high recommendation? No, it's a fairly good indie title developed by one man. It has a good and interesting mythos behind it, hell I have to give him credit for starting one of the biggest flame wars of 2014. It's definately different, not so much from it's predecssor, but if you've never played the first one, or a horror game in general, you'll probably get a few kicks out of it.

This review is written from the POV of a HUGE fan of the original dark souls.
Dark Souls 1 is one of my favorite games ever.  This game fails to grasp what made dark souls so enagaging, and instead goes for the "LOL YOU DIED THIS GAMES HARD LOLOLOL DANK MEMES"
You are going to see a lot of references to "difficulty" in this review. This is a criticism of the games approach to difficulty, which in my opinion is the wrong way to go about making a souls game.
Pros
-Beautiful game
-Optimized to the max
-Lore is cool and engrossing, as is per regular with souls games
-Zero Technical complaints
MAIN GRIPES
-This games "difficulty" is far too reliant on ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. With beginners being punished for stuff they could NOT have possibly known without prior knowledge. Dark Souls 1 was punsihing in its difficulty, yes, but it always felt fair. In Dark Souls II, there are more cheap deaths that are almost unavoidable in the first hours then there were in the entirety of Dark Souls I.

-Certain changes were made to the core game in order to make the game more "difficult" The health system has been changed to take away a little of the players max health every death. This can be restored by using human effigies, which are a limited item (save for online play) that mimic the function of humanity in the first game. This is an unnessacary addition to the game, and hurts the game by making more frustrating for the sake of "difficulty"
-More on the health system, the developers intoduced lifegems, whch are similar to the moon grass in demons souls. The introduction of another healing item, along with the nerfing of estus, what with the much slower healing time and smaller quantity from the start, RUINS the game. It creates a never ending cycle of having to buy lifegems, which you will do in lieu of levelling up because they nerfed estus so much, so then you will continually die because you have lower stats, so you will buy more life gems. The lifegem in itself is a self defeating item, and was only added to make the game more "difficult"
-Every enemy with a sword/weapon, which is most of the enemies in the game, (more on that later) has a tracking overhead attack. This attack can track you until the last split second, allowing enemies to redirect and turn nearly 360 degrees in order to hit you. This is in stark contrast to the first game, where enemies could track you to a degree, but their attacks had WEIGHT, IMPACT, and MEANING. It added to the fight when you dodged out of the way from an attack, and felt the ground shake beneath your character, and had to immediately decide what your next move is.  In dark souls II, the moment is ruined as most enemies will spend the fight pirouetting around until they hit the ground, and IMMEDIATELY wind up for the next attack. The challenge of the enemies doesn't feel legit in DS2, and instead feels like a crapshoot of luck if you actually dodge the enemy attack or not. Especially with the MASSIVE hitbox issues this game has for the sake of "difficulty"
Minor Gripes
-Every other enemy is a dude with sword/mace/etc. Moveset variations are virtually nonexistent from most of the enemies.
-What was once one difficult enemy in Dark Souls 1 is now several "difficult" enemies in Dark Souls 2. Rooms are filled with groups of enmies and the player is quickly swarmed, adding to the "difficulty"
-Area/Map design is messy and feels disorganized. In DS1, most of the areas felt very precisely thought out, and were a joy to traverse. Areas in this game feel very slapdash without any real thought to the path the player will take. It feels like the priority in the levels was the best enemy placement possible in order to kill the player. Which adds to the "difficulty"
I was so excited for this game, and am sorely dissapointed that i did not enjoy it.
If you have enevr played Dark Souls, you may find enjoyment in this game. But after playing the first game and enjoying it for its attention to detail, fair actual difficulty, and engrossing gameplay, this game feels like an absolute chore to play.
Cannot reccommend for returning souls players.

An immersive WW1 tactical FPS. What more could you ask for. Verdun is a welcome change to a genre dominated by modern-themed games. In Verdun you go back to the trenches and ditches of the ''The Great War'', as you battle from one trench line to the next.
Grab 3 friends and form a squad and level up as a cohesive fighting unit, the more you play with your friends the better your abilities will be with them. Or go solo and level up individually, and join or create a server for others to join.
Verdun truly captures the atrocities of the First World War, as you might navigate through ensnaring barbed wires, risking a quick peek over the trench, and even the dreadful ''No Man's Land". Where you can be cut down by an MG as soon as leave your little hole you call home.

It's amazing the freedom that you have in this game...
The map is huge and being able to use your grappling hook and all the vehicles that the game has to offer, makes this game really fun to explore.
I personally didn't find the missions "fun" and/or "exciting", but it's still a great game to play and even better if you have friends that own the game due to its multiplayer mod.

Wow. I've read through some reviews on this game, and I'm honestly kinda bummed out. I really like Gone Home.
I've noticed one of the biggest complaints against this game is "no real gameplay" or "walking simulator". Considering the game in question uses the concept of exploration and discovery to drive a personal and growing narrative, I think that these complaints are really unfair.
The story is arguably the greatest part of Gone Home. I hear so many people complain that the ending was  "obvious" and "lackluster", but I was kinda satisfied with it. Even if the ending wasn't exactly a "grand finale", it was the progression that was made me want to continue. Even coming across a few stories involving the other members of the family was really neat. You have to read between the lines, in most cases, and a lot of critics seemed to want the story fed to them through a straw.
Don't expect much from the "puzzles", though. Most, if not all, of the game's enjoyment comes from unraveling a very personal story about youth and ambition. If you buy this game expecting Amnesia, your going to be disappointed.

Probably one of the best games I have ever played. It's an action RPG that takes place in an eerie world that feels utterly hopeless. The great thing about the gloomy atmosphere is the fact you feel very much a part of the world you're in and not necessarily the central foretold-hero-that-would-save-the-planet cliche.
The story is there but in a way that you sort of unravel what's happened as you play. At times you may need to look up on wiki pages to get a handle on things going unfolding around you, but that's normal for everyone. That being said, the story won't leave you completely in the dark, it's just a bit different in pacing and storytelling than conventional means.
If you'd like a challenge and want to play a refreshing RPG, I can't recommend this game enough. Initially I stopped playing two hours in and put the game away for a few months, but once I picked it up again out of boredom, I could not put it down. The game is a bit challenging as anyone with eyes have probably read from either game critics or♥♥♥♥♥♥measuring forum posts, but don't let dying get to you. It is a lot like life in that failures will come and go, but once you start to adapt and become patient, you will ultimately start to see amazing progress in an unforgettable world.
This is certainly one of those games that is fun to discuss with friends after you play it.

So.  If you are a nine year old with nothing better to do than respawn all day, this is the game for you. is a game in which the player arrives home after a holiday overseas and finds their whole family (parents and sister) have gone AWOL.
The game itself is superbly well-executed. As you explore the house, you gradually learn more about the family that lives/lived there and their history, struggles, and dreams. The attention to detail is laudable, especially for the accurate period depiction of the mid-1990s, presumably so chosen so that most players would find the setting reminiscent of their own childhood (the average gamer age is 30-something, after all). Mix tapes, typewriters, and
abound.
It’s also a necessarily short experience – there’s only so large you can make a typical family’s house before it becomes ridiculous. I completed the game in under 3 hours after thoroughly exploring every room in the sizeable mansion. Indeed, the size of the home stretches believability at times, particularly as you explore the extensive basement, but perhaps that’s appropriate for rural Oregon, and the game is certainly no less immersive for it.
There are a number of “subplots” you discover as you explore the house. The mysterious superstition surrounding the house itself. The mother’s role at the Forestry Office. The father’s rocky career as a novelist. The environment is rife with knick-knacks and other paraphernalia which are in many cases more revealing of the family’s personalities than a personal conversation with them would be. In discerning facade from feelings you unearth numerous secrets in the family’s lives that vary from amusing to shocking. But the game directs you along a more specific narrative, subtly funneling you through the house in a predetermined path so as to unravel that story in the right order. The protagonist’s sister, Samantha, gradually becomes more intimate with another girl from school – Lonnie. It’s this flowering relationship that becomes the driving narrative of
, and what quickens your traversals from room to room as that narrative approaches its scandalous conclusion.

I can't start this without pointing out that I will compare this game/interactive story/gamified tale/not-a-game/kitchen sink/whatever-you-want-to-call-it with another one well known, Dear Esther... mainly because how contrasting my opinion of each game is. If you have played Dear Esther, I hope you see my point. If not, mainly my problem with Dear Esther is the main problem people had with the game, and while I can't stand Dear Esther, I find it dull and pointless.I found myself enjoying this game from beginning to end.
What makes this kind of product different to normal games is their focus on plot over gameplay, they don't have any difficult puzzle or reaction challenge, there is only the plot and the ambiance. I don't really want to call these games because they are not really focused on the play part but on giving a story. But even then there is still a need of interactivity, a need of making the player a part of the experience.
This is one the main problems I had with Dear Esther that I think Gone Home did right, in Dear Esther  you don't feel part of what's happening, you basically are taking a tour while some guy is telling you a story, the only thing you can do is either go along with the ride or stall it. Gone Home on the other hand feels like the story is there, you only need to find it, in fact, that's your main explicit objective, exploring an unknown house (for both you and your character) looking for what happened to your sister, and as you explore you get a good glimpses of you family's problems, mainly your sister's problems.
This is done not only on dialog but also on notes and parts of the house, most rooms serve some purpose to define some character or moment in the story, you only need to find it's purpose. While the only thing really connecting the story in Dear Esther is the dialog here every part of the game is focused on giving this simple (and a little predictable) but still effective story.
This is a good product, but like anything on this store, is not for everyone, if you want this product you should take in consideration that it is focused more in to giving a story than into what you could call playing, so you should be looking for that while “playing” this game.
Of course I cannot finish without pointing out the problem that is outside of the game itself, the game is too short for it's 20 USD pricetag, I would recommend to get this game if you can find it on sale. Right now I find it is just too expensive.

As a game, Gone Home doesn't exactly shine, but as an experience it greatly excels.  Many people flack this "game" for not properly being a game, but that's a very narrow minded approach.  To speak more braudly here, mediums of entertainment have always stretched the limit to what's possible in their very definition.  Books have spawned choose-your-own-adventure titles and Sci-Fi, movies have tried 3D and started a zombie craze, and music has taken many turns from the norm with astounding success.
Gone Home is the sort of game that doesn't necessarily fit into many genres of games besides maybe point-and-click.  It creates it's own genre with games like Proteus joining in the party.  Oh, and speaking of point-and-click, why does no one flack those types of games for being a non-game when they're very similar to Gone Home, only in 2D?  But I digress.  Wait, another idea, Gone Home could also be viewed as a linear shooter but without the shooting.  Does this make it not a game when you can't shoot and blow things up?  No!  Do players not often find themselves observing little quirks in the environment when going through levels?  Of course they do; we like to explore, we are a curious race.  Ok, moving on.
The main premise of Gone Home is exploring a house, trying to find clues to what's happened to your sister, Sam.  This kind of game could have been done very poorly, but The FullBright Company nailed it.  The first thing that makes this game great is how open it is to explore and pick various objects up throughout the house/mansion.  The physics might not be the greatest, but the freedom makes the game feel more real than most games where the objects scattered across a level are static and non moving (unless they can be pushed or blown up because explosions are cool).
The second thing that makes this game great is the house and objects themselves.  A lot of care was put into detailing the house and filling it to the brim with boxes, lamps, pots, cassette tapes, toilet paper, etc.  It looks and feels like a real house that people lived in.  Model-wise, all of the objects in the game are detailed very well even when viewed close up, which adds another layer of realism.
The third thing that makes this game great is the atmosphere.  From the lighting to the constant rainfall outside to the music playing from across the hall (although one knit pick is that they could have made the music louder when you're farther away because the volume drops down quite a bit when your only 5 feet away), Gone Home immerses you.  Aside from that, the voice acting scattered throughout the game in the form of journal entries is superb.  You can really read Sam's emotions from her voice.
Overall, this "game" is not something you should pick up if you're expecting your normal gaming experience.  But if you want a game with a great allowance for exploration and great story and backstory, this is for you.  For $20, though, I don't think it would be completely worth it, so definitely pick it up in a bundle or during a sale if you're interested.

Warface has great potential for a F2P fps. It has stunning graphics, using Crytek's famous Cryengine. It also receives monthly updates with new weapons, maps, and special operations. The special operations are very fun to play with and can satisfy the challenge that you want when playing against bots from Easy, to Medium, to Insane, and lastly, Nightmare.
Now the cons, Crytek, originally ran the servers in Europe and North America. Now they are run by
which have screwed up the economy severely which in return, caused many veterans of the game to leave. We now have to pay for random boxes using Kredits and the Auction House was completely removed. Now people who are willing to pay real cash to play the random boxes (which have no guaranteed drop chance so one guy could spend $3 and get a Gold Scar-H and another could spent $300 and get absolutely nothing) have a huge advantage over others, especially the new player base. New players will play no more than 10 hours of Warface because they will be isolated in the community, unable to play any PvP because of the major disadvantage they face and they can only fix that by putting in real cash.
Hackers. They are also one of the biggest problems of this game. Ranked matches are almost unplayable these days because that is where all of the hackers will lurk. Not only that, but many people will stay in these matches to benefit off the hackers. The anti-cheat does almost nothing and is useless and a waste of time. You can report the most obvious hacker in the game and he just won't get banned.
Warface is one of those games that will suck you right in when you find a group of friends to play with. The community is very connected (for the most part). The clans in this game are very competitive and at one point, you will join a clan because playing alone in a multiplayer specific game will get very boring for you.
Despite all of Warface's short comings, I find it one of the best Free To Play fps on the market and I highly recommend you try it for a couple hours and really give it a go.

If you loved the first Dark Souls, get ready to be ♥♥♥♥ing dissapointed with Dark Souls 2.
Seriously, this game butchered some of the greatest mechanics in the first one.
I hate having to build your own estus flask, finding shards in some really obscure area that you probably won't find unless you scour literally everywhere or are using a guide.
I hated having to level up adaptability so I could get more iframes so I could actually have a meaningful dodge instead of getting hit all the time.
The level design is complete garbage, unlike in Dark Souls where many areas loop around to different one providing a fast way to get to another area without warping, Dark Souls 2 provides zones that lead to another zone that will become a dead end with a boss fight. While this isn't that big of a deal in terms of gameplay, I missed finding all those short cuts.
The bigger problem is there being multiple places to choose from in the beginning. I have the oppurtunity from the very beginning to go two different routes, with a few more directions after I beat a boss and get an item. This means that when I choose to go a different direction, I am overleveled for that area because it considered a starting area.
In the first game, enemies would be placed typically slightly out of the way so you could run past them. Now, enemies are put right in your goddamn way.  Now you have to fight everything because they are in your way, and if you died, get ready to do it a-♥♥♥♥ing-gain til the enemies stop respawning. Also, some enemies can see you across the ♥♥♥♥ing map and will run at you forcing you to fight half a dozen enemies.
In this edition, enemies that are too powerful for their area are sprinkled all over. In the vanilla game, there was ONE heide knight in a beginning area and he was kind of tough. Now there is a ♥♥♥♥ton of them in another area and when the boss is defeated they become very aggressive from before when they wouldn't attack unless attacked.
Lastly, many bosses all feel very samey. Big enemy  where I just need to get to the side. Once you have sufficient iframes, these bosses are a piece of cake.
This game took the idea of the first game being difficult and ran with it. I don't feel like most of my deaths in DS2 are my fault, mostly me dealing with ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t hyper aggressive enemies with insane amount of tracking and instant attacks that can kill me in one hit. The game could be better. The original horror aspect is lessened by the threat of power (Which in this game means Foxy is going to get you, but others can be avoided easily.) The puppet is more of a pain in the rear than anything. It does give you more of a jump the first time the music box runs out, or the first few times that old Bonnie or Chica appear when you put the camera down, but after that there is a decrease in the scare factor. I have made it all the way to night 3 so far without dying, but the game was already as challenging as night 3-4 of the original. I wish there would have been more of a haunting atmosphere, which I will admit is hard to pull off with this being a (SPOILER ALERT) prequel. I still want to know what is up with Toy Chica losing her beak when she moves around, makes her look more like a round faced Pikachu than anything, but it is still creepy when you see it. There are some glitches in the game, such as Foxy jumping out from the walls when your not looking directly down the hallway, or him popping out of your camera from time to time. These really need to be fixed, maybe by having a slightly longer cut scene for it where it forces you to look down the hallway. It wouldn't hurt as well to give the animatronics some slightly different death animation and attack screams. Just like at Chuck E. Cheese, the animatronics each have different voices so that needs to be brought out more. That's why it was hard to tell in the first game whether Bonnie was a boy or a girl at first glance. And don't even get me started on BB.
Overall, the scares are still there and are hightened by the ammount of things that are going on, the number of animatronics, and the new mechanics. The only issue is that gameplay is interupted by the music box mechanic, but it redeems itself by adding time constrainted suspence. Do you go for the music box or make sure that Foxy doesn't jump you?

Not many of the reviews seem to be very positive. I get it, it's not a game for everyone. I, however, do like it. My only problem is that it was very, very short. I completed it in about an hour, and I did take time to do everything and uncover all the details and such. So because of that, I will say it is not worth the £14.99 pricetag. But I would still recommend it, especially if it was on a sale or a Humble Bundle (like I got it in). I am a great lover of story-based games and maybe that's the reason I liked this. It's got a nice, cute story telling the tale of the player's sister who falls in love with another girl and how their relationship progresses. It's a very personal story in that you are literally going through a family's house and you can see all the little details (Spoilers: Your dad has a porn stash!) and you can tell that a lot of care was put into it in that regard. It felt very real to me. There was no combat, no scares, no fighting. It was the telling of a story through a game and it was exceptionally well done for such an everyday life kind of story. It kept me intrigued the entire way through and I really loved following the story, exploring the house and getting to know all these characters without ever even meeting them. I heard someone say that this is not so much a game as it is an experience. And that's true. But that absolutely does not make it any less enjoyable. Another thing that the game has is puzzles. These puzzles are not challenging in any way as they are simple "search for the key" types of puzzles which I actually like because in this instance you are made to delve deeper into the story surrounding the family and such by hunting through everything. On top of that, you will find yourself going through a great many notes and letters and pictures which are scattered around the house and I found these rather enjoyable to read because it adds a realism layer to it all and really helps you get to know the family, their positions and who they are.
Overall, I would recommend this in general but I would definitely say to buy it when it's on sale or from a cheap bundle rather than full price, simply because of how short it is.

This game sucks. And I'm going to explain why with my flawless logic. As per usual.
To begin with, From Software sucks so much♥♥♥♥♥♥they cleaned out every gaybar from Kagoshima to Wakanai, and the team that worked on this isn't even entirely the original. Ports to PC have always been♥♥♥♥♥♥with them, always. So you'll be buying an xbox controller, unless you figure out the♥♥♥♥♥backward freeware configuration programs for ps3 and third party controllers.
If I stopped right there about From, I'd be ridiculously generous, to the point of misinformation. From can't fix their games and they never will. There are an absurd amount of easily fixed glitches present in this game. For those who say that they're mostly patched, might I remind you that in fact, they're reselling the game and splitting the online just to release these fixes? And that From soft bans anyone who uses any sort of modification, including the ones that fix these issues? Even if we ignore the blatant money grabbing, there is the matter of game balance. Despite the katanas in this title initially being blatantly overpowered (cough Chaos Blade cough), From decided to buff them. Yes, perfect. Even the Blacksteel Katana, which was perfectly fine as it was, a good solid weapon. Powerful, but not overwhelming. Now you can just spam away like every other katana. This is just an example. I have no particular beef with katanas, I love the Darkdrift.
Before I get people whining and saying I'm one of those nitpicks who thinks everything is overpowered in this game, you'd be wrong, if you are skilled enough, then you can beat any build. It can be done, you can beat the fast rolling max level fat ♥♥♥♥ turtle armor♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥with rice rapier, numbness, sacred oath, resonant flesh, great magic barrier, resonant weapon buffed dark shadow dagger, who've just downed an Elizabeth mushroom and have a monastery scimitar in their left hand. The question is, do you honestly want to fight that♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥i n g garbage? What do you think is going to happen over time as the multiplayer population fills up with the late comers? The scrubs who read the wikis and watch build videos till their eyes fall out their sockets and their thumbs rot off, so that all they can do is spam r1 and parry at you till you die? In any other game, this sort of unbalanced crap would not be ok. The problem is that From has been bad about this for so long, people are used to it.
One thing I must admit however, is that, so far, these sort of encounters have been rare for me. Also, it's more a matter of just how much of an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ the player in question decides to be.
Next is the story. Generally a non issue with From. But this time it felt a little stunted. It's just this general feeling of blandness that pervades at times. I got this with the Iron Keep as a whole. It was just so boring and unoriginal. Not even unoriginal in the sense that it was something From had done before, but instead in the sense that every other video game developper had done it before. Big fire lava castle with fire and death and iron knights and a demon who's on fire. Oh and the main boss is a big fire satan that wades through the lava at you. Yes it is a fire theme, but couldn't there be some level variety? Some added lore other than just, old king man dude builds castle in dumb spot out of pride, gets ♥♥♥♥ed because of it? It was beyond generic. This continues a bit into other aspects, the lore just does NOT go as deep as From has gone before.
Connection and lag problems are rampant. Period.
So over all, I love Dark Souls 2: Scholar of the First Sin.
This game has an excellent feeling of exploration and vastness. The Aerie is one of the coolest designs From has EVER put out. The PvP is fun as hell and so is co op. The people you meet online are often interesting and fun, whether it be the red invader that pits everything he can against you, the blue invader that falls off the ledge almost instantaneously, the cocky white phantom who does the Welcome gesture to bosses, invaders and defeated mobs, or finally, the sunbro who basically becomes your father/mother figure for the entirety of the summon, showing you every trick and secret.
The system of challenge and reward is so stable and rock solid. You want something? You have to earn it, you have to do well and learn from your mistakes. And it's just that, the game was never about difficulty, it's always been about proper fair challenge. A constant learning, figuring out patterns and how mobs work. Finding weaknesses. When you die in Dark Souls 2, you know exactly what you did wrong, every time. And when you win... The sense of accomplishment is unmatched in any game I've ever played before.
And that sense of accomplishment, that challenge, is all thanks to the PvE. The superb placement of mobs, the often excellent boss design. I drool at just the thought. There is no series of games that even comes close to matching this. None that I have ever played. It's absolutely incredible. A work of miracle.

There is a decent amount to like about Gone Home, but at the end of it all I can’t exactly recommend this game without explaining my gripes with it first-- from there you can form your own opinion. The concept is simplistic and surprisingly engrossing. The atmosphere is great, it’s a very interesting period piece, and a lot of the story is pretty engaging; however, the main problem with the game is that everything ends up feeling artificial. For those unfamiliar, you play as a young adult returning home a little past midnight and finding out that no one is home. As such, you let yourself into the house and begin exploring. Through your exploration you will slowly unravel the mysteries of where everyone is, the house, etc.
Honestly, it is a very interesting game and pretty well done. There is a sense of wonder exploring a relatively deserted and unfamiliar house—one your family calls home. The biggest gripe, though, is that the house doesn’t actually feel like a house at all. The layout and floor plan of the home you are exploring doesn’t really make much sense. I assume the home was designed in such a way as to guide players in the ‘correct’ direction, but honestly the house doesn’t really feel like a house. It feels more like a series of rooms that are connected by a maze of hallways. The room locations do not seem to make much sense, the hallways are incredibly long and winding, and honestly it just doesn’t feel like a home so much as it feels like a couple rooms held together by a thing wire.
Further detracting from the immersion is the fact that apparently every single member of the home has left incredibly personal papers, letters, and memos all over the house. For a family with so many secrets, you’d expect the mom to hide letters from her friend hinting at something sinister in a better place than any random cupboard in the house. Likewise, a note that isn’t exactly hidden at all saying ‘let’s do it at this location and this time’ more or less in plain sight makes little sense. This is pretty frustrating, particularly because there seems to have been a lot of effort put into the many different family storylines.
Perhaps most annoying is the character that is your sister. The letters she writes back and forth between her classmates and love interest are incredibly juvenile. Instead of presenting her as a highschool student graduating relatively soon—which she is--- the notes and slips of paper she has written read as though a third grader just found out that you can write an pass notes in class. It’s incredibly ridiculous and, for lack of a better word, lame. What really is disappointing is that your sister isn’t even the most interesting part of the story. What’s going on with your mom and dad is much more interesting, better paced, and frankly more believable. This is not to say that the story involving your sister is bad. The problem is that you can’t help but feel disillusioned by the juvenile and amateur writing of a supposed highschooler  with aspirations of attending a college for creative writing.
Gone Home could have been a really great game. Instead, it’s an okay game with a really interesting idea. In general I guess I recommend the game just to try it out and form your own opinion. There is a good deal to like. I just wouldn’t expect too much.

I honestly wanted to play a bit longer before reviewing this game, but I guess they deserve it.
This game is wonderful. Simple as that. Learning curve is not as steep as you'd imagine, and the first hours are a bit frustrating but eventually you will just learn how to survive more than 0.2 seconds in a row.
It's realistic, it's cool, and most importantly it's fun. Real fun. If you love WW1 you will love this game.
Entente Powers and Central Empires are divided in squads (4) each with their own abilities and roles, and each squad is divided into roles (4), each with their own weapons and charateristics, bonuses and maluses (32 players in total may seem few, but trust me, there's a lot of action going on all the time if both armies are full). Each squads also has an NCO providing forward spawn points, artillery, gas attacks, def/atk bonuses and whatnot, depending on the squad you're in. You start with basic equipment, and you can unlock more advanced one with experience points gained on the battlefield. Teamwork is highly valued and encouraged. In fact, highly teamworking teams will be awarded with several bonuses and better armour. Balancing system is extremely clever and fitting, too. Voting system is cool as well.
Just know that many actions involve real hardcore camping (just as you'd expect, I guess...), but it's fun nonetheless.
Also expect a lot of prone blocking.
And some major FPS drop from time to time.
But it's still a wonderful game.
Only flaw I can think of is the absence of a squad chat. That woulf fit A LOT.

Although this review comes with a "Thumbs Up" be aware that this isn't a wholehearted recommendation. This is more for people that played through Dark Souls 2 and are wondering if it is worth the money. Obviously if you are a newcomer then this is the best place to start considering it comes with all the DLC and a few minor improvements. Unless you are a newcomer to the franchise itself in which case you should definitely start with the first Dark Souls.
Scholar of the First Sin was announced immediately after the final expansion was released and I like many others was pretty irritated about. I purchased it recently on PC due to the sale although I also have the PS4 version as well. Having ignored it for nearly six months I feel I can look at this a little more objectively.
Whether this update is worth purchasing really depends on how much you enjoyed the vanilla version. Enemy placements have been tweaked, NPC summon signs and invasions are much more prominent and a few creative elements have been added in certain places (some of which are admittedly pretty interesting). There is also a ring in the game that allows you to control Soul Memory to a certain degree, although this is a band aid solution and doesn't really fix the core problem. Lighting seems to be improved and makes torches less optional in a couple of places but if you are looking for E3 levels of fidelity then you should probably keep moving. Lastly, a character very important to the lore makes multiple appearances. Speaking of lore, item descriptions have also been given the once over.
All in all, the game feels very familiar but also quite different. All the above mentioned tweaks and alterations to progression paths (you'll be using more Fragrant Branches of Yore than usual) make this update feel akin to a Director's Cut or Extended Edition bluray with all the added extras from the previous iterations. If you loved the regular game and don't mind starting from scratch (saves don't carry over) then it could be worth it. However the vanilla game has been updated via patch to include most of the features that aren't related to performance so it really does depend on how much you want the extra player count, slightly better lighting and enemy placement re-shuffle. If you weren't much of a fan to begin with then nothing here is going to change that.
So, should you buy it?
Newcomers... Definitely.
Longtime Players... Yes, if you want to spice things up a little. But Not essential.
Casual Players... Don't bother, you probably won't appreciate or care about any of the changes.

So over all, I love Dark Souls 2: Scholar of the First Sin.
This game has an excellent feeling of exploration and vastness. The Aerie is one of the coolest designs From has EVER put out. The PvP is fun as hell and so is co op. The people you meet online are often interesting and fun, whether it be the red invader that pits everything he can against you, the blue invader that falls off the ledge almost instantaneously, the cocky white phantom who does the Welcome gesture to bosses, invaders and defeated mobs, or finally, the sunbro who basically becomes your father/mother figure for the entirety of the summon, showing you every trick and secret.
The system of challenge and reward is so stable and rock solid. You want something? You have to earn it, you have to do well and learn from your mistakes. First off, if you judge a game's worth solely on how much actual play time you're going to get out of it, this isn't the game for you. For $20, it takes about 3-4 hours to play through and there isn't much reason to play through it more than once. That being said, if you judge a game's worth solely on the experience itself, I can not recommend this game enough. It is a truly unique experience that is hard to describe for lack of anything comparable. There are no people to encounter in the game; rather the characters and events of the story are expressed through the environment as well as audio journals. Ironically, the characters of Gone Home, which you never actually meet, are much more effectively portrayed in this way than most of the hyper-emotive digital actors seen in many recent triple-A titles. The puzzles (if they can really be called that) never get in the way and virtually solve themselves as you naturally progress through the game. There may be an ending, but there is no goal, only a curiosity to explore this house and unravel the story that took place while you were gone. If you enjoy a great story told in unconventional ways then please give Gone Home a try. I don't think you'll regret it.

Verdun has one fundametal flaw that is not clearly stated nowhere on the steam/www frontpage, raising many forum threads and questions in the game chat (it actually took me 12 hours of gameplay and ~1h or of wiki reading to understand the system myself).
If you play each time with different people, you have to grind co-op xp from the scratch over and over again. That means game heavily forces you to play with the same people all the time. This might not be that much of a problem for people who play only with their friends, but for everyone else it means that the game is turning from the WW1 first person shoother into the friend finding simmulator. If you don't have the stable gameplay schedule you are in disadvantage. Even if you do manage to find the people who will want to stick playing with you (squad consists of 4 players) and you will level up your team together to lvl 100, if one of those people will just quit playing the game for whatever reason you are losing 25% of all the XP lowering your squad to lvl 75. If two players will get bored of the game, you are loosing 50% of all the xp and your new squad members will have to grind all the required ammount of co-op xp from the start.
In summary: if you don't have a stable playing hours or group of friends who have bought the game as well to play with, you will be put at disadvantage against the other players. Definately not  a game for a lone wolfs!
